title: Why Lazarus Became a Threat to Religious Leaders After Resurrection
paragraphs: Why Lazarus Became a Threat to Religious Leaders After Resurrection
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like history and more like a courtroom where heaven places human hearts on trial.
The resurrection of Lazarus was one of those moments.
Not because a dead man walked out of a grave.
But because the miracle exposed people who looked alive on the outside while spiritually decaying underneath their robes, titles, traditions, and religious performances.
Most people think Lazarus became famous after resurrection.
That is not entirely true.
He became dangerous.
Not dangerous to Rome.
Not dangerous to the poor.
Not dangerous to sinners.
He became dangerous to religious systems that could survive around dead people but could not survive undeniable evidence that Jesus Christ truly carried the authority of God.
And the terrifying reality is this:
Some people do not hate miracles because miracles are fake.
Some hate miracles because miracles threaten their control.
The Gospel of John records one of the most chilling responses to a miracle ever written.
John 12:10–11 says:
“So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.”
Read that slowly.
Lazarus had already died once.
Now religion wanted him dead again.
Not because he committed violence.
Not because he preached rebellion.
Not because he stole power.
His existence itself became evidence.
And evidence terrifies people who built their identity around denying truth.
The name Lazarus comes from the Hebrew form Eleazar (אֶלְעָזָר), meaning:
“God has helped.”
That alone preaches.
Lazarus was not resurrected because he was powerful.
He was resurrected because God helps helpless people.
That is the Gospel.

The religious elite of Jesus’ day had built influence around controlling access to righteousness, temple authority, interpretation, and social standing. They wore holiness publicly while often resisting God privately.
Jesus repeatedly confronted this.
In Matthew 23:27, Jesus tells the Pharisees:
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness.”
The Greek phrase for “whitewashed tombs” is:
κεκονιαμένοις τάφοις (kekoniamenois taphois)
Beautiful externally.
Death internally.
Now think about the irony.
The religious leaders themselves had become spiritual tombs.
Then Jesus publicly stood before an actual tomb and reversed death itself.
Lazarus became living proof that Jesus could do what religion never could.
Religion could decorate death.
Jesus could conquer it.
That is why Lazarus became a threat.
Because every time people saw him breathing, they saw the failure of empty religion standing beside the power of the Son of God.
John 11 contains one of the most emotionally devastating scenes in the entire Bible.
When Jesus arrives after Lazarus has died, Martha confronts Him.
“Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
You can hear heartbreak inside those words.
Confusion.
Disappointment.
The feeling of praying while heaven stays silent.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You prayed.
You begged.
You fasted.
And still the relationship died.
Still the marriage collapsed.
Still the addiction stayed.
Still the depression swallowed your nights.
Still the grave stayed closed.
But Jesus was not late.
He was revealing something bigger than immediate rescue.
In John 11:25, Jesus declares:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
The Greek reads:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
“I AM the resurrection and the life.”
Not:
“I can perform resurrection.”
Not:
“I understand resurrection.”
Not:
“I teach resurrection.”
Jesus said resurrection is not merely an event.
It is a Person.
This statement shook theological foundations.
Because Jesus was not simply claiming prophetic authority.
He was identifying Himself with divine identity.
The phrase “ἐγώ εἰμι” (egō eimi) echoes the divine self-revelation in Exodus 3:14.
In Hebrew, God tells Moses:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)
“I AM THAT I AM.”
Jesus was not accidentally choosing words.
He was confronting everyone listening with a decision.
Either He was blasphemous.
Or He truly was who He claimed to be.
And Lazarus walking out of the grave became physical evidence attached to that claim.
This is why the miracle terrified the religious authorities.
Not because they lacked information.
But because truth was standing in front of them breathing.
John 11:47 records the panic meeting of the religious leaders:
“What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.”
Notice something deeply unsettling.
They did not deny the miracle.
They admitted it.
The Greek word for “signs” is σημεῖα (sēmeia).
Not random wonders.
Signs.
Evidence pointing somewhere.
The problem was never lack of proof.
The problem was surrender.
And this still happens today.
Some people say:
“If God would just show me a sign, I would believe.”
But Scripture repeatedly reveals that hardened hearts can stand in front of miracles and still refuse repentance.
The issue is often not intellectual.
It is spiritual.
Lazarus became dangerous because he embodied undeniable transformation.
Dead.
Buried.
Wrapped.
Stinking.
Then suddenly alive.
People can argue with sermons.
But transformed lives are harder to erase.
That is why genuine testimonies unsettle darkness.
A former addict suddenly free.
A violent man suddenly gentle.
A suicidal person suddenly carrying hope.
A broken marriage suddenly restored.
A lukewarm believer suddenly consumed with holiness.
There is something terrifying to darkness about people who were once spiritually dead becoming visibly alive through Christ.
Ephesians 2:1 says:
“And you were dead in the trespasses and sins.”
The Greek word for dead is νεκρούς (nekrous).
Spiritually lifeless.
Unable to save ourselves.
The story of Lazarus is not only about one man in Bethany.
It is the story of humanity.
And this is where the article becomes deeply personal.
Because many people reading this know what it feels like to live emotionally embalmed.
Still functioning.
Still posting.
Still smiling.
Still attending church.
But internally exhausted.
Numb.
Bound.
Rotting in hidden sin.
Covered by spiritual grave clothes.
Then Jesus enters the tomb of your life.
And everything changes.
John 11:43 says:
“He cried out with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out.’”
The Greek phrase:
Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω
(Lazare, deuro exō)
“Lazarus, come forth.”
Church history often notes something powerful here.
Jesus called Lazarus by name.
Because if He had simply shouted “Come out,” every grave might have emptied.
That is the authority of Christ.
And once Lazarus came out, everything changed politically, spiritually, socially, and prophetically.
The resurrection of Lazarus happened shortly before Jesus entered Jerusalem for His crucifixion.
It intensified public attention.
Crowds grew.
Belief spread.
Pressure increased.
John 11:48 reveals the fear of the leaders:
“If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him.”
Did you catch that?
Everyone will believe.
The fear was loss of influence.
Loss of control.
Loss of power.
Some leaders become so addicted to maintaining authority that they would rather attack evidence than repent before truth.
That spirit still exists.
There are environments today where transformed people become threats because their freedom exposes systems built on bondage.
A healed person threatens industries profiting from brokenness.
A delivered believer threatens lukewarm Christianity.
A bold testimony threatens counterfeit spirituality.
People often celebrate your resurrection until your transformation starts making them uncomfortable.
And this is why many believers quietly shrink back after God changes them.
Because resurrection attracts warfare.
The enemy does not panic over dead faith.
He panics over living evidence.
Lazarus did not even need to preach.
His existence preached.
Every breath became testimony.
Every step became evidence.
Every meal became proof.
Imagine sitting at a dinner table with a man who used to be decomposing.
Imagine hearing him laugh.
Imagine watching him eat bread.
Imagine realizing death failed.
No wonder people believed in Jesus.
And here is the terrifying irony.
The religious leaders plotted murder immediately after witnessing undeniable life.
Sin hardens people that deeply.
This is why external religion without surrender to God becomes dangerous.
Knowledge alone cannot save.
Position alone cannot save.
Tradition alone cannot save.
Only Christ saves.
The Hebrew concept of life throughout Scripture carries deeper meaning than mere biological existence.
The Hebrew word חַיִּים (chayyim) refers to fullness of living, vitality, flourishing life connected to God.
Jesus did not merely return Lazarus to breathing.
He restored him into visible life.
And ultimately, Lazarus points beyond himself.
Because Lazarus was resurrected temporarily.
Jesus would later resurrect permanently.
Lazarus came out still mortal.
Jesus came out glorified.
Lazarus would eventually die again.
Jesus conquered death forever.
That distinction matters.
Lazarus was a sign.
Jesus is the Savior.
And maybe the most emotionally overwhelming detail in the entire account is found in the shortest verse in the Bible.
“Jesus wept.”
John 11:35.
In Greek:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
(edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Not staged emotion.
Not detached theology.
The Son of God stood before human grief and entered it emotionally.
This destroys the lie that God is cold toward suffering.
Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
Yet He still wept.
Why?
Because love grieves.
Because death is horrific.
Because sin shattered creation.
Because God never intended humanity for graves.
Some of you reading this have cried secretly for months.
You feel forgotten.
Abandoned.
Buried alive emotionally.
But the same Christ who stood outside Lazarus’ tomb still sees hidden pain.
Still calls dead things back to life.
Still enters human suffering.
Still weeps with people before restoring them.
And maybe that is why this story hits so deeply across generations.
Because everyone knows what tombs feel like.
Some people are trapped in addiction.
Some inside shame.
Some inside trauma.
Some inside pornography.
Some inside bitterness.
Some inside anxiety.
Some inside hypocrisy.
Some inside silent unbelief while pretending to love God publicly.
But resurrection remains the business of Jesus.
And this is the part many people avoid.
When Jesus resurrects you, everyone around you must confront what changed you.
Some will celebrate.
Some will envy.
Some will mock.
Some will attack.
Because transformed lives force people to confront the possibility that Jesus truly is Lord.
Lazarus became a threat because he made unbelief harder to maintain.
His life confronted denial.
And if we are honest, many modern believers want the comfort of Christianity without the evidence of resurrection power.
But the early church exploded because people encountered transformed lives.
Christianity was never meant to be merely argued.
It was meant to be witnessed.
The Greek word for witness is μάρτυς (martys).
It is where we get the word martyr.
A witness is someone whose life becomes evidence.
Lazarus became evidence.
The question is:
Have we?
Can people see Jesus through the way we live?
Can they see resurrection after the addiction?
After the affair?
After the breakdown?
After the failure?
After the darkness?
Or have we settled for polished religion while remaining spiritually untouched?
One reason this story grips the human heart is because it reveals both the beauty of grace and the ugliness of pride at the same time.
One man exits a grave.
Another group plots murder.
One side surrenders.
The other side hardens.
The same miracle softens some hearts and exposes others.
And this still happens every day when people encounter Jesus Christ.
Some repent.
Some resist.
Some worship.
Some rage.
But nobody remains neutral forever.
There is another detail often overlooked.
When Lazarus came out, Jesus told the people:
“Unbind him, and let him go.”
John 11:44.
Even after resurrection, grave clothes remained.
This matters spiritually.
Many believers have truly encountered Jesus but still wear remnants of old bondage.
Fear.
Condemnation.
Toxic patterns.
Old identities.
Self-hatred.
Religious performance.
Healing sometimes unfolds in layers.
Resurrection can happen instantly.
Sanctification often unfolds progressively.
The Greek word λύσατε (lysate) means:
“Loose him.”
“Release him.”
This is what discipleship should do.
Help liberated people fully walk in freedom.
Not re-bury them in shame.
Not suffocate them with legalism.
Not weaponize their past.
The church should help remove grave clothes.
Not hand out new ones.
And perhaps that is why the story of Lazarus still shakes souls today.
Because deep down, humanity knows we cannot resurrect ourselves.
No amount of money can heal spiritual death.
No amount of achievement can erase guilt.
No amount of self-help can defeat sin.
Only Jesus Christ carries authority over the grave.
Romans 6:4 says:
“Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.”
The Greek phrase for “newness of life” is:
καινότητι ζωῆς
(kainotēti zōēs)
A completely new quality of living.
Not cosmetic improvement.
Transformation.
And this is why authentic Christianity terrifies darkness.
Because resurrection creates people who cannot be controlled by fear anymore.
People who know death already lost.
People who know grace personally.
People who have seen God pull life from impossible situations.
Lazarus became dangerous because he proved Jesus was not merely another teacher.
He proved Christ held authority over death itself.
That miracle accelerated the path toward the cross.
Because once resurrection power became undeniable, the religious system intensified its determination to eliminate Jesus.
Yet even their violence fulfilled prophecy.
The cross was never an accident.
The resurrection was never a backup plan.
The Lamb was always coming.
And maybe someone reading this feels spiritually entombed right now.
You think your addiction is too deep.
Your shame too disgusting.
Your hypocrisy too exposed.
Your wounds too old.
Your faith too weak.
But Lazarus was four days dead.
Jewish mourning tradition understood this as irreversible decay.
Even Martha warned:
“Lord, by this time there will be an odor.”
In Greek:
ἤδη ὄζει
(ēdē ozei)
“He already stinks.”
Yet Jesus still called him out.
This is the Gospel.
Christ enters situations humanity labels impossible.
And if Jesus can call a decomposing man from a tomb, He can still resurrect broken hearts, collapsing families, shattered minds, addicted souls, and spiritually numb believers.
That is why this story continues to spread across centuries.
Because people are desperate for hope stronger than death.
And the resurrection of Lazarus points directly to the greater resurrection power found in Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why the religious leaders feared Lazarus so deeply.
Because once someone has encountered resurrection personally, intimidation loses power.
Performance loses attraction.
Dead religion loses authority.
And systems built on fear begin collapsing when people discover living truth.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if you know someone trapped emotionally, spiritually, mentally, or secretly battling darkness, send this to them.
Some people do not need another motivational speech.
They need resurrection hope.
Because some graves are still waiting to hear your name called by Jesus.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Naging Banta si Lazaro sa mga Pinunong Panrelihiyon Matapos Siyang Buhayin Muli
May mga bahagi sa Kasulatan na parang hindi lang kuwento.
Parang hukuman.
Parang sandali kung saan inilalantad ng langit ang tunay na kalagayan ng puso ng tao.
Isa na rito ang muling pagkabuhay ni Lazaro.
Hindi lang dahil may patay na lumabas mula sa libingan.
Kundi dahil inilantad ng himala ang mga taong mukhang banal sa panlabas pero patay na espirituwal sa loob.
Mga taong nabubuhay sa tradisyon pero malayo sa Diyos.
Mga taong malakas sa relihiyon pero mahina sa pagsuko.
Karamihan iniisip na naging tanyag si Lazaro matapos siyang buhayin ni Jesus.
Pero ang totoo?
Naging mapanganib siya.
Hindi sa Roma.
Hindi sa gobyerno.
Hindi sa ordinaryong tao.
Naging banta siya sa sistemang panrelihiyon na kayang mabuhay kasama ng mga espirituwal na patay pero hindi kayang tanggapin ang malinaw na katotohanan na si Jesus talaga ang Anak ng Diyos.
At ang masakit na realidad ay ito:
May mga taong hindi galit sa himala dahil hindi sila naniniwala.
Galit sila sa himala dahil winawasak nito ang kontrol nila.
Sa Juan 12:10–11, sinabi:
“Ngunit nagpasya ang mga punong saserdote na ipapatay din si Lazaro, sapagkat dahil sa kanya ay maraming Judio ang humihiwalay at sumasampalataya kay Jesus.”
Isipin mo iyon.
Si Lazaro ay minsan nang namatay.
Ngayon gusto na naman siyang patayin ng relihiyon.
Hindi dahil kriminal siya.
Hindi dahil rebelde siya.
Hindi dahil nagnakaw siya ng kapangyarihan.
Kundi dahil ang mismong paghinga niya ay ebidensiya.
At ang ebidensiya ay kinatatakutan ng mga taong itinayo ang kanilang pagkatao sa pagtanggi sa katotohanan.
Ang pangalang Lazaro ay mula sa Hebreong pangalan na Eleazar:
אֶלְעָזָר
(Eleazar)
Ang ibig sabihin:
“Tumulong ang Diyos.”
Napakalalim niyan.
Hindi binuhay si Lazaro dahil makapangyarihan siya.
Binuhay siya dahil tumutulong ang Diyos sa mga taong walang kakayahang iligtas ang sarili nila.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Ang mga pinunong panrelihiyon noong panahon ni Jesus ay nagtayo ng impluwensiya sa pamamagitan ng kontrol.
Kontrol sa templo.
Kontrol sa batas.
Kontrol sa reputasyon.
Kontrol sa kung sino ang mukhang matuwid.
Pero paulit-ulit silang kinonpronta ni Jesus.
Sa Mateo 23:27 sinabi Niya:

“Sa aba ninyo, mga eskriba at mga Fariseo, mga mapagkunwari! Sapagkat kayo ay tulad sa mga pinaputing libingan na maganda sa labas ngunit sa loob ay puno ng mga buto ng mga patay at ng lahat ng karumihan.”
Sa Griyego:
κεκονιαμένοις τάφοις
(kekoniamenois taphois)
“Pinaputing libingan.”
Maganda sa labas.
Patay sa loob.
Napakalalim ng irony rito.
Ang mga lider na iyon ay naging espirituwal na libingan.
Pagkatapos tumayo si Jesus sa harap ng totoong libingan at ipinakita Niya ang kapangyarihang hindi kayang gawin ng relihiyon.
Kayang palamutian ng relihiyon ang kamatayan.
Pero si Jesus kayang talunin ito.
Kaya naging banta si Lazaro.
Dahil sa tuwing makikita siya ng mga tao na humihinga, nakikita nila ang pagkakaiba ng walang buhay na relihiyon at ng tunay na kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Sa Juan 11, makikita natin ang isa sa pinakamabigat na eksena sa Bibliya.
Pagdating ni Jesus matapos mamatay si Lazaro, sinabi ni Marta:
“Panginoon, kung narito ka sana, hindi namatay ang aking kapatid.”
Ramdam mo ang sakit.
Ang pagkalito.
Ang pakiramdam na nagdasal ka pero parang tahimik ang langit.
Maraming tao ang nakaka-relate rito.
Nagdasal ka.
Umiyak ka.
Nag-ayuno ka.
Pero namatay pa rin ang relasyon.
Nasira pa rin ang pamilya.
Bumalik pa rin ang kasalanan.
Nananatili pa rin ang depresyon.
At parang sarado pa rin ang libingan.
Pero hindi nahuli si Jesus.
May mas malalim Siyang ipinapakita.
Sa Juan 11:25 sinabi Niya:
“Ako ang muling pagkabuhay at ang buhay.”
Sa Griyego:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
“Ako ang pagkabuhay na muli at ang buhay.”
Hindi Niya sinabing:
“Kaya kong gumawa ng resurrection.”
Sinabi Niya:
“Ako mismo ang resurrection.”
Napakalaking pahayag nito.
Dahil inuugnay ni Jesus ang Kanyang sarili sa pangalan ng Diyos sa Exodo 3:14.
Sa Hebreo:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)
“Ako ang Ako Nga.”
Hindi aksidente ang mga salitang ginamit ni Jesus.
Hinaharap Niya ang lahat ng nakikinig:
Tatanggapin ba nila Siya?
O tatanggihan?
At nang lumabas si Lazaro mula sa libingan, naging pisikal na ebidensiya ang himala.
Kaya natakot ang mga lider.
Hindi dahil kulang sila sa impormasyon.
Kundi dahil humihinga na sa harap nila ang katotohanan.
Sa Juan 11:47 sinabi ng mga pinuno:
“Ano ang gagawin natin? Sapagkat ang taong ito ay gumagawa ng maraming tanda.”
Pansinin mo.
Hindi nila itinanggi ang himala.
Inamin nila ito.
Ang problema ay hindi kakulangan ng ebidensiya.
Ang problema ay ayaw nilang sumuko.
Ganito pa rin ngayon.
May mga taong nagsasabing:
“Kapag pinakita lang ng Diyos ang sarili Niya, maniniwala ako.”
Pero maraming beses sa Bibliya na kahit harap-harapan na ang himala, tumitigas pa rin ang puso ng tao.
Dahil hindi lang ito intelektuwal na laban.
Espirituwal ito.
Naging mapanganib si Lazaro dahil siya ay buhay na larawan ng pagbabago.
Patay.
Nakabalot.
Inilibing.
Nabubulok.
Tapos biglang buhay.
Kayang kontrahin ng tao ang sermon.
Pero mahirap kontrahin ang transformed life.
Kaya natatakot ang kadiliman sa tunay na testimonya.
Dating sugapa sa bisyo pero malaya na.
Dating puno ng galit pero maamo na.
Dating gustong magpakamatay pero ngayon may pag-asa na.
Dating malayo sa Diyos pero ngayon umiiyak na sa presensya Niya.
May kapangyarihan kapag ang dating patay espirituwal ay naging buhay kay Cristo.
Sa Efeso 2:1:
“Kayo ay dating mga patay dahil sa inyong mga pagsuway at mga kasalanan.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “patay” ay:
νεκρούς
(nekrous)
Espirituwal na walang buhay.
At dito nagiging personal ang kuwento.
Dahil maraming tao ang parang buhay sa panlabas pero pagod na pagod na sa loob.
Ngumingiti pero wasak.
Nagsisimba pero numb.
Nagpo-post pero umiiyak gabi-gabi.
Nakakulong sa hiya.
Takot.
Pornograpiya.
Kasalanan.
Pagkukunwari.
At pagkatapos pumapasok si Jesus sa libingan ng buhay nila.
At nagbabago ang lahat.
Sa Juan 11:43 sinabi:
“Sumigaw Siya nang malakas, ‘Lazaro, lumabas ka!’”
Sa Griyego:
Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω
(Lazare, deuro exō)
“Lazaro, lumabas ka.”
Sinasabi ng ilang Bible scholars:
Tinawag ni Jesus si Lazaro sa pangalan.
Dahil kung sinabi lang Niyang “Lumabas kayo,” baka nabuksan ang lahat ng libingan.
Ganoon ang awtoridad ni Cristo.
At mula nang lumabas si Lazaro, nagbago ang lahat.
Dumami ang naniniwala.
Lumakas ang pressure.
Nayanig ang relihiyosong sistema.
Sa Juan 11:48 sinabi ng mga lider:
“Kapag pinabayaan natin Siya, lahat ay sasampalataya sa Kanya.”
Iyan ang tunay nilang takot.
Mawawala ang kontrol.
Mawawala ang impluwensiya.
Mawawala ang kapangyarihan.
Hanggang ngayon may mga taong mas pinipiling atakihin ang katotohanan kaysa magsisi.
May mga sistema pa ring natatakot sa tunay na pagbabago.
Dahil ang tunay na kalayaan ay naglalantad ng pagkakakulong.
Kapag tunay kang binago ni Jesus, hindi lahat matutuwa.
May magdududa.
May maiinis.
May lalayo.
May sisira.
Dahil ang transformed life mo ay magiging paalala na totoo si Jesus.
Hindi nga nangaral si Lazaro.
Pero ang buhay niya mismo ay sermon.
Bawat hininga niya ay testimonya.
Isipin mo ang kumakain ka kasama ng taong dati nang naaagnas sa libingan.
Isipin mo marinig mo siyang tumatawa.
Isipin mong makita mo siyang buhay.
Parang sumisigaw ang buong eksena:
“Tinalo ni Jesus ang kamatayan.”
At dito mas lalong lumalalim ang kuwento.
Ang pinakamaikling talata sa Bibliya ay isa rin sa pinakamabigat.
“Umiyak si Jesus.”
Juan 11:35.
Sa Griyego:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
(edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Umiyak si Jesus.”
Hindi malamig ang Diyos.
Hindi Siya detached sa sakit ng tao.
Alam ni Jesus na bubuhayin Niya si Lazaro.
Pero umiyak pa rin Siya.
Bakit?
Dahil ang pag-ibig ay nasasaktan.
Dahil ang kamatayan ay hindi original na plano ng Diyos.
Dahil ang kasalanan ang sumira sa mundo.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na tahimik nang umiiyak.
Pagod ka na.
Pakiramdam mo nakalimutan ka ng Diyos.
Pakiramdam mo nakabaon ka na.
Pero ang parehong Jesus na tumayo sa harap ng libingan ni Lazaro ay nakikita ka rin.
Naririnig ka rin.
At kaya ka pa rin Niyang tawagin palabas.
Maraming tao ngayon ang buhay pero parang nakakulong sa sariling libingan.
Libingan ng trauma.
Libingan ng addiction.
Libingan ng hiya.
Libingan ng depression.
Libingan ng kasalanan.
Libingan ng religiosity na walang tunay na relasyon sa Diyos.
Pero si Jesus ay negosyo pa rin ang resurrection.
At ito ang katotohanang ayaw tanggapin ng marami:
Kapag tunay kang binuhay ni Cristo, mapipilitan ang mga tao sa paligid mo na harapin kung sino talaga ang nagbago sa iyo.
Kaya naging banta si Lazaro.
Dahil pinahirapan niyang manatili sa unbelief ang mga tao.
Ang buhay niya ay ebidensiya.
At ang tunay na Kristiyanismo ay hindi lang dapat pinapangaral.
Dapat nakikita.
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “witness” ay:
μάρτυς
(martys)
Dito nanggaling ang salitang martyr.
Ang witness ay taong ang buhay mismo ang ebidensiya.
Kaya ang tanong:
Nakikita ba kay Jesus sa atin?
Nakikita ba ang resurrection pagkatapos ng kasalanan?
Pagkatapos ng pagkawasak?
Pagkatapos ng addiction?
Pagkatapos ng depression?
O hanggang relihiyon lang tayo?
May isa pang detalye na madalas nakakalimutan.
Paglabas ni Lazaro sinabi ni Jesus:
“Kalagan ninyo siya at hayaan siyang makalakad.”
Juan 11:44.
Kahit buhay na si Lazaro, nakabalot pa rin siya ng grave clothes.
Napakalalim nito.
Maraming believers ang totoong nakilala si Jesus pero nakabalot pa rin sa dating takot.
Dating guilt.
Dating mindset.
Dating sugat.
Dating pagkatao.
Ang resurrection puwedeng instant.
Pero ang healing minsan process.
Ang salitang Griyego na λύσατε
(lysate)
ay nangangahulugang:
“Kalagan ninyo siya.”
“Palayain ninyo siya.”
Iyan ang dapat ginagawa ng church.
Hindi muling ilibing ang mga tao sa kahihiyan.
Hindi paulit-ulit ipamukha ang nakaraan nila.
Kundi tulungan silang mamuhay sa kalayaang ibinigay ni Cristo.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon tumatagos pa rin ang kuwento ni Lazaro.
Dahil alam ng tao sa kaibuturan niya:
Hindi natin kayang buhayin ang sarili natin.
Hindi kayang burahin ng pera ang guilt.
Hindi kayang talunin ng success ang spiritual death.
Si Jesus lang ang may awtoridad laban sa libingan.
Sa Roma 6:4:
“Kung paanong si Cristo ay muling binuhay mula sa mga patay… tayo rin ay mamuhay sa panibagong buhay.”
Sa Griyego:
καινότητι ζωῆς
(kainotēti zōēs)
“Bagong uri ng buhay.”
Hindi simpleng pagbabago.
Transformation.
Kaya natatakot ang kadiliman sa tunay na Kristiyanismo.
Dahil ang resurrection ay lumilikha ng mga taong hindi na kontrolado ng takot.
Mga taong alam na natalo na ang kamatayan.
Mga taong personal na nakaranas ng biyaya.
Mga taong alam kung paano sila hinugot ng Diyos mula sa imposible.
Maging tapat ka.
Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
At kung may kakilala kang parang nakakulong sa dilim, ipadala mo ito sa kanila.
May mga taong hindi motivational quote ang kailangan.
Kailangan nila ng resurrection hope.
Dahil may mga libingan pa ring naghihintay marinig ang pangalan nila mula sa bibig ni Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Elijah
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Elijah
There are moments in Scripture that feel too raw to be invented.
Moments where the pages stop sounding religious… and start sounding painfully human.
The story of Elijah is one of them.
Most people remember Elijah as the prophet who called down fire from heaven.
The fearless man who stood before kings.
The man who shut the heavens for three years.
The prophet who mocked false gods without trembling.
But very few people talk about what happened after the fire fell.
Very few people talk about the exhausted man underneath the mantle.

Very few people talk about the depression, the loneliness, the emotional collapse, the silence, the fear, the hidden tears, and the terrifying moment where one of the greatest prophets in history begged God to let him die.
This is the untold story of Elijah.
And if you have ever smiled in public while secretly collapsing inside… this story may expose parts of your soul nobody else can see.
Because Elijah was not just fighting prophets.
He was fighting exhaustion.
He was fighting disappointment.
He was fighting isolation.
He was fighting the crushing weight that comes after spiritual battles.
And maybe… so are you.
The first time Elijah appears in Scripture, he explodes onto the scene like thunder.
1 Kings 17:1 says:
“Now Elijah the Tishbite, from Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, ‘As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.’”
The Hebrew phrase for “before whom I stand” is:
לִפְנֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר־עָמַדְתִּי לְפָנָיו
Lifnei YHWH asher amadti lefanav
It carries the image of a servant standing in the direct presence of a king.
Elijah was not speaking from ego.
He was speaking from intimacy with God.
And that matters.
Because public power without private intimacy eventually destroys people.
The nation of Israel had fallen deep into idolatry under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel.
Baal worship had spread everywhere.
Child sacrifice.
Sexual immorality.
False prophets.
Corruption.
Spiritual compromise.
People still claimed to know God while bowing before idols.
Sound familiar?
Elijah was sent into a nation that wanted spiritual comfort without repentance.
A nation that preferred false prophets who entertained them instead of convicting them.
And honestly… not much has changed.
The drought Elijah announced was not random judgment.
It directly confronted Baal.
Baal was believed to be the storm god.
The god supposedly responsible for rain and fertility.
God was exposing the lie publicly.
For three years, heaven stayed shut.
No rain.
No crops.
No relief.
And during this time, Elijah himself was hidden.
First by the brook Cherith.
Then with a widow in Zarephath.
It is fascinating that before God used Elijah publicly, He isolated him privately.
Because hidden seasons are often where God strips dependency on human applause.
At the brook, ravens fed him.
Think about that.
Ravens were considered unclean animals under Jewish law.
Yet God used what was considered unclean to sustain His prophet.
Some of you keep rejecting the ways God is trying to help you because the package does not look spiritual enough.
But provision is still provision.
Then the brook dried up.
That detail matters deeply.
The brook dried up even though Elijah was obedient.
Many believers secretly think obedience guarantees comfort.
It does not.
Sometimes God allows brooks to dry up because your next assignment requires movement.
The Hebrew word for brook there is “נַחַל” (nachal).
It can describe a seasonal stream.
Temporary.
Not permanent.
Some relationships were seasonal.
Some places were seasonal.
Some blessings were seasonal.
And your pain is coming from trying to force permanence onto what God only intended for a season.
Then came Mount Carmel.
The confrontation.
The moment everybody talks about.
Hundreds of prophets of Baal gathered.
Elijah stood alone.
Imagine the pressure.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine standing against an entire culture by yourself.
Elijah tells the people in 1 Kings 18:21:
“How long will you go limping between two different opinions?”
The Hebrew phrase is extraordinary.
עַד־מָתַי אַתֶּם פֹּסְחִים עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים
Ad matai atem poschim al shtei hase’ifim
The word “פֹּסְחִים” (poschim) means limping, hobbling, wavering.
Israel was spiritually limping.
Trying to serve God while keeping idols.
Trying to hold truth and compromise together.
Trying to live double lives.
And some people reading this are exhausted because divided loyalty always drains the soul.
Elijah rebuilt the broken altar.
That detail is often overlooked.
Before the fire fell publicly… the altar had to be repaired privately.
Some of you keep asking God for fire while refusing to repair the altar.
Prayerlessness.
Hidden sin.
Compromise.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Secret addictions.
God does not bless performances.
He responds to surrender.
Then heaven answered.
Fire fell.
Not metaphorically.
Literally.
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּפֹּל אֵשׁ־יְהוָה
Vattipol esh-YHWH
“And the fire of the LORD fell.”
The people collapsed facedown.
Revival exploded.
It looked like victory.
The kind of moment modern Christians would clip into short videos and post everywhere.
But the next chapter becomes one of the darkest emotional collapses in Scripture.
And this is where the untold story begins.
After Elijah’s greatest victory… Jezebel sends one threat.
One message.
And suddenly Elijah runs.
Why?
Because spiritual highs do not erase human exhaustion.
Sometimes the strongest people break after the battle is over.
Adrenaline fades.
Emotion crashes.
Isolation settles in.
And Elijah collapses emotionally under a broom tree.
1 Kings 19:4 says:
“But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die.”
One chapter earlier he was calling down fire.
Now he wants to die.
This is one of the Bible’s clearest pictures that even mighty men of God can experience despair.
The Hebrew phrase is devastating.
רַב עַתָּה יְהוָה קַח נַפְשִׁי
Rav attah YHWH qach nafshi
“It is enough now, LORD, take my life.”
Elijah was depleted.
Burned out.
Emotionally crushed.
And notice something powerful.
God does not rebuke him immediately.
God lets him sleep.
Feeds him.
Gives him water.
Lets him rest.
That is astonishing.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a person can do is rest.
Not every exhausted believer needs another lecture.
Some need healing.
Some need sleep.
Some need nourishment.
Some need to stop carrying battles God never asked them to carry.
The angel tells Elijah:
“Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you.”
That line destroys pride.
Because even prophets have limits.
Even warriors break.
Even faithful believers become overwhelmed.
And pretending you are invincible is not faith.
It is denial.
Then Elijah goes to Horeb.
The mountain of God.
The same region connected to Moses.
The same place where God revealed Himself in power.
And Elijah hides in a cave.
God asks him:
“What are you doing here, Elijah?”
Not because God lacked information.
God was exposing Elijah’s heart.
Elijah responds:
“I alone am left.”
That sentence reveals the emotional distortion of isolation.
Loneliness makes people believe they are alone even when they are not.
Then comes one of the most misunderstood passages in Scripture.
There was wind.
Earthquake.
Fire.
But God was not in them.
Then came what English Bibles often translate as a “still small voice.”
The Hebrew phrase is:
קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַקָּה
Qol demamah daqqah
Literally:
“A voice of thin silence.”
Not hype.
Not spectacle.
Not noise.
Silence.
God met Elijah in quietness.
And this generation is terrified of silence.
Because silence exposes what distraction hides.
Many people know worship music.
Podcasts.
Sermons.
Content.
Noise.
But very few know how to sit quietly before God long enough to hear conviction.
The untold story of Elijah is not really about fire.
It is about what happens after the fire fades.
It is about discovering whether your identity was built on God… or on spiritual adrenaline.
And this is where many believers quietly fall apart.
Because they know how to fight publicly.
But they do not know how to heal privately.
Elijah expected revival to permanently change Israel.
But Jezebel was still there.
Evil still existed.
The nation was still unstable.
And disappointment crushed him.
Some of you are grieving because you expected one breakthrough to fix everything.
One answered prayer.
One relationship.
One church experience.
One opportunity.
One victory.
But life remained complicated.
And secretly you are wondering why God allowed the battle to continue.
Elijah’s story reveals that even after mountaintop moments… believers still walk through valleys.
And yet God never abandoned him.
Not once.
God corrected him gently.
Strengthened him patiently.
Spoke to him personally.
And reminded him:
“You are not alone.”
God tells Elijah there were still seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal.
Seven thousand.
Elijah’s despair distorted his perspective.
Pain often does that.
You start believing:
“Nobody understands.”
“Nobody cares.”
“I’m the only one struggling.”
But isolation lies.
One of the most beautiful details in Elijah’s story is that God eventually gives him Elisha.
Companionship.
Mentorship.
Relationship.
Even prophets needed people.
The hyper-independent version of Christianity many people promote today is not biblical.
God created believers for fellowship.
For encouragement.
For strengthening.
For sharpening.
For carrying burdens together.
And then comes Elijah’s departure.
The chariot of fire.
The whirlwind.
The mystery.
2 Kings 2 describes Elijah being taken up.
The Hebrew says:
וַיַּעַל אֵלִיָּהוּ בַּסְּעָרָה הַשָּׁמָיִם
Vaya’al Eliyahu basse’arah hashamayim
“And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.”
What a finish.
But do not miss the deeper truth.
Elijah was not remembered because he was flawless.
He was remembered because God stayed faithful to him through every extreme.
Fire.
Fear.
Faith.
Exhaustion.
Victory.
Depression.
Loneliness.
Power.
Weakness.
And maybe that is the real untold story.
That God does not only use fearless people.
He uses surrendered people.
People who break.
People who cry.
People who collapse.
People who become exhausted.
People who sometimes want to quit.
But keep turning back toward Him.
James 5:17 says:
“Elijah was a man with a nature like ours.”
The Greek says:
Ἠλίας ἄνθρωπος ἦν ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν
Elias anthropos ēn homoiopathēs hēmin
“Elijah was a human being with feelings like ours.”
That changes everything.
The Bible is not presenting Elijah as a mythological superhero.
He was human.
And if God could sustain Elijah through emotional collapse, fear, exhaustion, loneliness, disappointment, and spiritual warfare… He can sustain you too.
Maybe you are under your own broom tree right now.
Smiling outwardly while internally exhausted.
Still showing up.
Still functioning.
But secretly drained.
Listen carefully.
God did not abandon Elijah in the cave.
And He has not abandoned you either.
The enemy wants exhausted believers isolated.
Silent.
Ashamed.
Disconnected.
Because isolation magnifies despair.
But Jesus still calls weary people toward Himself.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for “rest” is:
ἀναπαύσω
anapausō
Refresh.
Relief.
Restoration.
Not temporary distraction.
True rest for the soul.
And the Gospel reveals something Elijah’s story was ultimately pointing toward.
A greater Prophet.
A greater Deliverer.
A greater Savior.
Jesus Christ.
Elijah called down fire.
Jesus carried judgment Himself.
Elijah fled into the wilderness.
Jesus walked willingly toward the cross.
Elijah felt alone.
Jesus was abandoned so sinners could be reconciled to God.
Elijah experienced exhaustion.
Jesus sweat drops like blood in Gethsemane.
Elijah was sustained by angels.
Jesus could have summoned angels but chose the cross instead.
And through Christ, broken sinners can become sons and daughters of God.
Not through works.
Not through performance.
Not through pretending to be spiritually strong.
But through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
And maybe the reason Elijah’s story feels so personal is because deep down… many people are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of carrying pain silently.
Tired of fighting secret battles.
Tired of spiritual emptiness.
But Jesus still heals.
Still restores.
Still forgives.
Still rescues.
Still calls people out of darkness.
Still rebuilds broken altars.
And maybe this article found you for a reason.
Maybe God is exposing what exhaustion has been hiding.
Maybe your soul has been starving while your life looked successful externally.
Maybe you have fire publicly… but despair privately.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone immediately came to your mind while reading this… share this with them.
Some people are losing battles silently.
Some fires are not sent to destroy you.
Some fires are exposing what was never surrendered.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Kwento ni Elias
May mga bahagi ang Biblia na parang sobrang totoo para imbentuhin lang.
Mga tagpong hindi na tunog relihiyon… kundi tunog ng totoong buhay.
Tunog ng pagod.
Tunog ng luha.
Tunog ng isang taong pilit lumalaban habang unti-unti nang nadudurog sa loob.
Isa sa mga kwentong iyon ay ang kwento ni Elias.
Kilala siya ng karamihan bilang propetang nagpababa ng apoy mula sa langit.
Ang lalaking humarap sa hari nang walang takot.
Ang propetang nagsara ng langit sa loob ng tatlong taon.
Ang taong hindi natinag sa harap ng daan-daang bulaang propeta.
Pero kakaunti ang nagsasalita tungkol sa nangyari pagkatapos bumaba ang apoy.
Kakaunti ang nagsasalita tungkol sa pagod sa likod ng tapang.
Kakaunti ang nakakapansin sa lungkot, pag-iisa, pagkapagod, takot, at emosyonal na pagbagsak ng isa sa pinakadakilang propeta sa kasaysayan.
Dahil may sandali sa buhay ni Elias na hiniling niyang kunin na ng Diyos ang kanyang buhay.
At kung naging masaya ka sa harap ng tao pero tahimik na umiiyak kapag mag-isa ka… baka mas malapit ka kay Elias kaysa sa inaakala mo.
Ang unang paglitaw ni Elias sa Biblia ay parang kulog.
Sa 1 Hari 17:1, sinabi niya:
“Buhay ang Panginoon, ang Diyos ng Israel, na aking pinaglilingkuran, walang hamog o ulan sa mga taong ito maliban kung sabihin ko.”
Sa Hebreo, ang katagang:
לִפְנֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר־עָמַדְתִּי לְפָנָיו
Lifnei YHWH asher amadti lefanav
ay may kahulugang:
“Nakatayo ako sa mismong harapan ng Diyos.”
Hindi nagsasalita si Elias mula sa pride.
Nagsasalita siya mula sa intimacy.
At mahalagang maintindihan iyon.
Dahil ang pampublikong kapangyarihan na walang pribadong relasyon sa Diyos ay unti-unting sisira sa tao.
Noong panahon ni Elias, nalubog ang Israel sa idolatriya.
Si Haring Ahab at Reyna Jezebel ang nagpasok ng pagsamba kay Baal.
Puno ng kompromiso.
Puno ng kasalanan.
Puno ng huwad na relihiyon.
Maraming taong nagsasabing kilala nila ang Diyos habang yumuyuko naman sa mga diyus-diyosan.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… parang hindi naiba sa panahon ngayon.
Maraming gustong sumunod kay Cristo basta walang pagsisisi.
Maraming gustong makarinig ng mensaheng komportable pero ayaw makarinig ng katotohanan.
Kaya isinara ng Diyos ang ulan.
Hindi iyon random na parusa.
Si Baal kasi ay tinatawag na diyos ng ulan at kasaganaan.
Parang ipinapakita ng Diyos:
“Wala siyang kapangyarihan. Ako lang ang Diyos.”
Tatlong taon walang ulan.
Walang ani.
Walang kasiguraduhan.
At habang nagugutom ang bayan… itinatago ng Diyos si Elias.
Una sa batis ng Kerit.
Pagkatapos sa bahay ng isang biyuda.
Nakakagulat isipin na bago gamitin ng Diyos si Elias nang makapangyarihan sa publiko… itinago muna siya sa pribado.
Dahil may mga panahon talagang aalisin ng Diyos ang lahat ng distraction para Siya lang ang matira.
Sa batis, mga uwak ang nagpapakain kay Elias.
Oo.
Mga uwak.
Sa batas ng Hudyo, maruming hayop ang uwak.
Pero ginamit pa rin iyon ng Diyos para buhayin ang propeta.
Minsan kasi, nire-reject natin ang tulong ng Diyos dahil hindi ito dumating sa paraang inaasahan natin.
Pero provision pa rin iyon.
Pagkatapos… natuyo ang batis.
At napakahalagang detalye niyan.
Natuyo ang batis kahit sumusunod si Elias.
Akala kasi ng maraming tao kapag obedient ka, magiging komportable na ang buhay.
Hindi.
Minsan pinapatuyo ng Diyos ang batis dahil oras na para lumipat ka.
May mga bagay kasing seasonal lang.
May mga relasyon.
May mga lugar.
May mga blessing.
At ang sakit minsan nanggagaling dahil pilit mong hinahawakan ang bagay na tapos na ang season.
Pagkatapos dumating ang pinakasikat na bahagi ng kwento.
Ang Bundok Carmel.
Ang laban.
Daang-daang propeta ni Baal laban kay Elias.
Isang tao laban sa buong sistema.
Imagine mo ang pressure.
Imagine mo ang katahimikan.
Imagine mong nakatayo ka mag-isa habang lahat laban sa iyo.
Sa 1 Hari 18:21, sinabi ni Elias:
“Hanggang kailan kayo mag-aalinlangan sa pagitan ng dalawang panig?”
Sa Hebreo:
עַד־מָתַי אַתֶּם פֹּסְחִים עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים
Ad matai atem poschim al shtei hase’ifim
Ang salitang “פֹּסְחִים” (poschim) ay nangangahulugang:
“Pilay.”
Lumpo.
Paika-ika.
Ganoon ang Israel.
Gusto ang Diyos pero gusto rin ang kasalanan.
Gusto ang katotohanan pero gusto rin ang compromise.
At maraming tao ngayon ang emotionally drained dahil doble ang buhay.
Pagod na pagod nang magpanggap.
Bago bumaba ang apoy… inayos muna ni Elias ang altar.
Napakalalim niyan.
Bago dumating ang apoy ng Diyos sa publiko… inayos muna ang sirang altar sa pribado.
Maraming gustong makaranas ng apoy ng Diyos pero ayaw ayusin ang altar.
Ayaw bitawan ang secret sin.
Ayaw magsisi.
Ayaw magpatawad.
Ayaw sumuko.
Ayaw magpakumbaba.
Pagkatapos bumagsak ang apoy.
Literal na apoy mula sa langit.
Sa Hebreo:
וַתִּפֹּל אֵשׁ־יְהוָה
Vattipol esh-YHWH
“At bumagsak ang apoy ng Panginoon.”
Lumuhod ang mga tao.
Nagkaroon ng revival.
Mukhang panalo na lahat.
Mukhang ito na ang moment na hindi na mawawala.
Pero dito nagsisimula ang hindi naikukuwentong bahagi.
Pagkatapos ng pinakamalaking victory ni Elias… isang mensahe lang mula kay Jezebel ang nagpayanig sa kanya.
Isang threat.
At tumakbo siya.
Bakit?
Dahil kahit ang pinakamatitibay na tao napapagod din.
Minsan bumabagsak ang tao pagkatapos ng laban.
Kapag tapos na ang adrenaline.
Kapag tahimik na ulit.
Kapag wala nang palakpak.
At doon bumigay si Elias.
Sa ilalim ng puno.
Sa ilang.
Mag-isa.
Sa 1 Hari 19:4, sinabi niya:
“Sapat na, Panginoon. Kunin Mo na ang aking buhay.”
Sa Hebreo:
רַב עַתָּה יְהוָה קַח נַפְשִׁי
Rav attah YHWH qach nafshi
“Sobra na, Panginoon.”
Imagine mo iyon.
Isang chapter lang ang pagitan.
Mula sa apoy ng langit… hanggang sa gusto nang mamatay.
At ito ang isa sa pinakamalinaw na patunay sa Biblia na kahit ang malalakas na lingkod ng Diyos ay puwedeng mapagod emotionally.
Puwedeng madepress.
Puwedeng madurog.
At napakaganda ng ginawa ng Diyos.
Hindi Niya agad sinermonan si Elias.
Pinatulog muna.
Pinakain.
Pinainom.
Pinagpahinga.
Minsan kasi, ang pinaka-spiritual na kailangan ng tao ay pahinga.
Hindi lahat ng pagod kailangan sermon.
May mga taong kailangan lang talagang gumaling.
May mga taong sobra nang may dinadalang laban.
Sinabi ng anghel:
“Tumayo ka at kumain ka, sapagkat napakalayo pa ng iyong lalakbayin.”
Napakabigat na linya.
Dahil kahit propeta may limitasyon.
Kahit warrior napapagod.
Kahit believer nadudurog.
At hindi kahinaan ang umamin na pagod ka.
Pagkatapos pumunta si Elias sa bundok ng Diyos.
At nagtago siya sa kuweba.
Doon tinanong siya ng Diyos:
“Ano ang ginagawa mo rito, Elias?”
Hindi dahil hindi alam ng Diyos.
Kundi dahil inilalabas Niya ang laman ng puso ni Elias.
At sinabi ni Elias:
“Ako na lang ang natitira.”
Ganyan magsinungaling ang loneliness.
Pinapaniwala ka nitong mag-isa ka.
Pagkatapos dumating ang hangin.
Lindol.
Apoy.
Pero wala roon ang Diyos.
Pagkatapos dumating ang:
קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַקָּה
Qol demamah daqqah
“Isang manipis na tinig ng katahimikan.”
Hindi sigaw.
Hindi ingay.
Hindi spectacle.
Kundi katahimikan.
At maraming tao ngayon takot sa katahimikan.
Dahil kapag tahimik na… lumalabas ang totoong kondisyon ng puso.
Ang hindi naikukuwentong kwento ni Elias ay hindi lang tungkol sa apoy.
Ito ay tungkol sa kung ano ang nangyayari pagkatapos mawala ang apoy.
Kapag wala na ang hype.
Kapag wala na ang crowd.
Kapag ikaw na lang at ang Diyos.
Doon nasusubok kung tunay bang nakaugat ang identity mo kay God.
Maraming believers marunong lumaban publicly.
Pero hindi marunong mag-heal privately.
Akala ni Elias magbabago na ang lahat pagkatapos ng Mount Carmel.
Pero nandiyan pa rin si Jezebel.
May kasamaan pa rin.
May laban pa rin.
At dinurog siya ng disappointment.
Baka may mga taong nagbabasa nito na ganyan din.
Akala mo kapag nakuha mo ang breakthrough magiging okay na lahat.
Kapag nasagot ang prayer.
Kapag bumalik siya.
Kapag nagbago ang sitwasyon.
Pero hindi.
At tahimik kang napapagod.
Pero hindi iniwan ng Diyos si Elias.
Hindi kahit isang beses.
Pinalakas Niya.
Kinorrect Niya.
Kinausap Niya.
At pinaalala:
“Hindi ka nag-iisa.”
May pitong libo pa raw sa Israel na hindi lumuhod kay Baal.
Pitong libo.
Ibig sabihin mali ang iniisip ni Elias na siya na lang mag-isa.
Kapag nasasaktan kasi ang tao… lumiliit ang perspective.
Akala mo wala nang nakakaintindi.
Wala nang nagmamahal.
Wala nang may pakialam.
Pero may mga taong ginagamit pa rin ang Diyos.
Isa sa pinakamagandang bahagi ng kwento ay binigyan ng Diyos si Elias ng kasama.
Si Eliseo.
Dahil kahit ang propeta kailangan ng tao.
Hindi biblical ang “ako lang at si God okay na.”
Ginawa tayo ng Diyos para sa fellowship.
Para sa encouragement.
Para sa accountability.
Para sa pagmamahalan.
At pagkatapos… dumating ang pagtatapos ni Elias.
Ang karwaheng apoy.
Ang ipoipo.
Ang pag-akyat sa langit.
Sa 2 Hari 2:
וַיַּעַל אֵלִיָּהוּ בַּסְּעָרָה הַשָּׁמָיִם
Vaya’al Eliyahu basse’arah hashamayim
“At si Elias ay iniakyat sa langit sa pamamagitan ng ipoipo.”
Napakalakas na ending.
Pero huwag mong mamiss ang totoong mensahe.
Hindi naging dakila si Elias dahil perpekto siya.
Naging dakila siya dahil naging tapat ang Diyos sa kanya sa bawat season.
Sa apoy.
Sa takot.
Sa victory.
Sa depression.
Sa loneliness.
Sa weakness.
At baka iyon din ang gustong ipaalala ng Diyos sa iyo ngayon.
Hindi lang Niya ginagamit ang malalakas.
Ginagamit Niya ang surrendered.
Mga taong umiiyak.
Mga taong pagod.
Mga taong minsang gustong sumuko.
Pero patuloy pa ring bumabalik sa Kanya.
Sa Santiago 5:17:
“Si Elias ay taong may likas na damdaming tulad natin.”
Sa Greek:
Ἠλίας ἄνθρωπος ἦν ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν
Elias anthropos ēn homoiopathēs hēmin
“Ibig sabihin si Elias ay taong may emosyon tulad natin.”
Hindi siya superhero.
Tao siya.
At kung kinaya siyang buhatin ng Diyos sa gitna ng pagod, fear, emotional collapse, at loneliness… kaya ka rin Niyang buhatin.
Baka nasa sarili kang kuweba ngayon.
Ngumingiti sa tao pero ubos na ubos na sa loob.
Tahimik.
Pagod.
At halos gusto nang sumuko.
Makinig ka.
Hindi iniwan ng Diyos si Elias sa kuweba.
At hindi ka rin Niya iiwan.
Gusto ng kaaway na manatiling tahimik ang mga pagod na believer.
Nakahiwalay.
Nahihiya.
Nag-iisa.
Dahil lumalakas ang despair sa isolation.
Pero patuloy pa ring tumatawag si Jesus sa mga pagod.
Sa Mateo 11:28 sinabi Niya:
“Lumapit kayo sa Akin, kayong lahat na napapagal at nabibigatan, at kayo’y Aking papapahingahin.”
Sa Greek, ang salitang:
ἀναπαύσω
anapausō
ay nangangahulugang:
Restoration.
Refreshment.
Kapahingahan ng kaluluwa.
At dito papasok ang pinakamahalagang bahagi.
Ang kwento ni Elias ay tumuturo sa mas dakilang Propeta.
Kay Jesus Cristo.
Si Elias nagpababa ng apoy.
Si Jesus ang tumanggap ng hatol para sa makasalanan.
Si Elias tumakbo sa ilang.
Si Jesus kusang naglakad papunta sa krus.
Si Elias nakaramdam ng pag-iisa.
Si Jesus iniwan upang tayo’y mailapit sa Diyos.
Si Elias napagod.
Si Jesus nagpawis ng dugo sa Getsemani.
At sa pamamagitan ni Cristo, may kapatawaran.
May bagong buhay.
May restoration.
May grace.
Hindi sa performance.
Hindi sa pagpapanggap.
Kundi sa pagsisisi at pananampalataya kay Jesus Cristo.
At baka kaya ka napahinto sa article na ito dahil may gustong ipakita ang Diyos sa puso mo.
Baka matagal ka nang pagod.
Baka matagal ka nang nagpapanggap na okay.
Baka may apoy ka sa harap ng tao pero may depression sa likod ng saradong pinto.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas tumama ito kaysa sa inaasahan mo.
May mga taong tahimik na nawawasak.
Minsan ang apoy ay hindi ipinadala para sirain ka.
Minsan ipinadala ito para sunugin ang mga bagay na hindi mo pa tunay na naisusuko sa Diyos.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Midwives Lied to Pharaoh to Save Hebrew Babies
paragraphs: Why the Midwives Lied to Pharaoh to Save Hebrew Babies
There are moments in Scripture that make people uncomfortable.
Moments where the Bible does not fit neatly inside religious systems.
Moments where survival, courage, terror, obedience, and moral tension collide in the dark.
This is one of those moments.
Two women stood between a murderous king and helpless newborn babies.
And they lied.
Not for money.
Not for selfish ambition.
Not for manipulation.
They lied because babies were about to be slaughtered.
And heaven saw everything.

Most people read Exodus quickly and miss the emotional weight buried inside the text. But if you slow down long enough to feel the terror of what was happening in Egypt, this story becomes devastatingly real.
This was not merely political oppression.
This was attempted extermination.
This was state-sponsored genocide against covenant children.
This was demonic fear trying to destroy the future before it could be born.
And strangely enough… the first recorded human heroes in the book of Exodus are not warriors.
Not prophets.
Not kings.
Not priests.
Midwives.
Women whose hands caught fragile babies while death waited outside.
Exodus 1:15–17 says:

“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah; and he said, ‘When you are helping the Hebrew women to give birth and see them upon the birthstool, if it is a son, then you shall put him to death; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.’ But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, but let the boys live.”
The Hebrew phrase used here is:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
“Vattirena hamyalledot et-haElohim”
“The midwives feared God.”
This changes everything.
The text does not first emphasize political rebellion.
It emphasizes fear of God.
The Hebrew word used for “feared” is יָרֵא (yare’).
This word means reverence, awe, trembling obedience, deep recognition of divine authority.
Their fear of God overpowered their fear of Pharaoh.
And that matters because Pharaoh was not merely a ruler.
In Egypt, Pharaoh was viewed as divine.
To disobey him was dangerous.
To oppose him could cost your life.
But these women understood something modern culture desperately needs to rediscover:
Earthly authority is never ultimate authority.
When human governments command evil, obedience to God becomes higher.
That is exactly why this passage has echoed through generations of persecuted believers.
Because sometimes righteousness is costly.
Sometimes doing what is holy puts you in danger.
Sometimes faithfulness requires courage while your hands shake.
And the terrifying part?
The midwives had no guarantee God would rescue them.
We read this story knowing the ending.
They did not.
Imagine the emotional tension.
Every Hebrew mother screaming in labor.
Every newborn son wrapped in cloth.
Every knock at the door potentially carrying death.
Every heartbeat filled with fear.
And still… these women chose life.
The names Shiphrah and Puah matter more than most readers realize.
Pharaoh’s personal name is not even mentioned in Exodus 1.
But God preserved the names of the midwives forever.
Think about that.
Empires collapse.
Tyrants rot.
But heaven remembers ordinary people who protect life.
Shiphrah likely comes from a Hebrew root associated with beauty or brightness.
Puah may carry ideas connected to crying out or splendor.
These women became beautiful in the eyes of God because they protected what evil wanted destroyed.
Then comes the moment that creates theological tension.
Exodus 1:18–19:

“So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them, ‘Why have you done this thing, and let the boys live?’ The midwives said to Pharaoh, ‘Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife can get to them.’”
This was not the whole truth.
And many people wrestle with this.
Did God approve of lying?
Was deception justified?
Why does Scripture appear to honor them afterward?
The answer requires careful biblical understanding.
The Bible does not explicitly praise the lie itself.
It praises their fear of God and their protection of innocent life.
Exodus 1:20–21 says:
“So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very mighty. Because the midwives feared God, He established households for them.”
Notice the repeated emphasis.
“Because the midwives feared God.”
Not:
“Because they lied skillfully.”
The text centers on covenant loyalty to God over participation in murder.
This distinction matters deeply.
Scripture consistently condemns false witness, deception for evil, manipulation, and dishonest gain.
Yet Scripture also recognizes moments where protecting innocent life under evil oppression creates morally tragic circumstances.
This is why many theologians compare this event to Rahab in Joshua 2.
Rahab hid the Israelite spies and misled the authorities searching for them.
Hebrews 11:31 later honors her faith.
James 2:25 highlights her actions flowing from faith.
Again, the emphasis is covenant loyalty and protection of life under wicked tyranny.
This does not create a universal permission slip for lying.
The Bible never teaches situational ethics where truth becomes meaningless.
Instead, these passages reveal the horror of living in a fallen world where evil regimes force people into impossible situations.
The moral burden in Exodus falls primarily on Pharaoh.
He was commanding infanticide.
He was weaponizing authority against babies.
And the midwives refused to become instruments of death.
This is one reason the story still grips people emotionally thousands of years later.
Because deep down, we recognize the weight of moral courage.
Most people imagine they would resist evil if history demanded it.
But reality is terrifying.
People lose jobs.
Families get threatened.
Reputations get destroyed.
Fear silences entire populations.
Yet these women stood in the gap.
Not with armies.
With conviction.
And if we are honest, this story exposes something painful inside many of us.
How often do we stay silent because speaking truth feels costly?
How often do we compromise because fear feels stronger than conviction?
How often do we protect comfort more than righteousness?
The midwives remind us that courage is rarely loud.
Sometimes courage looks like quietly refusing to participate in evil.
Sometimes holiness looks like protecting the vulnerable when nobody applauds.
Sometimes faithfulness happens behind closed doors where only God sees.
And there is something even deeper happening spiritually in Exodus.
Pharaoh was trying to kill Hebrew sons.
Centuries later, Herod would try to kill Hebrew sons again after hearing about the birth of Jesus.
Matthew 2 echoes Exodus intentionally.
Satan repeatedly targets covenant seed.
Why?
Because redemption was coming through a child.
The enemy often attacks what carries future deliverance.
That is why this story feels spiritually alive even now.
Some people reading this have spent years feeling like hell itself was trying to destroy them before they could become who God called them to be.
Some survived childhood trauma.
Abuse.
Addiction.
Depression.
Violence.
Rejection.
Suicidal thoughts.
And you still do not fully realize that your survival may itself be evidence of divine purpose.
The Hebrew babies Pharaoh wanted dead included Moses.
Imagine if the midwives had surrendered.
Imagine if fear won.
Imagine if they obeyed evil authority instead of God.
A deliverer would have died in infancy.
One act of courage can alter history.
One refusal to participate in evil can preserve generations.
One moment of fearing God more than man can become part of redemption itself.
That is why this passage cannot be reduced to shallow arguments online.
This is about the cost of righteousness in dark times.
And there is another detail many overlook.
The Hebrew word for midwives is מְיַלְּדֹת (meyalledot).
Its root relates to bringing forth birth.
These women were literally called to help life emerge.
Pharaoh commanded them to reverse their calling.
To turn deliverers of life into agents of death.
That is exactly how evil works.
Sin always tries to corrupt God-given purpose.
It tries to make protectors become predators.
It tries to make shepherds become wolves.
It tries to make truth-bearers become liars.
It tries to make image-bearers forget God.
But the midwives resisted corruption.
And because of that, their names still breathe through history.
There is also powerful theological significance in the phrase “let the boys live.”
The Hebrew says:
וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת־הַיְלָדִים
“Vattechayyena et-hayeladim”
“They caused the children to live.”
The root here is חָיָה (chayah), meaning “to live,” “to preserve alive,” “to revive.”
This same life-language echoes throughout Scripture.
God is repeatedly portrayed as the giver and sustainer of life.
The midwives aligned themselves with the life-giving heart of God instead of the death-producing agenda of Pharaoh.
That does not mean they were sinless.
It means they chose righteousness over participation in murder.
And perhaps that is part of what makes this story so emotionally overwhelming.
God works through flawed humans.
Not perfect humans.
Real humans.
Terrified humans.
Complicated humans.
Humans forced into difficult moments inside a fallen world.
Some readers struggle because they want every biblical situation reduced into simplistic formulas.
But Scripture often gives us reality instead.
Messy.
Painful.
Complex.
Human.
And through it all, God’s sovereignty remains intact.
The story also confronts modern believers with uncomfortable questions.
Would we protect the vulnerable if it endangered us?
Would we obey God if culture mocked us?
Would we stand against evil if the cost became personal?
Or have we become so addicted to comfort that conviction disappears under pressure?
This is why Exodus still cuts deep.
Because Pharaoh is not merely an ancient king.
Pharaoh represents every system that exalts itself against God.
Every power structure demanding compromise.
Every voice pressuring people to participate in evil for the sake of convenience, safety, acceptance, or survival.
And the midwives remind us that sometimes the holiest people in history are invisible to the world.
No stage.
No platform.
No empire.
Just courage.
Quiet courage.
Holy courage.
The kind of courage heaven never forgets.
There are people reading this who feel insignificant.
You think your obedience does not matter.
You think your quiet faithfulness goes unseen.
But Scripture says otherwise.
God recorded the names of two midwives forever.
Not because they were powerful.
Because they feared Him.
And maybe someone reading this right now has been compromising truth because fear has controlled your life.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of conflict.
Fear of losing people.
Fear of standing alone.
Fear of consequences.
But eventually every believer faces the same question the midwives faced:
Who do you fear more?
God?
Or Pharaoh?
That question still divides humanity.
Jesus Himself later said in Matthew 10:28:
“Do not fear those who kill the body but are unable to kill the soul; but rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
The Greek word for fear there is φοβέω (phobeó).
It carries the same deep reverential seriousness seen in the Hebrew concept of fearing God.
Biblical fear of God is not terror that pushes us away from Him.
It is awe that brings us under His authority.
The midwives understood this long before Sinai.
Long before the Law was formally given.
They recognized that innocent life mattered to God.
And their actions became part of preserving the line through which redemption history unfolded.
Moses survived.
Israel survived.
The covenant continued.
And ultimately, centuries later, Jesus Christ entered the world through that preserved covenant people.
This story points beyond itself.
It whispers about a greater Deliverer.
Because every rescued Hebrew child in Exodus foreshadows the God who rescues sinners from death.
Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior.
He came to rescue people enslaved under sin.
The same way Israel groaned under Pharaoh, humanity groans under bondage.
And Christ entered history to confront the kingdom of darkness itself.
That is why the Gospel matters.
Because every human eventually discovers that evil is not only outside us.
It is inside us too.
We have all lied.
Compromised.
Failed.
Broken trust.
Disobeyed God.
Fallen short.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek phrase “fall short” is ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai).
It carries the sense of lacking, failing to attain, coming behind.
Humanity cannot save itself through morality.
Not even heroic moments erase sin.
That is why we need grace.
The beauty of the Gospel is not that humans are flawless.
The beauty of the Gospel is that Jesus saves flawed people.
People like Moses.
People like Rahab.
People like David.
People like Peter.
People like us.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the overwhelming mercy of God.
Christ absorbed judgment so repentant sinners could receive forgiveness.
And maybe that is why this story lingers emotionally.
Because it reminds us that evil is real.
Fear is real.
Oppression is real.
But courage through faith is real too.
And God still sees those who choose righteousness when darkness grows loud.
Somebody needed this reminder today.
Your obedience matters.
Your refusal to compromise matters.
Your quiet faithfulness matters.
Your stand for truth matters.
And heaven notices what the world ignores.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than most people expected.
Sometimes the people who save generations are the ones history almost forgot.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Nagsinungaling ang mga Hilot kay Paraon Para Iligtas ang mga Sanggol na Hebreo
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na hindi komportable basahin.
Mga sandaling hindi kasya sa mabababaw na sermon.
Mga tagpong bumabangga ang takot, pananampalataya, buhay, kamatayan, kapangyarihan, at konsensya.
Ito ang isa sa mga iyon.
Dalawang babae ang tumayo sa pagitan ng isang mamamatay-taong hari at mga bagong silang na sanggol.
At nagsinungaling sila.
Hindi dahil gahaman sila.
Hindi dahil gusto nilang manloko.
Hindi dahil rebelde sila.
Nagsinungaling sila dahil may mga sanggol na malapit nang patayin.
At nakita iyon ng langit.
Karamihan sa mga tao mabilis basahin ang Exodo at hindi nararamdaman ang bigat ng nangyayari.
Pero kapag hinayaan mong lumubog ang puso mo sa takot ng panahong iyon… maiintindihan mo kung gaano ito kabigat.
Hindi ito simpleng pang-aapi.
Ito ay pagtatangkang lipulin ang isang buong lahi.
Ito ay sistematikong pagpatay sa mga anak ng tipan.
Ito ay takot ng kadiliman sa hinaharap na hindi pa ipinapanganak.
At nakakagulat… ang unang mga bayani sa aklat ng Exodo ay hindi hari.
Hindi propeta.
Hindi mandirigma.
Hindi pari.
Mga hilot.
Mga babaeng ang mga kamay ay humahawak ng bagong buhay habang naghihintay ang kamatayan sa labas.
Sinasabi sa Exodo 1:15–17:

“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah; and he said, ‘When you are helping the Hebrew women to give birth and see them upon the birthstool, if it is a son, then you shall put him to death; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.’ But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, but let the boys live.”
Ang ginamit na salitang Hebreo ay:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
“Vattirena hamyalledot et-haElohim”
“Natakot ang mga hilot sa Diyos.”
At dito nagbabago ang lahat.
Hindi unang binigyang-diin ng Kasulatan ang pagrerebelde nila.
Ang binigyang-diin ay ang kanilang takot sa Diyos.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “takot” ay יָרֵא (yare’).
Hindi lang ito simpleng takot.
Ito ay banal na paggalang.
Pagkamangha.
Panginginig sa harap ng awtoridad ng Diyos.
Mas malakas ang takot nila sa Diyos kaysa takot nila kay Paraon.
At mahalagang maunawaan iyon.
Si Paraon ay hindi lang hari.
Sa Egypto, itinuturing siyang parang diyos.
Ang pagsuway sa kanya ay maaaring ikamatay mo.
Pero naunawaan ng mga hilot ang isang katotohanang kailangan muling marinig ng mundo ngayon:
Ang kapangyarihan ng tao ay hindi kailanman mas mataas kaysa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Kapag inuutos ng tao ang kasamaan, mas mataas pa rin ang pagsunod sa Diyos.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napakalakas ng kuwentong ito kahit libo-libong taon na ang lumipas.
Dahil minsan mahal ang pagiging matuwid.
Minsan mapanganib ang paggawa ng tama.
Minsan nanginginig ka habang pinipili mong sumunod sa Diyos.
At ang nakakatakot?
Walang kasiguraduhan ang mga hilot na ililigtas sila ng Diyos.
Alam natin ang ending ng kuwento.
Sila, hindi.
Isipin mo ang tensyon.
Bawat inang Hebreo na sumisigaw sa panganganak.
Bawat sanggol na lalaki na iniluluwal.
Bawat katok sa pinto na maaaring may dalang kamatayan.
At sa kabila ng lahat… pinili pa rin nilang protektahan ang buhay.
Napakahalaga ng mga pangalang Shiphrah at Puah.
Ang pangalan ni Paraon mismo ay hindi binanggit sa Exodo 1.
Pero ang pangalan ng mga hilot… isinulat ng Diyos magpakailanman.
Pag-isipan mo iyon.
Nawawala ang mga imperyo.
Nabubulok ang mga diktador.
Pero hindi nakakalimutan ng langit ang mga ordinaryong taong nagprotekta ng buhay.
Pagkatapos nito dumating ang bahagi na madalas pagdebatehan.

“So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them, ‘Why have you done this thing, and let the boys live?’ The midwives said to Pharaoh, ‘Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife can get to them.’”
Hindi iyon buong katotohanan.
Kaya maraming nagtatanong:
Pinuri ba ng Diyos ang pagsisinungaling?
Pinapayagan ba ng Biblia ang panlilinlang?
Bakit tila pinagpala pa sila pagkatapos?
Mahalagang maging maingat dito.
Hindi pinuri ng Diyos ang kasinungalingan mismo.
Ang pinuri ng Diyos ay ang kanilang takot sa Kanya at ang kanilang pagtangging makibahagi sa pagpatay ng inosente.
“So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very mighty. Because the midwives feared God, He established households for them.”
Pansinin mo.
Paulit-ulit ang diin:
“Because the midwives feared God.”
Hindi sinabi:
“Because they lied well.”
Napakahalaga ng pagkakaibang iyon.
Hindi kailanman itinuro ng Biblia na okay lang magsinungaling para sa pansariling interes.
Kinokondena ng Kasulatan ang maling saksi, panlilinlang, at kasinungalingang nagdudulot ng kasamaan.
Pero ipinapakita rin ng Biblia ang bigat ng pamumuhay sa isang makasalanang mundo kung saan may mga pagkakataong pinipilit ng masasamang sistema ang tao sa napakahirap na sitwasyon.
Ang tunay na kasamaan sa kuwento ay si Paraon.
Siya ang nag-utos ng pagpatay sa mga sanggol.
Siya ang gumamit ng kapangyarihan laban sa mga inosente.
At tumanggi ang mga hilot na maging instrumento ng kamatayan.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon tumatama ito sa puso ng tao.
Dahil lahat tayo may sandaling kailangang pumili.
Mananahimik ba tayo dahil natatakot tayo?
O maninindigan tayo kahit may kapalit?
Madalas iniisip ng mga tao na magiging matapang sila kapag dumating ang kasamaan.
Pero ang totoo… nakakatakot.
May nawawalan ng trabaho.
May tinatakwil.
May pinapatahimik.
May inuusig.
Pero tumayo pa rin ang mga hilot.
Hindi gamit ang espada.
Kundi gamit ang paninindigan.
At kung magiging tapat tayo sa sarili natin, may inilalantad itong masakit.
Ilang beses na tayong nanahimik dahil mas mahalaga ang comfort kaysa katotohanan?
Ilang beses na tayong natakot mawalan ng tao kaya nagkompromiso tayo?
Ilang beses nating pinili ang seguridad kaysa pagsunod sa Diyos?
Ipinapaalala ng mga hilot na hindi laging maingay ang tapang.
Minsan tahimik lang itong pagtanggi na makibahagi sa mali.
Minsan kabanalan ang simpleng pagprotekta sa mahina kahit walang nakakakita.
At may mas malalim pang nangyayari rito.
Sinubukang patayin ni Paraon ang mga anak na lalaki ng Israel.
Pagkalipas ng maraming siglo, sinubukan ding patayin ni Herodes ang mga batang lalaki matapos marinig ang kapanganakan ni Jesus.
Sinasalamin ng Mateo 2 ang Exodo.
Paulit-ulit tinatarget ng kadiliman ang binhing may dalang pagtubos.
Bakit?
Dahil may darating na Tagapagligtas.
At madalas sinusubukan ng kaaway patayin ang layunin bago pa ito lumago.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pakiramdam nila buong buhay silang nilalabanan ng kadiliman.
Trauma.
Abuso.
Depresyon.
Pagkagumon.
Pagpapakamatay na isipin.
Pagkawasak.
At baka hindi mo pa rin lubos nauunawaan na maaaring dahilan kung bakit ka nabuhay ay dahil may layunin ang Diyos para sa iyo.
Kasama sa mga sanggol na gustong patayin ni Paraon si Moises.
Isipin mo kung sumuko ang mga hilot.
Isipin mo kung nanaig ang takot.
Maaaring namatay ang isang magiging tagapagligtas habang sanggol pa.
Minsan isang matapang na desisyon lang ang kayang baguhin ang kasaysayan.
Isang pagtanggi sa kasamaan.
Isang tao na mas natakot sa Diyos kaysa sa tao.
At may isa pang detalye na madalas hindi napapansin.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “mga hilot” ay מְיַלְּדֹת (meyalledot).
Nagmula ito sa ugat na may kaugnayan sa pagdadala ng buhay.
Ang calling nila ay tumulong magluwal ng buhay.
Pero gusto ni Paraon na gamitin sila para magdala ng kamatayan.
Ganiyan gumalaw ang kasamaan.
Sinisira nito ang orihinal na layunin ng Diyos.
Ginagawang mandaragit ang tagapangalaga.
Ginagawang manhid ang konsensya.
Ginagawang normal ang kasamaan.
Pero tumanggi ang mga hilot.
At dahil doon, buhay pa rin ang pangalan nila hanggang ngayon.
Sinasabi rin sa Exodo:
וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת־הַיְלָדִים
“Vattechayyena et-hayeladim”
“Pinanatili nilang buhay ang mga bata.”
Ang ugat ng salitang ito ay חָיָה (chayah).
Ibig sabihin: mabuhay, panatilihing buhay, magbigay-buhay.
Ang Diyos ay Diyos ng buhay.
At pinili ng mga hilot ang panig ng buhay kaysa kamatayan.
Hindi ibig sabihin nito perpekto sila.
Ibig sabihin pinili nilang huwag makibahagi sa pagpatay.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakalalim ng kuwentong ito.
Ginagamit ng Diyos ang mga totoong tao.
Hindi perpektong tao.
Takot na tao.
Sugatang tao.
Komplikadong tao.
Mga taong sinusubukang sumunod sa Diyos sa gitna ng magulong mundo.
At may tanong ang kuwentong ito para sa ating lahat.
Kapag dumating ang pressure… sino ang mas katatakutan mo?
Ang Diyos?
O si Paraon?
Iyan pa rin ang tanong hanggang ngayon.
Sinabi ni Jesus sa Mateo 10:28:
“Do not fear those who kill the body but are unable to kill the soul; but rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “fear” ay φοβέω (phobeó).
Hindi lang ito panic.
Ito ay malalim na paggalang at pagkilala sa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Naunawaan iyon ng mga hilot bago pa man ibigay ang Kautusan sa Sinai.
Naunawaan nila na mahalaga sa Diyos ang inosenteng buhay.
At dahil sa kanilang katapangan… nabuhay si Moises.
Nabuhay ang Israel.
Nagpatuloy ang tipan.
At paglipas ng maraming siglo… dumating si Jesucristo mula sa bayang iyon.
At dito lalong lumalalim ang kuwento.
Dahil hindi lang ito tungkol sa dalawang hilot.
Ito ay anino ng mas dakilang pagliligtas.
Gaya ng pagliligtas ng Diyos sa mga sanggol mula sa kamatayan, inililigtas din Niya ang mga makasalanan mula sa espirituwal na kamatayan.
Tayong lahat ay nagkasala.
Lahat tayo bumagsak.
Lahat tayo may kasinungalingan.
May kompromiso.
May sugat.
Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “fall short” ay ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai).
Ibig sabihin kulang.
Hindi sapat.
Hindi maabot ang pamantayan ng kabanalan ng Diyos.
Hindi kayang iligtas ng tao ang sarili niya.
Kaya kailangan natin si Cristo.
Ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo ay hindi dahil perpekto ang tao.
Ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo ay inililigtas ni Jesus ang mga hindi perpekto.
Mga taong tulad ni Moises.
Tulad ni Rahab.
Tulad ni Pedro.
Tulad natin.
Sa krus nakita natin kung gaano kaseryoso ang kasalanan.
Pero nakita rin natin kung gaano kalalim ang awa ng Diyos.
Inako ni Cristo ang hatol para makaranas tayo ng kapatawaran.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod na.
Takot na.
Tahimik na lumalaban.
Ito ang paalala mo:
Nakikita ng Diyos ang katapatan na hindi napapansin ng mundo.
Nakikita Niya ang tahimik mong paninindigan.
Nakikita Niya ang laban na hindi alam ng iba.
At hindi nasasayang ang pagsunod sa Diyos.
Maging tapat.
Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Minsan ang mga taong nagligtas ng mga henerasyon ay iyong mga halos nakalimutan ng kasaysayan.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Doeg the Edomite Became One of the Bible’s Darkest Side Characters
paragraphs: Why Doeg the Edomite Became One of the Bible’s Darkest Side Characters
Some villains announce themselves with armies.
Some arrive wearing crowns.
Some carry swords dripping with blood.
But some of the darkest people in Scripture walk quietly into the room unnoticed.
No thunder. No warning. No dramatic entrance.
Just a man standing in the background… listening. Watching. Waiting.
That was Doeg the Edomite.
A side character. A servant. A name most people skip while reading.
Yet hidden inside his story is one of the coldest betrayals in the entire Bible.
Not because he was powerful.
But because he had no fear of God.
And honestly… that is still one of the most dangerous types of people alive.

There are people who sit near worship but never surrender. People who stand around holy things while secretly loving darkness. People who know the language of faith but whose hearts are untouched by God.
Doeg was one of them.
And the terrifying part is this: He was close to the presence of God… but became a servant of destruction.
That is why his story still shakes the soul thousands of years later.
Because many people know what it feels like to be wounded by someone who stood close enough to holiness to appear safe.
Someone religious. Someone trusted. Someone inside the room.
And if we are honest… some people see parts of Doeg hiding inside themselves.
The jealousy. The ambition. The hunger for approval. The willingness to harm others to climb higher.
This is not just an ancient story.
This is a mirror.
And before this article ends, many people will realize why Scripture preserved Doeg’s name forever.
Not because he was important.
But because he became a warning.
A warning about what happens when a human heart chooses proximity to power over surrender to God.
Not to shame them. But because some wounds only begin healing when truth is finally spoken.
The first time Scripture introduces Doeg is in 1 Samuel 21.
David was running for his life.
Saul, the king of Israel, had become consumed by jealousy.
David had once played music to calm Saul’s torment. David fought Goliath. David served faithfully. David honored Saul repeatedly.
But jealousy can make people hate the very ones who helped them survive.
That spirit still exists today.
Some people celebrate you until your favor from God starts becoming visible.
The Hebrew language behind jealousy throughout Saul’s narrative carries the idea of burning zeal and possessive rage.
Saul could not control the fact that God’s hand rested upon David.
So instead of repenting… he tried to destroy him.
David fled to Nob, where the priests of the LORD were.
The priest Ahimelech gave David bread and the sword of Goliath.
But then Scripture quietly inserts a detail that almost feels insignificant.
1 Samuel 21:7 says:
“Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD; and his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul.”
Detained before the LORD.
That phrase matters deeply.
The Hebrew says:
"נֶעְצָר לִפְנֵי יְהוָה"
Transliterated:
“Ne’tsar lifnei YHWH.”
It carries the idea of being restrained, held, or lingering before the presence of the LORD.
Doeg was physically present around holy things.
But proximity to sacred places does not transform an unrepentant heart.
Judas walked with Jesus. Pharisees memorized Scripture. Cain brought an offering.
A person can stand inches from truth while remaining spiritually dead inside.
That should terrify every generation.
