Ang kuwento ni Moises ay hindi lang kuwento tungkol sa sampung salot, paghahati ng Dagat na Pula, o mga tapyas ng bato na isinulat ng daliri ng Diyos.
Ito ay kuwento ng isang lalaking halos buong buhay ay pakiramdam niya hindi siya sapat.
Isang lalaking iniligtas ng biyaya bago pa niya lubos na makilala ang Diyos na nagligtas sa kanya.
Isang lalaking may dalang pagtawag ng Diyos pero punong-puno ng takot, galit, pagod, pagdududa, trauma, at mga sugat na walang nakakakita.
Kilala ng karamihan ang mga himala ni Moises.
Pero kakaunti ang tunay na nakakaunawa sa mga sugat ni Moises.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon tumatagos pa rin ito sa kaluluwa ng tao.
Dahil sa ilalim ng aklat ng Exodo ay nakatago ang kuwento ng bawat taong minsang nagtanong:
“Magagamit pa ba ako ng Diyos kahit ganito ako?”
Nagsimula ang kuwento hindi sa nagliliyab na puno.
Nagsimula ito sa pagpatay.
Sa Exodo 1:22, iniutos ni Paraon:
“Bawat lalaking sanggol na ipanganak ay ihagis sa ilog.”
Sa Hebrew:
"כָּל־הַבֵּן הַיִּלּוֹד הַיְאֹרָה תַּשְׁלִיכֻהוּ"
(Kol-haben hayillod haye’orah tashlikhuhu)
Literal na ibig sabihin:
“Bawat batang lalaking ipinanganak ay ihagis sa Nile.”
Hindi ito simpleng batas.
Ito ay takot.
Takot ng kadiliman sa isang batang magiging tagapagligtas balang araw.
At kahit gustong patayin ng mundo si Moises… nabuhay pa rin siya.
Hindi dahil mahina si Paraon.
Kundi dahil may isinulat nang plano ang Diyos na hindi kayang burahin ng impiyerno.
Itinago siya ng kanyang ina nang tatlong buwan.
At dumating ang isa sa pinakamabigat na tagpo sa buong Kasulatan.
Isang ina ang naglagay ng kanyang sanggol sa basket at pinaanod sa ilog.
Ang nakakagulat… ang salitang ginamit sa Hebrew para sa basket ay:
"תֵּבָה" (tevah)
Ito rin mismo ang salitang ginamit para sa arka ni Noe.
Hindi ito aksidente.
Si Moises ay inilagay sa isang maliit na “arka.”
Isang sisidlan ng pagliligtas sa gitna ng tubig ng kamatayan.
Ang Nile sana ang magiging libingan niya.
Pero ginawa iyon ng Diyos na daan patungo sa kanyang destinasyon.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na akala nila tapos na ang buhay nila.
Akala mo winasak ka ng trauma.
Akala mo tinapos ka ng depresyon.
Akala mo walang saysay ang pag-iyak mo gabi-gabi.
Pero nabuhay ka pa rin.
At baka hindi mo pa alam… pero may dahilan kung bakit hindi ka pinabayaan ng Diyos.
Lumaki si Moises sa palasyo ni Paraon.
Isipin ang pagkalito niya.
Hebreo ang dugo.
Pero Ehipsiyo ang kultura.
Lumaking hindi lubos na tanggap saanman.
Acts 7:22:
“Tinuruan si Moises ng lahat ng karunungan ng mga Egipcio.”
May edukasyon siya.
Kapangyarihan.
Posisyon.
Pribilehiyo.
Pero walang nakapagpagaling sa digmaan sa loob niya.
Maraming tao ngayon ang ganyan.
Mukhang maayos sa labas.
Pero wasak sa loob.
At dumating ang araw na nagbago ang lahat.
Nakita ni Moises ang isang Egipcio na sinasaktan ang isang Hebreo.
May sumabog sa puso niya.
Exodo 2:12:
“Pinatay niya ang Egipcio.”
Sa Hebrew:
"וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַמִּצְרִי"
(Vayakh et-hamitzri)
Literal:
“Sinaktan niya hanggang mamatay.”
Galit iyon.
Matinding galit.
Gusto ni Moises ng hustisya.
Pero sinubukan niyang gawin ang plano ng Diyos gamit ang laman.
At hanggang ngayon, maraming tao pa rin ang gumagawa niyan.
Pinipilit ang calling gamit ang emosyon.
Pinapairal ang galit sa halip na pagsunod.
Kinokontrol ang lahat dahil takot masaktan muli.
Nang malaman ni Paraon ang nangyari, tumakas si Moises.
Ang prinsipe ng Egypt naging takas.
At dito nagsimula ang bahagi ng kuwento na madalas hindi pinapansin.
Ang ilang.
Apatnapung taon.
Apatnapung tahimik na taon.
Walang palakpakan.
Walang audience.
Walang himala.
Nag-aalaga lang ng tupa.
Ang dating nakatira sa palasyo… ngayon nasa disyerto.
At baka ito ang ayaw marinig ng modernong mundo.
Dahil gustong-gusto natin ng mabilis.
Pero madalas humuhubog ang Diyos sa katahimikan.
Mahilig tayo sa platform.
Pero ang Diyos gumagawa muna ng shepherd.
Mahilig tayo sa spotlight.
Pero ang Diyos naghahanda sa lihim.
Akala ni Moises tapos na ang buhay niya.
Hindi niya alam… inihahanda na pala siya ng langit.
May taong nagbabasa nito na frustrado dahil parang walang nangyayari sa buhay mo.
Pero ang mga nakatagong season ay hindi sayang.
May ginagawa ang Diyos kahit hindi mo nakikita.
At dumating ang nagliliyab na puno.
Exodo 3:2:
“Nagpakita ang anghel ng Panginoon sa apoy sa gitna ng isang mababang punongkahoy.”
Sa Hebrew:
"וַיַּרְא מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה אֵלָיו בְּלַבַּת־אֵשׁ"
(Vayera malakh YHWH elav belabbat-esh)
Ang “belabbat-esh” ay nangangahulugang:
“Sa puso ng apoy.”
Tinawag ng Diyos si Moises mula sa gitna ng apoy.
At ang nakakabigla…
Nasusunog ang puno.
Pero hindi nauubos.
Iyan ang larawan ng maraming mananampalataya ngayon.
Sugatan.
Pagod.
Sinubok.
Pero hindi pa rin tuluyang bumabagsak.
At tinawag siya ng Diyos:
“Moses, Moses.”
Mahalaga ang pag-uulit ng pangalan sa kultura ng Hebrew.
Ibig sabihin nito intimacy.
Pagmamahal.
Personal na pagtawag.
Hindi lang tinatawag ng Diyos ang isang lingkod.
Tinatawag Niya ang isang anak.
At sumagot si Moises:
"הִנֵּנִי"
(Hineni)
“Here I am.”
Hindi lang ito “nandito ako.”
Ibig sabihin nito:
“Handa ako.”
“Available ako.”
“Nakikinig ako.”
At pagkatapos nito… nakipagtalo si Moises sa Diyos.
Madalas hindi ito pinapansin sa mga sermon.
Punong-puno si Moises ng insecurity.
Exodo 4:10:
“Ako ay mabagal magsalita.”
Sa Hebrew:
"כְבַד־פֶּה וּכְבַד לָשׁוֹן"
(Khevad-peh ukhevad lashon)
Literal:
“Mabigat ang bibig at dila.”
Pakiramdam ni Moises hindi siya sapat.
Pero pinili pa rin siya ng Diyos.
At iyan ang bumabasag sa kasinungalingan ng maraming tao.
Hindi hinihintay ng Diyos na maging perpekto ka.
Hinahanap Niya ang surrender.
Maraming tao naghihintay maging fearless bago sumunod.
Pero ang Diyos humahanap ng willing.
At nagsimula ang laban kay Paraon.
Ang sampung salot ay hindi random.
Bawat isa ay pagwasak ng Diyos sa mga diyos-diyosan ng Egypt.
Ang Nile laban kay Hapi.
Ang kadiliman laban kay Ra.
Ang kamatayan ng panganay laban kay Paraon na itinuturing na diyos.
Pinapakita ng Diyos:
Walang diyos-diyosan ang makakatayo sa harapan Niya.
At hanggang ngayon ganoon pa rin.
Hindi kayang iligtas ng pera ang kaluluwa.
Hindi kayang pagalingin ng fame ang emptiness.
Hindi kayang punuin ng kasalanan ang espiritu.
Si Cristo lang.
At dumating ang Passover.
Ang dugo sa pintuan.
Ang kordero.
Ang pagliligtas.
Sa Hebrew:
"פֶּסַח" (Pesach)
Ibig sabihin:
“To pass over.”
“Lampasan.”
Ang dugo ang naging pagitan ng awa at paghatol.
At pagdating ni Jesus… nakita ng mundo ang tunay na Kordero ng Diyos.
John 1:29:
“Masdan ang Kordero ng Diyos na nag-aalis ng kasalanan ng sanlibutan.”
Mula pa noon… ibinubulong na ng Exodus ang tungkol kay Cristo.
Pagdating sa Dagat na Pula, natakot ang Israel.
Nasa likod nila ang hukbo ni Paraon.
Sa harap nila ang dagat.
At sinabi ni Moises:
“Stand firm.”
Sa Hebrew:
"הִתְיַצְּבוּ"
(Hityatzevu)
“Tumayo kayo.”
Huwag tumakbo.
Huwag sumuko sa takot.
Tumayo.
At saka hinati ng Diyos ang dagat.
Pero may bagay na madalas hindi napapansin.
Hindi nahati ang tubig hanggang hindi gumalaw si Moises.
Minsan hinihintay natin ang malinaw na ebidensya bago sumunod.
Pero ang tunay na pananampalataya kumikilos muna.
At nang makatawid sila… akala nila tapos na ang laban.
Hindi pa pala.
Dahil kahit nakalabas na sila sa Egypt… nasa puso pa rin nila ang Egypt.
At hanggang ngayon maraming tao ang ganyan.
Malaya na sana.
Pero bumabalik pa rin sa kasalanan.
Bumabalik sa toxic na relasyon.
Bumabalik sa addiction.
Bumabalik sa compromise.
Pagdating sa Sinai, ibinigay ng Diyos ang kautusan.
Pero ang salitang ginamit sa Hebrew para sa commandments ay:
"דְּבָרִים" (Devarim)
Ibig sabihin:
“Mga salita.”
Hindi lang nagbibigay ng rules ang Diyos.
Inihahayag Niya ang Kanyang puso.
At habang nasa bundok si Moises… gumawa naman ng gintong guya ang Israel.
Nainip sila.
At ang impatience madalas nagbubunga ng idolatry.
Kapag pakiramdam ng tao tahimik ang Diyos… gumagawa siya ng substitute.
Minsan relationship.
Minsan pera.
Minsan social media.
Minsan ministry mismo.
At kahit nagkasala ang Israel… nagpakita pa rin ng awa ang Diyos.
Paulit-ulit.
Pagkabigo ng tao.
Awa ng Diyos.
Rebellion ng tao.
Awa ng Diyos.
Kahinaan ng tao.
Awa ng Diyos.
At baka kailangan marinig ito ng isang tao ngayon.
Hindi ka naligtas dahil flawless ka.
Naligtas ka dahil maawain si Jesus.
At dumating ang pinakamasakit na bahagi ng kuwento.
Sinabihan ng Diyos si Moises na kausapin ang bato.
Pero hinampas niya ito.
Numbers 20:10:
“Makikinig ba kayo, kayong mga rebelde?”
Makikita ang frustration ni Moises.
At dahil dito… hindi siya nakapasok sa Promised Land.
Napakasakit isipin.
Matapos ang lahat ng sakripisyo.
Matapos ang lahat ng pagdurusa.
Pero kahit dito… may biyaya pa rin.
Dahil kalaunan nakita rin si Moises sa Promised Land.
Hindi sa Joshua.
Kundi sa Mount of Transfiguration kasama ni Jesus.
At doon naging malinaw ang mas malalim na katotohanan.
Si Moises ay hindi ang tunay na tagapagligtas.
Si Jesus.
Inilabas ni Moises ang Israel mula Egypt.
Pero inililigtas ni Jesus ang tao mula sa kasalanan.
Hinati ni Moises ang dagat.
Pero tinalo ni Jesus ang kamatayan.
Nagbigay si Moises ng kautusan sa bato.
Pero si Jesus nagsusulat ng pagbabago sa puso.
Ang buong kuwento ni Moises ay tumuturo kay Cristo.
At baka kaya ito sobrang tumatama sa tao.
Dahil nakikita natin ang sarili natin kay Moises.
Takot.
Pagod.
Sugatan.
Galit.
Nagkakamali.
Pero patuloy pa ring tinatawag ng Diyos.
At baka pakiramdam mo wala nang pag-asa para sa’yo.
Baka akala mo tapos na ang purpose mo.
Baka nilalamon ka ng shame.
Baka pakiramdam mo hindi ka na kayang gamitin ng Diyos.
Pero si Moises ay patunay:
Ginagamit pa rin ng Diyos ang mga sugatan.
Tinatawag pa rin Niya ang mga insecure.
Pinapatawad pa rin Niya ang mga bagsak.
At gumagawa pa rin Siya ng himala gamit ang nanginginig na kamay.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malalim ito kaysa simpleng impormasyon.
Dahil ang Biblia ay hindi lang history.
Salamin ito.
Ang parehong Diyos na nagligtas kay Moises sa ilog ay Siya ring Diyos na patuloy na nagliligtas sa mga taong pakiramdam nila nalulunod na sila.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Isaac
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Isaac
Most people remember Isaac as the quiet son.
The child Abraham almost sacrificed.
The miracle baby born to elderly parents.
The man standing silently between the towering stories of Abraham and Jacob.
But that is exactly why most people never truly see him.
Isaac is one of the most misunderstood men in Scripture.
Because silence does not mean weakness.
And gentleness does not mean absence.
There are believers everywhere carrying wounds so deep that they stopped speaking about them years ago.
People who survived impossible childhoods.
People who grew up under expectations they never asked for.
People who obeyed God while secretly bleeding inside.
People who inherited promises while also inheriting trauma.
Isaac was one of them.
And once you truly understand his story…
you may never read Genesis the same way again.
The first time Scripture introduces Isaac, heaven itself interrupts history.
God tells Abraham:
“Sarah your wife shall bear you a son indeed; and you shall call his name Isaac.”
The Hebrew name is:
יִצְחָק — Yitschaq
It literally means:
“He laughs.”
Not because life was funny.
But because impossible promises can make broken people laugh in disbelief.
Sarah laughed.
Abraham laughed.
Not mockery.
Shock.
Because God waited until their bodies were almost dead before revealing that His promise was still alive.
Romans 4 describes Abraham as:
“Now not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead…”
The Greek phrase Paul uses is:
νενεκρωμένον — nenekrōmenon
Meaning:
“already deadened.”
God intentionally waited until human ability died.
Because miracles shine brightest at funerals.
Some of you reading this have buried your hope already.
You stopped praying for restoration.
You stopped believing your family could heal.
You stopped believing your purpose could recover.
But Isaac’s birth was proof that God still moves after human possibility expires.
And maybe that is why the enemy attacks promised children so violently.
Because hell fears what heaven announced.
Isaac was not just a child.
He was covenant.
He was prophecy wrapped in skin.
He was living evidence that God keeps impossible promises.
But what many people overlook is this:
Isaac grew up carrying the emotional atmosphere of supernatural pressure.
Imagine being the miracle child everyone watched.
The promised son.
The answer to decades of tears.
The child your parents spoke about with trembling voices.
The one heaven mentioned by name before birth.
That kind of pressure changes people.
And then came Mount Moriah.
The moment most sermons rush through too quickly.
Genesis 22 says:
“And Isaac spake unto Abraham his father, and said, My father… behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
The Hebrew word for lamb is:
שֶׂה — seh
An innocent sacrificial animal.
Isaac knew exactly what sacrifices looked like.
He had seen blood before.
And suddenly he realized something horrifying.
There was no lamb.
Only him.
Most people imagine Isaac as a helpless little boy.
But historical Jewish scholarship and textual clues strongly suggest Isaac may have been a teenager or young adult.
Abraham was elderly.
Isaac could have resisted.
He could have run.
But Genesis never records resistance.
No screaming.
No fighting.
No rebellion.
Only surrender.
That changes everything.
Because Isaac became a living prophetic picture of Jesus Christ centuries before Calvary.
A beloved son.
Carrying wood uphill.
Submitted to the will of the father.
Willing to die.
The mountain of Moriah later became associated with Jerusalem itself.
The shadow was already forming.
The Gospel was already whispering through Genesis.
When Abraham says:
“God will provide himself a lamb…”
The Hebrew can carry the idea:
“God Himself will provide the lamb.”
And centuries later…
He did.
Jesus Christ.
יֵשׁוּעַ — Yeshua.
The Lamb of God.
The sacrifice Isaac never became.
But here is the part many believers miss.
Even though Isaac survived physically…
something inside him may never have forgotten that mountain.
Trauma leaves echoes.
Especially betrayal trauma.
Especially father wounds.
Especially moments where your life felt placed on an altar.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You survived.
But part of your heart still shakes when you remember what almost happened.
You still hear old voices.
Still replay old pain.
Still wonder why God allowed certain fires.
Isaac understood silent wounds.
And Scripture quietly reveals it.
After Genesis 22, something changes.
Sarah dies.
Abraham becomes increasingly distant in the narrative.
And Isaac appears quieter.
Almost withdrawn.
Genesis 24:63 says:
“And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide…”
The Hebrew word for meditate is fascinating:
לָשׂוּחַ — lasuach
It can imply meditation, prayer, lament, deep contemplation, even grieving communication.
Isaac was not merely relaxing.
He was carrying internal weight.
Some scholars believe he may have been mourning his mother.
Others believe he was processing the emotional aftermath of Moriah.
Maybe both.
This is the untold reality:
quiet people often carry the loudest pain.
The Bible says Rebekah saw him in the field before they met.
Not in a palace.
Not surrounded by crowds.
In solitude.
There are believers smiling publicly while privately wandering through emotional deserts.
And sometimes the holiest prayers are not shouted.
Sometimes they barely survive as whispers.
Because God still hears exhausted prayers.
Isaac eventually marries Rebekah.
And for a moment, it seems life is finally becoming peaceful.
But then another hidden wound emerges.
Infertility.
The same battle his parents endured.
Generation after generation.
Waiting.
Praying.
Crying.
The promise carrier now faces impossible delay himself.
Genesis 25:21 says:
“And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren…”
The Hebrew word translated “intreated” is:
וַיֶּעְתַּר — vaya‘tar
Meaning:
to plead earnestly,
to pray persistently,
to press deeply.
Isaac did not offer casual prayer.
He wrestled in intercession.
For twenty years.
Twenty.
Years.
Some people reading this are discouraged because heaven has not answered after six months.
Isaac waited two decades.
And still kept praying.
That kind of faith is rare now.
We live in a generation trained for instant gratification.
But covenant often grows slowly underground before it breaks through visibly.
God answered.
But even the answer carried struggle.
Rebekah conceived twins fighting within her womb.
Jacob and Esau.
Conflict before birth.
Division before identity formed.
And eventually Isaac’s family became fractured.
Favoritism.
Manipulation.
Deception.
Bitterness.
Many believers think godly families never struggle.
Genesis destroys that illusion.
The patriarchs were deeply human.
The Bible does not sanitize pain.
That is one reason Scripture feels so alive.
It tells the truth about humanity.
Isaac loved Esau.
Rebekah favored Jacob.
And division entered the home.
The enemy loves divided houses.
Because divided hearts become vulnerable hearts.
Then comes one of the saddest moments in Isaac’s life.
Genesis 27.
Jacob deceives his father.
Isaac is old.
His eyesight has faded.
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּכְהֶיןָ עֵינָיו — vatikhena ‘einav
“his eyes grew dim.”
But this story is deeper than physical blindness.
Sometimes pain clouds discernment.
Sometimes unresolved wounds distort perception.
Isaac could not see clearly anymore.
Neither physically.
Nor relationally.
And yet even in brokenness…
God’s covenant still moved.
That should encourage someone.
Because many believers secretly fear that their flaws disqualify them.
But Scripture repeatedly shows God accomplishing purposes through imperfect people.
Not because sin is acceptable.
But because grace is greater.
The Hebrew word for grace is often connected to:
חֵן — chen
Favor.
Kindness.
Unearned beauty.
God’s mercy reaches into dysfunctional places.
Into fractured homes.
Into grieving hearts.
Into exhausted minds.
Into wounded childhoods.
Into regret.
Into shame.
Into silence.
Isaac’s life proves something many people desperately need to hear:
You do not have to be loud to matter in the Kingdom of God.
Abraham was dramatic.
Jacob was intense.
Joseph was visionary.
Moses thundered.
David conquered.
Paul debated.
But Isaac?
Isaac dug wells.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Quiet obedience.
Patient endurance.
Faithfulness without applause.
Genesis 26 reveals enemies constantly stopping Isaac’s wells.
The Philistines filled them with dirt.
Imagine reopening life-giving wells only to watch people sabotage them repeatedly.
Some of you know that feeling.
Every time you start healing…
something tries to bury you again.
Every time you start rebuilding faith…
something attacks your mind again.
Every time you begin moving forward…
old pain resurfaces.
But Isaac kept digging.
That may be one of the most underrated acts of spiritual warfare in Scripture.
Not dramatic miracles.
Persistence.
Refusing to stop.
Refusing bitterness.
Refusing revenge.
Refusing surrender to despair.
Genesis 26:22 says:
“And he removed from thence, and digged another well…”
Another well.
Again.
This quiet man kept moving.
Kept rebuilding.
Kept trusting.
And eventually God made room for him.
The well was called:
רְחֹבוֹת — Rechovot
Meaning:
“broad places”
or
“room enough.”
After all the conflict, Isaac declares:
“For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.”
Somebody reading this has been fighting in cramped emotional spaces for years.
Anxiety.
Fear.
Rejection.
Spiritual exhaustion.
But God still creates Rechovot seasons.
Places where breathing returns.
Places where healing starts.
Places where peace finally enters the room.
Places where buried promises live again.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because Isaac’s story is not really about a weak forgotten man.
It is about hidden faithfulness.
The kind heaven sees even when crowds do not.
The kind of endurance that survives disappointment.
The kind of obedience that continues after trauma.
The kind of faith that quietly keeps digging wells.
The world celebrates noise.
God often honors endurance.
And maybe that is why Isaac matters so much right now.
Because there are countless believers carrying invisible burdens while still trying to trust God.
Single mothers praying quietly.
Men battling secret depression.
Young believers trying not to give up.
People attending church while internally collapsing.
Wounded Christians still worshipping through tears.
Isaac understands them.
He is proof that God still works through bruised people.
Still blesses quiet people.
Still walks with grieving people.
Still heals traumatized people.
Still uses emotionally exhausted people.
And perhaps the most powerful detail of all is this:
The covenant never left Isaac.
Not after Moriah.
Not after grief.
Not after delay.
Not after family dysfunction.
Not after deception.
Not after emotional scars.
God remained faithful.
Because covenant was never sustained by Isaac’s perfection.
It was sustained by God’s character.
That is the Gospel.
Humanity failing.
God remaining faithful.
Again.
And again.
And again.
2 Timothy 2:13 says:
“If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.”
The Greek word for faithful is:
πιστός — pistos
Trustworthy.
Reliable.
Steadfast.
God does not abandon His children when they struggle.
And ultimately Isaac’s entire life points toward Jesus Christ.
The true promised Son.
The true sacrifice.
The true Lamb.
The true covenant.
The true well of living water.
The true source of healing.
Where Isaac carried wood and survived…
Jesus carried the cross and died.
Where Isaac was spared…
Jesus was pierced.
Where Abraham said “God will provide”…
Calvary answered forever.
That is why salvation is not earned.
Because the Lamb was already provided.
Jesus Christ took the altar we deserved.
Took the judgment.
Took the nails.
Took the wrath.
So sinners could receive grace.
Forgiveness.
Adoption.
Redemption.
Eternal life.
If you have been carrying shame…
there is mercy.
If you have been carrying trauma…
there is healing.
If you have been carrying hidden exhaustion…
there is rest.
If you feel forgotten…
God still sees you.
And send this to someone silently carrying pain.
And for those hungry to go deeper:
Some wounds never made you weak.
They revealed where God kept sustaining you when you should have collapsed.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikuwentong Kwento ni Isaac
Karamihan sa mga tao, kilala lang si Isaac bilang tahimik na anak.
Ang batang muntik nang ialay ni Abraham.
Ang himalang sanggol na ipinanganak sa matandang magulang.
Ang lalaking halos natabunan ng napakalalaking kwento nina Abraham at Jacob.
Pero baka iyon mismo ang dahilan kung bakit hindi talaga siya nakikita ng marami.
Dahil ang katahimikan ay hindi kahinaan.
At ang pagiging mahinahon ay hindi nangangahulugang walang laban.
Maraming mananampalataya ngayon ang may sugat na napakalalim kaya tumigil na silang magsalita tungkol dito.
Mga taong lumaki sa pressure na hindi naman nila hiningi.
Mga taong sumunod sa Diyos habang palihim na dumudugo ang puso.
Mga taong nagmana ng pangako… pero kasama rin ang trauma.
Isaac was one of them.
At kapag naunawaan mo talaga ang kwento niya…
hindi mo na muling mababasa ang Genesis nang pareho.
Sa unang beses na ipinakilala si Isaac sa Biblia, parang huminto ang langit para magsalita.
Sinabi ng Diyos kay Abraham:
“Sarah your wife shall bear you a son indeed; and you shall call his name Isaac.”
Ang pangalan niya sa Hebrew ay:
יִצְחָק — Yitschaq
Ang ibig sabihin nito:
“Siya ay tatawa.”
Hindi dahil nakakatawa ang buhay.
Kundi dahil minsan, ang imposibleng pangako ng Diyos ay napakabigat paniwalaan kaya mapapatawa ka na lang sa gulat.
Tumawa si Sarah.
Tumawa si Abraham.
Hindi pangungutya.
Kundi pagkabigla.
Dahil hinintay ng Diyos na halos mawalan na sila ng kakayahang magkaanak bago Niya ipinakita na buhay pa rin ang Kanyang pangako.
Sa Roma 4, inilalarawan si Abraham bilang:
“Now not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead…”
Ang salitang Griyego ay:
νενεκρωμένον — nenekrōmenon
Ibig sabihin:
“parang patay na.”
Sadyang hinintay ng Diyos na mamatay muna ang kakayahan ng tao.
Dahil doon pinakamalinaw lumilitaw ang himala.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na matagal nang inilibing ang pag-asa.
Tumigil ka nang manalangin para sa pamilya mo.
Tumigil ka nang maniwalang may restoration pa.
Tumigil ka nang umasa na gagaling pa ang puso mo.
Pero ang kapanganakan ni Isaac ay patunay na gumagalaw pa rin ang Diyos kahit tapos na ang kakayahan ng tao.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit matinding inaatake ng kaaway ang mga taong may dalang pangako.
Dahil takot ang impiyerno sa inihayag ng langit.
Si Isaac ay hindi lang basta bata.
Siya ay tipan.
Siya ay propesiya na nabalot ng laman.
Siya ay buhay na patunay na tumutupad ang Diyos ng imposible.
Pero may isang bagay na hindi masyadong napapansin.
Lumaki si Isaac na pasan ang pressure ng pagiging “promised child.”
Isipin mo iyon.
Ikaw ang himalang anak.
Ikaw ang sagot sa dekadang pag-iyak ng magulang mo.
Ikaw ang batang binanggit ng Diyos bago pa ipanganak.
Ang ganoong pressure… may epekto iyon.
At pagkatapos dumating ang Mount Moriah.
Ang eksenang madalas minamadali sa mga sermon.
Sinasabi ng Genesis 22:
“And Isaac spake unto Abraham his father, and said, My father… behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “lamb” ay:
שֶׂה — seh
Isang inosenteng handog.
Biglang na-realize ni Isaac na may kulang.
Walang kordero.
Siya ang alay.
Karamihan iniisip na maliit pa si Isaac noon.
Pero maraming Jewish scholars ang naniniwalang maaaring teenager o young adult na siya.
Matanda na si Abraham.
Kayang tumakas ni Isaac.
Kayang lumaban.
Pero walang nakatalang paglaban.
Walang sigaw.
Walang pagtutol.
Puro pagsuko.
At doon nagiging napakalalim ng kwento.
Dahil si Isaac ay naging larawan ni Jesus Christ bago pa man mangyari ang Calvary.
Minamahal na anak.
May pasan na kahoy paakyat ng bundok.
Sumusunod sa kagustuhan ng Ama.
Handang mamatay.
Ang Mount Moriah ay kalaunang iniuugnay sa Jerusalem.
Parang matagal nang binubulong ng Genesis ang Ebanghelyo.
Nang sabihin ni Abraham:
“God will provide himself a lamb…”
Maaaring ipahiwatig ng Hebrew:
“Ang Diyos mismo ang magbibigay ng Kordero.”
At makalipas ang maraming siglo…
ginawa Niya.
Jesus Christ.
יֵשׁוּעַ — Yeshua.
Ang Kordero ng Diyos.
Ang handog na hindi kailanman naging si Isaac.
Pero eto ang bahagi na bihirang pag-usapan.
Kahit nabuhay si Isaac…
maaaring may bahagi sa kanya na hindi na nakaalis sa bundok na iyon.
May mga trauma na hindi basta nawawala.
Lalo na kapag galing sa taong dapat magprotekta sa’yo.
May mga taong buhay pa rin hanggang ngayon pero parang may bahagi sa puso nilang naiwan sa altar.
Ngumingiti.
Pero nanginginig pa rin kapag naaalala ang nangyari.
Nakakalakad.
Pero may sugat na hindi pa rin lubos naghihilom.
Naiintindihan iyon ni Isaac.
At tahimik itong ipinapakita ng Biblia.
Pagkatapos ng Genesis 22, parang may nagbago.
Namatay si Sarah.
Mas naging tahimik si Isaac.
Parang may lungkot na hindi niya masabi.
Genesis 24:63 says:
“And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide…”
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “meditate” ay:
לָשׂוּחַ — lasuach
Maaari itong mangahulugan ng:
pagmumuni,
panalangin,
malalim na pagdadalamhati,
o tahimik na pakikipag-usap sa Diyos.
Hindi lang nagpapahinga si Isaac.
May bigat siyang dala.
At may mga taong ganito rin ngayon.
Tahimik.
Pero pagod na pagod na sa loob.
Nagpo-post ng ngiti.
Pero umiiyak kapag mag-isa.
Uma-attend ng church.
Pero halos hindi na makahinga emotionally.
Dahil naririnig pa rin ng Diyos kahit ang halos pabulong na panalangin.
Kalaunan, pinakasalan ni Isaac si Rebekah.
At parang magiging maayos na sana ang lahat.
Pero dumating muli ang parehong laban ng kanyang mga magulang.
Infertility.
Paghihintay.
Pag-iyak.
Pagdarasal.
Genesis 25:21 says:
“And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren…”
Ang salitang Hebrew ay:
וַיֶּעְתַּר — vaya‘tar
Ibig sabihin:
malalim na pagsusumamo,
matinding panalangin,
patuloy na paghingi.
Hindi casual ang panalangin ni Isaac.
Dalawampung taon siyang naghintay.
Dalawampung taon.
At hindi siya tumigil.
May mga taong pinanghihinaan na matapos ang ilang buwan.
Si Isaac… dalawang dekada.
At nanatili pa rin.
Napakabihira na ng ganoong klase ng pananampalataya ngayon.
Gusto ng generation natin instant lahat.
Pero minsan, ang covenant ng Diyos ay tahimik munang tumutubo sa ilalim bago makita sa ibabaw.
At nang sumagot ang Diyos…
may laban pa rin.
Nagdalang-tao si Rebekah ng kambal na parang naglalaban na agad sa sinapupunan.
Jacob at Esau.
Conflict bago pa ipanganak.
At kalaunan, nagkaroon ng pagkakawatak-watak sa pamilya.
Favoritism.
Panlilinlang.
Sakit.
Manipulation.
Maraming tao ang iniisip na kapag pamilya ng Diyos, walang problema.
Pero sinisira ng Genesis ang ilusyon na iyon.
Napakahuman ng mga patriarchs.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit buhay na buhay ang Biblia.
Hindi nito tinatakpan ang sakit ng tao.
Mahal ni Isaac si Esau.
Mas paborito ni Rebekah si Jacob.
At unti-unting nabiyak ang tahanan.
Pagkatapos dumating ang isa sa pinakamalungkot na bahagi ng buhay ni Isaac.
Genesis 27.
Nilinlang siya ni Jacob.
Matanda na si Isaac.
Malabo na ang kanyang mga mata.
Sinasabi ng Hebrew:
וַתִּכְהֶיןָ עֵינָיו — vatikhena ‘einav
“lumabo ang kanyang paningin.”
Pero mas malalim pa iyon sa physical blindness.
Minsan, pinapalabo rin ng sakit ang discernment.
Minsan, kapag hindi nahilom ang sugat, nagugulo ang pagtingin natin.
At kahit ganoon…
hindi umalis ang covenant ng Diyos.
Kailangan marinig iyon ng maraming tao ngayon.
Dahil maraming believers ang lihim na natatakot na baka disqualified na sila dahil sa kahinaan nila.
Pero paulit-ulit ipinapakita ng Biblia na kumikilos pa rin ang Diyos kahit sa imperfect na tao.
Hindi dahil okay ang kasalanan.
Kundi dahil mas dakila ang biyaya.
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa grace ay:
חֵן — chen
Favor.
Kabutihan.
Hindi pinaghirapan.
Hindi deserve.
Ang awa ng Diyos umaabot hanggang sa sirang pamilya.
Sa wasak na isip.
Sa traumang dala-dala mo pa rin.
Sa tahimik na depression.
Sa hiya.
Sa guilt.
Sa pagod.
Pinapatunayan ng buhay ni Isaac ang isang bagay:
Hindi mo kailangang maging maingay para magamit ng Diyos.
Si Abraham dramatic.
Si Jacob intense.
Si David mandirigma.
Si Pablo matapang magsalita.
Pero si Isaac?
Naghukay lang siya ng balon.
Paulit-ulit.
Tahimik na faithfulness.
Tahimik na obedience.
Tahimik na endurance.
Sa Genesis 26, paulit-ulit tinatabunan ng mga Philistines ang mga balon ni Isaac.
Imagine mo iyon.
Tuwing may binubuo kang buhay…
may sumusubok ibaon ulit.
Tuwing nagsisimula kang mag-heal…
may lumang sakit na bumabalik.
Tuwing umaabante ka…
may humihila pababa.
Pero hindi tumigil si Isaac.
At baka iyon ang isa sa pinaka-underrated na spiritual warfare sa Biblia.
Hindi dramatic.
Hindi maingay.
Kundi pagpapatuloy.
Pagbangon.
Pagtitiwala pa rin.
Genesis 26:22 says:
“And he removed from thence, and digged another well…”
Isa na namang balon.
Muli.
At muli.
At muli.
Hanggang sa dumating siya sa:
רְחֹבוֹת — Rechovot
Ibig sabihin:
“maluwag na lugar”
“may sapat na espasyo.”
Matapos ang lahat ng laban, sinabi ni Isaac:
“For now the LORD hath made room for us…”
May mga taong sobrang tagal nang naiipit emotionally.
Sa anxiety.
Sa takot.
Sa rejection.
Sa spiritual exhaustion.
Pero may Rechovot pa rin ang Diyos.
May lugar pa ring ibinibigay ang Diyos para makahinga ka ulit.
Para gumaling.
Para makabangon.
Para mabuhay ulit.
Be honest.
Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
Dahil ang kwento ni Isaac ay hindi kwento ng mahinang lalaki.
Ito ay kwento ng tahimik na katapatan.
Tahimik na pagtitiis.
Tahimik na pananampalataya.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangan marinig ng generation ngayon.
Dahil maraming tao ang tahimik na lumalaban.
Mga lalaking depressed pero hindi makapagsalita.
Mga nanay na pagod na pero tuloy pa rin.
Mga kabataang gustong sumuko pero pilit pa ring kumakapit sa Diyos.
Mga believers na sugatan pero sumasamba pa rin.
Naiintindihan sila ni Isaac.
Patunay siya na ginagamit pa rin ng Diyos ang sugatan.
Pinapalakas pa rin Niya ang pagod.
At hindi Niya iniiwan ang tahimik na umiiyak.
At higit sa lahat…
ang buong buhay ni Isaac ay nagtuturo kay Jesus Christ.
Ang tunay na promised Son.
Ang tunay na Lamb.
Ang tunay na sacrifice.
Kung saan si Isaac ay nailigtas…
si Jesus ay ipinako.
Kung saan sinabi ni Abraham na “God will provide”…
sinagot iyon ng Calvary.
Iyon ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi tayo naligtas dahil mabuti tayo.
Naligtas tayo dahil may Korderong ibinigay ang Diyos.
Si Jesus ang tumanggap ng altar na para sana sa atin.
Tinanggap Niya ang parusa.
Ang pako.
Ang dugo.
Para tayo ay makatanggap ng kapatawaran.
Biyaya.
Pag-asa.
Bagong buhay.
Kung may dala kang hiya…
may awa ang Diyos.
Kung may dala kang trauma…
may healing kay Cristo.
Kung pagod ka na…
may pahinga kay Jesus.
At para sa mga gustong lalong lumalim:
Hindi lahat ng sugat ay sumira sa’yo.
Yung iba… doon mo lang nalaman na buong panahon ka palang binubuhat ng Diyos.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Dying on the Journey
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Dying on the Journey
Some deaths happen quietly.
Not because they are small.
But because heaven itself struggles to put words around the weight of what just happened.
Rachel’s death was one of those moments.
Most people remember it as a tragic Bible event tucked into a genealogy timeline. A woman dies giving birth. A husband buries her beside the road. The journey continues.
But if you slow down long enough to actually feel the scene… it becomes one of the most emotionally devastating moments in all of Scripture.
Because Rachel did not die in peace inside a home. She did not die surrounded by safety. She did not die after finally enjoying the life she suffered years to obtain.
She died on the road. Still traveling. Still unfinished. Still carrying promises she would never personally experience.
And millions of people silently understand that kind of pain.
The pain of finally reaching the season you prayed for… only to collapse emotionally while trying to hold it together.
The pain of carrying everyone else’s expectations while your own soul quietly bleeds underneath.
The pain of arriving at answered prayer while simultaneously losing strength to enjoy it.
This story is not just about Rachel.
It is about exhausted people who kept moving while dying internally.
It is about believers who smiled publicly while silently asking God why their journey became so heavy.
And hidden inside the Hebrew text is emotional depth most people never notice.
Genesis 35:16 says:
“Then they journeyed from Bethel. And when there was but a little distance to go to Ephrath, Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor.”
The Hebrew phrase for “hard labor” is:
קְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (Qeshoṯah Belidtah)
It carries the idea of severe difficulty, cruelty, intense suffering, unbearable pressure.
This was not ordinary pain.
This was overwhelming agony.
The kind of agony where breathing itself feels like warfare.
And what destroys me emotionally about this moment…
…is that Rachel had spent years crying for children.
Years.
Genesis 30:1 records her heartbreaking words to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
In Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי (Havah-li banim ve’im-ayin metah anokhi)
“Give me sons — if not, I am dying.”
Notice something terrifying.
The woman who emotionally said she would die without children… eventually dies while bringing forth a child.
Scripture is brutally honest.
Sometimes the thing we beg God for comes wrapped in pain we never anticipated.
Sometimes answered prayers arrive carrying weight we were never emotionally prepared to survive.
That does not mean God is cruel.
It means human beings often romanticize destinations while underestimating the suffering attached to purpose.
Rachel desperately wanted motherhood.
But motherhood did not remove sorrow from her life.
And if we are honest… many people today understand this exact emotional contradiction.
The marriage came. But so did loneliness.
The ministry grew. But exhaustion quietly grew with it.
The business succeeded. But anxiety followed every achievement.
The baby arrived. But postpartum darkness entered the room too.
The platform expanded. But private emptiness became unbearable.
People think blessing automatically removes struggle.
Rachel’s story destroys that illusion.
Sometimes blessings and breaking happen in the same season.
And that truth makes many believers uncomfortable.
Because we secretly thought obedience would protect us from emotional devastation.
But Scripture never promised a painless journey.
In fact, some of God’s most loved servants suffered deeply while still walking inside divine purpose.
Rachel’s death happened while Jacob’s family was moving toward destiny.
That detail matters.
Because many Christians mistakenly assume hardship means they left God’s will.
Not always.
Sometimes you are hurting precisely because you are still moving.
The text says they were close to Ephrath. Close.
The Hebrew wording implies nearness. They were almost there.
And isn’t that emotionally familiar?
Some of the deepest breakdowns happen when people are almost at the next chapter.
Right before breakthrough. Right before healing. Right before stability. Right before rest.
The enemy loves attacking exhausted people near transition.
Rachel was physically depleted. Emotionally strained. Travel-worn. And now labor contractions violently overtook her body.
Then comes one of the saddest verses in Genesis.
Genesis 35:17:
“And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.”
The Hebrew phrase:
אַל־תִּירְאִי (Al-Tira’i)
Means: “Do not fear.”
But think about this carefully.
Why would the midwife say “do not fear” unless Rachel herself was terrified?
This was not calm surrender.
This was panic.
This was a woman sensing death approaching.
A woman realizing she might not survive this moment.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully human.
Rachel is not merely a Bible character anymore.
She becomes every exhausted mother. Every emotionally overwhelmed believer. Every person who silently wondered if they could survive the pressure crushing them.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You kept showing up. Kept praying. Kept serving. Kept carrying responsibilities.
While internally thinking: “I don’t know how much more of this I can endure.”
And maybe nobody around you fully noticed.
Because wounded people often become experts at appearing functional.
Then Scripture delivers a sentence that emotionally shatters me every single time I read it.
Genesis 35:18:
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing…”
The Hebrew says:
בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ (Be-tzet nafshah)
“As her soul was going out.”
This language is deeply intimate.
The Bible does not merely say she died.
It describes her soul departing.
The Hebrew word:
נֶפֶשׁ (Nephesh)
Can mean soul, life, inner self, living being, breath, emotional essence.
Scripture slows down the moment intentionally.
As if heaven itself pauses beside this dying woman.
And during her final breaths… Rachel names the child:
בֶּן־אוֹנִי (Ben-Oni)
Meaning: “Son of my sorrow.” “Son of my affliction.” “Son of my pain.”
Can you feel the emotional gravity of that?
Her last act on earth was naming her pain.
Not hiding it. Not masking it. Not pretending strength.
She verbalized the sorrow.
And there are people reading this right now who have been carrying silent grief for years because church culture taught them to suppress emotional honesty.
But Rachel teaches us something important.
Acknowledging pain is not rebellion against God.
Pretending pain does not exist helps nobody.
Even Jesus openly wept.
In Greek, John 11:35 says:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Not performed. Not symbolically. Not emotionally detached.
He wept.
The Son of God Himself publicly entered grief.
So why do modern believers think emotional suppression equals holiness?
Rachel’s dying words expose a truth many Christians avoid:
People can deeply love God and still experience devastating emotional pain.
Then Jacob does something remarkable.
Genesis 35:18 continues:
“But his father called him Benjamin.”
In Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin)
Meaning: “Son of the right hand.” “Son of favor.” “Son of strength.”
Rachel named him from pain. Jacob renamed him through covenant identity.
This is one of the most beautiful emotional pictures of redemption in all of Scripture.
Because grief tried to define the child.
But destiny had another name.
And maybe this is where some of you need to breathe again.
Because your trauma is not your final identity.
Your depression is not your final name.
Your failure is not your final name.
Your addiction is not your final name.
Your shame is not your final name.
Your worst moment does not have authority to permanently define what God can redeem.
Jesus specializes in renaming broken stories.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham.
God repeatedly rewrites identities.
And maybe you have spent years calling yourself what pain named you.
Unwanted. Dirty. Too broken. Too late. Unlovable. Damaged. Disqualified.
But heaven speaks differently.
Isaiah 62:2 says:
“And thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.”
God renames people grace restores.
But there is still another heartbreaking layer inside Rachel’s story.
She was buried beside the road.
Genesis 35:19:
“So Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath.”
In the way.
On the journey.
Not at the destination.
And that reality hurts because many people expected life to finally become easier once they reached certain milestones.
Yet some seasons feel like endless movement without emotional arrival.
Always carrying. Always enduring. Always sacrificing. Always surviving.
Some of you are spiritually exhausted because your entire life has felt like one long road.
And maybe you secretly wonder if God still sees you there.
He does.
The Gospel is full of God meeting weary people on roads.
The Emmaus road. The Damascus road. The Jericho road.
Even Jesus carried His cross along a road toward Golgotha.
Christianity is not built around untouched people living painless lives.
It is built around a suffering Savior who entered human agony personally.
Isaiah 53:3 calls Him:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
In Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (Ish mak’ovot veyadua choli)
A man intimately familiar with suffering.
Jesus understands emotional pain from the inside.
Betrayal. Rejection. Abandonment. Grief. Exhaustion. Mockery. Loneliness.
This is why the Gospel matters so deeply.
Because Christianity is not God observing pain from a distance.
It is God entering pain Himself.
And maybe somebody reading this has been silently falling apart lately.
You still function. Still smile. Still attend church. Still answer messages. Still post online.
But deep down you are tired.
Tired of carrying invisible burdens. Tired of pretending strength. Tired of feeling emotionally stranded in the middle of your journey.
Rachel’s story reminds us that God sees exhausted travelers too.
Not just victorious people.
Not just strong people.
Not just emotionally polished believers.
He sees weary souls.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The Lord is near unto them that are of a broken heart.”
The Hebrew word for broken:
נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (Nishberei-lev)
Means shattered-hearted. Crushed internally.
God draws near to shattered people.
Not away from them.
And if you have secretly been losing emotional strength lately… hear this clearly:
You are not weak because the journey became painful.
Even faithful people bleed.
Even obedient people cry.
Even chosen people collapse emotionally sometimes.
Rachel’s death on the journey was tragic.
But it was not meaningless.
Because centuries later… another Son would arrive through another painful journey.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Rachel, Jesus willingly stepped into death so others could live.
The cross was not accidental.
It was love absorbing judgment. Grace carrying sin. Mercy entering suffering.
In Aramaic, one of Jesus’ cries from the cross was:
ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ (Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani)
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus entered the deepest human anguish imaginable.
So no broken believer could ever honestly say: “God does not understand suffering.”
He understands it completely.
And because He rose again, pain is never the final chapter for those who belong to Him.
That is the hope Rachel’s story whispers through tears.
The road is painful.
But resurrection still exists.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some people are still walking forward while quietly bleeding inside.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Nasasabi Tungkol sa Matinding Emosyonal na Sakit ni Rachel Habang Namatay sa Paglalakbay
May mga pagkamatay na tahimik.
Hindi dahil maliit ang sakit.
Kundi dahil kahit ang langit parang nahihirapang ilarawan kung gaano kabigat ang nangyari.
Isa doon ang pagkamatay ni Rachel.
Karamihan sa mga tao, nababasa lang ito bilang maikling bahagi ng kasaysayan sa Biblia. Isang babae ang namatay habang nanganganak. Inilibing siya sa tabi ng daan. Nagpatuloy ang paglalakbay.
Pero kapag pinabagal mo ang pagbabasa… kapag hinayaan mong maramdaman mo talaga ang eksena…
Biglang nagiging isa ito sa pinaka-masakit na tagpo sa buong Kasulatan.
Dahil si Rachel ay hindi namatay sa loob ng bahay. Hindi siya namatay sa ligtas na lugar. Hindi siya namatay pagkatapos niyang tuluyang ma-enjoy ang buhay na matagal niyang ipinaglaban.
Namatay siya habang nasa daan. Habang naglalakbay. Habang hindi pa tapos ang kuwento. Habang dala-dala pa rin ang mga pangakong hindi na niya personal na makikita.
At maraming tao ngayon ang tahimik na nakakarelate sa ganoong klaseng sakit.
Yung pakiramdam na finally dumating na ang ipinagdasal mo… pero ikaw mismo, unti-unti nang nauubos.
Yung pakiramdam na pinapasan mo ang expectations ng lahat habang tahimik na dumudugo ang kaluluwa mo.
Yung sakit na natanggap mo na ang blessing… pero nawawala na ang lakas mong i-enjoy ito.
Hindi lang ito kuwento tungkol kay Rachel.
Kuwento ito ng mga taong pagod na pero tuloy pa rin ang lakad.
Mga taong nakangiti sa harap ng iba habang tahimik na nagtatanong sa Diyos: “Lord… bakit parang sobrang bigat na ng journey?”
At sa orihinal na Hebrew text, may emosyonal na lalim na kadalasang hindi napapansin.
Genesis 35:16:
“Then they journeyed from Bethel. And when there was but a little distance to go to Ephrath, Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor.”
Ang Hebrew phrase para sa “hard labor” ay:
קְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (Qeshoṯah Belidtah)
Ibig sabihin nito: matinding paghihirap, malupit na sakit, halos hindi na kayaning pressure.
Hindi ito ordinaryong sakit.
Ito yung klaseng sakit na parang pati paghinga mo… laban.
At ang mas masakit dito…
…si Rachel ay matagal nang umiiyak para magkaroon ng anak.
Taon.
Genesis 30:1:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Sa Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי (Havah-li banim ve’im-ayin metah anokhi)
“Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak… kung wala, para na rin akong mamamatay.”
Napansin mo ba?
Yung babaeng nagsabing mamamatay siya kapag hindi nagkaanak…
…sa huli, namatay habang nanganganak.
Napaka-honest ng Biblia.
Minsan ang mga bagay na matagal nating ipinagdarasal… may kasamang sakit na hindi natin inaasahan.
Minsan ang answered prayer may kasamang pressure na hindi natin kayang kontrolin.
Hindi ibig sabihin nun malupit ang Diyos.
Ibig sabihin lang… madalas romanticized ang iniisip nating blessing, pero hindi natin naiintindihan ang bigat ng purpose.
Gustong-gusto ni Rachel maging ina.
Pero hindi ibig sabihin nawala lahat ng sakit sa buhay niya.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao ngayon ang nakakaramdam niyan.
Dumating nga ang marriage. Pero dumating din ang loneliness.
Lumago ang ministry. Pero kasabay nun, burnout.
Dumating ang baby. Pero kasama rin ang postpartum darkness.
Lumaki ang business. Pero lumala rin ang anxiety.
Dumami ang followers. Pero lalo ring naging empty sa loob.
Akala kasi ng marami, kapag blessed ka… wala ka nang struggle.
Sinisira ng kuwento ni Rachel ang maling paniniwalang iyon.
Minsan sabay dumarating ang blessing at breaking.
At uncomfortable iyon para sa maraming believers.
Kasi secretly… akala natin kapag sumusunod tayo sa Diyos, magiging madali na lahat.
Pero hindi kailanman nangako ang Diyos ng painless journey.
Sa katunayan, marami sa mga pinakamamahal ng Diyos sa Biblia ang dumanas ng matinding emotional pain.
At nangyari ang pagkamatay ni Rachel habang papunta sila sa destiny.
Mahalagang detalye iyon.
Kasi maraming Kristiyano iniisip na kapag nahihirapan sila, ibig sabihin wala na sila sa will ng Diyos.
Hindi palagi.
Minsan nasasaktan ka dahil nagpapatuloy ka pa rin.
Sabi ng text, malapit na sila sa Ephrath. Malapit na.
At hindi ba parang pamilyar iyon?
Minsan ang pinakamalalaking breakdown nangyayari kapag malapit ka na sa breakthrough.
Malapit na sa healing. Malapit na sa bagong chapter. Malapit na sa kapayapaan.
Mahilig umatake ang kaaway kapag pagod na pagod na ang tao.
Pagod na si Rachel. Pagod sa biyahe. Pagod sa katawan. Pagod emotionally.
Tapos biglang dumating ang matinding labor pain.
Pagkatapos, isa sa pinaka-masakit na verses sa Genesis.
Genesis 35:17:
“And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.”
Ang Hebrew phrase:
אַל־תִּירְאִי (Al-Tira’i)
Ibig sabihin: “Huwag kang matakot.”
Pero isipin mo ito.
Bakit sasabihin ng komadrona na “huwag kang matakot” kung hindi natatakot si Rachel?
Hindi ito calm surrender.
Ito ay panic.
Ito yung pakiramdam na alam mong may mali.
Yung pakiramdam na baka hindi ka na makaligtas.
At biglang nagiging sobrang human ng kuwento.
Si Rachel hindi na lang Bible character.
Nagiging representasyon siya ng bawat nanay na pagod. Bawat believer na emotionally overwhelmed. Bawat taong tahimik na nagtatanong: “Kaya ko pa ba talaga?”
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam na alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Tuloy lang sa trabaho. Tuloy lang sa ministry. Tuloy lang sa responsibilities. Tuloy lang sa pagngiti.
Pero sa loob-loob mo: “Pagod na pagod na ako.”
At baka wala talagang nakakapansin.
Kasi maraming sugatang tao… eksperto nang magmukhang okay.
Pagkatapos, dumating ang verse na talagang dumudurog sa puso.
Genesis 35:18:
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing…”
Sa Hebrew:
בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ (Be-tzet nafshah)
“Habang lumalabas ang kanyang kaluluwa.”
Napaka-intimate ng wording.
Hindi lang sinabi ng Biblia na namatay siya.
Parang pinabagal ng langit ang eksena.
Pinakita ang kaluluwa niyang unti-unting umaalis.
Ang Hebrew word na:
נֶפֶשׁ (Nephesh)
Ay maaaring ibig sabihin: kaluluwa, hininga, buhay, inner self, emotional essence.
At habang nalalapit siya sa kamatayan… pinangalanan niya ang bata:
בֶּן־אוֹנִי (Ben-Oni)
Ibig sabihin: “Anak ng aking kalungkutan.” “Anak ng aking sakit.”
Grabe iyon.
Ang huling ginawa ni Rachel sa mundo… ay pangalanan ang sakit niya.
Hindi niya itinago. Hindi niya pineke ang lakas.
At may mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na matagal nang nagtatago ng emotional pain dahil feeling nila bawal maging honest sa church.
Pero may itinuturo si Rachel.
Hindi kasalanan ang umamin na nasasaktan ka.
Maging si Jesus mismo umiyak.
John 11:35 sa Greek:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Hindi performance. Hindi drama.
Tunay na pag-iyak.
Kung ang Anak ng Diyos mismo umiyak… bakit maraming believers ang iniisip na bawal masaktan?
Ipinapakita ng kuwento ni Rachel na pwedeng mahal mo ang Diyos… at nasasaktan ka pa rin nang malalim.
Pero pagkatapos, may napakagandang ginawa si Jacob.
Genesis 35:18:
“But his father called him Benjamin.”
Sa Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין (Binyamin)
Ibig sabihin: “Anak ng kanang kamay.” “Anak ng pabor.” “Anak ng lakas.”
Pinangalanan siya ni Rachel mula sa sakit.
Pero ni-rename siya ni Jacob ayon sa covenant identity.
Napakagandang larawan nito ng redemption.
Sinubukan ng grief na pangalanan ang bata.
Pero may ibang pangalan ang destiny.
At baka may kailangang makarinig nito ngayon.
Hindi ikaw ang pangalan na ibinigay ng trauma mo.
Hindi ikaw ang addiction mo. Hindi ikaw ang shame mo. Hindi ikaw ang depression mo. Hindi ikaw ang worst mistake mo.
Marunong magbigay ng bagong pangalan ang Diyos.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham.
Paulit-ulit nire-rewrite ng Diyos ang identity ng tao.
At baka matagal mo nang tinatawag ang sarili mo base sa sakit.
“Walang kwenta.” “Madumi.” “Hindi na maaayos.” “Hindi lovable.”
Pero iba ang tawag ng langit sa’yo.
Isaiah 62:2:
“And thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.”
May bagong pangalan ang biyaya ng Diyos para sa mga taong akala nilang tapos na sila.
Pero may isa pang masakit na detalye.
Inilibing si Rachel sa tabi ng daan.
Genesis 35:19:
“So Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath.”
“In the way.”
Habang nasa journey.
Hindi pa sa destination.
At masakit iyon.
Kasi maraming tao ang umaasang gagaan ang buhay kapag narating na nila ang next chapter.
Pero minsan parang tuloy-tuloy lang ang laban.
Laging may pasan. Laging may pressure. Laging may pagod.
At baka may mga taong nagbabasa nito na emotionally exhausted na.
Pakiramdam mo buong buhay mo… puro biyahe.
At baka iniisip mo: “Lord… nakikita Mo pa ba ako?”
Oo.
Buong Gospel puno ng Diyos na sumasalubong sa pagod na tao habang nasa daan.
The Emmaus road. The Damascus road. The Jericho road.
Maging si Jesus dinala ang krus habang naglalakad papuntang Golgotha.
Ang Christianity hindi tungkol sa mga taong hindi nasasaktan.
Ito ay tungkol sa Tagapagligtas na piniling pasukin mismo ang sakit ng tao.
Isaiah 53:3:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
Sa Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (Ish mak’ovot veyadua choli)
Isang taong lubos na pamilyar sa paghihirap.
Alam ni Jesus ang betrayal. Alam Niya ang rejection. Alam Niya ang loneliness. Alam Niya ang exhaustion.
Kaya napakahalaga ng Gospel.
Dahil hindi lang minamasdan ng Diyos ang pain mo mula sa malayo.
Pinasok Niya ito mismo.
At baka may taong tahimik nang bumabagsak emotionally.
Nagagawa mo pa rin ang routine. Nakakangiti ka pa rin. Nakakapag-post ka pa rin. Nakakapag-serve ka pa rin.
Pero sa totoo lang… pagod ka na.
Pagod nang magpanggap. Pagod nang magdala ng invisible burdens. Pagod nang maging “strong” para sa lahat.
Ipinapaalala ng kuwento ni Rachel: Nakikita ng Diyos ang mga pagod na tao.
Hindi lang ang successful. Hindi lang ang mukhang okay.
Nakikita Niya ang mga basag ang puso.
Psalm 34:18:
“The Lord is near unto them that are of a broken heart.”
Ang Hebrew word:
נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (Nishberei-lev)
Ibig sabihin: basag, durog, crushed internally.
Lumalapit ang Diyos sa mga sugatang tao.
Hindi Siya lumalayo.
At kung pakiramdam mo lately nauubos ka na emotionally… pakinggan mo ito:
Hindi ka mahina dahil nahirapan ka.
Maging ang mga tapat na tao umiiyak. Maging ang mga obedient na tao napapagod. Maging ang mga chosen na tao minsang bumabagsak emotionally.
Tragic ang pagkamatay ni Rachel.
Pero hindi ito meaningless.
Dahil pagkalipas ng maraming taon… may isa pang Anak na darating sa pamamagitan ng isang masakit ding journey.
Si Jesucristo.
At hindi tulad ni Rachel, kusang pinasok ni Jesus ang kamatayan para mabuhay ang iba.
Ang krus ay hindi aksidente.
Pag-ibig itong sumalo ng hatol. Biyayang sumalo ng kasalanan. Awa na pumasok sa paghihirap.
Sa Aramaic, isa sa mga sigaw ni Jesus sa krus:
ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ (Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani)
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Pinasok ni Jesus ang pinakamalalim na anguish ng tao.
Kaya walang sugatang believer ang makakapagsabing: “Hindi naiintindihan ng Diyos ang sakit ko.”
Naiintindihan Niya.
At dahil Siya ay nabuhay muli… hindi pain ang final chapter ng mga kay Cristo.
Iyon ang bulong ng pag-asa sa kuwento ni Rachel.
Masakit ang daan.
Pero totoo pa rin ang resurrection.
Maging honest. Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
May mga taong tuloy pa ring naglalakad habang tahimik na dumudugo sa loob.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Jairus Had to Watch Jesus Stop for Someone Else First
paragraphs: Why Jairus Had to Watch Jesus Stop for Someone Else First
The crowd would not stop pressing.

Dust climbed into the air beneath hundreds of feet. Bodies shoved shoulder against shoulder. Desperation breathed heavily through the streets that day because whenever Jesus walked into a city, suffering followed Him.
Blind eyes searched for Him.
Broken bodies crawled toward Him.
Demons screamed when He came near.
And somewhere inside that chaos was a father trying not to collapse.
Not a fisherman. Not a beggar. Not an outcast.
A ruler.
A synagogue leader.
A respected man.
But pain has a way of stripping titles off people.
Because when your child is dying, reputation suddenly feels worthless.
His name was Jairus.
In Greek, the name appears as Ἰάειρος (Iaeiros), derived from the Hebrew יָאִיר (Ya'ir), meaning “he enlightens” or “God gives light.”
But that day, everything around Jairus probably felt dark.
Mark 5:22 says:
“Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing Him, he fell at His feet.”
The Greek phrase used here is:
πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ (piptei pros tous podas autou)
Literally: “he falls toward His feet.”
Not bows politely. Not greets respectfully.
Falls.
A collapsing father.
A man whose world was breaking in real time.
His little girl was dying.
Mark records her age carefully:
“She was twelve years of age.” (Mark 5:42)
Twelve.
Old enough to laugh loudly. Old enough to recognize her father’s footsteps. Old enough to still reach for his hand when afraid.
And Jairus watches her slipping away.
You can almost hear the panic in his voice when he begs Jesus:
“My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay Your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” (Mark 5:23)
The Greek word Jairus uses for “little daughter” is:
θυγάτριον (thygatrion)
It is intensely affectionate. A tender diminutive. Like saying: “My precious little girl.”
This was not theology to him.
This was survival.
And then Jesus says yes.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine Jairus feeling hope return for the first time in days.
Jesus is coming.
The miracle worker is walking toward his house.
His daughter might live.
But then something unbearable happens.
Jesus stops.
Not because of Jairus.
Because of someone else.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal for almost everyone who has followed God long enough.
Because many believers know exactly what it feels like to watch Jesus stop for someone else while your own prayer still feels unanswered.
You prayed first.
You begged first.
You were desperate first.
But somehow heaven seems to pause for another person while your crisis keeps bleeding.
And if we are honest, this part of the story hurts.
Because Jairus had to stand there and watch Jesus give attention to someone whose suffering interrupted his own emergency.
Mark says:
“And a great crowd followed Him and thronged about Him.” (Mark 5:24)
Then suddenly, hidden inside that crowd, was a woman.
Unnamed.
Bleeding.
Forgotten.
Mark 5:25 says she had suffered for twelve years.
The same amount of time Jairus had his daughter.
One father had twelve years of laughter with a child.
One woman had twelve years of isolation with pain.
Two completely different stories.
One Savior walking between both of them.
The woman suffered from what Scripture calls a “flow of blood.”
In Greek:
ῥύσει αἵματος (rhysei haimatos)
A continual hemorrhage. Constant bleeding.
According to Levitical law in Leviticus 15, her condition made her ceremonially unclean.
That means for twelve years:
People avoided her. People feared contamination from her. People likely withdrew physical affection from her.
No normal touch. No normal relationships. No normal life.
Imagine surviving twelve years without being embraced.
Some people reading this understand that kind of loneliness more than they want to admit.
She spent everything trying to get healed.
Mark says:
“She had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.” (Mark 5:26)
The Greek phrase for “suffered much” is brutal:
πολλὰ παθοῦσα (polla pathousa)
“Having endured many pains.”
Not only from disease.
From failed hope.
That kind of suffering exhausts the soul.
Then she hears Jesus is near.
And suddenly faith rises inside her.
Mark 5:28:
“For she said, ‘If I touch even His garments, I will be made well.’”
The Greek says:
ἐὰν ἅψωμαι κἂν τῶν ἱματίων αὐτοῦ σωθήσομαι (ean hapsōmai kan tōn himatiōn autou sōthēsomai)
Literally: “If I may touch even His clothes, I shall be saved/healed.”
The word σωθήσομαι (sōthēsomai) comes from σώζω (sōzō).
It means: Saved. Rescued. Delivered. Made whole.
She was not merely seeking symptom relief.
She wanted her life back.
So she reaches.
One touch.
And immediately the bleeding stops.
Immediately.
No delay. No process. No gradual recovery.
Instant healing.
And right there is where Jairus probably starts struggling internally.
Because Jesus stopped walking.
Toward his daughter.
Can you imagine the tension?
Every second matters.
Every delay feels dangerous.
And now Jesus turns around asking:
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples are confused.
The crowd is crushing Him from every direction.
Everyone is touching Him.
But Jesus is not talking about accidental contact.
He is talking about intentional faith.
Then the woman comes forward trembling.
Mark says she told Him “the whole truth.”
The Greek:
πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν (pasan tēn alētheian)
Everything.
All of it.
The shame. The pain. The loneliness. The failed treatments. The fear.
And Jesus listens.
He does not rush her.
Meanwhile Jairus is watching the clock on his daughter’s life disappear.
And then the nightmare happens.
Mark 5:35:
“While He was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, ‘Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?’”
Imagine hearing that sentence.
Your daughter is dead.
Too late.
And perhaps this is where many people secretly wrestle with God.
Because sometimes it feels like heaven delayed until the situation died.
The marriage died.
The dream died.
The opportunity died.
The relationship died.
The hope died.
And maybe what hurts even more is watching God move for other people while your own miracle seems buried.
Other people get healed.
Other people get breakthroughs.
Other people get restoration.
And you sit there wondering:
“Jesus… why did You stop?”
But then Jesus says something powerful to Jairus.
“Do not fear, only believe.” (Mark 5:36)
In Greek:
μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε (mē phobou, monon pisteue)
“Stop being afraid. Keep believing.”
The grammar matters.
Jesus was not merely commanding one moment of faith.
He was calling Jairus into continuing trust while everything looked irreversible.
That is harder.
Anyone can believe before the funeral.
Believing after the bad news arrives is different.
Jesus then enters the house.
People are already weeping.
Professional mourners had likely arrived.
The atmosphere is final.
Death has already written its conclusion.
But Jesus says:
“The child is not dead but sleeping.”
And they laugh at Him.
The Greek word used implies mockery.
Not nervous laughter. Cruel dismissal.
Because the world often mocks what Jesus is about to resurrect.
Then Jesus walks into the room.
Only Peter, James, John, and the parents remain.
And then one of the most beautiful moments in Scripture happens.
Mark preserves the original Aramaic words Jesus spoke.
“Talitha koum.”
ταλιθα κουμ
Mark even translates it for us:
“Little girl, I say to you, arise.” (Mark 5:41)
But the depth of this moment is astonishing.
“Talitha” was a tender word.
Not merely “girl.”
It could carry the warmth of saying: “Little lamb.” “Sweet child.”
“Koum” means: “Rise.” “Get up.”
The Creator of life stands over death itself and speaks gently.
No panic. No struggle. No uncertainty.
And immediately she rises.
Immediately.
The delay was never denial.
Jesus was not late.
He was revealing something Jairus could not have understood earlier.
If Jesus had arrived before her death, Jairus would have only known Jesus as healer.
But because Jesus delayed, Jairus discovered Jesus as resurrection.
Some of the hardest delays in life are actually revealing dimensions of Christ we would never encounter otherwise.
Many people want God to hurry.
But sometimes Jesus permits the situation to cross human impossibility because resurrection glory looks different than ordinary intervention.
Lazarus experienced this too.
In John 11:6, after hearing Lazarus was sick, Jesus intentionally stayed two more days.
He delayed on purpose.
And when He finally arrived, Martha said:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”
That sentence still lives in many hearts today.
“If You had moved sooner…”
“If You had answered faster…”
“If You had stopped this earlier…”
But Jesus operates with eternal vision while humans see only immediate pain.
Isaiah 55:8-9 says:
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the Lord.”
The Hebrew for “thoughts” is:
מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי (machshevotai)
It refers to intentions, plans, purposes.
God sees dimensions we cannot.
And that truth becomes painfully difficult when waiting collides with grief.
But the Gospel repeatedly shows something astonishing:
Jesus is never intimidated by what humans call impossible.
Dead daughters. Dead dreams. Dead hearts. Dead futures.
Nothing is beyond resurrection when Christ enters the room.
And perhaps someone reading this feels exactly like Jairus.
You begged.
You prayed.
You believed.
Then Jesus seemed to stop for somebody else.
Maybe you watched another person get the marriage restored. Another person get healed. Another person get blessed. Another person get the open door.
Meanwhile your own situation got worse.
And quietly, secretly, your heart started asking:
“Did Jesus forget me?”
But Jairus’ story says otherwise.
The delay was not abandonment.
The silence was not absence.
The interruption was not rejection.
Jesus was still walking toward his house the entire time.
That matters.
Even when heaven feels silent, Christ may still be moving toward you.
And there is another layer hidden inside this story that many miss.
Jairus had status.
The woman had shame.
Jairus was honored publicly.
The woman suffered privately.
Yet Jesus loved both fully.
The Gospel destroys human ranking systems.
Jesus stopped for the hidden woman while still caring for the influential father.
He is not limited by human urgency.
He can carry compassion for both at once.
And maybe that is part of what Jairus needed to learn.
Miracles are not competitions.
Someone else’s breakthrough is not proof God abandoned you.
Another person’s healing is not evidence that heaven skipped your name.
Jesus stopping for her did not mean He stopped loving Jairus.
Read that again.
Because envy quietly poisons many believers.
Social media intensifies it.
People celebrate testimonies while others suffer silently behind screens.
And sometimes wounded hearts ask:
“Why them first?”
But the Kingdom of God is not running out of mercy.
Jesus did not have to choose between the bleeding woman and Jairus’ daughter.
He was enough for both.
And He still is.
Romans 8:28 says:
“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good.”
Not all things are good.
Death is not good. Pain is not good. Grief is not good.
But God is able to work through even devastating moments toward eternal redemption.
The cross itself proves this.
The disciples thought everything was over.
Jesus was beaten. Mocked. Crucified. Buried.
For three days heaven looked silent.
But resurrection was already coming.
Christianity is built on the reality that God brings life out of what humans bury.
That is why believers still have hope.
Not because suffering is imaginary.
But because Christ defeated death itself.
The Greek word for resurrection is:
ἀνάστασις (anastasis)
Literally: “A standing up again.”
The Gospel is a resurrection story from beginning to end.
And maybe some people reading this need to hear something difficult but healing:
Jesus stopping for someone else first does not mean your story is over.
Sometimes heaven’s delay is preparing a deeper revelation of who Christ truly is.
Not merely healer.
Resurrection.
Not merely provider.
Savior.
Not merely comforter.
King.
The same Jesus who spoke “Talitha koum” over a dead child still speaks life today.
Not every earthly story ends the way people hope.
Scripture never promises a pain-free life.
But it does promise that those who belong to Christ are held by One stronger than death itself.
1 Corinthians 15:55 declares:
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”
And because of Jesus, death is no longer the final sentence for those who trust Him.
That changes everything.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment your faith has been exhausted.
Maybe you have been smiling publicly while grieving privately.
Maybe you have watched Jesus bless others while your own heart quietly breaks.
Do not assume silence means abandonment.
Jairus probably thought the story was over too.
Until Jesus walked into the room.
And maybe that is the line your soul needed today.
Jesus still walks into impossible rooms.
Be honest.
This story hits differently when you have already experienced disappointment.
And never forget this:
Sometimes Jesus lets the situation die because resurrection reveals His glory more deeply than rescue ever could.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Kailangang Panoorin ni Jairus si Jesus na Huminto Para sa Ibang Tao Muna
Maingay ang paligid.
Nagtutulakan ang mga tao.
Makapal ang alikabok sa daan habang pilit sinusundan ng karamihan si Jesus. May mga umiiyak. May mga sumisigaw. May mga umaasang makahawak man lang sa Kanya kahit sandali.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon, may isang ama na unti-unti nang nadudurog.
Hindi siya mahirap.
Hindi siya palaboy.
Hindi siya ordinaryong tao.
Isa siyang pinuno ng sinagoga.
May pangalan. May respeto. May posisyon.
Pero may isang bagay na kayang durugin kahit ang pinakamataas na tao.
Kapag ang anak mo na ang mamamatay.
Ang pangalan niya ay Jairus.
Sa Griyego:
Ἰάειρος (Iaeiros)
Mula ito sa Hebreong:
יָאִיר (Ya'ir)
Na ang ibig sabihin ay:
“God gives light.” “O ang Diyos ang nagbibigay ng liwanag.”
Pero sa araw na iyon, parang wala nang liwanag sa buhay niya.
Sinasabi ng Marcos 5:22:
“Dumating ang isa sa mga pinuno ng sinagoga, na ang pangalan ay Jairus; at pagkakita niya kay Jesus, siya ay nagpatirapa sa paanan nito.”
Sa orihinal na Griyego:
πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ (piptei pros tous podas autou)
Literal: “Bumagsak siya sa paanan Niya.”
Hindi simpleng yumuko.
Hindi pormal na pagbati.
Bumagsak.
Dahil minsan, ang sakit kayang iluhod kahit ang pinakamalakas.
Ang anak niyang babae ay mamamatay na.
At pansinin kung paano ito sinabi ni Jairus.
“My little daughter…”
Sa Griyego:
θυγάτριον (thygatrion)
Hindi lang basta “anak.”
May lambing. May lalim.
Parang:
“Aking munting anak.” “Aking mahal na bata.”
Maraming ama ang hindi umiiyak sa harap ng tao.
Pero sa araw na iyon, wala nang pride si Jairus.
Kailangan niya si Jesus.
At himalang-himala… pumayag si Jesus.
Naglakad Siya papunta sa bahay nila.
Isipin mo ang pag-asa na bumalik kay Jairus.
Baka iniisip niya:
“Makakaabot pa kami.”
“Hindi pa huli.”
“Bubuhayin ni Jesus ang anak ko.”
Pero pagkatapos… huminto si Jesus.
Hindi para kay Jairus.
Para sa ibang tao.
At dito nagiging sobrang personal ang kwentong ito.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ang nakaka-relate dito nang sobra.
Yung pakiramdam na:
Ikaw ang unang nagdasal. Ikaw ang desperado. Ikaw ang umiiyak gabi-gabi.
Pero parang ibang tao muna ang pinapansin ng Diyos.
Habang ikaw… naghihintay.
Masakit iyon.
At hindi natin kailangang magpanggap na hindi.
Habang naglalakad si Jesus kasama si Jairus, may isang babae sa gitna ng maraming tao.
Walang pangalan.
Walang posisyon.
Walang nakakapansin.
Labindalawang taon siyang dinudugo.
At nakakamangha ang detalye.
Ang anak ni Jairus ay labindalawang taong gulang.
Labindalawang taon ding naghihirap ang babae.
Habang si Jairus ay may labindalawang taon ng masasayang alaala kasama ang anak niya…
Ang babaeng ito naman ay may labindalawang taon ng sakit.
Ayon sa Kautusan sa Levitico 15, marumi siyang itinuturing dahil sa kondisyon niya.
Ibig sabihin:
Marahil matagal na siyang hindi nayayakap.
Hindi hinahawakan.
Iniiwasan.
Maraming taong buhay pero matagal nang walang nakakaramdam ng pagmamahal.
Baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na ganoon din ang pakiramdam.
Humingi siya ng tulong sa maraming manggagamot.
Ginastos niya lahat.
Pero lalo lang siyang lumala.
Marcos 5:26:
“She had suffered much…”
Sa Griyego:
πολλὰ παθοῦσα (polla pathousa)
“Maraming tiniis na sakit.”
Hindi lang sakit sa katawan.
Sakit ng paulit-ulit na pagkabigo.
Sakit ng pag-asang paulit-ulit na namamatay.
Pero nang marinig niyang dumadaan si Jesus, may nabuhay sa puso niya.
Pananampalataya.
Sinabi niya:
“Kahit mahawakan ko lang ang Kanyang damit, gagaling ako.”
Sa Griyego:
ἐὰν ἅψωμαι κἂν τῶν ἱματίων αὐτοῦ σωθήσομαι (ean hapsōmai kan tōn himatiōn autou sōthēsomai)
Ang salitang:
σωθήσομαι (sōthēsomai)
Ay hindi lang “gagaling.”
Ito rin ay:
“maliligtas.” “maibabalik.” “maibubuo muli.”
Hindi lang katawan niya ang sugatan.
Buong pagkatao niya.
Kaya lumapit siya.
Humawak.
At agad siyang gumaling.
Agad.
Walang delay.
Walang proseso.
At dito siguro nagsimulang mabiyak ang puso ni Jairus.
Kasi huminto si Jesus.
Habang ang anak niya… naghihingalo.
Isipin mo ang kaba.
Bawat segundo mahalaga.
Pero si Jesus nakikinig sa kwento ng ibang tao.
At minsan ganiyan din ang pakiramdam natin.
Parang:
“Lord… pwede bang ako naman muna?”
Habang nagsasalita pa si Jesus sa babae, may dumating.
At sinabi nila kay Jairus:
“Patay na ang anak mo.”
Iyon na siguro ang pinakamasakit na pangungusap na narinig niya sa buong buhay niya.
Patay na.
Tapos na.
Huli na.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na may sarili ring “patay na” sa puso.
Patay na relasyon.
Patay na pangarap.
Patay na pag-asa.
Patay na pananampalataya.
At minsan ang pinakamahirap tanggapin ay ito:
Habang ikaw nasasaktan… parang may ibang pinagpapala ang Diyos.
Pero pagkatapos sabihin iyon kay Jairus, may sinabi si Jesus na sobrang lalim.
“Do not fear, only believe.”
Sa Griyego:
μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε (mē phobou, monon pisteue)
Literal: “Tigilan mong matakot. Magpatuloy kang maniwala.”
Hindi sinabi ni Jesus:
“Maniwala ka sandali.”
Kundi:
“Patuloy kang maniwala.”
Mas mahirap iyon.
Madaling maniwala bago dumating ang masamang balita.
Pero paano kapag mukhang tapos na talaga?
Paano kapag parang wala nang pag-asa?
Pagdating nila sa bahay, umiiyak na ang lahat.
Nagluluksa na.
Final na para sa kanila ang lahat.
Pero sinabi ni Jesus:
“Hindi patay ang bata. Natutulog lang.”
At tinawanan Siya.
Ganiyan madalas ang mundo.
Tinatawanan nila ang mga bagay na bubuhayin ng Diyos.
Pagkatapos, pumasok si Jesus sa silid.
Kasama lang Niya sina Pedro, Santiago, Juan, at ang mga magulang.
At pagkatapos… sinabi Niya ang isa sa pinakamagandang linya sa buong Biblia.
“Talitha koum.”
Sa Aramaic:
ܛܠܝܬܐ ܩܘܡ
O sa transliteration:
Talitha koum.
Na ang ibig sabihin:
“Munting babae, bumangon ka.”
Ang “Talitha” ay may lambing.
Parang:
“Munting anak.” “Munting kordero.”
Hindi galit si Jesus.
Hindi Siya nagpanic.
Ang Maylikha ng buhay ay nagsalita lang.
At bumangon ang bata.
Agad.
At dito natin naiintindihan ang isang napakalalim na bagay.
Kung dumating si Jesus bago mamatay ang bata, makikilala lang sana Siya ni Jairus bilang manggagamot.
Pero dahil na-delay… nakilala niya si Jesus bilang muling pagkabuhay.
Minsan ang dahilan kung bakit hinahayaan ng Diyos na lumampas sa impossible ang sitwasyon… ay dahil may mas malalim Siyang gustong ipakita tungkol sa Kanyang sarili.
Hindi lang Siya healer.
Siya ang Resurrection.
Hindi lang Siya comforter.
Siya ang Hari kahit sa ibabaw ng kamatayan.
Maraming tao ang galit sa delay ng Diyos.
Pero ang delay ay hindi laging rejection.
Minsan preparation ito para sa mas dakilang kapahayagan.
Tingnan mo si Lazarus.
Na-delay din si Jesus.
At sinabi ni Marta:
“Lord, kung nandito Ka sana, hindi sana namatay ang kapatid ko.”
Ang daming tao ang may ganyang dasal.
“Lord, kung gumalaw Ka lang sana agad…”
“Lord, kung sinagot Mo lang sana ako noon…”
Pero ang nakikita natin ay kasalukuyang sakit.
Ang nakikita ng Diyos ay eternal na layunin.
Sabi sa Isaias 55:8:
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts…”
Sa Hebreo:
מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי (machshevotai)
Mga plano. Layunin. Intensyon.
May nakikita ang Diyos na hindi natin nakikita.
At minsan… sobrang hirap noon.
Pero paulit-ulit itong pinapakita ng Ebanghelyo:
Hindi natatakot si Jesus sa impossible.
Patay na pangarap. Patay na relasyon. Patay na puso. Patay na pananampalataya.
Kayang buhayin ng Diyos ang akala nating tapos na.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na parang si Jairus.
Pagod ka na.
Nagdasal ka na.
Umiyak ka na.
Pero parang iba muna ang pinagpapala.
At tahimik mong tinatanong:
“Lord… nakalimutan Mo na ba ako?”
Pero hindi iyon ang kwento ni Jairus.
Hindi siya iniwan ni Jesus.
Huminto lang sandali.
Pero tuloy pa rin Siyang naglalakad papunta sa bahay nila.
Napakalalim noon.
Kahit tahimik ang langit… maaaring papunta pa rin si Jesus sa sitwasyon mo.
At may isa pang bagay dito na madalas hindi napapansin.
Si Jairus may pangalan.
Ang babae wala.
Si Jairus respetado.
Ang babae itinago.
Pero pareho silang mahal ni Jesus.
Ganito ang Ebanghelyo.
Walang favoritism si Cristo.
Hindi porket pinagpala ang iba ay ibig sabihin nakalimutan ka na.
Hindi competition ang himala.
Hindi nauubusan ng awa ang Diyos.
Kayang hawakan ni Jesus ang sugat ng babae habang papunta pa rin Siya sa bahay ni Jairus.
At kaya rin Niyang hawakan ang sitwasyon mo ngayon.
Romans 8:28:
“All things work together for good…”
Hindi ibig sabihin lahat ay mabuti.
Hindi mabuti ang sakit.
Hindi mabuti ang kamatayan.
Hindi mabuti ang betrayal.
Pero kayang gamitin ng Diyos kahit ang pinakamasakit na bagay para sa mas dakilang redemption.
Kahit ang krus mukhang pagkatalo noon.
Pero doon dumating ang kaligtasan.
Tatlong araw tahimik ang langit.
Pero parating na pala ang resurrection.
Iyan ang pundasyon ng Kristiyanismo.
Hindi na ang kamatayan ang huling salita.
Dahil si Cristo ay nabuhay.
At baka ito mismo ang kailangan mong marinig ngayon:
Hindi porket huminto si Jesus para sa ibang tao ay tapos na ang kwento mo.
Hindi pa Siya tapos.
Baka papunta pa lang Siya sa silid ng impossible sa buhay mo.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malalim tamaan ng kwentong ito ang mga taong nasaktan na talaga.
At huwag mong kakalimutan ito:
Minsan hinahayaan ni Jesus na mamatay ang sitwasyon dahil ang resurrection ay magpapakita ng Kanyang kaluwalhatian nang mas malalim kaysa ordinaryong rescue.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Amos Said He Was “Not a Prophet”
paragraphs: Why Amos Said He Was “Not a Prophet”
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost dangerous.
Not because they are unclear.
But because they are too clear.
Too exposing.
Too personal.
Amos gives us one of those moments.

A shepherd from the south walks into a corrupt nation burning with religious activity, national pride, wealth, music, offerings, feasts, and public worship… and then says something that shocks everyone listening:
“I was no prophet.”
Not “I am no prophet.”
“I was no prophet.”
The Hebrew is brutally direct.
לֹא־נָבִיא אָנֹכִי
Lo-navi anokhi.
“I am not a prophet.”
And then he adds:
