“And for me, that utterance may be given to me, that I may open my mouth boldly to make known the mystery of the gospel.”
The Greek word for boldly is:
παρρησία (parrēsia)
It means fearless confidence. Courageous speech. Unashamed proclamation.
Even Paul needed prayer for courage.
Think about that.
The man who survived prison, beatings, persecution, shipwrecks, and riots still asked believers to pray for boldness.
Your pastor does not just need applause after sermons.
He needs intercession before sermons.

Pray for his purity. Pray for his mind. Pray for his marriage. Pray for his children. Pray for protection from temptation. Pray against discouragement. Pray that he never compromises truth to gain approval.
There are sermons your pastor will only survive because somebody prayed.
The second area is encouragement.
Not fake hype. Not shallow compliments.
Real encouragement. Biblical encouragement.
Many pastors spend their lives pouring strength into others while receiving very little in return.
And words matter more than people realize.
Proverbs 12:25 says:
“Anxiety in the heart of man causes depression, but a good word makes it glad.”
The Hebrew phrase for “good word” comes from:
דָּבָר טוֹב (dāḇār ṭôḇ)
It means a beneficial word. A healing word. A restorative word.
Never underestimate what one sincere message can do.
“Pastor, that sermon helped save my marriage.” “Pastor, thank you for preaching truth even when it’s hard.” “Pastor, your prayers helped me survive this season.”
Sometimes one honest testimony gives a weary shepherd enough strength to keep going another month.
Do not only speak when you disagree. Speak when God uses him.
The third area is service.
Some churches exhaust pastors because nobody volunteers unless they receive attention.
But the Kingdom of God advances through servants.
Galatians 5:13 says:
“Through love serve one another.”
The Greek word for “serve” is:
δουλεύετε (douleuete)
It literally means:
“To become a servant.” “To willingly place yourself in service.”
Modern culture glorifies being noticed.
Jesus glorified washing feet.
There are pastors trying to preach, counsel, administrate, clean, organize, fix problems, disciple people, handle conflict, visit hospitals, and lead ministries simultaneously.
Not because they want control.
But because too few believers step forward.
Some of the holiest ministry in your church may never happen on a stage.
Holding a crying child in nursery. Cleaning after service. Helping elderly members. Welcoming visitors. Setting up chairs. Preparing meals. Driving someone to church. Answering messages.
Heaven notices hidden faithfulness.
Jesus said in Mark 10:45:
“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.”
The King of Glory became a servant.
And somehow modern Christianity still struggles with humility.
The fourth area is protecting unity.
One of the greatest hidden pains pastors endure is church division.
Gossip destroys churches faster than persecution.
Satan does not always attack churches through atheists.
Sometimes he attacks through bitterness, offense, pride, jealousy, and careless words inside the congregation.
Proverbs 16:28 says:
“A whisperer separates close friends.”
The Hebrew idea behind whispering carries the image of secret slander. Quiet division. Poison spread slowly.
Some believers destroy spiritual families with their mouths while still singing worship songs on Sunday.
And pastors often stand in the middle trying to stop spiritual bleeding.
If you want to help your pastor...
Refuse gossip. Refuse division. Refuse unnecessary drama.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men.”
Peace is not weakness.
Biblical unity is spiritual warfare.
A united church becomes dangerous to hell.
The fifth area is generosity.
This topic makes some people uncomfortable.
But Scripture speaks clearly.
A faithful church supports faithful ministry.
1 Timothy 5:17 says:
“Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and doctrine.”
The phrase “labor” comes from the Greek:
κοπιῶντες (kopiōntes)
It means exhausting toil. Working to the point of weariness.
Biblical ministry is labor.
Deep labor. Emotional labor. Spiritual labor. Mental labor.
And many pastors quietly carry financial stress while trying to care for others.
Generosity is not about worshiping money.
It is about removing unnecessary burdens so ministry can flourish.
Some believers spend more money monthly on entertainment than they ever invest into the Kingdom of God.
Yet the local church is where souls are discipled. Marriages restored. Children taught Scripture. Broken people introduced to Jesus Christ.
Healthy giving is not manipulation.
It is worship.
The sixth area is simply standing beside your pastor during difficult seasons.
Because one of the loneliest moments in ministry is discovering people only loved the pastor when life was easy.
When criticism rises... When attacks come... When misunderstandings spread... When exhaustion shows...
Some people disappear.
But faithful believers stay.
Aaron and Hur understood this principle long before the modern church existed.
In Exodus 17, while Israel fought Amalek, Moses became physically exhausted holding up his hands.
As long as his hands stayed raised, Israel prevailed.
When his strength failed, Aaron and Hur stood beside him and held his arms up.
The Hebrew imagery here is powerful.
This was not passive support.
This was covenant strengthening.
And many pastors today are spiritually standing on hills with trembling arms.
Not because they do not love God.
But because ministry is heavy.
Some pastors are smiling publicly while privately asking God for strength not to quit.
Imagine how many shepherds would survive if more believers became modern-day Aarons and Hurs.
Not worshiping pastors. Not idolizing leaders.
But strengthening faithful servants of God.
Because even shepherds need support.
And maybe while reading this...
You suddenly realized your pastor has been carrying far more than you knew.
Maybe God is exposing areas where you became spiritually passive.
Maybe you attended church faithfully while forgetting the people sacrificing to help feed your soul.
The early church understood shared responsibility.
Acts 2 describes believers carrying burdens together, serving together, praying together, giving together, suffering together.
Church was never designed to be a weekly religious performance.
It was family.
Real family.
And families carry one another.
Your pastor does not need perfection from you.
But faithful partnership can become oxygen to a weary shepherd.
One prayer. One encouraging message. One act of service. One defense against gossip. One generous act. One loyal stand during hardship.
These things matter more than you think.
Because pastors are human.
They feel disappointment. They battle exhaustion. They experience grief. They fight temptation. They endure criticism. They carry invisible burdens.
Yet every Sunday many still stand up and preach Jesus Christ anyway.
That kind of faithfulness should never be taken lightly.
And if God has blessed your church with a pastor who truly preaches biblical truth... Protect that gift. Pray for that gift. Strengthen that gift.
Because biblically faithful shepherds are becoming increasingly rare in this generation.
1 Thessalonians 5:12–13 says:
“Recognize those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and esteem them very highly in love for their work’s sake.”
This does not mean pastors are above correction.
It means faithful spiritual leadership should not be treated casually.
One day many believers may realize too late how deeply their pastors fought to protect them spiritually.
And maybe tonight...
Somebody reading this suddenly feels convicted.
Not condemned.
Convicted.
Because the Holy Spirit is reminding you that church is not a place you consume.
It is a Body you help strengthen.
Some pastors silently read these testimonies and find strength to keep going.
Save this so you never forget the responsibility believers have toward those who watch over souls.
One exhausted shepherd strengthened by faithful believers can impact generations for the Kingdom of God.
Filipino Version:
6 Na Paraan Kung Paano Mo Matutulungan ang Iyong Pastor sa Simbahan
May mga laban ang pastor mo na malamang hindi mo kailanman makikita.
Hindi dahil magaling siyang magtago.
Kundi dahil maraming pastol ang tahimik na dumudugo.
Nakikita ng mga tao ang sermon. Naririnig nila ang panalangin. Napapansin nila ang ngiti. Humahanga sila sa karunungan.
Pero hindi nila nakikita ang bigat.

Hindi nila nakikita ang mga gabing walang tulog dahil may miyembrong gustong sumuko sa buhay. Hindi nila nakikita ang tahimik na pag-iyak matapos mag-counsel ng wasak na pamilya. Hindi nila nakikita ang spiritual warfare matapos mangaral ng katotohanan. Hindi nila nakikita ang pagod ng isang lalaking pasan ang mga kaluluwa habang unti-unti namang nauubos ang sarili niyang lakas.
At minsan...
Ang pinakamasakit na parte...
May mga pastor na napapalibutan ng maraming tao tuwing Linggo... pero pakiramdam nila mag-isa sila.
Naunawaan ito ni Apostol Pablo.
Sa 2 Corinthians 11:28 sinabi niya:
“Bukod pa sa ibang mga bagay, araw-araw ay nasa akin ang pagmamalasakit sa lahat ng mga iglesia.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “pagmamalasakit” ay:
ἡ μέριμνα (hē merimna)
Ibig sabihin nito:
matinding bigat, pressure, inner burden, malalim na pag-aalala.
Hindi simpleng stress lang ang tinutukoy ni Pablo.
Ang tinutukoy niya ay ang mabigat na responsibilidad ng pag-aalaga ng mga kaluluwa.
Kaya maling isipin na ang pastor ay parang makina lang na hindi napapagod.
Ang pastor ay hindi lang preacher.
Isa siyang taong may pananagutang espiritwal sa harap ng Diyos.
Sinasabi sa Hebrews 13:17:
“Sila’y nagpupuyat dahil sa inyong mga kaluluwa.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “nagpupuyat” ay:
ἀγρυπνοῦσιν (agrypnousin)
Literal itong nangangahulugang:
“manatiling gising,” “mawalan ng tulog,” “maging alerto espiritwal.”
Napakalalim niyan.
Ibig sabihin may mga pastor na nawawalan ng tulog dahil iniisip nila ang kalagayan ng mga tao sa simbahan.
Pero nakakalungkot...
Maraming believers ang lalapit lang sa pastor kapag may kailangan sila.
Kaunti lang ang nagtatanong:
“Pastor, paano po namin kayo matutulungan?”
Kailangan muling matutunan ng simbahan ang tunay na biblical partnership.
Hindi celebrity Christianity. Hindi consumer Christianity. Hindi entertainment church.
Kundi burden-sharing. Pagdadamayan. Pagmamahalan. Pananagutang espiritwal.
Dahil ang healthy na simbahan ay hindi itinayo ng isang pagod na pastor.
Itinayo ito ng mga mananampalatayang nauunawaan na ang ministry ay responsibilidad ng buong katawan ni Cristo.
Sa Ephesians 4:11–12:
“Upang ihanda ang mga banal sa gawain ng paglilingkod.”
Napakahalaga niyan.
Ang pastor ang naghahanda. Ang mga mananampalataya ang gumagawa ng ministry.
Hindi kailanman plano ng Diyos na isang tao lang ang bubuhat ng lahat habang ang iba ay nanonood lang.
At baka...
Baka may mga pastor ngayon na gusto nang sumuko hindi dahil iniwan sila ng Diyos...
Kundi dahil masyadong maraming believers ang nakalimot sa kanilang responsibilidad.
Kung may pastor ka na tapat na nangangaral ng Biblia... na pinoprotektahan ang katotohanan... na nananalangin para sa mga tao... na dinadala ang mga kaluluwa kay Jesus...
Mas pinagpala ka kaysa sa naiisip mo.
Kaya paano mo siya matutulungan?
Hindi sa puro papuri lang. Hindi sa fake loyalty. Hindi sa pagpapakitang-tao.
Kundi sa mga paraang itinuturo mismo ng Kasulatan.
Ang unang paraan ay panalangin.
Masyadong minamaliit ng maraming tao ang spiritual warfare laban sa mga pastor.
Kapag tapat na ipinapangaral ng isang pastor ang Ebanghelyo, nagiging target siya.
Ina-atake ang kanyang isip. Ang kanyang asawa. Ang kanyang mga anak. Ang kanyang purity. Ang kanyang emotional strength.
Kaya paulit-ulit humihingi si Pablo ng panalangin.
Sa Ephesians 6:19:
“Ipanalangin ninyo na ako’y pagkalooban ng pananalitang may katapangan.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “katapangan” ay:
παρρησία (parrēsia)
Ibig sabihin:
fearless confidence, walang takot na pangangaral, matapang na pagsasalita ng katotohanan.
Isipin mo iyon.
Kahit si Pablo nangailangan ng panalangin.
Hindi kailangan ng pastor mo ng palakpak lang pagkatapos ng sermon.
Kailangan niya ng mga taong mananalangin bago pa siya tumayo sa pulpito.
Ipanalangin mo ang kanyang isip. Ang kanyang pamilya. Ang kanyang holiness. Ang kanyang courage. Ang kanyang spiritual protection.
May mga sermon na nasusurvive lang ng pastor dahil may mga taong nananalangin.
Ang pangalawang paraan ay encouragement.
Hindi fake compliments. Hindi plastic.
Tunay na encouragement.
Maraming pastor ang buong buhay nagbibigay lakas sa iba habang tahimik namang nauubos.
At minsan isang mensahe lang ang kailangan nila para hindi sumuko.
Sinasabi sa Proverbs 12:25:
“Ang mabuting salita ay nagpapasaya ng puso.”
Ang Hebrew phrase dito ay:
דָּבָר טוֹב (dāḇār ṭôḇ)
Ibig sabihin:
healing word, restorative word, beneficial word.
Huwag mong maliitin ang simpleng:
“Pastor, salamat po sa sermon.” “Pastor, nakatulong po iyon sa pamilya namin.” “Pastor, salamat po dahil hindi ninyo kinokompromiso ang katotohanan.”
Minsan sapat na iyon para lumaban ulit ang isang pagod na pastor.
Ang pangatlong paraan ay paglilingkod.
May mga simbahan na sobrang napapagod ang pastor dahil walang gustong tumulong maliban kung mapapansin sila.
Pero ang Kaharian ng Diyos ay itinatayo ng mga lingkod.
Galatians 5:13:
“Sa pamamagitan ng pag-ibig ay maglingkuran kayo.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “maglingkuran” ay:
δουλεύετε (douleuete)
Literal na ibig sabihin:
“maging alipin sa paglilingkod,” “kusang maglingkod.”
Ang mundo gustong mapansin.
Si Jesus naghugas ng paa.
May mga pastor na nangangaral na nga... nagco-counsel pa... nag-aasikaso pa ng problema... nagvi-visit pa sa ospital... naglilinis pa... nag-aadjust pa ng sound system...
Hindi dahil gusto nila kontrolin lahat.
Kundi dahil kakaunti ang gustong tumulong.
Hindi lahat ng ministry nasa stage.
Minsan ang pinaka-holy na ministry ay:
pag-aalaga ng bata, pag-aayos ng upuan, pag-welcome ng bisita, paglilinis, pagdadala ng pagkain, pagtulong sa matatanda.
Nakikita ng langit ang mga bagay na hindi pinapansin ng tao.
Ang pang-apat na paraan ay protektahan ang unity.
Isa sa pinakamasakit na dinadala ng maraming pastor ay church division.
Mas maraming simbahan ang sinisira ng tsismis kaysa persecution.
Hindi laging sa labas nanggagaling ang atake ni Satanas.
Minsan nanggagaling ito sa bitterness, selos, pride, offense, at walang kontrol na dila.
Sinasabi sa Proverbs 16:28:
“Ang mapanirang tao ay naghihiwalay ng magkakaibigan.”
Ang larawan sa Hebrew nito ay tahimik na lason.
Whispering. Secret division. Slow destruction.
May mga taong sumisira ng spiritual family gamit ang bibig nila habang umaawit pa rin tuwing Linggo.
Kung gusto mong tulungan ang pastor mo...
Tumanggi kang makisali sa gossip. Tumanggi kang maghasik ng division. Tumanggi kang magpalala ng drama.
Ang united na simbahan ay napakadelikado para sa impyerno.
Ang pang-limang paraan ay generosity.
Alam kong uncomfortable ito para sa iba.
Pero malinaw ang Biblia.
Ang tapat na ministry ay dapat suportahan.
Sa 1 Timothy 5:17:
“Ang mga matandang namumuno nang mabuti ay karapat-dapat sa dobleng karangalan.”
Ang salitang “nagpapagal” ay mula sa Greek na:
κοπιῶντες (kopiōntes)
Ibig sabihin:
working to exhaustion, pagpapagal hanggang mapagod.
Mabigat ang tunay na ministry.
Emotional labor. Spiritual labor. Mental labor.
At maraming pastor ang tahimik na may financial burden habang iniintindi ang problema ng iba.
Ang generosity ay hindi tungkol sa pagsamba sa pera.
Ito ay tungkol sa pagtulong upang mas maging malaya ang ministry.
Napakaraming tao ang kayang gumastos para sa luho pero halos walang investment sa Kaharian ng Diyos.
Samantalang ang simbahan ang lugar kung saan:
naliligtas ang mga kaluluwa, naibabalik ang pamilya, natuturuan ang mga anak, at nakikilala si Jesus.
Ang pang-anim na paraan ay manatili sa tabi ng pastor sa mahihirap na panahon.
Dahil isa sa pinakamalungkot na bahagi ng ministry ay kapag nalaman mong mahal ka lang ng tao kapag maayos ang lahat.
Kapag may criticism... Kapag may attacks... Kapag may misunderstanding... Kapag pagod na ang pastor...
May mga taong biglang nawawala.
Pero ang tunay na faithful believers nananatili.
Sa Exodus 17, habang nakikipaglaban ang Israel, napagod si Moises sa pagtataas ng kanyang kamay.
Habang nakataas ang kamay niya, nananalo ang Israel.
Pero nanghina siya.
Kaya lumapit sina Aaron at Hur at inalalayan ang kanyang mga braso.
Napakagandang larawan nito.
Hindi nila sinamba si Moises.
Tinulungan nila siya.
At maraming pastor ngayon ang parang si Moises.
Pagod. Nanginginig. Lumalaban.
Hindi dahil kulang ang pagmamahal nila sa Diyos.
Kundi dahil mabigat ang ministry.
May mga pastor na nakangiti sa harap ng congregation habang tahimik na humihingi ng lakas sa Diyos para hindi sumuko.
Isipin mo kung gaano karaming shepherds ang mananatiling matatag kung mas maraming believers ang magiging modern-day Aaron at Hur.
Hindi idolizing pastors.
Kundi strengthening faithful servants.
Dahil kahit ang shepherd minsan kailangang alalayan.
At baka habang binabasa mo ito...
Pinapakita ng Diyos na naging passive ka sa ministry.
Baka faithful kang umaattend ng church... pero nakalimutan mong may mga taong nagsasakripisyo para maalagaan ang kaluluwa mo.
Ang simbahan ay hindi weekly religious show.
Pamilya ito.
At ang tunay na pamilya nagtutulungan.
Hindi kailangan ng pastor mo ng perfection.
Pero ang simpleng:
isang panalangin, isang encouragement, isang act of service, isang pagtatanggol laban sa gossip, isang faithful presence,
ay kayang magbigay ng bagong lakas sa isang pagod na shepherd.
Dahil tao rin ang mga pastor.
Nasasaktan sila. Napapagod. Nadidiscourage. Natutukso. Umiiyak.
Pero tumatayo pa rin sila tuwing Linggo para ipangaral si Cristo.
At hindi dapat basta-basta iyon.
Kung pinagpala ka ng Diyos ng pastor na tapat sa Biblia...
Ipanalangin mo siya. Protektahan mo siya. Tulungan mo siya. Pahalagahan mo siya.
Dahil unti-unting nagiging bihira ang mga tapat na shepherds sa panahon ngayon.
At baka ngayong gabi...
May tinatamaan ang Diyos sa puso mo.
Hindi condemnation.
Conviction.
Dahil pinapaalala ng Holy Spirit na ang simbahan ay hindi lugar na kino-consume mo lang.
Ito ay Katawan na dapat mong tulungang palakasin.
Minsan ang simpleng testimonya sa comments nagbibigay lakas sa mga pastor na gusto nang sumuko.
Minsan isang pastor lang na pinalakas ng tapat na believers ang ginagamit ng Diyos para baguhin ang buong henerasyon.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Ahimaaz Wanted to Run Even Without Good News
paragraphs: Why Ahimaaz Wanted to Run Even Without Good News
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully human.
Not polished. Not heroic. Not victorious.
Just painfully… human.
One of those moments lives inside 2 Samuel 18.
A battlefield still wet with blood. A father waiting at the gate. A kingdom fractured by betrayal. A son hanging dead beneath a tree. And in the middle of all of it…
A man named Ahimaaz desperately begging for permission to run.
But there was one problem.
He had no good news.
And somehow, that sounds exactly like many believers today.
Running fast. Posting constantly. Speaking loudly. Moving publicly. Being seen. Being noticed. Being active. Being involved.
Yet carrying no real message from God.
This story is deeper than most people realize. Because Ahimaaz was not evil. He was not rebellious. He was not wicked.
He simply wanted the platform before he carried the burden.
And that danger still exists today.
The Story Most People Read Too Quickly
The context of this moment is devastating.
Absalom, David’s son, had rebelled against his own father. He stole the hearts of Israel. He attempted to overthrow the kingdom. Civil war erupted.
David loved his son deeply despite Absalom’s betrayal.
Before the battle even began, David gave one emotional command:
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom.”
(2 Samuel 18:5)
But Absalom died anyway.
Joab ignored David’s heart.
The rebellion was crushed. But the victory felt like a funeral.
Then came the question:
Who will carry the news to the king?
Joab chose a Cushite messenger.
But Ahimaaz suddenly interrupted the moment.
Scripture says:
“Then said Ahimaaz the son of Zadok, Let me now run, and bear the king tidings, how that the LORD hath avenged him of his enemies.”
— 2 Samuel 18:19
The Hebrew wording is deeply revealing.
The phrase “bear tidings” comes from the Hebrew root בָּשַׂר (basar).
This word means:
• to announce news • to proclaim glad tidings • to bring a message of victory • to declare good news
This same root eventually becomes connected to the concept of gospel proclamation.
But here is the tragedy.
Ahimaaz wanted to carry “good news” in a moment where the king would not experience it as good news.
Because heaven’s victory can still feel devastating to a wounded heart.
Joab understood something Ahimaaz did not.
This was not a moment for excitement.
This was a moment requiring emotional weight.
Joab answered:
“Thou shalt not bear tidings this day…”
— 2 Samuel 18:20
In Hebrew:
לֹא־אִישׁ בְּשֹׂרָה אַתָּה הַיּוֹם
Transliteration: Lo ish besorah attah hayom.
Literal sense:
“You are not a man of news today.”
That line hits hard.
Because some people are called to speak in one season but not another.
Not every messenger is prepared for every assignment.
Sometimes zeal outruns maturity.
Sometimes passion outruns wisdom.
Sometimes ambition outruns discernment.
And sometimes people want to run because being seen feels more rewarding than carrying truth.
Ahimaaz Was Fast… But Empty
What happens next is one of the most overlooked warnings in the Bible.
Ahimaaz keeps insisting.
He begs to run.
Again. And again.
Finally Joab says:
“Run.”
And Ahimaaz outruns the Cushite.
He arrives first.
Imagine the scene.
David is trembling between hope and dread.
The watchman sees someone running.
Then another.
The king says:
“If he be alone, there is tidings in his mouth.”
(2 Samuel 18:25)
The anticipation builds.
Ahimaaz finally arrives.
And what does he say?
“All is well.”
But it was not well.
Not for David.
Not emotionally. Not spiritually. Not relationally.
Then David asks the question that mattered most:
“Is the young man Absalom safe?”
(2 Samuel 18:29)
And suddenly Ahimaaz collapses under the weight of the assignment he begged to carry.
He answers:
“When Joab sent the king’s servant, and me thy servant, I saw a great tumult, but I knew not what it was.”
This is astonishing.
He ran passionately. He arrived first. He looked impressive. He sounded confident.
But when the moment demanded truth…
He had nothing.
That should terrify every preacher. Every content creator. Every ministry leader. Every influencer. Every believer chasing visibility.
Because speed is not the same thing as substance.
Being first is not the same thing as being faithful.
Having an audience is not the same thing as carrying revelation.
Many people today are spiritually sprinting with empty hands.
And deep down… they know it.
The Difference Between Ahimaaz and the Cushite
The Cushite was slower.
Less celebrated. Less emotionally driven. Less eager for recognition.
But he carried the actual message.
He delivered the painful truth faithfully.
Sometimes the Kingdom is advanced more by faithful obedience than visible charisma.
The modern world rewards Ahimaaz.
Fast. Visible. Energetic. Impressive.
But heaven still values truth carriers.
The Greek language of the New Testament later captures this beautifully.
The word for gospel is:
εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion)
Meaning:
“good news” “glad tidings” “a message worth announcing”
But biblical good news was never about making people feel temporarily inspired.
It was about truth.
Even costly truth.
Even convicting truth.
Even truth that pierced hearts before healing them.
Paul told Timothy:
“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.”
— 2 Timothy 4:2
The Greek phrase “preach the word” is:
κήρυξον τὸν λόγον
(Kēruxon ton logon)
“Kēruxon” comes from κηρύσσω (kēryssō).
It means:
• to herald publicly • to proclaim with authority • to announce as an official messenger
A herald did not invent the message.
He carried the king’s message accurately.
That is the difference.
Ahimaaz wanted the run. The Cushite carried the burden.
One wanted movement. The other carried truth.
And modern Christianity is filled with people addicted to movement.
Posting. Talking. Uploading. Streaming. Performing. Reacting. Chasing relevance.
But God is still asking:
“Who actually carries My message?”
The Hidden Sin Nobody Talks About
Ahimaaz reveals something uncomfortable about the human heart.
Sometimes people want proximity to spiritual importance more than surrender to spiritual responsibility.
They want to feel involved.
They want visibility.
They want significance.
But they have not yet developed the weight required to carry truth through emotionally difficult moments.
That is why some believers disappear the moment ministry becomes painful.
The moment truth costs relationships. The moment obedience becomes lonely. The moment following Jesus stops feeling exciting.
Jesus never called people to perform spirituality.
He called them to die.
The Greek word for disciple is μαθητής (mathētēs).
Meaning:
• learner • follower • disciplined student
Not celebrity. Not personality. Not platform builder.
Follower.
Modern culture says:
“Build your audience.”
Jesus says:
“Carry your cross.”
Those are not the same mission.
And maybe this article hurts because some people recognize themselves in Ahimaaz.
Still running. Still exhausted. Still striving. Still posting. Still trying to prove they matter.
Yet secretly empty.
Secretly afraid that if someone finally asks the deeper question…
There will be no answer.
This Is Why Intimacy With God Matters More Than Visibility
The danger of public Christianity without private surrender is catastrophic.
Because eventually every runner reaches a moment where the king asks:
“What is the real condition?”
And charisma cannot answer that.
Only truth can.
Only intimacy can.
Only genuine relationship with God can sustain the weight of real ministry.
In John 15, Jesus said:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches.”
The Greek word for “abide” used repeatedly in this chapter is μένω (menō).
Meaning:
• remain • dwell • stay connected • continue intimately
Fruit does not come from frantic movement.
It comes from remaining connected to Christ.
Many believers are burning out because they are running faster than they are abiding.
Faster than they are praying. Faster than they are repenting. Faster than they are healing. Faster than they are listening.
And eventually the soul collapses under spiritual emptiness.
This article is not attacking passionate people.
Passion matters.
But passion without truth becomes noise.
Passion without surrender becomes performance.
Passion without intimacy becomes exhaustion.
God Is More Concerned About Faithfulness Than Visibility
One of the saddest realities in modern Christianity is how deeply people crave recognition.
Even spiritually.
Especially spiritually.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that God often works most deeply in hidden places.
David was hidden in fields. Moses was hidden in Midian. Elijah was hidden by the brook. John the Baptist lived in wilderness. Jesus spent thirty hidden years before three years of ministry.
Hiddenness is not punishment.
Sometimes it is preparation.
Ahimaaz wanted acceleration.
But spiritual weight takes time.
The Hebrew concept of glory helps explain this.
The Hebrew word כָּבוֹד (kavod) literally carries the idea of:
• heaviness • weight • substance • honor with gravity
Real spiritual authority carries weight.
Not theatrics. Not hype. Not performance.
Weight.
And weight is developed in hidden obedience.
Not public excitement.
Some of you reading this are frustrated because your life feels unseen.
You feel forgotten. Delayed. Overlooked.
But maybe God is protecting you from running ahead of your maturity.
Maybe heaven loves you too much to hand you a microphone before your character can survive it.
Maybe the silence is mercy.
Maybe the delay is protection.
Maybe God would rather develop depth inside you than speed around you.
And honestly…
That realization changes everything.
The Gospel Is Not About Looking Alive While Dying Inside
One reason this story hits so deeply is because many people know what it feels like to look spiritually active while internally exhausted.
Smiling publicly. Breaking privately.
Quoting Scripture publicly. Questioning everything privately.
Serving publicly. Bleeding privately.
But Jesus did not come merely to create religious runners.
He came to resurrect dead hearts.
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is transformation.
The Greek word μετανοέω (metanoeō), translated “repent,” means:
• to change the mind • to turn inwardly • to undergo spiritual transformation
Real Christianity is not cosmetic.
It is crucifixion followed by resurrection.
And maybe some people reading this are tired.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
Tired of pretending. Tired of performing. Tired of running. Tired of looking okay.
This is your reminder:
Jesus never asked you to impress Him.
He asked you to follow Him.
And there is mercy even for exhausted runners.
Peter failed publicly. Thomas doubted openly. Jonah ran away. David collapsed morally.
Yet grace still pursued them.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose empty people.
He restores them.
And maybe that is why this story lingers.
Because deep down, many people know what it feels like to outrun their own soul.
To move externally while dying internally.
To crave purpose while lacking peace.
To chase calling while neglecting communion with God.
But Jesus still stands calling weary people back to Himself.
Not into performance.
Into relationship.
Into truth.
Into surrender.
Into rest.
Maybe You Needed This More Than You Realize
Maybe this article exposed something hidden.
Maybe you have been running because slowing down would force you to confront what is actually happening inside your heart.
Maybe you have been terrified that if you stop moving… the pain will finally catch up.
But healing cannot happen in nonstop noise.
Sometimes God allows exhaustion because exhaustion finally breaks self-reliance.
Sometimes the collapse becomes the doorway to honesty.
And honesty is where healing begins.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if this reminded you of someone silently carrying spiritual exhaustion, share this with them.
Some people are smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
They need this reminder.
Some people are not exhausted because they have done too little.
They are exhausted because they have been running without carrying what only intimacy with Jesus can provide.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Gustong Tumakbo ni Ahimaaz Kahit Wala Siyang Magandang Balita
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na sobrang tao.
Hindi perpekto. Hindi makintab. Hindi parang pelikulang laging panalo.
Kundi sugatan. Mabigat. At totoo.
Isa sa mga tagpong iyon ay nasa 2 Samuel 18.
Isang digmaan na amoy dugo pa. Isang amang naghihintay sa tarangkahan. Isang kahariang nabiyak dahil sa pagtataksil. Isang anak na nakabitin nang patay sa puno.
At sa gitna ng lahat…
May isang lalaking desperadong gustong tumakbo.
Ang pangalan niya ay Ahimaaz.
Pero may problema.
Wala siyang magandang balita.
At kung tutuusin…
Maraming Kristiyano ngayon ang kamukha niya.
Laging gumagalaw. Laging may post. Laging may opinyon. Laging visible. Laging active. Laging gustong mapansin.
Pero walang tunay na dala mula sa presensya ng Diyos.
Mas malalim ang kuwentong ito kaysa sa inaakala ng karamihan.
Hindi masamang tao si Ahimaaz. Hindi siya rebelde. Hindi siya traydor.
Gusto lang niyang tumakbo bago niya talaga madala ang bigat ng mensahe.
At hanggang ngayon… nangyayari pa rin iyon.
Maraming gustong maging visible bago maging broken. Maraming gustong mangaral bago matutong sumunod. Maraming gustong mag-minister pero ayaw munang magpahubog.
At iyan ang delikado.
Ang Konteksto na Masyadong Minamadali ng Marami
Si Absalom, anak ni David, ay naghimagsik laban sa sarili niyang ama.
Inagaw niya ang puso ng Israel. Sinubukan niyang kunin ang trono. At sumabog ang digmaang sibil.
Pero kahit ganoon… mahal pa rin siya ni David.
Bago magsimula ang laban, sinabi ni David:
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom.”
(2 Samuel 18:5)
Pero namatay pa rin si Absalom.
Nanalo ang hukbo. Pero para kay David… parang wala ring panalo.
Pagkatapos ng digmaan, kailangang may magdala ng balita.
Pinili ni Joab ang Cushite messenger.
Pero biglang sumingit si Ahimaaz.
Sabi ng Kasulatan:
“Then said Ahimaaz the son of Zadok, Let me now run, and bear the king tidings…”
— 2 Samuel 18:19
Ang salitang “bear tidings” ay mula sa Hebrew na:
בָּשַׂר (basar)
Na ang ibig sabihin ay:
• magdala ng balita • magpahayag ng good news • mag-anunsyo ng tagumpay
Ito rin ang ugat ng konsepto ng “gospel” o mabuting balita.
Pero narito ang masakit.
Para kay Ahimaaz, magandang balita iyon.
Pero para kay David?
Patay ang anak niya.
Minsan kahit may panalo… masakit pa rin.
Naiintindihan iyon ni Joab.
Hindi ito oras para maging excited.
Ito ay oras na nangangailangan ng bigat.
Kaya sinabi niya:
“Thou shalt not bear tidings this day…”
Sa Hebrew:
לֹא־אִישׁ בְּשֹׂרָה אַתָּה הַיּוֹם
Lo ish besorah attah hayom.
Literal:
“Hindi ikaw ang taong dapat magdala ng balita ngayong araw.”
Napakalalim niyan.
Dahil hindi lahat ng masigasig ay handa.
Minsan nauuna ang excitement kaysa maturity. Minsan nauuna ang passion kaysa wisdom. Minsan nauuna ang ambition kaysa tunay na calling.
At minsan… gusto lang ng tao na mapansin.
Mabilis si Ahimaaz… Pero Walang Dalang Totoong Mensahe
Hindi tumigil si Ahimaaz.
Paulit-ulit siyang nagpilit.
Hanggang sa sinabi ni Joab:
“Sige. Tumakbo ka.”
At inunahan nga niya ang Cushite.
Siya ang unang dumating.
Isipin mo ang eksena.
Naghihintay si David. Kinakabahan. Umaasa. Natatakot.
Pagdating ni Ahimaaz, sinabi niya:
“All is well.”
Pero hindi naman talaga.
Hindi okay si David. Hindi okay ang puso niya. Hindi okay ang pamilya niya.
Pagkatapos tinanong ni David ang pinakamahalagang tanong:
“Ligtas ba si Absalom?”
At doon bumigay si Ahimaaz.
Hindi niya masagot.
Bigla niyang sinabi na hindi niya alam.
Napakasakit niyan.
Tumakbo siya. Mukhang confident. Mukhang passionate. Mukhang ready.
Pero nang kailangan na ng totoong sagot…
Wala siyang maibigay.
At kung tutuusin…
Maraming tao ngayon ang ganiyan.
Maingay online. Visible sa ministry. Active sa church. Laging may sinasabi.
Pero kapag tinanong mo:
“Kumusta talaga ang kaluluwa mo?”
Tahimik.
Dahil ang bilis ay hindi kapalit ng lalim.
Ang pagiging visible ay hindi kapalit ng intimacy kay God.
At ang audience ay hindi awtomatikong katumbas ng anointing.
Ang Kaibahan ni Ahimaaz at ng Cushite
Mas mabagal ang Cushite. Hindi siya flashy. Hindi siya dramatic.
Pero dala niya ang totoong mensahe.
Minsan mas ginagamit ng Diyos ang faithful kaysa famous.
Pero ang problema ngayon…
Mas gusto ng mundo ang mabilis.
Mas gusto ang viral. Mas gusto ang trending. Mas gusto ang performance.
Pero sa langit…
Truth still matters.
Sa Greek, ang salitang “gospel” ay:
εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion)
Ibig sabihin:
“mabuting balita.”
Pero ang tunay na mabuting balita ay hindi simpleng motivational speech.
Ito ay katotohanan.
Kahit minsan masakit. Kahit minsan nakaka-convict. Kahit minsan umiiyak ka habang naririnig mo.
Hindi tinawag ng Diyos ang mga tao para mag-perform.
Tinawag Niya silang mamatay sa sarili.
Ang salitang disciple sa Greek ay:
μαθητής (mathētēs)
Ibig sabihin:
• estudyante • tagasunod • disiplinadong learner
Hindi celebrity. Hindi influencer. Hindi performer.
Follower.
Sinasabi ng mundo:
“Build your platform.”
Sinasabi ni Jesus:
“Pasanin mo ang krus mo.”
Magkaibang landas iyon.
At baka kaya masakit itong basahin…
Dahil may mga nakakakita ng sarili nila kay Ahimaaz.
Pagod na. Pero tuloy pa rin sa takbo.
Visible. Pero empty.
Active. Pero disconnected kay God.
Bakit Mas Mahalaga ang Intimacy Kaysa Visibility
Darating ang punto na tatanungin ka rin ng Hari:
“Ano talaga ang kondisyon?”
At hindi sasagot diyan ang charisma.
Hindi sasagot diyan ang galing magsalita.
Tanging intimacy lang kay Jesus.
Sa John 15, paulit-ulit sinabi ni Jesus:
“Abide in Me.”
Ang Greek word na “abide” ay:
μένω (menō)
Ibig sabihin:
• manatili • manahan • manatiling konektado
Ang bunga ay hindi nanggagaling sa sobrang pagtakbo.
Nanggagaling ito sa pananatili kay Cristo.
Maraming believers ngayon ang burned out.
Hindi dahil kulang sila sa activity.
Kundi dahil mas mabilis silang tumatakbo kaysa manalangin. Mas mabilis mag-post kaysa makinig sa Diyos. Mas mabilis magsalita kaysa magsisi.
At eventually… bumabagsak ang kaluluwa.
Ang Diyos ay Mas Concerned sa Faithfulness Kaysa Fame
Napakaraming gustong mapansin.
Kahit spiritually.
Pero paulit-ulit sa Biblia:
Ginagamit ng Diyos ang mga taong hinubog sa lihim.
Si David nasa pastulan. Si Moises nasa disyerto. Si Elijah nasa brook. Si John the Baptist nasa wilderness.
Maging si Jesus…
Thirty years hidden.
Bago three years public ministry.
Hindi parusa ang hidden season.
Minsan preparation iyon.
Ang Hebrew word na:
כָּבוֹד (kavod)
na madalas isalin bilang “glory,” ay may idea ng:
• bigat • substance • spiritual weight
Ang tunay na authority may bigat.
Hindi puro hype. Hindi puro ingay. Hindi puro aesthetics.
At ang bigat na iyon…
nabubuo sa secret place.
Hindi sa clout.
Baka Kaya Ka Pinapabagal ng Diyos
May mga nagbabasa nito ngayon na feeling left behind.
Pakiramdam mo delayed ka. Hindi napapansin. Hindi ginagamit.
Pero baka proteksyon iyon.
Baka mahal ka ng Diyos para hayaang mauna ang platform kaysa character.
Baka ang katahimikan ay mercy.
Baka ang delay ay paghahanda.
Dahil kapag binigyan ka ng microphone nang hindi pa handa ang puso mo…
maaari kang masira.
At minsan ang pinakamalaking biyaya ay hindi acceleration.
Kundi formation.
Hindi Dumating si Jesus Para Magmukha Ka Lang Buhay
Maraming tao ang mukhang spiritually alive sa labas.
Pero patay na patay na sa loob.
Ngumingiti publicly. Umiiyak privately.
Nagpo-post ng verse. Pero gabi-gabing wasak.
Pero hindi dumating si Jesus para gumawa lang ng religious performers.
Dumating Siya para bumuhay ng patay na puso.
Ang salitang “repent” sa Greek ay:
μετανοέω (metanoeō)
Ibig sabihin:
• pagbabago ng isip • pagbabago ng direksyon • inward transformation
Ang Christianity ay hindi simpleng behavior modification.
Ito ay death and resurrection.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na sobrang pagod na.
Hindi physically.
Spiritually.
Pagod nang magpanggap. Pagod nang maging “okay.” Pagod nang tumakbo.
Ito ang paalala mo:
Hindi ka hinihingan ni Jesus ng performance.
Hinihingan ka Niya ng surrender.
At may awa pa rin para sa mga pagod na runner.
Hindi Tapos ang Diyos sa Iyo
Si Pedro bumagsak. Si Tomas nagduda. Si Jonas tumakbo. Si David nagkasala.
Pero hinabol pa rin sila ng biyaya ng Diyos.
Iyan ang Gospel.
Hindi lang tayo ine-expose ni Jesus.
Nire-restore Niya tayo.
At baka kaya tumama ito nang ganito kalalim…
Dahil alam mo ang pakiramdam ng tumatakbo habang ubos na ubos na sa loob.
At baka ngayon…
Tinatawag ka ni Jesus pabalik.
Hindi sa performance.
Kundi sa relationship.
Sa katotohanan. Sa pahinga. Sa Kanya.
Maging totoo ka.
Tinamaan ka nito, hindi ba?
May mga taong ngumiting okay sa labas habang unti-unti nang bumabagsak sa loob.
Kailangan nilang marinig ito.
May mga taong hindi pagod dahil kulang ang ginagawa nila.
Pagod sila dahil tumatakbo silang walang dalang kayang punuin lang ng presensya ni Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Mordecai Refused to Bow to Haman
paragraphs: Why Mordecai Refused to Bow to Haman
The room went silent the moment he refused.
Hundreds of knees bent.
One man stayed standing.
Not because he was arrogant. Not because he was rebellious. Not because he wanted attention.
But because somewhere deep inside his soul, there was a line he refused to cross.
And history changed because one exhausted Jewish exile decided he would rather risk death than violate the fear of God.
Most people read the story of Mordecai and Haman like an ancient political conflict.
It was not.
It was spiritual warfare hiding behind government authority.
It was the collision between pride and covenant.
Between ego and obedience.
Between a man demanding worship and another man remembering who worship belongs to.
And if we are honest…
Many of us bow every single day.
Not physically.
But emotionally.

We bow to approval. We bow to fear. We bow to popularity. We bow to compromise. We bow to culture. We bow to sinful relationships. We bow to money. We bow to lust. We bow to silence when God told us to stand.
That is why this story still burns after thousands of years.
Because Mordecai’s refusal confronts every hidden idol we protect.
The book of Esther says:

“After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him. And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.” — Esther 3:1–2
The Hebrew text carries tremendous weight here.
The phrase “bowed” comes from the Hebrew word “כָּרַע” (karaʿ), meaning to bend the knee, to kneel down, to submit oneself.
But the phrase “did him reverence” comes from “שָׁחָה” (shachah).
That changes everything.
Because “shachah” is not merely polite respect.
It is a word repeatedly associated throughout Scripture with worship, prostration, reverence given before deity, spiritual submission, and sacred honor.
This is the same Hebrew root used in passages involving worship before God.
Mordecai was not refusing simple workplace respect.
He was refusing an act that crossed into spiritual compromise.
And suddenly the story becomes terrifyingly personal.
Because many modern believers think compromise always looks dramatic.
Sometimes compromise is simply bowing emotionally where God told you to stand spiritually.
The text also tells us something else many people overlook.
Haman was not just any Persian official.
Scripture deliberately calls him “the Agagite.”
That detail is not random.
It is explosive.
Agag was the king of the Amalekites.
The Amalekites were ancient enemies of Israel.
Their hatred against God’s covenant people stretched back generations.
Exodus 17 records Amalek attacking Israel when they were weak and vulnerable in the wilderness.
God declared war against Amalek because of their brutality.
Later, in 1 Samuel 15, King Saul was commanded by God to destroy Amalek completely.
But Saul compromised.
He spared Agag.
And partial obedience created future destruction.
Now generations later, an Agagite named Haman rises to power with genocidal hatred against the Jewish people.
Compromise always grows teeth later.
What Saul tolerated, Esther’s generation suffered.
And what you entertain privately today may try to destroy your children tomorrow.
This is why biblical compromise is never harmless.
Sin survives longer than emotions do.
Mordecai understood something deeper than politics.
This was not merely about one man.
This represented a spiritual lineage hostile toward the covenant purposes of God.
There is another detail hidden in the text.
Mordecai himself was from the tribe connected to Kish.
Esther 2:5 says:
“Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite.”
Kish.
That name matters.
Why?
Because Saul, the king who failed to destroy Agag, was also the son of Kish.
The Bible is intentionally showing us unfinished spiritual warfare.
A Benjamite descendant connected to Kish now faces an Agagite descendant connected to Amalek.
The conflict was larger than personality.
It was covenant history colliding in one room.
And this time…
A man refused to compromise.
Mordecai would not repeat Saul’s failure.
This is what makes the story emotionally devastating.
One generation’s compromise became another generation’s battle.
Many people today are fighting inherited pain because someone before them bowed when they should have stood.

Some inherited addiction. Some inherited rage. Some inherited abuse. Some inherited silence. Some inherited spiritual lukewarmness. Some inherited father wounds. Some inherited cycles nobody talks about publicly.
But somewhere, somebody has to become the Mordecai of the family.
Somebody has to finally say:
“This cycle stops with me.”
That is why this story reaches so deeply into the human heart.
Mordecai was not just resisting Haman.
He was resisting generational surrender.
And Haman could not tolerate it.
Pride becomes violent when worship is denied.
The Bible says:
“And when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath.” — Esther 3:5
Not irritated.
Full of wrath.
Because pride demands validation.
And narcissistic power often becomes enraged when someone refuses to participate in false worship.
That still happens today.
People become uncomfortable when conviction enters the room.
Not because truth is weak.
But because darkness hates exposure.
Jesus Himself said in John 3:19:
“And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.”
The Greek word for “loved” here is “ἠγάπησαν” (ēgapēsan), from “agapaō.”
People emotionally attached themselves to darkness.
That is frightening.
Because humans can become emotionally loyal to the very thing destroying them.
Haman’s rage was not logical.
It was spiritual.
One uncompromising believer exposed the emptiness of his manufactured glory.
And this is where the story becomes painfully relevant.
Because culture still rewards bowing.

Bow to trends. Bow to sexual confusion. Bow to public opinion. Bow to corruption. Bow to entertainment addiction. Bow to greed. Bow to celebrity culture. Bow to self-worship. Bow to moral compromise. Bow to silence.
And when somebody refuses?
Mockery comes. Isolation comes. Pressure comes. Misunderstanding comes.
Sometimes even betrayal comes.
But Mordecai still stood.
Can you imagine the tension?
Every day he walked through the king’s gate knowing everyone saw him.
Every day people whispered.
Every day pressure increased.
Every day compromise would have been easier.
Yet he stood.
That kind of obedience costs something.
People love preaching about courage until courage threatens comfort.
The truth is many believers want heaven without confrontation.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that faithfulness often places people in collision with systems demanding spiritual compromise.
Daniel refused to stop praying. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar’s image. The apostles refused to stop preaching Christ.
Acts 5:29 says:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
The Greek says:
“Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις”
“Peitharchein dei Theō mallon ē anthrōpois.”
Literally:
“It is necessary to obey God more than men.”
Necessary.
Not optional.
And perhaps that is why Mordecai’s story still shakes hearts today.
Because every believer eventually faces a moment where obedience becomes expensive.
Somebody reading this is exhausted from pretending.
You have been bowing emotionally to people who are slowly crushing your spirit.
You fear rejection more than disobedience.
You silence conviction to maintain acceptance.
But deep inside, the Holy Spirit keeps whispering:
Stand.
Not in pride.
Not in arrogance.
Not in self-righteousness.
But in reverent loyalty to God.
Mordecai understood something modern Christianity sometimes forgets.
God does not always bless comfort.
Sometimes He blesses costly obedience.
The terrifying reality is this:
Standing may temporarily endanger your position.
But bowing may endanger your soul.
Jesus asked in Mark 8:36:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
The Greek word for soul is “ψυχή” (psychē).
It means life, soul, inner self, the essence of who someone truly is.
Many people gain temporary approval while losing themselves internally.
Mordecai refused that exchange.
And eventually his refusal exposed Haman completely.
That is another powerful truth.
Darkness often appears powerful… until God intervenes.
Haman built gallows for Mordecai.
But the very structure designed for the righteous became the instrument of judgment against evil.
Sin eventually collapses under its own arrogance.
Galatians 6:7 says:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
The Greek word for mocked is “μυκτηρίζεται” (myktērizetai).
It literally carries the sense of turning up the nose in arrogant contempt.
Human pride constantly believes it can outsmart God.
It never does.
Haman’s downfall reminds us that God sees every hidden act of pride, hatred, manipulation, corruption, and violence.
Nothing escapes Him.
And yet…
The deepest beauty of this story is not merely judgment.
It is preservation.
Because behind the scenes, God was protecting the lineage through which the Messiah would eventually come.
The book of Esther never directly mentions the name of God.
Not once.
And yet His fingerprints cover every chapter.
Coincidences align. Doors open. Timing shifts. Sleep disappears from a king. Hidden plots become exposed.
Providence moves invisibly.
That matters deeply for the person reading this while feeling abandoned.
Just because you cannot see God moving does not mean He stopped moving.
Sometimes heaven works silently.
And some of God’s greatest miracles happen behind curtains humans cannot yet see.
Maybe you are in a season where obedience feels unrewarded.
Maybe standing for Christ has cost friendships. Maybe purity cost relationships. Maybe conviction cost popularity. Maybe honesty cost opportunity. Maybe faithfulness cost comfort.
But Mordecai’s story reminds us that unseen obedience is never unseen by God.
Psalm 121:4 says:
“Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.”
While Haman obsessed over power, God was already arranging deliverance.
And eventually the man who refused to bow was elevated publicly.
Esther 8:15 says:
“And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold…”
The faithful exile became honored.
Not because he chased glory.
Because he feared God more than men.
There is something unforgettable about people who quietly refuse compromise.
Not loud. Not performative. Not attention-seeking.
Just faithful.
And in an age where almost everything bends to pressure, faithful people become impossible to ignore.
Maybe that is why this story survives.
Because every generation eventually meets its Hamans.
And every believer eventually chooses whether to bow.
Be honest.
What are you bowing to right now?
Approval? Fear? Addiction? Secret sin? Relationships? Bitterness? Pride? Comfort? Lust? Money? Social acceptance?
Some people are physically alive while spiritually kneeling before things destroying them internally.
But Jesus Christ still sets captives free.
That is the Gospel.
The cross was not merely forgiveness.
It was liberation.
Romans 6:6 says:
“Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed…”
The Greek phrase for “destroyed” is “καταργηθῇ” (katargēthē).
It means rendered powerless, brought to nothing, deprived of strength.
Christ did not die merely to improve behavior.
He came to break slavery.
And maybe somebody reading this feels exhausted because you have spent years bowing to things Jesus already paid to free you from.
You do not have to stay there.
Grace still reaches people in hiding.
Mercy still reaches addicts. Grace still reaches hypocrites. Mercy still reaches the ashamed. Grace still reaches prodigals. Mercy still reaches broken believers.
Jesus still rebuilds people.
That is why the Gospel is so powerful.
Because God specializes in restoring people who thought they were too compromised to recover.
Peter denied Christ publicly. David failed morally. Thomas doubted. Paul persecuted believers.
Yet grace rewrote their story.
And maybe that is why Mordecai’s refusal matters so much.
Because one faithful stand can shift generations.
One refusal to compromise can protect families. One act of obedience can preserve future lives. One surrendered heart can become the turning point for an entire bloodline.
Do not underestimate what God can do through one person who refuses to bow.
Somebody else reading your honesty may realize they are not alone.
One quiet decision to stand for God can echo through generations you may never live long enough to see.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Tumanggi si Mordecai na Yumuko kay Haman
Tumigil ang paligid nang tumanggi siyang yumuko.
Lahat ay lumuhod.
Pero may isang lalaking nanatiling nakatayo.
Hindi dahil mayabang siya. Hindi dahil rebelde siya. Hindi dahil gusto niyang magpasikat.
Kundi dahil may hangganan sa loob ng kanyang kaluluwa na hindi niya kayang tawirin.
At binago ng isang desisyon ang kasaysayan.
Karamihan sa mga tao ay binabasa ang kuwento nina Mordecai at Haman bilang simpleng alitan sa politika.
Pero hindi iyon simpleng politika.
Ito ay espirituwal na digmaan na nakatago sa likod ng kapangyarihan.
Banggaan ito ng kayabangan at katapatan sa Diyos.
Banggaan ng ego at pagsunod.
Banggaan ng isang lalaking gustong sambahin… at isang lalaking alam kung sino lang ang dapat sambahin.
At kung magiging totoo tayo…
Marami sa atin ang yumuyuko araw-araw.
Hindi man pisikal.
Pero emosyonal.

Yumuyuko tayo sa approval ng tao. Yumuyuko tayo sa takot. Yumuyuko tayo sa kasalanan. Yumuyuko tayo sa relasyon na alam nating inilalayo tayo sa Diyos. Yumuyuko tayo sa kultura. Yumuyuko tayo sa pera. Yumuyuko tayo sa makamundong validation.
Kaya hanggang ngayon, tumatagos pa rin ang kuwento ni Mordecai.
Dahil inilalantad nito ang mga diyos-diyosan na lihim nating pinoprotektahan.
Sinasabi ng Esther 3:1–2:

“Pagkatapos ng mga bagay na ito ay itinaas ni Haring Ahasuerus si Haman na anak ni Hammedatha na Agageo… At lahat ng lingkod ng hari… ay yumuyukod at nagbibigay-galang kay Haman… ngunit si Mordecai ay hindi yumuyukod ni nagbibigay-galang sa kanya.”
Sa orihinal na Hebreo, ang salitang “yumuyuko” ay “כָּרַע” (karaʿ), na nangangahulugang lumuhod o magpasakop.
Pero ang “nagbibigay-galang” ay mula sa “שָׁחָה” (shachah).
At dito lumalalim ang kuwento.
Dahil ang “shachah” ay salitang madalas gamitin sa Kasulatan para sa pagsamba.
Hindi simpleng respeto.
Ito ay kilos ng espirituwal na pagpapasakop.
Nauunawaan ni Mordecai na may hangganan ang paggalang sa tao.
At kapag ang hinihingi ng tao ay parang pagsamba na… hindi na iyon dapat ibigay.
Napakaraming Kristiyano ngayon ang unti-unting nakikipagkompromiso dahil iniisip nilang maliit na bagay lang.
Pero minsan, ang kompromiso ay simpleng pagyuko sa bagay na sinabi ng Diyos na dapat mong panindigan.
May isa pang detalye na madalas hindi napapansin.
Tinawag si Haman bilang “Agageo.”
Hindi random ang detalye na iyon.
Si Agag ay hari ng mga Amalecita.
At ang mga Amalecita ay matagal nang kaaway ng bayan ng Diyos.
Sa Exodus 17, sinalakay nila ang Israel habang mahina at pagod ang mga ito.
Kalaunan, inutusan si Haring Saul sa 1 Samuel 15 na lubusang lipulin ang Amalek.
Pero nagkompromiso si Saul.
Hindi niya pinatay si Agag.
At ang kompromisong iyon ay nagkaroon ng bunga makalipas ang mga henerasyon.
Ngayon, si Haman na Agageo ay gustong lipulin ang buong lahing Hudyo.
Ganito mapanganib ang kompromiso.
Ang kasalanang pinapayagan ngayon… maaaring sumira sa susunod na henerasyon bukas.
At dito nagiging emosyonal ang kuwento.
Dahil maraming tao ngayon ang lumalaban sa sakit na minana nila.
Minanang galit. Minanang addiction. Minanang trauma. Minanang katahimikan. Minanang espirituwal na pagiging malamig.
Pero may isang tao sa pamilya na kailangang maging parang Mordecai.
May isang taong kailangang magsabi:
“Dito na matatapos ang cycle na ito.”
Kaya hindi simpleng pagtanggi lang ang ginawa ni Mordecai.
Tumanggi siyang ulitin ang pagkakamali ng nakaraang henerasyon.
At galit na galit si Haman.
Sinasabi ng Esther 3:5:
“At nang makita ni Haman na si Mordecai ay hindi yumuyukod… siya ay napuno ng poot.”
Hindi simpleng inis.
Poot.
Dahil ang pride ay gustong sambahin.
At kapag may tumangging yumuko, nagagalit ang kayabangan.
Ganyan pa rin ngayon.
Kapag may taong tumatayo para sa katotohanan, may mga taong naiilang.
Hindi dahil mahina ang liwanag.
Kundi dahil ayaw ng dilim na mailantad.
Sabi ni Jesus sa Juan 3:19:
“…minahal ng mga tao ang kadiliman kaysa liwanag…”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “minahal” ay “ἠγάπησαν” (ēgapēsan).
Nakakatakot iyon.
Dahil posibleng mahalin ng tao ang mismong bagay na sumisira sa kanya.
At hanggang ngayon, marami pa ring “Haman” ang mundo.
Yumuko raw tayo sa kultura. Yumuko raw tayo sa kasalanan. Yumuko raw tayo sa compromise. Yumuko raw tayo sa pressure. Yumuko raw tayo sa maling sistema.
Pero may mga taong pinipili pa ring tumayo.
Kahit mahirap. Kahit nakakapagod. Kahit minsan mag-isa.
Araw-araw na dumadaan si Mordecai sa pintuan ng hari, alam niyang nakatingin ang lahat.
Alam niyang puwede siyang mapahamak.
Mas madali sanang sumunod.
Pero nanindigan siya.
At iyon ang problema ng modernong mundo.
Gusto natin ng langit nang walang paninindigan.
Gusto natin si Jesus pero ayaw natin ng sakripisyo.
Pero paulit-ulit ipinapakita ng Biblia na may halaga ang katapatan.
Tumangging manalangin sa diyus-diyosan si Daniel. Tumangging yumuko sa rebulto sina Shadrach, Meshach, at Abednego. Tumangging tumigil sa pangangaral ang mga apostol.
Sinasabi sa Gawa 5:29:
“Kailangang sundin namin ang Diyos kaysa tao.”
Sa Griyego:
“Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.”
Ibig sabihin:
“Kinakailangang sundin ang Diyos higit kaysa tao.”
Kinakailangan.
Hindi optional.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod nang magpanggap.
Pagod nang yumuko sa pressure. Pagod nang tahimik sa kasalanan. Pagod nang mag-compromise para lang tanggapin.
Pero may bumubulong pa rin sa espiritu mo:
“Tumayo ka.”
Hindi sa yabang.
Hindi sa self-righteousness.
Kundi sa takot sa Diyos.
Dahil minsan, ang pagtayo para kay Cristo ay may kapalit.
Puwedeng mawala ang comfort. Puwedeng mawala ang approval. Puwedeng mawala ang ilang relasyon.
Pero mas nakakatakot mawala ang kaluluwa.
Sabi ni Jesus sa Marcos 8:36:
“Sapagkat ano ang mapapakinabang ng tao kung makamtan man niya ang buong sanlibutan ngunit mawala naman ang kanyang kaluluwa?”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “kaluluwa” ay “ψυχή” (psychē).
Ito ang tunay na ikaw.
At maraming tao ngayon ang nakakakuha ng pansamantalang approval habang unti-unti namang nawawala ang sarili nila.
Tumanggi si Mordecai sa kapalit na iyon.
At kalaunan, ibinagsak ng Diyos si Haman.
Ang bitayan na inihanda para kay Mordecai… iyon din ang naging dahilan ng pagbagsak ni Haman.
Dahil hindi kayang lokohin ng kayabangan ang Diyos.
Sinasabi sa Galacia 6:7:
“Huwag kayong padaya; ang Diyos ay hindi napabibiro…”
Nakikita ng Diyos ang lahat.
Lahat ng lihim na pride. Lahat ng manipulasyon. Lahat ng kasinungalingan. Lahat ng pagtataksil.
Pero ang pinakamagandang bahagi ng kuwento ay ito:
Hindi pinabayaan ng Diyos ang Kanyang bayan.
Kahit hindi direktang binanggit ang pangalan ng Diyos sa aklat ng Esther… naroon Siya sa bawat pahina.
Tahimik Siyang kumikilos.
Nag-aayos ng timing. Nagbubukas ng pinto. Naglalantad ng lihim. Nag-iingat ng Kanyang plano.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito na pakiramdam ay tahimik ang langit.
Pero tandaan mo:
Hindi ibig sabihin na hindi mo nakikita ang Diyos ay tumigil na Siya sa pagkilos.
May mga milagro na nangyayari sa likod ng kurtina.
At gaya ni Mordecai, may gantimpala ang katapatan.
Sa huli, ang lalaking tumangging yumuko… siya ring pinarangalan.
Dahil ang Diyos ay marunong magtaas ng mga taong tapat.
At sa panahon ngayon kung saan halos lahat ay yumuyuko sa pressure… napakalakas ng testimony ng taong nananatiling matatag.
Maging totoo ka.
Ano ang pinagyuyukuran mo ngayon?
Takot? Kasalanan? Lust? Addiction? Pera? Validation? Relasyon? Pride?
Dahil si Jesus ay hindi lang dumating para magpatawad.
Dumating Siya para magpalaya.
Sinasabi sa Roma 6:6 na ang kapangyarihan ng kasalanan ay maaaring wasakin sa pamamagitan ni Cristo.
Ang salitang Griyego na “καταργηθῇ” (katargēthē) ay nangangahulugang gawing powerless.
May kalayaan kay Jesus.
May awa pa rin para sa mga taong pagod. May biyaya pa rin para sa mga taong nahulog. May pag-asa pa rin para sa mga taong gustong bumalik.
Kayang baguhin ni Jesus ang kahit sino.
At baka isang desisyon mo lang na tumayo para sa Diyos… ang magiging simula ng pagbabago ng buong pamilya mo.
Baka may ibang taong makabasa ng comment mo at marealize nilang hindi sila nag-iisa.
Isang tahimik na paninindigan para sa Diyos ang maaaring magbago ng mga henerasyong hindi mo man lang maaabutang makita.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind the Sons of Sceva Trying to Use Jesus’ Name
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind the Sons of Sceva Trying to Use Jesus’ Name
There are people who say the name of Jesus with tears in their eyes.
And there are people who say it like a password.
One changes eternity.
The other gets exposed.

Most believers know the story of the Sons of Sceva from a few verses buried inside Acts 19, but very few understand how terrifying, heartbreaking, prophetic, and painfully relevant this story truly is.
Because this was never just about seven Jewish exorcists.
This was about people trying to borrow intimacy with God that they never pursued themselves.
This was about using the name of Jesus without surrendering to the authority of Jesus.
This was about spiritual performance without relationship.
And if we are honest...
A generation is still doing it.
The room gets quiet whenever heaven exposes counterfeit spirituality.
Acts 19 does not read like a comfortable church story.
It reads like a warning siren.

The Apostle Paul had arrived in Ephesus, one of the darkest spiritual centers in the ancient world. Ephesus was consumed with idol worship, occult practices, magical arts, temple prostitution, and demonic activity. The city was famous for the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Sorcery was not hidden there.
It was culture.
Acts 19:11–12 says:

“God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.”
This shook the entire region.
Demons were fleeing.
People were being healed.
The authority of Christ was publicly destroying darkness.
And that is where the story becomes disturbing.
Because some men saw the power...
but never sought the Person.
Acts 19:13 says:
“Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus.”
The phrase “took upon them” comes from the Greek phrase:
ἐπεχείρησαν (epecheirēsan)
Meaning:
“To attempt arrogantly.” “To put one’s hand to something presumptuously.” “To undertake without authorization.”
This changes everything.
They were not moving in faith.
They were experimenting with holy things.
Jesus was not their Lord.
He was a technique.
And that is far more common today than many Christians want to admit.
People wear crosses but refuse surrender.
People quote Scripture without obedience.
People use Christian language while living in hidden rebellion.
People know worship songs but do not know God.
There are pulpits full of charisma without consecration.
Content creators chasing influence without prayer.
Church culture that knows branding better than brokenness.
And deep down...
many people are terrified that they have learned how to sound spiritual without actually being transformed.
The Sons of Sceva were not atheists.
That is what makes this story terrifying.
They operated around spiritual things.
Their father, Sceva, is described in Greek as:
ἀρχιερεύς (archiereus)
Meaning:
“Chief priest.”
Whether this title was official or self-appointed is debated among scholars, but the point remains:
These men were deeply connected to religious culture.
Yet demons still recognized they lacked authority.
Religion without relationship has always been powerless.
The seven sons approached a demonized man and declared:
“We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.”
Notice the wording carefully.
Not:
“The Jesus we serve.”
Not:
“The Jesus who saved us.”
Not:
“Our Lord.”
No.
“Jesus whom Paul preacheth.”
Borrowed faith.
Borrowed authority.
Borrowed intimacy.
Borrowed fire.
And hell immediately recognized the difference.
Acts 19:15 records one of the most chilling verses in the New Testament:
“And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?”
The Greek language here is incredibly revealing.
For “Jesus I know,” the demon uses:
γινώσκω (ginōskō)
Meaning:
“To know intimately.” “To recognize fully.”
For “Paul I know,” the Greek is:
ἐπίσταμαι (epistamai)
Meaning:
“To understand well.” “To be acquainted with.”
But when addressing the sons?
No recognition.
No spiritual identity.
No authority.
No heaven-backed relationship.
Just exposure.
Hell knew Jesus.
Hell recognized Paul.
But heaven had no record of surrendered intimacy from these men.
And then came the humiliation.
Acts 19:16 says the demonized man leaped on them, overpowered them, and they fled naked and wounded.
Naked.
The Greek word is:
γυμνούς (gymnous)
Exposed.
Stripped.
Uncovered.
This was not random embarrassment.
This was symbolic judgment.
Because counterfeit spirituality is eventually exposed.
You can fake power before people.
You cannot fake authority before hell.
That sentence alone should shake modern Christianity.
Because platforms can be purchased.
Followers can be manipulated.
Crowds can be emotionally moved.
But demons do not respond to branding.
Spiritual authority is born from surrender, obedience, prayer, holiness, intimacy, repentance, and submission to Christ.
Not performance.
Not aesthetics.
Not popularity.
There are people exhausted right now because they have been trying to use the language of faith while secretly starving spiritually.
They know how to post about Jesus.
But they do not spend time with Him.
They know how to quote verses.
But they avoid conviction.
They know Christian culture.
But not the cross.
And eventually, the soul begins collapsing under the weight of pretending.
This is why the story matters.
Not because God wanted to humiliate people.
But because Jesus refuses to be used like a magical incantation.

In Jewish culture during the first century, many itinerant exorcists believed certain names carried supernatural force. Ancient magical papyri from the Greco-Roman world reveal people invoking names of deities, angels, and spiritual beings as formulas for power.
The Sons of Sceva treated Jesus like one more formula.
But Jesus is not a spell.
His name is connected to His person.
His authority.
His kingdom.
His holiness.
Philippians 2:9–11 declares:
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.”
The Greek word for “name” here is:
ὄνομα (onoma)
But in biblical thought, a name represented identity, character, authority, and essence.
To invoke the name of Jesus while rejecting the Lordship of Jesus is spiritual contradiction.
And this is where many people feel pierced.
Because there are countless individuals sitting in churches while secretly feeling disconnected from God.
Some are performing Christianity because they fear disappointing people.
Some are trying to inherit faith from parents.
Some are living on old encounters.
Some know church language but have never fully surrendered their lives to Christ.
And beneath all the noise is a terrifying question:
Does heaven actually know me?
Not:
Do people know me.
Not:
Does social media know me.
Not:
Does my church know me.
But:
Does Jesus know me?
Matthew 7:22–23 echoes this same warning.
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
And Jesus responds:
“I never knew you.”
The Greek word for “knew” is again:
ἔγνων (egnōn)
Relational knowing.
Not awareness.
Intimacy.
Connection.
Covenant.
That verse should destroy every illusion that outward spiritual activity automatically equals inward transformation.
God has never been impressed with performance detached from surrender.
And yet...
The story does not end in hopelessness.
Because the aftermath of Acts 19 became one of the greatest revivals in Ephesus.
Fear fell upon the city.
People publicly repented.
Those practicing occult arts burned their books.
Acts 19:19 says the value of the burned books was fifty thousand pieces of silver.
This was not casual repentance.
This was costly surrender.
Real encounters with the holiness of God always expose what cannot remain.
The Greek word used for confessed in Acts 19:18 is:
ἐξομολογούμενοι (exomologoumenoi)
Meaning:
“To openly acknowledge.” “To confess fully.” “To admit without concealment.”
Revival began when people stopped hiding.
And maybe that is the real reason this story unsettles people.
Because it forces every believer to confront the difference between image and intimacy.
Between religion and relationship.
Between using Jesus and actually following Him.
The world does not need more Christians pretending to be perfect.
It needs surrendered believers who truly know Christ.
People who pray when nobody is watching.
People who repent quickly.
People who tremble at Scripture.
People who obey even when obedience costs them everything.
People who are broken enough to admit they need grace daily.
The Sons of Sceva wanted authority without surrender.
Power without holiness.
Spiritual influence without relationship.
And the result was exposure.
But Jesus still offers something better.
Not performance.
Relationship.
Not religious theater.
Transformation.
Not borrowed fire.
Personal intimacy.
Romans 10:13 says:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
The Greek word for “call upon” is:
ἐπικαλέσηται (epikalesētai)
Meaning:
“To invoke personally.” “To appeal to with dependence.” “To cry out toward.”
Not manipulate.
Not exploit.
Not imitate.
Depend.
The beauty of the Gospel is this:
Jesus does not reject broken people.
He rejects false masks.
He welcomes repentant sinners.
He restores failures.
He heals the ashamed.
He forgives the hidden.
He rescues the exhausted.
But He cannot be reduced into a religious accessory.
There are readers carrying secret fear right now.
Fear that their faith has become routine.
Fear that they have drifted.
Fear that they know church better than they know Christ.
But conviction is not condemnation.
Conviction is an invitation.
The fact that this unsettles your spirit may itself be evidence that God is still calling you closer.
The enemy wants people hiding.
Jesus wants people healed.
And maybe tonight is the night somebody finally stops pretending.
Maybe this is the moment somebody closes the hidden tabs.
Deletes the secret conversations.
Drops the spiritual performance.
Returns to prayer.
Returns to Scripture.
Returns to surrender.
Returns to Jesus.
Because one day every platform fades.
Every title disappears.
Every crowd vanishes.
And the only thing that will matter is whether we truly knew Christ...
and whether He truly knew us.
One of the most dangerous things a person can lose is the difference between sounding close to Jesus and actually knowing Him.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Katotohanan sa Likod ng mga Anak ni Sceva na Sinubukang Gamitin ang Pangalan ni Jesus
May mga taong binabanggit ang pangalan ni Jesus habang umiiyak.
At may mga taong ginagamit ito na parang password.
Ang isa ay nagdadala ng buhay na walang hanggan.
Ang isa naman ay nauuwi sa pagkakalantad.
Maraming Kristiyano ang alam ang kuwento tungkol sa mga Anak ni Sceva sa Gawa 19.
Pero kakaunti lang ang totoong nakakaunawa kung gaano ito kabigat, kabangis, at gaano ito kaakma sa panahon natin ngayon.
Dahil ang kuwentong ito ay hindi lang tungkol sa pitong lalaking Hudyo na nagtangkang magpalayas ng demonyo.
Ito ay kuwento ng mga taong gustong hiramin ang awtoridad ni Jesus nang hindi hinahanap ang relasyon kay Jesus.
Kuwento ito ng mga taong gustong gamitin ang pangalan ni Cristo pero ayaw magpasakop kay Cristo.
Kuwento ito ng relihiyosong performance na walang tunay na intimacy sa Diyos.
At kung magiging tapat tayo...
Marami pa ring gumagawa nito ngayon.
Tahimik ang buong espirituwal na mundo kapag inilalantad ng langit ang pekeng kabanalan.
Ang Ephesus noong panahon ni Pablo ay isa sa pinakamadilim na siyudad sa buong Roman Empire.
Punong-puno ito ng idolatriya.
Pangkukulam.
Mahikang espirituwal.
Mga ritwal.
Demonyong pagsamba.
Ang Temple of Artemis ay isa sa pinakatanyag na templo noon.
Ang kadiliman doon ay hindi lihim.
Parte ito ng kultura.
At doon dumating si Apostol Pablo.

“At gumawa ang Dios ng mga bukod na himala sa pamamagitan ng mga kamay ni Pablo: Ano pa't ang mga panyo o mga tapis na nanggaling sa kaniyang katawan ay dinadala sa mga may sakit, at nagsialis sa kanila ang mga sakit, at nagsilabas ang masasamang espiritu.”
Nanginginig ang buong siyudad.
Mga demonyo ang tumatakbo.
Mga maysakit ang gumagaling.
At doon nagsimulang mapansin ng iba ang kapangyarihan ni Jesus.
Pero may problema.
May mga taong nakita ang kapangyarihan...
pero hindi hinanap ang Presensya.
Gawa 19:13:
“Datapuwa't ang ilan sa mga Judiong pagala-galang nagpapalayas ng masasamang espiritu ay nagsikap na banggitin ang pangalan ng Panginoong Jesus.”
Ang salitang ginamit sa Greek para sa “nagsikap” ay:
ἐπεχείρησαν (epecheirēsan)
Ibig sabihin:
“Mapangahas na pagtatangka.” “Paggalaw nang walang pahintulot.” “Pag-abot sa bagay na hindi ipinagkaloob.”
Hindi sila gumagalaw sa pananampalataya.
Nag-eeksperimento sila sa banal.
Hindi nila kilala si Jesus.
Ginagamit lang nila Siya.
At iyon ang nakakatakot.
Dahil marami pa rin ang gumagawa niyan ngayon.
May mga taong marunong magsuot ng krus pero ayaw mamatay sa kasalanan.
May mga taong marunong mag-quote ng Bible verses pero ayaw magsisi.
May mga taong alam ang Christian language pero hindi kilala ang Diyos sa lihim.
May mga taong mahusay sa church culture pero hindi marunong manalangin.
May mga pulpito na puno ng charisma pero walang consecration.
May mga content creator na habol ay influence, hindi holiness.
At sa kailaliman ng puso nila...
natatakot silang baka natuto na lang silang magmukhang spiritual nang hindi talaga nababago.
Ang mas nakakatakot?
Hindi atheist ang mga Anak ni Sceva.
Relihiyoso sila.
Ang ama nilang si Sceva ay tinawag na:
ἀρχιερεύς (archiereus)
“Punong pari.”
Posibleng opisyal ang titulo.
Posibleng hindi.
Pero malinaw ang punto:
Malapit sila sa relihiyon.
Pero malayo sila sa tunay na awtoridad ng Diyos.
Dahil ang relihiyong walang relasyon kay Cristo ay walang tunay na kapangyarihan.
Lumapit sila sa lalaking sinasaniban ng demonyo at sinabi:
“Iniutos namin sa iyo sa pangalan ni Jesus na ipinangangaral ni Pablo.”
Pansinin mo iyon.
Hindi nila sinabing:
“Jesus na aming Panginoon.”
Hindi nila sinabing:
“Jesus na nagligtas sa amin.”
Hindi nila sinabing:
“Jesus na sinusunod namin.”
Hindi.
“Jesus na ipinapangaral ni Pablo.”
Hiram na pananampalataya.
Hiram na apoy.
Hiram na intimacy.
Hiram na awtoridad.
At agad itong nakilala ng impiyerno.
Gawa 19:15:
“At sumagot ang masamang espiritu at sinabi sa kanila, Nakikilala ko si Jesus, at kilala ko si Pablo; datapuwa't sino kayo?”
Nakakakilabot ang Greek dito.
Para kay Jesus, ginamit ang:
γινώσκω (ginōskō)
“Kilalang-kilala.” “May tunay na pagkakaugnayan.”
Para kay Pablo:
ἐπίσταμαι (epistamai)
“Kilala dahil sa awtoridad.” “Kilalang may espirituwal na reputasyon.”
Pero pagdating sa mga Anak ni Sceva?
Walang pagkilala.
Walang awtoridad.
Walang marka ng langit.
Walang intimacy.
At pagkatapos noon...
dumating ang kahihiyan.
Sinabi sa Gawa 19:16 na sinugod sila ng lalaking sinasaniban ng demonyo.
Natalo silang lahat.
At tumakas silang hubad at sugatan.
Hubad.
Sa Greek:
γυμνούς (gymnous)
“Nakalantad.”
“Walang takip.”
“At hayagang napahiya.”
Hindi aksidente iyon.
Simbolo iyon.
Dahil ang pekeng espirituwalidad ay laging nauuwi sa pagkakalantad.
Puwedeng malinlang ang tao.
Pero hindi ang impiyerno.
Napakalalim ng katotohanang iyon.
Dahil sa panahon natin ngayon, madaling bumili ng platform.
Madaling paramihin ang followers.
Madaling magmukhang spiritual online.
Pero hindi natitinag ang kadiliman sa aesthetics.
Ang tunay na awtoridad ay nanggagaling sa:
panalangin,
pagsuko,
kabanalan,
pagsisisi,
at intimacy kay Cristo.
Hindi sa performance.
Hindi sa branding.
Hindi sa pagiging viral.
Maraming tao ngayon ang pagod na pagod.
Dahil sinusubukan nilang dalhin ang image ng pagiging Kristiyano habang gutom na gutom ang kaluluwa nila.
Marunong silang mag-post tungkol kay Jesus.
Pero hindi sila gumugugol ng oras kasama Siya.
Marunong silang magsalita tungkol sa grace.
Pero tumatakbo sila palayo sa conviction.
Marunong silang sumamba sa harap ng tao.
Pero walang lihim na altar.
At unti-unting bumibigay ang kaluluwa sa bigat ng pagpapanggap.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit mahalaga ang kuwento.
Hindi dahil gusto ng Diyos na ipahiya ang tao.
Kundi dahil ayaw ni Jesus na tratuhin Siya bilang espirituwal na formula.
Noong unang siglo, maraming exorcist ang naniniwalang may supernatural na kapangyarihan ang ilang pangalan.
Ginagamit nila ang pangalan ng mga diyos, anghel, at espiritu bilang parang magical incantation.
At ganoon din ang ginawa ng mga Anak ni Sceva kay Jesus.
Pero hindi si Jesus spell.
Hindi Siya anting-anting.
Ang pangalan Niya ay konektado sa Kanyang pagkatao.
Sa Kanyang kabanalan.
Sa Kanyang kaharian.
Sa Kanyang awtoridad.
Filipos 2:9–11:
“Kaya naman siya'y totoong itinaas ng Dios, at binigyan siya ng pangalang lalo sa lahat ng pangalan.”
Ang salitang “pangalan” sa Greek ay:
ὄνομα (onoma)
Sa pag-iisip ng Biblia, ang pangalan ay hindi lang titulo.
Ito ay pagkakakilanlan.
Awtoridad.
Kaluwalhatian.
Katauhan.
Kaya imposibleng gamitin ang pangalan ni Jesus habang tinatanggihan ang pamumuno ni Jesus sa buhay.
At dito tinatamaan ang maraming tao.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ang tahimik na disconnected sa Diyos.
May mga nagsisimba pero walang tunay na surrender.
May mga umaasa lang sa pananampalataya ng magulang nila.
May mga nabubuhay na lang sa lumang encounter.
At sa ilalim ng lahat ng ito ay isang tanong:
Kilala ba talaga ako ni Jesus?
Hindi:
“Kilala ba ako ng church?”
Hindi:
“Kilala ba ako online?”
Hindi:
“May platform ba ako?”
Kundi:
“Kilala ba ako ng Langit?”

“Marami ang magsasabi sa akin sa araw na yaon, Panginoon, Panginoon, hindi baga nagsipanghula kami sa iyong pangalan?... At kung magkagayo'y ipahahayag ko sa kanila, Kailan ma'y hindi ko kayo nangakilala.”
Ang salitang “nakilala” ay:
ἔγνων (egnōn)
Hindi simpleng awareness.
Relasyon.
Intimacy.
Pagkakaugnayan.
Ito ang sumisira sa maling akala na sapat na ang religious activity para masabing transformed.
Hindi kailanman humanga ang Diyos sa performance na walang surrender.
Pero salamat sa Diyos...
Hindi nagtapos sa kadiliman ang kuwento.
Dahil matapos ang pangyayaring iyon, nagkaroon ng malaking revival sa Ephesus.
Natakot ang buong siyudad.
Nagsisi ang maraming tao.
Sinunog nila ang kanilang mga aklat ng mahika.
Gawa 19:19:
“At tinipon nila ang kanilang mga aklat, at sinunog sa paningin ng lahat.”
Napakamahal ng halaga ng mga iyon.
