May kakaibang takot kapag sama-samang gumagawa ng mali ang isang grupo.
Dahil kapag collective na ang kasamaan… nagiging mahal ang katapangan.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Ikaw lang ang nababagabag habang normal lang sa iba ang mali.
Ikaw lang ang nanginginig pa ang konsensya.
Ikaw lang ang tahimik na nananalangin:
“Diyos… mali ito.”
Pero imbes na direktang harapin ang kasamaan, pinili ni Ruben ang strategy kaysa surrender.
Genesis 37:22:
“At sinabi ni Ruben sa kanila, Huwag kayong magbubo ng dugo; ihulog ninyo siya sa balong ito na nasa ilang…”
At saka ipinakita ng Kasulatan ang tunay niyang plano:
“…upang mailigtas niya siya mula sa kanilang mga kamay, at maibalik siya sa kaniyang ama.”
Dito lalong sumakit ang kwento.
May awa si Ruben.
Pero kulang siya sa tapang.
May konsensya siya.
Pero kulang siya sa leadership.
Gusto niyang gumawa ng tama nang tahimik.
Gusto niyang iligtas si Jose nang walang confrontation.
At dito emosyonal na nasisira ang maraming believers.
Dahil ang kalahating pagsunod… may mabigat pa ring consequence.
Sinubukan ni Ruben na dayain ang kasamaan sa halip na direktang harapin ito.
Inisip niyang baka ma-delay niya ang evil hanggang mawala ang galit ng mga kapatid niya.
Pero maraming Kristiyano pa rin ngayon ang ganoon.
Tahimik sa corruption.
Tahimik sa compromise.
Tahimik sa gossip.
Tahimik sa spiritual decay.
Tahimik sa kasinungalingan.
Dahil umaasa silang sapat na ang pribadong disagreement.
Pero bihirang umatras ang kasamaan dahil lang may tahimik na taong hindi sang-ayon.
Maging ang hukay ay puno ng symbolism.
Sinasabi sa Genesis:
“Ang balon ay walang laman, walang tubig.”
Sa Hebrew:
“וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם”
“Vehabbor req, ein bo mayim.”
Walang tubig.
Walang buhay.
Walang comfort.
Hinubaran si Jose. Pinahiya. Itinapon.
At isa sa pinaka-mabigat na detalye sa buong kabanata ay ito:
Umupo ang magkakapatid para kumain.
Habang umiiyak si Jose sa hukay.
Hindi agad inilagay ng teksto ang iyak niya rito.
Pero sa Genesis 42:21, inamin mismo ng magkakapatid:
“Nakita namin ang paghihirap ng kaniyang kaluluwa nang siya’y nagsusumamo sa amin…”
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “paghihirap” ay:
“צָרַת”
“Tzarat.”
Matinding agony. Matinding distress. Matinding emotional suffering.
Nagmakaawa si Jose.
Isipin mong naririnig mo ang nakababatang kapatid mo na umiiyak mula sa madilim na hukay habang kumakain lang ng tinapay ang iba.
At alam ni Ruben na mali ito.
Alam niya.
Pero umalis siya.
Mahalaga ang detalye na iyon.
Genesis 37:29:
“At nagbalik si Ruben sa hukay; at narito, wala na si Jose…”
Nagbalik.
Ibig sabihin… umalis siya.
Wala siya noong ipinagbili si Jose.
At nang bumalik siya… wala na.
Maisip mo ba ang panic?
Ang biglang panlalamig ng sikmura niya?
Ang realization na pumalpak ang lihim niyang plano?
Sinasabi ng Kasulatan:
“Hinapak niya ang kaniyang mga damit.”
Sa Hebrew:
“וַיִּקְרַע אֶת־בְּגָדָיו”
“Vayiqra et begadav.”
Hindi ito simpleng frustration.
Sa kultura ng Hebrew noon, ang pagpunit ng damit ay simbolo ng matinding kalungkutan, horror, o pagsisisi.
Nabiyak emosyonal si Ruben.
At pagkatapos sinabi niya ang linyang nagpapakita ng totoong bigat na pasan niya.
“Wala na ang bata; at ako, saan ako pupunta?”
Hindi:
“Nasaan si Jose?”
Hindi:
“Ano ang ginawa ninyo?”
Kundi:
“Saan ako pupunta?”
Bakit?
Dahil may dati nang failure si Ruben bago pa ito.
Siya ang panganay.
Siya dapat ang leader.
Pero sa Genesis 35, natuklasang sinipingan niya si Bilha, ang babae ng kaniyang ama.
Nasira ang tiwala.
Nasira ang authority niya.
Nasira ang identity niya.
Ngayon… ang bagsak na panganay ay muli na namang nabigo.
At alam niyang dudurog ang puso ng kaniyang ama.
Hindi ito simpleng guilt.
Ito ay naipong kahihiyan.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na alam kung ano ang pakiramdam ng accumulated shame.
Hindi lang isang pagkakamali.
Kundi pattern.
Kasaysayan.
Paulit-ulit na pakiramdam na:
“Palagi kong nabibigo ang mga taong dapat kong protektahan.”
Ang sinabi ni Ruben ay parang lalaking gumuho na sa loob.
“Saan ako pupunta?”
Sa madaling salita:
“Paano ako mabubuhay dala ito?”
At dito pumapasok ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo.
Dahil ang Biblia ay hindi koleksyon ng perpektong bayani.
Ito ay kuwento ng Diyos na kumikilos sa mga sirang tao.
Nagkamali si Jacob.
Nagkamali si Moises.
Nagkamali si David.
Nagkamali si Pedro.
Nagkamali si Ruben.
Pero nakatago sa kwentong ito ang matinding babala tungkol sa passive righteousness.
Hindi sapat ang mabubuting intensyon kung walang tapang na sumunod.
May mga pagkakataong ang pananahimik ay nagiging pakikibahagi.
May mga pagkakataong ang delayed obedience ay nagiging disobedience.
May mga pagkakataong ang pagprotekta sa sarili mong comfort… nagiging dahilan para may ibang masaktan.
At napakasakit nitong tamaan ang modernong Kristiyanismo.
Dahil maraming believers ang pribadong hindi sang-ayon sa kadiliman… pero nananatiling neutral sa publiko.
Bulong ang katotohanan.
Tahimik ang conviction.
At umaasang maaayos ang lahat nang hindi kinakailangang manindigan.
Pero tuloy pa rin ang hukay.
At may isa pang mas mabigat na posibilidad.
Maaaring habang-buhay na inulit-ulit ni Ruben sa isip niya ang araw na iyon.
“Kung nagsalita lang sana ako nang mas matapang…”
“Kung dinala ko na lang sana si Jose…”
“Kung tumayo lang sana ako laban sa kanila…”
May mga regret na umaalingawngaw habambuhay.
Kaya mapanganib ang delayed obedience.
Hindi dahil hindi kayang magpatawad ng Diyos.
Kundi dahil may mga pagkakataong hindi na bumabalik.
May mga amang huli nang humingi ng tawad.
May mga inang huli nang nakipag-ayos.
May mga believers na huli nang nagsabi ng katotohanan.
At ang emotional burden ay:
“Alam kong tama… bakit hindi ko ginawa?”
Pero hindi nagtatapos ang kwento sa Genesis 37.
Dahil patuloy pa ring sumusulat ang Diyos kahit sa gitna ng failure.
Si Jose rin kalaunan ang ginamit ng Diyos para iligtas ang mismong pamilyang nagtaksil sa kaniya.
Diyos lang ang kayang gawing preparation ang hukay.
Diyos lang ang kayang gawing preservation ang betrayal.
Diyos lang ang kayang tubusin ang halos winasak ng kahinaan ng tao.
At dito lalong nagiging makapangyarihan si Jesucristo.
Dahil hindi tulad ni Ruben… hindi palihim na sinubukan ni Jesus na iligtas tayo.
Hayagan Siyang tumayo para sa atin.
Publiko.
Marahas.
Ganap.
Natakot si Ruben na mawalan ng sarili.
Pero si Jesus… kusang ibinigay ang Kaniyang sarili.
Sabi sa Juan 15:13:
“Walang hihigit pa sa pag-ibig ng taong nag-aalay ng kaniyang buhay para sa kaniyang mga kaibigan.”
Hindi ibinulong ni Jesus ang kaligtasan.
Dinala Niya ang krus sa harap ng lahat.
Pinahiya. Sinaktan. Itinakwil.
Para iligtas tayong mga makasalanan.
Ang Greek word para sa “pag-ibig” dito ay:
“ἀγάπη” (agapē)
Isang sakripisyal at self-giving na pag-ibig.
Hindi convenience.
Hindi lihim na loyalty.
Kumpletong surrender.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakasakit ng kwento ni Ruben.
Dahil nakikita natin ang sarili natin sa kaniya.
Ang takot.
Ang hesitation.
Ang compromise.
Ang mga pagkakataong muntik na tayong sumunod nang buo.
Muntik.
Pero mas dakila si Jesus kaysa sa ating “muntik.”
Mas dakila Siya kaysa sa ating hesitation.
Mas dakila Siya kaysa sa ating kahihiyan.
Mas dakila Siya kaysa sa ating failures.
Kahit si Pedro ay hayagang nagtakwil kay Cristo.
Pero ibinalik pa rin siya ni Jesus.
Hinahabol pa rin ng biyaya ang mga sirang tao.
Binabago pa rin ng biyaya ang mga duwag.
Ginagawang testimony ang failures.
Kung may tinamaan itong nakatagong bahagi sa puso mo… huwag mong takasan ang conviction.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan ng karamihan.
At may kakilala kang kailangang mabasa ito.
May mga taong hindi nasira dahil galit sila sa katuwiran.
Nasira sila dahil nag-atubili sila noong humihingi ng tapang ang katuwiran.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Phinehas Was Given a Covenant of Peace After Violence
paragraphs: Why Phinehas Was Given a Covenant of Peace After Violence
There are moments in Scripture that make people uncomfortable.
Moments so raw, so severe, so emotionally unsettling that modern readers almost instinctively step backward from the page.
The story of Phinehas is one of those moments.
A spear. A public execution. A plague. A holy God. And then something almost impossible to understand at first glance:
God rewards Phinehas with a covenant of peace.
Peace.
Not punishment. Not rebuke. Not correction. Peace.
For many people, this passage creates an immediate internal tension. How could violence lead to peace? How could zeal become covenant? How could judgment become mercy?
And maybe the deeper question hidden beneath all of it is this:
What kind of world had Israel become that such an act was even necessary?
Because Numbers 25 is not fundamentally about brutality. It is about spiritual collapse.
It is about a generation slowly dying from compromise while still carrying the appearance of covenant.
And if we are honest… that feels terrifyingly familiar.

Israel was not merely committing private sin. They were dissolving spiritually from the inside. The people whom God rescued from Egypt were now uniting themselves to the worship of Baal-peor. The Hebrew text says:
וַיִּצָּמֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַעַל פְּעוֹר (Vayyitzamed Yisra’el l’Ba‘al Pe‘or)
“Israel yoked itself to Baal of Peor.” — Numbers 25:3
The word וַיִּצָּמֶד (vayyitzamed) is deeply important. It means to bind, attach, yoke, cling together. This was not casual temptation. This was covenant-level attachment.
Israel was spiritually joining itself to another god.
What began with seduction became apostasy. What began with appetite became worship. What began in private became national rebellion.
And suddenly the camp of God’s people became infected.
The judgment that followed was not random rage. The plague was covenant judgment.
In the ancient Hebrew worldview, covenant was life itself. To abandon God was not merely moral failure. It was national suicide.

This is why the scene becomes so emotionally devastating. While Moses and the leaders are weeping before the Tabernacle… while people are literally dying under divine judgment… a man named Zimri openly brings a Midianite woman named Cozbi into the camp in full public view.
Not secretly. Not in shame. Publicly. Defiantly. Almost mockingly.
Imagine the horror of that moment. People collapsing from plague. Leaders grieving. The presence of God dishonored. And someone still proudly celebrating the very rebellion destroying the nation.
That is the atmosphere Phinehas walked into.
Most modern readings remove the emotional weight of the scene. But Scripture does not.
Phinehas was not acting from personal hatred. The text never presents him as bloodthirsty. In fact, the Bible frames his motivation through one central word:
קִנְאָה (qin’ah)
Zeal.
But this word means far more than emotional intensity. It carries the idea of covenant passion, jealous protection, burning devotion. It is even used of God Himself.
Exodus 34:14 says:
כִּי יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ (Ki YHWH qanna shemo)
“For the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.”
This is not sinful insecurity. It is covenant love refusing to share intimacy with destruction.
Phinehas mirrored this covenant zeal. Not perfectly as God does. Not divinely as God does. But representatively.
And this is the key most people miss:
Phinehas did not create violence. He interrupted a violence already consuming Israel.
The plague itself was violence. Idolatry was violence. Spiritual corruption was violence. The destruction of covenant identity was violence.
The spear did not begin death. The spear stopped it.
Numbers 25:11 says:
פִּינְחָס... הֵשִׁיב אֶת־חֲמָתִי (Pinchas... heshiv et-chamati)
“Phinehas… has turned back My wrath.”
The Hebrew phrase הֵשִׁיב אֶת־חֲמָתִי literally carries the idea of causing wrath to return or turn away. The judgment stopped. The plague ended. Mercy broke through.
Then comes the astonishing covenant declaration.
לָכֵן אֱמֹר הִנְנִי נֹתֵן לוֹ אֶת־בְּרִיתִי שָׁלוֹם
(Hineni noten lo et-beriti shalom)
“Behold, I give to him My covenant of peace.” — Numbers 25:12
Peace. Shalom.
But biblical shalom is much deeper than emotional calm. It means wholeness. Restoration. Order. Life flourishing under covenant harmony.
The covenant of peace was not celebrating death. It was restoring covenant order before total collapse consumed the nation.
This is where modern readers must slow down.
The Bible is not commanding believers today to imitate Phinehas physically. That would completely misunderstand redemptive history.

Phinehas operated within Israel’s covenant theocracy under direct divine judgment. The New Covenant radically transforms how God’s people engage evil. Jesus rebuked Peter for using the sword. The apostles advanced the Kingdom through suffering, witness, truth, prayer, and sacrificial love.
Yet the deeper spiritual principle behind Phinehas still remains alive.
God still honors holy zeal. God still hates destructive compromise. God still calls His people to confront sin before it destroys entire communities.
Only now the battlefield is primarily spiritual.
The terrifying reality is that many believers today no longer know the difference between peace and avoidance.
We call silence peace. We call compromise love. We call apathy maturity. We call moral surrender compassion.
But sometimes what looks peaceful externally is actually spiritual decay internally.

A father watches pornography in secret while leading family devotions. A worship leader lives in hidden adultery while singing about holiness. A church protects reputation more than repentance. A believer slowly starves spiritually while pretending everything is fine online.
And eventually entire souls become divided.
This is why the story of Phinehas still unsettles us. Because it confronts a generation that wants comfort without consecration.
We want covenant blessings without covenant surrender. We want resurrection without crucifixion. We want peace without repentance.
But biblical peace is never built upon protected rebellion.
Jesus Himself said:
“Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth. I did not come to bring peace but a sword.” — Matthew 10:34
Christ was not endorsing violence. He was revealing that truth divides. The Gospel exposes. The Kingdom confronts darkness. Real peace sometimes arrives only after deep spiritual surgery.
The cross itself proves this.
Calvary was violent. Brutal. Bloody. Unimaginably painful.
And yet through that violence came eternal peace between God and humanity.
Isaiah prophesied:
מוּסַר שְׁלוֹמֵנוּ עָלָיו (Musar shelomenu alav)
“The chastisement for our peace was upon Him.” — Isaiah 53:5
Jesus absorbed judgment so covenant peace could be offered to sinners.
This is why Phinehas ultimately points beyond himself.
He foreshadows the seriousness of sin. He foreshadows covenant zeal. He foreshadows the necessity of judgment. But Jesus fulfills the story at a far greater level.
Phinehas stopped a plague temporarily. Christ conquered the plague of sin eternally.
Phinehas used a spear. Jesus received one.
Phinehas stood between the living and the dead. Jesus became the bridge between holy God and dying humanity.
And maybe this is the part that reaches deepest into modern hearts.

Many people reading this are exhausted from hidden compromise. Not always dramatic rebellion. Sometimes just slow spiritual drifting. A cold prayer life. Secret addictions. Unforgiveness. Bitterness. Double lives. A soul smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
And somewhere inside you, you know God has been confronting you for a long time.
Not to destroy you. To save you.
Because conviction is not hatred. Conviction is rescue.
The same God who judged Israel is the same God who sent His Son for sinners. The same God who confronted compromise is the same God who stretches out mercy.
But mercy was never permission to remain chained.
There are moments when God’s love feels comforting. There are other moments when God’s love feels like surgery. Phinehas reminds us of the second kind.
Some compromises cannot be gently negotiated forever. Some spiritual infections must finally be confronted. Some hidden things must die so the soul can live again.
And that is why this story still matters.
Not because Christians are called to physical violence. We are not.
But because believers are still called to radical holiness in a dying world.
Romans 8:13 says:
“For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.”
Notice the language. Put to death.
The New Testament still carries spiritual severity. Not against people. Against sin. Against the corruption destroying souls from within.
The war is internal now. The spear becomes repentance. Confession. Truth. Surrender. Radical obedience. Cutting off what destroys intimacy with God.
And when believers finally surrender fully to Christ, something beautiful happens.
The plague stops.
Not because we became perfect. But because grace entered honestly confessed weakness.
Some of the most peaceful believers are not the ones who never fought sin. They are the ones who finally stopped defending it.
That is covenant peace.
Not pretending darkness does not exist. But allowing God to cleanse what we could never heal ourselves.

Maybe that is why this ancient story still feels so piercing. Because deep down many people know exactly what it feels like to carry hidden compromise while outwardly trying to appear spiritually alive.
And maybe you are tired. Tired of hiding. Tired of performing. Tired of carrying spiritual infections nobody else can see.
Jesus Christ is still able to cleanse what sin corrupted. Still able to restore what compromise damaged. Still able to heal what shame buried.
But healing begins where honesty starts.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
And send this to someone who has been slowly drifting spiritually but pretending everything is okay. Some people do not need another motivational speech. They need awakening.
It was meant to bring you back alive.
The most dangerous compromises are usually the ones we learned to survive with.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Binigyan si Phinehas ng Tipan ng Kapayapaan Matapos ang Karahasan
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na hindi madaling basahin.

Mga tagpong parang tumatagos sa dibdib. Mga kwentong hindi basta nagbibigay ng comfort kundi gumigising. Mga sandaling pinipilit tayong harapin ang katotohanan tungkol sa kasalanan, kabanalan, at Diyos.
Isa sa mga iyon ang kwento ni Phinehas.
Isang sibat. Isang pampublikong pagpatay. Isang salot. At pagkatapos… isang bagay na tila imposibleng maintindihan.
Binigyan siya ng Diyos ng tipan ng kapayapaan.
Kapayapaan.
Hindi parusa. Hindi pagsaway. Hindi pagkondena. Kapayapaan.
At dito nagsisimula ang pagkalito ng maraming tao.
Paano naging kapayapaan ang bunga ng karahasan? Paano naging pagpapala ang isang marahas na tagpo? Paano pwedeng parang pinuri ng Diyos ang ginawa ni Phinehas?
Pero baka ang mas malalim na tanong ay ito:
Gaano na kalalim ang pagkasira ng Israel para umabot sa ganoong sitwasyon?
Dahil ang Bilang 25 ay hindi simpleng kwento tungkol sa karahasan. Ito ay kwento tungkol sa isang bansang unti-unting namamatay espirituwal habang nagpapanggap pa ring bayan ng Diyos.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… parang pamilyar iyon ngayon.
Ang Israel ay hindi lang gumagawa ng personal na kasalanan. Unti-unti silang hinihigop ng idolatriya. Ang bayan na iniligtas ng Diyos mula sa Egypt ay nakipag-isa na ngayon kay Baal-peor.
Ganito ang sabi ng Hebrew text:
וַיִּצָּמֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַעַל פְּעוֹר (Vayyitzamed Yisra’el l’Ba‘al Pe‘or)
“Ang Israel ay nakiisa kay Baal-peor.” — Bilang 25:3
Ang salitang וַיִּצָּמֶד (vayyitzamed) ay napakalalim. Ibig sabihin nito ay dumikit, ikabit, itali, o makipagbuklod.
Hindi ito simpleng tukso. Hindi ito maliit na pagkakamali.
Ito ay covenant-level attachment.
Ikinakabit ng Israel ang sarili nila sa ibang diyos.
Nagsimula sa tukso. Nauwi sa pagsamba. Nagsimula sa laman. Nauwi sa pagkawasak ng espiritu.
At habang nangyayari iyon, nagsimulang bumagsak ang buong kampo.
Ang salot na dumating ay hindi random na galit. Ito ay covenant judgment.
Sa pananaw ng Lumang Tipan, ang tipan sa Diyos ang mismong buhay ng bayan. Kapag iniwan nila ang Diyos, hindi lang iyon moral failure. Iyon ay spiritual suicide.

Kaya napakabigat ng eksena. Habang umiiyak si Moises at ang mga pinuno sa harap ng Tabernakulo… habang may mga taong namamatay dahil sa salot… may isang lalaking nagngangalang Zimri na hayagang nagdala ng isang Midianitang babae sa loob ng kampo.
Hindi lihim. Hindi nahihiya. Hayagan. Mapanghamon.
Parang wala siyang pakialam sa kabanalan ng Diyos. Parang wala siyang pakialam sa mga taong namamatay.
Isipin mo ang bigat noon. May umiiyak. May namamatay. May paghuhukom. Pero may mga tao pa ring proud sa kasalanang sumisira sa buong bayan.
At iyon ang eksenang nadatnan ni Phinehas.
Maraming modernong pagbasa ang tinatanggal ang emotional weight ng kwento. Pero hindi iyon ginawa ng Biblia.
Hindi ipinakita si Phinehas bilang isang taong uhaw sa dugo. Hindi siya inilarawan bilang brutal na mamamatay-tao.
Sa halip, isang salita ang ginamit para ipaliwanag ang kanyang puso:
קִנְאָה (qin’ah)
Zeal.
Pero ang zeal sa Hebrew ay mas malalim kaysa simpleng emosyon. Ibig sabihin nito ay covenant passion. Burning devotion. Jealous protection.
Ito rin ang salitang ginagamit minsan para ilarawan ang Diyos.
Exodus 34:14:
כִּי יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ (Ki YHWH qanna shemo)
“Sapagkat ang Panginoon, na ang pangalan ay Seloso, ay isang selosong Diyos.”
Hindi ito insecure na selos. Ito ay banal na pag-ibig na ayaw hayaang sirain ng kasalanan ang relasyon ng Kanyang bayan sa Kanya.
At iyon ang zeal na nakita kay Phinehas.
Hindi niya sinimulan ang karahasan. Pinigilan niya ang karahasang sumisira na sa Israel.
Dahil ang salot ay karahasan. Ang idolatriya ay karahasan. Ang pagkasira ng covenant ay karahasan. Ang espirituwal na pagkabulok ay karahasan.
Hindi ang sibat ang nagsimula ng kamatayan. Ang sibat ang nagpahinto rito.
Ganito ang sabi sa Bilang 25:11:
פִּינְחָס... הֵשִׁיב אֶת־חֲמָתִי (Pinchas... heshiv et-chamati)
“Si Phinehas… ay nagpahupa ng Aking poot.”
Huminto ang paghuhukom. Tumigil ang salot.
At pagkatapos ay dumating ang nakakagulat na pangako.
הִנְנִי נֹתֵן לוֹ אֶת־בְּרִיתִי שָׁלוֹם (Hineni noten lo et-beriti shalom)
“Binibigyan Ko siya ng Aking tipan ng kapayapaan.” — Bilang 25:12
Kapayapaan. Shalom.
Pero ang shalom sa Biblia ay hindi lang katahimikan. Hindi lang emotional comfort.
Ang ibig sabihin nito ay wholeness. Restoration. Kaayusan. Buhay na nakaayon muli sa Diyos.
Hindi pinupuri ng Diyos ang dugo. Pinapanumbalik Niya ang covenant bago tuluyang mamatay ang buong bayan.
At dito kailangang maghinay-hinay ang mga modernong mambabasa.
Hindi ibig sabihin nito na dapat gayahin ng mga Kristiyano ngayon si Phinehas sa pisikal na paraan. Hindi.
Si Phinehas ay nabuhay sa ilalim ng covenant nation ng Israel kung saan may direktang divine judgment.

Sa Bagong Tipan, ibang paraan na ang ipinakita ni Cristo. Pinagsabihan ni Jesus si Pedro nang gumamit ito ng espada. Ang mga apostol ay hindi nagpalaganap ng Kaharian gamit ang dahas kundi gamit ang katotohanan, pag-ibig, sakripisyo, at pagtitiis.
Pero ang prinsipyo sa likod ng kwento ni Phinehas ay buhay pa rin.

Galit pa rin ang Diyos sa kasalanang sumisira ng kaluluwa. Mahalaga pa rin sa Diyos ang kabanalan. Tinatawag pa rin Niya ang Kanyang bayan na harapin ang kompromiso bago sila tuluyang mamatay espirituwal.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… marami sa atin ang hindi na alam ang kaibahan ng tunay na kapayapaan at simpleng pag-iwas.
Tinatawag nating peace ang pananahimik. Tinatawag nating love ang compromise. Tinatawag nating wisdom ang pagiging lukewarm.
Pero minsan, ang mukhang payapa sa labas ay unti-unti nang nabubulok sa loob.

Isang ama na lihim na nalululong sa pornography habang nagtuturo ng Bible verse sa pamilya. Isang worship leader na may tinatagong relasyon habang umaawit tungkol sa holiness. Isang Kristiyanong nakangiti online pero gabi-gabing umiiyak sa guilt.
Unti-unting naghahati ang kaluluwa.
Kaya mabigat pa rin ang kwento ni Phinehas hanggang ngayon. Dahil tinatamaan nito ang isang henerasyong gusto ng comfort pero ayaw ng consecration.
Gusto natin ng blessing pero ayaw natin ng surrender. Gusto natin ng peace pero ayaw natin ng repentance.
Pero ang tunay na kapayapaan ay hindi itinataas sa ibabaw ng tinatagong rebellion.
Maging si Jesus ay nagsabi:
“Huwag ninyong isipin na naparito Ako upang magdala ng kapayapaan sa lupa. Hindi kapayapaan kundi tabak.” — Mateo 10:34
Hindi ibig sabihin nito na gusto ni Jesus ng karahasan. Ipinapakita Niya na ang katotohanan ay naghihiwalay. Ang liwanag ay naglalantad ng dilim.
Minsan, bago dumating ang tunay na kapayapaan, kailangang may spiritual surgery muna.
At iyon mismo ang nangyari sa krus.
Ang Calvary ay marahas. Madugo. Masakit.
Pero mula roon dumating ang eternal peace sa pagitan ng Diyos at tao.
Sinabi ni Isaias:
מוּסַר שְׁלוֹמֵנוּ עָלָיו (Musar shelomenu alav)
“Ang parusa para sa ating kapayapaan ay nasa Kanya.” — Isaias 53:5
Inako ni Jesus ang paghuhukom para maibigay sa atin ang kapayapaan.
Kaya sa mas malalim na paraan, itinuturo tayo ni Phinehas kay Cristo.
Si Phinehas ay pansamantalang nagpahinto ng salot. Si Jesus ang tuluyang sumira sa kapangyarihan ng kasalanan.
Si Phinehas ay gumamit ng sibat. Si Jesus ay tinanggap ang sibat.
Si Phinehas ay tumayo sa pagitan ng buhay at kamatayan. Si Cristo ang naging tulay sa pagitan ng banal na Diyos at makasalanang tao.
At baka ito ang pinakamasakit na bahagi para sa maraming nagbabasa nito.
Marami ang pagod na. Pagod magpanggap. Pagod magtago. Pagod dalhin ang mga lihim na kasalanan na walang ibang nakakaalam.
At sa kaibuturan ng puso mo, alam mong matagal ka nang kinakausap ng Diyos.
Hindi para sirain ka. Kundi para iligtas ka.
Dahil ang conviction ay hindi hate. Conviction is rescue.
Ang parehong Diyos na humatol sa Israel ay Siya ring Diyos na nagpadala kay Jesus para iligtas ang mga makasalanan.
Pero ang biyaya ay hindi pahintulot para manatiling nakakadena.
May mga compromise na hindi na pwedeng alagaan habambuhay. May mga kasalanang kailangang putulin. May mga bagay na kailangang mamatay para muling mabuhay ang kaluluwa.
Kaya mahalaga pa rin ang kwento ni Phinehas.
Hindi dahil tinatawag tayong manakit ng tao. Hindi.
Kundi dahil tinatawag pa rin ang mga Kristiyano sa radical holiness sa mundong unti-unting namamatay.
Sabi sa Roma 8:13:
“Sapagkat kung nabubuhay kayo ayon sa laman, kayo ay mamamatay; ngunit kung sa pamamagitan ng Espiritu ay pinapatay ninyo ang mga gawa ng katawan, kayo ay mabubuhay.”
Pansinin ang salita. Pinapatay.
Sa Bagong Tipan, ang laban ay spiritual na. Ang sibat ngayon ay repentance. Confession. Truth. Surrender. Pagputol sa anumang sumisira sa intimacy natin sa Diyos.
At kapag tuluyan nang sumuko ang tao kay Cristo, may nangyayaring maganda.
Humihinto ang salot.
Hindi dahil naging perfect tayo. Kundi dahil pumasok ang biyaya sa wakas sa isang pusong naging tapat.
Ang pinaka-payapang mga mananampalataya ay hindi iyong mga hindi nakipaglaban sa kasalanan. Kundi iyong mga tumigil nang ipagtanggol ito.
Iyon ang covenant peace.
Hindi pagtatago ng dilim. Kundi pagpapalinis kay Cristo.
At baka kaya sobrang tumatagos pa rin ang kwentong ito hanggang ngayon… dahil maraming tao ang alam ang pakiramdam ng mukhang buhay sa labas pero unti-unti nang namamatay sa loob.
Pero si Jesus ay marunong pa ring magpagaling. Marunong pa ring maglinis. Marunong pa ring magpanumbalik.
Pero nagsisimula ang healing sa honesty.
Maging totoo ka. Tinamaan ka nito nang mas malalim kaysa inaakala mo.
May mga taong hindi na kailangan ng motivation. Kailangan nila ng awakening.
Ito ay para ibalik kang buhay.
Ang pinaka-mapanganib na compromise ay kadalasan iyong mga kasalanang natutunan na nating pakisamahan.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Shimei Cursed David While He Was Fleeing
paragraphs: Why Shimei Cursed David While He Was Fleeing
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully human.
Not polished. Not heroic. Not cinematic in the triumphant way people expect from “a man after God’s own heart.”
This was not David standing over Goliath. This was not David dancing before the Ark. This was not David writing worship songs beneath starlit skies.
This was David barefoot. Broken. Publicly humiliated. Weeping while fleeing Jerusalem.
And from the side of a dusty road came a man named Shimei screaming curses at the king.
Not whispers. Not subtle insults. Curses. Violent accusations. Public shame. Mockery while David was already bleeding emotionally.
And strangely… God allowed it.
That is what makes this story unforgettable.
Because if we are honest, many of us know exactly what it feels like to be wounded while already weak.
To be attacked when we are already exhausted. To be falsely accused while carrying real guilt. To be humiliated in front of others. To watch people kick us while we are already on the ground.
This moment in 2 Samuel is not merely ancient history. It is a mirror.
And hidden inside this heartbreaking scene is one of the deepest revelations about conviction, consequences, mercy, and the sovereignty of God.
The story begins during one of the darkest seasons of David’s life.
His own son, Absalom, had stolen the hearts of Israel. The prince had slowly manipulated the nation until a rebellion exploded against his father.
David was forced to flee Jerusalem to avoid civil war.
Imagine the emotional devastation.
The same king who once conquered giants was now escaping his own palace. The warrior who defeated enemies now watched his own household collapse.
And this was not random.
The roots of this tragedy reached back to David’s sin with Bathsheba.
When David committed adultery and orchestrated the death of Uriah, the prophet Nathan delivered a terrifying judgment from God:
“Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house.” — 2 Samuel 12:10
The Hebrew phrase used for “sword” is:
חֶרֶב (chereb)
It does not merely imply violence. It carries the imagery of devastation, destruction, warfare, and ongoing conflict.
David had been forgiven. But forgiveness did not erase earthly consequences.
That truth alone shatters modern shallow Christianity.
Many people want pardon without transformation. Grace without repentance. Mercy without consequences.
But Scripture never teaches that forgiven sin leaves no scars.
David was still loved by God. Still chosen. Still covenant-protected. Still redeemed.
Yet the ripple effects of sin were now tearing through his family.
And while David fled Jerusalem, another storm was waiting.
2 Samuel 16:5 says:
“And when king David came to Bahurim, behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei.”
Shimei belonged to Saul’s family line.
That detail matters deeply.

Because David’s rise to the throne had meant Saul’s dynasty lost power. Though David repeatedly refused to murder Saul, many from Saul’s household still viewed David as the destroyer of their family legacy.
Bitterness had likely been fermenting inside Shimei for years.
And now David looked vulnerable. Weak. Defeated. Exposed.
So Shimei unleashed everything he had buried in his heart.
Scripture says:
“And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial.” — 2 Samuel 16:7
The phrase “bloody man” comes from the Hebrew:
אִישׁ הַדָּמִים (ish ha-damim)
Literally: “man of bloods.”
This expression implied bloodguilt. A man stained by violence. A man carrying blood on his hands.
Then Shimei calls David:
אִישׁ הַבְּלִיַּעַל (ish ha-beliya'al)
Often translated “worthless man,” “wicked man,” or “man of Belial.”
The Hebrew concept of Belial referred to moral corruption, rebellion, lawlessness, and spiritual worthlessness.
This was not casual mockery. Shimei was publicly declaring David evil. Corrupt. Unworthy of kingship.
And then the accusations escalated.
“The LORD hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul.” — 2 Samuel 16:8
Ironically, this accusation was largely false.
David had repeatedly spared Saul. He mourned Saul’s death. He punished those who claimed to kill Saul. He even showed kindness to Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson.
Shimei’s accusations were distorted. Twisted. Emotionally fueled.
But here is what makes the scene spiritually terrifying.
Inside Shimei’s false accusations was still a painful shadow of truth.
David was not guilty of Saul’s blood. But David was guilty of bloodshed elsewhere.
Uriah’s blood.
And perhaps that is why David did not react defensively.
Because convicted people often recognize they deserve judgment somewhere… even when a specific accusation is inaccurate.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Sometimes the enemy accuses us unfairly. But sometimes the reason those accusations wound us so deeply is because there are other hidden areas where conviction already exists.
A person may falsely attack your motives. But maybe you know your heart has been drifting.
A person may exaggerate your failures. But maybe you know there are sins you never fully surrendered.
Shimei was wrong in specifics. But David knew he was not innocent before God.
That changes everything.
Then comes one of the most explosive moments in the story.
Abishai, David’s warrior, could not tolerate the disrespect.
“Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head.” — 2 Samuel 16:9
This was ancient warfare language. Abishai was essentially asking permission for immediate execution.
And honestly? Most leaders would have allowed it.
David had authority. Power. Loyal soldiers.
He could have silenced Shimei instantly.
But David responded with shocking restraint.
“What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? so let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David.” — 2 Samuel 16:10
This verse has confused readers for centuries.
Did God literally command Shimei to sin? No.
Scripture consistently teaches that God is holy and does not author evil.
The Hebrew understanding here is far deeper.
David recognized God’s sovereignty even over painful circumstances.
The Hebrew phrase:
יְהוָה אָמַר לוֹ קַלֵּל (YHWH amar lo qalel)
Literally: “Yahweh has said to him, curse.”
This reflects the biblical worldview that nothing touches God’s people outside His sovereign allowance.
David saw beyond Shimei. He saw the hand of God allowing humiliation as discipline.
That level of spiritual maturity is rare.
Most people spend their lives fighting human enemies while never asking whether God is trying to expose something deeper.
David understood something devastating: Sometimes God allows painful voices because pride still survives inside us.
And then David says something that breaks the heart:
“It may be that the LORD will look on mine affliction, and that the LORD will requite me good for his cursing this day.” — 2 Samuel 16:12
The Hebrew word for “affliction” here is:
עָוֹן (avon) in some manuscript traditions and interpretive connections, though many translations render the surrounding sense as misery, humiliation, or suffering.
The broader biblical concept of avon is powerful. It refers not only to sin itself but also the guilt and consequences carried from sin.
David was not merely enduring insults. He was carrying the crushing weight of consequence.
And this is where the Gospel quietly begins to emerge.
Because centuries later, another King would walk toward humiliation.
Another Son of David.
Another innocent King would be mocked publicly while enemies hurled accusations.
Except Jesus truly was innocent.
Isaiah prophesied:
“He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth.” — Isaiah 53:7
When Jesus stood before His accusers, He absorbed shame without retaliation.
The Greek word used repeatedly in the New Testament for reviling and insult is:
λοιδορέω (loidoreó)
Meaning: To abuse verbally. To insult. To heap disgrace upon.
1 Peter 2:23 says of Christ:
“Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again.”
David partially reflected this posture. Jesus fulfilled it perfectly.
This is why the story of Shimei matters far beyond ancient politics.
It exposes the human heart.

Shimei reveals what bitterness becomes when left unchecked. David reveals what conviction looks like when pride breaks. Abishai reveals our natural instinct toward revenge. And Jesus reveals the final perfect response to injustice.
But the story does not end there.
Years later, after Absalom’s rebellion collapsed, Shimei panicked.
He realized David was returning as king.
Suddenly the man who threw stones now fell at David’s feet begging for mercy.
Isn’t that human nature?
People curse you when they think you are finished. Then change their tone when they realize God was not done with you.
And astonishingly… David showed mercy.
Again.
That mercy reflected the heart of God.
Because the Gospel is not merely about exposing sinners. It is about transforming them.
Every one of us has been Shimei at some point.
We have spoken carelessly. Judged wrongly. Held bitterness. Misrepresented people. Cursed others in our hearts.
And every one of us has also been David.
Broken. Exposed. Ashamed. Facing consequences. Trying to survive seasons we created ourselves.
But above both stands Jesus Christ.
The true King. The innocent sufferer. The final Redeemer.
The One who carried not His own guilt… but ours.
The Hebrew prophet Isaiah declared:
“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows.” — Isaiah 53:4
The Hebrew word for “borne” is:
נָשָׂא (nasa)
Meaning: To lift. To carry. To bear away.
Jesus carried what would have crushed us forever.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement. Not religious performance. Not pretending to be spiritually strong.
It is surrender. Repentance. Grace. Mercy. Transformation.
Some people reading this are exhausted because you are fighting voices. Voices of shame. Voices of accusation. Voices from your past. Voices reminding you of failures.
And maybe some of those voices are unfair.
But maybe God is still using this season to draw you into deeper repentance, deeper humility, and deeper dependence on Him.
David did not lose his throne permanently. But he was changed by the valley.
And some of you are in that valley right now.
Crying privately. Smiling publicly. Trying to hold yourself together while your soul quietly bleeds.
Do not waste the wilderness.
God still speaks there.
And the same God who restored David through brokenness still restores sinners through Jesus Christ today.
And if this article exposed something buried deep inside your spirit, be honest about it.
Somebody else reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Some wounds are not destroying you. They are exposing the places where God is still rebuilding you.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Sinumpa ni Shimei si David Habang Tumatakas Siya
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na sobrang totoo.
Hindi makintab. Hindi parang perpektong pelikula. Hindi parang tagumpay na laging inaasahan ng mga tao mula kay David.
Hindi ito ang David na humarap kay Goliath. Hindi ito ang David na sumasayaw sa harap ng Kaban ng Tipan. Hindi ito ang David na sumusulat ng mga awit sa ilalim ng mga bituin.
Ito ang David na nakayapak. Wasak. Pinapahiya sa harap ng maraming tao. Umiiyak habang tumatakas palabas ng Jerusalem.
At habang naglalakad siya sa alikabok ng daan… may isang lalaking sumisigaw ng sumpa laban sa hari.
Ang pangalan niya ay Shimei.
Hindi simpleng insulto. Hindi pabulong na pangungutya. Kundi mabibigat na salita. Galit. Paghamak. Paglalantad.
At ang mas nakakagulat?
Hinayaan ito ng Diyos.
Diyan nagiging napakalalim ng kwentong ito.
Dahil kung magiging tapat tayo… marami sa atin ang nakaranas nang masaktan habang sugatan na.
Yung tipong pinapatay ka na nga ng problema… saka ka pa sisipain.
Yung tipong hirap ka nang huminga emotionally… tapos may mga taong lalo pang dudurog sa’yo.
At minsan ang pinakamasakit… may kaunting katotohanan ang ilan sa mga salitang ibinabato nila.
Ang kwento ni Shimei at David ay hindi lang lumang kasaysayan. Salamin ito ng puso ng tao.
Nagsimula ang lahat sa pinakamadilim na yugto ng buhay ni David.
Ang sarili niyang anak na si Absalom ay naghimagsik laban sa kanya. Unti-unti niyang ninakaw ang puso ng Israel hanggang sa bumaligtad ang bayan laban sa hari.
Napilitang tumakas si David mula sa Jerusalem.
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang dating mandirigmang kinatatakutan ng mga kaaway… ngayon tumatakbo para iligtas ang sariling buhay.
At hindi ito aksidente.
Ang sakit na ito ay may ugat.
Bumabalik ito sa kasalanan ni David kay Bathsheba.
Nang mangalunya si David at ipapatay si Uriah, nagsalita ang propetang si Nathan:
“Ngayon nga’y hindi hihiwalay ang tabak sa iyong sambahayan.” — 2 Samuel 12:10
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “tabak” ay:
חֶרֶב (chereb)
Hindi lamang ito literal na espada. Larawan ito ng tuloy-tuloy na kaguluhan, sugat, digmaan, at pagkawasak.
Pinatawad si David. Pero hindi ibig sabihin noon ay mawawala lahat ng bunga ng kasalanan.
Ito ang katotohanang ayaw tanggapin ng maraming tao ngayon.
Gusto ng iba ng grasya na walang pagsisisi. Kapatawaran na walang pagbabago. Kaligtasan na walang pagsuko.
Pero hindi ganoon ang Biblia.
Oo, mahal pa rin ng Diyos si David. Pinili pa rin siya. Hindi siya iniwan ng Panginoon.
Pero ang epekto ng kasalanan ay dumaan pa rin sa kanyang pamilya.
Habang tumatakas si David, dumating si Shimei.
Sinasabi ng 2 Samuel 16:5:
“At nang dumating ang haring si David sa Bahurim, naroon ang isang lalaking mula sa sambahayan ni Saul, na ang pangalan ay Shimei.”
Mahalaga iyon.
Dahil si Shimei ay kabilang sa pamilya ni Saul.
Para sa kanila, si David ang dahilan kung bakit bumagsak ang kanilang angkan.
Kahit paulit-ulit na iniligtas ni David si Saul noon… marami pa rin ang may lihim na galit laban sa kanya.
At ngayon nakita ni Shimei ang hari na mahina. Pagod. Wasak. Humiliated.
Kaya ibinuhos niya lahat ng lason na matagal nang nakatago sa puso niya.
“At ganito ang sabi ni Shimei habang siya’y sumusumpa, Lumayas ka, lumayas ka, ikaw na taong mabagsik at walang kabuluhan!” — 2 Samuel 16:7
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “taong mabagsik” ay:
אִישׁ הַדָּמִים (ish ha-damim)
Literal: “taong may dugo.”
Paratang ito na si David ay mamamatay-tao. Duguan. May kasalanang dugo.
Tinawag din siyang:
אִישׁ הַבְּלִיַּעַל (ish ha-beliya'al)
Ibig sabihin: masama, walang kwenta, rebeldeng tao.
Hindi biro ang ginagawa ni Shimei.
Pinapahiya niya ang hari sa harap ng lahat.
Pagkatapos sinabi pa niya:
“Ibinabalik ng PANGINOON sa iyo ang lahat ng dugo ng sambahayan ni Saul.” — 2 Samuel 16:8
At dito nagiging komplikado ang kwento.
Dahil technically… mali si Shimei.
Hindi pinatay ni David si Saul. Ipinagluluksa pa nga niya ito. Pinarusahan pa niya ang mga nagsabing sila ang pumatay kay Saul.
Pero kahit mali si Shimei sa detalye… may masakit pa ring katotohanan.
Hindi man dugo ni Saul ang problema ni David… may dugo pa rin siyang pasan.
Dugo ni Uriah.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit hindi lumaban si David.
Kapag ang isang tao ay totoong kinokonsensya ng Diyos… minsan alam niyang may mali talaga sa puso niya kahit hindi eksaktong tama ang paratang ng tao.
At dito tumatama nang malalim ang kwentong ito.
Minsan may mga taong mali ang sinasabi tungkol sa atin. Pero bakit sobrang sakit?
Dahil baka may ibang bahagi ng puso natin na alam nating hindi pa maayos sa Diyos.
Minsan unfair ang accusation. Pero may hidden conviction.
Minsan exaggerated ang paninira. Pero may lihim tayong kasalanan na matagal nang tinatago.
Alam iyon ni David.
Pagkatapos, gustong ipagtanggol ni Abishai si David.
“Bakit susumpain ng patay na asong ito ang aking panginoong hari? Hayaan mo akong pugutan siya ng ulo.” — 2 Samuel 16:9
At kung tutuusin?
Kayang-kaya ni David ipapatay si Shimei. Hari siya. May sundalo siya. May kapangyarihan siya.
Pero ang sagot ni David ay nakakagulat.
“Hayaan ninyo siya. Hayaan ninyong siya’y sumumpa, sapagkat sinabi ng PANGINOON sa kanya, ‘Sumpain mo si David.’” — 2 Samuel 16:10
Hindi ibig sabihin nito na ang Diyos ang may-akda ng kasalanan.
Ang ibig sabihin nito: Naiintindihan ni David na kahit ang sakit na ito ay pinahintulutan ng Diyos.
Nakikita niya ang kamay ng Diyos kahit sa gitna ng kahihiyan.
Napakalalim niyon.
Karamihan kasi sa atin… tao agad ang kalaban.
Hindi natin tinatanong: “Panginoon, may gusto Ka bang ituwid sa puso ko?”
Naintindihan ni David: Minsan ginagamit ng Diyos ang masasakit na season para durugin ang pride.
Pagkatapos sinabi ni David ang isa sa pinakamabigat na linya sa buong kwento:
“Marahil ay titingnan ng PANGINOON ang aking paghihirap at gagantihan Niya ako ng mabuti kapalit ng sumpa niya ngayon.” — 2 Samuel 16:12
Hindi na lumaban si David. Hindi na siya nagtanggol sa sarili.
Broken na siya.
At dito nagsisimulang sumilip ang larawan ni Jesus.
Dahil makalipas ang maraming taon… may isa pang Hari na lalakad patungo sa kahihiyan.
Isa pang Anak ni David.
Si Jesus.
Pinagtawanan. Ininsulto. Pinagbintangan. Dinuraan. Sinampal.
Pero hindi Siya gumanti.
Sinasabi sa 1 Pedro 2:23:
“Nang siya’y alipustain, hindi siya gumanti ng pag-alipusta.”
Ang salitang Griyego para rito ay:
λοιδορέω (loidoreó)
Ibig sabihin: insultuhin, laitin, pahiyain.
Bahagyang ipinakita ni David ang ugaling ito. Pero si Jesus ang perpektong katuparan nito.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napakahalaga ng kwento ni Shimei.

Ipinapakita nito kung ano ang nagagawa ng bitterness. Ipinapakita nito kung ano ang itsura ng pusong dinudurog ng conviction. Ipinapakita nito ang natural na desire ng tao para sa revenge. At ipinapakita nito ang awa ng Diyos.
Dahil kalaunan… nang bumalik si David bilang hari, natakot si Shimei.
Yung lalaking dati’y nagtatapon ng bato… ngayon nakaluhod at humihingi ng awa.
At nakakagulat… pinatawad siya ni David.
Ganyan ang Diyos.
Hindi lang Siya Diyos ng judgment. Siya rin ay Diyos ng awa.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… minsan tayo si Shimei.
Nanghusga. Nagsalita nang masama. Nagkimkim ng galit. Nagbitaw ng salitang nakasakit.
At minsan tayo rin si David.
Pagod. Wasak. Punong-puno ng guilt. Nahihirapang huminga emotionally.
Pero higit sa lahat… kailangan natin si Jesus.
Siya ang tunay na Hari. Siya ang walang kasalanan. Siya ang nagdala ng ating kahihiyan sa krus.
Sabi sa Isaias 53:4:
“Tunay na kaniyang dinala ang ating mga kapanglawan at pinasan ang ating mga kalungkutan.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “dinala” ay:
נָשָׂא (nasa)
Ibig sabihin: buhatin, pasanin, dalhin palayo.
Dinala ni Jesus ang bigat na dapat tayo ang magbayad magpakailanman.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi simpleng religion. Hindi performance. Hindi pagpapanggap na okay ka.
Kundi repentance. Pagsuko. Pagbabago. Biyaya. Kapatawaran.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod na pagod na.
Pagod nang lumaban. Pagod magpanggap. Pagod ngumiti kahit wasak na sa loob.
At baka itong season mo ngayon… hindi para sirain ka. Kundi para baguhin ka ng Diyos.
Huwag mong sayangin ang wilderness.
Minsan doon pinakamatinding nagsasalita ang Diyos.
At kung tinamaan ka nito nang malalim… maging totoo ka.
Baka ang testimony mo ang kailangan basahin ng ibang taong malapit nang sumuko.
Minsan ang sakit ay hindi ipinadala para tapusin ka. Kundi para ilantad kung anong bahagi ng puso mo ang gusto pang pagalingin ng Diyos.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story About Noah
paragraphs: The Untold Story About Noah
Most people think they know Noah.
An old man. A boat. Rain. Animals. A rainbow.
A children’s story painted onto nursery walls.
But Scripture does not present Noah as a bedtime story.
It presents him as a warning.
And maybe the most terrifying part of Noah’s story is not the flood.
Maybe it is how normal everybody felt before judgment came.
Because people were eating. Laughing. Building. Planning vacations. Getting married. Making money. Posting memories. Living life.
And not one of them believed the man building the ark.
Until the sky broke open.
Jesus Himself said:
“Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man.” — Luke 17:26
That means Noah’s story is not ancient history.
It is prophecy wearing yesterday’s clothes.
And if we are honest… many of us are closer to Noah’s generation than we want to admit.
The Bible says in Genesis 6:5:
“The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
The Hebrew language here is haunting.
The phrase “every intention” comes from the Hebrew word "יֵצֶר" (yetser), meaning formation, imagination, impulse, or inward shaping.
This was not merely sinful behavior.
Humanity’s inner world itself had become corrupted.
Their desires were diseased. Their imagination was infected. Their thoughts bent toward darkness continually.
Not occasionally. Not accidentally. Continually.
And the terrifying reality is this:
You can look successful while your soul quietly rots.
You can appear civilized while becoming spiritually violent.
Genesis says:
“Now the earth was corrupt in God’s sight, and the earth was filled with violence.” — Genesis 6:11
The Hebrew word for violence is “חָמָס” (ḥāmās).
It means brutality. Corruption. Destruction. Injustice. Cruelty.
Not just physical violence. A violent way of living. A violent way of using people. A violent culture that consumes innocence.
And suddenly Noah’s generation does not feel ancient anymore.
Because today people destroy each other emotionally. Spiritually. Digitally. Sexually. Financially. Psychologically.
People smile in public while secretly bleeding people dry behind closed doors.
And Scripture says God saw all of it.
Every hidden addiction. Every betrayal. Every abuse. Every secret conversation. Every hidden browser tab. Every fake version of ourselves we perform for applause.
Nothing escaped His sight.
Then suddenly, in the middle of worldwide corruption, one verse appears like lightning in darkness.
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.” — Genesis 6:8
Grace.
The Hebrew word is “חֵן” (chen).
Favor. Kindness. Acceptance.
Noah was not sinless. But Noah walked differently.
Genesis 6:9 says:
“Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God.”
The phrase “walked with God” in Hebrew carries the idea of ongoing movement and intimate fellowship.
Noah did not occasionally acknowledge God. He lived in step with Him.
And imagine how lonely that must have been.
Everybody else was moving one direction. Noah walked another.
Everybody else mocked holiness. Noah obeyed anyway.
Everybody else lived for the moment. Noah built for eternity.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because obedience to God will often make you look foolish before it makes sense.
Imagine building an ark while the world laughed.
Imagine hammering wood day after day while people mocked your faith.
Imagine preaching righteousness while nobody listened.
2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah “a preacher of righteousness.”
That means Noah did not merely build silently. He warned people.
For decades.
And nobody cared.
Can you imagine the heartbreak?
Watching people reject salvation while you build the very thing that could rescue them.
That is still happening today.
Mock repentance. Laugh at holiness. Treat Jesus like optional inspiration instead of Lord.
But one day the door closed.
And this is one of the most chilling moments in all Scripture.
Genesis 7:16 says:
“And the LORD shut him in.”
God shut the door.
Not Noah.
There came a moment when mercy’s invitation ended.
And then the rain began.
The Hebrew language describes the “fountains of the deep” bursting open. Creation itself seemed to collapse.
Water from above. Water from beneath. Judgment everywhere.
And suddenly the same people mocking Noah were clawing at the ark.
Too late.
The terrifying truth about judgment is this:
Nobody believes it is real until it arrives.
Jesus warned this same blindness would exist before His return.
Matthew 24:38-39 says:

“For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away…”
They were unaware.
Not because Noah stayed silent.
Because people preferred comfort over truth.
And honestly… that still describes millions today.
People want motivation without repentance. Heaven without surrender. Blessings without holiness. Christian identity without crucifixion of the flesh.
But Noah’s ark was not merely a boat.
It was a shadow.
A prophetic picture.
The ark represents Christ.
There was only one ark. One door. One rescue.
Jesus later said:
“I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.” — John 10:9
There were not multiple arks for different beliefs. There was one.
And everybody outside it perished.
Modern culture hates exclusivity.
But Scripture is unapologetically clear.
Acts 4:12 says:
“There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.”
Jesus is not one option among many.
He is the ark.
And maybe that is why Noah’s story still unsettles people.
Because deep down, humanity does not mind a loving God.
What humanity resists is a holy God.
A God who judges evil. A God who confronts sin. A God who refuses to call darkness light.
Yet even in judgment, mercy was screaming.
The ark itself was mercy.
Every hammer strike was mercy. Every warning was mercy. Every year Noah preached was mercy.
And maybe you have been mistaking God’s patience for His absence.
2 Peter 3:9 says:
“The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise… but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.”
Repentance.
The Greek word is “μετάνοια” (metanoia).
It means a change of mind leading to a transformed life.
Not fake guilt. Not emotional performance. A true turning.
And maybe that is what this article is really about.
Not Noah.
You.
Because somewhere deep inside, many people are exhausted.
Tired of pretending. Tired of carrying hidden sin. Tired of performing strength. Tired of smiling while spiritually drowning.
And the Gospel is this:
Jesus still saves drowning people.
The cross was God’s rescue plan long before the floodwaters of judgment ever arrive.
Noah floated above judgment inside the ark.
Believers stand above condemnation inside Christ.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
In Christ.
Not in religion. Not in self-improvement. Not in church performance.
In Christ.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years near Christianity without truly surrendering.
You know Bible verses. You know church language. You know worship songs.
But you have never fully given God your heart.
Noah’s story confronts us with one painful reality:
Eventually the door closes.
Life is fragile.
Tomorrow is not promised.
One heartbeat separates people from eternity every single day.
And yet Jesus still invites.
Still forgives. Still restores. Still heals. Still rescues.
Even Peter connected Noah’s story to salvation.
1 Peter 3:20-21 compares the flood narrative to rescue through Christ.
The point was never merely surviving water.
The point was entering covenant relationship with God.
And after judgment came something astonishing.
A rainbow.
The Hebrew word is “קֶשֶׁת” (qeshet).
Interestingly, the same word can also mean a battle bow.
Ancient readers would recognize the imagery.
God symbolically hung up His bow.
A picture of mercy after wrath.
A covenant sign.
Not human pride. Not rebellion. Not self-glorification.
A reminder that God keeps His promises.
Always.
And maybe the most overlooked part of Noah’s story is this:
After surviving the flood… Noah still struggled.
Genesis later records Noah becoming drunk and lying uncovered in his tent.
Why would Scripture include that?
Because the Bible does not sanitize human brokenness.
Even righteous men need grace.
Noah was not the ultimate Savior.
Jesus is.
Noah points forward. Christ fulfills.
Only Jesus lived perfectly. Only Jesus conquered sin completely. Only Jesus defeated death.
The Gospel is not “be Noah.”
The Gospel is:
Run to the greater ark.
Run to Christ.
Because floods still come.
Not always literal water.
Sometimes depression. Sometimes addiction. Sometimes grief. Sometimes shame. Sometimes anxiety. Sometimes secret sin. Sometimes unbearable loneliness.
And people are drowning quietly every day.
But Jesus still reaches into impossible storms.
Still calms chaos. Still resurrects ruined lives. Still saves.
That is why this message matters.
Not for entertainment. For eternity.
And maybe somebody reading this feels exposed right now.
Not by condemnation. By truth.
Because deep down you know God has been calling you.
Not toward religion. Toward surrender.
Toward repentance. Toward healing. Toward freedom. Toward Himself.
And if this stirred something inside you… do not ignore it.
The same God who warned through Noah now extends grace through Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to stay unchanged.
Grace transforms.
Grace convicts.
Grace resurrects dead hearts.
Be honest.
How long have you been pretending everything is fine while your soul quietly collapses?
And if someone came to your mind while reading this… share this with them.
Some people are smiling publicly while drowning privately.
One day the world laughed at the ark… until the rain started falling.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikuwentong Bahagi ng Buhay ni Noah
Karamihan sa tao akala nila kilala na nila si Noah.
Matandang lalaki. Barko. Ulan. Mga hayop. Bahaghari.
Isang simpleng kuwentong pambata na ipinipinta sa dingding ng nursery.
Pero hindi ganoon ipinakita ng Bibliya si Noah.
Hindi ito bedtime story.
Babala ito.
At baka ang pinaka nakakatakot na bahagi ng kuwento ni Noah ay hindi ang baha.
Kundi kung gaano ka-normal ang pakiramdam ng mga tao bago dumating ang paghuhukom.
Kumakain sila. Tumatawa. Nagpaplano ng buhay. Nagpapakasal. Nagnenegosyo. Nagpapakasaya. Namumuhay na parang walang mangyayaring masama.
At walang naniwala sa lalaking gumagawa ng arka.
Hanggang sa bumukas ang langit.
Mismong si Jesus ang nagsabi:
“Kung paano nangyari noong panahon ni Noe, ganoon din sa pagdating ng Anak ng Tao.” — Lucas 17:26
Ibig sabihin… hindi lang ito lumang kasaysayan.
Propesiya ito na nakasuot ng lumang panahon.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… mas kahawig natin ang henerasyon ni Noah kaysa gusto nating aminin.
Sinasabi ng Genesis 6:5:
“Nakita ng Panginoon na laganap ang kasamaan ng tao sa lupa, at ang bawat haka ng pag-iisip ng kanyang puso ay pawang masama sa buong panahon.”
Sa Hebrew, ang salitang ginamit para sa “haka” o “imagination” ay “יֵצֶר” (yetser).
Ibig sabihin nito ay paghubog ng kalooban, imahinasyon, o pinakaloob na pagnanasa.
Hindi lang masama ang ginagawa ng tao noon.
Maging ang laman ng isip nila ay nabubulok na.
Nasira na ang pagnanasa. Nahawa na ang isip. Nakatuon na ang puso sa kasamaan.
Hindi paminsan-minsan.
Palagian.
At ang masakit na katotohanan?
Posibleng mukhang maayos ang buhay mo habang unti-unting nabubulok ang kaluluwa mo.
Posibleng mukhang successful ka pero spiritually patay ka na.
Sinasabi rin ng Genesis:
“Ang lupa ay tiwali sa paningin ng Diyos, at puno ng karahasan.” — Genesis 6:11
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “karahasan” ay “חָמָס” (ḥāmās).
Hindi lang ito pisikal na pananakit.
Kasama rito ang kalupitan. Pang-aabuso. Korapsyon. Pagsasamantala. Pagwasak sa kapwa.
At biglang parang hindi na malayo ang panahon ni Noah.
Dahil ngayon…
Sinisira ng tao ang isa’t isa emosyonal. Espiritwal. Sekswal. Mental. Pinansyal.
Maraming nakangiti sa social media pero wasak na pala sa loob.
At nakita ng Diyos ang lahat.
Lahat ng sikreto. Lahat ng pagtataksil. Lahat ng addiction. Lahat ng kasinungalingan. Lahat ng kasalanang tinatago sa dilim.
Walang nakatago sa Kanya.
Pero sa gitna ng napakalawak na kasamaan, may isang talatang parang ilaw sa gitna ng kadiliman.
“Ngunit si Noe ay kinalugdan ng Panginoon.” — Genesis 6:8
Ang salitang “kinalugdan” ay mula sa Hebrew na “חֵן” (chen).
Ibig sabihin:
biyaya, pabor, hindi karapat-dapat na kabutihan.
Hindi perpekto si Noah.
Pero iba siyang lumakad.
Sinasabi ng Genesis 6:9:
“Si Noe ay isang matuwid na tao… lumakad siyang kasama ng Diyos.”
Sa Hebrew, ang “lumakad kasama ng Diyos” ay hindi simpleng pagkilala lang sa Diyos.
Ibig sabihin nito ay araw-araw na pakikipamuhay kasama Siya.
At isipin mo kung gaano siya ka-lonely.
Lahat tumatawa sa kabanalan. Pero si Noah sumunod pa rin.
Lahat nabubuhay para sa pansamantalang kasiyahan. Pero si Noah naghanda para sa walang hanggan.
At dito nagiging personal ang kuwento.
Dahil ang pagsunod sa Diyos kadalasan magmumukhang kabaliwan bago ito magmukhang tama.
Isipin mo gumagawa ka ng napakalaking arka habang pinagtatawanan ka ng buong mundo.
Araw-araw kang nagpapako ng kahoy habang iniinsulto ang pananampalataya mo.
At hindi lang basta gumawa si Noah.
Nangaral siya.
Tinawag siya ng 2 Pedro 2:5 na “mangangaral ng katuwiran.”
Ibig sabihin… binalaan niya ang mga tao.
Paulit-ulit. Sa loob ng maraming taon.
Pero walang nakinig.
At hanggang ngayon nangyayari pa rin iyon.
Maraming tao dinadaan-daanan ang katotohanan. Pinagtatawanan ang repentance. Ginagawang optional si Jesus.
Pero dumating ang araw na nagsara ang pinto.
At isa ito sa pinaka chilling na bahagi ng Bibliya.
Genesis 7:16:
“At isinara siya ng Panginoon sa loob.”
Ang Diyos ang nagsara ng pinto.
Hindi si Noah.
Dumating ang sandaling natapos ang paanyaya ng awa.
At nagsimula ang ulan.
Biglang bumagsak ang paghuhukom.
At siguro ang parehong mga taong tumatawa kay Noah noon… sila ring kumakatok sa arka kalaunan.
Pero huli na.
Ganito ang katotohanan tungkol sa paghuhukom:
Hindi ito pinaniniwalaan ng tao hanggang sa dumating na.
Ganito rin ang babala ni Jesus.
Sa Mateo 24:38-39:
“Kumakain at umiinom sila, nag-aasawa at ipinapakasal… hanggang sa dumating ang baha at tinangay silang lahat.”
Hindi sila unaware dahil walang nagbabala.
Unaware sila dahil mas gusto nila ang comfort kaysa katotohanan.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… maraming tao ngayon ganoon pa rin.
Gusto ng blessing pero ayaw ng surrender. Gusto ng langit pero ayaw magsisi. Gusto si Jesus bilang inspirasyon pero hindi bilang Panginoon.
Pero ang arka ay hindi lang barko.
Larawan ito.
Prophetic picture.
Ang arka ay simbolo ni Cristo.
Iisa lang ang arka. Iisa lang ang pinto. Iisa lang ang kaligtasan.
Sinabi ni Jesus:
“Ako ang pintuan; ang sinumang pumasok sa pamamagitan Ko ay maliligtas.” — Juan 10:9
Walang maraming arka para sa iba’t ibang katotohanan.
Isa lang.
At lahat ng nasa labas nito ay napahamak.
Ayaw marinig ng modernong mundo ang exclusivity ng katotohanan.
Pero malinaw ang Kasulatan.
Gawa 4:12:
“Walang kaligtasan sa kanino mang iba.”
Si Jesus ang arka.
At baka iyon ang dahilan bakit uncomfortable pa rin ang kuwento ni Noah.
Dahil okay lang sa tao ang Diyos na mapagmahal.
Pero ayaw nila sa banal na Diyos.
Diyos na humahatol sa kasalanan. Diyos na tumatawag sa pagsisisi. Diyos na hindi tinatawag na liwanag ang kadiliman.
Pero kahit sa paghuhukom… sumisigaw pa rin ang awa.
Ang arka mismo ay awa.
Bawat hampas ng martilyo ay awa. Bawat babala ay awa. Bawat taon na nangangaral si Noah ay awa.
At baka matagal mo nang napagkakamalan ang pasensya ng Diyos bilang kawalan Niya.
Sinasabi ng 2 Pedro 3:9:
“Ang Panginoon ay matiisin… hindi Niya nais na ang sinuman ay mapahamak kundi magsisi ang lahat.”
Ang salitang Greek para sa pagsisisi ay “μετάνοια” (metanoia).
Hindi ito simpleng guilty feeling.
Ito ay pagbabago ng isip na nagdudulot ng tunay na pagbabago ng buhay.
At baka hindi talaga tungkol kay Noah ang artikulong ito.
Baka tungkol ito sa’yo.
Dahil maraming tao ang pagod na.
Pagod nang magpanggap. Pagod nang magtago. Pagod nang ngumiti habang unti-unting lumulubog ang kaluluwa.
At ang mabuting balita?
Patuloy pa ring inililigtas ni Jesus ang mga taong nalulunod.
Ang krus ang tunay na rescue plan ng Diyos.
Si Noah ligtas sa loob ng arka habang bumabagsak ang paghuhukom.
Ang mga mananampalataya ligtas kay Cristo.
Sinasabi ng Roma 8:1:
“Kaya nga ngayon ay wala nang hatol sa mga na kay Cristo Jesus.”
Kay Cristo.
Hindi sa relihiyon. Hindi sa pagiging mabait. Hindi sa performance.
Kay Cristo.
At baka matagal ka nang malapit sa Christianity pero hindi ka pa talaga sumusuko sa Diyos.
Marunong ka ng Bible verses. Marunong ka ng church language. Marunong ka ng worship songs.
Pero hindi mo pa talaga ibinibigay ang puso mo.
At isang araw… magsasara rin ang pinto.
Hindi ipinapangako ang bukas.
Isang tibok lang ng puso ang pagitan ng tao at eternity.
Pero hanggang ngayon… nag-iimbita pa rin si Jesus.
Nagpapatawad. Nagpapalaya. Nagpapagaling. Nagliligtas.
At pagkatapos ng baha, may inilagay ang Diyos sa langit.
Bahaghari.
Ang salitang Hebrew para rito ay “קֶשֶׁת” (qeshet).
Nakakagulat dahil maaari rin itong mangahulugang battle bow.
Parang isinabit ng Diyos ang Kanyang pana.
Larawan ng awa pagkatapos ng galit.
Tipan. Pangako.
At may isa pang bahagi ng kuwento ni Noah na madalas hindi napapansin.
Pagkatapos niyang makaligtas… nagkamali pa rin siya.
Nalasing si Noah. Nadapa pa rin.
Bakit isinama iyon sa Bibliya?
Dahil hindi tinatakpan ng Kasulatan ang kahinaan ng tao.
Kahit ang matuwid na tao kailangan pa rin ng biyaya.
Hindi si Noah ang ultimate Savior.
Si Jesus.
Si Noah ay anino lamang. Si Cristo ang katuparan.
Si Jesus lang ang namuhay nang walang kasalanan. Si Jesus lang ang tumalo sa kamatayan. Si Jesus lang ang ganap na Tagapagligtas.
Hindi “maging parang Noah” ang mensahe ng Ebanghelyo.
Ang mensahe ay:
Tumakbo ka papunta kay Cristo.
Dahil hanggang ngayon may mga baha pa rin.
Hindi laging literal na tubig.
Minsan depression. Minsan addiction. Minsan guilt. Minsan anxiety. Minsan loneliness. Minsan lihim na kasalanan.
At maraming tao ang tahimik na nalulunod.
Pero hanggang ngayon… nagliligtas pa rin si Jesus.
At baka habang binabasa mo ito… may kinakausap ang Diyos sa puso mo.
Hindi ito condemnation.
Katotohanan ito.
At alam mong matagal ka nang tinatawag ng Diyos.
Hindi papunta sa relihiyon.
Kundi sa surrender.
Sa repentance. Sa healing. Sa freedom. Sa Kanya.
At kung may tinamaan sa puso mo habang binabasa ito… huwag mo itong balewalain.
May mga taong nakangiti sa harap ng iba pero tahimik nang lumulubog sa loob.
Pinagtawanan nila noon ang arka… hanggang sa nagsimula ang ulan.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind the Woman Who Hid the Ark Among the Reeds
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind the Woman Who Hid the Ark Among the Reeds
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost too small to matter.
A crying baby. A basket drifting between reeds. A desperate mother hiding tears behind silence. A daughter of empire walking toward a river.
But heaven never measures importance the way the world does.
Because hidden inside the reeds of the Nile was not merely a child.
Inside those reeds rested deliverance.
Most believers know the story of Moses. Few truly stop long enough to feel the terror of the woman who let him go.
Not Pharaoh’s daughter. Not Miriam.
Jochebed.
The mother who surrendered her son to the river because faith sometimes looks like losing what you love most.
And behind this story exists an overlooked mystery that changes everything once you understand it.
The Bible never simply says she made a basket.
In Exodus 2:3, Scripture uses a shocking Hebrew word:
"וַתִּקַּח־לוֹ תֵּבַת גֹּמֶא" (vattiqqach-lo tevat gome)
Translation: "She took for him an ark of bulrushes."
Not a basket.
An ark.
The Hebrew word is "תֵּבָה" (tevah).
This exact word is only used two times in the entire Old Testament.
One was Noah’s Ark. The other was Moses hidden among the reeds.
That is not coincidence. That is prophecy woven into language.
The same God who once preserved humanity through waters was now preserving Israel’s deliverer through waters.
And the woman who built this tiny ark was participating in something far bigger than she understood.
Can you imagine her hands shaking as she sealed the reeds with pitch?
Exodus 2:3 says:
"וַתַּחְמְרָה בַחֵמָר וּבַזָּפֶת"
"She covered it with bitumen and pitch."
The exact same preservation imagery used in Noah’s ark.
This was not random craftsmanship. This was covenant symbolism.
The Nile River was supposed to become Moses’ grave. Instead, God transformed it into transportation toward destiny.
And that is how God still works.
The place the enemy intended to destroy you becomes the very current God uses to carry you into purpose.
Some of you are grieving things you had to release. Dreams. Relationships. Children. Seasons. Versions of yourself.
But Jochebed teaches us something painful about faith:
Sometimes obedience requires putting what you love into God’s hands when you no longer have the power to protect it yourself.
The story begins under one of the darkest political climates Israel had ever known.
Pharaoh issued a genocidal decree.
Exodus 1:22:
"Every son that is born you shall cast into the Nile."
This was not merely oppression. This was satanic warfare against covenant destiny.
Because the enemy often attacks deliverers while they are still infants.
Before Moses ever split a sea… hell already knew he was dangerous.
And maybe that explains why some people have experienced warfare their entire lives.
Some battles began before you even understood your own calling.
Jochebed lived under terror. Romanized imagination often softens biblical stories into children’s lessons. But this was horror.
Hebrew mothers heard soldiers approaching homes. Babies crying became dangerous. A newborn son could become a death sentence.
Hebrews 11:23 says:
"By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king’s edict."
The Greek word for "beautiful" here is "ἀστεῖος" (asteios).
It means more than physically attractive. It carries the idea of markedness… distinction… divine favor.
His parents discerned something heaven had placed upon him.
Parents can sometimes sense destiny before the world ever sees it.
For three months she hid him.
Every cry threatened exposure. Every knock at the door could mean death. Every night required courage.
Then came the unbearable moment.
She could hide him no longer.
The reeds beside the Nile became an altar of surrender.
The Hebrew word for reeds is connected to the imagery of fragile vegetation bending under pressure. And isn’t that exactly what she was?
Bent. Not broken.
Faithful people are not always fearless people.
Sometimes they are simply people who keep obeying while trembling.
Jochebed placed the ark among the reeds.
Not in open waters. Not recklessly.
Wisdom and faith walked together.
Too many believers think faith means abandoning wisdom. But biblical faith is courageous obedience partnered with discernment.
Then Scripture introduces another woman.
Pharaoh’s daughter.
An Egyptian princess raised inside a system built on Hebrew suffering.
Yet somehow compassion interrupted conditioning.
Exodus 2:6 says:
"וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו" (vatachmol alav)
"She had compassion on him."
The Hebrew word "חָמַל" (chamal) means deep mercy… pity that moves someone toward action.
God can plant compassion inside places you least expect.
The enemy built an empire. God used the enemy’s own household to finance deliverance.
Think about the irony.
Pharaoh commanded Hebrew sons to die in the Nile. Pharaoh’s daughter drew Israel’s future deliverer out of the Nile.
Only God writes stories like this.
Moses’ very name reflects it.
"מֹשֶׁה" (Mosheh)
Derived from the Hebrew idea: "to draw out."
The child drawn out of water would later draw an entire nation out of slavery.
Nothing in Scripture is wasted.
Even names preach.
And then comes one of the most emotionally devastating details in the entire story.
Jochebed ends up nursing her own son… while being paid by Pharaoh’s house.
Read that again.
The empire that wanted her baby dead unknowingly funded the very child who would later dismantle its power.
When God moves, He does not merely protect. He overturns systems.
This story is not ultimately about motherhood. It is about hidden providence.
God was moving through: reeds, rivers, women, tears, fear, politics, infants, and impossible timing.
Everything looked fragile. Yet heaven was orchestrating deliverance.
Some of you think your life is too small for God to use.
But entire biblical revolutions have turned on unseen obedience.
A woman no army would remember. A hidden child. A riverbank.
And history changed forever.
There is another layer most people never notice.
Moses was hidden among reeds near the Nile, but later Israel would pass through waters again.
The Exodus itself mirrors birth imagery.
Israel emerged from water into covenant freedom.
Paul later connects this symbolically in 1 Corinthians 10:2:
"and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea."
The deliverer preserved through waters would later lead others through waters.
That is how redemption echoes.
God repeats themes intentionally.
The ark of Noah. The ark among reeds. Passing through the sea. The basket preserved by pitch. Baptism into Christ.
The Bible is not disconnected stories. It is one unified rescue narrative pointing toward Jesus.
Because centuries later, another child would be born under the threat of a murderous ruler.
Herod slaughtered infants trying to stop prophecy.
Again, hell attacked a deliverer during infancy.
Again, God preserved the child.
Again, salvation survived political violence.
Moses pointed forward. Jesus fulfilled what Moses foreshadowed.
Moses delivered Israel from Pharaoh. Jesus delivers humanity from sin and death.
Moses passed through waters. Jesus calmed waters.
Moses mediated covenant law. Jesus fulfilled covenant grace.
And just as Moses was hidden in an ark among reeds… our lives are now hidden in Christ.
Colossians 3:3 says:
"For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God."
Hidden does not mean abandoned.
Hidden things are often protected things.
Some of you feel forgotten because God concealed you. But concealment is not rejection. Sometimes God hides people until the right moment for revelation.
Moses spent years hidden. Jesus spent thirty years hidden. David was hidden in fields. Joseph was hidden in prisons.
Never confuse hidden seasons with wasted seasons.
Jochebed probably never fully grasped what her surrender would produce.
That is one of the hardest truths about obedience.
Sometimes you will never see the full harvest of your faithfulness on this side of eternity.
Yet heaven records every trembling act of trust.
Can you imagine the silence after she released the ark?
A mother standing near reeds. Trying not to scream. Trying to trust. Trying to believe God still sees.
Some readers understand that silence too well.
The silence after the diagnosis. The silence after betrayal. The silence after prayers felt unanswered. The silence after burying dreams.
But the reeds were never empty.
God was already moving feet toward the riverbank.
What looked delayed was actually divinely synchronized.
You may feel surrounded by reeds right now. Confused. Hidden. Trapped between fear and faith.
But heaven has not lost sight of you.
The same God who preserved Moses through impossible waters still specializes in preservation.
Not every miracle arrives like fire from heaven. Sometimes miracles float quietly through reeds.
And maybe that is why this story still grips the human soul.
Because all of us know what it feels like to lose control. All of us know what it feels like to release something precious into uncertainty. All of us know what it feels like to hope while terrified.
Jochebed’s faith was not loud. It was costly.
Real faith often is.
There are people reading this who have smiled publicly while privately surviving impossible spiritual pressure.
You kept praying. Kept believing. Kept showing up. Even while your heart felt exhausted.
And if you know someone quietly carrying fear, grief, uncertainty, or hidden battles, share this with them. They may need this reminder more than you realize.
And maybe the most terrifying moments of your life were never proof God abandoned you. Maybe they were the reeds hiding the beginning of your deliverance.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Madalas Ikukuwento Tungkol sa Babaeng Nagtago ng Arko sa Gitna ng mga Tambo
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na parang napakaliit para pansinin.

Isang umiiyak na sanggol. Isang basket na inaanod sa ilog. Isang ina na pilit nilulunok ang takot habang nanginginig ang mga kamay. Isang prinsesa na naglalakad papunta sa ilog nang hindi niya alam na babaguhin ng araw na iyon ang kasaysayan.
Pero ang langit ay hindi tumitingin sa mga bagay ayon sa tingin ng mundo.
Dahil sa gitna ng mga tambo sa Ilog Nile… hindi lang basta sanggol ang nakatago.
Nakatago roon ang pagliligtas.
Kilalang-kilala ng marami si Moises. Pero kakaunti ang tunay na humihinto para damhin ang sakit ng babaeng kinailangang bitawan siya.
Hindi si Miriam. Hindi ang anak na babae ni Faraon.
Kundi si Jochebed.
Ang ina na isinuko ang sarili niyang anak sa ilog dahil minsan… ang pananampalataya ay mukhang pagkawala.
At may isang detalye sa kuwentong ito na halos hindi napapansin ng marami.
Hindi lang sinabi ng Biblia na gumawa siya ng basket.
Sa Exodo 2:3, ginamit ang salitang Hebreo na:
"וַתִּקַּח־לוֹ תֵּבַת גֹּמֶא" (vattiqqach-lo tevat gome)
Na ang ibig sabihin ay:
"Gumawa siya para sa kanya ng isang arko na yari sa tambo."
Hindi basket.
Arko.
Ang salitang ginamit ay "תֵּבָה" (tevah).
At alam mo bang dalawang beses lang ginamit ang salitang ito sa buong Lumang Tipan?
Una… sa Arko ni Noe. Pangalawa… sa munting arko ni Moises sa gitna ng mga tambo.
Hindi aksidente iyon.
Iyon ay mensaheng nakatago sa wika mismo.
Ang Diyos na minsang nagligtas sa sangkatauhan sa pamamagitan ng tubig… siya ring Diyos na nagligtas sa magiging tagapagligtas ng Israel sa pamamagitan din ng tubig.
Habang binabalot ni Jochebed ang munting arko ng aspalto at alkitran, hindi niya alam na siya ay bahagi ng isang napakalaking plano ng Diyos.
Sinasabi sa Exodo 2:3:
"וַתַּחְמְרָה בַחֵמָר וּבַזָּפֶת"
"Pinahiran niya ito ng bitumen at alkitran."
Parehong larawan ng pag-iingat na ginamit din sa Arko ni Noe.
Ang Nile na dapat sana’y magiging libingan ni Moises… siya mismong naging daan papunta sa kanyang tadhana.
At ganoon pa rin kumilos ang Diyos hanggang ngayon.
Ang lugar na gustong gamitin ng kaaway para sirain ka… iyon mismo ang ginagamit ng Diyos para dalhin ka sa layunin mo.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na may mga bagay na kinailangan nilang bitawan.
Mga pangarap. Mga relasyon. Mga anak. Mga panalangin. Mga bahagi ng sarili nilang namatay habang tumatagal ang laban.
Pero may isang bagay na itinuturo si Jochebed tungkol sa pananampalataya:
Minsan, ang totoong pagtitiwala sa Diyos ay ang paglalagay ng pinakamamahal mo sa mga kamay Niya kapag wala ka nang kakayahang protektahan ito.
Nangyari ang lahat ng ito sa panahon ng matinding kadiliman.
Nag-utos si Faraon:
"Lahat ng lalaking sanggol ng mga Hebreo ay ihahagis sa Nile."
Hindi lang ito simpleng pang-aapi.
Ito ay espirituwal na digmaan laban sa plano ng Diyos.
Dahil madalas umatake ang kaaway habang bata pa ang mga tatawaging magligtas.
Bago pa hatiin ni Moises ang dagat… alam na ng impiyerno na delikado siya.
At baka iyon din ang dahilan kung bakit may mga taong parang buong buhay nang may laban.
May mga sugat na nagsimula bago mo pa maintindihan ang calling mo.
Tatlong buwan itinago ni Jochebed si Moises.
Bawat iyak maaaring magdala ng kamatayan. Bawat yabag sa labas ng bahay maaaring sundalo. Bawat gabi… kaba.
Pagkatapos dumating ang pinakamasakit na sandali.
Hindi na niya kayang itago pa ang anak niya.
Kaya dinala niya ito sa mga tambo.
Hindi sa gitna ng rumaragasang ilog. Hindi pabaya.
