May pananampalataya. May karunungan.
Maraming tao ang iniisip na ang faith ay walang takot. Pero minsan, ang faith ay umiiyak habang sumusunod pa rin.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang anak ni Faraon.
Isang babaeng lumaki sa palasyong itinayo sa paghihirap ng mga Hebreo.
Pero biglang may nangyari.
Habag.
Sabi sa Exodo 2:6:
"וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו" (vatachmol alav)
"Naawa siya rito."
Ang salitang Hebreo na "חָמַל" (chamal) ay malalim na awa na nagtutulak sa isang tao na kumilos.
Kayang magtanim ng Diyos ng awa kahit sa mga lugar na hindi mo inaasahan.
Ang mismong tahanan ng kaaway… siya pang ginamit ng Diyos para pondohan ang pagliligtas.
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang utos ni Faraon: patayin ang mga batang Hebreo sa Nile.
Pero ang sariling anak ni Faraon… siya ang kumuha sa magiging tagapagligtas ng Israel mula sa Nile.
Tanging Diyos lang ang kayang magsulat ng ganitong klase ng kuwento.
Kahit ang pangalan ni Moises ay may kahulugan.
"מֹשֶׁה" (Mosheh)
Mula sa ideya ng: "hinugot mula sa tubig."
Ang batang hinugot mula sa tubig… siya ring gagamitin ng Diyos para hugutin ang Israel mula sa pagkaalipin.
Walang sayang sa Biblia.
Kahit mga pangalan… nangangaral.
At isa sa pinakamasakit na bahagi ng kuwento?
Si Jochebed mismo ang naging tagapag-alaga ng sarili niyang anak… habang binabayaran ng bahay ni Faraon.
Ang sistemang gustong pumatay kay Moises… siya mismong ginamit ng Diyos para buhayin siya.
Kapag kumilos ang Diyos, hindi lang Siya nagpoprotekta. Binabaliktad Niya ang buong sistema.
Ang kuwentong ito ay hindi lang tungkol sa pagiging ina.
Ito ay kuwento tungkol sa nakatagong pagkilos ng Diyos.
Gumagalaw Siya sa: luha, takot, ilog, mga tambo, mga babae, mga sanggol, at imposibleng timing.
Lahat mukhang marupok. Pero kontrolado pa rin ng Diyos.
May isa pang napakalalim na koneksyon dito.
Si Moises ay iniligtas sa tubig. Kalaunan… siya rin ang gagamitin ng Diyos para akayin ang Israel sa pagtawid sa tubig.
Sa 1 Corinto 10:2:
"at silang lahat ay binautismuhan kay Moises sa ulap at sa dagat."
Ang tagapagligtas na iningatan sa tubig… siya ring gagamitin para akayin ang iba palabas ng pagkaalipin.
Paulit-ulit ginagawa ng Diyos ang mga larawan ng pagtubos.
Arko ni Noe. Arko sa mga tambo. Pagtawid sa Dagat na Pula. Bautismo.
At lahat ng ito… tumuturo kay Jesus.
Dahil makalipas ang maraming taon, may isa pang sanggol na ipinanganak habang may hari ring gustong pumatay ng mga bata.
Si Herodes.
Muli, tinarget ng kadiliman ang isang tagapagligtas habang sanggol pa.
Muli, iningatan ng Diyos ang bata.
Si Moises ay larawan lamang. Si Jesus ang katuparan.
Iniligtas ni Moises ang Israel mula kay Faraon. Inililigtas ni Jesus ang sangkatauhan mula sa kasalanan.
At gaya ni Moises na itinago sa munting arko sa gitna ng mga tambo… angako rin ang Diyos na ang buhay natin ay nakatago kay Cristo.
Colosas 3:3:
"Sapagkat kayo'y namatay na, at ang inyong buhay ay nakatagong kasama ni Cristo sa Diyos."
Ang pagiging nakatago ay hindi ibig sabihin na kinalimutan ka.
Minsan, ang mga bagay na tinatago ng Diyos… iyon ang Kanyang pinoprotektahan.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na pakiramdam nila nakalimutan na sila ng langit.
Pero baka ang totoo… iniingatan ka lang ng Diyos hanggang sa tamang panahon.
Si Moises ay matagal na nakatago. Si David ay nakatago sa parang. Si Jose ay nakatago sa bilangguan. Si Jesus mismo ay halos tatlumpung taon tahimik bago nagsimula ang ministeryo.
Huwag mong isipin na sayang ang mga panahong hindi ka nakikita.
Baka iyon mismo ang panahon ng paghahanda.
Siguro hindi naunawaan ni Jochebed kung gaano kalaki ang magiging bunga ng pagsuko niya.
At iyon ang isa sa pinakamahirap tanggapin sa pagsunod sa Diyos.
Minsan, hindi mo agad makikita ang buong epekto ng pananampalataya mo.
Pero bawat luha ng pagtitiwala… nakikita ng langit.
Naiisip mo ba ang katahimikan pagkatapos niyang bitawan ang arko?
Isang ina. Nakatayo sa tabi ng ilog. Pinipigilang sumigaw. Pinipigilang bumagsak. Pinipilit maniwala na nakikita pa rin siya ng Diyos.
May mga taong nakakarelate sa katahimikang iyon.
Yung katahimikan matapos ang betrayal. Matapos ang diagnosis. Matapos ang unanswered prayers. Matapos mawala ang bagay na pinakamamahal mo.
Pero hindi kailanman walang laman ang mga tambo.
Kumikilos na ang Diyos kahit hindi mo pa nakikita.
Ang tingin mong delay… baka divine timing.
Kung pakiramdam mo nasa gitna ka ng mga tambo ngayon— nalilito, natatakot, nakakubli, napapagod—
hindi ka nakalimutan ng Diyos.
Ang Diyos na nag-ingat kay Moises sa imposible niyang sitwasyon… kaya ka ring ingatan.
Hindi lahat ng himala may apoy mula sa langit.
Minsan… tahimik lang silang inaanod sa gitna ng mga tambo.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakalalim ng kuwentong ito.

Dahil lahat tayo alam kung ano ang pakiramdam ng mawalan ng kontrol. Lahat tayo alam kung ano ang pakiramdam ng manginig habang umaasa. Lahat tayo may mga bagay na kinailangang bitawan habang umiiyak.
Ang faith ni Jochebed ay hindi maingay. Pero totoo. At mahal.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na matagal nang lumalaban nang tahimik.
Ngumingiti sa harap ng iba habang pagod na pagod na sa loob.
Pero nandito ka pa rin. Nagdarasal pa rin. Lumalaban pa rin. Umaasa pa rin.
Baka ito ang reminder na kailangan nila ngayong gabi.
At baka ang mga pinakanakakatakot na sandali ng buhay mo… hindi pala ebidensya na iniwan ka ng Diyos.
Baka iyon pala ang mga tambo kung saan Niya itinatago ang simula ng pagliligtas mo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 7 Warnings You Should Never Ignore About Finances in Church
paragraphs: 7 Warnings You Should Never Ignore About Finances in Church
There are people sitting in church every Sunday carrying financial wounds nobody can see.
Some smile while drowning in debt.
Some give publicly but secretly resent God privately.
Some pastors preach faith while silently suffocating under pressure to maintain appearances.
Some ministries look successful online but are spiritually collapsing behind closed doors because money slowly replaced obedience.
And some believers were never taught the difference between biblical stewardship and spiritual manipulation.
This conversation is uncomfortable.
But it is necessary.
Because money has destroyed churches.
Money has divided families.
Money has corrupted leaders.
Money has turned altars into stages.
And if we are honest… some people no longer know whether they are following Jesus Christ or following religious systems built on financial performance.
The Bible never avoids this subject.
Jesus Himself spoke about money constantly because finances reveal what the heart worships.
In Matthew 6:21, Jesus says:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
The Greek word for “treasure” is θησαυρός (thēsauros).
It means a storehouse.
A treasury.
A place where someone deposits what they value most.
Jesus was not merely discussing coins.
He was exposing worship.
Because whatever controls your treasure eventually controls your heart.
And that is why the enemy attacks finances so aggressively inside churches.
Not because money itself is evil.
But because love of money becomes an idol powerful enough to compete with surrender to God.
The Apostle Paul warned Timothy with terrifying clarity.
1 Timothy 6:10 says:
“For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil.”
The Greek phrase for “love of money” is φιλαργυρία (philargyria).
It literally means affection for silver.
An unhealthy devotion to wealth.
Notice Paul did not say money is evil.
He said the obsession with it opens doors to destruction.
And history proves him right.
Churches have split over money.
Friendships have died over offerings.
Pastors have fallen because of greed.
Families have abandoned faith because manipulation disguised itself as ministry.
So before another generation confuses biblical stewardship with spiritual exploitation…
These warnings must be spoken clearly.
And some of them may hit closer to home than expected.
Someone else may be silently fighting the exact same battle.
The first warning is using giving to manipulate God.
Some people were taught that every financial seed guarantees earthly wealth.
That if they give enough, God becomes obligated to bless them materially.
But that is not biblical covenant.
That is transactional religion.
In Acts 8, Simon the Sorcerer tried to purchase spiritual power.
Peter rebuked him fiercely:
“May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money.”
The Greek word used for perish is ἀπώλεια (apōleia).
It means destruction.
Ruin.
Loss.
Peter understood something dangerous.
The moment people think money can control God, repentance disappears.
Giving is worship.
Not bribery.
You cannot purchase the Holy Spirit.
You cannot buy anointing.
You cannot manipulate heaven with offerings.
God is not a vending machine responding to financial pressure.
And yes… God blesses generosity.
But biblical blessing is deeper than cars, houses, or public success.
Sometimes blessing looks like peace during suffering.
Sometimes blessing looks like freedom from greed.
Sometimes blessing looks like surviving a season that should have destroyed you.
And sometimes the greatest blessing is God refusing to give you what would have become your idol.
The second warning is pressuring the poor while protecting the wealthy.
James directly confronted favoritism inside the church.
James 2:2-4 exposes believers who honored rich people while humiliating the poor.
The Greek word προσωπολημψία (prosōpolēmpsia) means partiality.
Favoritism based on external status.
Some churches still do this today.
A wealthy donor receives influence.
A struggling single mother becomes invisible.
A businessman gets platform access.
A broken believer gets ignored.
But heaven does not measure people by net worth.
Jesus Himself was born among the poor.
The King of Glory entered earth in humility.
Not luxury.
Church becomes spiritually dangerous when money determines honor.
Because eventually leaders stop hearing God and start protecting financial power.
And that corruption spreads quietly.
The third warning is living beyond your means to appear “blessed.”
This one hurts because social media intensified it.
Many believers are financially exhausted trying to maintain appearances.
Expensive lifestyles.
Designer image.
Forced success.
Fake prosperity.
Meanwhile anxiety grows privately.
Proverbs 22:7 says:
“The borrower is servant to the lender.”
The Hebrew word for servant is עֶבֶד (‘eved).
Bondman.
Slave.
Debt itself is not automatically sin.
But bondage becomes dangerous when image matters more than wisdom.
Some believers buy things to impress people they secretly envy.
Others overspend because they are emotionally empty.
And some ministry leaders feel trapped trying to sustain an image of constant success.
But pretending to be blessed while secretly drowning destroys peace.
God never called believers to fake prosperity.
He called them to faithful stewardship.
There is no shame in simplicity.
There is no shame in rebuilding.
There is no shame in saying:
“I need financial wisdom.”
The fourth warning is exploiting generosity for personal gain.
This is one of the most devastating wounds in modern Christianity.
Because spiritual authority carries sacred responsibility.
Ezekiel 34 rebukes shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock.
And sadly, history keeps repeating.
Some leaders use fear to control giving.
Some manipulate vulnerable people emotionally.
Some build personal kingdoms while calling it ministry.
And some believers gave sacrificially only to later discover corruption behind the scenes.
That pain is real.
But abuse does not erase biblical generosity.
It reveals why accountability matters.
True shepherds protect people.
They do not consume them.
Paul told the Corinthians:
“For I seek not what is yours but you.”
A real spiritual leader values souls more than offerings.
Always.
The fifth warning is neglecting generosity entirely.
Some believers swing to the opposite extreme.
After seeing manipulation, they harden their hearts completely.
But Scripture still commands generosity.
Not because God needs money.
Because generosity transforms the human heart.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“God loves a cheerful giver.”
The Greek word for cheerful is ἱλαρός (hilaros).
It means joyful.
Willing.
Glad-hearted.
Not pressured.
Not threatened.
Not guilted.
Biblical generosity flows from love.
And sometimes generosity is not even financial.
Sometimes it is feeding someone.
Helping quietly.
Supporting missions.
Paying for groceries.
Covering a struggling family in prayer and action.
The early church became powerful because believers cared for each other sacrificially.
And in a world obsessed with self-preservation… generosity still preaches the Gospel.
The sixth warning is trusting money more than God.
This can happen to rich people.
Poor people.
Church leaders.
Business owners.
Anyone.
Because money creates an illusion of security.
But economies collapse.
Jobs disappear.
Health changes.
Unexpected tragedy comes without warning.
Psalm 20:7 says:
“Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.”
Modern chariots simply changed forms.
Bank accounts.
Investments.
Status.
Connections.
Success.
None of those things are eternal.
Only Christ is.
And sometimes God allows uncomfortable seasons to expose where trust truly lives.
Because many people discover their faith was stable only while life felt financially secure.
The seventh warning is forgetting eternity completely.
This may be the most dangerous one.
Because entire lives can be consumed chasing temporary success.
Jesus asked:
“For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?”
The Greek word ψυχή (psychē) means soul.
Life.
Inner being.
A person can become financially successful and spiritually empty simultaneously.
And tragically… many do.
There are wealthy people who cannot sleep peacefully.
Successful people addicted secretly.
Influential people spiritually hollow.
Because nothing in creation can replace communion with God.
Not money.
Not applause.
Not influence.
Not possessions.
Only Jesus Christ satisfies the soul.
And deep down… many people reading this already know that.
Because no purchase healed the loneliness.
No paycheck removed the emptiness.
No material success silenced the fear.
Only the presence of God touches places money never can.
Maybe that is why this article found you.
Not to condemn you.
But to wake something up again.
To remind you that biblical stewardship is not merely about dollars.
It is about worship.
Trust.
Integrity.
Compassion.
Humility.
And surrender.
If you have been financially broken, manipulated, greedy, fearful, prideful, or exhausted… Jesus Christ still invites you closer.
Grace still exists.
Repentance still changes people.
Restoration still happens.
And your story is not over.
Be honest.
Someone else scrolling tonight may realize they are not alone because you chose vulnerability instead of silence.
One day, every dollar you touched will mean nothing… but every soul you helped lead toward Jesus Christ will echo into eternity.
Filipino Version:
7 Babala sa Pananalapi sa Simbahan na Hindi Mo Dapat Balewalain
May mga taong nakaupo sa loob ng simbahan tuwing Linggo na may dalang sugat sa pananalapi na walang nakakakita.
Ngumingiti sila… pero gabi-gabi umiiyak dahil sa utang.
Nagbibigay sila sa harap ng tao… pero palihim na nagtatanong sa Diyos kung bakit parang hindi naubos ang bigat.
May mga pastor na nangangaral tungkol sa pananampalataya habang lihim na dinudurog ng pressure na panatilihin ang imahe ng “pinagpapala.”
May mga ministry na mukhang matagumpay online pero sa likod ng kamera… unti-unti nang namamatay espirituwal dahil ang pera na ang naging sentro kaysa si Cristo.
At may mga mananampalataya na hindi na alam ang kaibahan ng tunay na biblical stewardship at spiritual manipulation.
Masakit itong pag-usapan.
Pero kailangan.
Dahil maraming simbahan ang nasira dahil sa pera.
Maraming pamilya ang nagkawatak-watak dahil sa pera.
Maraming lider ang bumagsak dahil sa kasakiman.
At maraming tao ang tuluyang lumayo kay Jesus dahil nasugatan sila ng maling paggamit ng pananalapi sa loob mismo ng simbahan.
Hindi iniiwasan ng Biblia ang usaping ito.
Sa katunayan, madalas magsalita si Jesus tungkol sa pera dahil ipinapakita nito kung sino talaga ang sinasamba ng puso.
Sa Mateo 6:21 sinabi ni Jesus:
“Sapagkat kung saan naroroon ang iyong kayamanan, doon din naman naroroon ang iyong puso.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “kayamanan” ay θησαυρός (thēsauros).
Ibig sabihin nito ay imbakan.
Taguan ng pinakamahalaga.
Hindi lang pera ang tinutukoy ni Jesus.
Pinapakita Niya kung ano talaga ang inuuna ng puso.
Dahil kung saan ka handang ibuhos ang lahat… iyon ang tunay mong sinasamba.
Kaya matindi ang atake ng kaaway pagdating sa pananalapi.
Hindi dahil masama ang pera.
Kundi dahil kayang palitan ng pag-ibig sa pera ang buong pagsuko sa Diyos.
Sinabi ni Apostol Pablo sa 1 Timoteo 6:10:
“Sapagkat ang pag-ibig sa salapi ay ugat ng lahat ng uri ng kasamaan.”
Ang salitang Griyego na φιλαργυρία (philargyria) ay nangangahulugang sobrang pagkagusto sa pilak o kayamanan.
Pansinin mo.
Hindi sinabi ni Pablo na masama ang pera.
Ang sinabi niya… ang sobrang pag-ibig dito ang nagbubukas ng pinto sa pagkawasak.
At totoo iyon.
May mga simbahan na naghiwalay dahil sa offerings.
May mga pagkakaibigan na namatay dahil sa pera.
May mga pastor na bumagsak dahil sa kasakiman.
At may mga mananampalatayang tuluyang nawalan ng gana sa pananampalataya dahil ang Gospel ay napalitan ng financial pressure.
Kaya bago tuluyang malito ang susunod na henerasyon tungkol sa tunay na biblical stewardship…
Kailangang malinaw itong sabihin.
At maaaring mas tumama ito sa puso mo kaysa inaasahan mo.
May ibang taong tahimik ding lumalaban sa parehong bagay.
Ang unang babala ay ang paggamit ng pagbibigay para manipulahin ang Diyos.
May mga taong tinuruan na kapag nagbigay sila nang malaki… obligado ang Diyos na pagyamanin sila.
Na parang ang offering ay investment para pilitin ang langit na magbigay ng material na kapalit.
Pero hindi iyon covenant.
Transactional religion iyon.
Sa Gawa 8, sinubukan ni Simon na bilhin ang kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
At matindi ang sagot ni Pedro:
“Mapahamak nawa kasama mo ang iyong salapi, sapagkat inakala mong mabibili mo ng salapi ang kaloob ng Diyos.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “mapahamak” ay ἀπώλεια (apōleia).
Pagkasira.
Pagkawasak.
Naiintindihan ni Pedro ang panganib.
Kapag iniisip ng tao na kayang kontrolin ng pera ang Diyos… nawawala ang tunay na pagsisisi.
Ang pagbibigay ay pagsamba.
Hindi panunuhol.
Hindi mo mabibili ang Banal na Espiritu.
Hindi mo mabibili ang anointing.
Hindi mo mapipilit ang Diyos gamit ang pera.
At oo… pinagpapala ng Diyos ang mapagbigay.
Pero ang biblical blessing ay mas malalim kaysa sasakyan, bahay, o social media success.
Minsan ang blessing ay kapayapaan sa gitna ng paghihirap.
Minsan ang blessing ay kalayaan mula sa kasakiman.
At minsan… ang pinakamalaking blessing ay ang hindi ibigay ng Diyos ang bagay na magiging diyos-diyosan mo.
Ang ikalawang babala ay ang pagpapabor sa mayaman habang hindi pinapansin ang mahirap.
Direktang kinondena ito ni Santiago.
Sa Santiago 2:2-4, pinagsabihan niya ang simbahan dahil mas mataas ang tingin nila sa mayaman.
Ang salitang Griyego na προσωπολημψία (prosōpolēmpsia) ay nangangahulugang favoritism.
Pagtingin sa halaga ng tao batay sa estado niya sa buhay.
At hanggang ngayon nangyayari pa rin ito.
Kapag mayamang donor… may espesyal na trato.
Kapag simpleng miyembro… halos walang nakakakita.
Kapag influential… may access.
Kapag mahirap… tahimik lang sa gilid.
Pero hindi sinusukat ng langit ang tao batay sa laman ng wallet.
Si Jesus mismo ay ipinanganak sa kababaang-loob.
Hindi sa palasyo.
Nagiging delikado ang simbahan kapag pera na ang basehan ng honor.
Dahil darating ang punto na mas poprotektahan na ang financial power kaysa katotohanan.
Ang ikatlong babala ay ang pamumuhay lampas sa kakayahan para lang magmukhang “blessed.”
Mas lumala ito sa panahon ng social media.
Maraming Kristiyano ang pagod na pagod na dahil pilit nilang pinapakita online na okay ang buhay nila.
Magandang damit.
Mamasa-masang posts.
Piliting image ng success.
Pero gabi-gabi kinakain ng anxiety.
Sabi sa Kawikaan 22:7:
“Ang nanghihiram ay alipin ng nagpapahiram.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa alipin ay עֶבֶד (‘eved).
Bondservant.
Nabubuhay sa ilalim ng kontrol.
Hindi lahat ng utang ay kasalanan.
Pero nagiging mapanganib ito kapag image na ang mas mahalaga kaysa wisdom.
May mga taong bumibili para magmukhang successful.
May iba namang gumagastos dahil sinusubukan nilang takpan ang emotional emptiness.
At may mga lider na lihim nang nalulunod sa pressure na panatilihin ang imahe ng “sobrang pinagpala.”
Pero walang kapayapaan sa pagpapanggap.
Hindi tayo tinawag ng Diyos para magmukhang mayaman.
Tinawag tayo para maging tapat.
Walang kahihiyan sa simpleng buhay.
Walang kahihiyan sa pagbangon ulit.
Walang kahihiyan sa pagsabing:
“Kailangan ko ng wisdom sa pananalapi.”
Ang ikaapat na babala ay ang paggamit sa generosity ng tao para sa personal na pakinabang.
Ito ang isa sa pinakamasakit na sugat sa modern Christianity.
Dahil sagrado ang spiritual authority.
Sa Ezekiel 34, kinondena ng Diyos ang mga shepherd na sarili lang nila ang pinapakain.
At nakakalungkot… paulit-ulit pa rin itong nangyayari.
May mga lider na gumagamit ng takot para makakuha ng pera.
May mga ministry na ginagamit ang emosyon ng tao para manipulahin sila.
May mga taong buong pusong nagbigay… tapos kalaunan nalaman nilang may corruption pala sa likod.
Totoong masakit iyon.
Pero ang abuse ay hindi ibig sabihin na mali na ang biblical generosity.
Ipinapakita lang nito kung bakit mahalaga ang accountability.
Ang tunay na shepherd… inuuna ang kaluluwa ng tao.
Hindi ang laman ng sobre.
Sinabi ni Pablo:
“Sapagkat hindi ang inyong ari-arian ang hinahanap ko kundi kayo.”
Ang tunay na lingkod ng Diyos… mas mahal ang tao kaysa offerings.
Palagi.
Ang ikalimang babala ay ang tuluyang pagsara ng puso sa generosity.
May mga tao na matapos masaktan sa church manipulation… ayaw nang magbigay kahit kailan.
Pero malinaw pa rin ang Biblia tungkol sa generosity.
Hindi dahil kailangan ng Diyos ang pera.
Kundi dahil binabago ng generosity ang puso.
Sa 2 Corinto 9:7:
“Iniibig ng Diyos ang nagbibigay na masaya.”
Ang salitang Griyego na ἱλαρός (hilaros) ay nangangahulugang joyful.
Maluwag sa loob.
Hindi pinipilit.
Hindi tinatakot.
Hindi ginuguilty.
Ang tunay na pagbibigay ay bunga ng pag-ibig.
At minsan… hindi pera ang pinakamalaking generosity.
Minsan oras.
Pagkain.
Panalangin.
Pagdamay.
Tahimik na pagtulong.
At sa mundong puro self-preservation… ang generosity ay nananatiling makapangyarihang pangangaral ng Ebanghelyo.
Ang ikaanim na babala ay ang pagtitiwala sa pera higit sa Diyos.
Puwedeng mangyari ito sa mayaman.
Puwedeng mangyari sa mahirap.
Puwedeng mangyari sa pastor.
Sa negosyante.
Sa kahit sino.
Dahil nagbibigay ang pera ng pakiramdam ng seguridad.
Pero puwedeng bumagsak ang ekonomiya.
Puwedeng mawala ang trabaho.
Puwedeng magkasakit.
Puwedeng magbago ang lahat sa isang iglap.
Sabi sa Awit 20:7:
“Ang iba ay nagtitiwala sa mga karo at ang iba naman ay sa mga kabayo, ngunit tayong lahat ay nagtitiwala sa pangalan ng Panginoon.”
Ngayon… iba na lang ang anyo ng “karo.”
Bank account.
Investments.
Status.
Connections.
Business.
Pero walang eternal doon.
Si Cristo lang.
At minsan hinahayaan ng Diyos ang uncomfortable seasons para ilantad kung saan talaga nakatayo ang tiwala natin.
Dahil maraming tao ang matatag lang ang faith habang stable ang finances.
Ang ikapitong babala ay ang pagkalimot sa eternity.
Ito marahil ang pinaka-mapanganib.
Dahil puwedeng ubusin ng tao ang buong buhay niya kakahabol ng temporary success.
Tinanong ni Jesus:
“Sapagkat ano ang mapapakinabang ng tao kung makamtan man niya ang buong sanlibutan ngunit mawala naman ang kanyang kaluluwa?”
Ang salitang Griyego na ψυχή (psychē) ay soul.
Inner life.
Tunay na pagkatao.
Posibleng yumaman ang tao habang unti-unting namamatay ang kaluluwa niya.
At maraming tao ang tahimik na nangyayari iyon.
May mayayamang hindi makatulog nang maayos.
May successful pero wasak emotionally.
May influential pero spiritually empty.
Dahil walang materyal na bagay ang kayang pumalit sa presensya ng Diyos.
Hindi pera.
Hindi applause.
Hindi influence.
Hindi fame.
Si Jesus lang ang kayang punuin ang kaluluwang pagod.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit nabasa mo ito ngayon.
Hindi para husgahan ka.
Kundi para gisingin ulit ang puso mo.
Para ipaalala na ang biblical stewardship ay hindi lang tungkol sa pera.
Tungkol ito sa pagsamba.
Katapatan.
Kababaang-loob.
Pagtitiwala.
At buong pagsuko kay Cristo.
Kung ikaw ay pagod na pagod na sa financial pressure… kung nasaktan ka ng church manipulation… kung nilalabanan mo ang greed, fear, pride, o anxiety… iniimbitahan ka pa rin ni Jesus na lumapit.
May grace pa rin.
May restoration pa rin.
May kapatawaran pa rin.
At hindi pa tapos ang kuwento mo.
Maging totoo ka.
May ibang taong nag-i-scroll ngayon na maaaring makahanap ng pag-asa dahil nakita nilang hindi sila nag-iisa.
Darating ang araw na mawawalan ng halaga ang lahat ng perang nahawakan mo… pero bawat kaluluwang nailapit mo kay Jesus Christ ay may eternal na epekto.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Wise Woman of Tekoa Was Sent to Confront David
paragraphs: Why the Wise Woman of Tekoa Was Sent to Confront David
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like history and more like someone secretly reading the human heart.
2 Samuel 14 is one of those moments.
A grieving king. A divided family. A nation watching silently. A father too wounded to move. And a woman from a small town carrying a message sharp enough to break open a palace.
Most people read the story of the Wise Woman of Tekoa and focus only on her speech. But the deeper question is this:
Why did she have to be sent at all?
Why was King David — the giant killer, the worshipper, the man after God’s own heart — suddenly unreachable?
Why did Joab believe only a wise woman could reach where armies, authority, and logic could not?
Because David was not dealing with politics.
He was dealing with hidden grief.
And grief, when buried long enough, can harden even the strongest believer into emotional paralysis.
The Wise Woman of Tekoa was sent because David had become trapped inside unresolved sorrow, guilt, and fatherly failure.
And sometimes God sends a voice into our lives not to destroy us…
…but to force us to finally face what we have been avoiding.
The story begins after one of the darkest tragedies inside David’s household.
Amnon, David’s son, violated his half-sister Tamar.
The Hebrew text uses violent and devastating language in 2 Samuel 13. The word for violation comes from the Hebrew root עָנָה (‘anah), meaning to afflict, humiliate, oppress, or violate.
This was not romance. This was destruction.
Tamar’s life was shattered. Absalom burned with rage. David became furious.
But he did nothing.
That silence became a seed.
And buried silence eventually becomes generational destruction.
Two years later, Absalom murdered Amnon and fled into exile.
Now David had lost two sons emotionally: One was dead. One was gone.
And the king who once ran toward Goliath could not move toward reconciliation.
Scripture says in 2 Samuel 14:1 that Joab “perceived that the king’s heart was toward Absalom.”
The Hebrew phrase is incredibly revealing.
לֵב הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל־אַבְשָׁלוֹם (lev ha-melekh al-Avshalom)
Literally: “The heart of the king was upon Absalom.”
David’s heart never stopped aching for his son.
But love without action becomes torment.
David missed Absalom. Yet he refused to confront the pain.
And this is where so many believers secretly live.
They love. They grieve. They remember. They ache.
But they never heal because healing requires confrontation.
So Joab sends for a wise woman from Tekoa.
Not a soldier. Not a prophet. Not a priest.
A wise woman.
The Hebrew describes her as:
אִשָּׁה חֲכָמָה (ishah chakamah)
A woman marked by wisdom, discernment, perception, and understanding.
Biblical wisdom was never merely intelligence.
Wisdom meant seeing beneath appearances. Wisdom meant understanding hearts. Wisdom meant speaking truth in a way that bypassed defenses.
Joab knew David could not be commanded into healing.
He had to be confronted through story.
So the woman comes before David pretending to be a grieving widow.
She tells him about two sons. One killed the other. Now the family demands vengeance. If justice is fully carried out, her remaining son will die too.
David immediately responds with mercy.
He promises protection.
Then the woman turns the story.
Suddenly David realizes he has judged himself.
This moment echoes the prophet Nathan confronting David after Bathsheba.
God often uses mirrors before He uses sermons.
Because people resist accusation. But stories slip past defenses.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking verses in the chapter.
2 Samuel 14:14.

“For we must needs die, and are as water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him.”
The Hebrew is emotionally staggering.
וְחָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת (vechashav machashavot)
“God devises plans.” “God invents ways.” “God thinks thoughts.”
For what purpose?
לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח (levilti yiddach mimennu nidach)
“So that the banished one may not remain cast away from Him.”
Pause there.
This woman was revealing something prophetic about the heart of God.
God is not merely holy. He is pursuing.
From Genesis to Revelation, Scripture reveals a God who keeps making ways to bring back the exiled.
Adam hiding in shame. Jacob running in fear. Israel wandering in rebellion. Peter drowning in failure.
And humanity itself banished because of sin.
Yet God keeps devising ways.
Ultimately, the greatest “way” was Jesus Christ.
The Greek language of the New Testament reveals this beautifully.
Jesus says in John 14:6:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς (ego eimi hē hodos)
“I am the way.”
Not merely a teacher. Not merely an example.
The way.
The Wise Woman of Tekoa spoke prophetically into a broken kingdom about the deeper heart of God:
God does not delight in permanent exile.
He seeks restoration.
But restoration without repentance becomes disaster.
And this is the tragic tension inside David’s story.
David brings Absalom back to Jerusalem. But he refuses to fully reconcile.
For two years Absalom lives near the palace yet never sees the king’s face.
Can you imagine that pain?
Close enough to see the kingdom. Too far away to feel loved.
This is one of the most devastating pictures of partial reconciliation in Scripture.
And partial reconciliation often creates deeper bitterness.
Absalom eventually turns the hearts of Israel against David. Civil war erupts. Thousands die. And David’s household collapses under the weight of unresolved sin.
The Wise Woman succeeded in confronting David.
But David still struggled to fully deal with the deeper issues beneath the surface.
This is what makes the story terrifyingly relevant.
Many people want restoration emotionally without transformation spiritually.
They want peace without repentance. They want healing without honesty. They want reunion without surrender.
But buried sin always grows roots.
The Hebrew worldview never separated spiritual decay from relational collapse.
David’s earlier compromise with Bathsheba did not remain isolated. Sin never stays contained.
The sword God warned about in 2 Samuel 12 continued cutting through David’s house.
And yet…
even here…
God’s mercy still shines.
Because the Wise Woman of Tekoa reveals something astonishing:
God keeps reaching toward broken people even when they created the mess themselves.
That is the Gospel.
Humanity ran. God pursued.
Humanity rebelled. God redeemed.
Humanity deserved exile. Jesus took the cross.
The cross itself becomes the ultimate fulfillment of:
“He devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.”
Jesus did not come merely to inspire sinners. He came to bring exiles home.
The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 5:8:
The Greek word for sinners is:
ἁμαρτωλῶν (hamartōlōn)
Those who missed the mark. The guilty. The wandering. The ruined.
That includes us.
Every hidden wound. Every secret addiction. Every fake smile in church. Every buried shame. Every silent compromise. Every private collapse.
Some people reading this have become emotionally exiled.
Not because God left.
Because pain hardened the heart slowly.
Like David, you still feel love somewhere deep inside. But unresolved grief has frozen movement.
You pray less. Trust less. Feel less. Hope less.
And maybe God sent this article like He sent the Wise Woman of Tekoa.
Not to shame you.
But to confront what has been silently destroying you.
Some wounds do not heal through time. They heal through surrender.
Some families do not break in one day. They break through years of avoided truth.
Some believers are physically present but spiritually distant. Just like Absalom living near Jerusalem but unable to see the king’s face.
And some people reading this have spent years performing Christianity while secretly feeling exiled from God.
But hear this clearly:
Jesus Christ still receives prodigals.
The Gospel is not self-improvement. It is reconciliation through the blood of Christ.
The Greek word for reconciliation in the New Testament is:
καταλλαγή (katallagē)
Restoration. Exchange. Peace after hostility.
That is what Christ purchased at Calvary.
Not religious performance. Not fake perfection.
Reconciliation.
And maybe that is why this story grips the soul so deeply.
Because everyone knows what it feels like to carry unresolved pain.
To miss someone. To regret something. To replay conversations. To wish time could reverse. To wonder if restoration is still possible.
The Wise Woman of Tekoa stood inside a broken kingdom and reminded David of the heart of God.
A God who devises ways. A God who pursues exiles. A God who still calls prodigals home.
But also a God who confronts what we bury.
Because mercy without truth is not love.
And truth without mercy crushes people.
Jesus came full of both.
John 1:14 says:
“Full of grace and truth.”
The Greek:
πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (plērēs charitos kai alētheias)
Completely filled with grace and truth.
Not one without the other.
That is the Savior still calling people today.
Maybe you have been running emotionally. Maybe pride has kept you silent. Maybe shame convinced you that God is finished with you.
But the cross says otherwise.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
Jesus still saves. Jesus still restores. Jesus still welcomes the banished.
And maybe the reason this story refuses to leave your mind is because deep down…
you know God has been confronting your heart too.
Some people are not running from God because they hate Him.
They are running because they are terrified He still wants them.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Isinugo ang Marunong na Babae ng Tekoa Upang Harapin si David
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na parang hindi lang kasaysayan.
Parang may humahawak sa pinakatagong bahagi ng puso mo habang binabasa mo.
Ang kuwento ng Marunong na Babae ng Tekoa sa 2 Samuel 14 ay isa doon.

Isang hari na puno ng pagsisisi. Isang amang wasak ang tahanan. Isang kahariang tahimik na nanonood. At isang babae mula sa maliit na bayan na may dalang mensaheng sapat para wasakin ang pader sa paligid ng puso ni David.
Karamihan sa mga tao, kapag binabasa ang kuwentong ito, iniisip lang na isa itong matalinong plano ni Joab.
Pero ang tunay na tanong ay ito:
Bakit kinailangan pang magsugo ng isang babae upang kausapin si David?
Bakit ang lalaking tumalo kay Goliath… ang sumulat ng mga Awit… ang tinawag na “lalaking ayon sa puso ng Diyos”…
ay naging emotionally unreachable?
Bakit tila hindi na siya kayang abutin ng simpleng katotohanan?
Dahil hindi lang politika ang problema ni David.
Sugatan ang puso niya.
At kapag ang sugat ay matagal mong tinatago… kahit ang pinakamalakas na tao ay unti-unting naninigas sa loob.
Ang Marunong na Babae ng Tekoa ay isinugo dahil si David ay nakakulong sa hindi niya hinaharap na sakit, guilt, at kabiguan bilang ama.
At minsan…
ang Diyos ay nagpapadala ng isang tinig sa buhay natin hindi para tayo ipahiya…
kundi para pilitin tayong harapin ang matagal na nating iniiwasan.
Nagsimula ang lahat matapos ang isa sa pinakamadilim na trahedya sa pamilya ni David.
Si Amnon, anak ni David, ay ginahasa ang kanyang kapatid na si Tamar.
Sa Hebrew text ng 2 Samuel 13, ginamit ang salitang:
עָנָה (‘anah)
Na nangangahulugang:
upang apihin, pahirapan, ibaba, o lapastanganin.
Hindi ito kuwento ng pag-ibig.
Ito ay kuwento ng pagkawasak.
Nasira si Tamar. Nagliyab sa galit si Absalom. Nagalit si David.
Pero wala siyang ginawa.
At ang katahimikang iyon ang naging binhi ng susunod na trahedya.
Dahil ang matagal na katahimikan tungkol sa kasalanan ay nagiging lason sa pamilya.
Pagkalipas ng dalawang taon, pinatay ni Absalom si Amnon at tumakas.
Ngayon dalawang anak na ang nawala kay David.
Ang isa ay patay. Ang isa ay malayo.
At ang hari na dating tumatakbo papunta sa laban… ngayon ay hindi makagalaw papunta sa reconciliation.
Sinasabi sa 2 Samuel 14:1:
“Ang puso ng hari ay nakatuon kay Absalom.”
Sa Hebrew:
לֵב הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל־אַבְשָׁלוֹם (lev ha-melekh al-Avshalom)
Literal na:
“Ang puso ng hari ay nasa ibabaw ni Absalom.”
Hindi tumigil si David sa pagmamahal sa kanyang anak.
Pero ang pag-ibig na walang pagkilos ay nagiging torture.
Miss niya si Absalom. Pero hindi niya kayang harapin ang sakit.
At maraming tao ang lihim na nabubuhay nang ganito.
Nagdarasal pero sugatan. Nagmamahal pero tahimik. Umaasa pero pagod. Nakangiti pero wasak.
At hindi sila gumagaling dahil ang tunay na paggaling ay nangangailangan ng confrontation.
Kaya nagsugo si Joab ng isang “marunong na babae” mula sa Tekoa.
Hindi sundalo. Hindi pari. Hindi propeta.
Isang babae.
Tinawag siya sa Hebrew na:
אִשָּׁה חֲכָמָה (ishah chakamah)
Ibig sabihin:
isang babaeng may karunungan, discernment, malalim na pang-unawa, at kakayahang makita ang nasa ilalim ng salita.
Sa Biblia, ang wisdom ay hindi lang talino.
Ang tunay na karunungan ay kakayahang maabot ang puso.
Alam ni Joab na hindi kayang pilitin si David na gumaling.
Kailangan niyang makita ang sarili niya sa kuwento.
Kaya nagkunwari ang babae bilang isang biyuda.
Ikinuwento niya na mayroon siyang dalawang anak. Nag-away. Napatay ng isa ang kanyang kapatid. Ngayon gusto ng buong pamilya na patayin din ang natitirang anak.
Nang marinig iyon ni David, agad siyang naawa.
Nangako siyang poprotektahan ang anak.
At doon binaliktad ng babae ang kuwento.
Biglang napagtanto ni David:
hinatulan niya ang sarili niyang sitwasyon.
Katulad ito nang komprontahin ni propeta Nathan si David matapos ang kasalanan niya kay Bathsheba.
Madalas gumagamit ang Diyos ng mga kuwento bago direktang magsalita.
Dahil maraming tao ang lumalaban kapag inaakusahan.
Pero kapag nakita nila ang sarili nila sa isang kuwento…
doon sila nababasag.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang isa sa pinakamakapangyarihang talata sa buong kabanata.
2 Samuel 14:14:
“Ngunit ang Diyos ay gumagawa ng paraan upang ang itinaboy ay hindi manatiling hiwalay sa Kanya.”
Sa Hebrew:
וְחָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת (vechashav machashavot)
“Ipinaplano ng Diyos.” “Gumagawa Siya ng paraan.” “Nag-iisip Siya ng paraan.”
Para saan?
לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח (levilti yiddach mimennu nidach)
“Upang ang itinaboy ay hindi manatiling hiwalay sa Kanya.”
Napakalalim nito.
Ipinapakita ng babaeng ito ang puso ng Diyos.
Hindi lang banal ang Diyos.
Hinahanap Niya ang mga nawawala.
Mula Genesis hanggang Revelation, paulit-ulit natin nakikita:
ang Diyos ay gumagawa ng paraan upang maibalik ang mga lumayo.
Si Adan na nagtago. Si Jacob na tumakas. Ang Israel na nagrebelde. Si Pedro na bumagsak.
At tayong lahat na nahiwalay dahil sa kasalanan.
Pero patuloy na gumagawa ng paraan ang Diyos.
At ang pinakadakilang “daan” ay si Jesucristo.
Sa John 14:6 sinabi ni Jesus:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς (ego eimi hē hodos)
“Ako ang daan.”
Hindi lang guro. Hindi lang mabuting halimbawa.
Siya ang daan pabalik sa Ama.
Ang kuwento ng Marunong na Babae ng Tekoa ay parang propetikong anino ng Ebanghelyo.
Dahil ang Diyos ay hindi natutuwa sa permanenteng pagkakahiwalay.
Gusto Niyang ibalik ang tao.
Pero narito ang problema.
Ibinalik ni David si Absalom sa Jerusalem. Pero hindi niya tunay na niyakap ang reconciliation.
Dalawang taon nanirahan si Absalom malapit sa palasyo ngunit hindi niya nakita ang mukha ng hari.
Isipin mo iyon.
Malapit pero malayo. Nasa kaharian pero walang relasyon.
Maraming tao ngayon ang ganito sa Diyos.
Nasa simbahan. Umaawit. Naglilingkod.
Pero sa loob nila, pakiramdam nila exiled pa rin sila.
At kapag hindi hinaharap ang sugat, nagiging bitterness ito.
Kalaunan, nagrebelde si Absalom laban kay David. Nagkaroon ng digmaan. Libo-libo ang namatay. At tuluyang gumuho ang tahanan ni David.
Ito ang mapait na katotohanan:
Ang kasalanang hindi kinakaharap ay hindi nananatiling maliit.
Lumalaki ito.
At ang compromise ni David kay Bathsheba ay patuloy na nagdala ng pagkawasak sa kanyang sambahayan.
Pero kahit dito…
makikita pa rin ang awa ng Diyos.
Dahil ipinapakita ng babaeng ito na kahit ang taong gumawa ng sarili niyang gulo…
hinahabol pa rin ng Diyos.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Tumakas ang tao. Hinabol ng Diyos.
Nagkasala ang tao. Nagbigay ng kaligtasan ang Diyos.
Karapat-dapat tayong mawalay. Pero si Jesus ang namatay sa krus para maibalik tayo.
Ang krus ang pinakadakilang patunay na:
“Ang Diyos ay gumagawa ng paraan upang ang itinaboy ay hindi manatiling hiwalay sa Kanya.”
Hindi dumating si Jesus para lang pagandahin ang buhay.
Dumating Siya upang ibalik sa Ama ang mga nawawala.
Sabi sa Romans 5:8:
“Ngunit ipinakita ng Diyos ang Kanyang pag-ibig sa atin, na noong tayo’y makasalanan pa, si Cristo ay namatay para sa atin.”
Ang salitang Greek para sa “makasalanan” ay:
ἁμαρτωλῶν (hamartōlōn)
Mga taong lumihis. Mga bumagsak. Mga nagkamali. Mga guilty.
Kasama tayo roon.
Bawat lihim na kasalanan. Bawat addiction. Bawat gabi ng pag-iyak. Bawat fake smile. Bawat tahimik na guilt.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na matagal nang emotionally exhausted.
Hindi dahil iniwan sila ng Diyos.
Kundi dahil unti-unting pinatigas ng sakit ang puso nila.
Katulad ni David.
Mahal pa rin nila ang Diyos. Pero hindi na sila marunong lumapit.
At baka itong article na ito ang “Wise Woman of Tekoa” sa buhay mo.
Hindi para husgahan ka.
Kundi para sabihin:
Hindi mo na kailangang magtago.
May mga sugat na hindi gumagaling sa paglipas ng panahon.
Gumagaling lang kapag isinuko sa Diyos.
May mga pamilya na hindi nasisira sa isang araw.
Nasasira sila dahil sa mga taon ng katahimikan.
At may mga Kristiyano na physically present pero spiritually malayo.
Pero pakinggan mo ito nang mabuti:
Hindi pa tapos si Jesus sa buhay mo.
Ang Ebanghelyo ay hindi tungkol sa pagiging perpekto.
Ito ay tungkol sa reconciliation.
Sa Greek, ang salitang reconciliation ay:
καταλλαγή (katallagē)
Pagpapanumbalik. Kapayapaan matapos ang alitan. Pagbabalik ng relasyon.
Iyan ang binili ni Cristo sa krus.
At marahil kaya napakalalim ng kuwentong ito…
kasi lahat tayo alam ang pakiramdam ng unresolved pain.
Ang magsisi. Ang mangulila. Ang mawasak. Ang gustuhing bumalik.
At ang magtaka kung tatanggapin pa ba tayo ng Diyos.
Ang Marunong na Babae ng Tekoa ay ipinadala upang ipaalala kay David ang puso ng Diyos.
Isang Diyos na gumagawa ng paraan. Isang Diyos na naghahabol sa mga lumalayo. Isang Diyos na tumatawag pauwi.
Pero isa ring Diyos na kinokompronta ang mga bagay na pilit nating ibinabaon.
Dahil ang awa na walang katotohanan ay hindi tunay na pag-ibig.
At ang katotohanang walang awa ay nakakadurog.
Si Jesus ay dumating na puno ng dalawa.
John 1:14:
πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (plērēs charitos kai alētheias)
“Puspos ng biyaya at katotohanan.”
Hindi lang biyaya. Hindi lang katotohanan.
Pareho.
At marahil habang binabasa mo ito…
alam mong matagal nang kinakausap ng Diyos ang puso mo.
Minsan ang mga taong pinakamalayong tumatakbo ay hindi dahil ayaw nila sa Diyos.
Kundi dahil natatakot silang baka mahal pa rin sila Niya.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Naming Ben-Oni Before She Died
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Naming Ben-Oni Before She Died
There are moments in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
A sentence. A name. A burial. Then the story moves on.
But hidden inside one dying mother’s final breath is a level of emotional pain so deep that many believers have never fully stopped to feel it.
Rachel did not simply die giving birth.
She died heartbroken.
And before her soul left this world, she gave her son a name that carried the full weight of her suffering.
Most people know him as Benjamin.
But Rachel never called him that.
Her final word over her child was Ben-Oni.
And if you understand what that name truly means in Hebrew… the entire scene becomes almost unbearable.
Genesis 35:18 says:
"And it came to pass, as her soul was departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin."
The Hebrew text reads:
וַיְהִי בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ כִּי־מֵתָה וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Transliteration:
Vayehi b’tzeit nafshah ki metah vatikra sh’mo Ben-Oni; v’aviv kara lo Binyamin.
The phrase "Ben-Oni" (בֶּן־אוֹנִי) is often translated:
"Son of my sorrow"
But the depth of the Hebrew is even heavier than that.
The word "Oni" comes from the Hebrew root:
אוֹן / אָוֶן
Depending on context, it can mean: • sorrow • affliction • misery • grief • suffering • anguish • emotional exhaustion • painful labor • crushing trouble
Rachel was not naming her son after joy.
She was naming him after agony.
This was not poetic.
This was trauma speaking.
A dying woman looked at the child who cost her everything and whispered:
"You are the son of my pain."
And suddenly the story feels painfully human.
Because some of us know what it feels like to associate people with wounds.
Some people walk into our lives through heartbreak.
Some relationships cost us pieces of ourselves.
Some seasons leave scars so deep that even beautiful things become connected to suffering.
Rachel’s story is not emotionally distant.
It is terrifyingly relatable.
Especially when you realize how long Rachel had suffered before this moment.
Rachel was Jacob’s beloved.
The woman he worked fourteen years for.
The woman Scripture describes with extraordinary affection.
Genesis 29:20 says:
"And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her."
But despite being deeply loved… Rachel lived under years of silent torment.
Infertility.
Comparison.
Competition.
Emotional humiliation.
Watching her sister Leah bear child after child while her own womb remained closed.
Genesis 30:1 says:
"And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die."
The Hebrew wording is emotionally explosive.
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, v’im-ayin metah anokhi.
Literally:
"Give me sons — and if not, I am dead."
Not physically dead.
Emotionally dead.
Internally collapsing.
Rachel was carrying years of buried grief before she ever reached Bethlehem.
People often assume biblical figures felt emotions softly.
But Scripture tells the truth about human pain.
Rachel was jealous. Rachel was desperate. Rachel was emotionally exhausted. Rachel felt forgotten. Rachel felt behind. Rachel felt broken.
And eventually God opened her womb.
She gave birth to Joseph.
Then later, during the journey near Ephrath — Bethlehem — labor became catastrophic.
Genesis 35:16-17 says:
"And they journeyed from Bethel; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour.
And it came to pass, when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also."
The Hebrew phrase for "hard labour" is:
בְּהַקְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ
B’hakshotah b’lid’tah.
This expression communicates severe difficulty, violent pain, extreme distress.
This was not ordinary childbirth.
Rachel was dying.
And the midwife’s encouragement becomes emotionally haunting when you realize Rachel probably understood she would not survive.
"Fear not; thou shalt have this son also."
As if heaven gave her the child she longed for… at the exact cost of her own life.
Can you imagine the emotions inside her final moments?
She waited years for children.
Begged for children.
Wept for children.
Compared herself over children.
And now the second son arrives wrapped in unbearable pain.
Some mothers reading this know the terrifying nearness between life and death in childbirth.
Some people understand what it means when answered prayers arrive with suffering attached.
Because sometimes God’s blessings enter our lives through blood, tears, loss, and breaking.
That truth makes people uncomfortable.
But the Bible never hides human anguish.
And Rachel’s final act reveals something devastating:
Pain was shaping her perspective in real time.
She could not yet see beyond the suffering.
So she named the child from the place of agony.
Ben-Oni.
Son of my sorrow.
But then Jacob intervened.
Scripture says:
"But his father called him Benjamin."
In Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין
Binyamin.
Commonly translated:
"Son of the right hand"
The right hand in Hebrew thought symbolized: • strength • favor • authority • blessing • honor • covenant position
Rachel named him from pain.
Jacob renamed him from promise.
And suddenly the story becomes one of the most powerful spiritual pictures in all of Genesis.
Because grief wanted to define the boy.
But covenant rewrote his identity.
Somebody reading this has been living under names that pain gave you.
Failure. Rejected. Damaged. Unwanted. Too late. Too broken. Addicted. Unlovable. Forgotten.
The enemy loves naming people in moments of suffering.
Pain speaks loudly.
Trauma speaks loudly.
Depression speaks loudly.
Shame speaks loudly.
But heaven still has the authority to rename what grief tried to define.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham. Jacob became Israel.
And Ben-Oni became Benjamin.
There are people smiling publicly while privately carrying identities born from wounds.
Some people were named by abusive fathers.
Some by betrayal.
Some by abandonment.
Some by church hurt.
Some by addiction.
Some by divorce.
Some by sexual trauma.
Some by failure.
Some by the worst day of their lives.
But one encounter with God can interrupt the label suffering placed on you.
This is what makes the Gospel so emotionally overwhelming.
Jesus does not merely forgive sinners.
He restores identity.
The Greek word often used for salvation in the New Testament is:
σωτηρία (sōtēria)
Which carries the idea of: • rescue • deliverance • preservation • healing • wholeness
Not just escaping hell.
Wholeness.
Christ heals what sorrow tried to rename.
Isaiah prophetically described Jesus as:
"a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief"
Isaiah 53:3.
The Hebrew says:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
Ish mak’ovot v’yadua choli.
A man deeply familiar with pain.
Jesus understands Rachel.
He understands mothers who bury dreams.
He understands people crushed by sorrow.
He understands tears nobody else sees.
And perhaps one of the most haunting details in Rachel’s story is where she died.
Bethlehem.
The same region where centuries later another Son would be born.
One Son was named from sorrow.
Another Son would carry sorrow for the world.
Matthew later connects Rachel symbolically to grief when describing the massacre of children under Herod.
Matthew 2:18 says:
"In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children…"
Rachel became an image of grieving motherhood itself.
The woman who once cried through her own suffering became a prophetic picture of generations mourning loss.
And yet even there… God was still writing redemption.
Because Bethlehem would not only become associated with death.
It would become associated with salvation.
This is the pattern of God.
He enters places of pain and rewrites endings.
The cross itself looked like defeat.
Roman execution. Blood. Humiliation. Public shame.
But three days later resurrection exposed heaven’s deeper story.
And some of you need to hear this clearly:
Just because pain named a season does not mean pain gets the final word.
Rachel’s grief was real.
Her suffering was real.
Her tears were real.
The Bible does not minimize any of it.
But the child survived.
And Benjamin later became part of the tribes of Israel.
From Benjamin eventually came: • kings • warriors • covenant history
Even the apostle Paul identified himself as from the tribe of Benjamin.
Romans 11:1 says:
"For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin."
Imagine that.
A child once named "son of my sorrow" became part of the lineage connected to kingdom history and Gospel expansion.
That is what God does.
He brings purpose out of broken places.
Some of the people God uses most powerfully are those who survived seasons that almost emotionally buried them.
And maybe that is why this story hits so hard.
Because deep down many of us are still carrying hidden Ben-Oni moments.
Memories tied to pain.
People tied to pain.
Dreams tied to pain.
Versions of ourselves tied to pain.
But Jesus still steps into graves, trauma, shame, and sorrow saying:
"I make all things new."
Revelation 21:5.
The Greek:
Ἰδοὺ καινὰ ποιῶ πάντα
Idou kaina poiō panta.
"Behold, I am making all things new."
Not some things.
All things.
Including identities wounded by grief.
Including hearts exhausted by suffering.
Including people who secretly feel emotionally shattered.
Somebody reading this has smiled for years while carrying silent sorrow.
Somebody has attended church while internally bleeding.
Somebody has prayed while secretly wondering whether God still sees the pain.
Rachel’s story proves God does not erase human emotion from Scripture.
He preserves it.
Because He knows broken people need to see that heaven still works through shattered hearts.
And maybe tonight you need to let God rename the thing sorrow attached itself to.
Maybe your entire identity has been shaped by the darkest season you survived.
Maybe you still hear pain introducing you.
But Jesus specializes in resurrection.
Not cosmetic repair.
Resurrection.
He speaks life into dead places.
He restores what trauma distorted.
He heals what shame buried.
He redeems what suffering touched.
And one day every grieving believer will finally understand that sorrow was never the end of the story.
Be honest.
This hit harder than many expected.
Some wounds gave you names heaven never intended you to keep.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Nasasabi Tungkol sa Matinding Sakit ni Rachel Nang Pangalanan Niyang Ben-Oni ang Kanyang Anak Bago Siya Mamatay
May mga talata sa Bibliya na madalas nating madaanan nang napakabilis.
Isang pangalan. Isang pangyayari. Isang kamatayan.
Tapos tuloy agad ang kuwento.
Pero may mga talata na kapag hinayaan mong tumagos sa puso mo… babaguhin ka nila.
At isa rito ang huling salita ni Rachel habang siya ay namamatay.
Hindi lang basta namatay si Rachel habang nanganganak.
Namatay siyang wasak.
At bago tuluyang humiwalay ang kanyang kaluluwa sa kanyang katawan, binigyan niya ng pangalan ang kanyang anak mula sa pinakamalalim na sugat ng kanyang puso.
Kilala natin siya bilang Benjamin.
Pero hindi iyon ang pangalang unang ibinigay ni Rachel.
Ang huling pangalan na binigkas niya ay:
Ben-Oni.
At kapag naintindihan mo kung gaano kabigat ang ibig sabihin nito sa Hebrew… mararamdaman mong parang may humahawak sa dibdib mo.
Genesis 35:18:
"At nang naghihingalo na siya, sapagkat siya’y namatay, ay pinanganlan niya ang bata ng Benoni: datapuwa't tinawag siya ng kaniyang ama na Benjamin."
Sa Hebrew:
וַיְהִי בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ כִּי־מֵתָה וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Transliteration:
Vayehi b’tzeit nafshah ki metah vatikra sh’mo Ben-Oni; v’aviv kara lo Binyamin.
Karaniwang isinasalin ang “Ben-Oni” bilang:
“Anak ng aking kalungkutan.”
Pero mas mabigat pa roon ang tunay nitong diwa.
Ang salitang “Oni” ay mula sa Hebrew root na:
אוֹן / אָוֶן
Na maaaring mangahulugan ng:
• paghihirap • matinding dalamhati • emosyonal na pagod • pagdurusa • affliction • misery • agony • crushing sorrow
Hindi pinangalanan ni Rachel ang kanyang anak mula sa saya.
Pinangalanan niya ito mula sa sakit.
Mula sa trauma.
Mula sa paghihingalo.
Isang ina na unti-unti nang namamatay ang tumingin sa kanyang anak at para bang bumulong:
“Ikaw ang anak ng aking sakit.”
At doon nagiging sobrang totoo ang kuwento.
Dahil marami sa atin ang may mga bagay na konektado sa sakit.
May mga alaalang hindi natin kayang balikan nang hindi umiiyak.
May mga tao tayong minahal na iniwan tayong wasak.
May mga panalangin tayong nasagot… pero may kapalit na sugat.
At iyon mismo ang nangyari kay Rachel.
Bago pa man siya makarating sa Bethlehem, matagal na siyang sugatan.
Si Rachel ang pinakamamahal ni Jacob.
Siya ang babaeng pinagtrabahuhan ni Jacob nang labing-apat na taon.
Genesis 29:20:
"At naglingkod si Jacob na dahil kay Rachel ay pitong taon; at naging parang ilang araw lamang sa kaniya, dahil sa pagibig niya sa kaniya."
Mahal siya.
Pero kahit mahal siya… hindi ibig sabihin noon ay hindi siya nasasaktan.
Dahil taon-taon niyang pinapanood si Leah na magkaanak habang siya ay baog.
Taon-taon niyang kinukumpara ang sarili niya.
Taon-taon siyang umiiyak sa katahimikan.
Genesis 30:1:
"Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak, o kung hindi ay mamamatay ako."
Sa Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, v’im-ayin metah anokhi.
Literal:
“Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak — kung hindi, para na rin akong patay.”
Hindi ito simpleng drama.
Ito ay sigaw ng isang pusong pagod na pagod na.
May mga taong nakangiti sa labas pero matagal nang patay ang loob sa loob.
At iyon si Rachel.
Kaya nang sa wakas ay buksan ng Diyos ang kanyang sinapupunan… dumating nga ang pagpapala… pero dumating din ang matinding sakit.
Genesis 35:16-17:
"At sila'y naglakbay mula sa Bethel… at si Rachel ay naghirap sa panganganak.
At nang siya'y mahirapan sa panganganak, sinabi sa kaniya ng hilot, Huwag kang matakot; sapagka't magkakaroon ka rin ng anak na lalake."
Ang Hebrew phrase para sa “nahirapan sa panganganak” ay:
בְּהַקְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ
B’hakshotah b’lid’tah.
Hindi ito ordinaryong labor pain.
Ito ay matinding paghihirap.
Violently painful.
Life-threatening.
At marahil alam na ni Rachel na hindi na siya makakaligtas.
Kaya sobrang bigat ng sinabi ng hilot:
“Huwag kang matakot; magkakaroon ka rin ng anak.”
Parang ibinigay ng langit ang matagal na niyang hinihintay… kasabay ng pagkuha ng kanyang buhay.
Ilang taon niyang ipinagdasal ang anak na iyon.
Ilang gabi siyang umiyak para doon.
Ilang beses niyang kinuwestiyon ang sarili niya.
At ngayon dumating nga ang bata… pero kasabay ng kanyang kamatayan.
May mga tao rito na naiintindihan ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Na minsan ang answered prayer ay may kasamang sugat.
Na minsan ang blessing ay dumadaan muna sa pagdurugo.
Hindi tinatago ng Bibliya ang sakit ng tao.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakatotoo nito.
Sa huling sandali ni Rachel, ang sakit ang nagsasalita.
Kaya tinawag niya siyang:
Ben-Oni.
Anak ng aking dalamhati.
Pero biglang may ginawa si Jacob.
Sabi ng Bibliya:
“Ngunit tinawag siya ng kanyang ama na Benjamin.”
Sa Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין
Binyamin.
Ibig sabihin:
“Anak ng kanang kamay.”
At sa kultura ng Hebrew, ang “kanang kamay” ay simbolo ng:
• lakas • pabor • karangalan • awtoridad • pagpapala
Napakalalim nito.
Pinangalanan siya ni Rachel mula sa sakit.
Pero pinangalanan siya ni Jacob mula sa pangako.
At dito pumapasok ang napakalalim na mensahe ng Diyos.
Dahil maraming tao ang nabubuhay gamit ang pangalan na ibinigay ng trauma.
“Wala kang kwenta.”
“Marumi ka.”
“Sirang-sira ka na.”
“Hindi ka na magbabago.”
“Hindi ka na kayang mahalin.”
“Palpak ka.”
“Hindi ka sapat.”
Maraming tao ang ipinakilala ng sakit.
Pero may kapangyarihan ang Diyos na baguhin ang pangalan na ibinigay ng sugat.
Si Abram naging Abraham. Si Jacob naging Israel. Si Simon naging Peter. Si Saul naging Paul.
At si Ben-Oni naging Benjamin.
May mga taong tahimik na lumalaban araw-araw habang dinadala ang identity na nilikha ng trauma.
At marahil kaya sobrang bigat ng kuwentong ito… dahil marami sa atin ang may sariling “Ben-Oni” moments.
Mga memoryang konektado sa sakit.
Mga panahong halos sumira sa atin.
Mga gabing umiyak tayo nang walang nakakaalam.
Pero ang ebanghelyo ni Cristo ay hindi lang tungkol sa kapatawaran.
Ito ay tungkol sa restoration.
Sa Greek, ang salitang madalas gamitin para sa “kaligtasan” ay:
σωτηρία (sōtēria)
Na hindi lang ibig sabihin ay “ligtas.”
Kasama rito ang:
• healing • wholeness • deliverance • rescue • restoration
Si Jesus ay hindi lang namatay para patawarin ka.
Namatay Siya para ibalik kung sino ka talaga sa mata ng Diyos.
Isaiah 53:3:
"Lalaki ng kapanglawan at bihasa sa pagdadalamhati."
Sa Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
Ish mak’ovot v’yadua choli.
Ibig sabihin:
Isang taong lubos na nakakakilala ng sakit.
Naiintindihan ni Jesus ang pagdurusa ni Rachel.
Naiintindihan Niya ang mga pusong tahimik na umiiyak.
Naiintindihan Niya ang mga taong pagod nang magpanggap na okay.
At napakalalim din na si Rachel ay namatay malapit sa Bethlehem.
Dahil makalipas ang maraming taon… isa pang Anak ang isisilang sa Bethlehem.
Ang isang anak ay pinangalanan mula sa kalungkutan.
Pero ang isa pang Anak… dadalhin ang kalungkutan ng buong mundo.
Si Jesus.
At doon mo makikita ang pattern ng Diyos.
Hindi Siya umiiwas sa lugar ng sakit.
Pumapasok Siya roon.
At binabago Niya ang ending.
Ang krus ay mukhang pagkatalo.
Dugo. Kahihiyan. Pagdurusa.
Pero pagkatapos ng tatlong araw… dumating ang resurrection.
At may mga taong kailangang marinig ito ngayon:
Hindi porket sakit ang nagbigay ng pangalan sa season mo… ibig sabihin sakit na ang may huling salita.
May plano pa rin ang Diyos.
May redemption pa rin.
May healing pa rin.
May resurrection pa rin.
At ang batang minsang tinawag na “anak ng aking kalungkutan”… naging bahagi ng kasaysayan ng Israel.
Mula sa tribo ni Benjamin nagmula ang mga mandirigma, mga lider, at maging si apostle Paul.
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang batang ipinanganak sa matinding sakit ay ginamit pa rin ng Diyos sa mas malaking layunin.
At baka iyon din ang ginagawa ng Diyos sa buhay mo ngayon.
Baka ang season na halos sumira sa’yo… iyon pa ang gagamitin Niya para magligtas ng iba.
Baka ang sugat na pilit mong tinatago… iyon pa ang magiging testimony mo.
Baka hindi pa tapos ang Diyos sa kuwento mo.
Maging totoo ka.
May mga sugat na matagal nating tinatago.
May mga pangalang ibinigay sa’yo ng sakit na hindi kailanman intensyon ng langit na manatili sa’yo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are few subjects in Christianity that have been surrounded with as much confusion, division, tradition, fear, and misunderstanding as baptism.
paragraphs: There are few subjects in Christianity that have been surrounded with as much confusion, division, tradition, fear, and misunderstanding as baptism.

Some have reduced baptism to a religious ceremony. Some treat it as a symbolic ritual with little spiritual weight. Others teach it as absolutely necessary for salvation in a way that removes the finished work of Jesus Christ. And many believers have never truly understood the difference between water baptism and the baptism of the Holy Spirit.
But Scripture does not leave us confused.
When we return to the Word of God carefully… slowly… honestly… and examine the original Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek context behind these passages, something powerful begins to emerge.
Baptism is not about religious performance. It is about identification. Death. Cleansing. Union. Transformation. Burial. Resurrection. Empowerment.
And ultimately… it is about Jesus Christ.
The modern world is full of people who want spiritual power without repentance. People who want heaven without surrender. People who want inspiration without crucifixion.
But biblical baptism points directly toward death before resurrection.
The old life buried. The new life raised.
Not perfection. Not performance. But surrender.
The English word “baptism” comes from the Greek word βαπτίζω (baptizō).
This word means:
to immerse to dip completely to submerge to overwhelm
It was used in ancient Greek culture for ships sinking beneath water, cloth being dyed until permanently changed, and objects being fully immersed.
This matters deeply.

Biblical baptism was never meant to be shallow religious symbolism. It represented complete identification. A total transition. A visible declaration that someone was leaving one life behind and entering another.
When John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness preaching repentance, the religious world was shaken.
Matthew 3:1–2 says:
“In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
The Greek word for repentance here is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It does not merely mean feeling sorry. It means:
a change of mind an inner turning spiritual reversal transformation of direction
John was not calling people into emotional guilt. He was calling them into radical surrender before God.
And then came the baptism.
Matthew 3:6 says:
“And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.”
Notice the connection. Repentance. Confession. Baptism.
Not empty ritual. Not cultural Christianity. Not family tradition.
The waters symbolized cleansing, humility, and preparation for the coming Messiah.
Yet John himself declared that his baptism was incomplete compared to what Jesus would bring.
Matthew 3:11:
“I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I… he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.”
The phrase “Holy Ghost” comes from the Greek:
ἐν Πνεύματι Ἁγίῳ (en Pneumati Hagiō)
Meaning:
in Holy Spirit with Holy Spirit by Holy Spirit
The word πνεῦμα (pneuma) means:
breath wind spirit life-force
This is deeply connected to the Hebrew word רוּחַ (ruach), which also means:
breath wind Spirit
In Genesis 1:2, the Spirit of God hovering over the waters is:
רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (Ruach Elohim)
The Breath of God. The Spirit of God. The divine life of God moving.
This connection matters because baptism is never merely external. God has always desired inward transformation.
Ezekiel 36:25–27 prophetically declares:
“Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean… A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you… and I will put my spirit within you.”
Even in the Old Testament, water and Spirit were connected.
External cleansing. Internal transformation.
When Jesus Himself came to John for baptism, John resisted.
Matthew 3:14:
“But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?”
Why?
Because Jesus had no sin.
Yet Jesus answered:
“Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.”
Jesus was not being baptized because He needed repentance. He was identifying Himself with humanity. He was stepping into the mission that would ultimately lead Him to the cross.
And when Jesus came out of the water, something extraordinary happened.
Matthew 3:16–17:

“And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
Notice the revelation of the Trinity.
The Son in the water. The Spirit descending. The Father speaking.
Baptism became a revelation point. A declaration point. A public unveiling.
And this is important because true baptism still confronts identity.
The world tries to define people by:
past failures sexual sin addiction trauma religion politics race status achievement
But biblical baptism announces:
“I belong to Jesus Christ now.”
That is why Romans 6 becomes one of the most important passages on baptism in the entire Bible.
Romans 6:3–4 says:

“Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.”
The Greek phrase for “newness of life” is:
καινότης ζωῆς (kainotēs zōēs)
Meaning:
freshness of life new quality of existence transformed living
This is why baptism is so serious.
It symbolizes burial.
The old self. The old rebellion. The old identity. The old slavery.
Buried.
Then resurrection.
A new creation.
Not sinless perfection overnight. But a new direction. A new Lord. A new heart.
Some people entered the water dry sinners and came out merely wet religious people because there was never repentance or faith in Jesus Christ.
Water alone cannot save.
Only Jesus saves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ.
Yet true faith produces obedience.
That is why throughout the book of Acts, believers repeatedly responded with repentance and baptism.
Acts 2:37–38 says:
“Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart… Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins…”
The Greek word for “pricked” is κατενύγησαν (katenugēsan).
Meaning:
to pierce deeply to wound emotionally to stab inwardly
This was conviction. Not manipulation. Not emotional hype.
The Holy Spirit was exposing hearts.
And notice again:
repentance faith baptism
The early church did not separate conversion from surrender.
Modern Christianity often tries to keep Jesus as Savior while rejecting Him as Lord.
But the Gospel calls people into complete surrender.
Now this leads to one of the most misunderstood subjects in Christianity:
the baptism of the Holy Spirit.
Some deny it entirely. Others distort it emotionally. Others reduce it to spiritual elitism.
But Scripture teaches clearly that the Holy Spirit is not an optional accessory for believers.
He is essential.
Jesus told the disciples in Acts 1:4–5:
“Wait for the promise of the Father… For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.”
Then Acts 1:8 says:
“But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me…”
The Greek word for power is δύναμις (dynamis).
This is where we derive the word dynamite.
It means:
miraculous power strength ability spiritual force
The baptism of the Holy Spirit was connected to empowerment for witness.
Not celebrity Christianity. Not spiritual entertainment. Not emotional chaos.
Power to testify. Power to endure. Power to obey. Power to remain faithful in persecution. Power to live holy.
And when Pentecost came in Acts 2, the Spirit filled the believers.
Acts 2:2–4 says:
“And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind… And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost…”
Again, notice the connection to breath and wind.
The same Spirit hovering in Genesis. The same breath that gave life. The same power promised by Jesus.
Now dwelling within believers.
The New Testament reveals several important truths about the Holy Spirit.
The Spirit convicts. The Spirit comforts. The Spirit teaches. The Spirit seals believers. The Spirit empowers. The Spirit produces holiness.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance…”
Real spiritual maturity is not measured merely by gifts. It is measured by Christlike transformation.
Someone can speak loudly about spiritual power while secretly living in pride, immorality, bitterness, greed, lust, or rebellion.
But the Holy Spirit always glorifies Jesus Christ.
John 16:13–14 says:
“Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth… He shall glorify me.”
This is critical.
Any movement that magnifies personalities above Jesus eventually becomes spiritually dangerous.
The Holy Spirit does not draw people toward human worship. He draws people toward Christ.
Now many believers ask:
Is water baptism necessary?
The answer requires biblical precision.
Water baptism itself does not magically remove sin. The blood of Jesus Christ removes sin.
Yet baptism is repeatedly presented in Scripture as the obedient response of genuine believers.
Jesus commanded it. The apostles practiced it. The early church honored it.
Matthew 28:19:
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.”
The word “name” here is singular in Greek:
ὄνομα (onoma)
Not “names.”
One divine name. One God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Baptism publicly identifies someone with Jesus Christ.
It is covenantal. Public. Visible.
This is why so many persecuted believers throughout history considered baptism deeply costly.
In many nations, people could secretly believe in Jesus. But baptism exposed them publicly.
Families rejected them. Governments targeted them. Communities expelled them.
Baptism declared:
“My old life is dead. Jesus Christ is Lord now.”
That declaration still matters.
Especially in a generation obsessed with private spirituality but terrified of surrender.
Now one major theological debate concerns infant baptism versus believer’s baptism.
When examining the New Testament carefully, baptism consistently follows personal faith and repentance.
Acts 8:36–38 records the Ethiopian eunuch asking:
“See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?”
Then Philip baptized him after belief.
Throughout Acts the pattern repeatedly appears:
hearing the Gospel believing in Christ repenting being baptized
This is why many Christians hold to believer’s baptism by immersion.
Not because immersion magically saves. But because immersion best reflects the biblical imagery of burial and resurrection.
Colossians 2:12 says:
“Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God…”
Again the imagery is unmistakable.
Burial. Resurrection. New life.
But beyond theological debates, many people avoid baptism for deeper reasons.
Fear. Pride. Shame. Delay. Attachment to sin. Fear of people. Fear of commitment.
Some know Jesus is calling them deeper… but they keep postponing obedience.
And sometimes the delay is not intellectual. Sometimes it is spiritual resistance.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that feels like.
God has been dealing with your heart for months. Maybe years.
You feel conviction late at night. You feel the emptiness after distractions fade. You feel the spiritual exhaustion from trying to control your own life.
But surrender still terrifies you.
Because baptism represents something deeper than getting wet.
It represents yielding control.
And human flesh hates surrender.
Yet Jesus said in Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
Christianity was never designed to be casual cultural attachment.
It is death to self. And life through Christ.
Now there is another dangerous error that must be addressed.
Some people chase supernatural experiences while neglecting holiness.
But Scripture never separates the Holy Spirit from sanctification.
1 Peter 1:15–16 says:
“But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation; Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.”
The Spirit of God does not empower people to continue comfortably in rebellion. He transforms. Corrects. Convicts. Purifies.
This does not mean believers never struggle. Every real Christian battles the flesh.
But there is a difference between struggling against sin and surrendering to sin.
The Holy Spirit produces warfare against darkness.
Romans 8:13–14 says:
“For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.”
The word “mortify” comes from the Greek θανατόω (thanatoō).
Meaning:
to put to death to execute to destroy
The Christian life is spiritual warfare.
Not against people. But against sin. Pride. Darkness. The flesh. The lies of Satan.
And the Holy Spirit empowers believers to fight.
Now one of the most beautiful pictures of baptism appears in 1 Corinthians 10, where Paul connects Israel crossing through the Red Sea with baptism.
Israel passed through the waters while Pharaoh’s army was destroyed behind them.
The imagery is profound.
Bondage behind. Deliverance ahead.
Many believers today are emotionally exhausted because they keep trying to drag Egypt into the Promised Land.
They want freedom while preserving the chains.
But God calls His people out.
Out of darkness. Out of compromise. Out of spiritual numbness.
Not into dead religion. Into relationship with Jesus Christ.
And this is ultimately the center of all true baptism.
Union with Christ.
Galatians 3:27 says:
“For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”
The phrase “put on” comes from the Greek ἐνεδύσασθε (enedysasthe).
Meaning:
to clothe oneself to be wrapped in to wear completely
The believer is spiritually identified with Christ.
His death. His resurrection. His righteousness.
Not because humans earn salvation. But because Jesus accomplished what sinners never could.
The cross is still the center.
Jesus Christ lived the sinless life humanity failed to live. He bore the wrath of sin on the cross. He died. He was buried. He rose again physically from the grave.
And now salvation is offered freely through repentance and faith in Him.
Not through rituals alone. Not through moral self-improvement. Not through church attendance. Not through human goodness.
Only through Jesus.
Acts 4:12 says:
“Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.”
The world offers endless counterfeit baptisms.
Immersion into entertainment. Immersion into pornography. Immersion into politics. Immersion into self-worship. Immersion into digital distraction. Immersion into materialism.
People are drowning spiritually while pretending to be fulfilled.
But Jesus still calls people into living water.
“If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me… out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”
The next verse explains:
“But this spake he of the Spirit…”
Only the Spirit of God can truly satisfy the human soul.
Not likes. Not money. Not lust. Not applause. Not success.
People can gain the entire world and still remain spiritually empty.
There are successful people crying themselves to sleep. Famous people addicted in secret. Religious people spiritually dead.
Because the human soul was created for communion with God.
And baptism points toward that union.
Cleansed. Buried. Raised. Filled.
Some reading this have spent years near Christianity without truly surrendering.
You know church language. You know worship songs. You know sermons.
But deep inside… you know there has never been full surrender.
And maybe God is confronting that right now.
Not to shame you. But to save you.
Conviction is mercy.
