Bawat sirang pamilya. Bawat libing. Bawat pagtataksil. Bawat gabi ng pag-iyak nang palihim. Bawat pusong pagod na pagod nang magpanggap na okay lang. Bawat taong nakatitig sa kisame habang tinatanong ang sarili:
“Paano ba nauwi ang buhay ko rito?”
Lahat ng iyon… nagsimula sa isang sandali sa Eden.
Kilala ng marami si Adan bilang unang taong nagkasala.
Pero kakaunti lang ang tunay na nakakaunawa kung sino talaga siya.
Siya ang lalaking nakakita sa pagbagsak ng perpektong mundo.
Siya ang unang taong nakarinig sa tunog ng Diyos… at nagtago.
Siya ang unang taong nakaranas ng hiya.
Siya ang unang taong nakakita ng kamatayan.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… kuwento rin natin ang kuwento ni Adan.
Dahil hanggang ngayon, likas pa rin sa tao ang magtago.
Sa Genesis 2:7, sinabi sa orihinal na Hebreo:
“וַיִּיצֶר יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם”
“Vayyitser YHWH Elohim et-ha’adam.”
Ang ibig sabihin:
“At nilalang ng PANGINOONG Diyos ang tao.”
Ang salitang ginamit para sa “nilalang” ay “יָצַר” (yatsar).
Ito ay larawan ng isang magpapalayok na maingat na hinuhubog ang putik gamit ang sariling mga kamay.
Hindi ginawa si Adan nang basta-basta.
Hindi siya aksidente.
Hindi siya random.
Hinubog siya ng Diyos nang personal.
Pagkatapos sinabi ng Kasulatan:
“וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים”
“Vayyipach be’appav nishmat chayyim.”
“At hiningahan Niya ng hininga ng buhay ang kanyang mga butas ng ilong.”
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang unang tibok ng puso ng tao… nanggaling mismo sa hininga ng Diyos.
Pagmulat ni Adan ng kanyang mga mata, ang unang mukhang nakita niya ay ang Diyos.
Walang trauma. Walang anxiety. Walang depression. Walang insecurity. Walang takot. Walang kahihiyan.
Kapayapaan lang.
Presensya lang ng Diyos.
At dito mali ang pagkaunawa ng mundo tungkol sa Eden.
Hindi pangunahing tungkol sa luho ang paraiso.
Tungkol ito sa malayang pakikipag-ugnayan sa Diyos.
Kaya maraming mayaman pero malungkot. Kaya maraming sikat pero walang kapayapaan. Kaya maraming successful pero empty sa loob.
Dahil nilikha ang tao para sa presensya ng Diyos bago pa man sa productivity.
Genesis 2:15:
“לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ”
“Le’ovdah uleshomrah.”
“Inalagaan at pinangalagaan niya ang hardin.”
May trabaho na bago pa dumating ang kasalanan.
Pero trabahong walang burnout.
Layuning walang pagod.
Isipin mong mabuhay nang walang pressure na magpanggap.
Ganito ang buhay ni Adan noon.
Ganap na kilala. Ganap na minamahal.
Pagkatapos dumating ang ahas.
At dito nagsimula ang pinakamapanganib na digmaan sa kasaysayan.
Hindi unang inatake ni Satanas ang kilos.
Inatake niya ang tiwala.
Sinabi ng ahas:
“אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים”
“Af ki-amar Elohim…”
“Talaga bang sinabi ng Diyos…?”
Hanggang ngayon, iyan pa rin ang taktika ng kaaway.
“Talaga bang mahal ka ng Diyos?” “Talaga bang mahalaga ang kabanalan?” “Talaga bang may kapatawaran pa para sa iyo?”
Maraming tao ang hindi agad nahuhulog dahil sa rebelyon.
Nahuhulog sila dahil nagsimula silang pagdudahan ang kabutihan ng Diyos.
Pagkatapos kumain si Eva.
At naroon si Adan.
Tahimik.
Isa ito sa pinakamabigat na detalye sa buong Bibliya.
Mukhang kasama niya si Eva habang nangyayari ang lahat.
Alam niya.
Nakita niya.
Pero nanahimik siya.
Hanggang ngayon, maraming buhay ang nasisira dahil sa katahimikan kung kailan dapat nagsasalita ng katotohanan.
Pagkatapos dumating ang isang kagat na sumira sa buong sangnilikha.
Sabi ng Genesis:
“וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם”
“Vattippaqachnah einei sheneihem.”
“At nabuksan ang kanilang mga mata.”
Pero hindi ito enlightenment.
Pagkasira ito.
Kaagad nilang naramdaman ang hiya.
Sa unang pagkakataon sa kasaysayan, nakaramdam ang tao ng guilt.
At hanggang ngayon dala pa rin ito ng mundo.
Yung fake smile. Yung lihim na addiction. Yung “okay lang ako” kahit wasak na sa loob. Yung buhay na puro filter pero puno ng sakit.
Simula Eden… patuloy nang nagtatago ang tao.
Pagkatapos narinig nila ang tunog ng Diyos.
Genesis 3:8:
“Narinig nila ang PANGINOONG Diyos na naglalakad sa hardin.”
Ang “קוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים” (“qol YHWH Elohim”) ay nangangahulugang “tinig” o “tunog” ng Diyos.
Ang dating nagbibigay ng kapayapaan… ngayon ay nagdulot ng takot.
Iyan ang ginagawa ng kasalanan.
Bago magkasala si Adan, tumatakbo siya papunta sa Diyos.
Pagkatapos magkasala… nagtago siya.
At baka ito ang isa sa pinakamalungkot na linya sa Bibliya:
“Nagtago sila mula sa presensya ng PANGINOONG Diyos.”
Pero ginagawa pa rin ito ng tao ngayon.
Nagtatago sa pera. Nagtatago sa relasyon. Nagtatago sa social media. Nagtatago sa relihiyon. Nagtatago sa achievement.
Pero walang pagtatagong nakakapagpagaling.
Pagkatapos tinanong ng Diyos si Adan:
“Ayekkah?”
“Nasaan ka?”
Hindi iyon dahil hindi alam ng Diyos.
Inaanyayahan Niya si Adan na umamin.
Ito ang awa ng Diyos.
Kahit pagkatapos ng rebelyon… Siya pa rin ang unang lumapit.
May mga taong matagal nang tumatakbo mula sa Diyos dahil sa kahihiyan.
Pero nagsisimula ang Ebanghelyo sa isang Diyos na naghahanap pa rin sa mga nagtatago.
Sinisi ni Adan si Eva. Sinisi ni Eva ang ahas. At hanggang ngayon… mahilig pa rin ang tao manisi ng iba.
Pero pumasok na ang sumpa.
Sakit. Pagod. Kamatayan. Kalungkutan.
Romans 5:12:
“Sa pamamagitan ng isang tao ay pumasok ang kasalanan sa mundo, at sa pamamagitan ng kasalanan ay pumasok ang kamatayan.”
Hindi lang simpleng utos ang sinuway ni Adan.
Nabasag niya ang buong sangnilikha.
Bawat sementeryo ngayon… bunga ng Eden.
Pero kahit sa gitna ng paghatol, may awa pa rin.
Genesis 3:21:
“Ginawan ng PANGINOONG Diyos ng kasuotan na yari sa balat sina Adan at Eva.”
Ito ang unang kamatayan sa Bibliya.
May inosenteng namatay para matakpan ang kahihiyan ng tao.
Dito pa lang… bumubulong na ang Ebanghelyo.
Dahil darating ang isa pang inosente.
Si Jesucristo.
Tinawag Siya ni Pablo bilang “Huling Adan.”
1 Corinthians 15:45:
“Ang unang taong si Adan ay naging may buhay; ang huling Adan ay naging espiritung nagbibigay-buhay.”
Ang unang Adan nagdala ng kamatayan.
Ang huling Adan nagdala ng kaligtasan.
Nabigo si Adan sa hardin.
Nagtagumpay si Jesus sa hardin.
Nagtago si Adan mula sa Diyos.
Si Jesus naman ay nagsabing:
“Hindi ang kalooban Ko kundi ang Iyo ang mangyari.”
Dahil kay Adan, pumasok ang tinik.
Dahil kay Jesus, sinuot Niya ang koronang tinik.
Dahil kay Adan, dumating ang kamatayan.
Dahil kay Jesus, natalo ang kamatayan.
At baka ito ang pinaka-tragic na bahagi ng kuwento ni Adan.
Naalala niya ang paraiso.
Naalala niya ang mundo bago ang kabaong. Bago ang luha. Bago ang trauma. Bago ang hiya.
Isipin mo si Adan habang hawak ang katawan ni Abel matapos siyang patayin ni Cain.
Ang unang ama… nakatingin sa unang patay na anak.
Doon niya lubos na nakita kung ano talaga ang ginawa ng kasalanan.
Ang kasalanan laging nangangako ng kalayaan.
Pero sa huli… nagdadala ito ng libing.
Pero hindi doon nagtapos ang kuwento.
Dahil paglipas ng maraming taon, may isa pang Lalaking pumasok sa isa pang hardin.
At sa pagkakataong ito… hindi Siya kayang pigilan ng kamatayan.
Muling nabuhay si Jesus.
Nabuksan ang libingan.
At natupad ang Genesis 3:15.
“הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ”
“Hu yeshufkha rosh.”
“Dudurugin niya ang iyong ulo.”
Mula pa lang sa simula… nakaplano na ng Diyos ang pagtubos.
Ibig sabihin may pag-asa pa.
Hindi pa tapos ang kuwento mo.
Hindi mas makapangyarihan ang kasalanan mo kaysa biyaya ng Diyos.
Hindi ka masyadong marumi para kay Cristo.
Ang Diyos na naglakad sa Eden para hanapin si Adan… Siya pa rin ang Diyos na naghahanap sa mga sugatang tao ngayon.
Hindi para wasakin sila.
Kundi para iligtas sila.
May taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod nang magpanggap.
Pagod nang ngumiti habang wasak sa loob.
Pagod nang magtago.
At baka ngayon na ang araw para bumalik kay Jesus.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Darating ang araw na lahat ng pagtatago ay mabibigo… at biyaya na lang ng Diyos ang matitira.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Absalom Burned Joab’s Field to Get Attention
paragraphs: Why Absalom Burned Joab’s Field to Get Attention
There are people reading this right now who never wanted to become destructive.
You did not wake up one morning hoping to become bitter. You did not plan to become angry. You did not want your pain to start spilling onto innocent people.
But ignored wounds eventually become dangerous fires.
That is the terrifying tension hidden inside one of the Bible’s most emotionally explosive moments.
A prince. A father who stopped speaking to him. A commander who ignored him. A broken son screaming for someone to finally look at him.
And suddenly… fields are burning.
Most people know Absalom as the rebellious son who tried to steal King David’s throne. But before Absalom became dangerous publicly… he was dying internally.
And one of the clearest cries for attention in all of Scripture came through smoke.
The story is found in 2 Samuel 14.
Absalom had spent years emotionally isolated.
After murdering his brother Amnon for violating Tamar, Absalom fled into exile for three years. Eventually Joab convinced King David to allow Absalom to return to Jerusalem.
But there was a brutal condition attached.
David refused to see his own son.
Imagine living in the same city as your father while being treated like you no longer exist.
The Hebrew language in 2 Samuel 14 carries emotional weight many readers never fully notice.
When Scripture says David would not see Absalom’s face, the Hebrew reads:
"וּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא רָאָה"
Transliterated: “U’penei ha’melekh lo ra’ah.”
Literal sense: “He did not see the face of the king.”
In ancient Hebrew culture, seeing someone’s face represented restored relationship, acceptance, reconciliation, and covenant peace.
This was not merely physical distance.
This was relational rejection.
Absalom was home… but emotionally fatherless.
And some people understand that kind of pain too well.
You can live in the same house with someone and still feel abandoned.
You can sleep beside someone and still feel invisible.
You can sit in church every Sunday and still feel spiritually unseen.
Absalom spent two full years in Jerusalem without seeing David.
Two years.
Silence changes people.
Ignored pain mutates.
Unaddressed wounds evolve.
And eventually Absalom reached a breaking point.
Scripture says he repeatedly called for Joab.
Joab ignored him.
Again. And again. And again.
Then comes one of the most cinematic moments in the entire Old Testament.
2 Samuel 14:30:
“Therefore he said unto his servants, See, Joab’s field is near mine, and he hath barley there; go and set it on fire.”
The Hebrew phrase for “set it on fire” is:
"וְהַצִּיתוּהָ בָאֵשׁ"
Transliteration: “Ve’hatzituha ba’esh.”
Literal meaning: “Consume it with fire.”
This was not accidental.
This was intentional destruction born from emotional desperation.
And suddenly Joab came running.
The same man who ignored Absalom repeatedly immediately showed up when his field started burning.
That detail is devastating.
Because Absalom learned something many wounded people quietly learn:
Sometimes destruction gets attention faster than honesty.

That is why some people explode. That is why some people sabotage relationships. That is why some people self-destruct publicly. That is why some people become toxic. That is why some people lash out online. That is why some people destroy the very people they love.
Not always because they are evil.
Sometimes because pain convinced them fire is the only language people respond to.
And before judging Absalom too quickly… some of us have done similar things emotionally.
Maybe not with literal fire.
But with words. With manipulation. With cold silence. With rage. With rebellion. With reckless decisions. With hidden addictions. With spiritual compromise.
Sometimes people burn things because they are screaming internally:
“Will somebody finally notice me?”
This story becomes even heavier when we understand Joab.
Joab was not merely a military commander.
He was the bridge between Absalom and David.
Absalom believed Joab had the power to restore connection.
But Joab stopped responding.
And neglected people often become emotionally unpredictable.
The tragedy is that Absalom never truly healed.
He learned how to gain attention.
But he never learned surrender.
There is a massive difference.
Attention can temporarily soothe pain. Only God can transform it.
That is why wounded people who receive visibility without healing often become more dangerous, not less.
Absalom eventually became obsessed with image, power, admiration, and control.
2 Samuel 14:25 says:
“Now in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty.”
The Hebrew word for beauty here is:
"יָפֶה"
“Yafeh.”
Meaning: Beautiful, attractive, pleasing, externally admirable.
Absalom mastered external appearance while internally decaying.
And that is still happening today.
Some people look successful publicly while bleeding privately.
Some social media smiles are covering emotional funerals.
Some loud personalities are hiding abandoned hearts.
Some rebellious behavior is actually unresolved grief wearing armor.
This is why Jesus did not merely address behavior.
He addressed hearts.
Religion often focuses on visible flames. Jesus investigates hidden wounds.
The Gospel reveals something extraordinary.
God does not wait for us to burn fields before responding.
One of the greatest differences between earthly relationships and Christ is this:
Jesus moves toward broken people before they self-destruct completely.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek phrase for “commendeth his love” is:
"συνίστησιν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην"
Transliteration: “Synistēsin tēn heautou agapēn.”
Meaning: God demonstrates, proves, establishes His own sacrificial love.
Not after perfection. Not after cleanup. Not after image management.
While we were still broken.
That changes everything.
Absalom had to create fire to get attention.
Jesus climbed onto a cross because Heaven already saw us.
And maybe that is the part somebody desperately needed to hear today.
You do not need to destroy yourself to be seen by God.
You do not need to perform pain for Heaven to notice you.
You do not need to become louder, darker, angrier, or more reckless for Jesus to care.
He already sees you.
The Hebrew concept of God “seeing” carries deep covenant intimacy.
In Genesis 16:13 Hagar calls God:
"אֵל רֳאִי"
“El Roi.”
Meaning: “The God who sees me.”
Not the God who merely watches.
The God who truly sees.
Your hidden exhaustion. Your disappointment. Your private grief. Your secret shame. Your fear. Your loneliness. Your resentment. Your confusion.
Some people reading this have spent years silently asking:
“Does anybody notice what I’m carrying?”
God does.
But there is another warning inside Absalom’s story that cannot be ignored.
Pain that is not surrendered to God eventually starts spreading.
Absalom’s unresolved wounds eventually divided an entire kingdom.
Hurt people often hurt people.
Not because pain excuses sin. But because untreated wounds become spiritual infection.
This is why forgiveness matters. This is why repentance matters. This is why healing matters. This is why humility matters.
Some people are one ignored wound away from becoming someone they never imagined.
And that is why we desperately need Christ.
Not motivational spirituality. Not image-based religion. Not church performance.
We need heart resurrection.
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is supernatural transformation.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
The Hebrew phrase:
"לֵב חָדָשׁ"
“Lev chadash.”
A new heart.
Not patched. Not cosmetically improved. Not temporarily distracted.
Made new.
There are people trying to heal eternal wounds with temporary attention.
It will never be enough.
More validation will not save you. More followers will not save you. More money will not save you. More applause will not save you. More distractions will not save you.
Only Jesus can reach the places pain buried alive.
And perhaps the saddest part of Absalom’s story is this:
The son who desperately wanted connection eventually died hanging from a tree.
Suspended between heaven and earth.
Broken by pride. Consumed by rebellion. Destroyed by unresolved pain.
David wept bitterly afterward.
2 Samuel 18:33:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee.”
One of the most heartbreaking cries in Scripture.
But unlike David… Jesus actually did die for us.
That is the Gospel.
Christ took the punishment rebellion deserved.
The Son of God stepped into the destruction human sin created.
And through the cross, broken sons and daughters can finally come home.
No more pretending. No more performing. No more burning fields to feel visible.
Grace sees you already.
And maybe this article exposed something hidden inside you.

Maybe you have been acting strong while quietly bleeding. Maybe your anger is actually grief. Maybe your rebellion is rooted in rejection. Maybe your exhaustion comes from carrying wounds nobody noticed.
Jesus is still calling you toward healing.
Not condemnation. Healing.
Your honesty might help someone else finally stop suffering silently.
Some wounds do not scream through tears. Sometimes they scream through fire.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Sinunog ni Absalom ang Bukirin ni Joab Para Lang Mapansin
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na hindi naman talaga gustong maging mapanira.
Hindi mo pinangarap maging galit. Hindi mo hiniling na maging malamig ang puso mo. Hindi mo gustong dumating sa puntong ang sugat mo ay nagsisimulang makasakit ng ibang tao.
Pero ang sakit na hindi pinapansin… kalaunan nagiging apoy.
At iyon ang isa sa pinakamabigat na emosyonal na eksena sa buong Biblia.
Isang prinsipe. Isang amang tumigil nang kausapin siya. Isang lalaking paulit-ulit siyang binale-wala. Isang sugatang anak na desperadong gustong mapansin.
At biglang… may nasusunog na bukirin.
Kilala ng marami si Absalom bilang rebeldeng anak ni David na nagtangkang agawin ang trono. Pero bago naging mapanganib si Absalom sa publiko… matagal muna siyang namatay sa loob.
At isa sa pinakamalalakas na sigaw para mapansin sa buong Kasulatan ay dumaan sa apoy.
Matatagpuan ang kuwento sa 2 Samuel 14.

Matapos patayin ni Absalom ang kapatid niyang si Amnon dahil sa ginawa nito kay Tamar, tumakas siya at namuhay sa pagkakatapon nang tatlong taon. Kalaunan, nakumbinsi ni Joab si Haring David na payagang makabalik si Absalom sa Jerusalem.
Pero may mabigat na kondisyon.
Ayaw siyang makita ng sarili niyang ama.
Isipin mong nasa iisang siyudad lang kayo ng ama mo… pero para kang hindi umiiral.
Sa Hebrew, nang sabihin ng Kasulatan na hindi nakita ni Absalom ang mukha ng hari, ito ang nakasulat:
"וּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא רָאָה"
Transliteration: “U’penei ha’melekh lo ra’ah.”
Literal na kahulugan: “Hindi niya nakita ang mukha ng hari.”
Sa kulturang Hebreo, ang “makita ang mukha” ay simbolo ng pagtanggap, pagkakasundo, at muling pagpapanumbalik ng relasyon.
Hindi lang ito simpleng distansya.
Ito ay emosyonal na pagtanggi.
Nasa bahay si Absalom… pero parang ulila pa rin.
At may mga taong nakakaramdam niyan hanggang ngayon.
Pwede kayong nasa iisang bahay… pero pakiramdam mo mag-isa ka.
Pwede kayong magkatabi sa kama… pero hindi ka na nakikita.
Pwede kang magsimba linggo-linggo… pero parang walang nakakakita sa totoong dinadala mo.
Dalawang taon nanatili si Absalom sa Jerusalem nang hindi man lang nakikita si David.
Dalawang taon.
Binabago ng katahimikan ang tao.
Kapag hindi ginagamot ang sugat… lumalala.
Kapag hindi inaayos ang sakit… kumakalat.
At dumating si Absalom sa sukdulan.
Paulit-ulit niyang ipinatawag si Joab.
Pero hindi siya pinansin.
Paulit-ulit.
Hanggang dumating ang isa sa pinaka-cinematic na tagpo sa Lumang Tipan.
2 Samuel 14:30:
“Kaya sinabi niya sa kaniyang mga alipin, Tingnan ninyo, ang bukid ni Joab ay malapit sa akin, at mayroon siyang sebada roon; puntahan ninyo at sunugin ninyo.”
Sa Hebrew, ang “sunugin” ay:
"וְהַצִּיתוּהָ בָאֵשׁ"
Transliteration: “Ve’hatzituha ba’esh.”
Literal na kahulugan: “Silaban ninyo ng apoy.”
Hindi ito aksidente.
Sinadya ito.
Desperadong sigaw ito ng isang pusong hindi na matiis na hindi mapansin.
At biglang dumating si Joab.
Ang lalaking paulit-ulit siyang hindi pinapansin… agad sumipot nang may nasusunog na.
Napakabigat ng detalye na iyon.
Dahil may mga sugatang tao ring natututong ganito:
“Minsan, mas mabilis mapansin ang gulo kaysa katotohanan.”

Kaya may mga taong sumasabog. Kaya may mga relasyon na sinisira. Kaya may mga taong unti-unting winawasak ang sarili nila. Kaya may mga taong nagiging toxic. Kaya may mga taong nagrerebelde. Kaya may mga taong lumalayo sa Diyos.
Hindi palaging dahil masama sila.
Minsan dahil naniwala silang ang apoy lang ang wikang pinapakinggan ng mundo.
At bago mo husgahan si Absalom… baka may mga pagkakataon ding parang ganoon tayo.
Hindi man literal na apoy.
Pero sa masasakit na salita. Sa galit. Sa pananahimik. Sa paglayo. Sa pagtatago. Sa bisyo. Sa kasalanan. Sa panlalamig.
May mga taong naninira dahil may sumisigaw sa loob nila:
“May makakapansin ba sa akin?”
Mas mabigat pa ang kuwento kapag naunawaan natin kung sino si Joab.
Hindi lang siya sundalo.
Siya ang tulay ni Absalom pabalik kay David.
At nang tumigil siyang sumagot… lalong naging magulo si Absalom.
Kapag matagal pinababayaan ang sugat… nagiging mapanganib ang puso.
Pero ang tunay na trahedya ay ito:
Natuto si Absalom kung paano kumuha ng atensyon.
Pero hindi siya natutong magpagaling.
Magkaibang bagay iyon.
Kayang pansamantalang patahimikin ng atensyon ang sakit. Pero Diyos lang ang kayang magbago ng puso.
Kaya maraming sugatang tao na kapag sumikat… lalo pang nasisira.
Kalaunan, naging obsessed si Absalom sa itsura, kapangyarihan, at paghanga ng tao.
2 Samuel 14:25:
“Sa buong Israel ay walang lalaking pinupuri nang higit kay Absalom dahil sa kaniyang kagandahan.”
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “kagandahan” ay:
"יָפֶה"
“Yafeh.”
Ibig sabihin: Maganda, kaaya-aya, kahanga-hanga sa panlabas.
Napaganda ni Absalom ang panlabas niyang anyo habang unti-unting nasisira ang loob niya.
At nangyayari pa rin iyon hanggang ngayon.
May mga mukhang masaya online… pero umiiyak kapag mag-isa.
May mga mukhang matatag… pero wasak na pala sa loob.
May mga taong maingay… dahil takot silang marinig ang katahimikan.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hindi lang ugali ang tinitingnan ni Jesus.
Puso ang hinahanap Niya.
Madalas ang relihiyon nakatuon sa nakikitang apoy. Pero si Cristo… diretso sa sugat.
At dito lalong gumaganda ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi hinihintay ng Diyos na sirain muna natin ang lahat bago Niya tayo lapitan.
Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Sa Greek:
"συνίστησιν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην"
Transliteration: “Synistēsin tēn heautou agapēn.”
Kahulugan: Ipinapakita at pinatutunayan ng Diyos ang Kaniyang pag-ibig.
Hindi pagkatapos nating maging malinis. Hindi pagkatapos nating magbago. Hindi pagkatapos nating ayusin ang sarili.
Habang makasalanan pa tayo.
Habang sugatan pa tayo.
Habang magulo pa tayo.
Hindi kailangang magsunog ng bukirin para mapansin ng Diyos.
Nakikita ka na Niya noon pa.
Sa Genesis 16:13, tinawag ni Hagar ang Diyos na:
"אֵל רֳאִי"
“El Roi.”
Ang ibig sabihin: “Ang Diyos na nakakakita sa akin.”
Hindi lang basta nanonood.
Kundi tunay na nakakakita.
Nakikita Niya ang pagod mo. Nakikita Niya ang lihim mong iyak. Nakikita Niya ang sugat na tinatago mo. Nakikita Niya ang bigat na hindi mo masabi. Nakikita Niya ang galit na hindi mo maintindihan.
At baka may nagbabasa nito na matagal nang nagtatanong:
“May nakakapansin pa ba sa akin?”
Oo.
Nakikita ka ng Diyos.
Pero may babala rin sa kuwento ni Absalom.
Ang sakit na hindi isinusuko sa Diyos… kalaunan nakakasakit din ng iba.
Ang sugat ni Absalom ay hindi lang sumira sa kaniya.
Hinati nito ang buong kaharian.
Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapatawad. Kaya mahalaga ang pagsisisi. Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapagaling. Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapakumbaba.
May mga taong isang sugat na lang ang layo bago maging taong hindi nila akalaing magiging sila.
At iyan ang dahilan kung bakit kailangan natin si Cristo.
Hindi lang religion. Hindi lang church attendance. Hindi lang magandang imahe.
Kailangan natin ng bagong puso.
Ezekiel 36:26:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
Sa Hebrew:
"לֵב חָדָשׁ"
“Lev chadash.”
Bagong puso.
Hindi patched. Hindi tinakpan lang. Hindi dinistract lang.
Bagong-bago.
Maraming tao ang sinusubukang pagalingin ang eternal na sugat gamit ang temporaryong atensyon.
Pero hindi iyon sapat.
Hindi followers ang makakapagligtas. Hindi validation. Hindi pera. Hindi kasikatan. Hindi applause.
Si Jesus lang.
At marahil ang pinakamalungkot sa kuwento ni Absalom ay ito:
Ang anak na desperadong gustong mapalapit… namatay na nakabitin sa puno.
Wasak ng pride. Nilamon ng rebelyon. Sinira ng sugat na hindi gumaling.
At umiyak si David.
2 Samuel 18:33:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee.”
Isa sa pinakamasakit na iyak sa buong Biblia.
Pero hindi tulad ni David… talagang namatay si Jesus para sa atin.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Pinasan ni Cristo ang parusang dapat sana ay atin.
Para ang mga sugatang anak ay makauwi na sa wakas.
Wala nang pagtatago. Wala nang pagpapanggap. Wala nang pagsusunog para lang mapansin.
Nakikita ka na ng biyaya.
At baka may tinamaan talaga sa puso mo habang binabasa ito.
Baka matagal ka nang pagod. Baka ang galit mo ay sugat lang pala. Baka ang pagrerebelde mo ay bunga ng rejection. Baka tahimik ka lang… pero unti-unti ka nang nasusunog sa loob.
Hindi ka pa tinatalikuran ni Jesus.
Tinatawag ka pa rin Niya papunta sa kagalingan.
Kung tumama ito sa puso mo, huwag mo lang basta i-scroll.
At maging totoo ka sa comments.
Baka ang honesty mo ang makatulong para may ibang taong hindi na magdusa nang tahimik.
May mga sugat na hindi sumisigaw sa pamamagitan ng luha. Minsan… apoy ang ginagamit nila.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Elisha
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Elisha
Nobody talks enough about how lonely Elisha must have felt.
Most people remember the miracles. The oil. The widow. The axe head floating. The dead boy breathing again. Naaman’s skin turning clean. The army blinded. The waters healed.
But very few people stop long enough to look into the exhausted eyes of the man behind the miracles.
Very few people notice the silence between the verses.
Because Elisha was not merely a prophet.
He was a man constantly carrying the grief of watching people reject the God who kept saving them.
And maybe that is why his story still feels painfully modern.
Because some of you know exactly what it feels like to keep pouring into people who only remember God when they are desperate.
Some of you know what it feels like to love people who only call heaven when their world catches fire.
Elisha understood that pain.
And the terrifying part is… he inherited it.
The day Elijah threw his mantle over Elisha, something far deeper than ministry was transferred.
A burden. A war. A loneliness. A calling that would cost him almost everything.
In 1 Kings 19:19, the Hebrew text says Elijah found Elisha while he was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen.
The Hebrew phrase is:
“שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר צְמָדִים” (Sheneim-Asar Tzemadim) “twelve pairs.”
This was not a poor farmer.
This represented wealth. Influence. Security. A future.
Elisha was not rescued from failure.
He walked away from comfort.
That changes everything.
Because following God is not always leaving brokenness. Sometimes it means leaving what already looks successful.
Some of the hardest callings in the Kingdom are not asking people to leave destruction. They are asking people to leave comfort.
And most people never do.
Elisha burned the plows. Killed the oxen. Fed the people. Walked away.
No backup plan. No safety net. No emergency exit.
Because real surrender removes the bridge back to your old life.
That sentence alone just exposed somebody.
You have been asking God for clarity while secretly preserving an escape route.
But Elisha understood something many believers still avoid.
Partial surrender is still rebellion.
What makes Elisha’s story even more devastating is that he spent years serving in obscurity before the public miracles ever happened.
Most people skip this part because modern culture worships visibility.
But before Elisha became powerful publicly, he became faithful privately.
2 Kings 3:11 describes him as:
“the one who poured water on the hands of Elijah.”
In Hebrew:
“יָצַק מַיִם עַל־יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ” (yatsaq mayim al-yedei Eliyahu)
He served. Quietly. Without applause. Without followers. Without a platform.
And this generation hates that stage.
People want mantles without mentorship. Authority without crushing preparation. Power without hidden obedience.
But heaven develops people in secret before trusting them in public.
Even Jesus spent approximately thirty years mostly hidden before three years of ministry.
And still people today panic when God takes too long.
The truth is horrifying.
Sometimes the delay is mercy.
Because premature promotion destroys people who have not yet been spiritually crucified.
Elisha watched Elijah be hated. Mocked. Threatened. Rejected.
He watched the emotional cost of carrying God’s voice in a rebellious generation.
Yet he stayed.
That matters.
Because loyalty is rare now.
People leave when correction comes. People disappear when offense rises. People abandon spiritual assignments the moment comfort dies.
But Elisha remained.
And eventually the day came when Elijah was taken.
The Jordan River split. The chariots of fire appeared. The whirlwind descended.
Imagine standing there.
Imagine watching the man who discipled you vanish into heaven.
Imagine the silence afterward.
2 Kings 2:12 says Elisha cried:
“My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!”
The Hebrew:
“אָבִי אָבִי רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו” (avi avi rekhev Yisra’el ufarashav)
This was not theatrical emotion.
This was grief.
Deep grief.
The kind of grief people feel when heaven removes someone they depended on.
And some of you are there right now.
You lost someone. A mentor. A parent. A spiritual covering. A season. A version of yourself.
And nobody understands the silence you have been carrying since.
But here is what most people miss.
Elisha picked up the mantle anyway.
Even while grieving.
That is maturity.
Still obeying God while your heart is shattered.
Still showing up while emotionally bleeding.
Still trusting heaven when life no longer feels familiar.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
One of the most misunderstood moments in Elisha’s story happens in 2 Kings 2:23–24.
A group of youths mocked him saying:
“Go up, you baldhead!”
Then bears came from the woods.
Many people reduce this to a strange angry reaction. But the Hebrew context is darker.
The phrase used:
“קֵרֵחַ” (qereach)
was likely more than an insult about appearance.
This was public contempt against the prophetic authority of God.
The phrase “Go up” may have also mocked Elijah’s ascension.
In other words:
“Why don’t you disappear too?”
This was rebellion. Mockery. Hatred toward the things of God.
And modern culture is filled with the same spirit.
People mock holiness. Mock repentance. Mock purity. Mock conviction. Mock surrender.
But scripture repeatedly warns that contempt toward God hardens the human heart.
Not because God is insecure. But because rebellion slowly destroys the soul from within.
The terrifying thing about sin is that eventually people stop feeling conviction.
And when conviction disappears, destruction usually follows.
That is why the Gospel matters so much.
Because Jesus did not merely come to improve behavior.
He came to resurrect dead hearts.
The Greek word for repentance is:
“μετάνοια” (metanoia)
It means a change of mind so deep it transforms direction.
Not performative religion. Not fake church language. Not social media Christianity.
Transformation.
Real transformation.
And Elisha’s life constantly pointed toward this deeper reality.
Even his miracles carried prophetic echoes of Christ.
When Elisha healed the poisoned waters in 2 Kings 2:21, he threw salt into the spring.
The Hebrew says:
“כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה רִפִּאתִי לַמַּיִם הָאֵלֶּה” (Koh amar YHWH rippiti la-mayim ha’eleh)
“Thus says the LORD, I have healed these waters.”
Notice carefully.
God did not merely treat symptoms. He healed the source.
That is exactly what Jesus does.
Religion modifies behavior externally. Christ transforms the source internally.
Some of you have spent years trying to manage symptoms while your soul still bleeds underneath.
But Jesus still heals at the source.
The addictions. The secret shame. The hidden bitterness. The trauma. The self-hatred. The exhaustion. The compromise.
He still restores human beings from the inside out.
One of the most breathtaking moments in Elisha’s story happens during famine.
Death surrounded the land. People were desperate. Fear was everywhere.
Sound familiar?
In 2 Kings 4, a widow faced losing her sons because of debt.
Elisha asked her:
“What do you have in your house?”
That question still echoes today.
Because people keep focusing on what they lost while God asks what remains.
The oil multiplied. The debt was covered. The family survived.
And hidden inside this miracle is one of the deepest spiritual truths in scripture.
God often multiplies surrendered emptiness.
But pride keeps people full.
That is why brokenness can become holy ground.
Because people who know they are desperate for God stop pretending they can save themselves.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:3:
“Blessed are the poor in spirit.”
The Greek:
“μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι” (makarioi hoi ptōchoi tō pneumati)
This means spiritually dependent. Completely aware of need.
And that is the doorway to grace.
Not self-righteousness. Not religious performance. Not polished appearances.
Dependency.
Some of you are exhausted because you have been trying to carry life without surrender.
But Christianity was never meant to be cosmetic behavior modification.
It was always about dying and being reborn through Christ.
And maybe that is why Elisha’s final miracle is so unforgettable.
Even after death… God still moved through him.
2 Kings 13:21 says a dead man was thrown into Elisha’s tomb. When the body touched Elisha’s bones, the man revived.
Think about that.
The anointing outlived the man.
His private obedience created impact beyond his lifetime.
That is legacy.
Not followers. Not fame. Not applause.
Transformation that survives your absence.
The world celebrates visibility. Heaven celebrates faithfulness.
And maybe the untold tragedy of Elisha’s story is this:
He performed twice as many miracles as Elijah. Yet most people still talk more about Elijah.
Can you handle obeying God without becoming the most remembered person in the room?
Can you stay faithful if someone else receives more recognition?
Because true surrender stops negotiating for human applause.
That silence just convicted somebody deeply.
And underneath everything in Elisha’s life was a greater prophetic shadow pointing toward Jesus Christ.
The One greater than every prophet. The One greater than every miracle. The One who did not merely raise the dead temporarily but conquered death itself.
Jesus did what no prophet could fully accomplish.
He became the sacrifice.
The Hebrew prophet Isaiah declared:
“וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ” (Vehu mecholal mip’shaeinu)
“But He was pierced for our transgressions.” — Isaiah 53:5
And centuries later Christ fulfilled it.
The Greek words Jesus cried on the cross in John 19:30 were:
“Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai)
“It is finished.”
Not “I am finished.”
“It is finished.”
The debt. The judgment. The separation. The price of sin.
Paid.
Completely.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement. Not religious cosmetics. Not trying harder.
Rescue.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to earn what Jesus already purchased through blood.
You have exhausted yourself pretending. Pretending you are strong. Pretending you are clean. Pretending you are okay.
But heaven is not waiting for your performance.
Heaven is calling for your surrender.
And maybe this article was not an accident.
Because beneath the noise… beneath the anxiety… beneath the distractions… beneath the hidden sin…
you still miss Him.
You still miss peace. You still miss innocence. You still miss truth.
And Jesus Christ is still calling people home.
Not perfect people. Broken people.
People tired of hiding. People tired of carrying shame. People tired of pretending darkness is freedom.
The cross still stands. The tomb is still empty. Grace is still available.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this… send this to them.
Some people are silently drowning while smiling publicly.
One day people will realize they were starving for God while feeding every other appetite.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Kwento ni Eliseo
Halos walang nag-uusap tungkol sa lungkot ni Eliseo.
Naalala ng karamihan ang mga himala. Ang langis na hindi naubos. Ang batang muling nabuhay. Ang palakol na lumutang. Ang ketong ni Naaman na gumaling. Ang mga sundalong nabulag.
Pero kakaunti lang ang tunay na tumitingin sa pagod na kaluluwa ng lalaking ginamit ng Diyos.
Kakaunti lang ang nakakaramdam ng katahimikan sa pagitan ng mga talata.
Dahil si Eliseo ay hindi lang propeta.
Isa siyang taong araw-araw na dinadala ang bigat ng makitang paulit-ulit na tinatalikuran ng tao ang Diyos na paulit-ulit namang nagliligtas sa kanila.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakalapit pa rin ng kwento niya sa panahon natin ngayon.
Dahil may mga taong nagbabasa nito na alam ang pakiramdam ng laging nagbibigay pero parang walang tunay na nagbabago.
Yung ikaw ang takbuhan kapag wasak na ang lahat… pero kapag maayos na ulit ang buhay nila, nakakalimutan ka na.
Naiintindihan iyon ni Eliseo.
Dahil minana niya ang sakit na iyon.
Noong isinuklob ni Elias ang balabal niya kay Eliseo, hindi lang ministeryo ang ipinasa.
Pasanin. Laban. Pag-iisa. Isang pagtawag na sisira sa dating buhay niya.
Sa 1 Hari 19:19, sinasabi sa Hebreo na si Eliseo ay nag-aararo kasama ang labindalawang pares ng baka.
“שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר צְמָדִים” (Sheneim-Asar Tzemadim)
Hindi mahirap si Eliseo.
May kaya siya. May seguridad. May kinabukasan.
Hindi siya iniligtas mula sa pagkabigo.
Iniwan niya ang komportableng buhay.
At iyon ang hindi kayang gawin ng karamihan.
Dahil minsan ang pagtawag ng Diyos ay hindi paglayo sa kasalanan.
Minsan paglayo ito sa bagay na mukhang maayos na.
Sinunog ni Eliseo ang araro. Pinatay ang mga baka. Ipinakain sa mga tao. At tuluyang umalis.
Walang backup plan. Walang reserve. Walang daan pabalik.
Dahil ang totoong pagsuko sa Diyos ay hindi nag-iiwan ng lihim na exit.
At baka may tinatamaan na dito.
Matagal ka nang humihingi ng linaw sa Diyos habang lihim mong pinoprotektahan ang daan pabalik sa dati mong buhay.
Pero naiintindihan ni Eliseo ang isang bagay na maraming Kristiyano ang iniiwasan.
Ang kalahating pagsunod ay pagsuway pa rin.
Bago naging makapangyarihang propeta si Eliseo, naging tahimik muna siyang lingkod.
At ayaw ng modernong mundo sa bahaging iyon.
Gusto ng tao ng platform nang walang proseso. Gusto ng authority nang walang pagdurog. Gusto ng anointing nang walang lihim na katapatan.
Pero bago pagkatiwalaan ng Diyos ang tao sa publiko, hinuhubog muna Niya ito nang palihim.
Sa 2 Hari 3:11, si Eliseo ay inilalarawan bilang:
“ang nagbubuhos ng tubig sa mga kamay ni Elias.”
“יָצַק מַיִם עַל־יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ” (yatsaq mayim al-yedei Eliyahu)
Tahimik siyang naglingkod. Walang spotlight. Walang papuri. Walang pangalan.
At doon sinusubok ang puso.
Dahil madaling sundan si Jesus kapag napapalakpakan ka.
Pero ibang usapan kapag tahimik ang langit at walang nakakakita sa sakripisyo mo.
Nanatili si Eliseo.
Nakita niyang kamuhian si Elias. Nakita niyang pagtawanan. Nakita niyang habulin.
Pero hindi siya umalis.
At dumating ang araw na inakyat si Elias sa langit.
Nahati ang Jordan. Dumating ang mga karo ng apoy. Umihip ang ipoipo.
At doon sumigaw si Eliseo:
“אָבִי אָבִי רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו” (Avi avi rekhev Yisra’el ufarashav)
“My father, my father…”
Hindi iyon drama.
Kalungkutan iyon.
Yung klaseng lungkot kapag may taong ginamit ng Diyos sa buhay mo… tapos biglang nawala.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na may ganoong sugat pa rin.
At ang mas matindi?
Pinulot pa rin ni Eliseo ang balabal.
Kahit sugatan. Kahit umiiyak. Kahit hindi handa.
Iyon ang maturity.
Ang sumunod pa rin sa Diyos kahit wasak ang puso mo.
Be honest. Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
Isa sa mga pinakamalalim na bahagi ng kwento ni Eliseo ay ang pagpapagaling niya sa maruming tubig.
Sa 2 Hari 2:21 sinabi niya:
“כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה רִפִּאתִי לַמַּיִם הָאֵלֶּה” (Koh amar YHWH rippiti la-mayim ha’eleh)
“Ganito ang sabi ng Panginoon: pinagaling Ko ang tubig na ito.”
Pansinin mo.
Hindi lang inayos ng Diyos ang sintomas.
Pinagaling Niya ang pinagmulan.
At iyon mismo ang ginagawa ni Jesus.
Hindi lang Niya inaayos ang panlabas mong kilos.
Binabago Niya ang puso.
May mga taong matagal nang sinusubukang itago ang sugat gamit ang ngiti.
Pero nakikita pa rin ng Diyos ang pagod. Ang trauma. Ang sikreto. Ang addiction. Ang guilt. Ang depression.
At hanggang ngayon… nagpapagaling pa rin si Cristo.
Sa panahon ng taggutom, isang biyuda ang lumapit kay Eliseo. Malulubog na sila sa utang. Mawawala na ang kanyang mga anak.
At tinanong siya ni Eliseo:
“Anong meron ka sa bahay?”
Napakalalim ng tanong na iyon.
Dahil abala ang tao sa pag-iisip kung ano ang nawala… habang tinitingnan ng Diyos kung ano pa ang natitira.
At doon nagsimulang dumami ang langis.
Dahil madalas minumultiply ng Diyos ang pusong surrendered.
Pero hindi Niya mapupuno ang pusong punong-puno na ng pride.
Kaya minsan ginagamit ng Diyos ang pagkabasag para ilapit tayo sa Kanya.
Hindi aksidente ang brokenness mo.
Baka iyon mismo ang lugar kung saan ka muling bubuhayin ni Cristo.
At marahil ang pinakamatinding bahagi ng kwento ni Eliseo ay ang huling himala niya.
Patay na siya. Mga buto na lang ang natira.
Pero nang mahipo ng isang patay na tao ang kanyang mga buto… nabuhay ito.
Isipin mo iyon.
Patay na ang propeta. Pero gumagalaw pa rin ang Diyos dahil sa buhay niyang naging tapat.
Iyan ang totoong legacy.
Hindi fame. Hindi followers. Hindi clout.
Kundi buhay na nababago kahit wala ka na.
At sa ilalim ng lahat ng ito, may mas malaking kwento.
Dahil si Eliseo ay anino lamang ng paparating na Mesiyas.
Si Jesus Cristo.
Ang mas dakila kaysa sa lahat ng propeta.
Siya na hindi lang pansamantalang bumuhay ng patay… kundi tumalo mismo sa kamatayan.
Sinabi sa Isaiah 53:5:
“וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ” (Vehu mecholal mip’shaeinu)
“Siya ay nasugatan dahil sa ating mga pagsalangsang.”
At nang mamatay si Jesus sa krus, sinabi Niya:
“Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai)
“It is finished.”
Bayad na. Tapos na. Kompleto na.
Ang kasalanan. Ang utang. Ang paghihiwalay natin sa Diyos.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito na pagod nang magpanggap.
Pagod nang magmukhang okay. Pagod nang magdala ng guilt. Pagod nang itago ang tunay na kalagayan.
Pero hindi ka tinatawag ni Jesus para magpanggap.
Tinatawag ka Niya para sumuko.
At baka hindi aksidente na binabasa mo ito ngayon.
Baka matagal nang gutom ang kaluluwa mo.
At sa ilalim ng lahat ng ingay… miss mo pa rin ang Diyos.
Miss mo pa rin ang kapayapaan. Miss mo pa rin ang katotohanan.
At hanggang ngayon… tumatawag pa rin si Jesus.
Hindi para sa perfect. Kundi para sa sugatan.
At kung may taong pumasok sa isip mo habang binabasa ito… ipadala mo sa kanila.
May mga taong nakangiti online pero tahimik nang nalulunod.
Darating ang araw na mare-realize ng tao na gutom sila sa Diyos habang pinapakain nila ang lahat ng ibang cravings ng laman.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Samuel
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Samuel
The Boy Who Heard God When a Nation Couldn’t
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost too quiet to notice.
No armies marching. No seas splitting. No giant collapsing beneath a stone.
Just a child. A whisper. A lamp flickering in the darkness.
And yet hidden inside that silence was one of the most terrifying spiritual conditions ever recorded in the Bible.
Israel still had religion. They still had priests. They still had sacrifices. They still had traditions.
But they no longer heard God.
That is where the story of Samuel truly begins.
Not with greatness. Not with prophecy. Not with leadership.
But with silence.
A terrifying silence.
1 Samuel 3:1 says:
“Now the boy Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.”
The Hebrew text says:
“וּדְבַר־יְהוָה הָיָה יָקָר בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם”
Transliterated:
“U’devar-YHWH hayah yaqar bayamim hahem.”
The word “yaqar” (יָקָר) does not merely mean rare.
It means costly. Precious. Scarce. Heavy in value because almost nobody possessed it anymore.
Imagine living in a generation where hearing from God became uncommon.
That was Israel.
People still attended worship. People still acted spiritual. People still wore religious garments.
But heaven had become quiet.
And if we are honest… that sounds painfully familiar.
Many people today know church culture but do not know the voice of God.
They know sermons. They know trends. They know religious language.
But inwardly?
They are exhausted. Numb. Disconnected. Spiritually starving.
Some have mastered appearing alive while silently dying inside.
And that is exactly the atmosphere Samuel was born into.
His mother Hannah understood pain long before Samuel understood purpose.
Before Samuel became a prophet, he was first an answer to tears.
Hannah was barren. Mocked. Humiliated. Emotionally shattered.
1 Samuel 1 reveals a woman pouring out agony before God while others misunderstood her brokenness.
Even Eli the priest thought she was drunk.
But she was not drunk.
She was desperate.
There is a kind of prayer that does not sound polished.
A prayer where words collapse. Where dignity disappears. Where your soul finally stops pretending.
The Hebrew phrase in 1 Samuel 1:15 says:
“וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה”
“Va’eshpokh et-nafshi lifnei YHWH.”
Literal meaning:
“I have poured out my soul before the LORD.”
Not a performance. Not ritual. Not public spirituality.
She poured out her soul.
Some of you reading this have cried like that.
In cars. In bathrooms. Late at night. While everyone else thought you were okay.
And here is the untold beauty of Hannah’s story:
God was listening the entire time.
Samuel was born from tears heaven refused to ignore.
Never underestimate what God can birth through suffering surrendered to Him.
Samuel’s very existence became evidence that God still hears hidden pain.
But what happened next is what makes this story devastatingly powerful.
Hannah kept her promise.
She released Samuel back to God.
Most people celebrate answered prayers. Very few surrender them.
Imagine the heartbreak.
After years of infertility… after ridicule… after finally holding her miracle… she brings Samuel to the temple.
And leaves him there.
The Hebrew mindset behind dedication was not symbolic ownership. It was total surrender.
Samuel did not belong to Hannah anymore. He belonged to God.
This is where modern Christianity often struggles.
We ask God to bless us. But resist releasing what He blesses.
We want promises without surrender. Calling without sacrifice. Purpose without obedience.
But Samuel’s life was forged inside surrender before it was ever revealed in public.
And while Samuel was growing… Israel was rotting spiritually.
Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests who abused the sacrifices and exploited people sexually.
Scripture does not hide corruption.
1 Samuel 2:12 says:
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.”
The Hebrew phrase “בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל” (bene beliyaal) means worthless, wicked, lawless men.
These were spiritual leaders functioning publicly while privately disconnected from God.
And this is one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable truths:
Religious position does not guarantee spiritual intimacy.
You can stand near holy things and still not know God.
You can wear ministry titles and still be spiritually empty.
You can appear righteous while secretly dying inside.
Samuel grew up witnessing corrupted leadership.
Yet he did not allow corruption around him to destroy the calling within him.
That matters.
Because many people today use woundedness as permission to abandon God completely.
Yes, church hurt is real. Yes, spiritual abuse is devastating. Yes, hypocrisy can scar deeply.
But Samuel teaches us something life-changing:
Corrupted people are not proof that God is false.
They are proof humanity desperately needs Him.
Then came the night everything changed.
1 Samuel 3 says:
“The lamp of God had not yet gone out.”
This detail seems small until you understand its symbolic depth.
The lamp represented God’s presence.
Israel was spiritually dark. Leadership was collapsing. Judgment was approaching.
But the lamp had not gone out.
And maybe that is the word someone needs right now.
Your faith may feel weak. Your heart may feel exhausted. Your soul may feel numb.
But the lamp has not gone out.
God is still calling.
Samuel hears a voice during the night.
Three times he runs to Eli. Three times Eli tells him to go back.
Finally Eli realizes something horrifying.
God was speaking… but the old priest could no longer recognize His voice personally.
Imagine being a spiritual leader who must rely on a child to hear what heaven is saying.
And then comes one of the most powerful lines in biblical history.
1 Samuel 3:10:
“Speak; for thy servant heareth.”
Hebrew:
“דַּבֵּר יְהוָה כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ”
“Dabber YHWH ki shomea avdekha.”
The word “shomea” (שֹׁמֵעַ) means more than hearing sound.
In Hebrew thought, listening and obeying are deeply connected.
Samuel was not saying:
“I hear noises.”
He was saying:
“I am ready to obey whatever You say.”
That is the difference between casual religion and true surrender.
Many want God to speak. Few want God to interrupt them.
Samuel became dangerous to darkness because he was available.
Not famous. Not experienced. Not powerful.
Available.
And God often chooses surrendered hearts over impressive resumes.
The untold tragedy of Samuel’s story is that his first prophetic assignment was delivering judgment.
Imagine being a child tasked with confronting the spiritual collapse of your own mentor’s house.
God tells Samuel that Eli’s household would face judgment because corruption had been tolerated.
This reveals another uncomfortable biblical truth:
God’s patience should never be mistaken for approval.
Delayed judgment is not absent judgment.
Modern culture celebrates tolerance at all costs. But Scripture repeatedly shows that unchecked sin destroys individuals, families, ministries, and nations.
And yet even inside judgment… God was raising restoration.
Samuel became the bridge between the broken era of the judges and the coming kings of Israel.
He anointed Saul. He anointed David. He established prophetic leadership.
But perhaps the most remarkable thing about Samuel is this:
The Bible records no moral scandal attached to his name.
In an era overflowing with compromise, Samuel remained faithful.
Not perfect. But faithful.
That matters more than most people realize.
We live in a generation fascinated with charisma. God is still searching for consecration.
People chase platforms. God looks at hearts.
Some reading this are secretly exhausted from performing spirituality.
You post encouraging captions while privately fighting despair. You smile publicly while battling hidden addictions. You attend church while silently wondering whether God still sees you.
Samuel’s story confronts something deeply personal:
God often begins His greatest work in hidden places nobody celebrates.
Before public impact came private obedience. Before national influence came nighttime surrender. Before leadership came listening.
And maybe your hidden season is not punishment.
Maybe God is teaching your spirit how to hear Him again.
The modern world is drowning in noise.
Notifications. Opinions. Algorithms. Distractions. Performance. Comparison.
Everyone is talking. Few are listening.
But God still whispers.
The tragedy is not that God stopped speaking.
The tragedy is that many stopped listening.
Jesus later echoes this same truth repeatedly:
“He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
In Greek:
“Ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω.”
The word “akouetō” (ἀκουέτω) carries the idea of attentive hearing that leads to response.
Biblical hearing is never passive. True hearing transforms.
And perhaps this is why Samuel’s story still pierces hearts thousands of years later.
Because deep down… many people are terrified God no longer speaks to them.
But the truth is far more hopeful.
God still calls names in the darkness.
He still reaches exhausted people. He still restores broken hearts. He still pursues prodigals. He still raises surrendered believers in compromised generations.
The lamp has not gone out.
Not yet.
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment your soul needed reminding.
God still sees you.
Not the fake version. Not the filtered version. Not the church version.
The real you.
The exhausted you. The grieving you. The struggling you. The doubting you.
The you nobody else fully understands.
And just like Samuel… God can still build something holy out of surrendered availability.
Not everyone reading this will become famous. But every surrendered believer can become faithful.
And heaven still moves through faithful people.
Maybe that is why Samuel’s story feels so emotionally haunting.
Because it reminds us that revival does not begin with crowds.
It begins when one person says:
“Speak Lord… I’m listening.”
And if this article exposed something hidden inside your soul… be honest about it.
Somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Sometimes the holiest thing a person can do… is become quiet enough to hear God again.
Filipino Version:

Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Kuwento ni Samuel
Ang Batang Nakinig sa Diyos Habang Tahimik ang Isang Buong Bansa
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na parang sobrang tahimik para mapansin.
Walang dagat na nahati. Walang higanteng bumagsak. Walang apoy na bumaba mula sa langit.
Isa lamang itong batang lalaki. Isang bulong. Isang ilawang nanginginig sa dilim.
Pero nakatago sa katahimikang iyon ang isa sa pinakamapanganib na kalagayang espirituwal na naranasan ng Israel.
May relihiyon pa sila. May templo pa. May mga saserdote pa. May pagsamba pa.
Pero hindi na nila naririnig ang Diyos.
Dito tunay na nagsimula ang kuwento ni Samuel.
Hindi sa kasikatan. Hindi sa pagiging propeta. Hindi sa kapangyarihan.
Kundi sa katahimikan.
Nakakatakot na katahimikan.
Sinasabi sa 1 Samuel 3:1:
“Now the boy Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.”
Sa Hebrew:
“וּדְבַר־יְהוָה הָיָה יָקָר בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם”
“U’devar-YHWH hayah yaqar bayamim hahem.”
Ang salitang “yaqar” (יָקָר) ay hindi lang nangangahulugang bihira.
Ibig sabihin nito ay mahalaga. Mabigat. Napakahalaga dahil kakaunti na lamang ang nakakatanggap nito.
Isipin mo iyon.
Isang henerasyon na bihira nang makarinig mula sa Diyos.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… parang ganoon din ngayon.
Maraming tao ang marunong sa relihiyon pero hindi kilala ang tinig ng Diyos.
Alam nila ang church culture. Alam nila ang Christian captions. Alam nila ang tamang sagot sa Bible study.
Pero sa loob?
Pagod. Manhid. Walang kapayapaan. Unti-unting namamatay ang kaluluwa.
May mga taong sanay magmukhang malakas habang lihim nang wasak.
At iyon mismo ang mundong kinalakihan ni Samuel.
Bago siya naging propeta… siya muna ay bunga ng pagluha.
Ang kanyang ina na si Hannah ay baog. Minamaliit. Dinudurog ng kahihiyan.
Habang ang iba ay nagdiriwang… siya ay umiiyak.
At isang araw, bumagsak na lamang siya sa harapan ng Diyos.
Hindi na maganda ang dasal. Hindi na maayos. Hindi na kontrolado.
Ang sabi niya sa Hebrew:
“וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה”
“Va’eshpokh et-nafshi lifnei YHWH.”
“Ibinuhos ko ang aking kaluluwa sa harapan ng Panginoon.”
Hindi performance. Hindi pagpapakitang banal.
Pagbubuhos ng kaluluwa.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Yung iyak sa gabi. Yung pagod na hindi mo masabi kahit kanino. Yung panalangin na wala nang eleganteng salita.
At narito ang nakakagulat:
Naririnig ka ng Diyos kahit tahimik kang umiiyak.
Si Samuel ay ipinanganak mula sa sakit na pinakinggan ng langit.
Huwag mong maliitin ang kayang gawin ng Diyos sa isang pusong sugatan pero sumusuko sa Kanya.
At pagkatapos maipanganak si Samuel… ginawa ni Hannah ang halos imposibleng gawin.
Binalik niya si Samuel sa Diyos.
Karamihan sa tao gusto ng pagpapala. Pero ayaw isuko ang pagpapala.
Pagkatapos ng mga taon ng pag-iyak… iniwan niya ang kanyang anak sa templo.
Iyon ang tunay na surrender.
At habang lumalaki si Samuel… unti-unting nabubulok ang espirituwal na kalagayan ng Israel.
Ang mga anak ni Eli na sina Hophni at Phinehas ay mga saserdoteng makasalanan.
Ginagamit nila ang posisyon para sa sariling pagnanasa.
At ipinapakita nito ang isang masakit na katotohanan:
Hindi porket malapit ka sa mga banal na bagay ay kilala mo na ang Diyos.
Maaaring nasa ministry ka pero malayo ang puso mo. Maaaring may titulo ka pero walang intimacy sa Diyos.
At maraming tao ngayon ang sugatan dahil sa religious hypocrisy.
Pero si Samuel?
Hindi niya hinayaang sirain ng corruption sa paligid ang calling sa loob niya.
Napakahalaga niyan.
Dahil maraming tao ang tuluyang lumalayo sa Diyos dahil nasaktan sila ng tao.
Oo, totoo ang church hurt. Oo, may spiritual abuse. Oo, maraming hypocrisy.
Pero ang corruption ng tao ay hindi patunay na hindi totoo ang Diyos.
Patunay iyon na desperado tayong lahat na kailangan Siya.
At pagkatapos dumating ang gabing nagpabago ng lahat.
Sinasabi ng Biblia:
“The lamp of God had not yet gone out.”
Napakaliit na detalye. Pero napakalalim.
Madilim na ang Israel. Corrupt na ang leadership. Paparating na ang judgment.
Pero hindi pa namamatay ang ilawan.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangan marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Pagod ka man. Manhid ka man. Pakiramdam mo man nawawala na ang pananampalataya mo.
Hindi pa namamatay ang ilawan.
Tinatawag ka pa rin ng Diyos.
Narinig ni Samuel ang tinig sa gabi. Tatlong beses siyang tumakbo kay Eli. Tatlong beses siyang pinabalik.
Hanggang sa naunawaan ni Eli:
Diyos na pala ang tumatawag.
At pagkatapos sinabi ni Samuel ang isa sa pinakamakapangyarihang linya sa buong Biblia:
“Speak Lord, for Your servant is listening.”
Sa Hebrew:
“דַּבֵּר יְהוָה כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ”
“Dabber YHWH ki shomea avdekha.”
Ang “shomea” ay hindi simpleng pakikinig.
Sa Hebrew understanding, ang tunay na pakikinig ay may kasamang pagsunod.
Parang sinasabi ni Samuel:
“Panginoon, handa akong sundin kahit ano ang sabihin Mo.”
At dito nagiging kakaiba ang tunay na surrender.
Maraming gustong marinig ang Diyos. Kaunti lang ang handang mabago ng Diyos.
Hindi naging makapangyarihan si Samuel dahil sikat siya.
Naging makapangyarihan siya dahil available siya.
At hanggang ngayon… mas gusto pa rin ng Diyos ang surrendered na puso kaysa impressive na reputasyon.
Ang unang prophetic assignment ni Samuel ay judgment.
Imagine mo iyon.
Isang bata na kailangang magsabi ng katotohanan tungkol sa pagbagsak ng spiritual leadership.
At ipinapakita nito ang isa pang katotohanan:
Ang pasensya ng Diyos ay hindi approval.
Kapag delayed ang judgment… hindi ibig sabihin absent ang judgment.
Pero kahit sa gitna ng judgment… may restoration pa ring inihahanda ang Diyos.
Si Samuel ang naging tulay mula sa magulong panahon ng judges papunta sa panahon ng mga hari.
Inanoint niya si Saul. Inanoint niya si David.
Pero isa sa pinakaimportanteng detalye tungkol kay Samuel ay ito:
Walang malaking scandal na naka-attach sa pangalan niya.
Sa panahong puno ng compromise… nanatili siyang faithful.
At sa panahon ngayon, bihira ang ganoon.
Abala ang mundo sa charisma. Pero ang Diyos naghahanap pa rin ng consecration.
Maraming tao ang pagod na pagod na sa pagpapanggap.
Nagpo-post ng “God is good” habang lihim na depressed. Ngumingiti sa church habang unti-unti nang nawawalan ng pag-asa.
At baka ito ang dahilan kung bakit napakalakas pa rin ng kuwento ni Samuel.
Dahil ipinapaalala nito na ang Diyos ay gumagawa muna sa lihim bago sa publiko.
Bago ang influence… may obedience. Bago ang platform… may surrender. Bago ang ministry… may pakikinig.
At baka ang season mong tahimik ay hindi punishment.
Baka tinuturuan ka lang ulit ng Diyos kung paano Siyang marinig.
Napakaingay ng mundo ngayon.
Notifications. Opinions. Distractions. Pressure. Comparison.
Lahat nagsasalita. Kakaunti ang tunay na nakikinig.
Pero nagsasalita pa rin ang Diyos.
Ang problema… maraming tumigil nang makinig.
At baka habang binabasa mo ito… may tinatawag na namang bahagi ng puso mo.
Yung bahagi mong matagal nang pagod. Yung bahagi mong takot nang umasa ulit. Yung bahagi mong gustong marinig ulit ang Diyos.
At katulad ni Samuel… kayang bumuo ng Diyos ng isang banal na buhay mula sa isang surrendered na puso.
Hindi lahat magiging sikat. Pero lahat pwedeng maging faithful.
At gumagalaw pa rin ang langit sa pamamagitan ng mga faithful.
Kaya baka oras na ulit para sabihin:
“Speak Lord… nakikinig pa rin ako.”
At kung may tinamaan sa puso mo habang binabasa ito… huwag kang matakot maging totoo.
Baka ang honesty mo ang maging dahilan para may ibang taong lumapit ulit kay Jesus.
Minsan… ang pinaka banal na bagay na kayang gawin ng tao… ay ang manahimik nang sapat para marinig ulit ang Diyos.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Nicodemus Defended Jesus Before Following Him Publicly
paragraphs: Why Nicodemus Defended Jesus Before Following Him Publicly
Jerusalem was loud that week.
Not loud with worship.
Loud with suspicion.

Men whispered in corners. Religious leaders tightened their grip on influence. Crowds argued about miracles. Some called Jesus a prophet. Some called Him dangerous. Some wanted Him crowned. Others wanted Him buried.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pressure stood a man who could lose everything.
His name was Nicodemus.
Not a fisherman. Not a rebel. Not an outcast.
A Pharisee. A ruler. A respected teacher of Israel. A man with status to protect.
John 3:1 introduces him carefully:
“Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.”
The Greek text says:
Ἦν δὲ ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων Νικόδημος ὄνομα αὐτῷ, ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
The word ἄρχων (archōn) means ruler, authority figure, one carrying influence and governance.
Nicodemus was not casually religious. He was deeply embedded inside the spiritual power structure of Israel.
And yet… something about Jesus disturbed him in a way religion never could.
Not because Jesus lacked truth.
Because Jesus carried too much of it.
Most people remember Nicodemus for visiting Jesus at night. But very few stop to ask why.
Why would a respected Pharisee secretly seek out a controversial teacher? Why defend Jesus before openly following Him? Why risk association before making public commitment?
Because Nicodemus represents something painfully human.
The war between conviction and fear.
And if we are honest… many believers still live there.
Some people think faith begins publicly. Scripture often shows the opposite.
Sometimes faith begins in hidden trembling. Sometimes discipleship starts with dangerous curiosity. Sometimes people defend truth long before they have courage to stand completely inside it.
Nicodemus was watching Jesus long before he was ready to lose everything for Him.
And maybe that is exactly why this story still feels uncomfortably personal.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to believe quietly.
Quietly at work. Quietly around unbelieving family. Quietly around mocking friends. Quietly inside churches where appearance matters more than surrender.
You know Jesus is real. But you are terrified of what full obedience could cost.
Nicodemus understood that fear.
When he first approached Jesus, he came at night. The Greek phrase from John 3:2 says:
οὗτος ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς
Literally:
“He came to Him by night.”
Some scholars argue the timing was practical. Others see symbolism. John’s Gospel repeatedly uses darkness and light as spiritual imagery.
And honestly… both may be true.
Nicodemus came in darkness externally because darkness already existed internally.
He was spiritually conflicted.
Not hardened. Conflicted.
There is a difference.
A hardened heart attacks truth. A conflicted heart wrestles with it.
Nicodemus did not come mocking Jesus. He came searching.
Listen carefully to his opening words:
“Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that You do unless God is with him.” — John 3:2
The Greek says:
οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος
“We know You have come from God as a teacher.”
Did you catch that?
“We know.”
Not “I know.”
“We know.”
Meaning Nicodemus was not the only religious leader wrestling privately with the reality of Jesus.
There were others.
Silent believers. Hidden wrestlers. Men trapped between revelation and reputation.
And before condemning them too quickly, remember this:
Social death can terrify people almost as much as physical death.
Especially in religious systems.
Nicodemus had everything to lose.
Honor. Position. Influence. Relationships. Identity.
Following Jesus was not socially inspiring in that moment. It was dangerous.
We read Scripture knowing the resurrection happened. Nicodemus did not.
At that point, publicly aligning with Jesus could destroy his entire life.
And yet even while afraid… he kept moving closer.
That matters.
Some people only see cowardice in Nicodemus. Jesus saw movement.
Because God notices trembling steps too.
Then Jesus says something that completely dismantles religious pride.
“Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3
The Greek phrase is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
This can mean:
“born again” or “born from above.”
Jesus was confronting Nicodemus with a devastating truth:
Religious status cannot produce spiritual life.
Knowledge cannot regenerate the soul. Position cannot save. Tradition cannot resurrect the heart.
Nicodemus had mastered theology. But he had not yet surrendered.
And millions still live there today.
Biblically informed. Spiritually unmoved.
Church attendance without transformation. Bible knowledge without repentance. Christian language without crucifixion of self.
Jesus shattered all of it in one conversation.
And Nicodemus did not walk away.
That is important.
He stayed. He listened. He wrestled.
Because deep down, something inside him knew Jesus was speaking with authority no rabbi possessed.
The Hebrew concept of truth is deeply connected to the word:
אֱמֶת (emet)
Meaning: truth, faithfulness, stability, ultimate reality.
Jesus did not merely teach truth. He embodied emet.
And Nicodemus felt it.
That is why conviction became unavoidable.
Real encounters with Christ destabilize comfortable religion.
You cannot truly meet Jesus and remain emotionally untouched.
Eventually the pressure around Jesus intensified. Religious leaders became increasingly hostile. The atmosphere became politically volatile.
Then comes one of the most underrated moments in Scripture.
John 7.
The Pharisees wanted Jesus arrested. Officers returned empty-handed because even they were overwhelmed by Jesus’ words.
The leaders mocked them.
Then suddenly… Nicodemus speaks.
Not publicly as a disciple. Not fully surrendered yet. But he speaks.
John 7:51:
“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”
The Greek says:
μὴ ὁ νόμος ἡμῶν κρίνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ πρῶτον παρ’ αὐτοῦ
“Does our law judge the man unless it first hears from him?”
This was not a sermon.
It was a crack in fear.
A fracture in silence.
A respected Pharisee publicly interrupting an unjust condemnation.
Do you understand how dangerous that was?
Nicodemus was defending Jesus inside hostile territory.
He still was not openly declaring discipleship. But conviction was beginning to overpower self-preservation.
And this is where many people emotionally connect with Nicodemus.
Because courage often grows progressively.
Not everyone transforms overnight.
Peter denied Jesus publicly. Thomas doubted openly. Jonah ran. Elijah collapsed emotionally. Moses resisted calling.
Yet God kept pursuing them.
The modern world glamorizes instant transformation. Scripture often reveals gradual surrender.
Nicodemus defended Jesus before following Him publicly because conviction had already begun changing him internally.
The process was unfolding.
And maybe somebody reading this needed to hear that.
Because you think your fear disqualifies you.
But conviction itself may already be evidence God is drawing you.
You still hesitate. Still wrestle. Still struggle. Still fear people. Still battle compromise.
Yet you cannot walk away from Jesus completely.
Why?
Because truth keeps haunting you.
That is what happened to Nicodemus.
Jesus got inside his conscience.
And once Christ enters the conscience, pretending becomes exhausting.
Then comes the final appearance of Nicodemus.
And this moment changes everything.
Jesus is dead.
Crucified. Humiliated. Rejected.
Most disciples disappeared. Fear spread everywhere.
Following Jesus publicly now carried enormous danger.
Yet suddenly… Nicodemus appears again.
Not at night.
In daylight.
John 19:39 says:
“Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.”
John intentionally reminds readers:
“who earlier had come by night.”
Why mention that?
Because the man hiding in darkness is no longer hiding.
The Greek says:
ἦλθεν δὲ καὶ Νικόδημος
“Nicodemus also came.”
He came.
When Jesus looked defeated. When association was costly. When reputation was threatened. When fear was justified.
He came.
And the amount of burial spices he brought was extravagant. Royal. Costly.
This was not secret admiration anymore.
This was public identification.
The fearful Pharisee had become courageous enough to honor a crucified Messiah.
And maybe that is the most beautiful part of the story.
Nicodemus did not arrive at boldness instantly.
He journeyed into it.
Slowly. Painfully. Honestly.
First curiosity. Then conviction. Then defense. Then devotion.
Some believers shame people still in process. Jesus did not.
Christ knew exactly how to bring Nicodemus from secrecy into surrender.
And perhaps some of the strongest believers today are still walking through that same painful transition.

There are people who quietly watch sermons after midnight. People secretly reading Scripture while pretending not to care. People hiding worship music under headphones. People terrified to tell family they believe. People trapped in intellectual pride while God keeps softening their heart. People defending Christianity publicly while privately battling whether to fully surrender.
Nicodemus speaks directly to them.
Because his story proves something powerful:
Jesus is patient with seekers who are honestly wrestling toward truth.
Not everyone begins bold. But many become bold after encountering Christ repeatedly.
The Hebrew word often connected to repentance is:
תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah)
Meaning: returning. Turning back. Coming home.
Nicodemus was slowly returning toward truth even before publicly identifying with Jesus.
And maybe right now you feel God pulling you the same way.
You cannot explain it.
But compromise feels heavier now. Sin feels emptier. Conviction hits harder. Worship affects you differently. The name of Jesus keeps disturbing your peace.
That is not accidental.
Christ still calls people out of darkness patiently.
The tragedy is not struggling.
The tragedy is resisting conviction until the heart becomes numb.
Nicodemus could have silenced his conscience forever. Instead, he kept moving closer to Jesus.
Even slowly.
And eventually hidden faith became visible devotion.
Somebody reading this has spent years intellectually near Jesus but emotionally distant from surrender.
You know verses. You understand theology. You can debate doctrine. But privately you still avoid complete obedience.
Nicodemus warns us that proximity to truth is not the same as transformation.
But he also gives hope.
Because people can change.
Fearful hearts can become courageous. Religious hearts can become reborn. Secret belief can become public devotion.
The Gospel still transforms people progressively.
And perhaps that is why Nicodemus defended Jesus before following Him publicly.
Because conviction was growing faster than his courage.
Until eventually courage caught up.
And maybe yours will too.
Be honest. This story probably felt closer to home than you expected.
Some people are not far from Jesus. They are just one surrendered step away from finally stepping into the light.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Ipinagtanggol ni Nicodemus si Jesus Bago Siya Sumunod Nang Hayagan
Maingay ang Jerusalem noong mga panahong iyon.
Hindi dahil sa pagsamba.
Kundi dahil sa takot.

May mga bulung-bulungan sa bawat sulok. May mga relihiyosong lider na pilit pinoprotektahan ang kanilang kapangyarihan. May mga taong namamangha sa mga himala ni Jesus. May iba namang gusto Siyang patahimikin.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon… may isang lalaking unti-unting winawasak ng katotohanan.
Ang pangalan niya ay Nicodemus.
Hindi siya ordinaryong tao.
Isa siyang Pariseo. Isang guro ng Israel. Isang lalaking may reputasyon. May impluwensya. May pangalan.
At iyon mismo ang dahilan kung bakit mahirap sundan si Jesus.
Dahil kung susunod siya kay Cristo nang hayagan… maaaring mawala ang lahat.
Sa Juan 3:1, maingat siyang ipinakilala:
“May isang taong mula sa mga Fariseo, na ang pangalan ay Nicodemo, isang pinuno ng mga Judio.”
Sa orihinal na Griyego:
ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων (archōn tōn Ioudaiōn)
Ang salitang archōn ay nangangahulugang:
pinuno, may kapangyarihan, may impluwensya.
Hindi simpleng relihiyoso si Nicodemus. Bahagi siya ng sistemang kumokontrol sa relihiyon ng Israel.
Pero may isang bagay kay Jesus na hindi niya matakasan.
Hindi siya mapalagay.
Dahil may kakaibang awtoridad si Jesus.
May katotohanang hindi kayang pantayan ng relihiyon.
Kaya isang gabi… lihim siyang pumunta kay Jesus.
At maraming tao ang agad siyang hinuhusgahan dahil doon.
“Bakit sa gabi?” “Bakit hindi siya naging matapang agad?”
Pero kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao pa rin hanggang ngayon ang katulad niya.
Tahimik na naniniwala. Tahimik na naghahanap. Tahimik na lumalaban sa takot.

May mga taong nanonood ng preaching nang madaling araw pero walang nakakaalam. May mga taong gustong sumunod kay Jesus pero takot sa sasabihin ng pamilya. May mga gustong magbago pero natatakot mawala ang dating buhay.
Si Nicodemus ang larawan ng taong hinahabol na ng Diyos… pero hindi pa handang isuko ang lahat.
Sa Juan 3:2, sinabi:
οὗτος ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς
Ibig sabihin:
“Pumunta siya kay Jesus sa gabi.”
Oo, gabi iyon literal.
Pero sa Ebanghelyo ni Juan, madalas ding simbolo ang dilim.
Dilim ng takot. Dilim ng pagdududa. Dilim ng pusong hindi pa tuluyang sumusuko.
Hindi lumapit si Nicodemus kay Jesus para kutyain Siya. Lumapit siya dahil may bumabagabag na sa kanyang konsensya.
Pakinggan ang sinabi niya:
“Rabbi, nalalaman naming ikaw ay gurong mula sa Diyos…” — Juan 3:2
Sa Griyego:
οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος
“Alam naming galing Ka sa Diyos.”
Pansinin mo iyon.
Hindi niya sinabi:
“Ako.”
Kundi:
“Kami.”
Ibig sabihin… hindi lang si Nicodemus ang lihim na naniniwala.
May iba pang relihiyosong lider na nakakakita rin kung sino talaga si Jesus.
Pero takot sila.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… nakakatakot talaga minsan ang pagsunod kay Cristo.
Dahil may mga taong mawawala. May mga relasyong masisira. May reputasyong babagsak. May pride na kailangang mamatay.
Kaya bago natin husgahan si Nicodemus… tandaan natin:
Hindi lahat ng transformation ay biglaan.
May mga taong dahan-dahang dinadala ng Diyos palabas ng dilim.
At iyon mismo ang ginawa ni Jesus kay Nicodemus.
Sinabi ni Jesus:
“Malibang ang tao’y ipanganak na muli ay hindi niya makikita ang kaharian ng Diyos.” — Juan 3:3
Sa Griyego:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
Maaaring isalin bilang:
“ipanganak na muli” o “ipanganak mula sa itaas.”
Winawasak ni Jesus ang maling akala ni Nicodemus.
Na sapat na ang relihiyon. Na sapat na ang kaalaman. Na sapat na ang posisyon.
Hindi.
Kailangan ng bagong puso.
At milyon-milyong tao pa rin ngayon ang nasa parehong sitwasyon.
Maraming alam tungkol sa Diyos. Pero hindi pa sumusuko sa Diyos.
May Bible verse sa bio. Pero walang tunay na repentance. May church attendance. Pero walang pagbabago.
At habang kausap ni Jesus si Nicodemus… unti-unting winawasak ang kanyang pride.
Pero hindi siya umalis.
Nanatili siya.
Dahil kahit natatakot siya… alam niyang may katotohanang hindi niya kayang takasan.
Pagdating ng Juan 7, lalo pang lumala ang galit ng mga Pariseo kay Jesus. Gusto na nila Siyang ipahuli.
At doon nangyari ang isang napakahalagang eksena.
Biglang nagsalita si Nicodemus.
Hindi pa siya public disciple. Hindi pa siya handang ipahayag ang lahat.
Pero ipinagtanggol niya si Jesus.
Juan 7:51:
“Hinahatulan ba ng ating kautusan ang isang tao nang hindi muna siya dinirinig?”
Sa Griyego:
μὴ ὁ νόμος ἡμῶν κρίνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ πρῶτον παρ’ αὐτοῦ
Hindi ito simpleng legal argument.
Ito ay unang bitak sa kanyang takot.
Unang pagkakataong pinili niyang manindigan kahit kaunti.
At minsan… doon nagsisimula ang tapang.
Hindi agad sa entablado.
Kundi sa maliliit na desisyong hindi na kayang manahimik ng konsensya.
Maraming tao ang gustong instant transformation.
Pero madalas sa Biblia… proseso ang surrender.
Unti-unti. Masakit. Totoo.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangan marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Dahil akala mo disqualified ka dahil natatakot ka pa.
Pero baka ang conviction na nararamdaman mo ay ebidensya nang kinikilos ka ng Diyos.
Hindi mo na ma-enjoy ang dating kasalanan. Hindi ka na mapalagay. Hindi mo maalis si Jesus sa isip mo.
Bakit?
Dahil kapag pumasok na si Cristo sa konsensya ng tao… mahirap nang bumalik sa dating dilim.
Pagdating ng Juan 19, namatay na si Jesus.
Pinako. Tinanggihan. Pinahiya.
At karamihan sa mga alagad… nagtago.
Pero si Nicodemus?
Lumabas.
Hindi na sa gabi.
Kundi hayagan.
Juan 19:39:
“Dumating din si Nicodemo, na noong una’y pumunta kay Jesus sa gabi…”
Bakit pa binanggit ni Juan ang “gabi”?
Dahil gusto niyang ipakita:
Hindi na nagtatago ang dating takot.
Ang lalaking dating lihim kung maniwala… ngayon ay handa nang maiugnay kay Cristo kahit patay na Siya.
At napakalaki ng dala niyang pabango para sa paglilibing.
Mahal. Marangal. Parang para sa hari.
Hindi na ito simpleng curiosity.
Ito na ay devotion.
At baka iyon ang pinakamagandang bahagi ng kwento.
Hindi naging matapang si Nicodemus overnight.
Unti-unti siyang binago ni Jesus.
Mula curiosity. Patungong conviction. Patungong pagtatanggol. Patungong surrender.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito na nasa gitna rin ng prosesong iyon.
Hindi ka pa perfect. Hindi ka pa matapang lagi. Hindi mo pa ma-let go lahat.
Pero hindi mo na rin kayang lumayo kay Jesus.
Dahil may katotohanang patuloy kang hinahabol.
Ang Hebrew word para sa repentance ay:
תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah)
Ibig sabihin:
pagbabalik. Pag-uwi. Paglapit muli sa Diyos.
At iyon ang nangyayari kay Nicodemus.
Unti-unti siyang bumabalik sa liwanag.
At baka ikaw rin.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malapit siguro sa puso mo ang kwentong ito kaysa inaamin mo.
May mga taong hindi malayo kay Jesus. Takot lang silang tuluyang lumabas sa dilim.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)
