At baka ito mismo ang dahilan kung bakit maraming tao ang hirap maniwala na magagamit pa sila ng Diyos.
Dahil pilit binubura ng relihiyon ang mga bahaging sadyang iniwan ng Diyos bilang patunay.
Hindi kahihiyan si Rahab sa Biblia.
Isa siyang ebidensya.
Ebidensya na iba tumingin ang Diyos kaysa tao.
Habang naghahanda ang Jericho para sa digmaan, natatakot ang buong siyudad.
Kumakalat ang usapan tungkol sa Diyos ng Israel.
Ang paghati ng Dagat na Pula. Ang pagbagsak ng mga hari. Ang mga imposibleng tagumpay. Ang nakakatakot na presensya ni Yahweh.
Pero habang buong siyudad ang nakarinig tungkol sa Diyos… iisang babae lang ang naniwala.
Dapat tayong matinag doon.
Buong siyudad may impormasyon. Isang wasak na babae ang nagkaroon ng pananampalataya.
Joshua 2:11:
“For the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “alam ko” ay:
יָדַעְתִּי
Yada’ti.
Hindi simpleng kaalaman.
Malalim na pagkakilala. Paniniwala. Kumbiksyon.
Hindi nanghuhula si Rahab.
Naniniwala siya bago pa niya makita.
At dito nagiging personal ang kuwento.
Dahil maraming taong nagsisimba linggo-linggo pero hindi talaga nagtitiwala sa Diyos.
Habang may isang single mother na pagod na. May isang addict na gustong makalaya. May isang kabataang gustong sumuko. May isang lalaking nilalamon ng kahihiyan. May isang babaeng hinusgahan ng lahat.
Isang bulong lang tungkol kay Jesus… naniwala agad sila.
Isinugal ni Rahab ang buhay niya dahil nagsimula na ang pananampalataya sa puso niya bago pa dumating ang mga espiya.
Akala ng iba pinagtaksilan niya ang Jericho dahil padalos-dalos siya.
Hindi.
Ginawa niya iyon dahil na-realize niyang wasak na talaga ang Jericho.
Darating ang punto sa buhay ng tao na maiisip niya:
“Kapag nanatili akong loyal sa mundong ito… mamamatay akong kasama nito.”
At binabago niyan ang lahat.
Hinahanap ng hari ng Jericho ang mga espiya.
Pero itinago sila ni Rahab.
Hindi lang iyon delikado.
Pagtataksil iyon.
Kapag nahuli siya, pwede siyang patayin.
Pwedeng patayin ang pamilya niya.
Pwedeng matapos ang lahat sa isang gabi.
Pero ginawa pa rin niya.
Bakit?
Dahil mas natakot siya sa Diyos kaysa kamatayan.
Ang konsepto ng takot sa Hebreo ay:
יִרְאָה
Yirah.
Hindi simpleng terror.
Paggalang. Pagkamangha. Pagkilala sa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Naunawaan ni Rahab ang bagay na marami pa ring hindi maintindihan hanggang ngayon.
Kapag tunay mong nakilala ang Diyos… hindi ka puwedeng manatiling neutral.
Susuko ka o lalaban.
Pero hindi ka mananatiling pareho.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito na matagal nang namumuhay sa gitna.
Kalahating surrendered. Kalahating makamundo. Kalahating totoo. Kalahating nagtatago.
Binabasag ng kuwento ni Rahab ang ilusyon na iyon.
Dahil noong naniwala siya… kumilos siya.
Ang tunay na pananampalataya sa Biblia ay hindi lang emosyon.
Ang salitang Griyego para sa faith ay:
πίστις
Pistis.
Pagtitiwala. Katapatan. Buong pagsandal.
Ang tunay na pananampalataya laging may kilos.
Laging may risk. Laging may surrender. Laging may kapalit.
At dito lalo nakakadurog ang kuwento.
Hindi lang sarili niya ang gustong iligtas ni Rahab.
Pati pamilya niya.
Joshua 2:12–13:
“Spare the lives of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them.”
Nakikita mo ba?
Ang babaeng tinawag na marumi ng lipunan… siya ang naging dahilan ng kaligtasan ng pamilya niya.
Ang rejected ang naging tulay ng awa.
May mga taong umiiyak dahil hindi maintindihan ng pamilya nila ang pananampalataya nila.
Pakiramdam mo nag-iisa ka.
Pero pinapakita ng kuwento ni Rahab na kayang gamitin ng Diyos ang isang surrendered na tao para baguhin ang buong pamilya.
Isang lola na hindi tumitigil magdasal. Isang dating addict na binago ni Cristo. Isang anak na ayaw bumitaw sa Diyos.
Huwag mong maliitin ang kayang gawin ng Diyos sa isang buhay na totoong sumuko.
At pagkatapos… dumating ang scarlet cord.
Joshua 2:18:
“Tie this scarlet cord in the window…”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa scarlet ay:
שָׁנִי
Shani.
Mapulang parang dugo.
Hindi aksidente ang simbolong ito.
Sa buong Kasulatan, ang scarlet ay konektado sa pagtubos, paghahandog, at pagtatakip.
Namarkahan ng scarlet ang bahay ni Rahab bago bumagsak ang paghuhukom.
Katulad ng mga mananampalatayang natatakpan ng dugo ni Cristo bago ang huling paghuhukom.
At dito sumasabog ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi lang iniligtas si Rahab.
Inampon siya.
Matthew 1:5 — kasama si Rahab sa genealogy ni Jesus.
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang dating patutot mula Jericho naging bahagi ng linya ng Mesiyas.
Buburahin sana siya ng relihiyon.
Pero isinulat siya ni Jesus sa kasaysayan.
May kailangang makarinig nito.
Hindi kayang sirain ng pinakamasama mong chapter ang future na gustong ibigay ng Diyos.
Paulit-ulit bumubulong ang kaaway:
“Masyado kang marumi.” “Tapos ka na.” “Hindi ka na mapapatawad.” “Hindi ka na magagamit ng Diyos.”
Dinudurog ng buhay ni Rahab ang lahat ng kasinungalingang iyon.
Hindi natatakot si Jesus sa iskandalo.
Espesyalista Siya sa redemption.
Ang salitang Griyego para sa salvation ay:
σωτηρία
Sōtēria.
Kaligtasan. Pagliligtas. Pagpapagaling. Buong restoration.
Hindi lang pagtakas sa impyerno.
Kumpletong rescue.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangan mo ngayon.
Hindi relihiyon.
Kundi rescue.
Dahil pagod na pagod na ang maraming tao sa pagtatago.
Pagod magpanggap. Pagod ngumiti kahit wasak. Pagod magkunwaring okay. Pagod lumaban mag-isa.
Pero ang Ebanghelyo ay hindi para sa perfect.
Ang Ebanghelyo ay para sa mga handang magsabi:
“Kailangan ko ng awa.”
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit buhay pa rin ang kuwento ni Rahab hanggang ngayon.
Dahil lahat ng tao alam ang pakiramdam ng nasa loob ng isang bumabagsak na Jericho.
Lahat alam ang pakiramdam ng takot.
Lahat minsang nagtatanong:
“May pag-asa pa ba para sa taong katulad ko?”
At sumasagot si Rahab gamit ang buong buhay niya.
Oo.
Oo, meron.
Pero tandaan mo ito.
Hindi iniligtas ni Rahab ang sarili niya.
Ang rescue nanggaling sa labas ng pader.
Katulad ng kaligtasan na nanggagaling lamang kay Cristo.
Ephesians 2:8:
“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa grace ay:
χάρις
Charis.
Hindi karapat-dapat na pabor. Kabutihan ng Diyos. Regalo.
Hindi inearn ni Rahab ang kaligtasan.
Tinanggap niya ito.
At ganoon din tayo.
Kung nababasa mo ito habang pagod na pagod ka na… hindi aksidente na nakita mo ito.
Baka pakiramdam mo wala nang pag-asa. Baka nilalamon ka ng kasalanan. Baka hindi mo na kayang magpanggap. Baka gusto mo nang sumuko.
Makinig ka.
Ang kuwento ni Rahab ay iniwan ng Diyos sa Biblia para ipaalala sa mga susunod na henerasyon:
Nakakarating pa rin ang biyaya ng Diyos sa pinakaimposibleng lugar.
At kung kayang baguhin ng Diyos ang kuwento ni Rahab… kaya rin Niyang baguhin ang kuwento mo.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
Ang Diyos na nagligtas kay Rahab noon ay Siya pa ring Diyos na humihila ng mga tao palabas ng mga gumuguhong buhay ngayon.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Noadiah Tried to Intimidate Nehemiah
paragraphs: Why Noadiah Tried to Intimidate Nehemiah
There are some battles that do not begin with swords.
They begin with whispers.
With carefully timed fear.
With spiritual manipulation disguised as concern.
With people who smile publicly while privately praying for your collapse.
Nehemiah discovered this the hard way.
He was not rebuilding a wall.
He was rebuilding identity.
He was rebuilding worship.
He was rebuilding obedience.
He was rebuilding a people who had forgotten who they belonged to.
And hell noticed.
That is why one of the most dangerous attacks against Nehemiah did not come through military invasion.
It came through intimidation.
And one of the names hidden inside that intimidation campaign was a woman named Noadiah.
Most people skip over her name.
But Scripture does not waste names.
Every name inside the Bible is there for a reason.
Especially the dangerous ones.
Nehemiah 6:14 says:
“Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear.”
The Hebrew phrase for “put me in fear” is:
יָרֵא — yare’
This word means:
• to terrify • to frighten • to cause trembling • to intimidate into submission • to make someone withdraw from obedience
This was not ordinary fear.
This was targeted spiritual intimidation.
Noadiah was attempting to weaponize fear against obedience.
And that is still one of Satan’s favorite strategies today.
Because if the enemy cannot stop the calling God placed on your life...
he will try to make you afraid of it.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You started getting closer to God... then suddenly anxiety increased.
You started praying more... then suddenly discouragement intensified.
You started separating from sin... then suddenly people began mocking you.
You started rebuilding your spiritual life... then suddenly emotional warfare exploded.
Because darkness becomes aggressive when restoration begins.
The Book of Nehemiah is not merely ancient Jewish history.
It is a spiritual blueprint for every believer trying to rebuild what the enemy tried to destroy.
And the enemy almost always sends intimidation before breakthrough.
Noadiah’s involvement is deeply disturbing because she was identified as a prophetess.
The Hebrew word used is:
נְבִיאָה — nevi’ah
meaning:
female prophet.
This is what makes the situation terrifying.
The intimidation was coming through someone carrying spiritual appearance.
Not every spiritual voice comes from God.
Not everyone who sounds religious is sent by Heaven.
Jesus warned about this repeatedly.
In Matthew 7:15, Christ said:
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
The Greek phrase for “false prophets” is:
ψευδοπροφητῶν — pseudoprophētōn
Pseudo.
False.
Imitation.
Counterfeit spirituality.
This is why discernment matters.
Because spiritual intimidation often arrives wearing spiritual language.
Noadiah was likely part of a coordinated effort alongside Sanballat and Tobiah to psychologically break Nehemiah before the wall was completed.
Why?
Because the wall represented separation.
Holiness.
Protection.
Identity.
Covenant.
And Satan hates boundaries that protect people from destruction.
The enemy does not panic when believers stay passive.
But he becomes threatened when people start rebuilding what sin destroyed.
That is why Nehemiah faced mockery first.
Then conspiracy.
Then lies.
Then false accusations.
Then fear tactics.
Then false prophecy.
This pattern still exists.
Some of you have experienced this yourself.
You were finally healing.
Then toxic voices returned.
You were finally escaping addiction.
Then temptation intensified.
You were finally pursuing purity.
Then loneliness attacked your mind.
You were finally stepping into purpose.
Then intimidation began whispering:
“Who do you think you are?”
“You’re going to fail again.”
“God cannot use someone like you.”
“People remember your past.”
“Stop before you embarrass yourself.”
Those whispers are not random.
They are spiritual warfare.
One of the most overlooked realities in Scripture is that fear itself can become a weaponized form of bondage.
Paul later wrote in 2 Timothy 1:7:
“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.”
The Greek word for fear here is:
δειλίας — deilias
meaning:
cowardice, shrinking back, timidation, fearfulness that causes retreat.
This was exactly the goal against Nehemiah.
To make him retreat.
To make him abandon the wall.
To make him emotionally collapse before completion.
Because incomplete obedience keeps people vulnerable.
That is why Nehemiah refused compromise.
Nehemiah 6:3 says:
“And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.”
That phrase “great work” in Hebrew is:
מְלָאכָה גְדוֹלָה — mela’khah gedolah
A great labor. A significant assignment. A divine task.
Nehemiah understood something many believers forget:
not every invitation deserves your attention.
Some distractions are demonic assignments.
Some conversations are traps.
Some relationships are strategically sent to pull you down from what God called you to build.
And if Nehemiah had come down from the wall...
Jerusalem would have remained vulnerable.
Sometimes the enemy does not need to destroy you.
He only needs to distract you long enough.
This is why spiritual intimidation is so dangerous.
It attacks momentum.
It attacks focus.
It attacks endurance.
It attacks confidence.
And eventually...
it attacks identity.
Noadiah tried to intimidate Nehemiah because intimidated people are easier to control.
Fearful believers become silent believers.
Silent believers stop rebuilding.
And broken walls leave entire generations exposed.
But Nehemiah did something powerful.
He prayed.
Not performative prayer.
Not shallow religious performance.
Real dependence.
Nehemiah repeatedly interrupted chaos with prayer.
This is one reason the enemy feared him.
Prayer keeps the soul anchored when intimidation attempts to drown the mind.
And notice something incredible.
Despite all the opposition...
the wall was completed.
Nehemiah 6:15 says:
“So the wall was finished.”
The Hebrew word for “finished” is:
וַתִּשְׁלַם — vatishlam
from the root:
שָׁלֵם — shalem
Meaning:
complete, whole, restored, fulfilled.
This is deeply connected to the word:
שָׁלוֹם — shalom
Peace. Wholeness. Restoration.
The enemy attacked Nehemiah because restored walls produce restored people.
And restored people become dangerous to darkness.
Some of you are in a Nehemiah season right now.
You are rebuilding after heartbreak.
Rebuilding after addiction.
Rebuilding after betrayal.
Rebuilding after secret sin.
Rebuilding after depression.
Rebuilding after spiritual exhaustion.
And intimidation has been whispering nonstop.
But hear this clearly:
The presence of intimidation does not mean God abandoned you.
Sometimes intimidation is proof you are getting close to breakthrough.
Satan does not waste warfare on spiritually dead territory.
And maybe the reason this article found you today is because you have been seconds away from giving up.
Maybe you were preparing to come down from the wall.
Maybe exhaustion convinced you quitting was easier.
Maybe fear convinced you your assignment was too heavy.
But Nehemiah’s story still echoes through history:
Do not come down.
Do not surrender your obedience to intimidation.
Do not abandon your rebuilding season because opposition became loud.
Do not let counterfeit spiritual voices redefine what God already spoke.
God did not call you this far to leave you unfinished.
Philippians 1:6 says:
“Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
The Greek phrase for “perform it” is:
ἐπιτελέσει — epitelesei
Meaning:
bring to completion, finish fully, carry through to the end.
God finishes what He truly begins.
Even when intimidation screams.
Even when fear shakes your emotions.
Even when opposition surrounds you.
Even when false voices rise against you.
Nehemiah survived because he feared God more than man.
And that remains the dividing line today.
Many people are controlled because they fear human opinion more than divine truth.
But Proverbs 29:25 warns:
“The fear of man bringeth a snare.”
The Hebrew word for snare is:
מוֹקֵשׁ — moqesh
A trap. A baited hook. A deadly entanglement.
Fear of people becomes spiritual captivity.
That is why Noadiah’s intimidation attempt mattered so much.
If Nehemiah had submitted to fear...
the rebuilding would have stopped.
And there are people connected to your obedience that you may never fully realize.
Your children.
Your future family.
Your ministry.
Your testimony.
Your influence.
Your future healing.
Your future freedom.
Sometimes your rebuilding season is bigger than you.
Sometimes Heaven is protecting generations through your obedience.
That is why the enemy fights so hard.
Because restored believers help restore others.
And broken chains become testimonies.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
Send this to someone rebuilding their life in silence.
And when it does... remember Nehemiah.
Remember the wall.
Remember that opposition often increases right before completion.
And never forget this:
The enemy attacks what Heaven intends to restore.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Tinangkang Takutin ni Noadias si Nehemias
May mga laban na hindi nagsisimula sa espada.
Nagsisimula sila sa takot.
Sa mga bulong.
Sa mga taong kunwari ay concern sa’yo pero lihim na hinihiling na bumagsak ka.
Sa spiritual manipulation na nakabalot sa relihiyosong salita.
Ito ang naranasan ni Nehemias.
Hindi lang siya nagtatayo ng pader.
Binubuo niya muli ang pagkakakilanlan ng bayan ng Diyos.
Binubuo niya muli ang pagsamba.
Binubuo niya muli ang pagsunod.
Binubuo niya muli ang mga taong matagal nang winasak ng kasalanan at pagkabihag.
At napansin iyon ng kadiliman.
Kaya isa sa pinaka-mapanganib na pag-atake laban kay Nehemias ay hindi galing sa digmaan.
Kundi sa intimidation.
At isa sa mga pangalang nakatago sa pag-atakeng iyon ay si Noadias.
Maraming tao ang hindi napapansin ang pangalan niya.
Pero walang sayang na pangalan sa Biblia.
Lahat ng pangalan ay may dahilan.
Lalo na ang mga mapanganib.
Sa Nehemias 6:14 sinabi:
“Alalahanin mo, Oh Dios ko, si Tobias at si Sanballat ayon sa kanilang mga gawa, at gayon din ang propetisang si Noadias at ang ibang mga propeta na nagsikap na takutin ako.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “takutin” ay:
יָרֵא — yare’
Ang ibig sabihin nito ay:
• takutin • sindakin • palabasin ang panghihina • piliting umatras dahil sa takot • pahinain ang loob ng isang tao upang tumigil siya sa pagsunod
Hindi simpleng fear ito.
Ito ay spiritual intimidation.
At hanggang ngayon, ito pa rin ang isa sa paboritong taktika ng kaaway.
Kapag hindi ka mapigilan ni Satanas sa calling mo...
susubukan ka niyang takutin palabas dito.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam na alam ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Noong nagsimula kang lumapit kay God... mas lumala ang anxiety.
Noong nagsimula kang magdasal... mas dumami ang discouragement.
Noong nagsimula kang umiwas sa kasalanan... mas dumami ang tukso.
Noong nagsimula kang ayusin ang buhay mo... biglang dumami ang spiritual attacks.
Dahil nagiging agresibo ang kadiliman kapag nagsisimula ang restoration.
Ang aklat ng Nehemias ay hindi lang history ng Israel.
Blueprint ito ng bawat believer na sinusubukang itayo muli ang winasak ng kaaway.
At halos palaging intimidation ang unang ipinapadala ni Satanas bago ang breakthrough.
Nakakatakot ang papel ni Noadias dahil tinawag siyang propetisa.
Sa Hebreo:
נְבִיאָה — nevi’ah
Ibig sabihin:
female prophet.
Ito ang masakit na katotohanan.
Ang intimidation minsan nanggagaling pa sa mga taong mukhang spiritual.
Hindi lahat ng nagsasalita tungkol sa Diyos ay galing sa Diyos.
Hindi lahat ng religious sounding ay Heaven-sent.
Kaya sinabi ni Jesus sa Mateo 7:15:
“Mag-ingat kayo sa mga bulaang propeta.”
Sa Greek:
ψευδοπροφητῶν — pseudoprophētōn
Pseudo.
Peke.
Counterfeit.
Pekeng spirituality.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napakahalaga ng discernment.
Dahil minsan ang intimidation ay dumarating na may dalang verses, prophecy, o religious language.
Malamang bahagi si Noadias ng planong psychologically sirain si Nehemias bago matapos ang pader.
Bakit?
Dahil ang pader ay simbolo ng:
holiness, protection, identity, obedience, at covenant.
At galit si Satanas sa anumang naglalagay ng boundaries laban sa pagkawasak.
Hindi natatakot ang kaaway sa passive Christians.
Pero natatakot siya sa mga taong nagsisimulang mag-rebuild.
Kaya unang ginamit laban kay Nehemias ang pangungutya.
Pagkatapos conspiracy.
Pagkatapos false accusations.
Pagkatapos intimidation.
Pagkatapos false prophecy.
Ganito pa rin hanggang ngayon.
Habang inaayos mo ang buhay mo... may gustong humila sa’yo pababa.
Habang nilalabanan mo ang addiction... may boses na bumubulong:
“Hindi ka magbabago.”
Habang tinatahak mo ang purity... may bumubulong:
“Babalik ka rin sa dati.”
Habang sinusunod mo si God... may bumubulong:
“Sino ka para gamitin ng Diyos?”
Hindi random ang mga boses na iyon.
Spiritual warfare iyon.
Sa 2 Timoteo 1:7 sinabi:
“Sapagka’t hindi tayo binigyan ng Dios ng espiritu ng katakutan.”
Ang Greek word para sa fear dito ay:
δειλίας — deilias
Ibig sabihin:
cowardice, shrinking back, intimidation na nagpapaatras.
Ito mismo ang gustong mangyari laban kay Nehemias.
Na umatras siya.
Na bumaba siya sa pader.
Na sumuko siya bago matapos.
Pero tumanggi si Nehemias.
Sa Nehemias 6:3 sinabi niya:
“Ako’y gumagawa ng dakilang gawain kaya hindi ako makabababa.”
Ang “dakilang gawain” sa Hebreo ay:
מְלָאכָה גְדוֹלָה — mela’khah gedolah
Divine assignment.
Mahalagang gawain.
Calling mula sa Diyos.
Naintindihan ni Nehemias ang bagay na nakakalimutan ng maraming believers:
Hindi lahat ng invitation ay dapat pansinin.
May mga distraction na demonic assignment.
May mga conversation na trap.
May mga tao na ipinadala para lang hilahin ka pababa mula sa calling mo.
At kung bumaba si Nehemias sa pader...
mananatiling vulnerable ang Jerusalem.
Minsan hindi ka kailangang sirain ng kaaway.
Kailangan ka lang niyang ma-distract.
Kaya napakadelikado ng intimidation.
Inaatake nito ang focus.
Inaatake nito ang confidence.
Inaatake nito ang endurance.
At kalaunan...
inaatake nito ang identity.
Tinangkang takutin ni Noadias si Nehemias dahil mas madaling kontrolin ang taong takot.
Kapag tahimik ang believer... mas madaling pabagsakin.
Kapag tumigil ang believer sa rebuilding... mananatiling bukas ang pader.
Pero may ginawa si Nehemias.
Nag-pray siya.
Hindi performance.
Hindi religious acting.
Totoong dependence sa Diyos.
At sa kabila ng lahat ng attacks...
natapos ang pader.
Sa Nehemias 6:15:
“So the wall was finished.”
Ang salitang “finished” sa Hebreo ay:
וַתִּשְׁלַם — vatishlam
Mula sa root na:
שָׁלֵם — shalem
Ibig sabihin:
complete, whole, restored.
Connected ito sa salitang:
שָׁלוֹם — shalom
Peace. Wholeness. Restoration.
Inatake ng kaaway si Nehemias dahil ang restored walls ay nagpo-produce ng restored people.
At ang restored people ay nagiging mapanganib sa kadiliman.
Baka nasa Nehemiah season ka ngayon.
Muling bumabangon pagkatapos ng heartbreak.
Pagkatapos ng addiction.
Pagkatapos ng betrayal.
Pagkatapos ng depression.
Pagkatapos ng secret sin.
At buong araw kang inuusig ng fear.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Ang presence ng intimidation ay hindi ibig sabihin iniwan ka ng Diyos.
Minsan sign ito na malapit ka na sa breakthrough.
Hindi nag-aaksaya si Satanas ng warfare sa territory na matagal nang patay.
At baka itong article na ito ang reminder na kailangan mo bago ka sumuko.
Baka pababa ka na sana sa pader.
Baka pagod ka na.
Baka gusto mo nang tumigil.
Pero ang kwento ni Nehemias ay sumisigaw pa rin hanggang ngayon:
Huwag kang bumaba.
Huwag mong isuko ang calling mo dahil lang sa intimidation.
Huwag mong hayaang takutin ka palabas sa assignment na ibinigay ng Diyos.
Hindi ka dinala ng Diyos hanggang dito para iwan kang unfinished.
Sa Filipos 1:6:
“Siya na nagpasimula ng mabuting gawa sa inyo ay siyang maglulubos nito.”
Sa Greek:
ἐπιτελέσει — epitelesei
Meaning:
bring to completion, finish fully.
Tinatapos ng Diyos ang totoong sinisimulan Niya.
Kahit maingay ang opposition.
Kahit nanginginig ka minsan sa fear.
Kahit maraming maling boses.
Nalampasan ni Nehemias ang intimidation dahil mas natakot siya sa Diyos kaysa sa tao.
At iyon pa rin ang malaking labanan ngayon.
Maraming believers ang kontrolado dahil mas takot sila sa opinion ng tao kaysa sa truth ng Diyos.
Pero sa Kawikaan 29:25:
“Ang takot sa tao ay nagdadala ng silo.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “silo” ay:
מוֹקֵשׁ — moqesh
Trap. Bitag. Deadly entanglement.
Kapag natakot ka sa tao... madaling mabihag ang spirit mo.
Kaya napakahalaga ng pagtanggi ni Nehemias sa intimidation.
Dahil kung sumuko siya... mahihinto ang rebuilding.
At may mga taong konektado sa obedience mo na hindi mo pa nakikita.
Ang future family mo.
Ang testimony mo.
Ang future ministry mo.
Ang healing mo.
Ang mga taong matutulungan mo balang araw.
Minsan mas malaki kaysa sa’yo ang rebuilding season mo.
Minsan buong henerasyon ang pinoprotektahan ng Diyos sa pamamagitan ng obedience mo.
Maging honest.
Mas tumama ito kaysa sa inaasahan mo.
At kapag dumating iyon... maalala mo sana si Nehemias.
Maalala mo ang pader.
Maalala mo na kadalasan pinakamalakas ang opposition bago dumating ang completion.
At huwag mong kakalimutan ito:
Pinaka-inaatake ng impiyerno ang gustong i-restore ng Langit.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Festus Thought Paul Was Insane
paragraphs: Why Festus Thought Paul Was Insane
There are moments in Scripture that feel so painfully human that you can almost hear the room breathing.
Acts 26 is one of those moments.

A chained apostle stands before governors, military commanders, political elites, intellectuals, religious authorities, and a king. The air is heavy with suspicion. Roman authority watches carefully. Jewish accusers burn with hatred. Pride fills the hall like smoke.
And then Paul starts talking about resurrection.
Not philosophy.
Not morality.
Not self-improvement.
Resurrection.
A dead man who walked out of His grave.
A blinding light from heaven.
A voice speaking from eternity.
A crucified Messiah who was alive.
And suddenly the governor Festus cannot contain himself anymore.
He interrupts Paul publicly.
Loudly.
Emotionally.
Almost desperately.
"Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." — Acts 26:24 (KJV)
The Greek text is even sharper.
"Μαίνῃ, Παῦλε" (Mainē, Paule).
Literally:
“Paul, you are insane.”
The Greek word μαίνῃ (mainē) comes from μαίνομαι (mainomai), meaning:
• to rage • to be out of one’s mind • to be mentally deranged • to speak as someone overtaken by madness
Festus was not politely disagreeing.
He was declaring that Paul had crossed the line between intelligence and insanity.
And honestly?
To the Roman mind… Paul sounded completely impossible.
Because the Gospel has always sounded irrational to people who worship power, image, control, status, logic without God, and earthly systems.
The tragedy is that many people still react to Jesus exactly like Festus did.
Some people hear the Gospel and feel conviction.
Others hear the Gospel and think believers have lost their minds.
Because resurrection destroys the illusion that this world is all there is.
And people become very uncomfortable when eternity interrupts their reality.
Festus could handle politics.
He could handle debates.
He could handle religion as long as it remained manageable.
But he could not process a man who stood before possible execution with supernatural peace while boldly declaring that death itself had already been defeated.
That terrified him.
Because Rome understood power.
But it did not understand surrender.
Rome understood conquest.
But it did not understand grace.
Rome understood gods made by men.
But it did not understand a God who became flesh and died for sinners.
And maybe that is why this moment still cuts so deeply today.
Because modern culture still celebrates confidence but mocks holiness.
People will believe crystals carry energy.
They will believe the universe sends signs.
They will believe strangers on social media can manifest destiny.
But the moment someone says:
“Jesus changed me.”
suddenly they become uncomfortable.
The world does not mind spirituality.
It minds surrender to Christ.
Paul’s testimony in Acts 26 was not theoretical theology.
It was collision.
A violent collision between darkness and divine mercy.
Paul was once Saul of Tarsus.
A persecutor.
A hunter of Christians.
A religious extremist convinced he was serving God.
In Philippians 3:5–6, Paul described himself as a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, zealous for the law.
Externally righteous.
Internally blind.
And then came Damascus.
Acts 26:13–14 records Paul’s words:
“At midday, O king, I saw in the way a light from heaven, above the brightness of the sun…”
The Greek phrase for “brightness” is:
ὑπὲρ τὴν λαμπρότητα τοῦ ἡλίου (hyper tēn lamprotēta tou hēliou)
Meaning:
“Beyond the brilliance of the sun itself.”
This was not imagination.
This was divine interruption.
Then Jesus speaks.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?”
And here something extraordinary happens.
Jesus speaks in Hebrew.
Acts 26:14 says:
“Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ” (Hebraidi dialektō)
“In the Hebrew language.”
Most scholars believe this likely refers to Aramaic, the common Semitic language spoken by Jews in Judea during that period.
The words:
“Saul, Saul…”
echo with deep covenant intimacy.
In Hebrew thought, repetition of a name carried emotional weight.
“Moses, Moses.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
“Martha, Martha.”
Now:
“Saul, Saul.”
Not condemnation.
Invitation.
Jesus was confronting the man destroying Christians… while still pursuing him in mercy.
And this is where the Gospel becomes offensive to proud hearts.
Because grace destroys the illusion that we can save ourselves.
Paul did not evolve into righteousness.
He was shattered into surrender.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You remember who you were.
The addictions.
The hidden sins.
The secret shame.
The bitterness.
The hypocrisy.
The nights you smiled publicly while privately collapsing.
Then somehow… Jesus found you.
Not because you were worthy.
But because He is merciful.
That kind of transformation confuses people.
Because the world understands behavior modification.
It does not understand rebirth.
The Greek word Jesus used in John 3 for “born again” is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen)
Meaning:
“born from above.”
Christianity is not self-help.
It is resurrection life entering spiritually dead people.
That is why Paul could stand before rulers without fear.
Because he was no longer living for earthly approval.
And this is what unsettled Festus most.
Paul had nothing to gain.
No political leverage.
No wealth.
No military power.
No public favor.
Yet he spoke with certainty.
Fearless certainty.
The kind that only comes from someone who has truly encountered Christ.
Festus likely thought:
“No sane man would suffer like this for a lie.”
But history proved Paul was telling the truth.
Because liars do not willingly embrace chains, beatings, shipwrecks, imprisonment, and execution for something they know is false.
Paul’s life became evidence.
His scars preached.
His suffering testified.
His endurance revealed that Jesus was not merely an idea to him.
Christ was alive.
And deep down, many people still resist Christianity for the same reason Festus did.
Because if Jesus truly rose from the dead… then everything changes.
If the resurrection happened, then sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Salvation is real.
Heaven is real.
Hell is real.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Truth matters.
And suddenly life is no longer about comfort.
It becomes about surrender.
That is why the cross offends human pride.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 1:18:
“For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness…”
The Greek word for “foolishness” is:
μωρία (mōria)
From where we derive the concept of moronic thinking.
To unbelieving minds, the Gospel sounds absurd.
A crucified Savior.
Salvation by grace.
Strength through weakness.
Life through death.
An eternal kingdom invisible to earthly eyes.
But Paul continued:
“…but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.”
The Greek word for power:
δύναμις (dynamis)
Divine explosive power.
The Gospel is not weak.
It is spiritually disruptive.
It breaks chains.
It convicts hearts.
It exposes darkness.
It resurrects dead souls.
And maybe some people reading this have secretly been afraid of fully surrendering to Jesus because you fear what others will think.
You fear being labeled extreme.
Religious.
Fanatical.
Brainwashed.
Crazy.
But remember this:
The same world that called Paul insane now studies his writings two thousand years later.
The same Roman Empire that mocked Christianity collapsed.
But Jesus Christ is still saving souls.
Still healing.
Still transforming.
Still forgiving.
Still calling sinners by name.
Still rescuing addicts.
Still restoring broken families.
Still delivering the hopeless.
Still raising spiritually dead people into new life.
Festus heard the Gospel and saw madness.
King Agrippa heard the Gospel and felt conviction.
Notice the difference.
Acts 26:28 says:
“Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.”
The room was divided.
One mocked.
One trembled.
And every person reading this will eventually respond one way or another.
Because nobody encounters the real Gospel neutrally.
Jesus forces a decision.
C.S. Lewis famously argued that Christ could not merely be considered a good moral teacher if His claims were true. The testimony of Scripture presents Him as Lord, not merely inspiration.
The resurrection stands at the center of Christianity.
If Christ did not rise, Paul himself said our faith is vain.
But if He did rise… then ignoring Him becomes the greatest tragedy imaginable.
And maybe that is the hidden fear beneath Festus’ outburst.
Because sometimes people call truth insanity when truth threatens the life they want to keep living.
Conviction can sound offensive when darkness has become comfortable.
Some of you reading this have been fighting conviction for months.
Maybe years.
You feel God calling you deeper.
Calling you out of compromise.
Out of addiction.
Out of sexual sin.
Out of lukewarm Christianity.
Out of hidden hypocrisy.
Out of performative religion.
Out of spiritual numbness.
But surrender feels terrifying because it changes everything.
Yet this is the beauty of the Gospel:
Jesus does not expose sin to destroy you.
He exposes sin to save you.
The cross was never proof that God hates sinners.
The cross is proof that God loves sinners enough to pay their debt Himself.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions…”
The Hebrew word for “wounded” is:
מְחֹלָל (mecholal)
Meaning:
pierced, profaned, violently wounded.
Christ was crushed beneath the weight of human rebellion.
Not symbolically.
Literally.
The Gospel is not sentimental.
It is bloody.
Costly.
Violent against sin.
And infinitely merciful toward sinners willing to repent.
That is why Paul could never stop preaching Jesus.
Because once you truly understand what Christ saved you from… silence becomes impossible.
Some people thought Paul was insane.
But maybe the real insanity is rejecting eternal life while obsessing over temporary things.
Maybe the real insanity is gaining worldly success while losing your soul.
Maybe the real insanity is pretending sin has no consequences.
Maybe the real insanity is spending your entire life avoiding the very God your heart was created for.
Paul was not crazy.
He was awake.
And awakened people unsettle sleeping worlds.
So if this exposed something hidden in your spirit… stop running.
Jesus Christ is still calling people out of darkness.
Still forgiving.
Still restoring.
Still welcoming prodigals home.
Still healing what religion could never heal.
And if you know someone who has been wrestling with faith, shame, doubt, addiction, depression, or spiritual confusion… share this with them.
Some people are one encounter away from complete transformation.
One day the voices that mocked your faith will stand before the same risen Christ they once rejected.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Inakala ni Festus na Baliw si Pablo
May mga eksena sa Bibliya na parang hindi lang basta mababasa.
Parang maririnig mo ang bigat ng katahimikan.
Parang mararamdaman mo ang tensyon sa hangin.
Ang Gawa 26 ay isa sa mga sandaling iyon.
Isang lalaking nakakadena ang nakatayo sa harap ng mga gobernador, sundalo, pinuno, relihiyosong lider, at hari.
At habang nagsasalita si Pablo… unti-unting nagiging hindi komportable ang buong silid.
Hindi dahil sumisigaw siya.
Hindi dahil agresibo siya.
Kundi dahil ang sinasabi niya ay imposible para sa isip ng tao.
Nagsasalita siya tungkol sa isang lalaking namatay… pero muling nabuhay.
Nagsasalita siya tungkol sa liwanag mula sa langit.
Isang tinig mula sa walang hanggan.
Isang Mesiyas na ipinako sa krus ngunit buhay.
At biglang sumabog si Festus.
“Pablo, nababaliw ka na!”
Iyon talaga ang diwa ng sinabi niya sa Gawa 26:24.
Sa orihinal na Greek:
“Μαίνῃ, Παῦλε” (Mainē, Paule)
Literal na ibig sabihin:
“Pablo, baliw ka.”
Ang salitang μαίνῃ (mainē) ay galing sa salitang μαίνομαι (mainomai), na nangangahulugang:
• mawalan ng katinuan • parang wala sa sarili • magwala na parang nababaliw • magsalita na tila nasisiraan ng isip
Hindi simpleng hindi pagsang-ayon ang ginawa ni Festus.
Para sa kanya… nawalan na ng bait si Pablo.
At kung tutuusin, sa pananaw ng Roma, parang imposible nga ang mga sinasabi ni Pablo.
Dahil ang Ebanghelyo ay palaging mukhang kahangalan sa mga taong sumasamba sa kapangyarihan, kayamanan, kontrol, pride, at makamundong sistema.
At hanggang ngayon… ganoon pa rin.
Kapag sinabi mong binago ka ni Jesus, may mga taong nagiging hindi komportable.
Maniniwala sila sa enerhiya.
Sa “manifesting.”
Sa universe.
Sa horoscope.
Sa spiritual vibrations.
Pero kapag sinabi mong:
“Binago ako ni Cristo.”
biglang parang ikaw ang kakaiba.
Dahil ayaw ng mundo sa tunay na pagsuko kay Jesus.
Ayaw ng tao sa ideya na may Hari na mas mataas kaysa sarili nilang kagustuhan.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit parang baliw si Pablo sa mata ni Festus.
Habang ang lahat ay takot mawalan ng posisyon… si Pablo ay may kakaibang kapayapaan kahit nakakadena.
Habang ang lahat ay protektado ng kapangyarihan ng Roma… si Pablo ay nakatayo lang dala ang katotohanan.
At iyon ang hindi maintindihan ni Festus.
Paano nagkakaroon ng ganoong katapang ang isang taong posibleng ipapatay?
Dahil si Pablo ay hindi na nabubuhay para sa approval ng tao.
Naranasan niya si Cristo.
Hindi relihiyon.
Hindi tradisyon.
Hindi philosophy.
Kundi si Jesus mismo.
Dati siyang si Saul ng Tarsus.
Mamamatay-tao ng mga Kristiyano.
Persecutor.
Relihiyosong extremist.
Akala niya tama siya.
Akala niya naglilingkod siya sa Diyos.
Pero sa daan papuntang Damascus… binasag ng langit ang kanyang kayabangan.
Sa Gawa 26:13–14 sinabi ni Pablo:
“Nakita ko ang isang liwanag mula sa langit na higit pa sa ningning ng araw.”
Sa Greek:
ὑπὲρ τὴν λαμπρότητα τοῦ ἡλίου (hyper tēn lamprotēta tou hēliou)
Ibig sabihin:
“Higit pa sa mismong liwanag ng araw.”
At pagkatapos ay nagsalita si Jesus.
“Saul, Saul, bakit mo Ako inuusig?”
Napakaganda ng detalye sa talatang iyon.
Sinasabi ng Kasulatan na nagsalita si Jesus sa “wikang Hebreo.”
“Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ” (Hebraidi dialektō)
Karamihan sa mga iskolar ay naniniwalang Aramaic ito — ang karaniwang wikang ginagamit noon ng mga Hudyo.
At ang pag-uulit ng pangalan:
“Saul, Saul…”
ay may malalim na emosyon sa kultura ng Hebreo.
“Moses, Moses.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
“Martha, Martha.”
Ngayon:
“Saul, Saul.”
Hindi ito simpleng galit.
Ito ay paanyaya.
Habang inuusig ni Saul ang mga Kristiyano… hinahabol pa rin siya ng awa ni Jesus.
At dito natitisod ang pride ng tao.
Dahil ipinapakita ng grasya na hindi natin kayang iligtas ang sarili natin.
Hindi unti-unting gumaling si Pablo.
Binagsak siya ng katotohanan hanggang siya ay sumuko.
At maraming tao ang makaka-relate dito.
May mga gabi kang umiiyak nang walang nakakaalam.
May mga kasalanang itinago mo nang matagal.
May addictions.
May shame.
May depression.
May double life.
Ngumingiti sa publiko.
Pero wasak sa pribado.
At pagkatapos… nakilala mo si Jesus.
Hindi dahil deserve mo.
Kundi dahil maawain Siya.
Iyan ang hindi maintindihan ng mundo.
Naiintindihan nila ang self-improvement.
Pero hindi nila maintindihan ang spiritual rebirth.
Sa Juan 3, sinabi ni Jesus ang salitang:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen)
“ipanganak mula sa itaas.”
Ang Kristiyanismo ay hindi simpleng pagiging mabuting tao.
Ito ay bagong buhay mula sa Diyos.
Kaya si Pablo ay nakatayo nang walang takot.
Wala siyang kayamanan.
Wala siyang political influence.
Wala siyang protection.
Pero mayroon siyang katotohanan.
At minsan… ang katotohanan ang pinaka-nakakatakot pakinggan.
Lalo na kapag alam mong babaguhin nito ang buhay mo.
Maraming tao hanggang ngayon ang tumatakbo sa conviction.
Ayaw nilang sumuko kay Jesus dahil natatakot silang may kailangang bitawan.
Kasalanan.
Pride.
Relasyon.
Addiction.
Lihim.
Kontrol.
Pero ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo ay ito:
Hindi inilalantad ni Jesus ang kasalanan para sirain ka.
Inilalantad Niya ito para iligtas ka.
Ang krus ay hindi patunay na galit ang Diyos sa makasalanan.
Patunay ito na mahal Niya tayo nang sapat para akuin Niya mismo ang parusa.
Sa Isaias 53:5:
“Siya ay nasugatan dahil sa ating mga pagsalangsang…”
Ang Hebrew word para sa “nasugatan” ay:
מְחֹלָל (mecholal)
Na nangangahulugang:
• tinusok • dinurog • marahas na sinaktan
Hindi simboliko ang krus.
Totoo ito.
Madugo.
Masakit.
Mahal.
At dahil doon… may pag-asa pa tayo.
Kaya hindi tumigil si Pablo sa pangangaral.
Kapag tunay mong naintindihan kung saan ka iniligtas ni Cristo… hindi ka na makakatahimik.
At baka iyon talaga ang dahilan kung bakit sinabi ni Festus na baliw si Pablo.
Dahil ang mga taong tunay na nabuhay para kay Jesus ay hindi na kayang kontrolin ng mundong ito.
Ang totoo?
Hindi baliw si Pablo.
Gising lang siya.
At ang mga gising… palaging istorbo sa mundong tulog.
Kung may tinamaan sa puso mo habang binabasa ito… huwag mo nang takbuhan ang conviction.
Tinatawag ka pa rin ni Jesus.
Hindi pa huli ang lahat.
May awa pa.
May kapatawaran pa.
May bagong simula pa.
May mga taong isang encounter na lang kay Jesus ang layo mula sa total transformation.
Darating ang araw na ang mundong tumawa sa pananampalataya mo ay haharap din sa parehong nabuhay na Cristo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why King Pekah Turned Against Judah
paragraphs: Why King Pekah Turned Against Judah
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully modern.
Moments where political betrayal looks like family betrayal.
Moments where wounded pride becomes national destruction.
Moments where fear makes leaders forget God.
And hidden inside one of the darkest political crises in the Old Testament is a king most people barely remember.
Pekah.
A warrior king. A conspirator. A murderer. A man consumed by resistance. A ruler who turned against Judah and helped drag an entire generation toward judgment.
But if we only read his story as politics, we completely miss the warning.
Because Pekah’s rebellion was never just military.
It was spiritual.
And if we are honest… many believers are fighting the exact same war inside themselves right now.
The story unfolds during a fractured season in Israel’s history.
The united kingdom established under David and Solomon had already split in two.
The northern kingdom kept the name Israel. The southern kingdom became Judah.
Two nations. One covenant heritage. One God. But divided hearts.

The northern kingdom had descended deeper and deeper into idolatry. Its kings repeatedly abandoned the covenant of Yahweh. Altars to false gods multiplied. Political survival became more important than holiness.
And into that chaos rose Pekah.
Second Kings 15:27 says:
“In the fifty and second year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned twenty years.”
But Pekah did not inherit peace.
He seized power through assassination.
Second Kings 15:25 tells us he conspired against King Pekahiah and murdered him inside the royal palace.
This matters.
Because Scripture is showing us something deeper than politics.
Violence born from ambition rarely stays contained.
The Hebrew language quietly reveals the darkness underneath.
The word used for “conspired” is:
קָשַׁר qashar
It carries the idea of binding together secretly, treasonously, forming an unlawful alliance.
Pekah’s kingdom was built on rebellion before he ever attacked Judah.
Sin almost always spreads beyond its original target.
A compromised heart eventually becomes a compromised nation.
At first, Pekah probably looked strong. Decisive. Aggressive. Nationalistic. A defender of northern Israel.
But strength without obedience to God becomes destruction wearing armor.
The real turning point came during the reign of Ahaz king of Judah.
Ahaz was deeply compromised spiritually.
Second Kings 16 describes horrifying idolatry.
He walked “in the way of the kings of Israel.” He practiced pagan worship. He even sacrificed his own son.
Judah was spiritually weak.
And Pekah saw opportunity.
But this was bigger than opportunism.
Pekah feared Assyria.
The Assyrian Empire was becoming a terrifying superpower swallowing nations whole. Kings throughout the region were panicking.
So Pekah formed an alliance with Rezin king of Aram.
Their goal was simple: Force Judah to join their anti-Assyrian coalition.
But Ahaz refused.
And rejection ignited war.
Isaiah 7 opens with chilling tension:
“When Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, King Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel marched up to fight against Jerusalem…”
Imagine the horror.
Brother kingdoms at war. Children of Abraham attacking children of Abraham. The covenant people tearing each other apart while pagan empires watched.
The Hebrew phrase used in Isaiah 7:2 says:
וַיָּנַע לְבָבוֹ va-yaná levavo
“His heart shook.”
The text says the hearts of Ahaz and the people shook “as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.”
This is not ordinary fear.
It is terror. Political panic. Spiritual collapse. The feeling that everything is about to fall apart.
And maybe that is exactly where some people are living right now.
You smile publicly. But internally your soul is shaking.
Your marriage. Your finances. Your hidden sin. Your exhaustion. Your future. Your faith.
Everything feels unstable.
This ancient war suddenly becomes deeply personal.
Because Pekah represents something larger than himself.
He represents what happens when fear replaces trust in God.
Instead of repentance, he chose coercion. Instead of humility, he chose aggression. Instead of seeking the Lord, he trusted political force.
And humanity still does this every day.
We manipulate. We pressure. We force. We control. We panic.
Because fear convinces us God cannot be trusted with outcomes.
But then something extraordinary happens.
God sends Isaiah.
Not first to rebuke. Not first to destroy. But to invite trust.
Isaiah tells Ahaz:
“Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted…”
The Hebrew phrase:
הִשָּׁמֵר וְהַשְׁקֵט hishamer ve-hashqet
Means: “Be careful… and be still.”
That command still confronts modern believers.
Because panic has become a lifestyle.
We doom-scroll. We catastrophize. We obsess over control. We trust strategies more than surrender.
Yet God was telling Judah: You do not survive by fear. You survive by faith.
Then comes one of the most devastating prophetic lines in the entire story.
Isaiah 7:9:
“If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”
The Hebrew uses a profound wordplay:
אִם לֹא תַאֲמִינוּ כִּי לֹא תֵאָמֵנוּ im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu
“If you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all.”
The root word carries the idea of firmness, reliability, faithfulness.
Faith is not emotional denial. Faith is stability rooted in God.
And this is where Pekah ultimately failed.
He trusted alliances more than Yahweh.
He believed political unity could save him. He believed force could secure the future. He believed human power could resist judgment.
But Assyria still came.
Second Kings 15:29 records devastating loss:
“In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah… and carried them captive to Assyria.”
The empire Pekah feared became the empire that crushed him.
Fear-driven rebellion often creates the very destruction it hoped to avoid.
And eventually Pekah himself was assassinated.
The man who rose through conspiracy died through conspiracy.
Scripture is brutally honest about the cycle of sin.
Violence multiplies. Pride multiplies. Fear multiplies. Compromise multiplies.
Until entire nations collapse spiritually.
But buried inside this tragedy is something astonishing.
God still extended mercy.
Even during rebellion. Even during political corruption. Even during idolatry. Even while kingdoms trembled.
The Lord still pursued people.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because humanity has always been Pekah in some way.
We resist surrender. We grasp for control. We trust human solutions. We build alliances with sin. We fight battles without prayer.
And yet God still sends His word. Still calls us back. Still warns. Still invites repentance.
The Greek New Testament later reveals this same spiritual crisis in another form.
Romans 10:17 says:
“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”
The Greek word for faith is:
πίστις pistis
It means trust, confidence, faithful reliance.
Not shallow positivity. Not motivational thinking.
True biblical faith is surrendering confidence into the character of God.
Pekah could not do that.
And many people today still cannot.
Some trust money more than God. Some trust politics more than God. Some trust relationships more than God. Some trust public image more than God. Some trust religious performance more than God.
But unstable foundations eventually collapse.
And maybe this article found you during your own internal civil war.
Part of you wants God. Part of you still wants control.
Part of you wants healing. Part of you still feeds hidden compromise.
Part of you wants peace. Part of you still fights battles your flesh created.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because the tragedy of Pekah is not merely that he fought Judah.
It is that he never truly surrendered before God.
History remembers military campaigns. Heaven examines hearts.
And this is why Jesus Christ changes everything.

Where earthly kings spread fear, Christ brings peace. Where earthly rulers seize power, Christ lays His life down. Where sinful kingdoms divide, Christ reconciles. Where rebellion deserves judgment, Christ offers mercy through the cross.
The prophet Isaiah — the same prophet who confronted this crisis — would later write about the coming Messiah:
And one of His names would be:
שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם Sar-Shalom
Prince of Peace.
Not temporary political peace. Not manipulated peace. Not fear-driven peace.
True peace with God.
The kind no collapsing kingdom can destroy.
And maybe that is what your exhausted soul has actually been searching for.
Not another strategy. Not another distraction. Not another performance.
But surrender.
Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior. He came to rescue rebels.
That includes fearful people. Proud people. Religious people. Broken people. Compromised people.
People like Pekah. People like Ahaz. People like us.
And if you know someone silently battling fear, compromise, anxiety, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them.
Some people are losing wars internally while pretending everything is fine publicly.
One day every kingdom built on fear will fall… but every soul anchored in Christ will still stand.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Tinalikuran ni Haring Pekah ang Juda
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na parang balita ngayon.
Mga panahong ang pagkakanulo sa politika ay parang pagkakanulo ng sariling pamilya.
Mga panahong ang takot ay mas malakas kaysa pananampalataya.
Mga panahong ang mga tao ng Diyos mismo ang naglalaban-laban.
At nakatago sa isa sa pinakamadilim na krisis ng Lumang Tipan ang isang haring halos hindi naaalala ng marami.
Si Pekah.
Isang mandirigma. Isang traydor. Isang mamamatay-tao. Isang haring nalunod sa paghihimagsik.
Ngunit kung politika lang ang makikita natin sa kanyang kwento… mamimiss natin ang tunay na babala.
Dahil ang laban ni Pekah laban sa Juda ay hindi lang militar.
Espirituwal ito.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao ngayon ang may parehong digmaan sa loob ng puso nila.
Nagsimula ang lahat matapos mabiyak ang kaharian ni Solomon.
Ang hilagang kaharian ay tinawag na Israel. Ang timog naman ay Juda.
Iisang kasaysayan. Iisang Diyos. Ngunit hati ang puso.
Habang lumilipas ang panahon, mas lumalalim ang hilagang Israel sa idolatriya.
Ang mga hari nito ay paulit-ulit na tumalikod kay Yahweh. Mas naging mahalaga ang kapangyarihan kaysa kabanalan. Mas naging mahalaga ang kaligtasan ng kaharian kaysa pagsunod sa Diyos.
At sa gitna ng kaguluhang iyon, umangat si Pekah.
Ngunit hindi siya naging hari sa mapayapang paraan.
Sa 2 Hari 15:25, makikita natin na nakipagsabwatan siya laban kay Haring Pekahias at pinatay niya ito sa loob mismo ng palasyo.
Mahalagang detalye iyon.
Dahil ipinapakita ng Kasulatan na ang kahariang itinayo sa paghihimagsik ay bihirang magtapos sa kapayapaan.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “nakipagsabwatan” ay:
קָשַׁר qashar
Ibig sabihin nito ay lihim na pagbuo ng pagtataksil. Pagkakaisa para sa rebelyon.
Bago pa lusubin ni Pekah ang Juda… may digmaan na sa loob ng kanyang puso.
At ganiyan din minsan ang tao.
Ang kasalanang kinukubli ay hindi nananatiling maliit.
Unti-unti nitong winawasak ang isip. Ang relasyon. Ang tahanan. Ang pananampalataya.
Noong una, maaaring mukhang malakas si Pekah. Matapang. Makabayan. Isang lider na handang lumaban.
Pero ang lakas na walang pagsunod sa Diyos ay nagiging pagkawasak na may suot na baluti.
Dumating ang pinakamahalagang bahagi ng kwento noong panahon ni Ahaz, hari ng Juda.
Si Ahaz ay espirituwal na mahina.
Ayon sa 2 Hari 16, lumakad siya sa kasalanan ng mga hari ng Israel. Sumamba siya sa mga diyus-diyosan. At mas masakit… inihandog pa niya ang sarili niyang anak.
Mahina ang Juda. At nakita iyon ni Pekah.
Pero may mas malalim pang dahilan.
Takot si Pekah.
Takot siya sa lumalakas na imperyo ng Asiria.
Sinakop ng Asiria ang mga bansa isa-isa. Lahat ng hari noon ay nangangamba.
Kaya nakipag-alyansa si Pekah kay Haring Rezin ng Aram.
Ang plano nila? Piliting sumama ang Juda sa kanilang laban kontra Asiria.
Pero tumanggi si Ahaz.
At doon nagsimula ang digmaan.
Sa Isaias 7, sinabi:
“Si Rezin na hari ng Siria at si Pekah na anak ni Remalias ay umahon laban sa Jerusalem upang salakayin iyon…”
Isipin mo iyon.
Magkapatid na kaharian. Mga anak ni Abraham. Ngunit nagpapatayan.
Habang pinapanood sila ng mga paganong imperyo.
Sinasabi ng Isaias 7:2:
וַיָּנַע לְבָבוֹ va-yaná levavo
“Nanginig ang kanyang puso.”
Hindi ito ordinaryong takot.
Ito iyong klase ng takot na parang mawawasak na ang lahat.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na ganiyan ang nararamdaman.
Ngumingiti ka sa harap ng iba. Pero sa loob… pagod na pagod ka na.
Takot ka sa mangyayari sa pamilya mo. Takot ka sa kinabukasan. Takot ka sa kasalanang hindi mo mabitawan. Takot ka na baka lumalayo ka na sa Diyos.
At biglang nagiging personal ang kwento ni Pekah.
Dahil si Pekah ay larawan ng taong pinamumunuan ng takot kaysa pagtitiwala sa Diyos.
Sa halip na magsisi… nanakot siya. Sa halip na magpakumbaba… lumaban siya. Sa halip na hanapin si Yahweh… umasa siya sa politika at kapangyarihan.
At hanggang ngayon, ginagawa pa rin iyon ng tao.
Kinokontrol natin ang lahat. Pinipilit natin ang gusto natin. Nagpapanic tayo. Nag-ooverthink tayo.
Dahil minsan… hindi talaga tayo nagtitiwala na kayang hawakan ng Diyos ang buhay natin.
Pero dito naging makapangyarihan ang kwento.
Nagpadala ang Diyos ng propeta.
Hindi agad para manira. Hindi agad para humatol.
Kundi para tawagin silang magtiwala.
Sinabi ni Isaias kay Ahaz:
“Mag-ingat ka at manahimik ka; huwag kang matakot…”
Sa Hebreo:
הִשָּׁמֵר וְהַשְׁקֵט hishamer ve-hashqet
“Mag-ingat… at maging payapa.”
Napakalalim ng utos na iyon.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ngayon ang nabubuhay sa panic.
Laging balisa. Laging natatakot. Laging may iniisip.
Pero sinasabi pa rin ng Diyos: Hindi ka mabubuhay sa takot. Mabubuhay ka sa pananampalataya.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang isa sa pinakamabibigat na talata sa kwento.
Isaias 7:9:
“Kung hindi kayo mananampalataya, tiyak na hindi kayo matatatag.”
Sa Hebreo:
אִם לֹא תַאֲמִינוּ כִּי לֹא תֵאָמֵנוּ im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu
Kung wala kang pananampalataya… wala kang matatag na pundasyon.
At dito tuluyang nabigo si Pekah.
Mas nagtiwala siya sa alyansa kaysa kay Yahweh. Mas naniwala siya sa lakas ng tao kaysa sa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Pero dumating pa rin ang Asiria.
Sa 2 Hari 15:29, sinakop nila ang mga lungsod ng Israel at dinala ang mga tao bilang bihag.
Ang kinatatakutan ni Pekah… iyon mismo ang sumira sa kanya.
Ganiyan minsan ang buhay.
Kapag takot ang nagpapatakbo sa atin, madalas tayo mismo ang gumagawa ng pagkawasak na gusto nating iwasan.
At kalaunan… pinaslang din si Pekah.
Ang taong umangat sa pamamagitan ng pagtataksil ay bumagsak din sa parehong paraan.
Napakatapat ng Biblia.
Ang kasalanan ay lumalaki. Ang pride ay lumalaki. Ang takot ay lumalaki.
Hanggang sa bumagsak ang buong tao.
Pero kahit sa gitna ng kaguluhan… may awa pa rin ang Diyos.
Iyon ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo.
Dahil kahit paulit-ulit tayong pumapalya… patuloy pa rin Siyang tumatawag.
Patuloy Siyang nagbababala. Patuloy Siyang naghihintay. Patuloy Siyang nag-aalok ng kapatawaran.
At dito pumapasok si Jesucristo.
Dahil ang problema ng tao ay hindi lang politika. Hindi lang emosyon. Hindi lang trauma.
Kasalanan.
At si Jesus ang dumating para iligtas ang mga rebelde.
Mga takot. Mga pagod. Mga nagtatago. Mga wasak. Mga taong pilit kinokontrol ang lahat.
Mga taong katulad natin.
Sinasabi sa Roma 10:17:
“Ang pananampalataya ay nanggagaling sa pakikinig, at ang pakikinig ay sa pamamagitan ng salita ng Diyos.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “pananampalataya” ay:
πίστις pistis
Ibig sabihin: Buong pagtitiwala. Buong pag-asa. Buong pagsandal.
Hindi fake positivity. Hindi pagpapanggap na okay ka.
Kundi tunay na pagsuko sa Diyos.
At baka iyon talaga ang kailangan mo ngayon.
Hindi panibagong distraction. Hindi panibagong kontrol. Hindi panibagong pagtatago.
Kundi pagsuko.
Dahil habang ang mga hari sa lupa ay nagdadala ng takot… si Cristo ay nagdadala ng kapayapaan.
Habang ang mundo ay naghahati-hati… si Jesus ay nagkakasundo.
Habang ang kasalanan ay sumisira… si Cristo ay nagliligtas.
At ang parehong propetang si Isaias na nakakita ng kaguluhan ni Pekah ay nagsulat din tungkol sa darating na Mesiyas.
Tinawag niya Siyang:
שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם Sar-Shalom
Prinsipe ng Kapayapaan.
Hindi pansamantalang kapayapaan. Hindi kapayapaang gawa ng politika.
Kundi tunay na kapayapaan sa Diyos.
At kapag si Cristo ang pundasyon mo… kahit gaano kalakas ang bagyo, mananatili kang nakatayo.
May mga taong mukhang okay sa labas pero wasak na pala sa loob.
Darating ang araw na lahat ng kahariang itinayo sa takot ay babagsak… pero ang pusong nakatanim kay Cristo ay mananatiling nakatayo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why King Zedekiah Secretly Asked Jeremiah for the Truth
paragraphs: Why King Zedekiah Secretly Asked Jeremiah for the Truth
The palace was still standing.
The walls of Jerusalem had not fully collapsed yet.
The priests were still performing rituals.
The officials still wore their robes.
The king still sat on a throne.
But underneath the gold… Judah was already dying.
And deep inside the palace, a terrified king was secretly searching for a prophet he publicly refused to obey.
This is not merely the story of a weak ruler.
This is the story of every person who already knows the truth… but is afraid of what obedience will cost.
The Bible says in Jeremiah 38:14:

“Then Zedekiah the king sent and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the LORD: and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me.”
That verse feels heavy when you truly understand it.
Because Zedekiah did not ask Jeremiah publicly.
He asked secretly.
Quietly.
Behind closed doors.
Away from the crowds.
Away from the officials.
Away from the people influencing him.
He wanted truth… but not exposure.
He wanted clarity… but not surrender.
He wanted God’s voice… without God’s consequences.
And millions are still doing the exact same thing today.
Some people secretly watch sermons at night after spending all day pretending they do not care about God.
Some secretly pray after publicly living rebellious lives.
Some secretly know their relationship is sinful.
Some secretly know they are destroying themselves.
Some secretly know God has been warning them for years.
But like Zedekiah… they fear people more than they fear the Lord.
That is where this story becomes terrifyingly personal.
Because Zedekiah was not ignorant.
He was convicted.
There is a massive difference.

The Hebrew behind Jeremiah’s warnings carries the weight of covenant judgment. Jeremiah repeatedly declared that Babylon would conquer Jerusalem because Judah had violated God’s covenant through idolatry, injustice, bloodshed, and rebellion.
In Jeremiah 38:17, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah:
“If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon’s princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire…”
The Hebrew phrase for “thy soul shall live” is:
וְחָיְתָה נַפְשֶׁךָ
“Vechayetah nafshekha.”
Literally:
“Your life shall live.”
This was mercy being offered in the middle of judgment.
God was still extending an escape.
Even after years of rebellion.
Even after ignored warnings.
Even after national corruption.
The Lord was still saying:
“Obey Me now… and live.”
But Zedekiah hesitated.
Why?
Because fear of people can make cowards out of kings.
Jeremiah 38:19 reveals the true reason:
“And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid…”
That sentence exposes the entire tragedy.
“I am afraid.”
Not confused.
Not unconvinced.
Afraid.
The Hebrew word used here is:
יָגֹר
“Yagor.”
It means to dread, fear, or live in terror.
Zedekiah feared humiliation.
He feared rejection.
He feared what people would think.
He feared political embarrassment.
He feared losing approval.
And because he feared man more than God… he lost both.
This is exactly why Proverbs 29:25 says:
“The fear of man bringeth a snare.”
The Hebrew word for “snare” is:
מוֹקֵשׁ
“Moqesh.”
A trap.
A hidden noose.
Something that slowly tightens around your life.
Zedekiah was trapped long before Babylon broke the walls.
His real prison was internal.
And some people reading this understand exactly what that feels like.
You know God has been convicting you.
But you are terrified of losing relationships.
Terrified of being mocked.
Terrified of changing.
Terrified of surrender.
Terrified of letting go of sin.
Terrified of becoming “too serious” about Jesus.
So you keep God in secret compartments.
Private prayers.
Hidden tears.
Silent conviction.
Secret spiritual panic.
That was Zedekiah.
He kept consulting Jeremiah privately while publicly refusing to fully obey.
And eventually the clock ran out.
Babylon breached Jerusalem.
The city burned.
The temple was destroyed.
Zedekiah watched his sons slaughtered before his eyes.
Then the Babylonians blinded him.
The last thing he ever saw was judgment.
Second Kings 25:7 says:
“And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah…”
The tragedy is unbearable.
Because it did not have to happen.
This was not the destruction of a man who never heard truth.
This was the destruction of a man who repeatedly heard truth… but delayed obedience.
That is one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions possible.
Hearing truth without surrender hardens the heart.
The New Testament echoes this warning powerfully.
In James 1:22, the Greek says:
Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ ἀκροαταὶ μόνον
“Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē akroatai monon.”
“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.”
The word “ἀκροαταὶ” (akroatai) refers to passive listeners.
People who hear.
People who nod.
People who understand.
But never transform.
Zedekiah was an “akroates.”
A hearer.
Not a surrenderer.
And modern Christianity is filled with people secretly asking Jeremiah for truth while refusing to fully obey God publicly.
They love conviction as long as it stays emotional.
But conviction is supposed to lead somewhere.
To repentance.
To surrender.
To transformation.
To Christ.
This is what makes Jeremiah such a painful prophet.
He was not popular.
He was not celebrated.
He was hated because he refused to alter God’s message.
The false prophets promised peace.
Jeremiah warned judgment.
The false prophets comforted rebellion.
Jeremiah confronted sin.
And Zedekiah kept bouncing between what felt good and what was true.
That is still happening today.
Many people do not want truth.
They want reassurance.
They want spiritual anesthesia.
They want motivation without repentance.
Blessing without holiness.
Encouragement without correction.
But the real Word of God does not merely comfort.
It cuts.
Hebrews 4:12 says:
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword…”
The Greek word for “sharper” is:
τομώτερος
“Tomōteros.”
It means cutting deeply.
Piercing completely.
The Word of God exposes what we try to hide.
That is why Zedekiah kept meeting Jeremiah in secret.
Truth makes hidden things tremble.
And maybe that is why this story is hitting your spirit right now.
Because deep down… you already know.
You know what God has been convicting you about.
You know where compromise entered.
You know what you keep postponing.
You know the conversations you avoid.
You know the surrender you fear.
You know the sin you defend.
You know the wounds you hide behind sarcasm, pride, lust, anger, addiction, ambition, or distraction.
You know.
And still… Jesus stands ready to forgive.
That is the part many people miss.
Jeremiah’s warnings were severe, but God kept extending mercy.
The Lord kept sending prophets because He desired repentance.
God warns because God loves.
Judgment was never His first desire.
Even Ezekiel 33:11 says:
“I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live.”
The Hebrew word for “turn” is:
שׁוּב
“Shuv.”
It means to return.
To come back.
To reverse direction.
This is the heartbeat of repentance.
Not perfection.
Return.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because where Zedekiah failed… Jesus succeeded.
Zedekiah feared people.
Jesus feared the Father perfectly.
Zedekiah hid from truth.
Jesus declared:
“I am the truth.”
Zedekiah compromised under pressure.
Jesus stood silent before mockers and still obeyed unto death.
Zedekiah lost his kingdom.
Jesus established an eternal Kingdom through the cross.
The Gospel is not merely a lesson about ancient kings.
It is the rescue of spiritually collapsing people.
Jesus Christ stepped into our rebellion and carried the judgment we deserved.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions…”
The Hebrew word for “wounded” is:
מְחֹלָל
“Mecholal.”
Pierced.
Profaned.
Broken open.
Christ was crushed so sinners could return.
That means your story does not have to end like Zedekiah’s.
You do not have to keep secretly asking for truth while publicly resisting God.
You can surrender.
Right now.
Fully.
Not halfway.
Not emotionally.
Not temporarily.
Completely.
Because delayed obedience is still disobedience.
And hidden conviction eventually becomes visible destruction if ignored long enough.
But mercy is still reaching for you.
That is why you are reading this.
Not by accident.
Not randomly.
Not casually.
God is still calling people back before the walls collapse.
Before the consequences fully arrive.
Before the numbness becomes permanent.
Before the heart hardens completely.
The terrifying thing about Zedekiah is not that he asked for the truth.
It is that he heard it clearly… and still refused to fully obey.
Do not let that become your story.
And if this article reminded you of someone silently battling fear, compromise, addiction, shame, or hidden conviction, share this with them now.
Some people are one warning away from surrender.
Others are one step away from collapse.
Do not stay silent.
One day the hidden conversations in your soul will become visible in your life.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Palihim na Humingi si Haring Zedekias ng Katotohanan kay Jeremias
Nakatayo pa ang palasyo.
Hindi pa ganap na bumabagsak ang mga pader ng Jerusalem.
Patuloy pa rin ang mga pari sa kanilang mga ritwal.
Nakasuot pa rin ng kanilang mahahabang kasuotan ang mga pinuno.
Nakaupo pa rin ang hari sa kaniyang trono.
Pero sa ilalim ng lahat ng karangyaan… unti-unti nang namamatay ang Juda.
At sa loob mismo ng palasyo, isang natatakot na hari ang palihim na naghahanap sa propetang matagal na niyang hindi sinusunod.
Hindi lang ito kuwento tungkol sa isang mahinang hari.
Ito ang kuwento ng bawat taong alam na ang katotohanan… pero takot sa magiging kapalit ng pagsunod.
Sinasabi sa Jeremias 38:14:
“At ipinatawag ni haring Zedekias si Jeremias na propeta… at sinabi ng hari kay Jeremias, ‘May itatanong ako sa iyo; huwag kang maglihim sa akin ng anuman.’”
Mabigat ang talatang iyon kapag talagang naunawaan mo.
Dahil hindi tinanong ni Zedekias si Jeremias sa harap ng bayan.
Palihim niya itong ginawa.
Tahimik.
Nakatago.
Malayo sa mga opisyal.
Malayo sa mga taong nakakaimpluwensya sa kaniya.
Gusto niya ang katotohanan… pero ayaw niya ng kahihiyan.
Gusto niya ang tinig ng Diyos… pero ayaw niya ng kabuuang pagsunod.
At milyon-milyon pa rin ang gumagawa nito hanggang ngayon.
May mga taong lihim na umiiyak habang nananalangin gabi-gabi pero buong araw ay nagpapanggap na okay lang sila.
May mga taong alam na nilang mali ang kanilang relasyon pero ayaw nilang bitawan.
May mga taong alam nang unti-unti silang sinisira ng kasalanan pero pinipili pa rin nilang manatili rito.
May mga taong matagal nang kinakausap ng Diyos… pero mas takot sila sa opinyon ng tao kaysa sa utos ng Panginoon.
Dito nagiging personal ang kuwento ni Zedekias.
Hindi siya ignorante.
Kinukumbinsi na siya ng Diyos.
Malaki ang pagkakaiba ng dalawang iyon.
Sa Jeremias 38:17, sinabi ni Jeremias:
“Kung ikaw ay lalabas… mabubuhay ka, at ang lungsod na ito ay hindi susunugin sa apoy.”
Sa Hebreo, ang pariralang:
וְחָיְתָה נַפְשֶׁךָ
“Vechayetah nafshekha.”
Ay literal na nangangahulugang:
“Ang buhay mo ay mabubuhay.”
Kahit sa gitna ng paghatol… nag-aalok pa rin ang Diyos ng awa.
Kahit paulit-ulit na silang sumuway.
Kahit paulit-ulit na nilang binale-wala ang babala.
Patuloy pa ring sinasabi ng Diyos:
“Sumunod ka ngayon… at mabuhay ka.”
Pero nagdalawang-isip si Zedekias.
Bakit?
Dahil kayang gawing duwag ng takot sa tao kahit ang isang hari.
Sinasabi sa Jeremias 38:19:
“Natatakot ako…”
Iyan ang ugat ng kaniyang trahedya.
Hindi siya nalilito.
Hindi siya walang alam.
Takot siya.
Ang salitang Hebreo rito ay:
יָגֹר
“Yagor.”
Nangangahulugan itong mabuhay sa matinding takot o pangamba.
Takot si Zedekias mapahiya.
Takot siyang mawalan ng pagtanggap.
Takot siyang husgahan.
Takot siyang mawalan ng kontrol.
At dahil mas natakot siya sa tao kaysa sa Diyos… nawala sa kaniya pareho.
Ito mismo ang babala sa Kawikaan 29:25:
“Ang takot sa tao ay nagdadala ng silo.”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “silo” ay:
מוֹקֵשׁ
“Moqesh.”
Bitag.
Patibong.
Tahimik na lubid na unti-unting sumasakal.
Hindi nagsimula ang pagkawasak ni Zedekias nang bumagsak ang Jerusalem.
Matagal na siyang bihag sa loob.
At may mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam mismo ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Alam mong kinakausap ka na ng Diyos.
Pero takot kang mawalan ng mga tao.
Takot kang magbago.
Takot kang bitawan ang kasalanan.
Takot kang maging seryoso kay Cristo.
Kaya ginagawa mong lihim ang Diyos.
Lihim na panalangin.
Lihim na pag-iyak.
Lihim na conviction.
Iyan si Zedekias.
Paulit-ulit niyang hinahanap si Jeremias nang palihim habang tumatanggi pa ring lubusang sumunod sa Diyos.
At dumating ang araw na naubos ang oras.
Sinakop ng Babilonia ang Jerusalem.
Nasunog ang lungsod.
Nawasak ang templo.
Pinatay sa harap niya ang kaniyang mga anak.
Pagkatapos… binulag siya.
Ang huling nakita niya ay paghatol.
Napakasakit isipin na hindi sana iyon kailangang mangyari.
Hindi siya napahamak dahil wala siyang narinig na katotohanan.
Napahamak siya dahil paulit-ulit niyang narinig ang katotohanan… pero ipinagpaliban niya ang pagsunod.
At iyan ang isa sa pinaka-mapanganib na kondisyon ng kaluluwa.
Ang paulit-ulit na pakikinig sa katotohanan nang walang pagsunod ay nagpapatigas ng puso.
Sa Santiago 1:22, sinasabi sa Griyego:
Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ ἀκροαταὶ μόνον
“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.”
Ang salitang:
ἀκροαταὶ
“Akroatai.”
Ay tumutukoy sa mga tagapakinig lamang.
Nakikinig.
Nauunawaan.
Natatamaan.
Pero hindi sumusuko.
Maraming tao ngayon ang parang si Zedekias.
Mahilig sa conviction.
Mahilig sa sermons.
Mahilig sa truth posts.
Pero ayaw ng tunay na surrender.
Gusto nila ng comfort na walang repentance.
Blessing na walang holiness.
Encouragement na walang correction.
Pero ang tunay na Salita ng Diyos ay hindi lang nagbibigay-ginhawa.
Ito ay sumusugat upang magpagaling.
Sinasabi sa Hebreo 4:12:
“Sapagkat ang salita ng Diyos ay buhay at makapangyarihan, at higit na matalas kaysa alinmang tabak na may dalawang talim…”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “matalas” ay:
τομώτερος
“Tomoteros.”
Nangangahulugang tumatagos nang malalim.
Inilalantad ng Salita ng Diyos ang mga bagay na pilit nating itinatago.
Kaya lihim na hinahanap ni Zedekias si Jeremias.
Dahil nanginginig ang mga nakatagong bagay kapag dumadating ang katotohanan.
At marahil kaya ito tumatama nang malalim sa puso mo ngayon.
Dahil alam mo.
Alam mo kung ano ang matagal nang kinukumbinsi sa iyo ng Diyos.
Alam mo kung saan nagsimula ang compromise.
Alam mo kung anong kasalanan ang pilit mong dine-depensa.
Alam mo kung anong surrender ang iniiwasan mo.
Pero heto ang mabuting balita.
Handa pa ring magpatawad si Jesus.
Iyan ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo.
Patuloy na nagbabala ang Diyos dahil mahal Niya ang tao.
Hindi Kaniyang kagustuhan ang kapahamakan.
Sinasabi sa Ezekiel 33:11:
“Ako’y walang kaluguran sa kamatayan ng masama; kundi ang masama ay manumbalik…”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “manumbalik” ay:
שׁוּב
“Shuv.”
Bumalik.
Manumbalik.
Magbago ng direksyon.
Ito ang puso ng tunay na pagsisisi.
Hindi pagiging perpekto.
Kundi pagbabalik kay Diyos.
At dito lalong nagiging napakaganda si Cristo.
Kung saan nabigo si Zedekias… nagtagumpay si Jesus.
Natakot si Zedekias sa tao.
Pero si Jesus ay lubos na sumunod sa Ama.
Itinago ni Zedekias ang sarili mula sa katotohanan.
Pero sinabi ni Jesus:
“Ako ang katotohanan.”
Nabigo si Zedekias sa ilalim ng pressure.
Pero si Cristo ay nanatiling tapat hanggang kamatayan sa krus.
Ang Ebanghelyo ay hindi lang kuwento tungkol sa sinaunang hari.
Ito ay kuwento ng pagliligtas ng Diyos sa mga pusong unti-unti nang bumabagsak.
Si Jesus ang tumanggap ng hatol na para sana sa atin.
Sinasabi sa Isaias 53:5:
“Siya ay nasugatan dahil sa ating mga pagsalangsang…”
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “nasugatan” ay:
מְחֹלָל
“Mecholal.”
Tinusok.
Dinurog.
Sinugatan.
Si Cristo ang nasaktan upang makabalik ang mga makasalanan.
Kaya hindi kailangang magtapos ang kuwento mo gaya ng kay Zedekias.
Hindi mo kailangang manatiling lihim na naghahanap ng katotohanan habang patuloy na lumalaban sa Diyos.
Maaari kang sumuko kay Cristo ngayon.
Buo.
Totoo.
Walang pagtatago.
Dahil ang ipinagpapalibang pagsunod ay pagsuway pa rin.
Pero habang may hininga… may awa pa.
May mga taong isang katotohanan na lang ang layo mula sa pagsuko kay Jesus.
Balang araw… ang mga lihim na pakikipaglaban ng puso mo ay makikita rin sa direksyon ng buhay mo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Men of Jabesh-Gilead Risked Their Lives for Saul’s Body
paragraphs: Why the Men of Jabesh-Gilead Risked Their Lives for Saul’s Body
There are moments in Scripture that feel too human to be invented.
Moments where grief breathes.
Moments where loyalty bleeds.
Moments where broken men carry the weight of memory deeper than fear.
And buried in the ashes of Saul’s tragic downfall is one of the most emotionally devastating acts of courage in the entire Old Testament.
Not from mighty kings.
Not from prophets.
Not from armies.
But from forgotten men.
The men of Jabesh-Gilead.
Men who walked through the darkness of enemy territory… risking torture, execution, and humiliation… just to recover the mutilated body of a fallen king.
A king who had failed.
A king rejected by God.
A king who died in fear.
A king whose final chapter looked like disgrace.
Yet they still came for him.
And once you understand why… this story becomes one of the deepest pictures of covenant memory, gratitude, honor, redemption, and the terrifying cost of loyalty.
Most people read this account quickly.
But if you slow down long enough… it feels less like ancient history and more like the story of every person who has ever wondered:
“Will anybody still come for me after I fail?”
The story unfolds in 1 Samuel 31.
Israel has collapsed under Philistine attack.
Mount Gilboa has become a graveyard.
Saul’s sons are dead.
Jonathan is dead.
Israel’s first king has fallen by his own sword.
The Philistines strip Saul’s armor, cut off his head, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth-shan as public humiliation.
Scripture says:
“Then the valiant men arose and walked all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan; and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.”
— 1 Samuel 31:12
The Hebrew phrase for “valiant men” is:
חַיִל אִישׁ
Transliterated:
"ish chayil"
This does not merely mean brave men.
It carries the idea of men of strength, substance, valor, moral force, military courage, and noble character.
These were not reckless thrill-seekers.
These were men who understood exactly how dangerous this mission was.
Beth-shan was occupied by Philistines.
Saul’s body was displayed as a political trophy.
To retrieve it meant entering hostile territory under the cover of darkness.
One mistake meant death.
Yet they went anyway.
Why?
Because decades earlier… Saul had done something nobody else would do.
To understand Jabesh-Gilead’s loyalty, you must return to 1 Samuel 11.
Before Saul became corrupted by jealousy.
Before paranoia consumed him.
Before his rebellion against God.
Before David.
Before the madness.
There was a city crying for help.
Jabesh-Gilead.
Nahash the Ammonite surrounded the city and offered horrifying terms of surrender.
Scripture records his words:
“On this condition I will make a covenant with you, that I may thrust out all your right eyes, and bring reproach on all Israel.”
— 1 Samuel 11:2
The Hebrew expression here is deeply violent.
The phrase:
נְקֹר לָכֶם כָּל־עֵין יָמִין
"neqor lakhem kol-ein yamin"
Literally means:
“to gouge out every right eye.”
This was not random cruelty.
Ancient warfare understood the right eye as strategically important for combat because shields often protected the left side while the right eye guided attack.
Nahash was not merely threatening pain.
He was planning permanent humiliation and military crippling.
He wanted Israel weakened.
Disgraced.
Ashamed.
Powerless.
And no one came.
No tribe moved.
No army marched.
No savior appeared.
Until Saul heard.
Scripture says:
“And the Spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard those tidings, and his anger was kindled greatly.”
— 1 Samuel 11:6
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּצְלַח רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים
"vatitzlach ruach Elohim"
Meaning:
“The Spirit of God rushed powerfully upon him.”
This is important.
Because many only remember Saul’s collapse.
But there was a time when God genuinely empowered him.
A time when Saul fought for the helpless.
A time when Saul delivered the oppressed.
A time when Saul looked like the king Israel hoped for.
And Jabesh-Gilead never forgot.
Years passed.
Kings rise.
Kings fall.
People move on.
Crowds change allegiance.
But some people never forget the person who came for them when nobody else would.
That is what makes this story so emotionally devastating.
When Saul died… most of Israel ran.
But Jabesh-Gilead remembered.
Not the madness.
Not the spear-throwing.
Not the jealousy.
Not the rebellion.
They remembered mercy.
They remembered rescue.
