They remembered the day Saul saved their families from mutilation and shame.
And now the man who once rescued them hung publicly dishonored.
So they walked all night.
Imagine it.
No guarantee of survival.
No applause.
No reward.
No headlines.
Only gratitude.
Only loyalty.
Only honor.
There is something deeply Christlike hidden in this story.
Because the Gospel itself is the story of Someone who came for dishonored people.
The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 5:8:
The Greek phrase:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν
"eti hamartolon onton hemon"
Means:
“while we were still sinners.”
Not cleaned up.
Not fixed.
Not worthy.
Still sinners.
Jesus came for humanity while humanity was spiritually hanging on the wall of shame.
Exposed.
Broken.
Humiliated.
And this is why the story of Jabesh-Gilead grips the human heart.
Because every soul longs for someone who will still come after failure.
Someone who will not define us only by our worst chapter.
Saul’s life became tragic because partial obedience eventually becomes total destruction.
That is one of the terrifying theological truths of Saul’s story.
Delayed obedience is still disobedience.
Religious appearance without surrender eventually collapses.
Saul wanted kingdom benefits without fully submitting to God’s authority.
And many people today are trying to do the same.
They want the crown without repentance.
Anointing without obedience.
Blessing without surrender.
Public Christianity without private holiness.
But Saul’s story warns us that hidden rebellion eventually becomes public ruin.
Yet even in Saul’s collapse… grace flickers through the darkness.
Because God allowed men from Jabesh-Gilead to preserve Saul’s dignity after death.
That matters.
Deeply.
Even David later honors their actions.
In 2 Samuel 2:5, David says:
“Blessed be ye of the LORD, that ye have shewed this kindness unto your lord, even unto Saul, and have buried him.”
The Hebrew word for “kindness” here is:
חֶסֶד
"chesed"
One of the most powerful covenant words in the Old Testament.
It means steadfast love.
Loyal covenant mercy.
Faithful lovingkindness.
Sacrificial loyalty.
This was not ordinary kindness.
This was covenant remembrance.
The men of Jabesh-Gilead showed chesed.
And Scripture remembers them forever because of it.
There are people reading this right now who secretly believe their failures have erased every good thing God ever did through them.
You remember your collapse more than your calling.
Your shame more than your purpose.
Your weakness more than His mercy.
But one of the stunning truths of the Bible is that God tells stories honestly.
Scripture does not hide Noah’s drunkenness.
David’s adultery.
Peter’s denial.
Thomas’ doubt.
Moses’ anger.
Or Saul’s downfall.
Because the Bible is not propaganda.
It is revelation.
And revelation tells the truth about humanity.
The truth that all have sinned.
The truth that pride destroys.
The truth that unchecked flesh consumes.
But also the truth that God still moves toward broken people.
Some of the most dangerous spiritual words a person can say are:
“I’m too far gone.”
That is not humility.
That is unbelief.
The cross already settled how far God is willing to go to rescue sinners.
In Aramaic, one of the cries associated with Jesus on the cross is:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לְמָא שְׁבַקְתַּנִי
"Eli, Eli, lama shabaqtani"
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Matthew 27:46 preserves this cry because heaven wanted humanity to understand the cost of redemption.
Jesus entered abandonment so sinners could enter reconciliation.
He entered shame so believers could receive righteousness.
He entered death so humanity could receive eternal life.
And unlike Saul… Christ is the King who never failed.
The perfect King.
The righteous King.
The obedient King.
The resurrected King.
The King who does not merely rescue Jabesh-Gilead.
He rescues the world.
This is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Not behavior modification.
Heart transformation.
Not religious cosmetics.
Total surrender.
Somebody reading this has been carrying hidden shame for years.
You smile publicly.
But privately you feel spiritually nailed to the wall.
Exposed.
Disgraced.
Haunted.
You wonder if anybody would still come for you if people knew the whole story.
But Jesus specializes in walking into impossible places to recover what looked lost forever.
That is who He is.
That is what He does.
And this article is not an accident.
God may be confronting something buried deep inside you right now.
The exhaustion.
The compromise.
The hidden addiction.
The bitterness.
The double life.
The spiritual numbness.
The secret despair.
The performance.
The pretending.
You can keep hiding.
Or you can surrender.
One path leads deeper into darkness.
The other leads to Christ.
And only one of those paths ends in life.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Your honesty may become the testimony that helps somebody else return to God.
And if this article reminded you of someone struggling silently… share this with them.
Some people only love you while you are winning.
Jesus loved you knowing every chapter you would fail.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Isinugal ng mga Lalaki ng Jabesh-Gilead ang Kanilang Buhay Para sa Bangkay ni Saul
May mga bahagi ang Biblia na parang hindi gawa-gawa lamang.
Mga tagpong humihinga ang dalamhati.
Mga tagpong dumudugo ang katapatan.
Mga tagpong may mga lalaking pasan ang bigat ng alaala nang higit pa sa kanilang takot.
At sa gitna ng madilim na pagbagsak ni Haring Saul… may isang kwento ng katapangan na halos hindi nabibigyan ng sapat na pansin.
Hindi ito kwento ng mga propeta.
Hindi ito kwento ng mga hari.
Hindi ito kwento ng mga tanyag na mandirigma.
Ito ay kwento ng mga lalaking hindi nakalimot.
Mga lalaki mula sa Jabesh-Gilead.
Mga lalaking naglakad sa dilim… tumawid sa teritoryo ng kaaway… handang mamatay… para lamang kunin ang katawan ng isang bagsak na hari.
Isang haring nabigo.
Isang haring itinakwil ng Diyos.
Isang haring namatay sa takot.
Isang haring ang huling kabanata ay puno ng kahihiyan.
Pero pinuntahan pa rin nila siya.
At kapag naunawaan mo kung bakit… mararamdaman mong hindi lang ito kasaysayan.
Parang kwento ito ng bawat taong natatakot na baka wala nang babalik para sa kanila pagkatapos nilang magkamali.
Nagsimula ang lahat sa 1 Samuel 31.
Natalo ang Israel.
Naging sementeryo ang Bundok Gilboa.
Patay ang mga anak ni Saul.
Patay si Jonathan.
At ang unang hari ng Israel ay bumagsak sa sarili niyang espada.
Pagkatapos noon, pinutol ng mga Filisteo ang ulo ni Saul at isinabit ang kanyang katawan sa pader ng Beth-shan bilang pampublikong kahihiyan.
Pero may nangyari sa gabi.
Sinasabi ng Kasulatan:
“Lahat ng magigiting na lalaki ay tumindig at naglakad buong gabi, at kinuha ang bangkay ni Saul at ang mga bangkay ng kanyang mga anak mula sa pader ng Beth-shan.”
— 1 Samuel 31:12
Sa Hebrew, ang salitang ginamit para sa “magigiting na lalaki” ay:
חַיִל אִישׁ
"ish chayil"
Hindi lang ito simpleng “matapang.”
Ibig sabihin nito ay mga lalaking may dangal, lakas ng loob, moral na tibay, at tapang na handang mamatay para sa tama.
Alam nila ang panganib.
Alam nilang maaaring hulihin sila.
Maaaring patayin.
Maaaring pahirapan.
Pero pumunta pa rin sila.
Bakit?
Dahil maraming taon bago bumagsak si Saul… siya ang taong dumating para iligtas sila noong walang ibang gustong tumulong.
Bumalik tayo sa 1 Samuel 11.
Bago pa nasira si Saul ng inggit.
Bago siya nilamon ng kayabangan.
Bago siya naging suwail sa Diyos.
Napapalibutan noon ang Jabesh-Gilead ng mga Ammonita.
At ang kanilang hari na si Nahash ay nagbigay ng nakakakilabot na kondisyon:
“Papayag lang ako kung bubunutin ko ang kanang mata ng bawat isa sa inyo.”
— 1 Samuel 11:2
Sa Hebrew:
נְקֹר לָכֶם כָּל־עֵין יָמִין
"neqor lakhem kol-ein yamin"
Literal na ibig sabihin:
“dukutin ang bawat kanang mata.”
Hindi ito simpleng kalupitan.
Plano nitong pahinain ang Israel.
Pahiyain sila.
Gawing inutil sa pakikipagdigma.
At walang tumulong.
Walang tribo ang kumilos.
Walang hukbo ang dumating.
Hanggang marinig ito ni Saul.
Sinasabi ng Biblia:
“At sumakanya ang Espiritu ng Diyos nang may kapangyarihan.”
— 1 Samuel 11:6
Sa Hebrew:
וַתִּצְלַח רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים
"vatitzlach ruach Elohim"
Ibig sabihin:
“Makapangyarihang dumating sa kanya ang Espiritu ng Diyos.”
Mahalagang maintindihan ito.
Dahil maraming tao ang si Saul lang na bumagsak ang naaalala.
Pero may panahon na tunay siyang ginamit ng Diyos.
May panahon na ipinaglaban niya ang mahihina.
May panahon na iniligtas niya ang mga desperado.
At hindi iyon nakalimutan ng Jabesh-Gilead.
Lumipas ang mga taon.
Nagbago ang mga tao.
Nagbago ang pulitika.
Nagbago ang katapatan ng marami.
Pero may mga taong hindi nakakalimot sa taong dumating para sa kanila noong wala nang iba.
Kaya nang mamatay si Saul… habang tumatakbo ang iba… may mga lalaking naglakad papunta sa panganib.
Hindi nila naalala ang kabaliwan ni Saul.
Hindi nila naalala ang pagseselos niya kay David.
Hindi nila naalala ang kanyang pagbagsak.
Naalala nila ang awa.
Naalala nila ang pagliligtas.
Naalala nila ang araw na may isang hari na tumayo para sa kanila.
At ngayon… ang haring iyon ay nakasabit sa pader sa kahihiyan.
Kaya pumunta sila.
Buong gabi.
Walang kasiguraduhan kung mabubuhay pa sila.
Walang papuri.
Walang gantimpala.
Kundi utang na loob.
Katapatan.
Pagmamahal.
At may mas malalim pang dahilan kung bakit napakalakas ng kwentong ito.
Dahil larawan ito ng Ebanghelyo.
Tayong lahat ay parang si Saul.
Mga taong bumagsak.
Mga taong may kahihiyan.
Mga taong may kasalanang hindi maitago.
At si Jesus ang Hari na dumating para kunin tayo mula sa espirituwal na kahihiyan.
Sinasabi sa Roma 5:8:
“Subalit ipinakita ng Diyos ang Kanyang pag-ibig sa atin, na noong tayo’y makasalanan pa, si Cristo ay namatay para sa atin.”
Sa Greek:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν
"eti hamartolon onton hemon"
Ibig sabihin:
“habang makasalanan pa tayo.”
Hindi noong maayos na tayo.
Hindi noong banal na tayo.
Hindi noong karapat-dapat na tayo.
Habang makasalanan pa tayo.
Iyan ang klase ng pag-ibig ni Cristo.
Maraming tao ang naniniwalang ang kanilang pagkakamali ang katapusan ng kanilang kwento.
Pero ang Biblia ay paulit-ulit na nagpapatunay na ang Diyos ay lumalapit pa rin sa mga wasak.
Si Pedro ay itinanggi si Jesus.
Si David ay nagkasala nang malalim.
Si Tomas ay nagduda.
Si Moises ay nagalit.
At si Saul ay bumagsak.
Pero ipinapakita ng Kasulatan ang katotohanan dahil ang Biblia ay hindi propaganda.
Ito ay rebelasyon.
At ang rebelasyon ay nagsasabi ng katotohanan tungkol sa tao.
Na lahat tayo ay makasalanan.
Na kayang sirain ng pride ang tao.
Na ang lihim na rebelyon ay nagiging pampublikong pagkawasak.
Pero ipinapakita rin nito na mas malalim ang biyaya ng Diyos kaysa kasalanan ng tao.
May taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod na.
Pagod nang magpanggap.
Pagod nang ngumiti habang wasak sa loob.
Pagod nang magtago.
At baka pakiramdam mo… kapag nalaman ng tao ang totoo tungkol sa iyo… wala nang babalik para iligtas ka.
Pero si Jesus ay espesyalista sa paglapit sa mga lugar na puno ng kahihiyan.
Hindi Siya natatakot sa wasak.
Hindi Siya umatras sa makasalanan.
Hindi Siya lumayo sa sugatan.
Siya ang Hari na bumababa para kunin ang mga nawawala.
At baka hindi aksidente na binabasa mo ito ngayon.
Baka kinakausap ka ng Diyos.
Baka may bagay na matagal mo nang tinatago.
Ang lihim na kasalanan.
Ang addiction.
Ang galit.
Ang spiritual numbness.
Ang doble buhay.
Ang depresyon.
Ang pagod.
Ang guilt.
At ngayon… tinatawag ka ni Cristo na sumuko.
Hindi para husgahan ka.
Kundi para iligtas ka.
Maging tapat ka.
Mas tumama ito kaysa inaasahan mo.
Ang testimony mo ay maaaring maging dahilan para may isang taong bumalik kay Jesus.
May mga taong mahal ka lang kapag malakas ka.
Pero minahal ka ni Jesus kahit alam Niya lahat ng pagbagsak mo.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Abraham
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Abraham
There are some people in Scripture whose names became so familiar that we accidentally stopped feeling their humanity.
Abraham is one of them.
We say “father of faith” so often that we forget he once stood in the middle of a dark night wondering if God had abandoned him.
We quote his obedience while ignoring the terror inside it.
We celebrate the promise while skipping over the silence.
But the untold story of Abraham is not just about a man who believed God.
It is about a broken human being who kept walking even when heaven felt painfully quiet.
And maybe that is why his story still shakes souls thousands of years later.
Because deep down, many people are still living in Ur.
Still trapped. Still afraid. Still successful externally while spiritually starving internally. Still hearing whispers from God while pretending not to.
The first mention of Abraham does not even begin with greatness.
It begins with interruption.
Genesis 12:1 says:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee.”
The Hebrew phrase for “Get thee out” is:
לֶךְ־לְךָ
Transliterated:
Lech-Lecha
This phrase carries deeper meaning than most English translations reveal.
It does not merely mean “leave.”
It carries the idea:
“Go for yourself.” “Go toward your true self.” “Go into the purpose I created for you.”
God was not only calling Abraham away from a location.
He was calling him away from the false version of himself.
Away from inherited idols. Away from familiar chains. Away from generational patterns. Away from comfort. Away from predictable living.
And some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Because God has been disturbing your comfort lately.
You cannot enjoy the sin the same way anymore. You cannot fit into the old conversations anymore. You cannot ignore conviction anymore.
Something inside you has been hearing:
“Leave.”
Leave the bitterness. Leave the compromise. Leave the secret addiction. Leave the lukewarm Christianity. Leave the version of yourself that survives without surrender.
And the terrifying part is this:
God did not initially tell Abraham where he was going.
Hebrews 11:8 says:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Not knowing.
That phrase destroys modern Christianity.
Because most people want guarantees before obedience.
But biblical faith has always moved before explanations arrived.
Abraham walked with incomplete details.
And honestly, that is where many believers lose their courage.
Because uncertainty exposes whether we truly trust God or merely trust outcomes.
Some of the deepest faith seasons are not loud miracles.
They are quiet obedience.
The untold story of Abraham is filled with waiting.
Years. Decades. Silence.
God promised him descendants while Sarah’s womb remained empty.
Imagine the emotional warfare.
Every birthday becoming another reminder. Every gray hair screaming impossibility. Every month ending in disappointment.
And yet God had said:
“So shall thy seed be.”
Genesis 15 records one of the rawest moments in Scripture.
Abraham looks into the heavens while God speaks about descendants more numerous than stars.
The Hebrew says:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
Vehe’emin BaYHWH
“And he believed in the LORD.”
The Hebrew word here for “believed” comes from:
אָמַן
Aman
The same root where we get “Amen.”
It means:
To support. To uphold. To lean the full weight upon.
Abraham’s faith was not intellectual agreement.
It was collapsing his full weight onto God when everything visible contradicted the promise.
That changes everything.
Real faith is not pretending doubts do not exist.
Real faith is choosing to lean on God while doubts scream in your face.
And Abraham did struggle.
Scripture does not hide his failures.
He lied. He doubted. He tried to manufacture God’s promise through Hagar. He made fearful decisions.
The Bible never sanitizes its heroes.
Because the point was never human perfection.
The point was God’s faithfulness.
One of the most misunderstood parts of Abraham’s story is the covenant in Genesis 15.
Most people miss how shocking this moment really was.
In ancient covenant rituals, animals were split in half and both parties walked between the pieces, symbolizing:
“If I break this covenant, let this happen to me.”
But in Genesis 15, Abraham falls into deep sleep.
And only God passes through.
A smoking furnace. A burning lamp.
God alone walked the covenant path.
Why does that matter?
Because God knew Abraham would fail.
And yet He still bound Himself to the promise.
That is grace.
The covenant rested ultimately on God’s faithfulness, not Abraham’s perfection.
Somebody reading this has been drowning in shame because you think your failures disqualified you.
But Abraham’s story proves something powerful:
God already knew your weakness before He called you.
He was never shocked by your humanity.
This does not excuse sin.
But it destroys the lie that grace belongs only to flawless people.
Then came the waiting.
Long waiting.
Some theologians estimate nearly 25 years between the promise and Isaac’s birth.
Twenty-five years.
Most people cannot endure twenty-five minutes of silence anymore.
But God develops giants in hidden seasons.
The name change itself carried prophetic weight.
Abram:
אַבְרָם
“Exalted father.”
Abraham:
אַבְרָהָם
“Father of many.”
God changed his identity before changing his circumstances.
And sometimes God speaks to who you are becoming before your life visibly reflects it.
That process feels painful.
Because heaven will call you healed while you are still bleeding. Heaven will call you chosen while you still feel rejected. Heaven will call you free while chains are still falling off.
Then Isaac finally arrives.
The miracle child.
The laughter after decades of tears.
The promise fulfilled.
And then comes Genesis 22.
The chapter that leaves many people emotionally shaken.
“Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest…”
The Hebrew phrase “whom thou lovest” is:
אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ
Asher-Ahavta
“The one you love deeply.”
This is the first explicit mention of love in the Bible.
And it appears in the context of surrender.
Not romance. Not pleasure. Not comfort.
Surrender.
That is breathtaking.
God asked Abraham to place even the promise itself on the altar.
Because gifts can never become idols.
Not even sacred gifts.
Some people idolize relationships. Others idolize ministry. Others idolize success. Others idolize dreams God Himself gave them.
But Abraham’s test revealed whether he loved God more than what God provided.
The mountain was never about child sacrifice.
God had already condemned pagan child sacrifice elsewhere in Scripture.
The deeper revelation was prophetic.
Abraham tells Isaac:
“God will provide himself a lamb.”
In Hebrew:
אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה
Elohim Yir’eh-Lo HaSeh
This becomes connected to:
יְהוָה יִרְאֶה
YHWH Yireh
“Jehovah Jireh”
Often translated:
“The Lord will provide.”
But the Hebrew idea is even richer.
It literally carries the sense:
“The Lord will see.” “The Lord will see ahead.” “The Lord will foresee the need before it arrives.”
God already had provision waiting on the mountain Abraham feared.
And many believers need to hear this today:
The ram was already prepared before Abraham climbed the mountain.
God’s provision is not panic response.
He already sees tomorrow.
The untold story of Abraham ultimately points beyond Abraham.
It points to Christ.
A beloved son. A father willing to surrender. A mountain. Wood carried upward. A substitute provided.
Genesis whispers the Gospel long before Calvary arrived.
Jesus Himself said in John 8:56:
“Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.”
Even Abraham’s journey was ultimately pointing toward redemption through Jesus Christ.
And maybe the reason Abraham’s story still grips hearts is because we see ourselves in it.
We know what it feels like to wait.
To fear. To fail. To wonder. To obey while trembling. To carry promises through painful seasons. To wrestle between faith and visible reality.
The untold story of Abraham is not the story of a fearless man.
It is the story of a man who kept moving toward God despite fear.
That changes everything.
Because many people secretly think faith means never struggling.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals something different.
Faithful people still cry. Faithful people still wrestle. Faithful people still ask questions. Faithful people still collapse emotionally.
Yet they keep returning to God.
And maybe that is you right now.
Maybe you are in a season where God feels silent.
Maybe the promise feels delayed. Maybe your heart is exhausted. Maybe you feel disqualified because of your failures. Maybe you have secretly wondered whether God forgot you.
Abraham’s story still answers across generations:
God is faithful even in the waiting.
Not one promise of God has ever died because human weakness existed.
And the greatest promise was never land, descendants, or earthly blessing.
The greatest promise was Jesus.
Galatians 3 reveals that ultimately the covenant pointed toward Christ through whom all nations would be blessed.
The Gospel was hidden inside Abraham’s story from the beginning.
That means your story can also become redemption territory.
Your failures are not the final sentence. Your waiting is not wasted. Your wilderness is not proof of abandonment.
God still calls broken people. Still transforms wandering hearts. Still restores ruined lives. Still writes impossible stories.
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment you needed it.
Not accidentally.
Because there are people reading this who have been smiling publicly while silently collapsing internally.
People exhausted from pretending. People tired of carrying hidden pain. People wondering whether God could still use them.
Abraham’s story says yes.
Not because humans are strong.
But because God remains faithful.
Be honest. This reached deeper than information.
Some mountains are actually places where God reveals who He has always been.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikuwentong Bahagi ng Buhay ni Abraham
May mga tao sa Bibliya na sobrang madalas nating marinig ang pangalan kaya nakalimutan na nating tao rin pala sila.
Isa na roon si Abraham.
Madalas natin siyang tawaging “ama ng pananampalataya,” pero bihira nating isipin na may mga gabi ring halos mawalan siya ng pag-asa.
Pinupuri natin ang kanyang pagsunod, pero hindi natin nararamdaman ang takot na kasama noon.
Ikinukuwento natin ang pangako ng Diyos, pero nilalampasan natin ang mahabang katahimikan sa pagitan.
At baka iyon ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon, tinatamaan pa rin ng kuwento ni Abraham ang puso ng tao.
Dahil marami pa ring tao ang parang nasa “Ur.”
Nakakulong. Takot. Mukhang maayos sa labas pero wasak sa loob. Naririnig ang tawag ng Diyos pero nagpapanggap na hindi.
Nagsimula ang kuwento ni Abraham hindi sa tagumpay.
Nagsimula ito sa pagputol ng Diyos sa dati niyang buhay.
Genesis 12:1:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country…”
Sa Hebrew:
לֶךְ־לְךָ
Lech-Lecha
Hindi lang ito simpleng “umalis ka.”
Mas malalim ang ibig sabihin.
“Humayo ka para sa tunay mong pagkatao.” “Lumakad ka patungo sa layunin ko para sa’yo.”
Hindi lang si Abraham pinapaalis ng Diyos sa isang lugar.
Pinapaalis siya ng Diyos sa lumang bersyon ng sarili niya.
Sa maling identidad. Sa nakasanayang kasalanan. Sa mga bagay na humahadlang sa tawag ng Diyos.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na nakakaramdam din niyan.
Hindi mo na ma-enjoy ang dati mong kasalanan. Hindi ka na mapalagay sa dati mong buhay. May bumabagabag sa puso mo.
At paulit-ulit mong naririnig:
“Umalis ka.”
Umalis ka sa lihim na kasalanan. Umalis ka sa pagpapanggap. Umalis ka sa pagiging malamig sa Diyos. Umalis ka sa buhay na walang surrender.
At ang pinakamahirap?
Hindi agad sinabi ng Diyos kay Abraham kung saan siya dadalhin.
Hebrews 11:8:
“…and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Hindi niya alam.
At doon nasusubok ang totoong pananampalataya.
Dahil karamihan gusto muna ng kasiguruhan bago sumunod.
Pero ang totoong faith sa Bibliya, sumusunod muna bago makita ang buong plano.
Lumakad si Abraham kahit kulang ang detalye.
At maraming Kristiyano ang bumibigay dito.
Kapag tahimik ang langit. Kapag delayed ang pangako. Kapag hindi malinaw ang susunod.
Pero doon madalas gumagawa ng malalalim na tao ang Diyos.
Sa paghihintay.
Matagal naghintay si Abraham.
Taon. Dekada.
Habang tumatanda si Sarah. Habang parang imposibleng mangyari ang pangako.
Pero sinabi pa rin ng Diyos:
“So shall thy seed be.”
Genesis 15:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
Vehe’emin BaYHWH
“And he believed in the LORD.”
Ang salitang “believed” ay mula sa Hebrew na:
אָמַן
Aman
Dito rin nanggaling ang salitang “Amen.”
Ibig sabihin:
Buong bigat mong sumandal.
Hindi lang intellectual agreement.
Si Abraham sumandal sa Diyos kahit mukhang imposible ang lahat.
Iyon ang totoong pananampalataya.
Hindi kawalan ng takot.
Kundi pagpili sa Diyos kahit may takot.
At oo, nagkamali rin si Abraham.
Nagsinungaling siya. Nagduda siya. Sinubukan niyang tulungan ang pangako ng Diyos sa pamamagitan ni Hagar.
Hindi tinatago ng Bibliya ang kahinaan ng mga bayani nito.
Dahil ang bida talaga ay hindi si Abraham.
Ang bida ay ang katapatan ng Diyos.
Isa sa pinakamalalim na bahagi ng kuwento niya ay Genesis 15.
Sa covenant noon, parehong dadaan ang dalawang partido sa pagitan ng hinating hayop bilang simbolo:
“Kapag sinira ko ang kasunduang ito, mangyari rin sana ito sa akin.”
Pero sa kuwento ni Abraham, nakatulog siya.
At Diyos lang ang dumaan.
Ibig sabihin?
Alam na ng Diyos na magkakamali si Abraham.
Pero pinili pa rin Siyang maging tapat.
Iyan ang grasya.
May nagbabasa nito ngayon na pakiramdam disqualified ka na dahil sa failures mo.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Hindi nagulat ang Diyos sa kahinaan mo.
Alam na Niya lahat bago ka pa Niya tawagin.
Hindi excuse ang kasalanan.
Pero patunay ito na ang grasya ay para sa mga sirang tao.
At pagkatapos ng mahabang paghihintay, dumating si Isaac.
Ang anak ng pangako.
Ang himala pagkatapos ng maraming luha.
Pero pagkatapos noon, dumating ang pinakamabigat na pagsubok.
Genesis 22.
“Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest…”
Sa Hebrew:
אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ
Asher-Ahavta
“Ang anak na mahal na mahal mo.”
Nakakagulat na ang unang malinaw na paggamit ng salitang “love” sa Bibliya ay konektado sa surrender.
Hindi romance. Hindi comfort.
Kundi pagsuko.
Hiniling ng Diyos kay Abraham na ilagay maging ang pangako sa altar.
Dahil kahit ang mga biyaya ng Diyos puwedeng maging idolo.
May mga taong ginagawang diyos ang relasyon. Ang iba career. Ang iba ministry. Ang iba pangarap.
Pero ipinakita ng Diyos kay Abraham:
Walang dapat mas mahal kaysa sa Diyos mismo.
At habang paakyat sila ng bundok, sinabi ni Abraham:
“God will provide himself a lamb.”
Sa Hebrew:
יְהוָה יִרְאֶה
YHWH Yireh
Jehovah Jireh.
Madalas itong isalin bilang:
“The Lord will provide.”
Pero mas malalim pa roon.
“The Lord will see ahead.”
Nakikita na ng Diyos ang pangangailangan mo bago pa ito dumating.
Nakahanda na ang lalaking tupang ipapalit kay Isaac bago pa sila umakyat ng bundok.
At baka may kailangang makarinig nito ngayon:
Hindi nahuhuli ang provision ng Diyos.
Nakikita na Niya ang bukas mo.
Ang buong kuwento ni Abraham ay tumuturo kay Jesus.
Isang minamahal na anak. Isang ama. Isang bundok. Kahoy na pasan. Isang kapalit na handog.
Mula pa Genesis, bumubulong na ang Ebanghelyo.
At baka kaya malalim tumama ang kuwento ni Abraham dahil nakikita natin ang sarili natin sa kanya.
Takot. Paghihintay. Pagkabigo. Pagdududa. Pagod.
Pero patuloy pa ring lumalakad papunta sa Diyos.
At baka ikaw iyon ngayon.
Pagod ka na. Tahimik ang langit. Pakiramdam mo delayed ang pangako. Pakiramdam mo hindi ka na magagamit ng Diyos.
Pero sumisigaw pa rin ang kuwento ni Abraham:
Tapat pa rin ang Diyos.
Hindi pa tapos ang kuwento mo.
At ang pinakamagandang pangako ng Diyos ay hindi lupa o kayamanan.
Si Jesus.
Siya ang katuparan. Siya ang pag-asa. Siya ang dahilan kung bakit may redemption pa.
Maging totoo ka. Mas malalim ito kaysa simpleng article.
May mga bundok na akala mo katapusan mo, pero doon pala ipapakilala ng Diyos kung sino talaga Siya.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Should Christians Celebrate Christmas?
paragraphs:
Should Christians Celebrate Christmas?
The Question That Has Divided Homes, Churches, and Hearts for Generations
Some believers whisper it quietly because they are afraid of being judged.
Others preach about it loudly like they alone discovered hidden truth.
Some families decorate trees while singing worship songs to Jesus.
Other families throw every ornament away, convinced Christmas dishonors God.
And somewhere in the middle of all the noise…
there are exhausted Christians sitting in silence wondering:
“Am I offending God if I celebrate Christmas?”
That question is not small.
Because nobody who truly loves Jesus wants to accidentally dishonor Him.
Nobody wants to stand before God one day and discover they turned holy worship into empty tradition.
But at the same time…
many believers also fear becoming cold, legalistic, joyless, suspicious of everything beautiful, and disconnected from the very heart of the Gospel.
So what is the truth?
Should Christians celebrate Christmas?
Or has the modern Church inherited a tradition that God never wanted?
The answer requires honesty.
Not emotional reactions.
Not conspiracy videos.
Not cultural pressure.
Not nostalgia.
Not internet rage.
Truth.
Biblical truth.
Historical truth.
Spiritual truth.
And maybe…
before this article ends…
you may realize this conversation was never ultimately about trees, lights, gifts, or December 25.
It was always about the condition of the human heart.
Because people can reject Christmas and still reject Christ.
And people can celebrate Christmas while never truly knowing Jesus.
That is the terrifying part.
The Apostle Paul warned Timothy that in the last days people would have “a form of godliness” while denying its power.
External appearance.
No transformed heart.
Religious performance.
No surrender.
And honestly…
that danger exists on both sides of this argument.
Some worship culture.
Others worship being “right.”
Both can miss Jesus.
The Hebrew word often translated as “heart” is לֵב (lev).
Not merely emotions.
The center of will.
Mind.
Desire.
Identity.
God has always been after the lev.
Not empty rituals.
Not performative religion.
Not self-righteousness.
Not spiritual pride.
When the prophet Samuel looked at Eliab and assumed he looked kingly, God responded:
“Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”
The Hebrew there again points toward the lev.
The inner person.
The hidden self.
That changes everything.
Because before we ask whether Christians should celebrate Christmas…
we must first ask:
Why are we doing anything at all?
To honor Christ?
To imitate culture?
To feel included?
To prove superiority?
To appear spiritually deeper than others?
To make memories with family?
To preach the Gospel?
Motives matter deeply to God.
The Greek word Jesus often used when confronting religious hypocrisy was ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs).
Originally it referred to actors.
Performers.
People wearing masks.
That should unsettle every believer reading this.
Because it is possible to condemn Christmas publicly while privately living in pride, bitterness, gossip, lust, greed, and unforgiveness.
And it is equally possible to celebrate Christmas while genuinely loving Jesus with sincerity and truth.
So let us walk carefully.
Not emotionally.
Biblically.
Historically.
Honestly.
One of the most common arguments against Christmas is this:
“Jesus was not born on December 25.”
That statement is almost certainly true.
Scripture never gives an exact birth date for Christ.
Many historians believe Jesus was likely born during a different season based on shepherd activity described in Luke 2.
So if December 25 is not His actual birthday… does that automatically make Christmas sinful?
Not necessarily.
The Bible never commands believers to celebrate Christ’s birth.
But the Bible also never forbids remembering and honoring the incarnation.
That distinction matters.
Very deeply.
The incarnation is one of the greatest miracles in human history.
God entering human flesh.
The eternal stepping into time.
The Creator entering creation.
The invisible becoming visible.
The Gospel of John says:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
The Greek says:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
(Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.)
“The Word became flesh.”
Not symbolic flesh.
Not partial humanity.
Real humanity.
Real tears.
Real exhaustion.
Real suffering.
Real blood.
Real nails.
Real death.
That is staggering.
The word λόγος (logos) carries immense depth.
Reason.
Divine expression.
Ultimate revelation.
Jesus was not merely a teacher sent by God.
He is God revealed.
And whether someone remembers that reality in December, April, or July…
the incarnation itself remains holy.
Some believers argue Christmas has pagan roots.
This is where careful truth matters more than sensationalism.
Yes, certain winter festivals existed in pagan cultures before Christian observances of Christmas became formalized.
Yes, some traditions later attached themselves culturally to Christmas celebrations.
Yes, many modern practices today are commercialized and worldly.
But Christians must be careful not to oversimplify history.
Having historical overlap does not automatically make every practice pagan worship.
If that standard were applied consistently, many aspects of modern life would become impossible to use.
Wedding rings existed in pagan cultures.
Names of weekdays have pagan associations.
Buildings, calendars, customs, architecture, and civic traditions across the world contain historical layers from various civilizations.
The issue is not merely historical origin.
The issue is present worship.
In Scripture, God repeatedly condemns syncretism.
That means mixing the worship of Yahweh with false gods.
Israel constantly fell into this trap.
They wanted God…
and idols.
Holiness…
and compromise.
Truth…
and surrounding culture.
That danger absolutely still exists today.
A Christmas celebration centered entirely around greed, drunkenness, vanity, lust, materialism, and self-indulgence does not honor Christ.
Not because trees are evil.
But because the human heart drifts easily.
Very easily.
The prophet Isaiah warned:
“These people honor Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.”
That warning reaches across generations.
A person can sing worship songs while spiritually numb.
Buy Christian decorations while secretly addicted to pornography.
Post Bible verses online while refusing to forgive people in private.
Appear holy publicly while decaying internally.
Christmas cannot save anyone.
Only Christ can.
And maybe this is where many believers become convicted.
Because sometimes the debate about Christmas becomes a distraction from the deeper issue:
Have we actually surrendered to Jesus?
Not admired Him.
Not quoted Him.
Not debated theology online.
Surrendered.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a transformed mind.
A turning.
A change of inner direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
Judas felt guilt.
Repentance changes allegiance.
And honestly…
many Christians arguing online about Christmas have never truly experienced deep metanoia.
That is why conversations become toxic.
Harsh.
Proud.
Cold.
Cruel.
Unteachable.
Jesus said the world would know His disciples by their love.
Not by their seasonal debates.
Love does not mean abandoning truth.
But truth without love becomes a weapon.
Paul wrote in Romans 14 about disputable matters among believers.
Some esteemed certain days.
Others did not.
Paul did not command uniformity in every non-salvation issue.
Instead he emphasized conviction before God.
He wrote:
“One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.”
That passage matters enormously in this conversation.
Because Scripture does not present Christmas observance as a salvation issue.
A believer who celebrates Christmas unto Christ is not automatically rebelling against God.
And a believer who abstains from Christmas to honor God is not automatically legalistic.
The issue becomes sinful when pride, judgment, condemnation, arrogance, hatred, or hypocrisy enter the picture.
Paul continued:
“Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?”
That should humble everyone.
Especially social media theology warriors.
Especially believers addicted to outrage.
Especially Christians who feel spiritually superior because they discovered information others have not.
Knowledge alone does not produce holiness.
Satan knows Scripture.
Transformation requires surrender.
The enemy loves when Christians become obsessed with secondary arguments while neglecting prayer, holiness, evangelism, forgiveness, discipleship, purity, and obedience.
Think about it carefully.
If Satan cannot destroy the Church externally…
he often distracts it internally.
Endless arguments.
Division.
Suspicion.
Pride.
Accusation.
No fruit.
No brokenness.
No compassion.
No evangelism.
No intimacy with God.
Just noise.
And the world watches.
Meanwhile millions are depressed.
Addicted.
Suicidal.
Spiritually lost.
Terrified.
Fatherless.
Numb.
Hopeless.
People are not desperately searching for Christians who can merely win arguments.
They are searching for people who genuinely carry the presence of Jesus.
People whose lives look transformed.
People who radiate grace and truth.
People whose peace cannot be explained naturally.
People who forgive when wounded.
People who repent quickly.
People who love deeply.
People who refuse compromise.
People who are alive spiritually.
That is rare now.
Very rare.
Some believers reading this grew up with traumatic Christmas experiences.
Abuse.
Alcoholism.
Family division.
Financial pressure.
Loneliness.
Broken homes.
Loss.
For some people, Christmas does not feel joyful.
It feels painful.
Heavy.
Haunted.
And God sees that too.
The Psalms repeatedly reveal a God attentive to human suffering.
The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) means more than peace.
Wholeness.
Restoration.
Completeness.
The Messiah came to restore shattered things.
Not merely create religious holidays.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful opportunities during Christmas is this:
pointing hurting people toward the true source of shalom.
Jesus.
Not commercialism.
Not temporary emotion.
Not expensive gifts.
Not social status.
Christ.
The Savior born into poverty.
Wrapped in cloth.
Placed in a feeding trough.
Rejected by many.
Worshiped by some.
Eventually crucified for sinners.
Including us.
Especially us.
The angel announced in Luke 2:
“Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people.”
The Greek phrase μεγάλην χαρὰν (megalēn charan) means great joy.
Not shallow happiness.
Not emotional hype.
Deep joy rooted in divine rescue.
Because humanity needed saving.
Still does.
Nothing about Christmas matters if Jesus is reduced to decoration.
Nothing.
Not nativity scenes.
Not songs.
Not candles.
Not church attendance.
Not aesthetics.
Not tradition.
If Christ is absent from the heart…
everything becomes empty religion.
But when Christ truly becomes central…
even ordinary moments become holy.
Families praying together.
Repentance around dinner tables.
Forgiveness between estranged relatives.
Scripture being read aloud.
Children learning about Jesus.
The lonely being invited in.
The poor being helped.
The Gospel being preached.
That honors God.
Deeply.
Some Christians avoid Christmas because of conscience.
Romans 14 protects that conscience.
They should not be mocked.
Others celebrate Christmas sincerely unto Christ.
They should not be condemned.
But every believer should examine themselves honestly.
Is Jesus truly Lord of my life?
Or have I built a version of Christianity centered around appearance?
Because outward separation from holidays does not automatically equal holiness.
And outward celebration does not automatically equal compromise.
God sees deeper than behavior.
He sees the lev.
The heart.
The hidden motives.
The private life.
The secret thoughts.
The desires nobody else sees.
That should sober every one of us.
There is another uncomfortable truth many avoid.
Some people reject Christmas passionately…
but never preach the Gospel passionately.
They expose traditions.
But never expose sin.
They attack symbols.
But never call people to repentance.
They study controversy.
But rarely demonstrate Christlike love.
That imbalance reveals something serious.
Jesus did not command His disciples to become experts in seasonal arguments.
He commanded them to make disciples.
To preach repentance.
To care for the poor.
To love one another.
To deny themselves.
To take up their cross.
To follow Him.
Somebody reading this has spent years arguing online while their prayer life quietly died.
Somebody else stopped celebrating Christmas externally…
but secretly became prideful and spiritually cold.
Somebody else celebrates Christmas every year…
but still feels empty inside because they know they are far from God.
This article is not ultimately about defending a date.
It is about confronting the soul.
Because eternity is real.
Heaven is real.
Hell is real.
Sin is real.
Grace is real.
And Jesus Christ truly came into this world to save sinners.
The name “Jesus” comes from the Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua).
Meaning:
“Yahweh saves.”
That is the center.
Not the tree.
Not the calendar.
Not the controversy.
Salvation.
The cross.
Redemption.
The empty tomb.
The Gospel.
Never lose the center.
Because culture constantly pulls believers toward extremes.
One extreme worships consumerism.
The other sometimes worships intellectual superiority.
Both can become idols.
Colossians 2 warns against man-made regulations that appear wise externally but lack true power against fleshly indulgence.
Externalism alone cannot transform the soul.
Only Christ can.
And maybe that is why some of the most broken people still cry when hearing worship songs about Jesus during Christmas season.
Because deep down many people are starving spiritually.
Starving for hope.
Starving for forgiveness.
Starving for meaning.
Starving for home.
And whether someone celebrates Christmas or abstains from it…
the mission remains unchanged:
point people to Jesus.
Not ourselves.
Not our knowledge.
Not our image.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Some readers may still ask:
“So should Christians celebrate Christmas or not?”
Here is the most biblically honest answer:
A Christian may celebrate Christmas unto Christ with a clear conscience before God.
A Christian may also abstain from Christmas unto God with a clear conscience.
But neither side should despise the other.
Neither side should weaponize conviction.
Neither side should elevate this issue above the Gospel itself.
And neither side should forget that holiness is measured far deeper than seasonal practice.
If you celebrate Christmas…
make Christ central.
Reject greed.
Reject vanity.
Reject drunkenness.
Reject hypocrisy.
Preach the Gospel.
Love people deeply.
Help the hurting.
Honor Jesus sincerely.
And if you abstain from Christmas…
walk humbly.
Do not become arrogant.
Do not treat fellow believers with contempt.
Do not confuse personal conviction with universal salvation law.
And above all…
never stop loving people.
Because the world already has enough angry voices.
What it desperately lacks…
is transformed believers.
People who genuinely resemble Christ.
People whose lives preach louder than their arguments.
Maybe that is why Paul wrote:
“If I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge… but have not love, I am nothing.”
Nothing.
That verse should terrify pride.
Especially religious pride.
Especially performative Christianity.
Especially online spirituality.
At the center of Christianity is not a holiday.
It is a crucified and risen Savior.
And one day every argument will disappear.
Every trend.
Every controversy.
Every platform.
Every cultural war.
Every temporary distraction.
But Jesus Christ remains forever.
The same yesterday.
Today.
And forever.
So maybe the better question is no longer:
“Should Christians celebrate Christmas?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“Does my life actually reflect Christ?”
Be honest.
Not performative.
Not defensive.
Honest.
Have you truly repented?
Have you forgiven people?
Are you secretly living in sin?
Have you surrendered fully to Jesus?
Do you love truth?
Do you love people?
Do you obey God privately?
Would your hidden life glorify Christ if exposed publicly?
Those questions matter eternally.
Far more than December 25.
And maybe somebody reading this feels conviction right now.
Not condemnation.
Conviction.
There is a difference.
Condemnation pushes people away from God.
Conviction pulls people toward repentance and healing.
The Holy Spirit still calls people home.
Even now.
Even after all the failures.
Even after hypocrisy.
Even after hidden sin.
Even after spiritual numbness.
Grace still reaches.
That is the miracle of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come for perfect people.
He came for sinners willing to repent.
For the exhausted.
The addicted.
The prideful.
The ashamed.
The grieving.
The wandering.
The broken.
The pretending.
The hiding.
The spiritually dead.
And maybe this Christmas season…
or this non-Christmas season…
God is not primarily asking whether you have the right decorations.
Maybe He is asking for your heart.
Your lev.
Fully.
Completely.
No masks.
No performance.
No divided loyalty.
Just surrender.
One day the lights, gifts, arguments, and traditions will all fade away… but the condition of your soul before Jesus Christ will remain forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Joseph
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Joseph
There are some people in the Bible we admire too quickly.
We quote their victories. We celebrate their endings. We preach their promotions.
But we rarely sit inside their loneliness long enough to understand what obedience actually cost them.
Joseph is one of those people.

Because before the palace… there was betrayal. Before authority… there was abandonment. Before dreams were fulfilled… there was silence so heavy it probably felt like heaven itself had forgotten his name.
And maybe that is why this story still cuts so deep.
Because some of you know exactly what it feels like to obey God and still end up in a pit.
Some of you know what it feels like to be hated for something you never did.
To be misunderstood. To be isolated. To be thrown away by people you would have died for.
Joseph’s story is not just about dreams.
It is about surviving seasons where nothing around you looks like the promise God gave you.
And that is where most believers quietly break.
Genesis 37:3 says:
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children…”
The Hebrew phrase used here is:
“אָהַב” (ahav)
Meaning: not merely affection, but deep covenantal love, attachment, favor, relational devotion.
Jacob’s favoritism toward Joseph was visible. Painfully visible.
The coat given to Joseph was not merely colorful clothing.
The Hebrew description “כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים” (ketonet passim) likely described a long-sleeved royal garment associated with honor, distinction, and inheritance.
It represented status. Authority. Selection.
And sometimes the favor of God on your life becomes the reason people resent you.
Not because you hurt them.
But because your existence reminds them of what they refuse to surrender to God.
Joseph’s brothers did not hate him overnight. Jealousy grew slowly. Quietly. Like mold in darkness.
Genesis 37:4 says:
“They hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.”
The Hebrew wording is haunting.
“וְלֹא יָכְלוּ דַּבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם”
Literally: “They were unable to speak shalom to him.”
Shalom does not simply mean peace.
It means wholeness. Completeness. Harmony. Welfare.
Their hearts had become so corrupted by envy they could no longer release wholeness from their mouths.
Jealousy changes language.
People consumed by bitterness eventually lose the ability to speak life.
And some of you have been wounded by words spoken from spiritually sick hearts.
But Joseph’s story becomes even more devastating when God gives him dreams.
Not fantasies. Not ego trips. Dreams.
The Hebrew word is:
“חֲלוֹם” (chalom)
A revelatory dream. A divine communication.
Joseph did not invent the future God showed him.
God revealed it.
Yet revelation without maturity can create unnecessary wounds.
Joseph shared dreams before learning wisdom.
And sometimes young believers mistake revelation for readiness.
The brothers’ hatred intensified.
Genesis 37:11 says:
“And his brothers envied him…”
The Hebrew word:
“וַיְקַנְאוּ־בוֹ” (vayekanu-bo)
Carries the sense of burning jealousy. A consuming fire of resentment.
Envy is terrifying because it can make people justify evil while still believing they are right.
Eventually Joseph’s brothers strip him.
Not just physically. Emotionally. Relationally. Mentally.
Genesis 37:23:
“They stripped Joseph of his coat…”
Because the enemy always attacks identity before destiny.
Then comes the pit.
The Hebrew word:
“בּוֹר” (bor)
A cistern. An empty hole. A place associated with death, confinement, isolation, desperation.
And this is the part many sermons rush through.
Joseph was seventeen.
Seventeen.
Imagine the confusion.
Imagine screaming for help while hearing your own brothers debate whether you deserved to live.
Imagine watching the people you trusted eat bread while you cried inside a pit.
Genesis 37:25 says:
“And they sat down to eat a meal.”
One of the coldest verses in Scripture.
Joseph’s pain became background noise to people consumed by their own hardness.
Some of you know this pain.
You broke privately while everyone around you kept scrolling, laughing, posting, living.
But what is fascinating is this:
The pit was not the end.
It was transportation.
Because sometimes God allows burial-looking seasons that are actually preparation.
Joseph is sold into slavery.
The Hebrew word for slave:
“עֶבֶד” (eved)
A servant. A bondman. Someone owned.
The dreamer became property.
Can you imagine the emotional violence of that transition?
One moment favored son. Next moment chained merchandise.
And still… God never abandoned him.
Genesis 39:2 repeatedly says:
“The LORD was with Joseph.”
The Hebrew:
“וַיְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף”
YHWH hayah et Yosef.
God was with him in slavery. God was with him in false accusation. God was with him in prison.
Notice: The presence of God did not prevent suffering.
This modern idea that favor guarantees comfort is biblically bankrupt.
Sometimes God’s presence is most visible in endurance.
Joseph prospers inside Potiphar’s house.
Then temptation comes.
Potiphar’s wife repeatedly pressures Joseph sexually.
Genesis 39:9 records Joseph saying:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
The Hebrew word for wickedness:
“רָעָה” (ra’ah)
Moral evil. Corruption.
Notice Joseph did not define sin by culture. By opportunity. By secrecy. By desire.
He defined it by God.
Modern culture says: “If it feels good, do it.”
Joseph said: “How could I sin against God?”
Purity is not outdated. It is warfare.
And the terrifying thing is this:
Doing the right thing still got Joseph falsely accused.
Some of you are angry because obedience did not immediately reward you.
But Scripture never promised instant vindication.
Joseph is imprisoned. Again.
Forgotten. Again.
The Hebrew prison term carries the sense of confinement under authority.
Years pass.
Years.
Do not miss this.
God often develops identity in hiddenness before revealing assignment publicly.
The prison was training Joseph for governance.
Pain was teaching him discernment.
Isolation was building endurance.
Humiliation was killing pride.
Then Pharaoh dreams.
And suddenly the gift hidden in Joseph becomes necessary for a nation.
Your calling may feel invisible now. But one day the very thing people ignored may become the answer to someone else’s survival.
Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s dreams.
The wisdom shocks Egypt.
Genesis 41:38 says:
“Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”
The Hebrew phrase:
“רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים” (Ruach Elohim)
The Spirit of God.
Even pagan rulers recognized something supernatural resting on Joseph.
And suddenly the prisoner becomes ruler.
In one day.
Because God can change a life faster than suffering convinced you He could.
But the true untold story of Joseph is not the promotion.
It is the forgiveness.
Because years later the brothers stand before Joseph without recognizing him.
The same brothers. The same betrayal. The same trauma.
And Joseph weeps.
The Hebrew verb:
“בָּכָה” (bakah)
Deep emotional crying. Lamenting. Overwhelming release.
Joseph never became emotionless. Healing did not erase memory.
Some believers think maturity means feeling nothing.
No.
Biblical healing means wounds no longer control your obedience.
Then comes one of the most powerful statements in all of Genesis.
Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good…”
The Hebrew wording is astonishing.
“אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה”
The word “חָשַׁב” (chashav) means: To weave. To plan. To devise. To calculate.
What they designed for destruction… God rewove into deliverance.
That is redemption.
Not denial. Not pretending evil never happened.
Redemption means God is so sovereign He can take human betrayal and still produce purpose.
Joseph’s life ultimately points beyond himself.
Like Joseph, Jesus was beloved by the Father.
Like Joseph, Jesus was rejected by His own.
Like Joseph, Jesus was stripped.
Like Joseph, Jesus was sold for silver.
Like Joseph, Jesus suffered though innocent.
Like Joseph, Jesus descended before being exalted.
And like Joseph, Jesus became the source of salvation for the very people who rejected Him.
The Old Testament was always whispering His name.
Yeshua.
Jesus.
And maybe this is why Joseph’s story still destroys people emotionally.
Because deep down, we are not just reading about Joseph.
We are reading about ourselves.
The pit. The betrayal. The waiting. The loneliness. The silent prayers. The years where heaven seemed quiet.
Some of you are in Genesis 37 right now.
The dream feels attacked.
Some of you are in Genesis 39. Trying to stay pure in a filthy culture.
Some of you are in the prison years. Wondering if God forgot your name.
But Joseph’s story proves something powerful:
God is still working in hidden places.
Your suffering is not always punishment. Sometimes it is preparation.
And one encounter with God can rewrite an entire future.
If Joseph had quit in the pit, Egypt would have starved.
Your survival may be connected to someone else’s deliverance.
Do not surrender your faith because the process hurts.
And maybe tonight, what hurts the most is not what people did to you.
Maybe it is the fear that your life no longer has purpose.
But Joseph’s story screams across generations:
God still writes endings human hands cannot destroy.
Even now.
Especially now.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some people survived because they discovered God was closest in the seasons that hurt the most.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Bahagi ng Buhay ni Jose
May mga kuwento sa Bibliya na madalas nating minamadali.
Nakikita natin ang tagumpay. Naririnig natin ang mga himala. Ipinapangaral natin ang pagtatagumpay.
Pero bihira nating damhin ang bigat ng sakit na dinaanan bago dumating ang tagumpay.
Isa si Jose sa mga taong iyon.
Dahil bago ang palasyo… may hukay.
Bago ang karangalan… may pagtataksil.
Bago ang katuparan ng panaginip… may mga gabing tila tahimik ang langit.
At marahil kaya hanggang ngayon ay tumatagos pa rin ang kuwento niya…
Dahil maraming tao ang marunong maniwala habang maayos ang lahat.
Pero kakaunti ang nananatiling tapat kapag parang iniwan na sila ng Diyos.
Genesis 37:3:
“Minahal ni Israel si Jose nang higit kaysa sa lahat niyang anak…”
Ang salitang Hebreo na ginamit dito ay:
“אָהַב” (ahav)
Hindi lang simpleng pagmamahal. Ito ay malalim na pagmamahal ng tipan. Pagpili. Pabor. Pagkakabit ng puso.
Kita ng lahat ang pabor kay Jose. At minsan… ang pabor ng Diyos sa buhay mo ang mismong dahilan kung bakit ka kinamumuhian ng iba.
Hindi dahil may ginawa kang masama.
Kundi dahil may nakikita silang calling sa’yo na ayaw nilang isuko sa Diyos.
Ang balabal ni Jose ay hindi lang makulay na damit.
Ang “כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים” (ketonet passim) ay malamang simbolo ng dangal, awtoridad, at mana.
Ibig sabihin: May espesyal na layunin si Jose.
At doon nagsimula ang galit.
Genesis 37:4:
“Kinamuhian nila siya at hindi nila siya makausap nang mapayapa.”
Sa Hebreo:
“וְלֹא יָכְלוּ דַּבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם”
Literal: “Hindi nila kayang magsalita ng shalom sa kanya.”
Ang “shalom” ay hindi lang peace.
Ito ay kabuuan. Kapayapaan. Kagalingan. Kaayusan.
Ganito kalala ang inggit.
Kapag nalason ang puso, nawawala ang kakayahang magsalita ng buhay.
At baka may ilan dito na nasugatan ng mga salita ng mga taong puno ng galit.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang mga panaginip.
Ang salitang:
“חֲלוֹם” (chalom)
Ay banal na rebelasyon.
Hindi gawa-gawa ni Jose ang nakita niya. Diyos ang nagpakita.
Pero minsan, kapag bata pa ang pananampalataya, akala natin handa na tayo dahil may natanggap tayong revelation.
Hindi pa alam ni Jose na may timing ang wisdom.
Lalong lumalim ang galit ng kanyang mga kapatid.
Hanggang dumating ang araw na hinubaran siya.
Genesis 37:23:
“Hinubaran nila si Jose ng kanyang balabal…”
Dahil bago sirain ng kaaway ang destiny mo, una niyang aatakihin ang identity mo.
Pagkatapos ay itinapon siya sa hukay.
“בּוֹר” (bor)
Isang malalim na hukay. Lugar ng kadiliman. Pagkakulong. Pagkahiwalay.
At ito ang bahagi ng kuwento na madalas minamadali ng mga sermon.
Labing pitong taong gulang lang si Jose.
Isipin mo iyon.
Siguro sumisigaw siya. Siguro umiiyak. Siguro hinihintay niyang maawa ang mga kapatid niya.
Habang sila… nakaupo at kumakain.
Genesis 37:25:
“At sila’y naupo upang kumain.”
Napakalamig na talata.
Habang si Jose ay nadudurog, normal lang ang araw para sa kanila.
May mga taong ganito rin ang pinagdaanan.
Ikaw ang umiiyak. Pero tuloy lang ang mundo.
Pagkatapos, ipinagbili si Jose bilang alipin.
“עֶבֶד” (eved)
Isang alipin. Pag-aari ng iba.
Mula sa paboritong anak… naging produkto.
Pero kahit ganoon, hindi siya iniwan ng Diyos.
Genesis 39:2:
“At ang Panginoon ay sumasa kay Jose.”
Sa Hebreo:
“וַיְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף”
Kasama siya ng Diyos sa pagkaalipin. Kasama siya sa maling paratang. Kasama siya sa kulungan.
Napakahalagang maintindihan ito:
Ang presensya ng Diyos ay hindi nangangahulugang walang paghihirap.
Minsan, pinaka-malapit ang Diyos sa mga panahong halos hindi mo na kaya.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang tukso.
Inakit si Jose ng asawa ni Potifar.
Pero sinabi ni Jose:
“Paanong gagawin ko ang malaking kasamaan na ito at magkakasala laban sa Diyos?”
Genesis 39:9
Ang “רָעָה” (ra’ah) ay moral na kasamaan.
Hindi ibinase ni Jose ang tama sa kultura. Sa laman. Sa lihim. Sa emosyon.
Ibinase niya ito sa Diyos.
At nakakatakot isipin:
Kahit tama ang ginawa niya, nakulong pa rin siya.
Maraming tao ang nanlamig sa Diyos dahil akala nila ang pagsunod ay laging may instant reward.
Pero hindi iyon ang itinuturo ng Bibliya.
Minsan, ang obedience ay magdadala muna sa’yo sa proseso bago sa promotion.
Lumipas ang mga taon.
Nakalimutan si Jose.
Tahimik. Nakakulong. Naghihintay.
Pero habang akala niya nasasayang ang buhay niya, hinuhubog pala siya ng Diyos.
Ang kulungan ang naghanda sa kanya para mamuno.
Ang sakit ang nagturo ng wisdom.
Ang kahihiyan ang pumatay sa pride.
Pagkatapos, nanaginip si Paraon.
At biglang naging mahalaga ang regalong binale-wala noon.
Minsan, yung bagay na minamaliit ng tao sa’yo ngayon ang magiging dahilan ng pagliligtas ng iba balang araw.
At sa isang iglap, ang preso ay naging pinuno.
Pero ang pinakamakapangyarihang bahagi ng kuwento ni Jose ay hindi ang promotion.
Kundi ang pagpapatawad.
Dahil nang muli niyang makita ang mga kapatid niya, may kapangyarihan na siyang gumanti.
Pero umiyak siya.
“בָּכָה” (bakah)
Malalim na pag-iyak. Paglabas ng matagal nang sakit.
Hindi naging manhid si Jose.
Hindi ibig sabihin ng healing ay wala ka nang nararamdaman.
Ibig sabihin lang: Hindi na kontrolado ng sugat mo ang pagsunod mo sa Diyos.
At pagkatapos ay sinabi niya ang isa sa pinakamagandang linya sa buong Bibliya.
Genesis 50:20:
“Binalak ninyo ang masama laban sa akin, ngunit binalak iyon ng Diyos para sa ikabubuti…”
Ang salitang:
“חָשַׁב” (chashav)
Ay mangahulugang: maghabi, magplano, bumuo.
Yung plano nilang sirain siya… hinabi ng Diyos para maging kaligtasan.
Iyan ang redemption.
Hindi paglimot. Hindi pagdedeny ng sakit.
Kundi ang kakayahan ng Diyos na gawing may layunin kahit ang pinakamadilim na pagtataksil.
At higit sa lahat, ang buhay ni Jose ay larawan ni Cristo.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay minahal ng Ama.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay itinakwil ng sarili Niyang bayan.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay ipinagbili.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay nagdusa kahit inosente.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay ibinaba bago itinaas.
At tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ang naging daan ng kaligtasan para mismo sa mga taong tumanggi sa Kanya.
Yeshua.
Jesus.
At baka kaya ka tinatamaan ng kuwento ni Jose ngayon…
Dahil hindi mo lang nakikita si Jose.
Nakikita mo ang sarili mo.
Ang paghihintay. Ang sakit. Ang betrayal. Ang tahimik na gabi. Ang mga panahong parang walang sagot ang Diyos.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Hindi tumitigil ang Diyos gumalaw kahit tahimik Siya.
Ang hukay ay hindi dulo ng kuwento.
At ang proseso ay hindi ebidensya na iniwan ka na ng Diyos.
Kung sumuko si Jose sa hukay, may bansang mamamatay sa gutom.
Maaaring may mga taong nakakabit ang future sa katapatan mo ngayon.
Kaya huwag kang bibitaw.
Kahit pagod ka na. Kahit umiiyak ka na. Kahit hindi mo maintindihan ang ginagawa ng Diyos.
Maging totoo ka. Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Minsan, doon mo mararamdaman na pinakamalapit ang Diyos… sa panahong akala mo iniwan ka na Niya.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Widow of Nain Never Expected Jesus to Stop the Funeral
paragraphs: Why the Widow of Nain Never Expected Jesus to Stop the Funeral
There are pains so deep that even prayer feels exhausted.
Some grief does not scream. It just walks slowly behind a coffin.
The widow of Nain was not looking for a miracle. She was simply trying to survive the walk to the cemetery.
Most people read Luke 7 quickly. Too quickly. They remember the resurrection. They celebrate the miracle. They quote the power.
But very few stop long enough to feel the unbearable silence hanging over that funeral procession.
This was not just a woman crying over her son. This was a woman watching her entire future disappear in front of her eyes.
And that is exactly why what Jesus did becomes even more devastatingly beautiful.
Because she never asked Him to stop the funeral.
She did not run to Him. She did not beg Him. She did not kneel before Him. She did not even speak.
Jesus interrupted her grief before she had enough faith left to ask.
That changes everything.
Luke records the moment with painful precision:
“In the city called Nain… behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow.” (Luke 7:11–12)
The Greek text is stunning.
Luke writes:
καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐξεκομίζετο τεθνηκὼς μονογενὴς υἱὸς τῇ μητρὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὴ ἦν χήρα.
Transliterated:
“Kai idou exekomizeto tethnekōs monogenēs huios tē mētri autou kai autē ēn chēra.”
The word μονογενὴς (monogenēs) means “only begotten,” “only one,” “unique child.”
This is not accidental wording.
Luke is intentionally emphasizing total loss.
One son. Gone.
And then comes the crushing final phrase:
καὶ αὐτὴ ἦν χήρα
“And she was a widow.”
In the ancient Jewish world, this was catastrophic.
A widow without a son often faced social vulnerability, poverty, instability, and isolation. There were no modern safety systems. No insurance. No government support. No retirement.
Her husband was dead. Now her son was dead.
This funeral was not only about death. It was about the destruction of covering, provision, protection, inheritance, and hope.
And the horrifying part is this:
By this point, she probably expected nothing from God anymore.
Because grief changes people.
Especially delayed grief. Repeated grief. Layered grief.
The kind of grief where heaven already seemed silent once before.
We do not know how long ago her husband died. But we know this:
She already buried one person she loved.
Now she was burying another.
There comes a point where some people stop expecting rescue.
Not because they hate God. Not because they stopped believing.
But because disappointment exhausted their imagination.
That is where many people secretly live right now.
Still attending church. Still posting Bible verses. Still smiling publicly.
But privately?
They no longer expect Jesus to intervene.
They pray mechanically. They worship tired. They survive spiritually instead of living spiritually.
Because too many funerals happened inside them.
Dead dreams. Dead purity. Dead hope. Dead relationships. Dead passion. Dead trust. Dead innocence.
And eventually people stop asking God to stop the funeral procession.
They simply learn how to walk beside the coffin.
That is why Luke 7 hits differently when you truly understand it.
Because Jesus was not invited there.
He arrived anyway.
The widow never sent word. No messenger reached Him. No one requested a healing service. No one gathered intercessors.
Jesus encountered her pain while entering the city gate.
One crowd was following Jesus. Another crowd was following death.
And when the two processions collided, death lost.
Luke 7:13 says:
“When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her.”
The Greek word for compassion here is deeply emotional.
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
Transliterated:
“esplagchnisthē.”
This word comes from σπλάγχνα (splanchna), referring to the inward organs — the bowels, the guts, the deepest inner parts of a person.
Biblically, compassion was not viewed as shallow sympathy. It was something felt violently inside. A gut-level emotional movement.
Jesus was not emotionally detached from her pain.
He felt it.
Deeply.
This destroys the false image many people have of Christ.
Jesus is not cold toward suffering. He is not distant from broken people. He is not irritated by exhausted believers.
He sees grief humans cannot explain. He sees private funerals nobody else notices.
And sometimes He moves toward people before they even know how to pray anymore.
Then Jesus says something almost offensive:
“Do not weep.”
At first glance that sounds insensitive. Cruel, even.
How do you tell a mother not to cry at her only son’s funeral?
But Jesus was not dismissing her grief.
He was about to confront the reason for it.
Then Scripture says:
“Then He came and touched the open coffin.”
This moment is shocking.
Under Jewish law, touching death made someone ceremonially unclean.
Numbers 19:11 says:
“He who touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days.”
Yet Jesus touched the bier anyway.
Because Jesus was never afraid of contamination from death.
Death was about to become contaminated by Him.
Religion avoids brokenness to stay clean. Jesus enters brokenness to make people whole.
That difference changes lives.
Then Jesus spoke directly to the dead son.
“Young man, I say to you, arise.”
In Greek:
νεανίσκε, σοὶ λέγω, ἐγέρθητι.
Transliterated:
“Neaniske, soi legō, egerthēti.”
ἐγέρθητι (egerthēti) means “be raised,” “wake up,” “rise.”
And immediately, the dead man sat up and began to speak.
Imagine the screaming. The shock. The terror. The collapse of human logic in real time.
One second there was a funeral. The next second there was a resurrection.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear.
Jesus can interrupt hopeless situations without warning.
He can step into places people already gave up on.
He can resurrect things everyone declared permanently dead.
Not every earthly story ends with physical resurrection. Scripture never teaches that every funeral becomes reversed in this life.
But Luke 7 reveals something eternally important:
Jesus is Lord even over irreversible situations.
Even funerals. Even impossible endings. Even sealed outcomes.
The widow expected burial. Jesus brought restoration.
And the terrifying truth is that many people today have silently accepted emotional death as normal.
They function. They work. They laugh occasionally.
But inside?
Something has been carried toward burial for years.
Their prayer life. Their intimacy with God. Their identity. Their purity. Their hunger for Scripture. Their emotional health. Their trust after betrayal.
Some people reading this are exhausted from carrying internal coffins nobody else sees.
But Jesus still walks into funeral processions.
And sometimes He waits until the situation looks completely impossible so nobody confuses resurrection with self-improvement.
That is the Gospel.
Humanity was spiritually dead. Not weak. Not bruised. Dead.
Ephesians 2:1 says:
“And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.”
The Greek word there is νεκρούς (nekrous). Dead. Lifeless. Unable to save ourselves.
Christianity is not behavior modification. It is resurrection.
That is why Jesus later declares in John 11:25:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
In Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
“Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.”
ἀνάστασις (anastasis) means resurrection. ζωή (zōē) means true life, divine life.
Jesus does not merely improve dead things. He resurrects them.
And perhaps the most beautiful detail in the entire story appears at the very end.
Luke says:
“And He presented him to his mother.”
Jesus did not resurrect the boy merely to demonstrate power.
He restored a broken mother.
This miracle was deeply personal.
Because Jesus is not only concerned with public displays of glory. He cares about devastated hearts.
Some people think God only moves through giant platforms, famous ministries, or dramatic stages.
But Luke 7 reveals Christ stopping an entire funeral procession for one shattered woman.
One.
Never underestimate how personally Jesus sees pain.
The enemy wants exhausted believers to think heaven stopped noticing them.
But Christ still sees the widow walking behind the coffin.
He still notices silent suffering. He still notices hidden grief. He still notices people barely surviving emotionally.
And sometimes the greatest miracles begin when people no longer even have enough strength left to ask.
That is grace.
Not that we climbed to God. But that Christ came toward us.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we fixed ourselves. Not after we became worthy. Not after we became spiritually impressive.
While we were still broken.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus walks toward funerals. Toward sinners. Toward failures. Toward grieving people. Toward exhausted hearts. Toward impossible situations.
And He still speaks life.
Maybe this article found you during your own funeral procession.
Maybe something inside you already accepted defeat. Maybe your faith became survival instead of relationship. Maybe disappointment slowly buried your expectation.
But Luke 7 reminds us that Jesus can enter a hopeless scene uninvited and completely rewrite the outcome.
And maybe that is why the widow of Nain never expected Jesus to stop the funeral.
Because she thought death already had the final word.
Until Jesus arrived.
Be honest. This hit deeper than some people expected.
Sometimes the miracle begins the moment you realize Jesus was walking toward your funeral long before you noticed Him coming.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Hindi Inasahan ng Balo ng Nain na Hihintuin ni Jesus ang Libing
May mga sakit na sobrang lalim… kahit panalangin napapagod.
May mga lungkot na hindi umiiyak nang malakas. Tahimik lang itong naglalakad sa likod ng kabaong.
Ang balo ng Nain ay hindi naghahanap ng himala. Sinusubukan lang niyang mabuhay habang papunta sa sementeryo.
Masyadong mabilis basahin ng karamihan ang Lucas 7. Naalala nila ang himala. Naalala nila ang pagkabuhay muli. Naalala nila ang kapangyarihan.
Pero kakaunti lang ang tunay na humihinto para maramdaman ang bigat ng katahimikang bumabalot sa prusisyon ng libing na iyon.
Hindi lang ito kwento ng isang ina na nawalan ng anak. Ito ay kwento ng isang babaeng nakitang mamatay ang natitira niyang kinabukasan.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit mas lalong napakaganda ng ginawa ni Jesus.
Dahil hindi niya kailanman inasahang pipigilan ni Jesus ang libing.
Hindi siya tumakbo kay Jesus. Hindi siya nakiusap. Hindi siya lumuhod. Hindi nga siya nagsalita.
Si Jesus mismo ang huminto sa kanyang pagdadalamhati bago pa siya magkaroon ng sapat na lakas para humingi ng tulong.
Binabago niyan ang lahat.
Sabi ng Lucas 7:11–12:
“Sa bayang tinatawag na Nain… may inilalabas na isang patay, ang kaisa-isang anak na lalaki ng kanyang ina, at ang ina ay isang balo.”
Sa orihinal na Greek:
καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐξεκομίζετο τεθνηκὼς μονογενὴς υἱὸς τῇ μητρὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὴ ἦν χήρα.
Ang salitang μονογενὴς (monogenēs) ay nangangahulugang “nag-iisa,” “tanging anak.”
Isang anak. At ngayon patay na.
Pagkatapos idinagdag pa ni Lucas:
καὶ αὐτὴ ἦν χήρα
“At siya ay isang balo.”
Sa kulturang Hudyo noon, napakabigat nito.
Walang asawa. Ngayon wala na ring anak.
Hindi lang ito emosyonal na pagkawala. Maaaring mawala rin ang proteksyon, kabuhayan, seguridad, at kinabukasan.
At marahil dito pinakamasakit ang lahat:
Malamang matagal na siyang tumigil sa pag-asang may gagawin pa ang Diyos.
Dahil may klase ng sakit na unti-unting pinapatay ang expectation.
Hindi dahil galit ka sa Diyos. Hindi dahil wala ka nang pananampalataya.
Kundi dahil napagod ka nang umasa.
May mga taong ganito ngayon.
Nagsisimba pa rin. Nagpo-post pa rin ng Bible verse. Ngumingiti pa rin sa publiko.
Pero sa loob?
Hindi na talaga nila inaasahang kikilos pa si Jesus.
Paulit-ulit na kasing may namatay sa loob nila.
Patay na pangarap. Patay na passion. Patay na purity. Patay na tiwala. Patay na excitement sa Diyos. Patay na pag-asa.
At kalaunan… natututo na lang silang maglakad katabi ng kabaong.
Kaya sobrang bigat ng Lucas 7 kapag naintindihan mo ito nang mas malalim.
Dahil hindi inimbitahan si Jesus.
Dumating Siya pa rin.
Walang messenger. Walang prayer request. Walang special service.
Bigla na lang sinalubong ni Jesus ang kanyang sakit sa may pintuan ng lungsod.
Isang grupo sumusunod kay Jesus. Isang grupo sumusunod sa kamatayan.
At nang magtagpo ang dalawang prusisyon… natalo ang kamatayan.
Sabi ng Lucas 7:13:
“Nang makita siya ng Panginoon, nahabag Siya sa kanya.”
Sa Greek:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
“esplagchnisthē.”
Ito ay mula sa salitang σπλάγχνα (splanchna), na tumutukoy sa pinaka-loob ng damdamin. Parang sakit na ramdam hanggang sikmura.
Hindi malamig si Jesus sa pagdurusa. Hindi Siya detached.
Ramdam Niya ang sakit ng babae.
At iyon ang gustong kalimutan ng kaaway.
Gusto niyang paniwalaan ng mga sugatan na hindi na sila napapansin ng langit.
Pero nakikita pa rin ni Cristo ang mga taong tahimik na umiiyak.
Nakikita Niya ang mga taong pagod nang lumaban. Nakikita Niya ang mga taong hindi na alam paano manalangin.
At minsan… gumagalaw Siya bago pa tayo makahingi ng tulong.
Pagkatapos sinabi ni Jesus:
“Huwag kang umiyak.”
Parang ang sakit pakinggan.
Paano mo sasabihin iyon sa isang inang nawalan ng kaisa-isang anak?
Pero hindi minamaliit ni Jesus ang kanyang pagdadalamhati.
Papatayin Niya ang dahilan ng kanyang pag-iyak.
Pagkatapos hinawakan Niya ang kabaong.
Napakalaking bagay nito.
Sa kautusang Hudyo, ang paghawak sa patay ay nagiging sanhi ng pagiging marumi sa seremonyal na paraan.
Pero hinawakan pa rin ito ni Jesus.
Dahil hindi natatakot si Jesus na mahawahan ng kamatayan.
Ang kamatayan ang mahahawahan ng buhay na nasa Kanya.
Iyan ang kaibahan ng relihiyon at ni Cristo.
Ang relihiyon lumalayo sa wasak para manatiling malinis. Si Jesus lumalapit sa wasak para magbigay ng buhay.
Pagkatapos sinabi Niya:
“Binata, sinasabi Ko sa iyo, bumangon ka.”
Sa Greek:
νεανίσκε, σοὶ λέγω, ἐγέρθητι.
At agad na umupo ang patay na lalaki at nagsimulang magsalita.
Isipin mo ang sigawan. Ang takot. Ang pag-iyak. Ang pagkagulat.
Isang segundo may libing. Sa susunod na segundo may resurrection.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangang marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Kayang pasukin ni Jesus ang sitwasyong matagal nang isinuko ng tao.
Kayang buhayin ni Cristo ang mga bagay na idineklara nang patay.
Hindi lahat ng kwento sa mundo nagtatapos sa pisikal na resurrection. Hindi iyan ang itinuturo ng Biblia.
Pero malinaw ang Lucas 7:
Si Jesus ay Panginoon kahit sa mga sitwasyong mukhang tapos na.
Kahit sa libing. Kahit sa impossible. Kahit sa wasak.
At maraming tao ngayon ang buhay sa labas… pero patay sa loob.
Gumagana. Nagtatrabaho. Tumatawa minsan.
Pero may kabaong silang pasan na walang nakakakita.
Patay na prayer life. Patay na intimacy sa Diyos. Patay na identity. Patay na emotional strength.
Pero si Jesus… lumalakad pa rin papunta sa mga funeral procession.
At minsan hinihintay Niyang maging imposible ang sitwasyon para walang magkamaling isipin na self-improvement lang ang nangyari.
Dahil ang Christianity ay hindi simpleng pagbabago ng ugali. Ito ay resurrection.
Sabi ng Juan 11:25:
“Ako ang muling pagkabuhay at ang buhay.”
Sa Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
Hindi lang inaayos ni Jesus ang patay. Binubuhay Niya ito.
At marahil ang pinakamagandang bahagi ng kwento ay ang dulo.
Sabi ng Biblia:
“At ibinigay Niya ito sa kanyang ina.”
Hindi lang ginawa ni Jesus ang himala para ipakita ang kapangyarihan.
Ginawa Niya ito para ibalik ang puso ng isang wasak na ina.
Napakapersonal ni Cristo.
Kaya huwag mong isipin na hindi ka na nakikita ng Diyos.
Nakikita pa rin Niya ang mga tahimik na umiiyak. Nakikita Niya ang mga pagod nang lumaban. Nakikita Niya ang mga halos sumuko na.
At minsan… ang biyaya ng Diyos dumarating bago pa tayo makapagsalita.
Baka itong article na ito ang paraan ng Diyos para ipaalala sa iyo:
Hindi pa tapos si Jesus.
Maging totoo ka. Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Minsan nagsisimula ang himala sa sandaling marealize mong matagal nang naglalakad si Jesus papunta sa funeral mo bago mo pa Siya napansin.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Tertullus Flattered Felix Before Accusing Paul
paragraphs: Why Tertullus Flattered Felix Before Accusing Paul
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully modern.
Moments where truth enters a room… but manipulation speaks first.
Acts 24 is one of those moments.

The Apostle Paul stood chained before a corrupt governor. His enemies burned with hatred. Religious leaders traveled nearly sixty miles from Jerusalem to Caesarea just to destroy one man. But before they launched accusations against Paul, something disturbing happened.
A lawyer named Tertullus began with flattery.
Not truth.
Not justice.
Flattery.
And what makes this scene unforgettable is that everyone in the room knew the praise was exaggerated.
Even Felix knew.
That is how powerful manipulation can become.
It can survive even when everyone recognizes it.
The terrifying part is this:
Many people still use the spirit of Tertullus today.
Not only in politics.
Not only in courtrooms.
But in churches.
In relationships.
In leadership.
In social circles.
Even in spiritual warfare.
Because sometimes people flatter others, not because they honor them… but because they want permission to destroy someone else.
And that is exactly what happened before Paul ever opened his mouth.
The courtroom atmosphere in Acts 24 feels cinematic.
