Behind YouTube thumbnails covered in flames.
Behind red moons, microchips, collapsing governments, conspiracy theories, and countdown predictions.
For decades, millions of believers have opened the Book of Revelation with clenched fists instead of open hearts.
Some were taught Revelation is primarily about decoding world events.
Others were told every headline is another fulfilled prophecy.
Some grew up believing the book was written mainly to terrify humanity into obedience.
But what if much of modern Christianity has misunderstood Revelation entirely?
What if the final book of Scripture was never designed to produce panic… but perseverance?
What if Revelation is less about identifying the Antichrist… and more about remaining faithful to Jesus Christ?
And what if many believers have accidentally turned a book about worship into a book about fear?
That question unsettles people.
Because Revelation has become deeply commercialized.
Fear sells.
Panic spreads faster than peace.
Speculation attracts more clicks than surrender.
But Scripture was never written to entertain our obsession with hidden timelines.
It was written to reveal Jesus.
Not merely events.
Not merely symbols.
Jesus.
The very first verse destroys countless modern assumptions.
Revelation 1:1 says:
“The revelation of Jesus Christ…”
In Greek, the word is:
ἀποκάλυψις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Apokalypsis Iēsou Christou.
“Apokalypsis” does not mean catastrophe.
It means unveiling.
Disclosure.
Revealing what was hidden.
The Book of Revelation is not fundamentally “the revelation of the end times.”
It is the revelation OF Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Because many believers approach Revelation asking:
“Who is the beast?”
“When is the tribulation?”
“What nation is Babylon?”
“What technology is the mark?”
But the book itself is screaming another question:
“Do you truly see Jesus for who He is?”
The modern church often treats Revelation like a codebook.
The early church treated it like oxygen.
That difference matters.
Deeply.
Because Revelation was originally written to suffering believers under Roman oppression.
Christians were being hunted.
Marginalized.
Executed.
Publicly humiliated.
Some were burned alive.
Others were fed to wild animals.
The Roman Empire demanded ultimate allegiance.
Caesar wanted worship.
And Christians who confessed “Jesus is Lord” were declaring war against imperial idolatry.
That context changes the emotional gravity of the book.
Revelation was not written primarily to comfortable Christians trying to predict politics from a couch.
It was written to persecuted believers trying not to abandon Christ.
The book was a survival document for faithful endurance.
Not entertainment for speculative obsession.
John writes from Patmos.
An island prison.
Not a luxury conference.
Not a podcast studio.
A prison.
Revelation emerged from suffering.
And suddenly the symbolism begins making more sense.
The beasts.
The dragons.
Babylon.
The harlot.
The blood.
The martyrs.
The cosmic warfare.
These images were not random fantasy imagery.
They were apocalyptic literature.
A literary style deeply rooted in Jewish tradition.
And many modern readers miss this entirely.
Apocalyptic writing used vivid symbols, heavenly imagery, poetic visions, numerical patterns, and prophetic metaphors to communicate spiritual realities.
Daniel uses it.
Ezekiel uses it.
Zechariah uses it.
Isaiah contains echoes of it.
Even Jesus uses apocalyptic imagery in Matthew 24.
The language was symbolic, layered, emotional, and theological.
Not simplistic newspaper prediction.
This does not mean Revelation is meaningless symbolism.
It means biblical symbolism must be interpreted biblically.
And that requires humility.
For example, many modern Christians read “666” and instantly jump to futuristic technology.
But first-century readers would have recognized the practice of gematria — assigning numerical values to letters.
Many scholars note that “Nero Caesar” transliterated into Hebrew letters corresponds numerically to 666.
Nero represented monstrous imperial persecution.
The beast was not merely future.
It reflected systems of anti-Christ power already operating in the world.
That matters.
Because Scripture repeatedly teaches the spirit of antichrist is already active.
1 John 4:3 says:
“Every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist…”
The Greek:
τὸ τοῦ ἀντιχρίστου
To tou antichristou.
Not merely one future individual.
But a recurring satanic opposition against Christ.
This is where many believers unintentionally narrow Revelation into a timeline chart instead of a discipleship confrontation.
The book forces us to ask:
What powers are discipling our loyalty?
Who receives our worship?
What empire owns our heart?
Because Revelation is saturated with worship scenes.
Heaven sings constantly.
The throne dominates the narrative.
The Lamb appears central again and again.
And this is perhaps the greatest shock in the entire book.
Jesus conquers like a Lamb.
Not like Caesar.
Not like earthly empires.
Not through domination.
Through sacrificial victory.
Revelation 5 changes everything.
John hears about the Lion of Judah.
But when he turns… he sees a slain Lamb.
That detail is breathtaking.
The Greek says:
ἀρνίον ἑστηκὸς ὡς ἐσφαγμένον
Arnion hestēkos hōs esphagmenon.
“A Lamb standing as though slain.”
Standing.
Yet slaughtered.
Alive.
Yet scarred.
Victorious.
Yet pierced.
This is the Kingdom of God.
And many Christians miss the emotional earthquake of this image because they rush too quickly into speculation.
The Lamb is central.
Not our charts.
Not our theories.
Not our internet arguments.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
And perhaps this is where Revelation becomes painfully personal.
Because many believers are obsessed with identifying Babylon while secretly bowing to Babylon’s values.
Consumerism.
Pride.
Sexual immorality.
Greed.
Power worship.
Nationalistic idolatry.
Spiritual compromise.
Self-exaltation.
Revelation is not merely exposing future evil.
It exposes present compromise.
The letters to the seven churches prove this.
Those churches were real congregations.
Real people.
Real spiritual struggles.
Ephesus lost its first love.
Laodicea became lukewarm.
Sardis looked alive but was spiritually dead.
Pergamum tolerated corruption.
Thyatira compromised morally.
And if we are honest…
many churches today still do the same.
We fear the beast while tolerating worldliness.
We debate prophecy while neglecting repentance.
We analyze symbols while ignoring holiness.
We obsess over future persecution while refusing present obedience.
That tension should convict us.
Because Revelation never intended to merely inform us.
It intends to transform us.
The Hebrew mindset behind biblical prophecy was rarely about satisfying curiosity.
It was about covenant faithfulness.
The prophets called people back to God.
Back to holiness.
Back to repentance.
Back to worship.
Even the terrifying judgments in Revelation echo the Exodus story.
Plagues.
Deliverance.
A tyrannical empire.
God protecting His people.
The Bible is deeply interconnected.
And Revelation is saturated with Old Testament echoes.
Some scholars estimate there are hundreds of allusions to Old Testament passages throughout Revelation.
In many ways, Revelation is less understandable if we ignore the Hebrew Scriptures.
For example, when Revelation calls Jesus “Alpha and Omega,” it reflects God’s eternal sovereignty.
In Greek:
Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
Egō eimi to Alpha kai to Ō.
“I am the Alpha and the Omega.”
The beginning.
The end.
The One outside time itself.
And suddenly Revelation becomes less about trying to control the future…
and more about trusting the One who already holds it.
That is emotionally different.
One produces anxiety.
The other produces worship.
But here is where things become even more uncomfortable.
Some Christians have become addicted to prophetic fear.
Every crisis becomes “proof.”
Every war becomes “the final war.”
Every invention becomes “the mark.”
Every election becomes “the end.”
Yet Jesus Himself warned against hysteria.
In Matthew 24, Christ said:
“See that you are not alarmed.”
The Greek phrase:
μὴ θροεῖσθε
Mē throeisthe.
Do not panic.
Do not be terrified.
Do not lose stability.
That command matters.
Especially now.
Because fear-driven Christianity often produces exhaustion instead of endurance.
And exhausted believers become vulnerable believers.
Some eventually abandon faith entirely because every failed prediction slowly erodes trust.
History is filled with prophetic date-setting disasters.
Generations confidently predicted exact endings.
They were wrong.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Yet Revelation itself repeatedly emphasizes something far more important than prediction.
Faithful endurance.
Revelation 14:12 says:
“Here is a call for the endurance of the saints…”
The Greek word:
ὑπομονή
Hypomonē.
Steadfast perseverance.
Remaining under pressure without abandoning Christ.
That is one of Revelation’s central themes.
Not obsession.
Endurance.
And perhaps this is why Revelation feels so emotionally overwhelming.
Because the book exposes the war happening inside every human heart.
Who will you worship?
The Lamb?
Or the world?
Truth?
Or comfort?
Faithfulness?
Or compromise?
The conflict is cosmic.
But also deeply personal.
Every believer understands this battle.
The temptation to drift.
The exhaustion.
The secret sin.
The spiritual numbness.
The fear.
The loneliness.
The pressure to blend into culture.
Revelation tears the veil away and reminds suffering Christians that heaven still sees them.
That God is still on the throne.
That evil does not win forever.
That Babylon falls.
That Christ reigns.
That resurrection is coming.
That tears will not have the final word.
Revelation 21 carries one of the most emotionally devastating promises in all Scripture.
“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”
In Greek:
ἐξαλείψει πᾶν δάκρυον
Exaleipsei pan dakryon.
Every tear.
Not some.
Every.
The tears nobody saw.
The grief hidden behind smiles.
The betrayal.
The depression.
The prayers whispered through shaking hands.
The nights of despair.
The funerals.
The addictions.
The trauma.
The regret.
The shame.
The loneliness.
Every tear.
That is the destination Revelation points toward.
Not terror.
Restoration.
And this changes how we read judgment itself.
Because modern readers often struggle emotionally with Revelation’s severe imagery.
But biblical judgment is not random cruelty.
It is God confronting evil.
Destroying what destroys.
Ending oppression.
Overthrowing wickedness.
Defeating death.
Justice matters because love matters.
A God who never judges evil would not actually be good.
And yet even in judgment, Revelation repeatedly reveals mercy.
Warnings are given.
Calls to repentance appear.
God’s patience remains astonishing.
The tragedy is not that God warns humanity.
The tragedy is humanity refusing Him.
And maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortably personal for all of us.
Because many people want Revelation to explain world events while avoiding personal surrender.
We want information.
Jesus wants transformation.
We want certainty.
Jesus calls for trust.
We want to decode symbols.
Jesus calls us to carry crosses.
The terrifying reality is that someone can know every prophecy chart and still not truly know Christ.
And Revelation warns about this constantly.
Religious appearance without genuine devotion.
External Christianity without surrendered worship.
A church that looks powerful externally while spiritually dying internally.
That should shake us.
Because Revelation is ultimately not asking:
“Can you predict the future?”
It is asking:
“Will you remain faithful to Jesus no matter the cost?”
That question costs more.
And perhaps this explains why Revelation repeatedly returns to worship scenes.
Songs.
Thrones.
Crowns.
Falling before God.
Holy.
Holy.
Holy.
The book keeps redirecting our eyes upward.
Because fearful Christians stare constantly at the beast.
Faithful Christians keep staring at the Lamb.
And whatever captures your gaze eventually shapes your soul.
This is why some believers live in continual panic while others walk in supernatural peace during chaos.
One is consumed with signs.
The other is consumed with Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
Even historically, Christians across centuries interpreted Revelation differently.
Some viewed portions symbolically.
Others historically.
Others futuristically.
Faithful believers have debated these issues for generations.
But mature theology requires humility where Scripture allows mystery.
Dogmatism about speculative details has fractured countless believers unnecessarily.
Meanwhile the clearest themes remain undeniable.
Jesus wins.
Evil falls.
The saints endure.
Worship belongs to God alone.
And the Kingdom of Christ will never be overthrown.
Daniel 7:14 echoes this beautifully:
“His dominion is an everlasting dominion.”
In Aramaic:
שָׁלְטָנֵהּ שָׁלְטָן עָלַם
Sholtaneh sholtan alam.
An eternal dominion.
Not temporary.
Not fragile.
Not threatened.
Christ reigns.
Right now.
Even when the world looks chaotic.
Even when evil appears loud.
Even when suffering feels unbearable.
The throne in heaven is never panicking.
That line alone might save someone reading this.
Because some believers secretly feel exhausted.
Emotionally numb.
Spiritually anxious.
Terrified by the future.
Drowning in endless prophecy content online.
Waiting constantly for disaster.
But Revelation was never given to imprison Christians in fear.
It was given to anchor suffering believers in hope.
Hope stronger than Rome.
Hope stronger than death.
Hope stronger than persecution.
Hope stronger than hell itself.
The resurrection of Jesus already changed history.
The cross already secured victory.
The empty tomb already announced the collapse of death’s final authority.
And Revelation reveals the completion of what Christ began.
Not uncertainty.
Completion.
This does not mean Christians should ignore prophecy.
Biblical prophecy matters deeply.
Jesus Himself spoke prophetically.
The apostles taught about Christ’s return.
Scripture calls believers to readiness.
But readiness is not hysteria.
Readiness is faithful obedience.
Holiness.
Love.
Repentance.
Perseverance.
Watching with oil in our lamps.
Living awake.
Living surrendered.
Living ready to meet Christ whether He returns tomorrow or centuries from now.
That is biblical vigilance.
And perhaps the greatest misunderstanding about Revelation is this:
Many think the central message is “Be afraid.”
But over and over again, Scripture says:
“Do not fear.”
To the frightened churches.
To persecuted believers.
To suffering saints.
To exhausted disciples.
Jesus says:
“Fear not.”
In Revelation 1:17:
“Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last.”
The Greek:
Μὴ φοβοῦ
Mē phobou.
Stop being afraid.
Why?
Because Christ is alive.
Because the grave lost.
Because death does not own the final chapter.
Because the Lamb reigns.
Because the King is coming.
And because faithful believers belong to Him.
That is not escapist fantasy.
That is Christian hope.
Real hope.
Ancient hope.
Blood-bought hope.
And maybe someone reading this needed permission to breathe again.
To stop obsessively chasing panic.
To stop feeding spiritual anxiety.
To stop treating every news cycle like another apocalypse countdown.
To open Revelation again and actually see Jesus.
The scarred Lamb.
The risen King.
The faithful witness.
The ruler of kings.
The One walking among the lampstands.
The One who still holds His Church.
Even now.
Especially now.
So… could Christians be misunderstanding Revelation?
Some probably are.
But maybe the deeper question is this:
Have we been reading Revelation looking for fear instead of faithfulness?
Looking for speculation instead of surrender?
Looking for secrets instead of the Savior?
Because the greatest tragedy would not be misunderstanding symbols.
The greatest tragedy would be missing Jesus while studying the book that reveals Him.
And maybe that realization hits harder than expected.
Be honest.
Has fear ever shaped the way you viewed Revelation?
The book was never meant to make you fear the darkness more than you trust the Lamb.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Zerubbabel: The Man Who Rebuilt While Carrying Ruins Inside Him
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Zerubbabel: The Man Who Rebuilt While Carrying Ruins Inside Him
Most people remember kings.
Warriors.
Prophets who called down fire.
Men whose names thunder through history.
But Scripture hides some of its deepest pain inside quiet names.
Zerubbabel was one of them.
A man born in exile. A prince without a throne. A leader carrying the memory of a kingdom he never personally saw. A builder standing among broken stones while older men cried around him.
His story does not begin with victory.
It begins with collapse.
Jerusalem had fallen. The Temple had been burned. The holy city was turned into smoke and rubble by Babylon. The people of God were dragged away in chains.
And inside the ashes of national judgment, a child would eventually be born whose very name carried the sound of Babylon.
זְרֻבָּבֶל — Zerubbāḇel.
Most scholars understand the name to mean: “Seed of Babylon” or “Born in Babylon.”
Imagine carrying that name your entire life.
Every introduction reminding you where your people were humiliated. Every breath connected to exile. Every memory tied to consequences your nation created.
Some people today know exactly what that feels like.
Being born into generational damage. Being raised inside the aftermath of someone else’s rebellion. Being handed trauma you did not personally create.
Zerubbabel did not choose Babylon.
But Babylon shaped him.
And maybe that is why his story matters more than most people realize.
Because countless believers love God while secretly carrying exile inside their soul.
They worship. But still feel displaced.
They pray. But still feel internally ruined.
They believe. But parts of them still smell like captivity.
And this is where God enters the story.
Not after the healing. Not after perfection. Not after the wounds disappear.
But right in the middle of the rubble.
The Persian king Cyrus eventually issued a decree allowing Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem.
Ezra 2 records the names of those returning. And there he is.
Zerubbabel.
Not hiding. Not running. Not remaining comfortable in Babylon.
Returning.
The journey itself was brutal. Hundreds of miles. Dangerous terrain. Uncertain future. A destroyed homeland waiting ahead.
And yet he went.
Some people never leave Babylon because Babylon becomes familiar.
Bondage can become comfortable when people live in it long enough.
That is one of the most terrifying realities in spiritual life.
Some believers know Egypt better than freedom. Some know addiction better than holiness. Some know compromise better than surrender.
But Zerubbabel walked away from the system that shaped him.
And the moment he arrived in Jerusalem, reality hit.
The city was devastated.
The Temple of Solomon — once breathtaking beyond imagination — was gone.
The Hebrew word used repeatedly around this devastation carries imagery of desolation and waste.
חָרֵב — ḥārēḇ.
Ruined. Destroyed. Desolate.
This was not cosmetic damage.
This was generational heartbreak.
Imagine elderly survivors standing among burned stones remembering what once existed.
Imagine younger generations trying to understand glory they never personally witnessed.
Imagine leading people who are emotionally exhausted before rebuilding even begins.
That was Zerubbabel’s assignment.
Not celebrity. Not applause.
Rebuilding.
Some people think God only calls people into exciting assignments.
But many times God calls people into restoration work.
Repairing marriages. Repairing families. Repairing churches. Repairing trust. Repairing spiritual disciplines. Repairing souls.
And restoration work is exhausting because you constantly see evidence of what was lost.
Ezra 3 describes the moment the foundation of the Second Temple was laid.
The younger generation shouted with joy.
But the older men wept loudly.
Why?
Because they remembered Solomon’s Temple.
The new foundation looked smaller. Weaker. Less glorious.
And suddenly Zerubbabel faced one of the cruelest emotional battles in leadership:
Building something people constantly compare to the past.
That still destroys many believers today.
Comparison.
People compare their healing to someone else. Their ministry to someone else. Their growth to someone else. Their marriage to someone else. Their spiritual life to who they used to be.
And comparison suffocates gratitude.
But God was not asking Zerubbabel to rebuild Solomon’s Temple.
God was asking him to obey.
There is a difference.
Some of you are collapsing emotionally because you are trying to recreate old glory instead of stewarding present obedience.
And then opposition arrived.
Of course it did.
Because hell rarely stays silent when God starts rebuilding ruins.
Enemies mocked the workers. Threatened them. Manipulated political systems. Created fear. Spread discouragement.
Eventually construction stopped.
Years passed.
Imagine the shame.
Half-built foundations. Unfinished calling. Public disappointment. Private exhaustion.
Many believers know this feeling.
Starting strong. Then stalling. Then silently wondering if God has abandoned the assignment.
But God had not forgotten Zerubbabel.
God raised prophets.
Haggai. Zechariah.
And suddenly Heaven spoke directly into the paralysis.
One of the most famous verses connected to Zerubbabel appears in Zechariah 4:6.
In Hebrew:
לֹא בְחַיִל וְלֹא בְכֹחַ כִּי אִם־בְּרוּחִי
Transliteration: Lo ḇəḥayil wəlo ḇəḵoaḥ ki ʾim-bərūḥi.
True translation: “Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit.”
The word רוּחַ — ruaḥ — means spirit, breath, wind.
God was telling Zerubbabel:
“You will not finish this through human strength.”
That word still confronts modern believers.
Because many people are trying to heal themselves through discipline without dependence on God.
Trying to conquer temptation through willpower alone. Trying to rebuild spiritually while prayer remains empty. Trying to carry burdens Heaven never asked them to carry alone.
But the rebuilding of sacred things has always required the Spirit of God.
Then comes one of the most emotional moments in Zerubbabel’s story.
Zechariah 4:10 says:
“For who has despised the day of small things?”
In Hebrew:
כִּי מִי בַז לְיוֹם קְטַנּוֹת
Ki mi baz leyom qetannoth?
The word בַז — baz — means to despise, scorn, treat as insignificant.
God was rebuking people who mocked small beginnings.
And honestly?
Many believers secretly despise small beginnings.
Small progress. Small healing. Small obedience. Small victories. Small faithfulness.
But Heaven celebrates what pride ignores.
One prayer can begin restoration. One act of repentance can change generations. One surrendered heart can transform an entire family.
Never underestimate what God starts quietly.
The world worships visible greatness.
But God often hides eternity inside small obedience.
And then Zechariah gives Zerubbabel a promise that feels impossible.
“The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it.” — Zechariah 4:9
Imagine hearing that while surrounded by resistance.
God declared completion before circumstances confirmed it.
That is faith.
Not pretending pain does not exist.
But believing God remains sovereign inside unfinished places.
There are people reading this right now who feel spiritually unfinished.
You started rebuilding. Then fear returned. Temptation returned. Depression returned. Exhaustion returned.
But hear this clearly:
God is not intimidated by incomplete construction.
The Builder of souls has always worked through process.
Even the Greek language of the New Testament repeatedly carries this idea of ongoing transformation.
One powerful example appears in Philippians 1:6.
ἐπιτελέσει — epitelesei.
“He will complete it.”
Not abandon. Not forget. Not discard.
Complete.
God finishes what He truly authors.
Eventually the Temple was completed.
Not as grand outwardly as Solomon’s. But filled with something deeper.
Faithfulness.
The rebuilt Temple became proof that judgment was not the end of Israel’s story.
Grace still spoke.
And then comes the detail many overlook.
Zerubbabel appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:12.
A man born in exile becomes part of the bloodline leading to the Messiah.
Read that slowly.
The “seed of Babylon” becomes part of the lineage of redemption.
Only God writes stories like that.
Only God takes exile and turns it into testimony. Only God takes ruins and creates restoration. Only God takes broken history and weaves grace through it.
Some of you have spent years believing your past disqualified you.
Your failures. Your addictions. Your compromises. Your secret battles. Your wasted years.
But Zerubbabel’s story screams something powerful:
God still uses people born in the middle of ruins.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because many people are exhausted from pretending they are spiritually stronger than they really are.
But God never asked Zerubbabel to pretend the rubble did not exist.
He asked him to rebuild anyway.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for polished people.
He came for ruined people.
The Greek word often used for salvation in the New Testament is:
σῴζω — sōzō.
It means: To save. To rescue. To heal. To make whole.
Not merely legal forgiveness.
Restoration.
Jesus does not merely forgive sinners. He rebuilds them.
Brick by brick. Prayer by prayer. Surrender by surrender.
And some rebuilding hurts.
Because God cannot restore what pride refuses to expose.
Some readers need to stop hiding.
You are exhausted. Spiritually numb. Secretly battling sin. Losing hope. Pretending everything is fine while your soul quietly collapses.
But the God who walked with Zerubbabel among ruins still walks among ruins today.
He still rebuilds.
Even now.
Especially now.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because some people are not reading for entertainment anymore.
They are searching for hope before they completely fall apart.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Nakukuwentong Istorya ni Zerubbabel: Ang Lalaking Nagtayo ng Templo Habang Wasak Din ang Loob
May mga pangalan sa Biblia na madalas nating marinig.
David. Moises. Elijah.
Pero may mga taong halos hindi napapansin… kahit dala nila ang isa sa pinakamabibigat na kwento sa buong Kasulatan.
Isa doon si Zerubbabel.
Hindi siya lumaki sa palasyo. Hindi siya isinilang sa panahon ng tagumpay.
Isinilang siya sa pagkabihag.
Ang pangalan niyang זְרֻבָּבֶל — Zerubbāḇel — ay may kahulugang: “Binhi ng Babylon” o “Isinilang sa Babylon.”
Isipin mo iyon.
Habang buhay mong dala ang pangalan ng lugar kung saan nadurog ang bayan ng Diyos.
Jerusalem wasak. Ang templo sinunog. Ang Israel bihag.
At sa gitna ng kahihiyan ng buong bansa… doon isinilang si Zerubbabel.
Maraming tao ngayon ang ganyan din ang pakiramdam.
Lumaki sa sirang pamilya. Lumaki sa trauma. Lumaki sa kasalanang hindi naman sila ang nagsimula.
Parang minana nila ang pagkawasak.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakalalim ng kwento ni Zerubbabel.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ang nagmamahal kay Jesus… pero may Babylon pa rin sa loob nila.
Ngumingiti. Pero sugatan.
Naglilingkod. Pero pagod na pagod.
Nananalangin. Pero parang wasak pa rin ang kaluluwa.
At dito nagsisimulang kumilos ang Diyos.
Hindi pagkatapos maayos ang lahat. Hindi pagkatapos maging malinis.
Kundi habang may guho pa.
Nang payagan ni Haring Cyrus ang mga Hudyo na bumalik sa Jerusalem, isa si Zerubbabel sa unang bumalik.
Pwede naman siyang manatili sa Babylon.
Mas komportable doon. Mas ligtas. Mas pamilyar.
Pero may mga tao na kahit komportable na sa pagkabihag… may tinig pa rin ang Diyos na humihila pabalik.
At nang makarating sila sa Jerusalem, tumambad ang realidad.
Wasak lahat.
Ang templo ni Solomon na minsang simbolo ng kaluwalhatian ng Diyos… abo na lang.
Ang salitang Hebrew na ginagamit para sa pagkawasak ay:
חָרֵב — ḥārēḇ.
Desolate. Ruined. Wasak.
Hindi simpleng sira.
Parang buhay ng maraming tao ngayon.
Mukhang maayos sa labas. Pero sa loob… guho.
At iyon ang assignment ni Zerubbabel.
Hindi kasikatan. Hindi komportableng buhay.
Kundi magtayo muli.
At minsan iyon ang pinakamahirap gawin.
Mag-rebuild habang ikaw mismo sugatan.
Ezra 3 describes one of the most heartbreaking moments.
Nang ilagay ang pundasyon ng bagong templo, ang mga kabataan nagsisigawan sa tuwa.
Pero ang matatanda umiiyak.
Dahil nakita nila ang dating templo.
Mas maganda. Mas engrande. Mas maluwalhati.
At doon pumapasok ang isa sa pinakamalalaking laban ng tao:
Comparison.
Kinukumpara natin ang healing natin sa iba. Ang faith natin sa dati nating sarili. Ang buhay natin sa nakikita natin online.
At unti-unting pinapatay ng comparison ang gratitude.
Pero hindi hinihingi ng Diyos kay Zerubbabel na gayahin si Solomon.
Ang hinihingi ng Diyos ay obedience.
May pagkakaiba iyon.
Hindi ka tinawag ng Diyos para maging ibang tao. Tinawag ka Niya para maging tapat.
Pero syempre dumating ang opposition.
Dahil kapag may nire-restore ang Diyos… hindi tahimik ang kaaway.
May pananakot. May discouragement. May pagod. May delays.
At dumating sa puntong tumigil ang pagtatayo.
Maraming taon.
Imagine the shame.
Half-finished calling. Incomplete assignment. Public disappointment.
Maraming believers ang nandiyan ngayon.
Nagsimula nang malakas. Pero napagod. Natakot. Nanlamig.
Pero hindi nakalimutan ng Diyos si Zerubbabel.
Nagpadala Siya ng salita.
Sa Zechariah 4:6:
לֹא בְחַיִל וְלֹא בְכֹחַ כִּי אִם־בְּרוּחִי
Lo ḇəḥayil wəlo ḇəḵoaḥ ki ʾim-bərūḥi.
“Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit.”
Ang salitang רוּחַ — ruaḥ — ay nangangahulugang hininga, hangin, Espiritu.
Parang sinasabi ng Diyos:
“Hindi mo ito matatapos sa sarili mong lakas.”
At totoo iyon hanggang ngayon.
Maraming tao ang pilit inaayos ang sarili nila nang walang presensya ng Diyos.
Trying to heal without surrender. Trying to survive without prayer. Trying to rebuild habang ubos na ubos na.
Pero may mga bagay na tanging Espiritu ng Diyos lang ang kayang buuin muli.
Then comes one of the most powerful verses.
Zechariah 4:10:
“For who has despised the day of small things?”
Hebrew:
כִּי מִי בַז לְיוֹם קְטַנּוֹת
Ki mi baz leyom qetannoth?
Maraming tao minamaliit ang small beginnings.
Maliit na progress. Maliit na healing. Maliit na pagbabago.
Pero ang mga bagay na maliit sa tao… madalas doon nagsisimula ang himala ng Diyos.
Isang prayer. Isang repentance. Isang surrender.
Pwedeng baguhin ang buong future.
At pagkatapos ng lahat ng delays, opposition, at pagod… natapos din ang templo.
Hindi man kasing engrande ng dati.
Pero may dala itong mas malalim:
Faithfulness.
At dito lalo lumalim ang kwento.
Lumabas ang pangalan ni Zerubbabel sa genealogy ni Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:12.
Ang lalaking ipinanganak sa Babylon… naging bahagi ng linya ng Mesiyas.
Only God can write stories like that.
Ang taong galing sa pagkawasak… ginawang bahagi ng redemption story.
Kaya kung pakiramdam mo disqualified ka dahil sa nakaraan mo…
Makinig ka.
Hindi hadlang sa Diyos ang ruins.
Minsan doon pa Siya nagsisimulang magtayo.
Ang Greek word na ginagamit sa New Testament para sa salvation ay:
σῴζω — sōzō.
Hindi lang “save.”
Kundi: Heal. Restore. Make whole.
Hindi lang pinapatawad ni Jesus ang tao.
Binubuo Niya ulit.
Pira-piraso.
At baka iyon ang kailangan marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Hindi pa tapos ang Diyos sa’yo.
Kahit pagod ka na. Kahit umiiyak ka na nang tahimik. Kahit parang wasak ulit ang buhay.
Hindi pa tapos.
Save this para balikan mo kapag pakiramdam mo maliit lang ang progress mo.
Dahil may mga taong hindi na naghahanap ng entertainment.
Naghahanap sila ng pag-asa bago sila tuluyang madurog.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Secret Mystery Behind Why God Asked for Firstfruits
paragraphs: The Secret Mystery Behind Why God Asked for Firstfruits
There is something deeply mysterious about the very first thing.
The first breath. The first cry. The first seed. The firstborn. The first harvest. The first surrender.
God has always asked humanity for the first.
Not because He is poor. Not because Heaven lacks resources. Not because the Creator of galaxies needed grain, lambs, oil, wine, or money.
So why did God establish the principle of firstfruits?

Why did He speak about it so intensely throughout Scripture? Why did entire blessings and judgments seem connected to whether people honored Him first? Why did Cain and Abel’s offerings end differently? Why did Jericho belong entirely to God? Why was Israel commanded never to eat certain first harvests until they were offered? Why did Jesus Himself become called the “firstfruits”?
The mystery goes far deeper than agriculture.
Firstfruits was never merely about farming.
It was always about trust. Identity. Order. Covenant. Worship. Kingship. And the war over who truly owns your future.
Most people think firstfruits means “giving God something first.”
Biblically, it means something much more terrifying and beautiful.
It means declaring that God owns the source before you ever touch the supply.
And that changes everything.
In Hebrew, the word for firstfruits is:
בִּכּוּרִים Bikkurim
The root comes from:
בָּכַר Bakar
Meaning: “the firstborn,” “the earliest,” “the choicest,” “that which opens first.”
This is critical.
God was never asking for leftovers.
He was asking for the opening.
The first opening of the womb. The first opening of the harvest. The first opening of increase. The first opening of blessing. The first opening of trust.
Because whatever opens first reveals what reigns most.
Exodus 13:2 says:
"Consecrate to Me every firstborn male. The first offspring of every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, whether human or animal."
In Hebrew:
קַדֶּשׁ־לִי כָל־בְּכוֹר Kaddesh-li kol-bekhor
“Set apart unto Me every firstborn.”
The word kaddesh means: “to sanctify,” “to make holy,” “to separate unto divine purpose.”
God claimed the first because the first represented the whole.
This is one of the greatest hidden mysteries in all of Scripture.
The first sanctifies the rest.
Romans 11:16 reveals this exact principle:
"If the firstfruit is holy, the whole lump is holy."
In Greek:
εἰ δὲ ἡ ἀπαρχὴ ἁγία ei de hē aparchē hagia
The word:
ἀπαρχή aparchē
means: “the beginning sacrifice,” “the initial offering,” “the first portion dedicated to God.”
Paul reveals an ancient spiritual law.
The first portion determines the spiritual condition of what follows.
This was never superstition.
It was covenant order.
The reason God asked for firstfruits was because He was teaching Israel a terrifying truth:
If God is not first, eventually something else becomes god.
Human hearts naturally drift toward self-dependence.
So God created systems of remembrance.
Firstfruits forced people to remember:
“The harvest did not come from me.” “The increase did not come from my strength.” “My future does not belong to fear.” “Provision does not begin with my labor.” “It begins with God.”
This is why Proverbs 3:9–10 says:
"Honor the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing."
The Hebrew word for “honor” is:
כַּבֵּד Kabbed
from:
כָּבוֹד Kavod
Meaning: “weight,” “glory,” “substance,” “importance.”
To honor God with firstfruits meant:
“You carry more weight in my heart than survival itself.”
That is why firstfruits required faith.
Because you gave before knowing the final harvest.
Anyone can give after abundance appears.
But firstfruits demanded surrender before certainty.
That is why Cain and Abel matter so deeply.
Genesis 4 never simply describes two random offerings.
It reveals two different heart postures.
Scripture says Abel brought:
"the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions."
But Cain merely brought:
"some of the fruits of the soil."
The Hebrew structure implies intentional distinction.
Abel brought the first and the best. Cain brought an offering without covenant priority.
One recognized God as source. The other treated God as optional.
The issue was never vegetables versus animals.
The issue was firstness.
Hebrews 11:4 later explains:
"By faith Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain."
Faith was connected to the first.
Because firstfruits is fundamentally an act of trust.
And trust exposes worship.
This is also why Jericho became untouchable.
Most people miss this mystery entirely.
Jericho was the first city conquered in the Promised Land.
And God commanded Israel not to touch the spoils.
Why?
Because the first conquest belonged entirely to Him.
Joshua 6:19 says:
"All the silver and gold and articles of bronze and iron are sacred to the LORD and must go into His treasury."
Jericho was firstfruits.
And when Achan stole from it, the sin was not merely theft.
It was violation of firstfruits.
Achan touched what represented God’s ownership over the entire conquest.
This explains why judgment came so severely.
Because firstfruits declares:
“The future victory already belongs to God.”
There is another mystery hidden in Leviticus 23.
God commanded Israel to wave the first sheaf before Him during Passover season.
Leviticus 23:10–11:

"When you enter the land I am going to give you and you reap its harvest, bring to the priest a sheaf of the first grain you harvest. He is to wave the sheaf before the LORD so it will be accepted on your behalf."
The Hebrew phrase:
רֵאשִׁית קְצִירְכֶם Reshit qetsirkhem
means: “the beginning of your harvest.”
This offering happened before the full harvest arrived.
Again: God demanded trust before visible completion.
But then something extraordinary happens in the New Testament.
Jesus becomes the fulfillment of firstfruits itself.
1 Corinthians 15:20:
"But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep."
In Greek:
ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων aparchē tōn kekoimēmenōn
Jesus is called the firstfruits of resurrection.
This is staggering.
It means His resurrection was not isolated.
It was the first portion guaranteeing the full harvest to come.
Just as the first sheaf prophetically sanctified the future harvest, Christ’s resurrection guarantees the resurrection of all who belong to Him.
This is why the resurrection happened during the Feast of Firstfruits.
Nothing in Scripture is accidental.
Jesus fulfilled the prophetic pattern perfectly.
The firstfruit offering in ancient Israel was lifted before God.
And Christ Himself was lifted from the grave as Heaven’s firstfruits.
The pattern had always been pointing toward Him.
This is why James 1:18 says believers themselves become:
"a kind of firstfruits of His creatures."
God always desired a people fully consecrated to Him.
Firstfruits was never ultimately about crops.
It was about hearts.
Hearts surrendered first. Hearts yielded first. Hearts trusting first. Hearts loving God before comfort.
This is why Jesus said in Matthew 6:33:
"Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness."
The Greek word for first is:
πρῶτον prōton
Meaning: “first in order,” “first in priority,” “first in rank.”
The Kingdom is not supposed to be added somewhere into life.
It must become the governing first.
Because whatever comes first shapes everything after it.
This is the hidden mystery behind firstfruits.
God was never after fruit.
He was after enthronement.
The first thing reveals the ruling thing.
What gets your first attention? Your first affection? Your first obedience? Your first energy? Your first thoughts? Your first loyalty? Your first trust?
That is your functional god.
This is why firstfruits remains spiritually powerful even beyond ancient agricultural systems.
People often reduce it to money.
But biblically, firstfruits touches every area of life.
The first moments of your morning. The first response during pain. The first instinct during fear. The first reaction during crisis. The first place your mind runs.
Those reveal worship.
Some people wake up and reach for anxiety first. Others reach for social media first. Others reach for lust first. Others reach for ambition first.
But God says:
“Seek Me first.”
Not because He is insecure.
Because He understands the architecture of the human soul.
Whatever comes first eventually governs what follows.
This is why Satan constantly fights for first place.
The enemy does not merely want moments.
He wants precedence.
Because precedence creates influence.
And influence shapes identity.
That is why Scripture repeatedly warns against idolatry.
An idol is not merely a carved object.
An idol is anything enthroned before God.
Anything trusted more deeply. Anything obeyed more quickly. Anything feared more intensely. Anything loved more completely.
The war over firstfruits is ultimately the war over kingship.
Who reigns first?
That is the real question.
And this is exactly why Jesus said the greatest commandment is:
"Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength."
Totality. Priority. Firstness.
The Gospel itself begins with firstness.
John 3:16 says:
"For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son."
Before humanity ever surrendered anything to God… God gave first.
Before repentance, He loved first. Before obedience, He pursued first. Before restoration, He sacrificed first.
Even firstfruits ultimately reflects the character of God Himself.
He never asks humanity to do something He did not first reveal through His own nature.
Romans 5:8 says:
"While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
God moved first.
This changes the entire emotional meaning of firstfruits.
It is no longer religious transaction.
It becomes relational response.
We give God the first because He first loved us.
1 John 4:19:
"We love because He first loved us."
In Greek:
ἡμεῖς ἀγαπῶμεν ὅτι αὐτὸς πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς Hēmeis agapōmen hoti autos prōtos ēgapēsen hēmas
The word:
πρῶτος prōtos
Again means: “first.”
God initiates covenant.
Humanity responds.
That is the mystery.
The principle of firstfruits was never about enriching Heaven.
It was about transforming hearts enslaved to fear, self-reliance, greed, control, and idolatry.
Because the first thing surrendered breaks the illusion that we are our own source.
And honestly… this is where many people struggle.
Not because they hate God.
But because surrendering the first requires trust deeper than emotion.
It means:
“I believe You are faithful before I see the outcome.”
That is terrifying to the flesh.
The flesh wants guarantees. The flesh wants visible proof. The flesh wants control.
But covenant trust often requires obedience before evidence.
That is why firstfruits always carried spiritual weight.
It exposed whether people truly believed God.
This is why Malachi 3 became so confrontational.
Israel had stopped honoring God properly.
Their worship became partial. Mechanical. Convenient. Leftover.
And God rebuked them because covenant had become empty performance.
The issue was never divine greed.
It was spiritual drift.
Their priorities revealed their hearts had moved away from Him.
Jesus later confronts the same issue repeatedly.
People honored God externally while enthroning other things internally.
Religious activity without surrendered priority.
And that still happens now.

People sing worship songs while fear rules their decisions. People quote Scripture while lust rules their habits. People attend church while ambition rules their identity. People say “God first” while giving Him whatever remains.
But God sees firstness.
He sees what reigns.
And this is why repentance matters so deeply.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad.
In Greek, repentance is:
μετάνοια metanoia
Meaning: “a change of mind,” “a turning,” “a transformation of inner direction.”
Real repentance restores God to first place.
That is why revival always begins with reordered love.
Not emotional hype. Not performance. Not appearances.
But restored firstness.
The church in Ephesus in Revelation had doctrine. Service. Perseverance. Orthodoxy.
But Jesus said:
"You have forsaken your first love."
In Greek:
τὴν ἀγάπην σου τὴν πρώτην tēn agapēn sou tēn prōtēn
Your first love.
The earliest. The primary. The ruling affection.
Even mature believers can slowly lose firstness.
And that is dangerous.
Because Christianity without first love eventually becomes religious machinery.
This is why the mystery of firstfruits still matters today.
It is not merely an Old Testament ritual.
It is a revelation about spiritual order.
God must remain first.
Not because He needs position.
But because humanity collapses when anything else occupies the throne.
Money makes a cruel god. Pleasure makes a cruel god. Approval makes a cruel god. Success makes a cruel god. Politics makes a cruel god. Self makes a cruel god.
Only Christ can sit on the throne without destroying the soul.
That is the secret mystery.
Firstfruits was always preparing humanity to understand Jesus.
The true Firstborn. The true Offering. The true Beginning. The true Consecrated One. The true Resurrection. The true King.
Colossians 1:18 says:
"He is the beginning and the firstborn from among the dead."
In Greek:
πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν prōtotokos ek tōn nekrōn
Meaning: “the supreme firstborn.”
Jesus is Heaven’s declaration that a new creation has begun.
And everyone who belongs to Him becomes part of that future harvest.
This is why firstfruits ultimately points beyond offerings.
It points toward redemption.
Toward resurrection. Toward surrender. Toward restored worship. Toward covenant intimacy. Toward Christ Himself.
And maybe that is what hurts some hearts while reading this.
Because deep down… many people already know something else has quietly taken first place.
A hidden addiction. A relationship. A wound. An obsession. A fear. A secret compromise. A constant distraction.
And the Holy Spirit keeps whispering:
“Return to Me.”
Not because God wants empty ritual.
But because He wants your heart alive again.
The enemy wants believers spiritually numb. Distracted. Fragmented. Exhausted. Double-minded.
But God still calls people back to first love. First surrender. First trust. First devotion.
And the beautiful part is this:
Jesus does not merely demand first place.
He is worthy of it.
No one has loved humanity like Christ. No one has bled like Christ. No one has forgiven like Christ. No one has pursued broken sinners like Christ. No one has conquered death like Christ.
The cross forever settled His worthiness.
And maybe today is the day someone finally stops giving God leftovers.
Not out of religious pressure.
But because they finally understand:
He gave Himself first.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
One surrendered first thing can change the direction of an entire life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People?
paragraphs: Why Do Bad Things Happen to Good People?
There are nights when heaven feels silent.
Not poetic silence. Not peaceful silence. Not the kind preached about in polished sermons.
The kind of silence that sits beside a hospital bed. The kind that stares back from an empty chair at the dinner table. The kind that shows up after the funeral when everybody else goes home.
The kind that makes even faithful people whisper:
“God… where were You?”
Because if we are honest, this question has lived inside humanity since the dust of Eden first tasted sorrow.
Why do bad things happen to good people?

Why does cancer invade praying homes? Why are children buried before parents? Why are loyal spouses betrayed? Why are the righteous crushed while the wicked seem to flourish? Why do some of the most faithful believers carry the heaviest scars?
And maybe the hardest part of all…
Why does God sometimes allow pain He could stop?
Most people do not lose faith because they studied too much. They lose faith because they suffered too deeply.
The tears became louder than the theology.

And yet buried inside Scripture is a truth so raw, so piercing, and so beautiful that it has carried martyrs through prisons, widows through grief, addicts through withdrawal, and shattered believers through nights they thought they would never survive.
This is not an easy article.
But it may be the article somebody has been praying for.
Because some wounds only heal when truth finally touches them.
The Bible never actually says good people suffer.
That sentence alone shocks many Christians.
Because according to Scripture, no human being is truly righteous on their own.
The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 3:10:
The Greek word Paul uses is:
δικαιος (dikaios)
Meaning: just, righteous, perfectly upright before God.
Not mostly good. Not morally decent. Not better than others.
Perfect.
And Scripture says nobody qualifies.
Not pastors. Not churches. Not influencers. Not religious leaders. Not the person who gives to charity.
Nobody.
That changes the entire conversation.
The question is not actually: “Why do bad things happen to good people?”
Biblically speaking, the deeper question becomes:
“Why does a holy God continue showing mercy to sinful people living in a broken world?”
That is not meant to sound harsh. It is meant to reveal the seriousness of sin.
Because modern culture talks about sin casually while heaven speaks about it catastrophically.
In Genesis 3, humanity rebelled against God.
The Hebrew word for sin later used throughout the Old Testament is:
חטא (chata)
Meaning: “To miss the mark.”
Humanity missed the holiness of God.
And when sin entered the world, death entered with it. Disease entered. Violence entered. Decay entered. Corruption entered.
Creation itself became fractured.
Romans 8 says creation groans.
Not humanity alone. Creation.
The oceans. The earth. The body. The mind. Everything.
This world is not functioning the way God originally designed it.
That matters.
Because many people blame God for things God actually hates.
God hates death. God hates evil. God hates injustice. God hates abuse. God hates sin.
Jesus wept at Lazarus’ tomb even though He knew resurrection was minutes away.
Think about that.
The Son of God stood face to face with death and still cried.
The Greek text in John 11:35 simply says:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
“Jesus wept.”
Two words.
Yet oceans of theology live inside them.
God is not emotionally detached from human suffering.
He enters it.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not the story of a distant God observing pain from heaven.
It is the story of God stepping into human suffering Himself.
Jesus did not come wrapped in political power. He came wrapped in vulnerability.
He was betrayed. Rejected. Mocked. Beaten. Abandoned. Falsely accused. Tortured. Crucified.
Isaiah 53 calls Him:
“A man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew phrase for “acquainted with grief” carries the idea of intimate familiarity.
Not surface-level awareness. Deep experience.
Jesus understands suffering from the inside.
Somebody reading this has secretly asked:
“If God loved me, why would He allow this?”
But the cross answers differently.
The cross says:
“I loved you enough to suffer with you.”
There are pains God removes.
And there are pains God redeems.
That distinction is life-changing.
Paul begged God three times to remove what he called a “thorn in the flesh.”
But instead of removal, God gave grace.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness.”
The Greek word for sufficient is:
ἀρκέω (arkeo)
Meaning: to be enough, to satisfy completely.
God was telling Paul:
“My grace will carry what your strength cannot.”
Some people only know God as Savior.
Others meet Him as Sustainer.
And strangely, suffering often introduces believers to dimensions of God comfort never could.
Nobody wants the valley.
But valleys reveal things mountaintops cannot.
In comfort, people quote Scripture. In suffering, they cling to it like oxygen.
Job understood this better than almost anyone.
He lost wealth. Children. Security. Health. Reputation.
And yet one of the most staggering verses in Scripture comes from a broken man sitting in ashes:
“Though He slay me, yet will I trust Him.”
That is not shallow Christianity.
That is war-tested faith.
Job never got every answer.
That bothers modern people.
We want explanations. Timelines. Reasons. Clarity.
But God often gives presence before explanation.
And sometimes the greatest miracle is not immediate deliverance.
Sometimes the greatest miracle is surviving without losing your soul.
There are believers reading this who never thought they would make it through what they survived.
But somehow… God carried them.
Not perfectly. Not cleanly. Not without tears.
But He carried them.
You may still cry when nobody is around. You may still wrestle with fear. You may still have questions.
But you are still here.
And that matters more than you know.
Because there are people silently reading this who need to know they are not alone.
One of the deepest misunderstandings in modern Christianity is the belief that obedience guarantees earthly ease.
It does not.
Jesus never promised believers a painless life.
He promised believers a faithful Savior.
In John 16:33, Jesus says:
“In this world you will have tribulation.”
The Greek word is:
θλῖψις (thlipsis)
Meaning: pressure, affliction, crushing weight.
Jesus did not hide suffering from His followers.
He prepared them for it.
But He continued:
“Take heart; I have overcome the world.”
Not “might overcome.” Not “hopefully overcome.”
Have overcome.
Victory was already secured through Christ.
That does not erase pain. But it gives pain an expiration date.
For believers, suffering is never the final chapter.
Resurrection always has the last word.
The enemy wants suffering to convince people God abandoned them.
But often suffering becomes the very place God transforms them.
Peter, once terrified of a servant girl, became fearless after brokenness refined him.
Joseph was betrayed before he was elevated.
David was hunted before he was crowned.
Paul was imprisoned before he shook nations.
Even Jesus wore a crown of thorns before a crown of glory.
Sometimes God develops eternal strength through temporary suffering.
Not all pain is punishment.
That truth needs to be heard carefully.
Some suffering comes from personal sin. Some from living in a fallen world. Some from spiritual warfare. Some from the consequences of other people’s choices.
And sometimes… suffering remains mysterious.
Anybody who pretends to fully explain every tragedy is speaking beyond Scripture.
Even the disciples once asked Jesus regarding a blind man:
“Who sinned, this man or his parents?”
Jesus answered:
“Neither.”
That shattered their assumptions.
Not every wound is direct punishment.
Some pain becomes a platform where God reveals His glory in ways human understanding cannot fully comprehend.
Still… that does not make suffering emotionally easy.
Somebody reading this prayed for healing and buried the person anyway.
Somebody begged God to save the marriage and watched it collapse.
Somebody fasted for breakthrough and still lost the job.
And the hardest battles are often the invisible ones.
The depression nobody notices. The anxiety hidden behind jokes. The secret addiction. The exhaustion. The loneliness. The silent disappointment with God.
Some believers feel guilty for struggling.
But Scripture is full of emotionally overwhelmed people.
David cried. Jeremiah lamented. Elijah collapsed emotionally. Even Jesus sweat blood under agony in Gethsemane.
Biblical faith is not pretending pain does not exist.
Biblical faith is bringing pain honestly before God.
The Hebrew word often translated as peace is:
שָׁלוֹם (shalom)
But shalom means far more than emotional calm.
It means: wholeness, restoration, completeness, things brought back into proper order.
That means God’s ultimate plan is not temporary distraction.
It is full restoration.
One day death will die. One day graves will open. One day suffering will end. One day Christ will wipe away every tear.
Revelation does not end with pain. It ends with restoration.
That is the Christian hope.
Not escapism. Not denial.
Resurrection.
And until that day, believers live in tension.
We grieve. But not without hope.
We suffer. But not abandoned.
We bleed. But not without purpose.
The enemy whispers: “Your suffering proves God left you.”
But Calvary says the opposite.
The nails say God stayed.
There is another uncomfortable truth many avoid.
Some people become spiritually awake only after suffering strips away illusions.
Comfort can make people independent from God.
Pain often exposes how fragile human control really is.
C.S. Lewis once wrote:
“God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains.”
Many believers discovered their deepest intimacy with God inside seasons they would never choose again.
Not because pain itself is holy.
But because desperation often destroys pride.
And pride is one of the greatest barriers between humanity and surrender.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to appear strong while secretly collapsing.
You do not have to hide anymore.
Your honesty may help another wounded believer breathe again.
The Gospel does not promise a life untouched by suffering.
It promises a Savior who conquered sin, death, hell, and the grave.
The resurrection of Jesus changes the meaning of suffering forever.
Because if Christ truly rose from the dead, then pain is temporary.
Death is temporary.
Even the grave becomes temporary.
That is why early Christians faced persecution singing.
Not because suffering felt good.
But because they believed eternity was real.
Modern culture lives almost entirely for temporary comfort.
Scripture lives for eternal reality.
Paul called present suffering “light affliction” compared to eternal glory.
And Paul wrote those words after beatings, imprisonment, hunger, rejection, and persecution.
This was not naïve optimism.
It was eternal perspective.
Some wounds on earth will not fully heal until heaven.
That truth hurts.
But it is honest.
Christianity does not offer fake positivity.
It offers resurrection after crucifixion.
That difference matters.
Because many people want a crown without a cross.
But the Gospel has always been about surrender before glory.
And maybe the greatest mystery of all is this:
God can take what was meant to destroy someone and use it to rescue somebody else.
The addict becomes the voice that frees addicts. The grieving mother comforts grieving mothers. The survivor becomes the lighthouse.
What the enemy intended for destruction, God can transform into testimony.
The Hebrew word for compassion is:
רַחֲמִים (rachamim)
It carries imagery connected deeply to the womb.
Tender mercy. Deep compassion. Protective love.
That is the heart of God toward broken people.
Not disgust. Not coldness. Not abandonment.
Compassion.
Jesus did not avoid wounded people.
He moved toward them.
Toward lepers. Toward sinners. Toward the grieving. Toward the outcast. Toward the demonized. Toward the ashamed.
Toward people exactly like us.
And perhaps that is why suffering often softens believers.
People who have walked through fire tend to recognize smoke on others.
They become gentler. More compassionate. More aware of hidden battles.
Pain handled through Christ can produce profound spiritual maturity.
Not automatically. But redemptively.
Some people become bitter through suffering. Others become broken open before God.
The difference is often surrender.
And surrender is terrifying.
Because surrender means trusting God even when answers do not arrive immediately.
Faith is easy when prayers are instantly answered.
Faith becomes real when heaven feels silent and you still refuse to walk away.
Somebody reading this almost gave up.
But you are still searching. Still reading. Still hoping somewhere deep inside.
That matters.
God is closer than your pain is telling you.
The cross proves that.
And if Jesus walked out of His grave, then hopelessness never gets the final word.
There are people silently drowning who need to know healing is still possible.
Maybe you clicked this article because your heart is exhausted.
Maybe disappointment hardened you.
Maybe tragedy made you question everything.
Maybe religion failed you. Maybe people claiming to represent God wounded you deeply.
But Jesus is not the abuse you survived.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy you witnessed.
Jesus is not the betrayal that shattered your trust.
Jesus is the One who entered suffering to rescue sinners.
The One who touched lepers. The One who forgave criminals. The One who wept. The One who bled. The One who rose again.
And salvation is not earned through human goodness.
It is received through grace.
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις (charis)
Meaning: unearned favor, divine kindness, gift.
That means nobody comes to Christ because they were perfect.
People come because they desperately need mercy.
And mercy is available.
No matter how shattered the past feels. No matter how dark the addiction became. No matter how numb the soul has grown. No matter how many nights were wasted.
Jesus still saves.
Still forgives. Still restores. Still heals. Still calls people home.
The Gospel is not for flawless people.
It is for ruined people willing to surrender.
Be honest.
This article hit harder than you expected.
One day you will understand why God kept you alive through battles that should have destroyed you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Don’t call me Naomi,” she said. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.” — Ruth 1:20
paragraphs: “Don’t call me Naomi,” she said. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.” — Ruth 1:20
There are moments in Scripture where God allows us to see a wound so deep that most people rush past it because it feels too uncomfortable to examine.
Naomi is one of those wounds.
Most people remember the Book of Ruth as a beautiful love story. Redemption. Restoration. Boaz. The lineage of David. The shadow of Christ.
But hidden beneath the surface is a woman who became spiritually exhausted under the crushing weight of loss.
A woman who no longer recognized herself.
A woman who believed God Himself had turned against her.
And if we are honest, many believers secretly understand Naomi more than they admit.
They still attend church. They still know Scripture. They still speak respectfully about God.
But deep inside, there is bitterness they never healed from.
God saw it.
You knew.
The Meaning Hidden Inside Naomi’s Name
The Hebrew name Naomi is:
נָעֳמִי
Transliterated:
Na‘omi
The root word comes from the Hebrew:
נֹעַם (no‘am)
Meaning:
“pleasantness,” “sweetness,” “delight,” “beauty,” or “favor.”
Naomi’s very identity was tied to sweetness.
But by the time we encounter her in Ruth chapter 1, sweetness had been replaced by sorrow.
She says:
“אַל־תִּקְרֶאנָה לִי נָעֳמִי קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא”
Al-tiqre’nah li Na‘omi; qre’nah li Mara
“Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara.”
The word “Mara” in Hebrew:
מָרָא
comes from:
מַר (mar)
Meaning:
“bitter,” “embittered,” “painful.”
This was not merely sadness.
This was identity transformation through suffering.
Naomi was essentially saying:
“The woman you once knew no longer exists.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Naomi did not become bitter overnight.
Bitterness almost never begins with rebellion.
It begins with unresolved grief.
The Famine That Started Everything
Ruth 1:1 says:
“In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land.”
The Hebrew word for famine is:
רָעָב
ra‘av
Meaning:
“Hunger,” “starvation,” “emptiness.”
This famine struck Bethlehem.
Bethlehem in Hebrew:
בֵּית לֶחֶם
Beit Lechem
Literally means:
“House of Bread.”
Read that again.
There was no bread in the House of Bread.
God intentionally allows that tension to appear in the text.
Sometimes the very place that once fed you becomes the place where you feel empty.
Some believers know this pain.
The marriage that once felt alive becomes cold. The ministry that once burned with passion becomes mechanical. The prayer life that once felt intimate becomes silent.
And in desperation, people begin leaving spiritually familiar territory searching for survival.
That is exactly what Naomi’s family did.
Leaving Bethlehem — The Spiritual Symbolism
Ruth 1:1-2 tells us Naomi’s husband Elimelech took his family to Moab.
Moab was not merely another country.
Moab carried spiritual history.
The Moabites descended from Lot’s incestuous relationship with his daughter in Genesis 19.
Their origins were marked by shame.
Throughout Scripture, Moab often represents compromise, opposition, and spiritual distance from covenant life.
Psalm 60:8 says:
“Moab is my washpot.”
The Hebrew phrase:
מוֹאָב סִיר רַחְצִי
Mo’av sir rachtsi
carries imagery of humiliation.
Yet famine drove Naomi’s family there.
Pain has a way of pushing people into places they never thought they would go.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Sometimes suffering does not instantly destroy faith.
It slowly relocates the heart.
The Deaths That Shattered Naomi
The text moves brutally fast.
Elimelech dies.
Then Naomi’s sons marry Ruth and Orpah.
Then both sons die too.
Three graves.
One woman left standing in silence.
The Hebrew text in Ruth 1:5 says:
Vattisha’er ha’ishah
“And the woman was left.”
Left.
That word carries emotional devastation.
Not simply surviving.
Abandoned by circumstance.
Stripped.
Empty.
There are believers carrying this exact feeling.
People moved on. The world kept spinning. Church services continued. But internally they remained standing beside emotional graves nobody else understood.
And this is where bitterness begins to grow.
Not because someone hates God.
But because pain remained unanswered too long.
Naomi’s Theology Begins To Collapse
Naomi says something shocking in Ruth 1:13:
“The hand of the LORD has gone out against me.”
Hebrew:
יָצְאָה בִי יַד־יְהוָה
yatse’ah bi yad-YHWH
Meaning:
“The hand of Yahweh has come against me.”
Then later:
“I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.”
Hebrew:
אֲנִי מְלֵאָה הָלַכְתִּי וְרֵיקָם הֱשִׁיבַנִי יְהוָה
Ani mele’ah halakhti, vereiqam heshivani YHWH
“Full I departed, but empty Yahweh has returned me.”
Notice something important.
Naomi still believed in God.
She still used His covenant name.
But she interpreted every loss through the lens of divine hostility.
This is one of the most dangerous forms of spiritual bitterness.
Not atheism.
Not open rebellion.
But wounded belief.
A faith that still acknowledges God’s existence while quietly accusing His character.
Many people sitting in churches today are spiritually here.
They worship externally.
But internally they carry hidden accusations:
“Why did You allow this?” “Why didn’t You stop it?” “Why did You stay silent?”
God heard every one of those thoughts.
God saw it.
You knew.
The Difference Between Grief And Bitterness
Scripture never condemns grief.
Jesus Himself wept.
In Greek, John 11:35 says:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
edakrysen ho Iēsous
“Jesus wept.”
The Son of God openly entered human sorrow.
But bitterness is different.
The New Testament uses the Greek word:
πικρία
pikria
Meaning:
“resentment,” “poisoned bitterness,” “sharp hostility.”
Ephesians 4:31 says:
“Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you.”
Bitterness becomes dangerous because it slowly poisons perception.
A bitter person no longer interprets life clearly.
Pain becomes the lens.
Naomi could no longer see God’s mercy unfolding beside her.
Ruth was literally standing next to her.
Future redemption was walking beside her.
But bitterness blinded her to hope.
That is what bitterness does.
It convinces wounded people that the story already ended.
Ruth — The Grace Naomi Could Not Yet Recognize
One of the most powerful contrasts in the Book of Ruth is that Naomi speaks emptiness while heaven quietly sends provision.
Ruth tells Naomi:
“Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
In Hebrew:
כִּי אֶל־אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ
Ki el-asher telkhi elekh
This is covenant loyalty.
The Hebrew concept behind Ruth’s devotion connects deeply to:
חֶסֶד
chesed
Meaning:
steadfast love, loyal covenant mercy, faithful lovingkindness.
Even while Naomi believed God had abandoned her, God had already positioned Ruth as part of her restoration.
But Naomi could not yet see it.
Some people are asking God where He is while He is already moving through people, circumstances, warnings, delays, and unseen protection.
But bitterness narrows vision.
Naomi’s Bitterness Was Honest — But Incomplete
This is where careful biblical interpretation matters.
Naomi spoke honestly.
Scripture does not hide her anguish.
The Bible is brutally truthful about human emotion.
But Naomi’s interpretation was incomplete.
She believed the story was over.
Heaven knew redemption was approaching.
This is why temporary pain should never become permanent theology.
A single season cannot fully interpret God’s eternal intentions.
Isaiah 55:8-9 says:
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD.”
Hebrew:
כִּי לֹא מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי מַחְשְׁבוֹתֵיכֶם
Ki lo machshevotai machshevoteikhem
Human beings often judge God from unfinished chapters.
Naomi did.
Many still do.
The Hidden Prophecy Inside Naomi’s Story
The Book of Ruth eventually reveals Boaz as the kinsman redeemer.
In Hebrew:
גֹּאֵל
go’el
Meaning:
redeemer, restorer, one who rescues family inheritance.
This points directly toward Jesus Christ.
Because humanity also became spiritually empty.
Sin devastated us.
Isaiah 53:6 says:
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
The Hebrew word for astray:
תָּעִינוּ
ta‘inu
means wandering, losing the path.
Humanity wandered spiritually far from God.
But Christ entered our emptiness.
The Gospel is not merely self-improvement.
It is divine redemption.
Jesus became our Go’el.
The New Testament reveals this through the Greek word:
λυτρόω
lytroō
Meaning:
“To redeem,” “To ransom,” “To release by payment.”
Titus 2:14 says:
“[Jesus] gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.”
The cross was not symbolic sentiment.
It was redemption purchased with blood.
Naomi’s story whispers this long before Bethlehem would eventually receive another child — Jesus Christ.
And this is no coincidence.
Jesus Himself was born in Bethlehem.
The House of Bread eventually received the Bread of Life.
The Danger Of Secret Bitterness Toward God
Some people do not hate God openly.
They simply stopped trusting Him.
That is the quieter tragedy.
Bitterness often disguises itself as disappointment.
But underneath is accusation.
“God failed me.” “God abandoned me.” “God took too much.”
Hebrews 12:15 warns:
“See to it that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble.”
The Greek word for root:
ῥίζα
rhiza
indicates something underground.
Hidden.
Growing silently.
Many people manage symptoms while the root remains alive.
They become cynical. Emotionally detached. Spiritually numb. Unable to celebrate others. Unable to trust God fully.
But here is the terrifying reality.
Bitterness eventually rewrites identity.
Naomi no longer wanted to be called Naomi.
Pain became her name.
And many people have done the same thing internally.
Their wound became their identity.
Their betrayal became their identity. Their divorce became their identity. Their addiction became their identity. Their failure became their identity.
But Jesus did not die merely to improve behavior.
He came to restore identity.
Naomi’s Restoration Began Before She Felt It
One of the deepest truths in Ruth is that God was already restoring Naomi before Naomi emotionally recognized restoration.
That matters.
Because modern culture often treats feelings as ultimate truth.
Scripture does not.
God’s activity is not dependent upon human emotional awareness.
Even in Naomi’s bitterness, providence was moving.
The Hebrew concept of divine providence silently saturates Ruth.
No miracles split the sea. No fire falls from heaven. No angels visibly appear.
Yet God orchestrates everything quietly.
A field. A meeting. A harvest. A redeemer. A lineage. A future King.
And eventually…
The Messiah.
Some of God’s greatest works happen silently.
That is why believers must be careful not to interpret silence as absence.
The Gospel Answer To Bitterness
The answer to bitterness is not pretending pain never happened.
Naomi truly suffered.
The answer is not motivational positivity.
The Gospel confronts suffering honestly.
The answer is redemption through Christ.
Romans 8:28 says:
“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good.”
This does not mean all things are good.
Death is not good. Sin is not good. Betrayal is not good.
But God is powerful enough to redeem what humans cannot repair.
That is the center of Christianity.
At Calvary, humanity saw defeat.
Three days later, heaven revealed redemption.
The cross looked like the end.
It became salvation.
And some people reading this have been interpreting their lives from Friday while God is still writing Sunday.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
If bitterness is never surrendered, it can harden the soul against the very mercy meant to heal it.
Naomi Eventually Held Redemption In Her Arms
At the end of Ruth, Naomi holds Obed — the grandfather of King David.
Ruth 4:17 says:
“A son has been born to Naomi.”
Notice the beauty.
The woman who called herself empty became part of the lineage leading to Jesus Christ.
God was writing a larger story than Naomi understood.
And He still does that today.
Some people think their suffering disqualified them.
But throughout Scripture, God repeatedly enters broken stories.
Abraham was old. Moses was insecure. David failed. Peter denied Christ. Paul persecuted believers.
Yet grace rewrote everything.
That is the Gospel.
Not human perfection.
Divine redemption.
Jesus Christ — The Greater Redeemer
Boaz redeemed Ruth and restored Naomi’s household.
Jesus Christ does infinitely more.
Humanity stands guilty before a holy God because of sin.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek word for sinned:
ἥμαρτον
hēmarton
means:
“To miss the mark.”
Sin is not merely bad behavior.
It is rebellion against God’s holiness.
And bitterness itself can become sin when humans place themselves in judgment over God.
But Christ came to rescue sinners.
John 3:16 says:
“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son.”
The Greek word for loved:
ἠγάπησεν
ēgapēsen
refers to sacrificial, covenant love.
Jesus lived the sinless life humanity could not live.
He died on the cross for sinners.
The wrath against sin fell upon Him.
Then He rose again victorious over death.
This is the Gospel.
Not religion.
Not self-help.
Not moral performance.
Redemption through Jesus Christ alone.
Some People Are Still Living As Mara
They smile publicly.
But privately they still call themselves bitter.
They still define themselves by what they lost.
But Christ can restore what bitterness tried to bury.
Not always by recreating the old life.
But by creating something redeemed.
God never promised believers a painless existence.
Jesus said:
“In the world you will have tribulation.”
Greek:
θλῖψιν
thlipsin
Meaning:
pressure, affliction, crushing.
But Christ also said:
“Take heart; I have overcome the world.”
The resurrection changes everything.
Even grief.
Even bitterness.
Even ruined years.
Even you.
The Question Naomi’s Story Leaves Behind
Will pain become your permanent identity?
Or will you allow Christ to redeem even the places that broke you?
Because many people know Scripture intellectually while secretly living emotionally as Mara.
And the terrifying part is that bitterness can survive inside religious language for years.
But Jesus still calls the weary.
Still heals. Still restores. Still redeems.
The cross remains proof that God can bring resurrection out of devastation.
If this pierced something hidden in you, do not ignore it.
Confession is not weakness.
Bitterness grows in secrecy.
Bring it into the light.
Somebody reading this has blamed God for years while still pretending everything is fine.
God saw it.
You knew.
But His mercy is still reaching for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS BE DEMON POSSESSED?
paragraphs:
CAN CHRISTIANS BE DEMON POSSESSED?
The Question That Terrifies Churches, Haunts Secret Sin, and Exposes What Many Believers Never Truly Understood About Spiritual Warfare
There are people sitting in church every Sunday who secretly wonder if the darkness inside them is bigger than the faith they confess.
They worship with shaking hands.
They sing while hiding addictions.
They quote Scripture while hearing tormenting thoughts they cannot silence.
They love Jesus… but still battle rage, lust, depression, self-hatred, fear, intrusive thoughts, nightmares, spiritual heaviness, and cycles they cannot seem to break.
And eventually the terrifying question arrives.
“Am I oppressed… or possessed?”
Few topics create more fear, confusion, fake theology, emotional manipulation, and internet nonsense than this one.
Some Christians believe believers can be fully possessed by demons.
Others mock the entire discussion as superstition.
Some blame every struggle on demons.
Others deny spiritual warfare entirely.
Meanwhile real people are suffering in silence.
Some are genuinely demonized.
Some are mentally exhausted.
Some are trapped in unrepented sin.
Some are spiritually oppressed.
Some simply never learned what the Bible actually teaches.
And hidden underneath all the arguments is a deeper fear nobody wants to say out loud.
“If the Holy Spirit lives inside me… why do I still feel this war inside my mind?”
That question deserves honesty.
Not theatrics.
Not sensationalism.
Not social media deliverance performances.
Truth.
Biblical truth.
And the answer is more serious… and more hopeful… than most people realize.
Because Scripture does not paint believers as fragile victims abandoned to darkness.
But it also does not pretend demons are imaginary.
The Bible takes spiritual warfare terrifyingly seriously.
And the modern church often doesn’t.
The Apostle Paul wrote in Ephesians 6:12:
“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.”
The Greek word for wrestle here is “πάλη” (palē).
It refers to close combat.
Hand-to-hand struggle.
Violent conflict.
Not casual inconvenience.
Not symbolic discomfort.
War.
The Christian life was never promised to be demon-free.
It was promised to be Christ-covered.
And those are not the same thing.
One of the greatest mistakes modern Christianity makes is confusing temptation, oppression, torment, and possession as if they are identical categories.
They are not.
The New Testament uses extremely specific language.
And understanding the language matters.
In many Gospel passages, the phrase translated “demon possessed” comes from the Greek word “δαιμονίζομαι” (daimonizomai).
This word does not literally mean “owned completely by a demon.”
It more accurately means:
“To be under demonic influence, affliction, torment, or control.”
That distinction changes everything.
Because Western culture often imagines possession like horror movies.
Total takeover.
Head spinning.
Instant loss of all humanity.
But Scripture describes varying degrees of demonic influence.
Some people were physically tormented.
Some mentally afflicted.
Some spiritually bound.
Some self-destructive.
Some mute.
Some violent.
Some isolated among tombs.
The demonic realm attacks human beings differently.
And the Bible never treats spiritual warfare as entertainment.
