It treats it like a deadly reality.
Still… can a true born-again believer be possessed?
The clearest biblical answer is this:
A genuine believer sealed by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by Satan.

But believers absolutely can experience oppression, torment, deception, temptation, spiritual attack, and even severe bondage when living in unrepented sin, rebellion, occult involvement, or persistent compromise.
That distinction matters because ownership belongs to God.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19:
The Greek word for temple is “ναός” (naos).
Not outer courtyard.
Inner sanctuary.
Sacred dwelling place.
A true believer is indwelt by the Spirit of God.
Romans 8:9 says:
“Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.”
That means the defining mark of salvation is the indwelling Holy Spirit.
The New Testament never presents a redeemed believer as jointly owned by both Christ and demons.
Never.
But before people relax too quickly, understand this carefully.
The Bible absolutely warns believers not to “give place” to the devil.
Ephesians 4:27:
“Neither give place to the devil.”
The Greek word for place is “τόπος” (topos).
Opportunity.
Foothold.
Ground.
Territory.
Paul was writing to Christians.
Not pagans.
Believers can open doors.
Not ownership doors.
Influence doors.
Bondage doors.
Destructive doors.
And some Christians have opened doors so wide that their spiritual lives look indistinguishable from captivity.
Hidden pornography.
Occult practices.
Hatred.
Abuse.
Persistent rebellion.
Drug dependency.
Unforgiveness.
Sexual immorality.
Pride.
Secret violence.
Bitterness.
Many people want freedom without repentance.
But Jesus never separated the two.
In John 8:34, Jesus says:
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
The Greek word for servant is “δοῦλος” (doulos).
Slave.
Sin enslaves.
And Satan exploits slavery.
That does not automatically equal possession.
But it absolutely creates spiritual destruction.
One reason this conversation becomes emotionally explosive is because many believers secretly fear their struggles mean they are fake Christians.
They think:
“If I still battle darkness this badly… maybe God never saved me.”
But Scripture repeatedly shows believers struggling intensely.
Even Paul writes in Romans 7:
The Christian life involves warfare between flesh and Spirit.
Galatians 5:17 says:
“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.”
The word flesh here is “σάρξ” (sarx).
Not merely skin.
The fallen sinful nature.
Believers still battle fallen desires.
That internal war itself is often evidence of spiritual life.
Dead people do not fight sin.
The truly terrifying condition is not struggling against sin.
It is becoming comfortable with it.
Still, we must not swing to the opposite extreme and deny demonic activity.
Jesus cast out demons constantly throughout the Gospels.
The early church confronted spiritual darkness directly.
The demonic realm is real.
Satan is real.
Hell is real.
Spiritual warfare is real.
1 Peter 5:8 warns believers:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.”
The Greek word for devour is “καταπίνω” (katapinō).
To swallow whole.
Destroy.
Consume.
Peter wrote that to Christians.
Not unbelievers.
Demons cannot steal a believer’s salvation.
But they absolutely seek to destroy joy, peace, testimony, effectiveness, marriages, purity, mental stability, boldness, and intimacy with God.
And many Christians underestimate how strategic darkness actually is.
The enemy studies compromise.
Studies wounds.
Studies isolation.
Studies exhaustion.
Studies bitterness.
Studies pride.
Satan loves spiritually isolated believers.
Especially the ones pretending they are fine.
Some readers feel exhausted right now because you have spent years hiding what is happening in your mind.
You smile publicly.
But privately you feel hunted.
You pray but still feel tormented.
You repent but still battle temptation.
You love God but still hear accusing thoughts.
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same voice.
The Holy Spirit convicts specifically to restore.
Satan condemns endlessly to destroy.
Revelation 12:10 calls Satan “the accuser of our brethren.”
In Greek:
“ὁ κατήγωρ” (ho katēgor).
The prosecutor.
The accuser.
The one who weaponizes shame.
Many believers are not demon possessed.
They are demon accused.
And they have mistaken spiritual warfare for proof God abandoned them.
But Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
Not less condemnation.
None.
That verse has rescued countless believers from suicidal despair.
But there is another side Christians rarely discuss.
Some people claiming Christianity have never actually surrendered to Christ.
Church attendance is not salvation.
Christian language is not salvation.
Emotional worship moments are not salvation.
Family tradition is not salvation.
Jesus said in Matthew 7:21:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
That warning should sober everyone.
Because religious performance without regeneration leaves people spiritually vulnerable.
The Holy Spirit does not merely improve behavior.
He transforms identity.
2 Corinthians 5:17:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.”
The Greek word for new is “καινός” (kainos).
Not repaired.
Entirely new in nature.
This is why the question cannot merely become:
“Can Christians be possessed?”
The deeper question is:
“Has my life truly been surrendered to Jesus Christ?”
Because Christianity is not demon management.
It is spiritual rebirth.
And rebirth changes ownership.
Colossians 1:13 says Christ:
“Hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son.”
The word translated is “μεθίστημι” (methistēmi).
Transferred.
Relocated.
Removed from one dominion into another.
The believer no longer belongs to darkness.
That does not mean spiritual attacks stop.
It means Satan no longer has legal claim over the redeemed soul.
That truth matters more than many people realize.
Because some churches accidentally glorify demons more than Jesus.
Every problem becomes a demon.
Every weakness becomes possession.
Every emotional struggle becomes spiritual takeover.
But Scripture calls believers repeatedly toward responsibility, repentance, obedience, endurance, renewal of the mind, and submission to God.
James 4:7 says:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Notice the order.
Submit.
Then resist.
Many people want authority over darkness without surrender to Christ.
But biblical authority flows from obedience.
Not theatrics.
Not volume.
Not viral deliverance clips.
Not emotional hype.
Jesus never treated demons casually.
But He also never appeared intimidated by them.
The demons feared Him.
And that same Christ lives within true believers.
1 John 4:4:
“Greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world.”
The Greek word for greater is “μείζων” (meizōn).
Stronger.
Superior.
More powerful.
Christian… hear this deeply.
Your fear is not stronger than Christ.
Your torment is not stronger than Christ.
Your addiction is not stronger than Christ.
Your past is not stronger than Christ.
Your nightmares are not stronger than Christ.
Demons tremble before the authority of Jesus.
The cross was not symbolic.
It was conquest.
Colossians 2:15 says Jesus:
“Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.”
The image is military victory.
Public humiliation of defeated enemies.
The resurrection of Jesus was heaven’s declaration that darkness does not get the final word.
Still… some readers are carrying secret chains.
You know certain things in your life are opening spiritual doors.
You know compromise has been choking your soul.
You know God has been convicting you.
And maybe you clicked this article hoping for information… but encountered confrontation.
That is mercy.
Not rejection.
The enemy wants secrecy.
Jesus calls people into light.
1 John 1:7:
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.”
All sin.
Not partial sin.
Not manageable sin.
All.
The blood of Christ is stronger than the darkest thing hiding in your life.
But freedom begins with honesty.
Not pretending.
Not religious performance.
Honesty.
Some people reading this need repentance more than deliverance.
Some need healing.
Some need biblical counseling.
Some need mature Christian community.
Some need to destroy occult objects.
Some need to confess hidden addiction.
Some need to stop feeding darkness while asking God for peace.
Some need sleep.
Some need medical help.
Some need discipleship.
And some truly need spiritual warfare prayer.
But every single person needs Jesus.
Not a version of Jesus.
Not motivational spirituality.
The real Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The resurrected Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Christ who still sets captives free.
One of the most dangerous lies Satan whispers to struggling believers is:
“You are too far gone.”
But the Gospel says otherwise.
Mary Magdalene had seven demons cast out.
The Gerasene demoniac was restored.
Peter was restored after denying Christ.
Paul was transformed from persecutor to apostle.
The cross has always been a rescue mission.
Not a museum for perfect people.
And maybe that is what this conversation is really about.
Not obsession with demons.
But desperation for freedom.
People are tired.
Tired of fake peace.
Tired of hidden bondage.
Tired of secret shame.
Tired of smiling while spiritually bleeding.
Tired of pretending church automatically equals healing.
And Jesus still says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for rest in Matthew 11:28 is “ἀναπαύω” (anapauō).
Relief.
Refreshment.
Recovery.
Breathing again.
That invitation still stands.
Right now.
For addicts.
For anxious minds.
For exhausted believers.
For spiritually oppressed people.
For doubters.
For religious hypocrites.
For people secretly afraid of themselves.
For those terrified God has abandoned them.
Christ still rescues.
Christ still forgives.
Christ still breaks chains.
Christ still heals.
Christ still restores.
And no demon in hell can overpower the Savior who walked out of the grave.
So can Christians be demon possessed?
Biblically speaking, a true believer indwelt and sealed by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by demons.
But believers absolutely can experience severe spiritual warfare, oppression, deception, temptation, bondage through sin, and devastating attacks from darkness.
That is why Scripture repeatedly calls Christians to vigilance, repentance, prayer, holiness, discernment, submission to God, renewal of the mind, and dependence upon Christ.
This is not a game.
But neither is it hopeless.
The victory belongs to Jesus.
And maybe the most important thing you could do after reading this is stop hiding.
Talk to a mature biblical believer.
Confess what has been poisoning your soul.
Turn from compromise.
Run toward Christ instead of away from Him.
You do not need to perform your way into freedom.
You need surrender.
You need truth.
You need grace.
You need Jesus.
Be honest.
This hit harder than many expected.
The chains you hide in darkness only grow stronger until they are dragged into the light of Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Thaddeus
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Thaddeus
Nobody talks about Thaddeus.
Peter walked on water. John leaned on the chest of Jesus. Thomas doubted. Judas betrayed. Paul wrote letters that shook empires.
But Thaddeus?
Most Christians could not even tell you his other name.
And maybe that is exactly why his story matters.
Because hidden inside the silence of Scripture is a terrifying truth most believers never notice: God has always built some of His greatest Kingdom work through people the world barely remembers.
The forgotten. The overlooked. The unnamed. The quiet faithful.
The disciples nobody preached sermons about.
And if you have ever felt unseen… ignored… spiritually small… emotionally exhausted… or like your life would never matter in God’s plan…
then the story of Thaddeus may hit your soul harder than you expected.
His name appears only a few times in Scripture. No recorded miracles. No massive speeches. No books of the Bible. No famous moments.
Yet Jesus personally chose him.
Not accidentally. Not randomly. Not as filler.
Jesus looked into the eyes of this quiet man and said: “You. Follow Me.”
That single detail destroys the lie that visibility equals value.
Because Heaven does not measure greatness the way social media does.
And somewhere deep inside this forgotten disciple is a message the modern Church desperately needs.
Especially now.
Especially in a generation addicted to being seen.
Especially for believers secretly wondering if their hidden obedience even matters anymore.
The name “Thaddeus” appears in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18, but Luke and Acts call him “Judas the son of James.” This has caused confusion for centuries.
In Greek, the name used in Luke 6:16 is:
Ἰούδαν Ἰακώβου (Ioudan Iakōbou)
Usually translated: “Judas son of James.”
But to separate him from Judas Iscariot, early Christians commonly referred to him as “Thaddeus.”
Some scholars believe “Thaddeus” was a nickname derived from the Aramaic root:
תדי (Taddai)
Possibly meaning: “heart,” “courageous,” or “beloved.”
Others connect it to the Syriac and Aramaic idea of a warm-hearted or tender-chested person.
Imagine that.
A disciple remembered not for power… but possibly for his heart.
Not for fame. Not for influence. Not for platform.
But for quiet loyalty.
That changes the atmosphere immediately.
Because we live in a time where loudness is mistaken for anointing. Where visibility is mistaken for calling. Where algorithms often shape identity more than prayer does.
But Thaddeus stands in Scripture like a whisper from Heaven:
“You do not have to be famous to be faithful.”
And honestly?
Some people needed to hear that more than they realize.
The Gospel writers barely mention him, but one moment suddenly opens a window into his soul.
In John 14:22, during the final hours before the crucifixion, Scripture says:
“Judas (not Iscariot) said to Him, ‘Lord, how is it that You will manifest Yourself to us, and not to the world?’”
The Greek text says:
Κύριε, τί γέγονεν ὅτι ἡμῖν μέλλεις ἐμφανίζειν σεαυτὸν καὶ οὐχὶ τῷ κόσμῳ;
Transliterated: “Kyrie, ti gegonen hoti hēmin melleis emphanizein seauton kai ouchi tō kosmō?”
A deeply literal rendering: “Lord, what has happened that You are about to reveal Yourself to us and not to the world?”
This question is devastatingly human.
Thaddeus could not understand why Jesus would not simply reveal His glory publicly. Why not overwhelm Rome? Why not expose Himself before the crowds? Why not force the world to believe?
And if we are honest… we still ask that same question today.
“Jesus, why stay hidden?”
“Why not prove Yourself louder?”
“Why do evil people seem to win?”
“Why does faith sometimes feel invisible?”
“Why does obedience happen in secret?”
Thaddeus asked the question millions still carry silently.
And Jesus answered him with one of the deepest spiritual truths in the Gospel of John.
John 14:23:
“If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word, and My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.”
The Greek phrase for “make Our home” is:
μονὴν παρ’ αὐτῷ ποιησόμεθα (monēn par’ autō poiēsometha)
Meaning: “We will establish a dwelling place with him.”
Not a temporary visit. Not an emotional moment. Not religious performance.
A dwelling.
Jesus answered Thaddeus by explaining that God’s greatest revelation would not happen primarily through public spectacle.
It would happen inside surrendered hearts.
That changes everything.
Because many people keep waiting for God to reveal Himself through massive signs while ignoring the quiet invasion of His presence inside obedience.
The Kingdom often arrives silently before it arrives visibly.
And some of the deepest moves of God happen in rooms nobody livestreams.
In private repentance. In exhausted prayers. In hidden tears. In late-night surrender. In secret forgiveness. In silent warfare.
The world celebrates noise. Heaven celebrates transformation.
That is the hidden theology inside Thaddeus’ question.
A disciple almost nobody remembers accidentally revealed one of the deepest spiritual tensions in human history.
Visible glory versus inward transformation.
External religion versus indwelling presence.
Crowd fascination versus covenant intimacy.
And maybe this is where the article becomes personal.
Because there are people reading this who feel spiritually invisible.
You love Jesus. You pray. You fight sin. You keep showing up. You worship while grieving. You smile while mentally exhausted. You serve while secretly bleeding.
But nobody sees the battle.
Nobody applauds hidden obedience.
Nobody posts about your private faithfulness.
And the enemy has been whispering: “Your life doesn’t matter.”
But Thaddeus stands inside Scripture as living proof that Heaven sees differently.
Jesus chose twelve men. Not because they were influencers. Not because they were wealthy. Not because they were impressive.
But because He knew what grace could build through surrendered hearts.
The Church today knows almost nothing about the later ministry of Thaddeus with certainty because historical traditions vary.
Some early traditions connect him with Edessa. Others say he preached in Syria, Mesopotamia, Persia, or Armenia. Some traditions identify him with Jude, associated with the Epistle of Jude.
What is historically important is this:
The earliest believers remembered him as faithful.
Not flashy. Faithful.
And honestly? That may be one of the highest compliments Heaven can give a human being.
Because when your life ends, popularity will not matter.
Faithfulness will.
The applause of crowds disappears. The opinion of culture shifts constantly. The internet forgets people overnight.
But Heaven records obedience eternally.
That is why Jesus said in Matthew 25:21:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Not famous servant. Not viral servant. Not impressive servant.
Faithful.
In Greek:
εὖ, δοῦλε ἀγαθὲ καὶ πιστέ
“Eu, doule agathe kai piste.”
“Faithful” comes from πιστός (pistos).
Trustworthy. Loyal. Steadfast. Reliable.
That sounds like Thaddeus.
And maybe… that is what God is trying to build in you too.
There is another heartbreaking reality hidden in the life of Thaddeus.
History remembers celebrities. God remembers servants.
Those are rarely the same people.
Modern culture trains people to chase recognition.
But the Gospel repeatedly trains believers toward surrender.
John the Baptist said:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
In Greek:
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι
“Ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai.”
That is the opposite of modern self-exaltation.
And maybe that is why so many people feel spiritually empty despite endless attention.
Because the soul was never designed to survive worshiping itself.
Thaddeus reminds us that hiddenness is not abandonment.
Sometimes God hides people before He deepens them.
Moses spent years hidden in Midian. David was hidden in caves. Elijah hid near the brook Cherith. Paul disappeared into Arabia. Even Jesus spent thirty hidden years before three public years.
Hidden seasons are not proof God forgot you.
Sometimes they are proof He is preparing you.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Somebody reading this has been measuring their worth through visibility. Through likes. Through followers. Through recognition. Through who notices them.
But the Kingdom of God has never operated on celebrity metrics.
In fact, some of the strongest believers in history died unknown on earth while shaking Hell through prayer.
That includes mothers. Fathers. Intercessors. Missionaries. Workers. Grandparents. The exhausted believer trying not to quit.
You may never trend online. But your obedience can still echo through eternity.
And this is where Thaddeus becomes deeply prophetic for modern Christianity.
Because many believers secretly think:
“If God really loved me, my life would look bigger.”
But Scripture never teaches that.
The Gospel teaches that the greatest life is the surrendered one.
Jesus Himself said:
“For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.”
The Greek word for “life” there is:
ψυχή (psychē)
Meaning not merely biological existence, but the soul-self.
The identity. The ego. The self-driven life.
Jesus was saying:
The person obsessed with preserving themselves loses themselves.
But the person surrendered to Christ discovers who they truly are.
That is terrifying.
And freeing.
Because it means your value is no longer chained to public validation.
It means God can use hidden people powerfully.
It means your prayers matter. Your repentance matters. Your faithfulness matters. Your unseen obedience matters.
Even when nobody claps.
Even when nobody notices.
Even when your name never becomes famous.
Thaddeus is proof that obscurity does not cancel calling.
And maybe the most painful thing about modern Christianity is that many people would rather be seen than transformed.
But Jesus never said: “Follow Me and become admired.”
He said: “Follow Me and die.”
Die to pride. Die to self-worship. Die to sin. Die to ego. Die to performance.
And through that death comes resurrection.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement. Not motivational spirituality. Not religious branding.
Transformation through surrender to Jesus Christ.
Thaddeus disappears into history quietly.
But maybe that silence itself preaches.
Because maybe the point was never for the disciple to become unforgettable.
Maybe the point was for Jesus to become unforgettable.
And somewhere along the way, the modern world reversed it.
Many people now want Christianity to make them famous instead of holy.
But the disciples did not spend their lives building personal platforms.
They spent their lives preaching a crucified and risen Christ.
That difference matters more than people realize.
The Hebrew idea of remembrance is deeply powerful.
In Hebrew, “remember” is:
זָכַר (zakar)
But biblical remembrance is not merely mental recall. It carries covenant weight. Action. Recognition. Faithfulness.
When God “remembers,” He acts.
And Scripture repeatedly shows that God remembers people others overlook.
Hagar in the wilderness. Hannah in grief. David in the fields. Mary in obscurity. The thief on the cross.
And yes… even forgotten disciples.
You may feel unseen by people. But you are not unseen by God.
Psalm 139 destroys the illusion of abandonment.
“You have searched me and known me.”
In Hebrew:
חֲקַרְתַּנִי וַתֵּדָע
“Chaqartani vateda.”
God knows.
The tears nobody heard. The anxiety nobody noticed. The temptation nobody saw. The nights you almost quit. The prayers whispered through exhaustion.
He knows.
And if Thaddeus teaches us anything, it may be this:
Your hidden faithfulness still matters in Heaven.
Even if history forgets your name.
Somebody reading this has been dangerously close to giving up spiritually.
Not because you stopped believing in God.
But because you stopped believing your life mattered.
The enemy loves convincing believers that quiet obedience is useless.
But that is a lie from Hell.
Every act of obedience matters. Every hidden prayer matters. Every resisted temptation matters. Every act of forgiveness matters. Every surrender matters.
Nothing done for Christ is wasted.
First Corinthians 15:58 says:
“Your labor in the Lord is not in vain.”
The Greek phrase for “not in vain” is:
οὐκ ἔστιν κενὸς
Meaning: Not empty. Not meaningless. Not useless.
Read that again slowly.
Your faithfulness is not empty.
Even if nobody else sees it.
There is something else people overlook about Thaddeus.
Jesus kept him close.
That matters.
Out of the thousands following Christ, only twelve were chosen as apostles. And Thaddeus was among them.
Not because he was the loudest. Not because he was the most charismatic. Not because he demanded attention.
But because Jesus wanted him there.
That truth alone can heal wounded hearts.
You do not have to earn Christ’s invitation through perfection.
The disciples themselves were flawed, confused, fearful, impulsive, and broken.
Yet Jesus called them anyway.
That includes you.
The Gospel is not the story of impressive people reaching God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing broken people through Jesus Christ.
And the cross stands at the center of that rescue.
In Aramaic, one of the final cries of Jesus was:
ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ
“Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani?”
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus entered human agony fully. Isolation. Pain. Suffering. Abandonment.
So no wounded believer could ever say: “God does not understand.”
He does.
And through His death and resurrection, Jesus made reconciliation with God possible.
That is why the Gospel is not merely inspiration.
It is salvation.
Not behavior modification. Not religious performance.
Redemption.
Through the blood of Christ.
The story of Thaddeus ultimately points beyond Thaddeus.
It points to the kind of King Jesus is.
A King who notices hidden people. A King who calls ordinary people. A King who transforms surrendered people. A King who values faithfulness over fame.
And maybe that is why this forgotten disciple still matters two thousand years later.
Because millions of believers secretly live like him.
Quiet. Overlooked. Faithful. Fighting battles nobody sees.
And Heaven has not forgotten a single one of them.
One day, many people the world ignored will hear Heaven say, “Well done.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Aholah and Aholibah — The Sisters Who Became a Prophetic Warning
paragraphs: Aholah and Aholibah — The Sisters Who Became a Prophetic Warning
There are passages in Scripture people avoid reading publicly. Not because they are unimportant. Because they are uncomfortable. Graphic. Exposing. Painfully honest about the human heart.
Ezekiel 23 is one of those chapters.

Many believers know the names Aholah and Aholibah, but few truly understand what God was saying through them. Some reduce the chapter to symbolism. Others avoid it entirely because of the explicit imagery. But this prophecy was never written merely to shock people. It was written because God was revealing how deeply spiritual adultery wounds His heart.

This chapter is not ultimately about two immoral women. It is about two covenant-breaking nations. It is about God exposing what His people became after abandoning Him. It is about idolatry, political compromise, lust for worldly power, false security, and spiritual betrayal.
And if we are honest… modern believers can still become Aholah and Aholibah.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what it feels like to slowly drift from God while still pretending everything is fine publicly. Save this for the night conviction hits harder than distraction.

The names appear in Ezekiel 23. The prophet Ezekiel ministered during one of the darkest periods in Israel’s history — the Babylonian exile. Jerusalem was collapsing spiritually before it collapsed physically. God raised Ezekiel as a watchman to confront rebellion that had become normalized.
The chapter begins:
“Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.” — Ezekiel 23:2
In Hebrew:
בֶּן־אָדָם שְׁתַּיִם נָשִׁים בְּנוֹת אֵם אַחַת הָיוּ
Transliteration:
Ben-adam, shtayim nashim benot em achat hayu.
Literal understanding:
“Son of man, two women, daughters of one mother, existed.”
The “one mother” points back to the united covenant people that emerged from Israel’s history. The sisters symbolize the divided kingdoms:
Aholah = Samaria = Northern Kingdom of Israel Aholibah = Jerusalem = Southern Kingdom of Judah
God gives them symbolic names with devastating meaning.
Aholah in Hebrew:
אָהֳלָה
Transliteration:
Oholah
Root word:
אֹהֶל (ohel)
Meaning:
“tent”
Aholah literally means:
“Her own tent.”
Aholibah in Hebrew:
אָהֳלִיבָה
Transliteration:
Oholivah
Meaning:
“My tent is in her.”
This distinction matters profoundly.

“Her own tent” points to Samaria creating false worship systems outside God’s ordained presence. The Northern Kingdom established counterfeit worship centers under Jeroboam. They created alternative religion. Alternative priesthood. Alternative devotion. Alternative truth.
Aholibah, however, was Jerusalem. God says, “My tent is in her.” Jerusalem contained the Temple. The priesthood. The sacrifices. The visible covenant signs.
This makes Judah’s sin even more severe.
One sister corrupted herself without the Temple. The other sinned while carrying the very presence of God among her.
That should terrify modern Christianity.
It is possible to have worship music, church attendance, sermons, conferences, Bible verses in your bio, and still become spiritually unfaithful.
Some people are surrounded by Christian culture while emotionally belonging to Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, lust, greed, pride, validation, politics, or compromise.
That is why this chapter still burns with relevance.
God describes the sisters committing harlotry in Egypt. This language shocks modern readers because God intentionally uses marital imagery to describe covenant unfaithfulness.
Ezekiel 23:3 says:
“They played the harlot in Egypt.”
Hebrew:
וַתִּזְנֶינָה בְמִצְרַיִם
Transliteration:
Vatiznenah b’Mitzrayim.
The Hebrew root here is:
זָנָה (zanah)
Meaning:
to commit fornication, to act as a prostitute, to become unfaithful.
Throughout the Old Testament, idolatry is repeatedly described as adultery. Why? Because covenant with God was relational. Not merely legal.
Israel was not just violating rules. They were betraying intimacy.
The modern church often treats sin casually. As weakness. As a mistake. As “just struggling.”
But Scripture frequently describes rebellion as relational betrayal against a holy God.
Not because God is insecure. Because He is covenantally faithful.
And this is where Ezekiel 23 becomes deeply uncomfortable.

God begins describing the political alliances Israel and Judah pursued. The nations around them became objects of fascination. They lusted after foreign power. Foreign protection. Foreign identity. Foreign culture.
Aholah desired Assyria. Aholibah desired Babylon.
Instead of trusting God, they trusted empires.
Instead of repentance, they pursued strategic compromise.
Instead of holiness, they wanted acceptance.
Nothing has changed.
People still abandon obedience because they fear being rejected. Churches still dilute truth to gain cultural approval. Believers still crave worldly validation while claiming loyalty to Christ.
And slowly… without realizing it… hearts become spiritually divided.
Somebody reading this has been trying to satisfy spiritual emptiness with distraction instead of surrender.

The prophetic imagery intensifies because God wants Israel to feel the ugliness of their rebellion. Modern readers sometimes accuse passages like this of being “too graphic,” but the graphic nature is intentional. Sin is not sanitized in heaven.
Ezekiel 23:19 says:
“Yet she multiplied her harlotries.”
Hebrew:
וַתַּרְבֶּה אֶת־תַּזְנוּתֶיהָ
Transliteration:
Vatarbeh et-taznuteha.
Literal sense:
“She increased her acts of unfaithfulness.”
Notice something terrifying. Sin rarely stays still.
Compromise grows. Numbness deepens. Conviction weakens. What once shocked the conscience eventually becomes normal.
That is one of the most frightening spiritual realities in Scripture.

People do not usually wake up one morning fully hardened against God. It happens gradually. One tolerated compromise at a time. One hidden addiction at a time. One secret fantasy at a time. One delayed repentance at a time.
This chapter also reveals something devastating about human nature: people often run back toward the very things that destroyed them before.
Israel had experienced suffering because of pagan nations repeatedly. Yet they still desired those same systems.
That is humanity without repentance.
People return to toxic relationships. Return to addictions. Return to lust. Return to pride. Return to emotional idols. Return to secret sins they promised God they would leave forever.
And many do it while still attending church.
Aholibah especially represents deeper accountability because she sinned despite greater revelation. She had the Temple. The covenant signs. The prophets. The priesthood.
Jesus later echoes this principle. Greater revelation means greater accountability.
This is why religious hypocrisy angers God throughout Scripture. Not because He hates broken people. But because people pretend closeness to God while loving rebellion internally.

There are people posting Bible verses online while privately starving spiritually. People leading worship while secretly enslaved. People preaching while emotionally distant from God. People smiling in church while dying internally.
And Ezekiel 23 confronts all of it.
The chapter reaches a devastating climax when judgment finally comes. The nations they trusted eventually destroy them.
This becomes one of Scripture’s repeated patterns. The idols people worship eventually become the instruments of their suffering.
The approval they crave controls them. The lust they entertain enslaves them. The pride they protect isolates them. The secret sin they hide consumes them.
Sin promises comfort. Then steals peace.
Sin promises freedom. Then creates chains.
Sin promises identity. Then destroys the soul.
That is why repentance is mercy. Not punishment.
Many modern believers misunderstand repentance. They see it as God trying to ruin happiness. But repentance is God rescuing people from self-destruction.
The Hebrew concept behind repentance is:
שׁוּב (shuv)
Meaning:
to return, to turn back, to come home again.
Repentance is not merely guilt. It is returning.
Returning after compromise. Returning after rebellion. Returning after spiritual numbness. Returning after hidden sin. Returning after pretending too long.
The terrifying thing about Aholah and Aholibah is not merely that they sinned. It is that they resisted returning.
Conviction ignored long enough becomes hardness.
And that is a warning every generation desperately needs.
Especially this generation.

A generation drowning in distraction. Endless scrolling. Fake intimacy. Performative spirituality. Emotional exhaustion. Pornography addiction. Identity confusion. Public image obsession. Private loneliness.
People are more connected digitally than ever while becoming spiritually emptier than ever.
And many believers no longer know the difference between feeling inspired and actually being transformed.
Aholah and Aholibah remind us that external religion without covenant faithfulness means nothing.
God was not impressed by ceremonies while hearts belonged elsewhere.
This connects directly to the words of Jesus in the New Testament.
Jesus confronts religious hypocrisy repeatedly because external spirituality without surrendered hearts is still spiritual adultery.
In Greek, the New Testament often uses the word:
μοιχαλίς (moichalis)
Meaning:
adulteress.
James 4:4 says:
“You adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?”
Greek:
Μοιχαλίδες, οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ἡ φιλία τοῦ κόσμου ἔχθρα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστίν;
Transliteration:
Moichalides, ouk oidate hoti hē philia tou kosmou echthra tou Theou estin?
James is echoing the exact covenant imagery found in Ezekiel.
Spiritual adultery did not disappear in the New Testament. It remained a warning to believers.
Friendship with the corrupt values of the world system can slowly pull the heart away from devotion to God.
That does not mean believers isolate from society. It means loyalty matters. Affection matters. Worship matters.
Whatever owns the heart eventually shapes the life.
That is why idols are so dangerous.
An idol is not merely a statue. An idol is anything loved, trusted, feared, desired, or obeyed above God.

Career can become an idol. Relationships can become idols. Validation can become an idol. Politics can become an idol. Ministry itself can become an idol. Even religious reputation can become an idol.
And idols always demand sacrifice.
People sacrifice peace. Purity. Integrity. Truth. Time. Conviction.
Some people have not completely abandoned God. They have simply divided their loyalty.
That was the tragedy of the sisters.
And still… in the middle of all this judgment… God’s heart reveals something astonishing.
The warnings themselves were mercy.
Ezekiel’s prophecies were not written because God enjoyed punishment. They were written because God was pleading before destruction fully arrived.
That is still true today.
Conviction is mercy. The discomfort you feel reading certain Scriptures can be mercy. The exposure of hidden compromise can be mercy.
Because God disciplines those He loves.
Somebody reading this has been sensing conviction for months. Not condemnation. Conviction. There is a difference.
Condemnation says: “There is no hope for you.”
Conviction says: “Come back before this destroys you.”
Jesus Christ did not die merely to improve behavior. He died to reconcile people back to God.
The Gospel is not self-help. It is resurrection for spiritually dead people.
And this is where the story changes.
Because Ezekiel’s warnings ultimately point forward to humanity’s need for a faithful covenant keeper. Israel failed. Judah failed. Humanity fails.
But Jesus succeeds where humanity collapses.
He remains faithful where people become unfaithful.
The New Covenant is established not through human perfection, but through the righteousness of Christ.
This is why grace is so astonishing. Not because sin is small. But because mercy is greater.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the depth of God’s love simultaneously.
Some readers carry secret shame so heavy they believe restoration is impossible. But Scripture repeatedly shows God restoring repentant people.
David committed grievous sin. Peter denied Christ. The prodigal son rebelled openly. Yet repentance opened the door to restoration.
God does not forgive because sin is harmless. He forgives because Jesus paid the price.
Isaiah 1:18 says:
“Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.”
Hebrew:
אִם־יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ
Transliteration:
Im-yihyu chata’eikhem kashanim kasheleg yalbinu.
The Gospel does not excuse rebellion. It transforms rebels.
That transformation begins with honesty.
Honesty about idols. Honesty about compromise. Honesty about hidden sin. Honesty about emotional exhaustion. Honesty about spiritual numbness.
God already sees what people spend years trying to hide.
Aholah and Aholibah are warnings, but they are also mirrors.
They force readers to ask uncomfortable questions.
What owns my heart? What competes with God for my loyalty? Where have I normalized compromise? What have I loved more than obedience? What have I protected instead of surrendering?
Those questions matter eternally.
Especially in a culture teaching people to follow feelings above truth.
Feelings are real. But they are not always trustworthy.
Scripture repeatedly calls believers toward holiness, faithfulness, repentance, and surrender because unchecked desires can destroy lives.
And yet God still invites broken people home.
That invitation remains open through Jesus Christ.
Not through performance. Not through pretending. Not through religious image management.
Through repentance and faith.
The Gospel exposes sin because God wants healing deeper than surface appearances.
Somebody you love is secretly losing a war nobody else sees. Share this before they convince everyone they are okay.
There are believers exhausted from pretending. Exhausted from performing spirituality. Exhausted from smiling while internally collapsing.
Jesus never asked people to perform perfection. He called people to follow Him honestly.
That includes repentance. That includes surrender. That includes dying to self. But it also includes mercy. Forgiveness. Restoration. And transformation.

Aholah and Aholibah stand in Scripture as permanent reminders that spiritual compromise is never harmless. But they also remind readers that God speaks warnings because He desires restoration before judgment.
The same God who exposed Israel’s rebellion also promised future redemption.
Ezekiel later prophesies about new hearts and new spirits.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.”
Hebrew:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם
Transliteration:
Venatati lakhem lev chadash veruach chadashah eten b’kirbekhem.
That promise ultimately finds fulfillment through Christ.
God does not merely command transformation. He provides the power for transformation through the Holy Spirit.
This matters because many people secretly believe they are too far gone. Too addicted. Too compromised. Too hypocritical. Too broken.
But Jesus specializes in restoring what sin destroys.
No amount of darkness is stronger than the mercy of God.
One day every hidden loyalty will be exposed before God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Jair’s Daughter Was Laughingly Declared Dead Before Jesus Entered
paragraphs: Why Jair’s Daughter Was Laughingly Declared Dead Before Jesus Entered
The room was already preparing for grief before Jesus even touched the door.
Professional mourners had arrived.
Flutes were crying.
Voices were collapsing into rehearsed sorrow.
The atmosphere smelled like finality.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it… a twelve-year-old girl lay motionless.
The Gospel account in Mark 5, Matthew 9, and Luke 8 does not merely tell the story of a miracle.
It exposes something terrifying about the human heart.
People declared death before Life Himself even entered the room.
And what makes the scene unforgettable is this:
They laughed at Jesus.
Not doubted.
Not questioned.
Laughed.
Mockery filled the house before resurrection stepped inside.
Many believers today live inside that same room.
Dreams pronounced dead.
Marriages pronounced dead.
Purity pronounced dead.
Calling pronounced dead.
Faith pronounced dead.
Hope pronounced dead.
People around them already rehearsing funeral songs over things Jesus has not finished touching.
That is why this story still shakes souls two thousand years later.
Because some of the loudest voices around you may already be burying what Jesus still intends to resurrect.
Mark 5:35 says:
“While He yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogue’s house certain which said, Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further?”
The Greek phrase for “is dead” is:
“ἀπέθανεν” (apethanen)
It comes from “ἀποθνῄσκω” (apothnēskō), meaning:
“To die fully.”
“To perish.”
“To become separated from life.”
In their minds, the situation had crossed beyond possibility.
Notice the next phrase carefully:
“Why trouble the Master any further?”
That sentence reveals more than despair.
It reveals limitation.
They believed Jesus could heal sickness.
But resurrection?
That was too far.
Some people can believe God for improvement.
But not restoration.
They believe Jesus can make life slightly better.
But cannot revive what already collapsed.
And that is where many modern Christians secretly struggle.
They trust God with manageable pain.
But not impossible situations.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly waits until situations appear completely dead before revealing His glory.
Lazarus was buried four days.
Abraham’s body was “as good as dead” according to Romans 4:19.
Sarah’s womb had passed natural ability.
Israel stood trapped between Pharaoh and the Red Sea.
The valley in Ezekiel 37 was not filled with wounded men.
It was filled with dry bones.
God specializes in entering rooms where humans have already surrendered.
But the detail most people miss is what happened when Jesus arrived.
Matthew 9:23-24 says:

“And when Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise, He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed Him to scorn.”
The phrase “laughed Him to scorn” comes from the Greek:
“κατεγέλων αὐτοῦ” (kategelōn autou)
It means:
“To ridicule openly.”
“To mock contemptuously.”
“To laugh someone down as foolish.”
This was not casual laughter.
This was aggressive unbelief.
They were convinced Jesus had misunderstood reality.
Imagine mocking the Creator of breath while standing beside borrowed breath.
Imagine laughing at Resurrection while your own heartbeat depends on Him.
Human pride becomes dangerous when people think visible reality is the highest authority.
But Heaven has never been intimidated by human conclusions.
Then Jesus says something astonishing.
“The maid is not dead, but sleepeth.”
Critics often misunderstand this statement.
Jesus was not denying physical death.
Luke’s Gospel confirms clearly that “her spirit returned” (Luke 8:55), proving literal death had occurred.
So why did Jesus call it sleep?
Because Jesus speaks from divine perspective.
What humans call irreversible, God can reverse with a word.
For Christ, death itself was temporary.
The New Testament repeatedly uses sleep imagery for believers because resurrection is guaranteed through Christ.
The Greek word for sleep here is:
“καθεύδει” (katheudei)
It can mean literal sleep, but spiritually it also communicates temporary interruption.
Jesus viewed the girl’s condition through resurrection authority.
Everyone else saw an ending.
Jesus saw an awakening.
And that difference changes everything.
Some of you reading this were declared finished by people who only understand earthly conclusions.
Maybe they saw your addiction.
Your divorce.
Your depression.
Your compromise.
Your relapse.
Your failure.
Your secret shame.
And they assumed your story was over.
Some even said it spiritually:
“There’s no hope for them anymore.”
But they forgot something.
Jesus has a history of walking into impossible rooms.
The most powerful moment in the story may not even be the resurrection itself.
It may be the removal.
Mark 5:40 says:
“And they laughed Him to scorn. But when He had put them all out…”
Read that slowly.
“He had put them all out.”
Before resurrection happened, unbelief was removed from the room.
Not everyone deserves front-row access to what God is reviving in your life.
Some voices suffocate faith.
Some atmospheres feed despair.
Some people are more committed to your funeral than your healing.
Jesus removed the noise.
Removed the mockers.
Removed the atmosphere of death.
Then He spoke life.
The Gospel of Mark preserves the original Aramaic words Jesus spoke:
“Talitha koum.”
Mark 5:41 says:
“And He took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.”
In Aramaic:
“טליתא קומי” (Talitha qumi)
“Talitha” means:
“Little girl” or “little lamb.”
A deeply tender expression.
“Qumi” means:
“Arise.”
“Get up.”
The Creator of galaxies stood beside a dead child and spoke with the gentleness of a loving father waking his daughter in the morning.
No panic.
No struggle.
No ceremony.
No incantation.
Just authority wrapped in tenderness.
And immediately, life returned.
Mark 5:42 says:
“And straightway the damsel arose, and walked.”
The Greek word for “straightway” is:
“εὐθύς” (euthys)
Meaning:
“Immediately.”
“Without delay.”
When Jesus decides resurrection time has come, death does not negotiate.
The miracle happened instantly.
But there is another layer most readers overlook.
Jairus was a synagogue ruler.
A respected religious leader.
For him to publicly fall before Jesus was costly.
Especially in a culture where many religious leaders opposed Christ.
Mark 5:22 says Jairus:
“fell at His feet.”
The Greek phrase:
“πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ” (piptei pros tous podas autou)
describes complete desperation and surrender.
His status could not save his daughter.
His position could not stop death.
His reputation could not heal his home.
And sometimes God allows situations where titles, money, intellect, and influence all fail… so people finally realize they need Jesus more than image.
Some people only seek Jesus when their control dies.
Jairus had reached that moment.
And maybe you have too.
Maybe beneath your smile, something in your life feels lifeless.
Maybe you are exhausted pretending everything is okay.
Maybe everyone around you has already accepted defeat.
But this story survives through generations because it confronts every hopeless heart with one terrifyingly beautiful truth:
Jesus walks into dead places.
Not symbolic dead places.
Actual dead places.
The cross itself looked like Heaven had lost.
Jesus was mocked there too.
Laughed at.
Spat on.
Humiliated.
People assumed the story had ended.
But three days later, the stone moved.
The same Christ who stood in Jairus’ house stepped out of Joseph’s tomb alive.
Death itself became temporary because of Jesus Christ.
That is why believers do not grieve like those without hope.
Because resurrection is not merely an event.
It is a Person.
The enemy wants you to think your situation is beyond recovery.
Beyond forgiveness.
Beyond healing.
Beyond restoration.
But Scripture says in Ephesians 2:1:
“And you hath He quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.”
The Greek word for “quickened” is:
“συνεζωοποίησεν” (synezōopoiēsen)
Meaning:
“To make alive together.”
Christianity itself is a resurrection story.
We were spiritually dead.
Christ made us alive.
That means Jairus’ daughter is not just history.
She is a picture.
A picture of every soul Jesus still calls out of darkness.
A picture of every broken believer God restores.
A picture of every prodigal who thinks it is too late.
A picture of every exhausted Christian barely hanging on.
A picture of grace walking into rooms already filled with hopelessness.
And maybe this article found you during your own funeral atmosphere.
Maybe you have spent months listening to voices that declared your faith dead.
Your purpose dead.
Your joy dead.
Your relationship with God dead.
But people laughed before Jesus entered Jairus’ house too.
And they were wrong.
Be careful whose conclusions you accept before Christ speaks.
Because Heaven has interrupted funerals before.
Some funerals end the moment Jesus walks into the room.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Idineklarang Patay ang Anak ni Jairus Habang Pinagtatawanan Pa si Jesus Bago Siya Pumasok
Bago pa man pumasok si Jesus sa bahay… tapos na agad ang laban sa isip ng mga tao.
May mga umiiyak na.
May mga musikero nang tumutugtog ng awit ng pagluluksa.
May mga taong kumbinsidong wala nang pag-asa.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon… naroon ang isang labindalawang taong gulang na batang babae na walang buhay.
Pero ang pinakamasakit na bahagi ng kwento ay hindi ang kamatayan.
Kundi ang katotohanang pinagtawanan nila si Jesus.
Hindi lang nagduda.
Hindi lang nagtaka.
Tinawanan.
Nilait.
Minura ang posibilidad ng himala.
At hanggang ngayon… marami pa ring tao ang nabubuhay sa parehong klaseng silid.
Silid ng hopelessness.
Silid ng pagod.
Silid kung saan may mga taong matagal nang nagdeklara na patay na ang iyong pangarap.
Patay na ang relasyon.
Patay na ang pananampalataya.
Patay na ang pag-asa.
Patay na ang calling mo.
Patay na ang espiritu mo.
Pero ang problema… hindi pa pumapasok si Jesus.
Sa Mark 5:35, sinabi ng mga tao kay Jairus:
“Patay na ang iyong anak; bakit mo pa ginugulo ang Guro?”
Sa Greek, ang salitang ginamit para sa “patay” ay:
“ἀπέθανεν” (apethanen)
Ibig sabihin:
“Ganap nang namatay.”
“Wala nang natitirang buhay.”
Sa isip nila, tapos na ang lahat.
At dito lumalabas ang limitasyon ng pananampalataya ng tao.
Naniniwala silang kayang magpagaling ni Jesus.
Pero bumuhay ng patay?
Sobra na iyon para sa kanila.
At kung magiging tapat tayo… maraming Kristiyano ngayon ang ganito rin.
Naniniwala tayo sa maliit na himala.
Pero kapag sobrang sira na ang sitwasyon… pakiramdam natin imposible na kahit kay God.
Pero paulit-ulit itong pinapakita ng Diyos sa Biblia:
Kapag sinabi ng tao na “tapos na”… doon pa lang nagsisimula ang Diyos.
Si Lazarus apat na araw nang nakalibing.
Si Abraham halos wala nang lakas para magkaanak.
Si Sarah lampas na sa natural na kakayahang magdalang-tao.
Nakulong ang Israel sa harap ng Red Sea.
At sa Ezekiel 37, hindi sugatang tao ang nakita ng propeta.
Kundi tuyong mga buto.
Mahilig ang Diyos pumasok sa mga sitwasyong matagal nang sinukuan ng tao.
Sa Matthew 9:24 sinabi ni Jesus:
“Hindi patay ang bata; natutulog lamang.”
At ano ang ginawa ng mga tao?
“Pinagtawanan nila Siya.”
Sa Greek:
“κατεγέλων αὐτοῦ” (kategelon autou)
Ibig sabihin:
“Hayagang paglapastangan.”
“Mapanlibak na pagtawa.”
Kumbinsido silang mali si Jesus.
Imagine.
Pinagtatawanan nila ang Maylikha ng buhay habang ang sarili nilang hininga ay galing din sa Kanya.
Minsan ganyan ang tao.
Kapag masyado tayong nakatingin sa nakikita… nakakalimutan natin na mas mataas ang kapangyarihan ng Diyos kaysa sa realidad na nakaharap natin.
Pero bakit sinabi ni Jesus na natutulog lang ang bata kung patay naman talaga?
Dahil iba ang perspective ni Jesus.
Ang impossible sa tao ay temporary lang sa Diyos.
Sa Luke 8:55 malinaw na sinabi:
“At nagbalik ang kanyang espiritu.”
Ibig sabihin totoong namatay siya.
Pero kay Jesus… pansamantala lang iyon.
Dahil ang kamatayan mismo ay walang permanenteng kapangyarihan sa harap ng Anak ng Diyos.
At may isang detalye rito na sobrang lalim.
Bago binuhay ni Jesus ang bata… pinalabas muna Niya ang mga taong puno ng unbelief.
Mark 5:40:
“But when He had put them all out…”
Hindi lahat dapat kasama sa silid kung saan bubuhayin ng Diyos ang isang bagay sa buhay mo.
May mga taong mas committed sa funeral mo kaysa sa restoration mo.
May mga taong komportable kapag bagsak ka.
May mga taong gusto kang manatiling wasak dahil naiintimidate sila kapag binuhay ka ulit ng Diyos.
Kaya minsan… kailangan munang alisin ng Diyos ang maling boses bago Niya ilabas ang himala.
Pagkatapos noon, hinawakan ni Jesus ang kamay ng bata.
At sinabi Niya ang original na Aramaic words:
“Talitha qumi.”
“טליתא קומי”
Ang “Talitha” ay:
“Munting babae.”
Parang mapagmahal na tawag ng ama.
At ang “Qumi” ay:
“Bumangon ka.”
Imagine the scene.
Walang panic.
Walang struggle.
Walang drama.
Ang Hari ng kalangitan nagsalita lang nang may lambing.
At agad bumalik ang buhay.
Ang salitang “agad” sa Mark 5:42 ay:
“εὐθύς” (euthys)
Meaning:
“Kaagad-agad.”
“Walang delay.”
Kapag dumating ang oras ng Diyos para buhayin muli ang isang bagay… walang makakapigil.
At baka habang binabasa mo ito… may bahagi ng buhay mo na matagal nang dineklarang patay.
Baka ng ibang tao.
Baka ng pamilya.
Baka ng sarili mong isip.
Baka spiritually exhausted ka na.
Baka pakiramdam mo wala nang pag-asa.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Pinagtawanan din si Jesus bago Niya binuhay ang anak ni Jairus.
At mali silang lahat.
Ang Cross mukhang pagkatalo.
Mukhang katapusan.
Mukhang funeral ng pag-asa.
Tinawanan din Siya roon.
Nilait.
Dinuraan.
Pinahiya.
Pero makalipas ang tatlong araw… gumalaw ang bato.
Nabuhay si Cristo.
At dahil nabuhay Siya, may pag-asa pa rin kahit sa mga sitwasyong mukhang patay na.
Kaya mag-ingat ka kung kaninong boses ang pinapaniwalaan mo.
Dahil maraming tao ang nagdeklara ng “katapusan” bago pa magsalita si Jesus.
May mga funeral na natatapos sa mismong sandaling pumasok si Jesus sa silid.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Benaiah Became One of the Most Feared Warriors in Israel
paragraphs: Why Benaiah Became One of the Most Feared Warriors in Israel
There are men in Scripture whose names arrive like thunder.
David. Samson. Elijah. Goliath.
And then there is Benaiah.

A man most believers barely talk about. A warrior hidden between genealogies, battle records, and royal transitions. A lion-killer. A giant-slayer. A man trusted so deeply by King David that he eventually became commander over Israel’s army under Solomon.
But what made Benaiah terrifying was not merely his strength.
It was his willingness to descend into places other men avoided.
Because the most feared warriors in Scripture are never merely physically dangerous.
They are spiritually unshakable.
And maybe that is why this story feels personal.
Because some of you are fighting battles nobody else sees. Battles inside your mind. Inside your home. Inside your habits. Inside your silence.
And deep down, you wonder whether God can still raise warriors from exhausted people.
Benaiah’s story answers that question.
The answer is yes.
But God will often build warriors in pits before He places them in palaces.
The Bible introduces Benaiah in a way that almost feels cinematic.
2 Samuel 23:20 says:

“Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a valiant fighter from Kabzeel, who performed great exploits. He struck down Moab’s two mightiest warriors. He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion.”
The Hebrew language here is fascinating.
The phrase “valiant fighter” comes from the Hebrew:
בֶּן־אִישׁ חַיִל Ben ish chayil
The word חַיִל (chayil) does not simply mean strong. It carries the idea of valor, wealth of strength, capability, military excellence, courage, force, and proven power.
This was not a reckless fighter. This was a tested man.
A man whose courage survived reality.
And then Scripture says something almost unbelievable.
“He went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion.”
Most people read that too quickly.
Slow down.
A pit means limited movement. Snow means unstable footing. A lion means certain death for most men.
Everything about the environment favored the predator.
Yet Benaiah went down anyway.
The Hebrew phrase for “went down” is:
וְהוּא יָרַד vehu yarad
It literally means “he descended.”
That matters.

Because most people spend their lives avoiding uncomfortable places. Avoiding confrontation. Avoiding repentance. Avoiding honesty. Avoiding surrender. Avoiding the deep places where God transforms people.
But Benaiah descended.
And some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You descended into depression. Into grief. Into betrayal. Into addiction. Into loneliness. Into nights where your prayers felt unanswered.
Yet somehow… God kept you alive.
This article is not really about lions.
It is about what happens when faith enters terrifying places.
Because spiritually speaking, many believers want resurrection power without crucifixion reality.
But warriors are not created in comfort.
They are forged in places where survival itself becomes prayer.
The lion in Scripture often represents destructive spiritual opposition.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.”
The Greek says:
ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος ho antidikos hymōn diabolos
“Your adversary, the accuser, the slanderer.”
And the word for devour:
καταπιεῖν katapiein
Means to swallow completely. Consume entirely. Destroy utterly.
That is the enemy’s goal. Not merely temptation. Consumption.
And suddenly Benaiah’s story becomes more than military history.
It becomes prophetic.
Because every believer eventually faces a pit where the enemy believes you will not survive.
Some people lost themselves there.
Others met God there.
The snowy pit was not the end of Benaiah.
It was the revelation of who he already was.
And maybe your hardest season is not exposing your weakness.
Maybe it is exposing the warrior God has been building quietly.
What makes Benaiah even more remarkable is that he did not rise to fame through self-promotion.
No podcasts. No platform. No branding. No public image management.
Just faithfulness.
Modern culture rewards visibility. Heaven rewards obedience.
That difference changes everything.
Some of the strongest believers alive right now are completely unknown online. Unknown publicly. Unknown socially.
But hell recognizes them.
Because darkness has always recognized people who genuinely walk with God.
There is another detail many overlook.
Benaiah also killed an Egyptian warrior described as impressive in appearance.
2 Samuel 23:21 says:

“And he struck down a huge Egyptian. Although the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club. He snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.”
Do not miss this.
Benaiah defeated a superior weapon using inferior equipment.
That should encourage someone reading this.
Because many of you think you cannot be used by God until you become more qualified. More polished. More educated. More prepared. More healed.
But throughout Scripture, God repeatedly uses surrendered people carrying ordinary things.
Moses had a staff. David had a sling. The disciples had fishing nets. The widow had oil. The boy had bread.
And Benaiah had a club.
Yet faith turned ordinary things into impossible victories.
That is the pattern of God.
The Apostle Paul wrote:
“But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise.”
The Greek word for foolish is:
μωρὰ mōra
It refers to what the world dismisses as weak, absurd, unimpressive, or insignificant.
God specializes in using what pride overlooks.
Which means your weakness may not disqualify you.
It may actually position you.
That truth hits differently when life has humbled you.
Because eventually everyone discovers they are not strong enough alone.
Eventually everyone meets a pit.
And some of you are there now.
Smiling publicly. Bleeding privately.
You worship on Sunday while quietly fighting despair Monday through Friday. You encourage others while wondering who would notice if you disappeared. You pray while secretly battling exhaustion.
But Benaiah’s story reminds us that hidden battles still matter to God.
The world often celebrates crowns. God watches caves. Pits. Wildernesses. Prayer closets.
The hidden places reveal who we truly are.
That is why Jesus Himself often withdrew into lonely places to pray.
Luke 5:16 says:
“But Jesus often withdrew to lonely places and prayed.”
The Greek word for withdrew is:
ὑπεχώρει hypechōrei
Meaning to retreat intentionally. Not from weakness. But for spiritual strengthening.
Even Christ modeled dependence on the Father.
So why do we act ashamed when we need God desperately?
Some of you reading this were taught to hide struggle. Hide weakness. Hide emotion. Hide trauma. Hide temptation.
But hidden wounds become dangerous when never surrendered to Christ.
Benaiah became feared because he confronted what others avoided.
And spiritually, that still separates warriors from spectators.
Some believers spend years pretending. Others finally surrender.
One finds exhaustion. The other finds freedom.
The terrifying thing about real faith is that it eventually demands honesty.
Not performance. Not religious vocabulary. Not image management.
Honesty.
David himself wrote in Psalm 51 after his sin:
“Behold, You desire truth in the inward being.”
The Hebrew word for truth here is:
אֱמֶת emet
Meaning faithfulness, reliability, truthfulness, firmness, reality.
God is not impressed by fake holiness.
He desires truth in the hidden places.
And maybe that is why this article hurts a little.
Because deep down, many people are exhausted from pretending they are okay.
But Jesus never called people to perform healing.
He called them to come to Him.
Matthew 11:28 says:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek phrase:
Δεῦτε πρός με Deute pros me
Means: “Come here toward Me.”
Not away. Toward.
That invitation still stands.
For the addicted. For the ashamed. For the angry. For the exhausted. For the hypocrite. For the doubter. For the wandering believer. For the prodigal.
Jesus still says come.
And that changes everything.
Benaiah eventually became one of David’s elite mighty men.
But the deeper truth is this:
His private courage prepared him for public responsibility.
That principle appears throughout Scripture.
Joseph survived prison before leadership. David survived wilderness before kingship. Peter survived failure before preaching. Paul survived blindness before ministry.
God often develops people in obscurity before releasing them publicly.
Which means your hidden season may not be punishment.
It may be preparation.
Read that again.
Preparation.
The pit was not proof God abandoned Benaiah.
It became the evidence that fear no longer controlled him.
And maybe your current battle is teaching you the same thing.
Somebody reading this has survived things that should have destroyed you.
You cried privately. You broke privately. You questioned God privately.
Yet somehow… you are still here.
That is not accidental.
There are battles heaven knows about that people around you never saw.
And maybe that is why this article found you today.
Because God still raises warriors from wounded places.
Not perfect people. Redeemed people.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement. Resurrection.
Not image management. Transformation.
Not pretending. Redemption.
The Cross of Christ is where defeated sinners become redeemed sons and daughters.
Isaiah prophesied this hundreds of years before Jesus was crucified.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities.”
The Hebrew word for pierced:
מְחֹלָל mecholal
Carries the idea of being wounded through, profaned, pierced violently.
Jesus endured brutality so humanity could receive mercy.
That is not religion.
That is rescue.
And maybe someone reading this has spent years believing they are too far gone.
Too dirty. Too hypocritical. Too broken. Too addicted. Too numb.
But Scripture repeatedly shows Christ moving toward broken people.
Not away from them.
The woman at the well. Zacchaeus. Peter after denial. Thomas after doubt. Mary Magdalene. The thief on the cross.
Grace reaches people religion often gives up on.
That is why the Gospel still changes lives.
Not because Christians are perfect.
But because Jesus saves sinners.
Even now.
Even still.
And perhaps the greatest reason Benaiah became feared was not because he killed lions.
But because he developed a reputation for unwavering courage under impossible conditions.
Fear loses power when someone fully trusts God.
That kind of faith unsettles darkness.
The early church carried this same spiritual boldness.
Acts 4:13 says:
“Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John… they recognized that they had been with Jesus.”
The Greek word for boldness is:
παρρησία parrēsia
Meaning fearless confidence. Frankness. Open courage.
And notice the source.
Not personality.
Presence.
“They recognized that they had been with Jesus.”
That is the difference.
Real spiritual authority cannot be manufactured. It flows from genuine intimacy with Christ.
And maybe that explains why some believers radiate peace in storms.
They have been with Jesus.
Maybe that is what your soul actually longs for.
Not another motivational speech. Not another distraction. Not another temporary escape.
Jesus.
The One who still enters pits. Still heals hearts. Still breaks chains. Still forgives sinners. Still resurrects dead things.
The One who walked into death itself and conquered the grave.
The Gospel is not merely inspiration.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is Lord. That sin can be forgiven. That repentance leads to life. That mercy is available. That eternity is real.
And one day every hidden thing will be revealed.
Which means the question is no longer whether you appear strong.
The question is whether you truly belong to Christ.
Because eventually every warrior lays down his weapon. Every kingdom fades. Every platform disappears. Every earthly reputation dies.
But eternity remains.
That truth strips away illusion.
And maybe right now the Holy Spirit is confronting something you have avoided for years.
The hidden addiction. The secret bitterness. The compromise. The numbness. The pride. The exhaustion.
Do not ignore conviction.
Conviction is often mercy before destruction.
Jesus Christ did not die so people could continue pretending.
He died so people could finally become free.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Still sinners.
Not after perfection. Before it.
That changes the entire story.
Because salvation was never earned through human strength.
It was purchased through Christ’s sacrifice.
And that means even the exhausted person reading this right now can come home to God.
Right now.
No performance. No pretending. No delay.
Just surrender.
Benaiah descended into the pit and emerged victorious.
Jesus descended into death itself and emerged resurrected.
That is why Christians still have hope.
Not because life is easy.
But because Christ conquered the grave.
And when someone truly understands that… fear begins to lose its grip.
Maybe that is what made Benaiah terrifying.
Not merely skill.
But courage formed through trust.
The kind of trust only forged when someone has survived deep waters with God.
Some of you are still alive because grace carried you.
You know it.
You should have quit. Should have collapsed. Should have lost your mind.
Yet somehow Christ sustained you.
That is not weakness.
That is testimony.
And one day the very pit that almost destroyed you may become the story God uses to rescue somebody else.
Pray. Repent. Come back to Christ. Tell the truth. Forgive somebody. Ask for help. Open the Bible again.
Your soul is too valuable to keep dying silently.
Be honest. Some of you have been fighting battles nobody around you even knows exist.
“I’m still fighting.”
Let people know they are not alone.
Some people do not need another argument.
They need hope.
One day you will realize the pit was not where God abandoned you. It was where He revealed who you were becoming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Joanna Supported Jesus Financially in Secret
paragraphs: Why Joanna Supported Jesus Financially in Secret
Most people never notice Joanna.
That is exactly why her story matters.
She is mentioned only a few times in Scripture, hidden quietly between the names of louder disciples, stronger personalities, fishermen, zealots, and public miracle moments.
But heaven noticed her.
Jesus noticed her.
And if you have ever loved God silently while carrying pain privately… this story may expose parts of your soul you have hidden from everyone.
Because Joanna was not just another woman following Jesus.
She was connected to power.
Connected to money.
Connected to Herod’s palace.
And somehow… she still chose Christ.
That decision could have cost her everything.
Luke records something most people read too quickly.
Luke 8:1–3 says:

“And also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.”
The Greek phrase used here is:
“διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς”
Transliterated:
“diēkonoun autois ek tōn hyparchontōn autais”
Literal meaning:
“They were serving them out of what belonged to them.”
This was not symbolic generosity.
This was financial support.
Personal resources.
Provision.
Money.
Food.
Possibly property.
Travel expenses.
Jesus and the disciples were being supported by Joanna and these women.
That alone shocks many people.
But the deeper shock is who Joanna was married to.
Luke calls her:
“Ἰωάννα γυνὴ Χουζᾶ ἐπιτρόπου Ἡρῴδου”
“iōanna gynē chouza epitropou hērōdou”
Translation:
“Joanna, wife of Chuza, manager/steward of Herod.”
The word “ἐπιτρόπου” (epitropou) means administrator, financial manager, steward, trusted overseer.
Chuza was not a random servant.
He handled the affairs of Herod Antipas.
The same Herod Antipas who mocked Jesus.
The same Herod connected to the murder of John the Baptist.
The same corrupt political household soaked in paranoia, compromise, lust, manipulation, and fear.
And inside that darkness… was Joanna.
Can you imagine her life?
Surrounded by wealth.
Surrounded by political conversations.
Surrounded by Roman influence.
Surrounded by people pretending righteousness while serving power.
And then she hears about Jesus.
Not palace religion.
Not performance.
Not dead tradition.
Truth.
Authority.
Purity.
Compassion.
The Kingdom of God.
And something inside her broke.
Because money can decorate pain without healing it.
Status can silence loneliness without curing it.
Luxury can distract the soul while the spirit slowly dies.
Many people today are living exactly like Joanna before Christ.
Beautiful outside.
Dying inside.
Successful publicly.
Empty privately.
Still smiling in photos.
Still crying when nobody sees.
The Gospel reaches people religion ignores.
And Jesus was never intimidated by powerful households.
He walked straight toward them.
One of the most overlooked details is this:
Luke says these women had been healed.
Joanna’s healing is not specified, but the wording groups her among women transformed deeply by Christ.
Something happened to her.
Something personal.
Something life-altering.
And healed people become dangerous to darkness.
Because once Jesus rescues your soul, money stops being your master.
You start using resources for eternity instead of identity.
This is why Joanna supported Jesus.
Not because she was manipulated.
Not because she was emotionally pressured.
Not because Christianity was fashionable.
Following Jesus was dangerous.
Especially from Herod’s circle.
This may explain why her support was likely discreet.
Not necessarily hidden from Jesus.
But likely hidden from political eyes.
Because supporting a rabbi gaining influence while connected to Herod’s administration could become catastrophic.
Imagine the tension.
Joanna hearing reports inside Herod’s world.
Then secretly helping fund the ministry of the Messiah they feared.
Some scholars believe Joanna may have had access to inside political knowledge through Chuza’s position.
While Scripture does not explicitly state every detail, the contextual implications are powerful.
She lived between two kingdoms.
Earthly power.
And the Kingdom of God.
And eventually she chose which King truly mattered.
This is where many readers feel exposed.
Because some people love Jesus privately but fear losing worldly approval publicly.
Some people attend church but still belong emotionally to Herod’s palace.
Still addicted to status.
Still chained to appearance.
Still terrified of what people think.
Joanna’s story whispers something uncomfortable:
You can live near power and still be starving spiritually.
But you can also surrender everything and finally become alive.
The Hebrew understanding behind stewardship also deepens this.
In Hebrew thought, wealth was never meant to become an idol.
The word often connected to stewardship concepts is:
“שָׁלִיט” (shalit) or stewardship principles tied to entrusted authority.
Biblically, everything belonged ultimately to God.
Psalm 24:1 says:
“The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof.”
Joanna understood something many modern believers forget.
Resources are tools.
Not gods.
She leveraged earthly wealth to support eternal truth.
That is why heaven remembers her name while history barely remembers Herod’s servants.
One kingdom faded.
The other remains eternal.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking moments.
Joanna appears again.
At the resurrection.
Luke 24:10:
“Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles.”
Joanna was still there.
Still faithful.
Still following.
Still near Jesus even after crucifixion trauma.
Do you understand how powerful that is?
Many followed Jesus when miracles multiplied.
But Joanna stayed through public humiliation.
Through Roman execution.
Through fear.
Through uncertainty.
Some people only follow God while life feels blessed.
Joanna followed Him through devastation.
That is real discipleship.
Not motivational Christianity.
Not performance spirituality.
Covenant loyalty.
This is also deeply connected to the Greek word for ministry and service:
“διακονέω” (diakoneō)
Meaning:
To serve, minister, attend to, care for.
This is where we later derive concepts related to deacons and ministry service.
Joanna’s financial support was not secondary spirituality.
It was ministry.
Holy ministry.
Kingdom service.
Some people think only preachers matter.
But heaven sees every hidden sacrifice.
Every meal provided.
Every seed sown.
Every quiet act that advances the Gospel.
Joanna reminds believers that unseen obedience still shakes eternity.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because many people secretly know God has been calling them out of compromise.
Out of lukewarm living.
Out of performative religion.
Out of double-minded loyalty.
But fear keeps them chained.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of losing relationships.
Fear of losing comfort.
Fear of losing status.
Joanna had those same crossroads.
And she still chose Jesus.
There are people reading this right now who feel spiritually exhausted because they keep feeding two kingdoms.
You cannot fully belong to Herod’s palace and Christ’s Kingdom simultaneously.
Eventually one will expose the other.
And maybe that is why this article found you.
Not by accident.
But because God is confronting hidden loyalties.
Some people hide sin.
Others hide surrender.
Joanna likely hid generosity because the environment around her was hostile to truth.
Yet Jesus still received her faith.
That should give hope to every believer trapped in difficult environments.
God sees secret obedience.
God sees hidden tears.
God sees silent faithfulness.
And no sacrifice for Christ is ever wasted.
Maybe you feel unnoticed.
Maybe your prayers feel invisible.
Maybe you have supported others while battling private pain yourself.
Joanna’s story proves heaven remembers names the world overlooks.
And the greatest tragedy is not losing status.
The greatest tragedy is standing near Jesus your whole life while never truly surrendering.
Herod had proximity to truth and still hardened his heart.
Joanna had proximity to corruption and still chose Christ.
The difference was surrender.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if this article reminded you of someone trapped between worldly pressure and spiritual hunger, share this with them.
One day heaven will reveal how many souls were touched by sacrifices nobody on earth applauded.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Palihim na Sinuportahan ni Joanna si Jesus Gamit ang Kanyang Kayamanan
Karamihan sa mga tao… hindi napapansin si Joanna.
At baka iyon mismo ang dahilan kung bakit napakalalim ng kanyang kuwento.
Hindi siya katulad nina Pedro.
Hindi siya katulad nina Juan.
Wala siyang mahabang sermon.
Wala siyang sikat na himala.
Kaunting beses lang siyang nabanggit sa Biblia.
Parang isang tahimik na pangalan na mabilis lampasan ng mga tao habang nagbabasa.
Pero napansin siya ng langit.
Napansin siya ni Jesus.
At kung minsan ka nang nasaktan nang tahimik…
Kung minsan ka nang naglingkod sa Diyos habang walang nakakaalam ng laban mo…
Maaaring tamaan ka ng kuwentong ito nang mas malalim kaysa inaasahan mo.
Dahil si Joanna ay hindi basta simpleng babae lamang na sumusunod kay Cristo.
May koneksyon siya sa kapangyarihan.
May koneksyon siya sa pera.
May koneksyon siya sa palasyo ni Herodes.
At sa kabila ng lahat ng iyon… pinili pa rin niya si Jesus.
Maaaring ikasira iyon ng kanyang buhay.
Sa Lucas 8:1–3, may isang detalyeng madalas minamadali ng mga tao.
Sinasabi ng Kasulatan:
