Only dependence on God.
And sometimes God allows seasons where human strength collapses so we discover whether He truly is enough.
That does not mean your suffering is meaningless.
Romans 8:28 does not say everything is good.
It says God works all things together for good to those who love Him.
Even grief.
Even betrayal.
Even seasons that made you question everything.
Some of the deepest intimacy with God is born in places nobody would voluntarily choose.
Jacob limped after wrestling with God.
Paul carried a thorn.
Joseph suffered in prison.
And Jesus Himself was “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Gospel never promises a painless life.
It promises a Savior who enters suffering with us.
And here is where this story becomes even more powerful.
The widow in the parable kept approaching an unjust judge.
But believers today approach a loving Father through Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace.”
The Greek word for “boldly” is:
παρρησίας (parrēsias)
Meaning:
Freedom in speaking. Confidence in access. Fearless honesty.
Because of Christ, believers are not unwanted beggars outside heaven’s courtroom.
Jesus tore the veil.
The cross opened access.
The resurrection secured reconciliation.
And now broken people can come directly before God.
Not because we deserve it.
But because Christ paid for it.
That changes everything.
The widow feared rejection.
Believers approach through grace.
The widow hoped the judge might care.
Believers know the Father already loves them.
The widow fought alone.
Believers have an Advocate.
1 John 2:1 says:
“We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
The Greek word for advocate is:
παράκλητον (paraklēton)
Meaning:
One who comes alongside. A defender. An intercessor. A helper in court.
Jesus stands for His people.
Even now.
Which means your story is not abandoned.
Your prayers are not wasted.
Your tears are not unseen.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“Put thou my tears into thy bottle.”
In Hebrew thought, this painted the image of God treasuring every sorrow.
Not forgetting.
Not dismissing.
Not ignoring.
Remember that the next time suffering tries to convince you heaven is silent.
Silence is not absence.
Delay is not denial.
And waiting is not proof God stopped caring.
Sometimes God develops endurance before deliverance.
Sometimes He strengthens faith before changing circumstances.
Sometimes the greatest miracle is not immediate rescue…
but a soul that keeps trusting Him through the darkness.
Somebody reading this nearly gave up recently.
You smiled publicly while privately collapsing.
You almost stopped praying.
Almost stopped believing.
Almost stopped fighting.
But somehow… you are still here.
Still breathing.
Still reading.
Still searching for hope.
Do not ignore that.
God often keeps people alive emotionally long before they recognize He is sustaining them spiritually.
And if this article found you at the exact moment you needed it… maybe this is your reminder that heaven has not forgotten your name.
Maybe your story is not ending in despair.
Maybe the Judge of all the earth is still working behind scenes you cannot yet see.
Genesis 18:25 asks:
“Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?”
Yes.
He will.
Not always according to our timing.
Not always according to our expectations.
But perfectly according to His wisdom, justice, mercy, and eternal purpose.
The widow kept knocking because she believed somebody eventually would answer.
The Gospel reveals something greater.
The door has already been opened through Jesus Christ.
That is why believers continue praying.
Not to manipulate God.
Not to force heaven’s hand.
But because relationship with God refuses to surrender even when pain remains unresolved.
Faith is not pretending everything feels okay.
Faith is continuing to trust Christ when everything inside you wants to quit.
And maybe that is why this widow’s story survived for thousands of years.
Because every generation eventually discovers what it feels like to beg heaven for justice, healing, breakthrough, peace, mercy, or rescue.
Every generation eventually becomes the widow.
And every generation must decide:
Will disappointment silence my faith?
Or will I keep coming to God anyway?
And if somebody you love is silently losing hope, share this with them today.
Some people are fighting battles they have never told anyone about.
The people who keep crying out to God are often far stronger than they realize.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Zebulun and Naphtali Were Called More Honorable Than Others
paragraphs: Why Zebulun and Naphtali Were Called More Honorable Than Others
There are names in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
Names buried in genealogies. Names hidden between wars. Names mentioned once in prophecy and forgotten by the next chapter.
But heaven never wastes names.
And sometimes the tribes nobody expected became the tribes God chose to honor publicly.
Zebulun. Naphtali.
Two tribes from the northern region of Israel. Two tribes constantly threatened. Two tribes exposed to invasion. Two tribes overlooked politically. Two tribes surrounded by darkness.
Yet somehow... when God spoke through Isaiah about the coming glory of the Messiah... He mentioned them first.
Not Judah. Not Benjamin. Not Levi.
Zebulun and Naphtali.
That alone should make every serious Bible reader stop and ask: Why?
Why would God intentionally spotlight these two tribes? Why did Scripture connect them to honor, light, glory, courage, and Messiah Himself? Why did Jesus begin His ministry there?
Because buried inside their story is one of the greatest revelations about how God chooses people.
And maybe one of the deepest comforts for wounded believers.
Because God has always loved bringing light into places everybody else gave up on.
Isaiah 9:1–2 says:

“Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations. The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.”
Most people quote this at Christmas and never slow down enough to realize what God was actually saying.
This was not random geography.
This was redemption.
The Hebrew phrase for “great light” is:
אוֹר גָּדוֹל
'Or gadol.
Not a weak light. Not temporary inspiration. Not emotional positivity.
A massive divine light. A heaven-breaking light. A covenant light.
And where did God send it first?
Into wounded territory.
Zebulun and Naphtali were the first regions devastated by Assyrian invasion.
2 Kings 15:29 records that Tiglath-Pileser attacked these northern territories first.
They suffered humiliation before others. They experienced darkness before others. They were exposed before others.
And that matters.
Because many people assume honor means protection from suffering.
But biblically... God often honors people by trusting them with battle first.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew word often connected to honor is:
כָּבֵד
Kaved.
It literally means “weighty,” “heavy,” “significant,” or “glorious.”
Honor in Scripture is not celebrity. Honor is spiritual weight.
God gave Zebulun and Naphtali spiritual weight because they endured darkness without losing prophetic destiny.
Most people cannot handle prolonged darkness without becoming bitter.
These tribes did.
And God remembered.
This is one of the most misunderstood patterns in all Scripture:
The places attacked hardest are often the places God plans to reveal Himself through most powerfully.
The enemy strikes territories prophetically.
That means some people reading this have hated themselves for wounds that may actually reveal where heaven intends to shine brightest.
Your deepest warfare may be connected to your deepest assignment.
The enemy does not waste attacks.
Neither does God.
When Matthew quoted Isaiah concerning Jesus beginning His ministry in Galilee, he intentionally connected Christ directly to Zebulun and Naphtali.
Matthew 4:13–16 says:
“And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet...”
Jesus could have launched His ministry anywhere.
Jerusalem would have made political sense. The temple would have made religious sense. The capital would have made strategic sense.
But heaven chose wounded territory.
Again.
Do you see the pattern?
God intentionally starts glory where shame once lived.
This is why the Gospel is so offensive to pride.
Because God repeatedly bypasses human systems of importance.
He chooses:
David over Saul. Joseph in prison. Gideon hiding. Ruth the outsider. Mary from Nazareth. Fishermen over scholars. The cross over the throne.
And Zebulun and Naphtali over religious prestige.
The religious mind struggles with this because religion believes honor is earned through visibility.
But Scripture shows honor is often hidden inside endurance.
Some of the most honored people in heaven were barely noticed on earth.
And some believers reading this have secretly believed:
“If God loved me, my life would not have been this painful.”
But Zebulun and Naphtali tell another story.
Sometimes the first territory attacked becomes the first territory illuminated.
That is not rejection.
That is prophetic positioning.
In Genesis 49, Jacob prophetically blesses his sons before death.
When he speaks over Zebulun, he says:
“Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships.”
The Hebrew phrase carries imagery of openness, access, commerce, movement, and connection.
Zebulun became associated with reaching outward.
Naphtali, meanwhile, receives this blessing:
“Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words.”
The Hebrew phrase for “goodly words” can imply beautiful speech, fruitful declarations, elegant expression.
Freedom. Expression. Movement.
One tribe connected to expansion. One tribe connected to release.
Then centuries later... Jesus walks directly into their region carrying the Kingdom of God.
Nothing in Scripture is accidental.
Not geography. Not timing. Not tribal placement. Not prophecy.
Even the location of Christ’s ministry reveals God’s heart toward broken regions.
Galilee itself carried stigma.
In John 1:46, Nathanael asked:
“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?”
That was not a compliment.
Galilee was often viewed as spiritually compromised, culturally mixed, and less prestigious.
Yet Jesus intentionally rooted Himself there.
Why?
Because God loves invading despised places with undeniable glory.
And honestly... this destroys human pride.
Because many believers still think God moves most powerfully through polished people.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals God moving through surrendered people.
There is a difference.
One performs. One depends.
One seeks applause. One seeks Christ.
And Zebulun and Naphtali remind us that God can transform devastated territory into holy ground.
This is why Isaiah’s prophecy matters so deeply.
The people walking in darkness saw great light.
Notice:
They were still walking.
They were wounded... but still moving.
Confused... but still moving.
Surrounded by darkness... but still moving.
And then the light came.
Somebody reading this is exhausted because you expected God to remove the darkness immediately.
But many times God develops endurance before revelation.
The Greek word used for endurance in the New Testament is:
ὑπομονή
Hypomonē.
It means steadfastness. Remaining under pressure. Refusing to quit. Faithfulness under burden.
Zebulun and Naphtali carried hypomonē before the Messiah arrived.
And some believers are one season away from seeing why the warfare was so intense.
The enemy wanted them to quit before the light appeared.
That is still happening today.
Some people abandoned prayer too early. Some surrendered purity too early. Some walked away from God too early. Some lost hope too early.
And hell celebrated prematurely.
Because what looked like devastation was actually preparation.
The Gospel changes how suffering is interpreted.
Without Christ, suffering looks meaningless.
With Christ, suffering can become transformation.
Romans 8:18 says:
“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.”
Notice Paul did not deny suffering.
He compared it.
That changes everything.
The glory outweighs the pain.
The resurrection outweighs the cross. The restoration outweighs the betrayal. The healing outweighs the wound. The Kingdom outweighs the darkness.
And Zebulun and Naphtali became prophetic proof.
God did not forget wounded territory.
He visited it personally.
There is another detail many people miss.
When Deborah and Barak fought Sisera in Judges 4 and 5, Zebulun and Naphtali were among the tribes that courageously entered battle.
Judges 5:18 says:
“Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field.”
That verse is explosive.
Because many tribes hesitated. Some stayed comfortable. Some remained distant.
But Zebulun and Naphtali risked themselves.
The Hebrew imagery carries sacrificial courage.
Not convenience. Not safety.
Courage.
That matters spiritually.
Because heaven notices who remains faithful when obedience becomes costly.
Modern Christianity often celebrates platforms.
But Scripture celebrates surrender.
The Kingdom of God was never built by comfortable spectators.
It was built by surrendered people willing to carry crosses.
And these tribes did.
No wonder God later associated them with light.
People who survive darkness with faith intact become dangerous to hell.
There are believers reading this who feel disqualified because of previous pain.
But the Bible repeatedly shows God using scarred territory.
Thomas doubted. Peter failed. Moses stuttered. David fell. Paul persecuted Christians. Mary Magdalene carried deep torment before freedom.
Yet Jesus redeemed all of it.
The enemy loves convincing wounded believers that they are permanently unusable.
But Christ specializes in resurrection.
Not improvement.
Resurrection.
There is a difference.
Improvement modifies. Resurrection restores life where death existed.
And that is exactly what happened prophetically in Zebulun and Naphtali.
Light invaded devastated territory.
The Messiah walked into forgotten regions.
Heaven honored places others dismissed.
And maybe that is why this story hits so personally for so many people.
Because deep down... most people know what it feels like to carry hidden darkness.
Some hide depression behind smiles. Some hide addiction behind church attendance. Some hide lust behind theology. Some hide exhaustion behind productivity. Some hide grief behind humor.
But Jesus still walks toward dark places.
Not away from them.
That is the Gospel.
John 1:5 says:
“And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.”
The Greek word for “comprehended” is:
κατέλαβεν
Katelaben.
It can mean overcome, overpower, seize, suppress.
Darkness could not overpower the Light.
That means your darkness is not stronger than Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than Christ. Your addiction is not stronger than Christ. Your past is not stronger than Christ. Your fear is not stronger than Christ.
The Light still wins.
Always.
And maybe somebody needed to hear that today more than they needed another motivational speech.
Because motivational speeches cannot resurrect dead souls.
Only Jesus can.
This is why the Gospel is not self-help.
It is supernatural rebirth.
The Greek phrase Jesus used in John 3 for “born again” is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
Gennēthē anōthen.
Born from above.
Not behavior modification. Not image management. Not religious cosmetics.
A new heart. A new spirit. A new creation.
And the same God who brought light into Zebulun and Naphtali still brings light into shattered lives today.
That is why no testimony is too broken. No past too filthy. No addiction too strong. No family too damaged. No mind too tormented.
Jesus still walks into Galilee.
He still enters wounded regions.
He still calls ordinary people.
And He still changes everything.
Maybe that is why this story refuses to die.
Because people recognize themselves in it.
The forgotten. The ashamed. The exhausted. The attacked. The spiritually numb. The ones wondering if God still sees them.
Zebulun and Naphtali answer:
Yes.
God sees wounded territory.
And sometimes... He chooses it first.
And if you know somebody walking through darkness right now, share this with them because some people are closer to breakthrough than they realize.
The places you thought disqualified you may become the exact places where Christ reveals His glory most powerfully.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Gideon Needed Confirmation Again and Again
paragraphs: Why Gideon Needed Confirmation Again and Again
There are people who pretend they have never doubted God.
And then there are honest people.
The kind who pray, then pray again because fear returned five minutes later.
The kind who open the Bible searching for peace… only to ask heaven the same question tomorrow.
The kind who believe… but still tremble.
That was Gideon.
Not weak.
Not faithless.
Human.
And maybe that is exactly why God chose him.
Because some of the most dangerous spiritual lies ever taught are the lies that say real believers never struggle, never question, never need reassurance, never feel afraid.
But Scripture never hides the shaking hands of the people God used.
Moses doubted.
Elijah collapsed.
David wept.
Thomas questioned.
Peter sank.
And Gideon needed confirmation again… and again… and again.
The story begins in Judges 6.
Israel had abandoned God repeatedly, and the consequence was devastating oppression under Midian. Crops were stolen. Families were starving. Entire communities lived in fear.
The Hebrew text describes Israel as being brought “very low.”
The phrase used is:
מְאֹד דָּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
Me’od dalal Yisra’el.
It carries the sense of being emptied, weakened, reduced, brought into utter helplessness.
This was not merely political suffering.
It was spiritual exhaustion.
And in the middle of national fear, Gideon is found hiding.
Not fighting.
Not preaching.
Hiding.
Judges 6:11 says he was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
A winepress was not designed for threshing wheat.
Threshing normally happened in open elevated areas where wind could separate grain from chaff.
But Gideon was underground.
Secretive.
Afraid.
Trying to survive.
And then heaven interrupted him.
“The LORD is with you, mighty warrior.”
In Hebrew:
יְהוָה עִמְּךָ גִּבּוֹר הֶחָיִל
YHWH immekha gibbor heḥayil.
“Gibbor heḥayil” means mighty warrior, mighty man of valor, courageous fighter.
Imagine hearing that while hiding.
Imagine God calling you what nobody else sees.
Imagine heaven speaking destiny over someone still shaking.
That alone is enough to make some people cry.
Because many believers know exactly what it feels like to love God while secretly feeling terrified.
To worship publicly while panicking privately.
To smile in church while fighting silent wars in the mind.
And this is where Gideon becomes painfully relatable.
Because he does not respond like a fearless superhero.
He responds like someone drowning in confusion.
“If the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us?”
That question has echoed through millions of bedrooms at 2 AM.
If God is with me… why am I exhausted?
Why did the relationship die?
Why did the prayer feel unanswered?
Why does anxiety still follow me?
Why does obedience sometimes still hurt?
Gideon was not questioning God’s existence.
He was struggling to reconcile God’s promises with present pain.
And many believers are secretly there right now.
They believe in God.
But they are trying to understand their suffering.
What is astonishing is that God does not destroy Gideon for asking questions.
The Lord answers him.
Patiently.
Mercifully.
This matters deeply because religion often punishes honesty while Jesus consistently moved toward it.
God tells Gideon he will save Israel.
And immediately Gideon asks for confirmation.
“Please, Lord, how can I save Israel?”
He points to his weakness.
His insignificance.
His insecurity.
“My clan is the weakest… and I am the least in my father’s house.”
That sentence reveals something devastating.
Gideon did not merely doubt the mission.
He doubted himself.
Many people do not struggle believing God is powerful.
They struggle believing God could use them.
That is a different wound.
And sometimes it comes from years of failure.
Years of rejection.
Years of shame.
Years of hidden sin.
Years of hearing voices that convinced them they are too broken to matter.
So Gideon asks for a sign.
Not because he wants entertainment.
Because fear is choking him.
He prepares an offering.
The angel touches it.
Fire rises from the rock.
The offering is consumed.
The supernatural explodes in front of him.
And still… Gideon struggles later.
That detail is critical.
Because one encounter with God does not automatically erase every human fear.
Some believers think if they were truly spiritual, one sermon, one worship moment, one answered prayer, one breakthrough would permanently eliminate all insecurity.
But Scripture paints a more honest picture of sanctification.
Growth is often progressive.
Healing can happen in layers.
Faith can coexist with trembling.
Even after experiencing God.
That night God commands Gideon to tear down the altar of Baal.
And Gideon obeys.
But Judges 6:27 says he did it at night because he was afraid.
Read that carefully.
He obeyed while afraid.
That may describe someone reading this right now.
Still anxious.
Still struggling.
Still uncertain.
But still obeying.
And heaven honors that.
Perfect fearlessness is not the requirement for obedience.
Trusting God while afraid is still faith.
Then comes the moment most people know Gideon for.
The fleece.
Gideon asks God for confirmation again.
And again.
First dew only on the fleece.
Then dew only on the ground.
Many people mock Gideon here.
But they should not.
Because countless believers still place out modern fleeces.
“God, if this door opens…”
“Lord, if they call me back…”
“If this verse appears…”
“If peace comes…”
“If You really want me to do this, confirm it.”
The issue is not that Gideon lacked all faith.
The issue is that the assignment in front of him felt impossibly overwhelming.
God was asking a fearful man to confront a nation’s idolatry and lead an army against impossible odds.
And underneath Gideon’s repeated requests was a deeply human cry:
“Please don’t let me fail out there.”
That cry still exists today.
People feel it before marriage.
Before ministry.
Before leadership.
Before forgiveness.
Before stepping away from addiction.
Before leaving toxic relationships.
Before surrendering fully to Christ.
Because obedience can feel terrifying when it costs everything familiar.
And this is where the story becomes overwhelming.
God keeps answering him.
Patiently.
Again.
And again.
Not because God enjoys unbelief.
But because God understood Gideon’s frame.
Psalm 103:14 says:
“For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust.”
In Hebrew:
כִּי־הוּא יָדַע יִצְרֵנוּ
Ki hu yada yitzrenu.
“He knows our formation.”
God understands human fragility better than humans do.
This does not mean endless unbelief is healthy.
But it does reveal something beautiful:
God is extraordinarily patient with sincere struggling hearts.
Then comes another astonishing moment.
In Judges 7, before battle, God Himself initiates another confirmation.
Gideon did not even ask this time.
God tells him to go listen to the enemy camp.
There Gideon hears a Midianite describing a dream about Gideon defeating them.
And suddenly Gideon worships.
Do you see it?
God knew Gideon still needed strengthening.
Some people imagine God as constantly irritated with wounded believers.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a Father who strengthens weak people into courage.
This changes how many people see themselves.
Because some believers are drowning in shame for still struggling.
They think repeated fear means God is disappointed in them.
But Gideon’s story reveals something different.
Needing reassurance did not disqualify him.
God still used him.
Powerfully.
In fact, Gideon’s weakness became the stage where God’s power became undeniable.
The army is reduced from 32,000 to 300.
No human could claim glory afterward.
The victory would belong entirely to God.
And maybe that is one reason God allows some people to feel their weakness so deeply.
Because when breakthrough finally comes, nobody will confuse it with human strength.
The Apostle Paul later writes something that sounds strangely connected to Gideon’s story.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”
In Greek:
ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
Hē gar dynamis mou en astheneia teleitai.
“My power is brought to completion in weakness.”
Not after weakness.
In weakness.
That changes everything.
Because modern culture worships confidence.
The Kingdom often works through dependence.
And some of the people God uses most are the people who know they cannot survive without Him.
Gideon eventually moves.
Leads.
Fights.
Wins.
Not because he became naturally fearless.
But because God patiently transformed a trembling man into a vessel of deliverance.
Somebody reading this has spent years condemning themselves for being “too emotional,” “too anxious,” “too uncertain,” “too damaged.”
But maybe your repeated prayers are not proof that God abandoned you.
Maybe they are evidence that you keep returning to Him instead of walking away.
That matters.
There is also another side to Gideon’s story many people avoid discussing.
Repeated confirmation-seeking can become unhealthy if it becomes chronic refusal to trust God after He has spoken clearly.
At some point faith must move.
At some point obedience must walk.
At some point the boat must be stepped out of.
God comforted Gideon.
But God also sent Gideon.
And there are believers trapped in endless hesitation because they are waiting for one more sign while ignoring the confirmations already given through Scripture.
The Word of God must remain higher than emotional impulses.
Feelings fluctuate.
Truth does not.
That distinction matters.
Biblical confirmation never contradicts biblical revelation.
God will not “confirm” sin.
He will not endorse rebellion.
He will not contradict His own nature.
And this is why Scripture matters so deeply.
Feelings can deceive.
Culture can deceive.
Even spiritual experiences can be misunderstood.
But the Word of God anchors believers in truth.
The Greek word often translated “truth” in the New Testament is:
ἀλήθεια
Alētheia.
It carries the idea of reality unveiled.
Truth uncovered.
What is genuine.
Jesus did not merely teach truth.
He declared:
“I am the truth.”
Not a truth.
The truth.
And ultimately Gideon’s story points beyond Gideon.
It points to humanity’s deeper need.
Because every fearful heart eventually reaches the same crossroads:
Will I trust God enough to surrender fully?
Not partially.
Not publicly while secretly resisting privately.
Fully.
The Gospel itself is the greatest confirmation ever given.
God did not merely send signs.
He sent His Son.
Jesus Christ entered human suffering, carried human sin, endured the cross, defeated death, and rose again so fearful, broken, sinful people could be reconciled to God.
The cross is not proof that believers will never struggle.
It is proof that God loves struggling sinners enough to rescue them anyway.
That is why grace is so overwhelming.
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις
Charis.
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift no human could earn.
And maybe someone reading this has been secretly waiting for one final confirmation before finally surrendering fully to Jesus.
But deep down… you already know He has been calling you.
Through conviction.
Through pain.
Through sermons.
Through sleepless nights.
Through this article.
And maybe the real issue is not lack of evidence.
Maybe it is fear of what surrender will cost.
Gideon understands that fear.
But he also proves something extraordinary:
God can transform trembling people into surrendered people.
God still uses imperfect people.
God still calls fearful people.
God still restores doubting people.
God still strengthens exhausted people.
And Jesus Christ is still saving people today.
Do not suffer silently.
Somebody else reading your honesty may realize they are not alone.
One day you will realize God kept answering you because He never planned to abandon you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Barzillai Refused Fame and Stayed Home Instead
paragraphs: Why Barzillai Refused Fame and Stayed Home Instead
Most people dream about being noticed.
They dream about finally being invited into rooms where kings speak.
They want influence. They want recognition. They want the seat beside power.
But one old man in Scripture was offered everything most people spend their entire lives chasing… and he quietly said no.
No spotlight. No palace. No prestige. No public applause.
And somehow… that refusal became one of the most unforgettable moments in the Bible.
His name was Barzillai.

Most believers skip over him. Most sermons barely mention him. But hidden inside his story is one of the deepest revelations about humility, aging, loyalty, discernment, and eternal reward found anywhere in Scripture.
And if you have ever felt overlooked… exhausted… forgotten… or tempted to prove yourself to people who only value visibility… this story may hit you harder than you expected.
Because Barzillai understood something modern Christianity often forgets:
Not every calling is public. Not every reward is earthly. And not every faithful servant is supposed to stand on a stage.
The story unfolds during one of the darkest moments in King David’s life.
His own son Absalom had betrayed him. Jerusalem was thrown into political chaos. David fled the city humiliated, grieving, and vulnerable.
This was not the David who killed Goliath. This was not the celebrated king surrounded by victory songs.
This was an aging king running barefoot through heartbreak.
And during David’s suffering, many people abandoned him.
But a few remained loyal.
One of them was Barzillai.
Scripture introduces him in 2 Samuel 17:27-29.
The Hebrew text calls him:
בַּרְזִלַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי
Transliterated:
Barzillai HaGiladi
Meaning:
“Barzillai the Gileadite.”
The name “Barzillai” is connected to the Hebrew root:
בַּרְזֶל (barzel)
Meaning:
“Iron.”
And that is exactly who he was.
Not flashy. Not loud. Not performative.
Strong. Steady. Faithful.
Iron in a collapsing world.
When David was starving, weary, rejected, and vulnerable in the wilderness, Barzillai showed up carrying provision.
Beds. Basins. Wheat. Barley. Flour. Beans. Honey. Curds. Sheep. Cheese.
While others calculated political survival… Barzillai simply served.
He risked his reputation helping a rejected king.
And here is what makes this moment extraordinary:
At the time, David’s future looked uncertain.
Supporting him was dangerous.
Barzillai was not serving from convenience. He was serving from covenant loyalty.
The Hebrew word often associated with this kind of faithful covenant love throughout the Old Testament is:
חֶסֶד (chesed)
A word deeper than simple kindness.
It means loyal love. Faithful mercy. Steadfast covenant devotion.
Barzillai embodied chesed.
He served when it cost him something.
That is the kind of faithfulness Heaven remembers.
Not the faithfulness that appears after the victory.
The faithfulness that appears during humiliation.
Some people only stand beside you when your crown is shining.
Others carry bread to you in the wilderness.
Learn the difference.
Eventually Absalom’s rebellion collapsed. David reclaimed the kingdom. The crisis ended.
And then came the moment most people would have dreamed of.
David looked at Barzillai and offered him royal privilege.
2 Samuel 19:33 says:
“Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem.”
The king himself was inviting Barzillai into the palace.
Honor. Comfort. Recognition. Security. Influence.
This was the reward.
Most people would have accepted before David even finished speaking.
But Barzillai answered in a way that feels almost shocking in today’s world.
He said:
“How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?”
Then he continues:
“Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?”
This is one of the most emotionally mature speeches in all of Scripture.
Barzillai was not bitter. He was not insecure. He was not rejecting David.
He simply understood the season of his life.
Modern culture teaches people to chase relevance until death.
Barzillai understood something wiser.
There comes a point where peace matters more than prestige.
He was around eighty years old according to the text.
The Hebrew phrase says:
בֶּן־שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה
Ben-shemonim shanah.
“A son of eighty years.”
And with breathtaking humility, he basically says:
“I do not need the palace anymore.”
Can you imagine the freedom inside a soul like that?
No obsession with image. No desperate hunger for validation. No addiction to applause.
Just peace.
He had already learned what many never learn.
Earthly glory has an expiration date.
The music fades. The celebrations end. The palace eventually becomes dust.
But faithfulness to God echoes into eternity.
Barzillai did not need proximity to power to feel significant.
That sentence alone could heal thousands of believers.
Some people are destroying themselves trying to be seen.
Trying to build platforms. Trying to manufacture importance. Trying to convince the world they matter.
Meanwhile Heaven is often watching the hidden servant carrying bread in obscurity.
Jesus Himself later taught this same kingdom principle.
In Greek, Jesus says in Matthew 6:1:
Προσέχετε τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς
Meaning:
“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them.”
The phrase:
πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι
Means:
“To be gazed at.” “To be publicly admired.” “To be visibly noticed.”
That temptation is ancient.
Many people do not want purpose. They want visibility.
Barzillai was different.
He already knew who he was without public admiration.
And maybe that is why his story still carries so much spiritual weight.
Because inwardly secure people do not need constant attention.
There is another heartbreaking beauty in his response.
Barzillai says he wants to die near the grave of his father and mother.
This reveals something deeply biblical.
He was rooted.
Modern culture glorifies endless mobility. Always chasing bigger. Always chasing louder. Always chasing newer.
But Barzillai treasured home.
The Hebrew understanding of inheritance and family land was deeply sacred.
Home was not merely geography.
It represented identity. Memory. Legacy. Belonging. Covenant continuity.
Barzillai was not clinging to comfort.
He was honoring sacred roots.
There is wisdom in knowing where your soul belongs.
Not every faithful believer is called to the palace.
Some are called to remain planted.
To quietly finish well.
That matters more than most people realize.
And yet the story becomes even more beautiful.
Barzillai did not become selfish in old age.
Instead of taking the royal opportunity for himself, he asked David to bless Chimham.
Likely his son.
That moment reveals generational humility.
Barzillai was content letting someone else receive the visible reward.
Few people are spiritually mature enough for that.
Many people only celebrate opportunities when they personally benefit.
But Barzillai found joy in blessing the next generation.
That is kingdom maturity.
John the Baptist carried this same spirit centuries later.
In Greek, John says about Jesus in John 3:30:
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι
Meaning:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Modern flesh hates that verse.
Everything in worldly culture screams:
Increase yourself. Promote yourself. Protect your image. Build your empire. Stay relevant.
But kingdom people understand something deeper.
Your worth is not measured by how loudly the world celebrates you.
Your worth was settled at Calvary.
Barzillai reminds us that obscurity is not failure.
Sometimes obscurity is faithfulness.
Some of the holiest people alive will never trend online.
They will never fill stadiums. They will never become famous. They will never have millions of followers.
But Heaven knows their names.
That is enough.
One of the enemy’s greatest lies is convincing believers that hidden obedience has little value.
But Scripture repeatedly shows the opposite.
God notices hidden faithfulness.
The widow with two mites. The unnamed woman washing Jesus’ feet with tears. The boy carrying loaves and fish. Joseph silently protecting Mary. Barzillai carrying provisions to a grieving king.
Heaven watches differently than culture watches.
Even Jesus was born away from worldly prestige.
Isaiah 53:2 says there was no outward beauty in Him that people should desire Him.
The Messiah entered history without earthly glamour.
And still humanity was redeemed through Him.
Never underestimate quiet obedience.
Some of the greatest kingdom impact happens far away from public applause.
There are tired believers reading this right now who feel invisible.
You served. You gave. You stayed faithful. You carried others emotionally. You prayed privately. You endured silently.
And maybe nobody thanked you.
Barzillai’s story is proof that God sees hidden loyalty.
Nothing surrendered to Christ is forgotten.
Galatians 6:9 says:
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.”
The Greek phrase for “grow weary” is:
ἐγκακέω (enkakeō)
Meaning:
“To lose heart.” “To collapse inwardly.” “To surrender emotionally.”
Some of you have been spiritually exhausted.
But God has not overlooked your faithfulness.
Barzillai teaches us that you do not need fame to matter.
You do not need a platform to be powerful.
You do not need public recognition for Heaven to call your life significant.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of all…
Barzillai disappears quietly from the biblical narrative.
No grand farewell. No monument. No public ceremony.
Just faithful service. Then home.
And somehow that silence speaks loudly.
Because real spiritual maturity no longer needs to announce itself.
The older many believers become, the more they crave attention.
But the older Barzillai became, the more content he was with peace.
That is rare.
That is holy.
That is unforgettable.
Maybe you are in a season where God is teaching you the same lesson.
To stop chasing visibility. To stop comparing your calling. To stop measuring your worth by public response.
Maybe God is teaching you to become faithful in secret.
To become rooted. To become steady. To become iron.
Like Barzillai.
And maybe the reason this story hurts so deeply is because many believers secretly fear being forgotten.
But the Gospel changes that fear forever.
Because in Christ, your identity is not built on earthly applause.
It is built on redemption.
Jesus Christ did what no human could ever do.
He carried our sin to the cross. He took judgment upon Himself. He defeated death through His resurrection.
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις (charis)
Meaning:
Unearned favor. Divine gift. Mercy freely given.
Salvation is not earned through status. Not through fame. Not through influence.
It is received through Christ.
Ephesians 2:8 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
The Gospel dismantles human pride.
At the foot of the cross, kings and servants stand equally desperate for mercy.
And maybe that is why Barzillai’s spirit feels so Christlike.
He was content serving without needing glory.
That spirit points toward Jesus Himself.
Philippians 2 says Christ “made Himself nothing.”
The Greek phrase:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
“He emptied Himself.”
The King of kings embraced humility.
And because of Him, hidden faithfulness now carries eternal meaning.
If this article exposed something hidden inside your heart, be honest about it.
And if someone you love is exhausted from trying to prove themselves to the world, send this to them.
One day, many people celebrated on earth will be forgotten… while hidden servants welcomed by Jesus will shine forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Emotional Burden of Carrying Gomer Back Home Again
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Burden of Carrying Gomer Back Home Again
Nobody talks enough about the walk home.
We preach about Hosea obeying God. We preach about Gomer’s unfaithfulness. We preach about redemption. We preach about covenant.
But almost nobody stops long enough to feel the unbearable silence of a broken prophet walking beside the woman who shattered him… while leading her back home again.
That is where this story stops feeling ancient. That is where it becomes terrifyingly personal.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to carry back someone who wounded us deeply.

Some know what it feels like to forgive while still bleeding. Some know what it feels like to love someone who embarrassed you publicly. Some know what it feels like to stay awake wondering why your loyalty was not enough.
And some know the strange emotional exhaustion of praying for people who keep running toward the very darkness destroying them.
The Book of Hosea is not merely a prophetic warning to Israel. It is one of the most emotionally devastating portraits of covenant love ever recorded in Scripture.
And when understood in the original Hebrew context, the story becomes even heavier.
In Hosea 1:2, the Lord commands Hosea:
“Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms.”
The Hebrew reads:
"לֵךְ קַח־לְךָ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים"
Transliterated:
“Lekach-lecha eshet zenunim.”
The phrase “eshet zenunim” does not merely imply isolated immoral mistakes.
The Hebrew word “זְנוּנִים” (zenunim) carries the sense of repeated harlotry, habitual unfaithfulness, spiritual prostitution, and ongoing covenant betrayal.
This was not God asking Hosea to prepare for one bad season. This was God asking him to enter emotional warfare.

And before someone misunderstands this passage, Scripture never glorifies abuse, manipulation, or destructive relationships. The purpose of Hosea’s marriage was prophetic symbolism ordained uniquely by God to reveal Israel’s spiritual adultery against Him.
This is not permission for people to remain in danger. This is revelation about the depth of divine covenant love.
Hosea’s pain was prophetic.
Imagine the humiliation.
The whispers in the marketplace. The side-eyes. The silent pity. The rumors. The shame.
“Did you hear where Gomer was seen?” “Did you hear who she left with?” “Did you hear what happened?”
And still… Hosea stayed obedient.
Most people can handle serving God publicly. Very few can handle obeying Him privately when obedience humiliates them.
That is the hidden burden.
There are wounds that happen behind closed doors that nobody applauds.
Some people reading this are carrying secret heartbreak while still smiling in church. Still worshipping. Still serving. Still posting Scriptures. Still trying not to collapse emotionally.
And the terrifying part is this: You can be deeply loved by God and still emotionally shattered at the same time.
The modern church sometimes teaches a version of faith that leaves no room for grief. But Scripture never hides the emotional agony of God’s servants.
David wept. Jeremiah broke. Elijah collapsed. Paul despaired. Even Jesus sweat blood in Gethsemane.
Biblical strength was never emotional numbness.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly show that covenant faithfulness often costs tears.
Then comes the part almost nobody emotionally enters.
Hosea 3.
Gomer is gone again.
And now she is no longer simply wandering. She appears enslaved. Broken. Owned. Reduced.
Then God says something staggering.
Hosea 3:1:
“Then said the LORD unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress...”
The Hebrew opening is breathtaking:
"עוֹד לֵךְ אֱהַב אִשָּׁה"
“Od lech ehav ishah.”
“Go again, love a woman.”
Go again.
Not after an apology. Not after changed behavior. Not after restored trust. Not after public repentance.
Go again.
Some of the deepest pain in human existence is loving people who repeatedly break your heart.
Now imagine Hosea walking toward the place where Gomer was being sold.
The crowd. The smell of dirt. The humiliation. The transaction.
And Hosea purchasing back the woman who already belonged to him.
Hosea 3:2 says:
“So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley.”
The Hebrew:
"וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי"
“Va’ekreha li.”
“I bought her for myself.”
Do you understand how emotionally crushing that is?
To pay for what should have never been lost.
This is where the story stops being about ancient Israel and starts exposing us.
Because this is exactly what sin did to humanity.
We belonged to God. Yet humanity wandered. Sold itself into spiritual slavery. Chased idols. Loved darkness. Betrayed covenant.
And then Christ came to purchase back what already belonged to Him.
The Gospel was never cheap.
In the Greek New Testament, the language of redemption carries marketplace imagery.
The word “ἀγοράζω” (agorazō) means “to buy in the marketplace.”
1 Corinthians 6:20 says:
“For ye are bought with a price.”
Greek:
"ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς"
“Egorasthete gar times.”
“You were purchased with a price.”
Jesus did not merely forgive from a distance. He entered the marketplace of human brokenness.
He stepped into our filth. Our rebellion. Our shame. Our addictions. Our hypocrisy. Our secret sin. Our pride. Our wandering.
And He paid for us with His own blood.
The emotional weight of Hosea points directly toward Christ.
Many people picture the crucifixion only physically. But Scripture reveals enormous emotional suffering too.
Isaiah 53 says:
“He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew phrase “מַכְאֹבוֹת” (mak’ovot) literally carries the sense of pains, sorrows, sufferings, emotional anguish.
Jesus was not emotionally detached from human betrayal.
Judas betrayed Him. Peter denied Him. The crowds abandoned Him. The religious leaders mocked Him.
Yet still… He carried humanity home.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we were lovable. But that Christ remained loving.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek phrase “ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν” means “while we were still sinners.”
Not after perfection. Not after cleanup. Not after religious performance.
While still broken.
Somebody reading this has spent years believing you are too filthy for God. Too inconsistent. Too compromised. Too hypocritical. Too addicted. Too emotionally unstable. Too far gone.
But Hosea destroys that lie.
Because the story was never about Gomer earning rescue. It was about covenant love pursuing the undeserving.
Still… there is another side to this story most people ignore.
The emotional burden carried by faithful people.
Some believers are exhausted. Not because they stopped loving God. But because they kept loving people who kept hurting them.
Parents praying for prodigal children. Spouses grieving hardened hearts. Friends carrying betrayal. Pastors carrying hidden loneliness. Believers silently fighting disappointment.
Sometimes obedience to God feels emotionally expensive.
And here is the dangerous moment: When pain tempts people toward emotional numbness.
Some stop loving deeply because loving deeply hurt too much.
But Jesus never became cold.
Wounded? Yes. Rejected? Yes. Crucified? Yes.
But still loving.
Luke 23:34 records Jesus saying:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
The Greek:
"Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς"
“Pater, aphes autois.”
“Father, forgive them.”
Mercy while bleeding.
That is supernatural love.
Not weak love. Not enabling love. Not foolish love.
Holy love.
The kind only God can sustain inside a shattered heart.
And maybe that is why Hosea hurts so deeply.
Because many of us are not just reading about Gomer. We are reading about ourselves.

We know what it means to wander. We know what it means to fail God repeatedly. We know what it means to promise change and still struggle. We know what it means to hide shame. We know what it means to feel spiritually dirty.
Yet Christ still comes looking.
Still calling. Still redeeming. Still inviting. Still healing.
There is something terrifyingly beautiful about realizing Jesus knew every future failure before the cross… and still chose the cross.
He knew every relapse. Every compromise. Every secret. Every hidden thought. Every betrayal.
And still said yes to Calvary.
That kind of love breaks people.
Not emotionally manipulated religion. Not performance Christianity. Not fake holiness.
Real grace.
The kind that exposes sin while still offering redemption.
The modern world is filled with people starving for this kind of truth.
Not watered-down spirituality. Not motivational speeches disguised as sermons.
People need the Gospel.
The real Gospel.

The Gospel that says sinners can become sons. The Gospel that says shame does not have the final word. The Gospel that says Jesus still restores shattered lives. The Gospel that says redemption is possible.
But redemption is never permission to continue destroying yourself.
Hosea did not buy Gomer back so she could continue living in slavery.
Hosea 3:3 says:
“Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot...”
Redemption leads toward restoration. Toward transformation. Toward covenant faithfulness.
Grace is not God approving sin. Grace is God rescuing people from sin.
That distinction matters.
Somebody reading this has been pretending to be okay. But deep inside, your soul feels exhausted.
You smile publicly. But privately you feel spiritually numb.
Maybe you wandered. Maybe you compromised. Maybe you slowly drifted from intimacy with God. Maybe your heart became cold. Maybe secret sin quietly chained you.
But Jesus still calls people home.
Not because they deserve it. But because He is merciful.
And maybe the most emotional part of Hosea’s story was not purchasing Gomer.
Maybe it was the walk home afterward.
The silence. The tears. The awkwardness. The rebuilding. The healing. The learning to trust again.
Real restoration is rarely instant.
Some scars take time. Some healing takes surrender. Some freedom takes daily dying to self.
But Jesus does not abandon the restoration process.
Philippians 1:6 says:
“He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
The Greek “ἐπιτελέσει” (epitelesei) means to complete fully, accomplish, bring to maturity.
God finishes what He starts.
That matters for people who feel unfinished.
Some of you are in the middle of restoration right now. Not fully free yet. Not fully healed yet. Not fully restored yet.
But still being carried home.
Do not confuse process with abandonment.
God has not forgotten you.
And for the faithful ones carrying emotional burdens nobody sees… The ones who kept praying. Kept forgiving. Kept serving. Kept believing. Kept loving despite heartbreak.
God sees every hidden tear.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle.”
The Hebrew imagery is deeply personal. God is portrayed as preserving every tear. Not ignoring them. Not dismissing them.
Seen. Remembered. Held.
That changes everything.
One day every faithful act of unseen obedience will matter eternally.
One day every burden carried for Christ will make sense.
One day every redeemed prodigal will testify that mercy found them before destruction consumed them.
And one day every knee will bow before the Savior who carried humanity home through blood, nails, rejection, grief, and resurrection power.
Jesus is still rescuing Gomers.
And astonishingly… many of us were one.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this… share this with them. They may be carrying silent heartbreak nobody else sees.
Some people are still alive today only because mercy came looking for them one more time.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE WE LIVING IN THE LAST DAYS?
paragraphs:
ARE WE LIVING IN THE LAST DAYS?
The Question Keeping Millions Awake at Night
There is a silence that falls over a room when someone finally asks the question out loud.
Not casually. Not joking. Not as entertainment.
But with trembling honesty.
“Are we living in the last days?”
You can feel it in the air now.

Wars multiplying. Earthquakes shaking nations. Families collapsing. Churches compromising. People becoming colder. Anxiety becoming normal. Children growing up without peace. Truth being mocked. Evil becoming celebrated.
Even people far from God feel it.
Something is changing.
Something feels close.
And deep inside millions of hearts is the terrifying realization that maybe humanity is not evolving upward the way society promised.
Maybe Scripture was telling the truth all along.

But before fear hijacks the conversation… before sensationalism twists prophecy into entertainment… before social media turns biblical warnings into clickbait… we must return to the only source that can answer this honestly.
The Word of God.
Not conspiracy theories. Not viral predictions. Not date-setting false prophets. Not emotionally manipulative fear preaching.
Scripture.
Because Jesus never commanded believers to panic. He commanded believers to watch.
And there is a difference.
The night before the flood came in Noah’s generation, people were still eating, marrying, buying, selling, laughing, planning vacations, building futures, ignoring warnings.
Judgment did not arrive to a terrified world.
It arrived to a distracted one.
That is what makes this conversation so haunting.
The most dangerous sign may not be chaos itself.
It may be how normal chaos has become.
In Matthew 24, Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives overlooking Jerusalem after His disciples privately asked Him:
“What will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?”
The Greek phrase used in Matthew 24:3 is:
“συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος” (synteleias tou aiōnos)
It literally means: “the completion of the age.”
Not the destruction of existence. Not annihilation.
The closing of one era and the arrival of another.
Jesus answered with terrifying precision.
He warned of deception first. Not war. Not earthquakes. Not famine.
Deception.
“Take heed that no one deceives you.” — Matthew 24:4
The Greek word for deceive is:
“πλανήσῃ” (planēsē)
It means: “to cause someone to wander away from truth.”
That changes everything.
The greatest danger of the last days is not merely destruction around us.
It is spiritual confusion inside us.
People assuming they know God while drifting further from Him.
Church culture replacing surrender. Christian branding replacing holiness. Internet theology replacing Scripture. Feelings replacing repentance.
Jesus said many would come in His name. Many.
Not a few.
Many.
Some would preach parts of truth while hiding the cost of discipleship. Some would build platforms instead of altars. Some would attract crowds while never leading people to genuine repentance.
And people would follow them because they prefer inspiration over transformation.
The Apostle Paul warned Timothy with language so accurate it feels like today’s headlines.
“But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.” — 2 Timothy 3:1
The Greek phrase for “times of difficulty” is:
“καιροὶ χαλεποί” (kairoi chalepoi)
It means: “fierce, savage, dangerous seasons.”
Then Paul described humanity:
Lovers of self. Lovers of money. Proud. Arrogant. Disobedient. Unholy. Without self-control. Brutal. Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.
What makes this passage devastating is that Paul was not primarily describing pagan empires.
He was describing people who still had a form of godliness.
External religion. Internal emptiness.
And suddenly the issue becomes personal.
Because this article is not merely about identifying signs in the world.
It is about identifying signs in ourselves.
That is where conviction begins.
Not with pointing fingers at society.
But by asking:
Has my own heart grown cold?
Jesus warned:
“Because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold.” — Matthew 24:12
The word “love” there is the Greek word:
“ἀγάπη” (agapē)
This is not casual affection.
This is covenant love. Sacrificial love. Holy love. God-centered love.
Jesus warned that many hearts would slowly freeze spiritually.
Not overnight.
Gradually.
A little compromise. A little bitterness. A little hidden sin. A little prayerlessness. A little numbness.
Until eventually people no longer burn for God the way they once did.
And maybe that is why so many people secretly feel exhausted right now.
Not just physically.
Spiritually.
Because no human soul was designed to survive disconnected from its Creator.
People are drowning in entertainment while starving for peace. Scrolling endlessly while feeling emptier. Laughing publicly while breaking privately.
And beneath all the noise is a deeper fear many do not know how to articulate.
What if eternity is real?
The Bible never presents the last days merely as a timeline issue.
It presents them as a wake-up call.
The Hebrew prophets warned generations repeatedly that judgment follows persistent rebellion.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word often associated with repentance is:
“שׁוּב” (shuv)
It means: “to return.”
Not merely feeling guilty.
Returning.
Returning to God. Returning to truth. Returning to holiness. Returning to obedience. Returning to intimacy with the Lord.
That changes the entire emotional atmosphere of this conversation.
Because the message of the last days is not ultimately: “Be terrified.”
It is: “Come back to God while there is still time.”
Even now, mercy is still being extended.
Every sunrise is proof.
The cross still stands. The tomb is still empty. Grace is still available. Forgiveness is still possible. Jesus is still saving broken people.
That is why prophecy without the Gospel becomes dangerous.
Because biblical prophecy was never meant to entertain curiosity while leaving hearts unchanged.
Its purpose was repentance.
The Apostle Peter wrote:
“The Lord is not slow concerning His promise… but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” — 2 Peter 3:9
The Greek word for repentance is:
“μετάνοια” (metanoia)
It means: “a change of mind that results in a transformed life.”
Not temporary emotion. Transformation.
And maybe that is the real miracle happening quietly right now around the world.
In the middle of darkness, people are waking up spiritually.
Former atheists finding Christ. Addicts being delivered. Muslims encountering Jesus in dreams. Young people opening Bibles again. Broken marriages being restored. Prodigals returning home.
Light shines brightest in darkness.
The enemy wants people to believe the last days are only about fear.
But Scripture also says there will be an unprecedented harvest of souls.
The Gospel is spreading globally faster than ever before.
And this matters deeply because many believers have unknowingly developed an unhealthy obsession with signs while neglecting intimacy with Christ.
They know timelines. But not prayer.
They study beasts in Revelation. But ignore the Beatitudes.
They analyze world events. But refuse to forgive people.
Yet Jesus never said the world would recognize His disciples by their prophecy charts.
He said they would recognize them by love.
Real love. Holy love. Sacrificial love.
Still… we cannot ignore the weight of what Scripture reveals.
Israel’s existence. Global instability. Increasing deception. Moral collapse. Technological control. Growing hostility toward biblical truth.
These realities understandably cause many believers to wonder how close we are.
But one of the most misunderstood truths about biblical prophecy is this:
Jesus explicitly warned against date setting.
“But concerning that day and hour no one knows…” — Matthew 24:36
No one.
That includes influencers. That includes viral prophecy personalities. That includes self-proclaimed watchmen predicting exact dates.
Every generation of believers has seen shadows of the end.
But Scripture teaches us to live ready rather than obsessed.
There is a profound difference.
Because fear-driven obsession produces anxiety.
But readiness produces holiness.
The early church lived with urgency, but also with hope.
One of the most powerful Aramaic expressions connected to the return of Christ is:
“מָרַנָא תָא” (Marana Tha)
Found in 1 Corinthians 16:22.
It means: “Our Lord, come.”
This was not spoken with terror.
It was spoken with longing.
The first Christians were not merely trying to escape earth.
They loved Jesus deeply enough to desire His appearing.
And maybe that is the question hiding beneath this entire article.
Do we fear the return of Christ because we love sin too much?
That question cuts deeper than most people expect.
Because many want heaven someday while still clinging to the very darkness Jesus died to free them from.
But the Gospel is not behavior management.
It is resurrection.
The same Jesus who warned about judgment also touched lepers. Forgave prostitutes. Restored failures. Wept with the grieving. Died for sinners. Rose again.
The cross proves God’s holiness.
And simultaneously proves His love.
That is why the last days message cannot stop at warning.
It must end with invitation.
Because no matter how dark the world becomes, no human being is beyond redemption while breath still remains.
The thief on the cross found mercy in his final moments. Peter found restoration after denial. Paul found grace after persecuting Christians.
And maybe someone reading this right now believes they have gone too far.
Too dirty. Too addicted. Too compromised. Too numb. Too hypocritical. Too broken.
But the Gospel declares something culture never can.
Jesus still saves.
Not because humanity deserves it.
But because His mercy is greater than human rebellion.
In Hebrew, one of the most beautiful words connected to God’s covenant love is:
“חֶסֶד” (chesed)
It describes steadfast mercy. Loyal love. Faithful covenant compassion.
This is the heart of God toward repentant sinners.
Not weak tolerance of sin.
Holy mercy that invites transformation.
So… are we living in the last days?
Maybe.
Many signs described in Scripture undeniably echo louder now than ever before.
But the deeper question is not: “When will Jesus return?”
The deeper question is:
Will He find us faithful when He does?
Will He find us loving people? Forgiving enemies? Living holy? Walking humbly? Sharing the Gospel? Repenting sincerely? Seeking truth? Serving faithfully?
Or merely distracted?
The danger of the last days is not only persecution.
It is spiritual sleep.
That is why Romans 13:11 says:
“The hour has come for you to wake from sleep.”
And perhaps that is exactly what God is doing through this generation.
Waking people up.
Not merely to fear the end.
But to finally see their need for Jesus Christ.
Because in the end, prophecy is not mainly about charts.
It is about a King.
A returning King.
And the same Savior who promised He would come again also promised this:
“Whoever comes to Me I will never cast out.” — John 6:37
That invitation still stands.
Right now.
For the addict. For the doubter. For the exhausted believer. For the secret sinner. For the lukewarm Christian. For the atheist. For the prodigal. For the wounded. For the ashamed.
Grace still has an open door.
But none of us are promised tomorrow.
And maybe that is why this conversation matters so deeply.
Not because fear sells.
But because eternity is real.
And if you know someone silently wrestling with fear, doubt, anxiety, compromise, or spiritual exhaustion… send this to them.
Some people do not need another motivational speech.
They need truth.
One day, the sky will split open… and nobody will care who won the argument online.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Woman at the Well Left Her Waterpot Behind
paragraphs: Why the Woman at the Well Left Her Waterpot Behind
There are moments in Scripture that seem small until you realize Heaven hid an earthquake inside a sentence.
John 4:28 says:
“Then the woman left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men…”
She left her waterpot behind.
Most people read past that line.
But nothing in Scripture is accidental.
That waterpot carried more than water.
It carried routine.
Shame.
Survival.
Isolation.
Years of disappointment.
And when she encountered Jesus Christ, she walked away from the very thing that represented the life she used to live.
This was not absent-mindedness.
This was transformation.
And if we are honest… many of us are still carrying waterpots we should have dropped a long time ago.
The story begins in John 4, where Jesus travels through Samaria. Jews and Samaritans carried generations of hostility between them. Many Jews intentionally avoided Samaritan territory altogether.
Yet John 4:4 says:
“He must needs go through Samaria.”
The Greek phrase used here is:
δεῖ δὲ αὐτὸν διέρχεσθαι διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας
“Dei de auton dierchesthai dia tes Samareias.”
The word δεῖ (dei) means “it is necessary,” “it is required,” or “it must happen.”
This was not geographical convenience.
This was divine appointment.
Jesus was not wandering.
Heaven had a meeting scheduled.
One broken woman was about to collide with the Messiah.
And maybe this is the part people need to hear today:
Jesus still walks into places religious people avoid.
He still enters messy lives.
He still sits beside exhausted souls.
He still waits at wells where thirsty hearts keep pretending they are fine.
The Bible says Jesus sat by Jacob’s well around the sixth hour.
That matters.
The sixth hour was around noon.
The hottest part of the day.
Women normally gathered water in the cooler hours with other women.
But this woman came alone.
Loneliness was already preaching before she ever opened her mouth.
People who have been publicly broken often learn how to move quietly.
They avoid crowds.
Avoid conversations.
Avoid eye contact.
Avoid reminders.
Some wounds become schedules.
When Jesus asked her for water, she was shocked.
John 4:9 says:
“How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria?”
Everything about this moment shattered cultural barriers.
Jewish men typically avoided prolonged public conversations with women.
Jews despised Samaritans.
Yet Jesus initiated the conversation.
Because grace always moves first.
Religion says, “Clean yourself first.”
Jesus says, “Come talk to Me first.”
Then Jesus says something that changes the atmosphere forever.
John 4:10:
“If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.”
The Greek phrase for “living water” is:
ὕδωρ ζῶν
“Hydor zon.”
Not stagnant water.
Not temporary satisfaction.
Not religious performance.
Living water.
Flowing.
Breathing.
Transforming.
Alive.
Jesus was offering something deeper than physical relief.
He was confronting the drought inside her soul.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because many people are still trying to satisfy spiritual thirst with temporary wells.
Relationships.
Attention.
Money.
Addictions.
Success.
Validation.
Pornography.
Platforms.
Followers.
Drunkenness.
Achievement.
Even religion without intimacy with God.
But temporary water always creates permanent thirst.
That is why people can sleep beside someone they love and still feel emotionally abandoned.
Why celebrities overdose.
Why wealthy people still feel empty.
Why applause cannot heal trauma.
Why lust never cures loneliness.
Why secret sin always asks for more.
The woman at the well understood disappointment.
Jesus reveals:
“Thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband.”
Notice something powerful.
Jesus exposed her truth without humiliating her.
Conviction is not the same as condemnation.
The enemy exposes sin to destroy people.
Jesus exposes sin to rescue people.
The Hebrew concept connected to repentance carries the idea of turning back.
The word שׁוּב (shuv) means “to return,” “to turn back,” or “to come home again.”
Real repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is returning to God.
And this woman was finally encountering the One her soul had actually been searching for through every failed relationship.
Many people criticize her history.
But broken relationships often reveal deeper hunger.
People search for eternal healing inside temporary humans.
No human being can successfully carry the weight of becoming someone’s savior.
Only Jesus Christ can heal the thirst beneath the thirst.
And then the moment happens.
The unveiling.
The revelation.
The collision between shame and Messiah.
John 4:26:
Jesus saith unto her, “I that speak unto thee am he.”
In Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι
“Ego eimi.”
“I AM.”
The same divine echo connected to God’s revelation in Exodus.
In Exodus 3:14, God tells Moses:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
“Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh.”
“I AM THAT I AM.”
This was not merely a teacher speaking.
This was God revealing Himself to a rejected woman beside a well.
Think about the scandal of grace.
Religious elites argued.
Powerful leaders resisted Him.
Yet one of the clearest early revelations of His identity was given to a Samaritan woman with a shattered reputation.
Because Jesus specializes in revealing Himself to people the world counts out.
And then Scripture says:
“The woman then left her waterpot…”
The Greek word for waterpot is:
ὑδρία
“Hydria.”
This was not some tiny cup.
It was an important vessel.
Necessary.
Practical.
Valuable.
Yet she abandoned it.
Why?
Because when living water touched her soul, the old thirst lost its authority.
The very reason she came to the well became irrelevant compared to what she found there.
This is what happens when people genuinely encounter Jesus.
Old appetites begin dying.
Old chains begin breaking.
Old identities begin collapsing.
Things that once controlled you suddenly lose power.
Not because self-help saved you.
Not because religion impressed you.
But because Christ transformed you.
The waterpot represented survival.
But she discovered salvation.
The waterpot represented routine.
But she discovered resurrection life.
The waterpot represented temporary water.
But she discovered eternal water.
Some people are emotionally dying because they keep carrying what Jesus already told them to release.
Old bitterness.
Old labels.
Old addictions.
Old shame.
Old identities.
Old guilt.
Old versions of themselves.
You cannot fully grab hold of living water while clinging to dead weight.
And notice what happened next.
The isolated woman became an evangelist.
The woman who arrived alone suddenly ran back into the city.
John 4:29:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
People who truly encounter Jesus cannot stay silent forever.
One authentic encounter with Christ can turn private pain into public testimony.
And maybe the most beautiful part is this:
She was not fully educated.
Not fully healed.
Not fully discipled.
Not fully polished.
Yet God still used her.
Some people keep postponing obedience because they think God only uses perfect people.
But Scripture repeatedly destroys that lie.
Moses stuttered.
David failed.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet grace rewrote their story.
The Samaritan woman did not have a theological degree.
She simply had an encounter she could not deny.
And honestly… some of the most powerful witnesses are people who remember exactly what Jesus rescued them from.
Because gratitude creates boldness.
Religion often produces performance.
But mercy produces worship.
And maybe this is why the story still pierces hearts today.
We know what it feels like to carry invisible thirst.
To smile publicly while collapsing privately.
To crave love while sabotaging ourselves.
To chase distractions because silence forces us to hear our own pain.
To appear functional while spiritually exhausted.
To pretend everything is okay while secretly asking:
“Why do I still feel empty?”
This woman thought she came for water.
But Jesus knew she came for Him.
Even if she did not realize it yet.
Some of you reading this have spent years carrying emotional waterpots.
Trying to survive.
Trying to numb pain.
Trying to outrun guilt.
Trying to satisfy cravings that never stay satisfied.
But Jesus still sits beside wells today.
Still speaking.
Still calling.
Still offering living water.
Still healing sinners.
Still restoring prodigals.
Still forgiving the ashamed.
Still welcoming the exhausted.
And the invitation remains.
Isaiah 55:1 says:
“Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters…”
The Hebrew word for thirst is:
צָמֵא
“Tsame.”
A desperate thirst.
A deep craving.
A consuming need.
God has always addressed thirsty souls.
Not fake perfection.
Not polished masks.
Not religious acting.
Thirsty souls.
And maybe the tragedy today is not that people are thirsty.
The tragedy is that many people keep drinking from poisoned wells.
Social media validation.
Lust.
Self-worship.
Bitterness.
Occult spirituality.
Pride.
Greed.
Temporary pleasure.
Sin always overpromises and underdelivers.
The enemy markets chains like freedom.
But Jesus offers actual freedom.
John 7:37 says:
“If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.”
Christianity is not ultimately about behavior modification.
It is about reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Christ died for sinners.
Was buried.
Rose again.
And through repentance and faith, broken people become new creations.
Not perfect overnight.
But transformed.
Alive.
Redeemed.
And maybe someone reading this has been wondering if God could still want them after everything they have done.
Look at the woman at the well.
Jesus already knew every chapter of her story before He spoke to her.
And He stayed.
That alone destroys the lie that grace only belongs to clean people.
No.
Grace is for sinners willing to come to Christ.
Grace is for exhausted people.
Grace is for addicts.
Grace is for prodigals.
Grace is for hypocrites tired of pretending.
Grace is for people who secretly hate who they have become.
Grace is for thirsty souls.
And perhaps the reason this story survives centuries later is because humanity still keeps arriving at wells carrying empty hearts.
We keep thinking another relationship will fix us.
Another paycheck.
Another achievement.
Another thrill.
Another compromise.
Another distraction.
But nothing temporary can permanently satisfy an eternal soul.
Only Christ can.
The woman left her waterpot because she finally found something worth more than what she came carrying.
And maybe that is the question echoing through this story today:
What are you still carrying that Jesus is asking you to leave behind?
The addiction?
The secret sin?
The shame?
The unforgiveness?
The fake image?
The rebellion?
The spiritual apathy?
The hidden exhaustion?
The self-hatred?
The pride?
The fear?
Some people need to stop decorating the very chains Jesus died to break.
You do not need another motivational speech.
You need living water.
And the beautiful reality is this:
Jesus still saves.
Still heals.
Still restores.
Still forgives.
Still changes lives.
Still calls sinners by name.
Still walks into Samaria.
Still waits at wells.
Still loves the people society labels unreachable.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if this reminded you of someone who has been spiritually exhausted, drowning silently, or running from God, share this with them.
Some people are still carrying waterpots because they have never realized the Messiah is already waiting at the well.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind the Silent Years of Ishmael After Abraham Died
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind the Silent Years of Ishmael After Abraham Died
There are some people in Scripture whose pain is so deep… God only gives us fragments.
Not because their story did not matter.
But because some grief is too heavy for paragraphs.
Ishmael is one of them.
Most believers know him as “the son sent away.”
The child born before the promise.
The boy Abraham loved… but history slowly forgot.
And somewhere between sermons, theology debates, and generational conflict, many stopped asking one haunting question:
What happened to Ishmael after Abraham died?
Not politically.
Not ethnically.
Not culturally.
Personally.
Emotionally.
Spiritually.
What does it feel like to grow up knowing your father loved you… but could never fully keep you?
What does it do to a son’s heart to hear heaven’s promises spoken over another child while you stand nearby listening?
What happens in the silent years after rejection?
Scripture becomes strangely quiet about Ishmael.
And silence in the Bible is never accidental.
Sometimes silence is where the deepest wounds live.
Sometimes silence is where God hides the details because He knows humanity would not know how to carry them.
Genesis tells us something most people miss.
When Abraham died, Ishmael came back.
Not to fight.
Not to steal Isaac’s inheritance.
Not to destroy the covenant line.
He came home.
Genesis 25:9 says:
“His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah…”
Notice the order.
Isaac.
And Ishmael.
Together.
Two brothers separated by jealousy, prophecy, pain, mothers, inheritance, and history… standing over the grave of the same father.
The Hebrew wording here matters deeply.
The word used for buried is:
קָבַר (qābar)
Meaning:
“To bury, to lay to rest, to place into the earth with honor.”
This was not a rushed disposal.
This was dignity.
Respect.
Closure.
And perhaps… reconciliation.
Imagine the scene.
Abraham is gone.
The man who once held Ishmael as an answered prayer.
The father who taught him survival in the wilderness.
The father whose silence after the separation may have hurt more than the exile itself.
Now dead.
And Ishmael returns older.
Weathered.
No longer the crying child under the desert shrub.
No longer the mocked son.
No longer simply “Hagar’s boy.”
Now a man carrying decades of memories no one wrote down.
Some of you understand this kind of pain too well.
You know what it feels like to love someone who wounded you.
You know what it feels like to spend years pretending rejection did not shape you.
You know what it feels like to hear people celebrate someone else’s calling while wondering why your own life feels hidden.
Ishmael’s silent years speak loudly to forgotten people.
To abandoned sons.
To overlooked daughters.
To believers who feel spiritually secondary.
To people who smile publicly while privately wondering if they were the “almost blessing.”
But the Bible never says God abandoned Ishmael.
That changes everything.
In fact, long before Abraham died, God already spoke directly concerning Ishmael.
Genesis 17:20:
“And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee…”
In Hebrew:
וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שְׁמַעְתִּיךָ
(U’leYishma’el shema‘ticha)
Literally:
“And concerning Ishmael, I have heard you.”
The name Ishmael itself comes from:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishma‘el)
Meaning:
