Maybe this article found you at the exact moment your spirit needed it.
Maybe this was confirmation. Maybe this was correction. Maybe this was rescue.
But whatever God is saying to you right now… do not ignore Him.
One day you will realize God’s delays protected you as much as His answers carried you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF REHOBOAM
paragraphs:
THE UNTOLD STORY OF REHOBOAM
The King Who Inherited a Kingdom… and Lost a Nation
There are some people in Scripture we judge too quickly.
We reduce them to one terrible decision. One foolish moment. One catastrophic mistake.
But behind every fallen king is usually a wounded son.
And few stories reveal this more painfully than Rehoboam.
Most believers know him as the arrogant king who split Israel. The stubborn ruler who answered wisdom with pride. The son of Solomon who destroyed what David built.
But the deeper you go into the biblical text… the more terrifyingly human his story becomes.
Because Rehoboam was not born evil.
He was born into impossible expectations.
He inherited pressure. He inherited legacy. He inherited comparison. He inherited a crown too heavy for the soul carrying it.
And somewhere between insecurity, pride, fear, and the desperate need to appear strong… he destroyed a kingdom with words.
Not swords. Words.
And maybe that is why this story still feels painfully modern.

Because entire families still split over pride. Churches still fracture over ego. Friendships still collapse because someone refused humility. And people still lose what God gave them because they needed to sound powerful more than they needed to be wise.
The tragedy of Rehoboam is not ancient history.
It is happening every single day.
And most people do not realize they are becoming him.
The Bible introduces Rehoboam in 1 Kings 11 after the spiritual collapse of Solomon.
Solomon — the wisest king who ever lived — had slowly drifted into compromise. His heart turned toward foreign gods because of the influence of the wives he loved more than the God who enthroned him.
The kingdom still looked glorious externally. Gold still filled the palace. The temple still stood. The music still played. The ceremonies still continued.
But spiritually? Decay had already begun.
That is one of the most dangerous realities in human life.
Things can appear successful long after they have started dying internally.
And Rehoboam inherited the consequences of sins he did not personally create.
Many people understand this pain.
Some inherited broken homes. Others inherited generational anger. Some inherited addiction cycles. Some inherited spiritual confusion. Some inherited emotional wounds they never asked for.
Rehoboam inherited a fractured spiritual atmosphere.
And Scripture quietly reveals something many overlook.
His mother was Naamah the Ammonite.
The text says:
“וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ נַעֲמָה הָעַמּוֹנִית”
Transliteration: “Ve’shem immo Na’amah ha’Ammonit.”
Translation: “And his mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.”
— 1 Kings 14:21
This detail matters.
The Ammonites worshiped false gods including Molech. A demonic deity associated with child sacrifice.
Imagine growing up in Solomon’s palace.
Wisdom on one side. Idolatry on the other. Glory publicly. Confusion privately.
That environment shapes people.
Rehoboam grew up watching a father celebrated by nations while simultaneously compromising before God.
And this is where many modern believers secretly struggle.
Confusion caused by inconsistent spiritual leadership.

People who preached holiness publicly but lived differently privately. Parents who quoted Scripture while emotionally wounding their children. Leaders who looked anointed but were spiritually collapsing behind closed doors.
It creates instability in the soul.
And unstable souls often overcompensate later through control, anger, dominance, pride, or insecurity.
By the time Rehoboam ascended the throne, Israel was exhausted.
Solomon’s building projects had become financially crushing. The labor burdens were immense. The people were weary.
So Israel approached the new king with a simple request.
Lighten the load.
That was it.
Not rebellion. Not mutiny. Not revolution.
Compassion.
The elders who had served Solomon wisely advised Rehoboam:
“If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them and grant them their petition and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever.” — 1 Kings 12:7
That advice reflected the heart of godly leadership.
True authority in Scripture is never rooted in intimidation. It is rooted in servanthood.
Jesus Himself would later say:
“The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.” — Mark 10:45
But Rehoboam rejected the elders.
Why?
Because pride often prefers voices that protect ego instead of voices that protect destiny.
So he turned to younger men. Friends. Peers. People raised with him.
And they gave him toxic advice drenched in insecurity.
“Tell them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.’” — 1 Kings 12:10
The Hebrew wording carries a brutal tone of domination and humiliation.
This was not strength.
It was performative masculinity. It was insecurity disguised as authority.
And countless people still do this today.
They weaponize harshness because they fear appearing weak. They dominate because they secretly feel powerless. They raise their voice because they cannot govern their spirit.
The loudest person in the room is often the most fragile emotionally.
Then came the sentence that shattered a nation.
“My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.” — 1 Kings 12:11
In Hebrew:
“אָבִי יִסַּר אֶתְכֶם בַּשּׁוֹטִים וַאֲנִי אֲיַסֵּר אֶתְכֶם בָּעַקְרַבִּים”
Transliteration: “Avi yissar etkhem ba-shotim va’ani ayasser etkhem ba’aqrabbim.”
Literal meaning: “My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
The word “scorpions” likely referred to brutal multi-thonged whips embedded with metal or sharp fragments.
Rehoboam thought cruelty would establish loyalty.
Instead… he triggered division.
Immediately the northern tribes revolted.
The united kingdom fractured forever.
Ten tribes separated. Only Judah and Benjamin remained.
One speech destroyed generations of unity.
This is why Scripture repeatedly warns about the tongue.
Words build worlds. Words also bury them.
Marriages die through words. Children carry wounds from words. Churches split because of words. Nations burn because of words.
Some of the deepest scars on earth were never caused by knives.
Only sentences.
And what makes Rehoboam’s story devastating is this:
God had already warned Solomon this division would happen because of covenant unfaithfulness.
Rehoboam was walking into consequences larger than himself.
Yet Scripture still holds him responsible for how he responded.
That tension matters deeply.
Because inherited pain is real.
But inherited pain does not excuse sinful responses.
You may not have created your trauma. But you are still responsible before God for what you do with it.
That truth hurts.
But it also liberates.
Because it means your future is not chained forever to your past.
Then comes one of the most overlooked moments in the entire story.
Rehoboam prepares for civil war.
He gathers 180,000 warriors.
Imagine the rage. The humiliation. The embarrassment. The desperation to reclaim control.
But then God intervenes through the prophet Shemaiah.
“Thus says the LORD, ‘You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from Me.’” — 1 Kings 12:24
And astonishingly… Rehoboam listened.
That matters.
Because even flawed people can still respond to God.
The Bible does not hide the failures of its characters. It exposes them honestly.
That authenticity is one reason Scripture carries such supernatural weight.
It does not present fake heroes.
It presents broken humans desperately needing God.
And maybe that is why so many people emotionally connect to biblical stories more than polished modern performances.
Because Scripture tells the truth about humanity.
Even after catastrophic failure, Rehoboam’s story was not entirely hopeless.
But sadly… he never fully surrendered.
2 Chronicles 12:14 gives one of the coldest spiritual evaluations in the Bible:
“He did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.”
In Hebrew:
“וַיַּעַשׂ הָרַע כִּי לֹא הֵכִין לִבּוֹ לִדְרוֹשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה”
Transliteration: “Vaya’as hara ki lo heikhin libbo lidrosh et-YHWH.”
Literal meaning: “He acted wickedly because he did not prepare his heart to seek Yahweh.”
That phrase “prepare his heart” is devastating.
Because spiritual collapse rarely happens suddenly.
It usually happens through unprepared hearts.
Hearts that drift. Hearts that delay repentance. Hearts that love image more than surrender. Hearts that want blessing without obedience.
Many people today are trying to fix external chaos while neglecting internal surrender.
But the soul can never heal properly apart from God.
Success cannot heal it. Relationships cannot heal it. Money cannot heal it. Followers cannot heal it. Attention cannot heal it.
Only Christ can restore what pride destroys.
And this is where Rehoboam’s story quietly points us toward Jesus.
Because Jesus is the better King.
Rehoboam answered the people harshly. Jesus answered the broken gently.
Rehoboam increased burdens. Jesus said:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28
Rehoboam divided a kingdom. Jesus unites people from every tribe and nation.
Rehoboam ruled through intimidation. Jesus washes the feet of sinners.
Rehoboam protected pride. Jesus carried a cross.
The contrast is overwhelming.
And maybe this article is confronting some readers more deeply than expected because they recognize parts of Rehoboam inside themselves.
The defensiveness. The need to control. The fear of appearing weak. The hidden insecurity. The struggle with pride. The inherited wounds. The refusal to soften.
Be honest.
How many relationships have suffered because ego spoke louder than humility?
How many apologies died because pride refused to kneel?
How many people are exhausted from pretending to be strong while spiritually collapsing internally?
This story is not merely about a king from ancient Israel.
It is about every human heart tempted to choose self-protection over surrender.
But the Gospel still offers hope.
Because Jesus specializes in rebuilding what pride shattered.
Peter failed. David failed. Moses failed. Paul failed.
Yet surrender transformed them.
And maybe that is the invitation here.
Not condemnation. Repentance.
There is a difference.
Conviction says: “Come back to God.”
Condemnation says: “Run from Him.”
The enemy wants people hiding. Jesus wants people healed.
And some readers need to hear this clearly:
You do not have to continue the destructive spiritual patterns you inherited.
Generational dysfunction is not stronger than the power of Christ.
Pride can break. Anger can heal. Addiction can lose its chains. Families can change. Souls can recover.
But only surrendered hearts experience resurrection.
The terrifying reality about Rehoboam is not merely that he lost a kingdom.
It is that he never fully dealt with the deeper war inside himself.
And many people are doing the same thing now.
Fighting external battles while ignoring internal bondage.
But hidden pride eventually becomes public destruction.
Always.
The Gospel invites something different.
Not image management. Transformation.
Not religious performance. Relationship.
Not domination. Servanthood.
Not self-exaltation. Surrender.
And that invitation still stands today.

For the exhausted father. For the angry son. For the wounded daughter. For the leader secretly collapsing internally. For the believer battling hidden pride. For the person who feels spiritually numb. For the soul tired of pretending.
Jesus still restores shattered kingdoms inside human hearts.
And maybe that is why Rehoboam’s story matters so much.
Because it warns us what pride destroys… while simultaneously revealing what grace can still redeem.
Some people do not realize how close they are to destroying relationships they may never recover.
One uncontrolled moment of pride can destroy what took generations to build.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of the Woman Who Shared Her Last Oil
paragraphs: The Untold Story of the Woman Who Shared Her Last Oil
Nobody remembers her name.
Scripture never tells us.
No title. No legacy attached to her bloodline. No social status. No platform. No crowd applauding her sacrifice.
Just a starving widow. A dying son. An empty future. And one final drop of oil.
But Heaven remembered her.
And maybe that is the part modern believers still do not understand.
Because we live in a world obsessed with abundance. God often moves through surrender.
The story hides inside 1 Kings 17. Buried between drought, national judgment, idolatry, and famine. Most people read it quickly. Few actually sit inside the agony of it.
But if you slow down long enough... this story becomes terrifyingly personal.
Because sooner or later, every believer reaches a moment where God asks for the thing that feels impossible to release.

The story begins with judgment across the land. Israel had abandoned the LORD under King Ahab and Jezebel. The prophet Elijah declared drought over the nation. No rain. No harvest. No stability. No certainty.
The Hebrew word used in 1 Kings 17:1 for drought is connected to the shutting up of heaven itself. The heavens became restrained. Held back. Closed.
And when Heaven closes... human strength gets exposed very quickly.
Fields die. Savings disappear. Fear spreads. Faith gets tested.
The famine became so severe that even Elijah himself depended completely on God. First ravens fed him. Then the brook dried up.
Even the prophet experienced emptiness.
That detail matters.
Because many believers secretly think struggle means God abandoned them.
But Scripture repeatedly shows us something different. Sometimes God leads people directly into impossible conditions so dependence can become deeper than comfort.
Then comes the moment that changes everything.
1 Kings 17:8–9 says:
“Then the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee.”
The place matters.
Zarephath was in Sidon. Jezebel’s territory. Pagan territory. Enemy territory.
God sent His prophet outside Israel. To a Gentile widow.
Even this shattered religious expectations.
And the name Zarephath itself carries weight.
In Hebrew: צָרְפַת — Tsarephath
It comes from the root צָרַף (tsaraph), meaning: “to smelt,” “to refine,” “to purify through fire.”
This was not just a location. It was a spiritual furnace.
And some of you reading this already know exactly what that feels like.
You have prayed. Cried. Waited. Watched things dry up. Watched relationships collapse. Watched hope weaken. Watched your strength disappear.
And secretly you keep asking: “God… why does obedience sometimes feel like fire?”
Because refinement is painful.
Gold does not become pure without heat.
Neither do hearts.
When Elijah arrives, he sees her gathering sticks.
Not preparing for tomorrow. Preparing for death.
Scripture says in 1 Kings 17:12:
“And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse…”
The phrase “a little oil” in Hebrew carries the idea of insufficiency. Barely enough. Almost gone. The final remains.
Oil throughout Scripture often symbolizes: anointing, presence, consecration, light, healing, and the sustaining work of God.
Yet this woman possessed almost none.
And honestly… that is where many believers are right now.
Still showing up to church. Still smiling online. Still telling people they are okay.
But internally?
Exhausted. Emotionally empty. Spiritually running on fumes. Trying to survive off “a little oil.”
The widow then says something devastating.
“…that we may eat it, and die.”
She had already accepted death.
Not metaphorically. Literally.
This was not poetic sadness. This was starvation. A mother watching her child slowly approach the end.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Elijah responds in a way modern culture would probably hate.
He says:
“Fear not… but make me thereof a little cake first…” — 1 Kings 17:13
First.
Before her. Before her son. Before her security.
At first glance, it almost sounds cruel.
Until you understand what God was actually exposing.
Fear always clutches. Faith always releases.
The widow stood between two kingdoms:
The kingdom of scarcity. Or the kingdom of trust.
And the terrifying thing about trust is this: real faith usually costs something.
David said in 2 Samuel 24:24:
“Neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing.”
Modern Christianity often celebrates convenience. Biblical faith usually demands surrender.
And here is the part almost nobody talks about.
God could have fed Elijah another way.
He already used ravens. He could have sent angels. He could have multiplied food from the ground.
But instead… He involved a broken widow.
Why?
Because God was not only rescuing Elijah. He was rescuing her heart from the prison of fear.
Some miracles arrive disguised as impossible instructions.
The widow obeyed.
And this changes everything.
1 Kings 17:15–16 says:
“And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days.
And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD…”
The Hebrew wording here is beautiful.
The oil did not “fail.”
לֹא חָסֵר — lo chaser
Meaning: not lacking, not diminished, not exhausted.
God did not necessarily flood her with abundance overnight.
He sustained her daily.
And that may be one of the hardest lessons in the Christian life.
Sometimes God gives enough for today. Not enough to control tomorrow.
Because dependence keeps the heart close.
Israel gathered manna one day at a time. Jesus taught believers to pray: “Give us this day our daily bread.”
Daily.
Not lifetime guarantees. Daily trust.
Some of you want God to show you the entire future before you obey Him.
But Scripture repeatedly shows God revealing provision step by step.
And maybe that frustrates us because control feels safer than surrender.
But control has never produced intimacy with God.
Trust does.
Then the story becomes even heavier.
Her son dies.
After all that obedience. After all that sacrifice. After all that faith.
The boy stops breathing.
And suddenly every hidden question erupts from her soul.
“Art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance, and to slay my son?” — 1 Kings 17:18
This is one of the rawest emotional moments in the Old Testament.
Because suffering has a way of exposing buried guilt.
Many people carry secret shame. Old failures. Private regrets. Hidden sin.
And when tragedy strikes… they immediately assume God is punishing them.
But watch what happens next.
Elijah carries the dead child upstairs. Cries out to the LORD. Stretches himself upon the child three times.
And Scripture says:
“And the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.” — 1 Kings 17:22
This becomes the first recorded resurrection in Scripture.
Think about that.
The first resurrection miracle in the Bible did not happen in a palace. Not through royalty. Not before crowds.
It happened inside the hidden suffering of a widow who shared her last oil.
God entered the house nobody noticed.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to hear that tonight.
He still does.

God still walks into forgotten houses. Still sees exhausted mothers. Still sees grieving fathers. Still sees anxious believers. Still sees people crying silently at night while pretending they are strong during the day.
You are not invisible to Him.
The Gospel itself echoes this widow’s story.
Because Jesus also became poor.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 8:9:
Christ poured Himself out. Completely.
Philippians 2 describes Him emptying Himself.
In Greek: ἐκένωσεν — ekenōsen
Meaning: He emptied, poured out, made Himself of no reputation.
Jesus became the true and better provision.
The widow gave her final oil. Christ gave His own blood.
And unlike temporary bread during famine, Jesus said in John 6:35:
“I am the bread of life.”
The world promises satisfaction. Only Christ sustains souls.
This story was never merely about survival.
It was about revelation.
The widow discovered who God truly was in the middle of impossible surrender.
And some people will never understand God deeply because they refuse to trust Him beyond comfort.
That is why trials often become sacred places.
Pain strips illusions. Weakness exposes idols. Need reveals dependency.
And sometimes the very season you prayed against becomes the season that introduces you to the deepest intimacy with God you have ever known.
The heartbreaking truth is that many people only want God as emergency provision. Not as Lord.
But the widow moved from survival faith… into surrendered faith.
At the end of the chapter she says:
“Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth.” — 1 Kings 17:24
Truth.
Not motivational optimism. Not emotional hype. Not prosperity fantasies.
Truth.
And truth changes people.
This story still exposes modern hearts.
Because many believers say they trust God until obedience threatens comfort.
Until generosity costs something. Until surrender hurts. Until waiting becomes exhausting. Until prayers remain unanswered longer than expected.
Then fear starts screaming louder than faith.
But the widow teaches something unforgettable:
What looks insufficient in your hands becomes supernatural in God’s hands.
A little oil. A little meal. A hidden house. A broken mother.
And Heaven built one of the most unforgettable stories in Scripture from it.
Maybe that is your story too.
Maybe you feel emotionally depleted. Spiritually dry. Mentally exhausted. Afraid about finances. Afraid about family. Afraid about the future.
And maybe you keep thinking: “I do not have enough.”
But God has always specialized in multiplying surrendered weakness.
Moses only had a staff. David only had stones. The disciples only had loaves and fish. The widow only had oil.
God does extraordinary things through surrendered insufficiency.
Not self-sufficiency.
And maybe the deepest tragedy today is not that people lack resources.
It is that people no longer trust God enough to release what they have.
The widow’s story survived thousands of years because it confronts every generation with the same question:
Will you trust God when obedience feels terrifying?
That question still divides hearts today.
Some will cling tightly to fear. Others will release everything into God’s hands.
Only one path leads to deeper intimacy.
And maybe that is why Jesus later praised another widow.
In Mark 12, He watched wealthy people give from abundance while a poor widow gave two mites.
Tiny. Insignificant by worldly standards.
Yet Jesus said she gave more than everyone else.
Why?
Because Heaven measures surrender differently than Earth.
God sees what costs you.
He sees the prayers nobody hears. The tears nobody notices. The obedience nobody applauds. The sacrifice nobody celebrates.
And none of it is wasted.
Not one drop of surrendered oil.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
One surrendered drop of oil can become the doorway to a miracle bigger than your fear.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
paragraphs:
DID GOD CREATE EVIL?
The Verse That Terrified Generations… and the Truth Most People Never Heard
There are verses in Scripture that comfort people.
Then there are verses that stop people cold.
Verses that feel dangerous.
Verses that sound like they could shatter everything believers think they know about God.
Isaiah 45:7 is one of them.
In the King James Version, God says:
“I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the Lord do all these things.”
Create evil.
For centuries, skeptics have weaponized those words.
Some believers quietly avoid them.
Others read the verse once… then bury the discomfort deep enough to never revisit it again.
Because if God created evil… then what does that mean?
Did God create murder?
Did He create rape?
Did He create hellish atrocities?
Did God create Satan to become evil?
Did He design human suffering?
And if God is holy… how can evil come from Him?
This is not a shallow question.
This is the kind of question people cry about at 2 a.m.
The kind of question whispered after funerals.
The kind of question asked by exhausted believers trying to reconcile God’s goodness with the horrors they’ve survived.
And maybe the hardest part is this:
The Bible never runs away from difficult questions.
God never panics when humans wrestle.
Scripture invites investigation.
Truth survives examination.
But to understand Isaiah 45:7 correctly, we must step into the language, culture, theology, and context the verse was originally written in.
Because one mistranslated English word has confused millions.
And the truth hiding underneath it is breathtaking.
The Hebrew text of Isaiah 45:7 reads:
“יוֹצֵר אוֹר וּבוֹרֵא חֹשֶׁךְ עֹשֶׂה שָׁלוֹם וּבוֹרֵא רָע”
Transliterated:
“Yotzer or u-vorei choshekh, oseh shalom u-vorei ra.”
Literal rendering:
“Forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating ra.”
The entire controversy revolves around one Hebrew word:
“Ra” (רָע)
Most people assume “ra” always means moral evil.
But Hebrew is deeper than that.
Far deeper.
The Hebrew word “ra” has a broad semantic range.
Depending on context, it can mean:
• calamity • disaster • distress • adversity • sorrow • affliction • misery • trouble • judgment • harmful consequences
Sometimes it refers to moral evil.
But often it does not.
Context determines meaning.
And Isaiah 45 is not discussing moral corruption.
It is discussing God’s sovereignty over nations, kings, war, judgment, restoration, and history itself.
In modern translations, Isaiah 45:7 is more accurately rendered:
“I make peace and create calamity.”
The ESV says:
“I make well-being and create calamity.”
The NASB says:
“Causing well-being and creating disaster.”
The CSB says:
“I make success and create disaster.”
Suddenly the verse changes entirely.
Not because Scripture was altered.
But because the original Hebrew context was restored.
God is not claiming to manufacture moral wickedness.
He is declaring absolute sovereignty over judgment and national calamity.
The surrounding context proves this.
Isaiah 45 is addressed primarily to Cyrus, the Persian king God would use to judge nations and later allow Israel’s restoration.
God is declaring:
“I alone rule history.
I raise kings.
I remove kings.
I bring peace.
I permit judgment.
I control outcomes.
Nothing escapes My authority.”
This theme echoes throughout Scripture.
In Amos 3:6:
“Does disaster come to a city, unless the Lord has done it?”
Again, the context is judgment.
Not moral evil.
In Lamentations 3:38:
“Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come?”
Again:
calamity.
judgment.
discipline.
national consequences.
Not moral corruption originating inside God.
Because Scripture is crystal clear about God’s moral nature.
1 John 1:5 says:
“God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all.”
The Greek text says:
“Ὁ Θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν, καὶ σκοτία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδεμία.”
“Ho Theos phos estin, kai skotia en auto ouk estin oudemia.”
No darkness at all.
James 1:13 says:
“God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man.”
The Greek word for evil there is:
“κακῶν” (kakon)
Moral evil.
Corruption.
Wickedness.
God is not morally corrupt.
Ever.
Habakkuk 1:13 says of God:
“You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong…”
So the Bible cannot contradict itself.
If God is perfectly holy… then Isaiah 45:7 cannot mean God creates moral evil.
And it does not.
But that still leaves another difficult question.
If God did not create evil… where did evil come from?
The answer is both terrifying and deeply personal.
Evil is not a created substance.
It is the corruption of what was originally good.
Darkness is not a created thing.
Darkness is the absence of light.
Cold is the absence of heat.
Rot is the corruption of life.
Evil is the rebellion against God’s goodness.
Scripture teaches that God created angels good.
Lucifer was not created evil.
Ezekiel 28:15 says:
“You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.”
Found in you.
Not implanted by God.
Isaiah 14 describes Lucifer’s pride:
“I will ascend.”
“I will exalt my throne.”
“I will make myself like the Most High.”
Sin began with rebellion.
Not divine corruption.
Then humanity repeated the same rebellion in Eden.
Genesis never portrays God injecting Adam and Eve with evil.
He gave genuine choice.
And love without choice is not love.
A forced relationship is slavery.
Real obedience requires the possibility of rejection.
That possibility opened the door for sin.
And humanity walked through it willingly.
That truth becomes uncomfortable fast.
Because people often want evil explained in abstraction.
But Scripture keeps bringing it back to the human heart.
Jesus said in Mark 7:21-23:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
The Greek phrase:
“ἔσωθεν γὰρ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας”
“Esōthen gar ek tēs kardias.”
From within the heart.
Humanity does not merely encounter evil.
Humanity produces it.
Wars.
Abuse.
Betrayal.
Greed.
Pride.
Violence.
Lust.
Corruption.
The Bible refuses to let humanity pretend innocence.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not just dictators.
Not just criminals.
Not just visibly broken people.
All.
Which means the question is not merely:
“Why does evil exist?”
The deeper question is:
“Why would a holy God still love people capable of it?”
And this is where the Gospel explodes with unbearable beauty.
Because Christianity is not the story of a God who created evil.
It is the story of a holy God stepping into the devastation evil caused.
Jesus did not watch suffering from a distance.
He entered it.
The cross is God confronting evil head-on.
Not by becoming evil.
But by absorbing its consequences.
Isaiah 53 says:
“He was pierced for our transgressions.”
The Hebrew word for pierced:
“מְחֹלָל” (mecholal)
Wounded.
Profaned.
Crushed open.
The Son of God stepped into human violence.
Human hatred.
Human betrayal.
Human sin.
And endured it willingly.
The greatest proof that God did not create moral evil is the cross itself.
Because evil murdered perfection.
Yet even there, God remained sovereign.
Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered up according to:
“the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.”
Human beings committed evil.
God redeemed through it.
That distinction matters.
Deeply.
God permits free will.
Humans commit evil.
God remains sovereign over history without becoming morally corrupt.
And some people struggle with that tension.
Because they want a God who removes all possibility of evil immediately.
But that would also remove freedom.
Love.
Choice.
Relationship.
Redemption.
The same free will that allows rebellion also allows repentance.
The same mouth that lies can worship.
The same heart that hated can be transformed.
The same sinner that fell can be redeemed.
That is the entire miracle of grace.
And maybe this hits differently when suffering becomes personal.
Maybe you were abused.
Maybe you buried someone too early.
Maybe evil did not feel philosophical to you.
Maybe it felt devastatingly real.
Maybe you asked:
“Where was God?”
Scripture never mocks those cries.
David cried them.
Job cried them.
Jeremiah cried them.
Even Jesus cried:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
The Bible is brutally honest about pain.
But it never concludes God is evil.
Instead, it reveals a God patient enough to allow freedom temporarily while preparing final justice eternally.
Revelation promises a coming day where evil ends completely.
No more death.
No more mourning.
No more tears.
No more curse.
The story is not over yet.
And that matters.
Because some people judge God before reading the final chapter.
But until then, humanity stands in a terrifying tension:
We want justice for evil done against us.
But mercy for evil done by us.
And only the Gospel resolves both.
At the cross, justice and mercy kissed.
Sin was not ignored.
It was paid for.
Holiness remained intact.
Love remained available.
Forgiveness became possible.
This is why the question “Did God create evil?” cannot merely become an intellectual debate.
Eventually it becomes personal.
Because every human being must answer another question:
“What will I do with my own sin?”
Not your neighbor’s.
Not your government’s.
Not the culture’s.
Yours.
The Gospel does not simply explain evil.
It exposes it.
Then offers redemption through Jesus Christ.
And maybe the most haunting truth of all is this:
Many people spend their entire lives accusing God of evil while secretly refusing to surrender their own.
That silence gets heavy.
Especially at night.
Especially when nobody else sees the thoughts.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The lust.
The pride.
The hidden hatred.
The pretending.
But the Gospel still reaches there.
Still.
No matter how far someone ran.
No matter how dirty the past became.
No matter how many nights were wasted.
Grace still reaches.
Romans 5:20 says:
“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
Not permission to continue in sin.
But proof that Christ is greater than the wreckage.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years angry at God because of what evil did to your life.
You are not weak for wrestling.
But do not mistake human rebellion for God’s character.
The cross reveals His character.
Jesus reveals His character.
Mercy reveals His character.
Patience reveals His character.
The empty tomb reveals His character.
God did not create moral evil.
But He did create a rescue plan before humanity even realized it would need saving.
That changes everything.
Because the story of Scripture is not:
“God created evil.”
The story is:
Humanity embraced evil.
And God came to save humanity anyway.
That is the scandal of grace.
That is the unbearable mercy of Christ.
That is the Gospel.
And maybe this article exposed questions you buried for years.
Maybe it reopened wounds.
Maybe it challenged assumptions.
Maybe it confronted hidden anger toward God.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone you love is wrestling with doubt, suffering, anger, trauma, or confusion about God… share this with them.
One day every hidden thing will stand before perfect holiness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Secret Meaning Behind the Scarlet Cord of Rahab
paragraphs: The Secret Meaning Behind the Scarlet Cord of Rahab
There is a moment in Scripture that feels almost too small to notice.
A single cord.
A scarlet thread hanging from the window of a woman the world had already condemned.
Most people read past it.
But heaven did not.

That scarlet cord in the window of Rahab became one of the most prophetic symbols in all of Scripture — a shadow of redemption, a whisper of the cross, and a revelation of how God saves people nobody expected Him to save.
The story appears in Joshua 2.
Israel is standing at the edge of promise. Moses is gone. Joshua is now leading the people toward Canaan. Jericho stands in front of them like an impossible wall.
And inside Jericho lives a woman named Rahab.
A prostitute.
An outsider.
A Gentile.
A woman whose entire life looked disqualified.
Yet somehow… her name would eventually appear in the genealogy of Jesus Christ Himself.
That alone should make every believer stop and think.
Because God has always specialized in rewriting stories people thought were too ruined to redeem.
The Hebrew text introduces her in Joshua 2:1:
“And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho. And they went, and came into a harlot’s house, named Rahab, and lodged there.”
The Hebrew word used for harlot is:
זוֹנָה — zonah
This word comes from the Hebrew root zanah, meaning:
“to commit fornication, prostitution, unfaithfulness, or harlotry.”
The Bible does not sanitize Rahab’s past.
God never hides the brokenness of the people He redeems.
That matters deeply.
Because religion often edits people’s stories to make them look respectable.
But Scripture leaves the scars visible so grace becomes undeniable.
Rahab lived in Jericho — a city devoted to destruction because of its wickedness.
Yet while an entire city resisted God, one woman believed.
That is astonishing.
Joshua 2:9 records Rahab speaking to the spies:
“I know that the LORD hath given you the land…”
The Hebrew says:
יָדַעְתִּי כִּי־נָתַן יְהוָה לָכֶם אֶת־הָאָרֶץ
Transliterated:
Yada‘ti ki natan YHWH lakhem et-ha’aretz
The word yada‘ti means:
“I know.”
Not “I wonder.” Not “I heard rumors.” Not “Maybe.”
This is conviction.
Rahab had heard about the God of Israel.
She heard about the Red Sea. She heard about Egypt. She heard about the victories of Israel.
But while everyone else in Jericho hardened their hearts in fear… Rahab surrendered in faith.
That is one of the greatest dividing lines in human history.
Some people hear about God and become harder.
Others hear about Him and fall to their knees.
Rahab chose surrender.
Then comes the scarlet cord.
Joshua 2:17–18:

“And the men said unto her, We will be blameless of this thine oath which thou hast made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by…”
The Hebrew phrase for “scarlet thread” is:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat chut ha-shani
This phrase is incredibly powerful.
Let’s break it down carefully.
Tiqvah (תִּקְוָה) means:
“hope.”
But it also literally means:
“cord.” “line.” “attachment.”
This is breathtaking.
The very word used for the scarlet cord also carries the meaning of hope.
Rahab’s hope hung outside her window.
Her salvation hung visibly for all to see.
The root idea behind tiqvah comes from something twisted together like a rope.
Biblically, hope is not wishful thinking.
Biblical hope is something you hold onto.
Something anchored.
Something tied tightly.
Then comes:
Chut (חוּט) — thread, cord, line.
And:
Shani (שָּׁנִי) — scarlet, crimson.
Scarlet throughout Scripture carries deep theological symbolism.
In Isaiah 1:18:
“Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow…”
The Hebrew word again is:
שָּׁנִי — shani
Scarlet represented blood-guilt, sin, sacrifice, cleansing, and atonement.
This is why the scarlet cord matters so much.
Rahab was not merely hanging decoration outside her house.
She was prophetically placing her faith under a blood-colored sign of deliverance.
And suddenly the story starts sounding familiar.
Because centuries earlier, Israel itself had once been saved under a sign of blood.
Exodus 12 describes the Passover.
The blood of the lamb was placed on the doorposts.
When judgment came through Egypt, every house marked by blood was spared.
Now in Joshua 2, Rahab’s house becomes another house marked for salvation.
Not because she deserved it.
But because she believed.
This is one of the clearest Old Testament foreshadowings of salvation through Jesus Christ.
The New Testament confirms Rahab’s faith.
Hebrews 11:31 says:
“By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not…”
The Greek phrase says:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη
Transliterated:
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē
The word pistei means:
“by faith.”
And the word pornē means:
“prostitute.”
Again, Scripture refuses to erase her past.
Yet heaven remembers her for faith more than failure.
That should break something religious inside us.
Because many believers secretly think their past is stronger than God’s grace.
Rahab’s story destroys that lie.
Then James 2:25 says:
“Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works…?”
The Greek word for justified is:
ἐδικαιώθη — edikaiōthē
Meaning:
“declared righteous.” “vindicated.” “shown to be right.”
Rahab’s faith produced action.
Real faith always does.
She hid the spies. She risked her life. She rejected Jericho. She aligned herself with the God of Israel.
Faith is not merely agreeing with facts about God.
Faith changes allegiance.
And perhaps that is one of the deepest meanings behind the scarlet cord.
Rahab publicly declared where her trust now belonged.
That cord became separation.
One house marked. One family rescued. One woman transferred from judgment into covenant.
When Jericho fell, her house remained standing.
Imagine the terror.
Walls collapsing. Dust filling the air. Screams echoing through the city.
And there — one scarlet-marked window untouched by destruction.
Mercy in the middle of judgment.
That is the Gospel.
The scarlet cord also points prophetically toward the blood of Jesus.
In the New Testament, the Greek word for scarlet appears as:
κόκκινος — kokkinos
Meaning scarlet or crimson.
Scarlet appears repeatedly around the crucifixion narrative.
Matthew 27:28 says Jesus was dressed in a scarlet robe.
The mocked King wore the color of sacrifice.
The color of blood.
The color of atonement.
The color hanging from Rahab’s window.
Nothing in Scripture is accidental.
The Bible is a woven revelation.
Genesis to Revelation tells one redemption story.
And hidden inside Joshua is a prophetic whisper:
One day salvation would come through scarlet blood again.
There is another mystery many overlook.
Rahab lived on the wall.
Joshua 2:15 says:
“for her house was upon the town wall…”
Spiritually this is powerful imagery.
Rahab lived between two worlds.
Inside Jericho. Yet reaching toward Israel.
Still surrounded by corruption. Yet moving toward covenant.
Many people live there spiritually.
Caught between the old life and the new.
But eventually the scarlet cord forced a decision.
Either trust God completely… or perish with Jericho.
The Gospel still confronts humanity that way.
Jesus did not come merely to improve lives.
He came to rescue people from destruction.
Rahab understood something many religious people still miss.
God’s mercy is available even to the guilty.
Especially to the guilty.
Jesus Himself later declared in Matthew 21:31:
“The publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.”
Why?
Because broken people often recognize their need for grace faster than self-righteous people do.
Rahab knew she needed saving.
That humility opened the door for mercy.
Then comes one of the most shocking details in Scripture.
Matthew 1 includes Rahab in the genealogy of Christ.
A former prostitute became part of the Messianic bloodline.
Only God writes stories like that.
The same woman once known for sexual sin became an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
Think about the scandal of grace.
The religious world would have excluded her.
But heaven included her.
This is why the scarlet cord matters so deeply.
It is not merely ancient symbolism.
It is the announcement that no life is beyond redemption.
The cord testified:
Grace can enter condemned places. Faith can exist in ruined people. Mercy can rewrite identities. Blood can still save.
And maybe that is why so many people feel emotional when reading Rahab’s story.
Because somewhere deep inside, we know we are Rahab.
We all have places of shame. Hidden compromise. Broken history. Things we hope nobody discovers.
Yet the Gospel declares that salvation does not come through perfection.
It comes through faith in the One who saves.
Ephesians 2:8 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith…”
The Greek says:
χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
Transliterated:
chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs
Grace. Faith. Salvation.
Rahab experienced all three long before the cross was physically raised.
The scarlet cord became a prophetic preview.
A sign that judgment passes over those who trust in God’s redemption.
And there is still one more layer.
Jewish tradition and early Christian interpretation often saw scarlet as connected to cleansing through sacrifice.
In Leviticus, scarlet thread was associated with purification rituals.
In Hebrews, blood becomes the center of covenant.
Hebrews 9:22 says:
“without shedding of blood is no remission.”
The Greek word for remission is:
ἄφεσις — aphesis
Meaning:
“release.” “forgiveness.” “freedom.”
Rahab’s scarlet cord prophetically pointed toward release through blood.
Not animal blood.
But ultimately the blood of Christ.
The cross was hidden in Joshua long before Calvary arrived.
And maybe the most beautiful part is this:
Rahab did not fully understand all the theology behind the scarlet cord.
She simply trusted.
Sometimes faith begins before full understanding arrives.
She obeyed. She hung the cord. She waited. And God honored her faith.
Somebody reading this feels disqualified from God.
You think your history ruined your future.
You think your failures are too dark.
You think your secret sins permanently defined you.
Rahab’s scarlet cord says otherwise.
The blood of Jesus still reaches into condemned places.
Still rescues broken people.
Still rewrites names.
Still saves.
Romans 10:13 says:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
The Greek word for saved is:
σωθήσεται — sōthēsetai
Meaning:
“rescued.” “delivered.” “preserved.” “made whole.”
That is the Gospel hidden inside Rahab’s window.
A scarlet cord hanging in the middle of judgment.
A visible declaration:
“I believe God can save me too.”
And maybe that is why this story still shakes hearts thousands of years later.
Because every believer alive today stands under the same reality.
Not saved by our goodness. Not rescued by religious performance. Not redeemed because we earned mercy.
Saved by grace. Through faith. Under the covering of scarlet blood.
If this stirred something inside your spirit, do not ignore it.
Be honest. Rahab’s story hits differently when you realize grace found you too.
The scarlet cord outside Rahab’s window was never just thread.
It was heaven whispering that mercy was already coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind the Young Prophet Crushed by a Lion
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind the Young Prophet Crushed by a Lion
There are some Bible stories people avoid.
Not because they are boring.
Because they are terrifying.
Because somewhere deep inside, they expose something uncomfortable about us.
And few stories in Scripture are more unsettling than the mysterious death of the young prophet who was killed by a lion… after delivering a message from God.
Most people read it once and move on.
But if you sit with this story long enough, it begins to feel less like ancient history… and more like a mirror.
Because this is not just a story about a prophet.
It is a warning to anyone who has ever heard God clearly… and still drifted.
It is a warning to gifted people.
To preachers.
To worship leaders.
To believers who once burned with conviction.
To Christians who know exactly what God said… but slowly allowed another voice to sound more comforting.
And what makes this story unforgettable is this:
The young prophet was not destroyed in rebellion first.
He was destroyed after compromise.
The story is found in 1 Kings 13.
And hidden inside it is one of the most emotionally devastating truths in the entire Bible.
The chapter opens during the reign of King Jeroboam.

Jeroboam had already begun leading Israel into corruption and idolatry. God’s people were drifting away from covenant worship. Altars were being raised in rebellion. Truth was being replaced with convenience.
And then suddenly, God sends a prophet.
Scripture says:
“Behold, there came a man of God out of Judah by the word of the LORD unto Bethel.” — 1 Kings 13:1
The Hebrew phrase used for “man of God” is:
אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים
Transliterated:
Ish ha-Elohim.
It literally means:
“A man belonging to God.”
Not self-appointed.
Not self-made.
Not platform-built.
He carried heaven’s authority.
And God gave him extremely specific instructions.
After delivering the prophetic judgment against Jeroboam’s altar, God commanded him:
“Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.” — 1 Kings 13:9
This mattered deeply.
Because throughout Scripture, obedience is often tested in details that appear small.
The Hebrew word for “commanded” here is:
צִוָּה
(Tsivvah)
It means:
To appoint, charge, commission with authority.
This was not advice.
This was a divine directive.
And at first… the prophet obeyed.
Completely.
King Jeroboam himself tried to reward him.
The king offered food.
Honor.
Hospitality.
Influence.
The prophet refused.
Imagine that moment.
A corrupt king standing before a faithful prophet.
The prophet had enough discernment to reject a king.
But not enough discernment to reject an older compromised prophet.
And that is where the story begins to cut deep.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual danger is not open wickedness.
It is familiar religious voices.
Scripture says an old prophet living nearby heard what happened and pursued the young prophet.
Eventually he found him sitting under an oak tree.
That detail matters.
He stopped moving.
He paused where God never told him to pause.
Weariness is dangerous when discernment is weak.
The old prophet invited him home for a meal.
The younger prophet refused at first because he remembered God’s instruction.
But then the old prophet said something chilling:
“I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD.” — 1 Kings 13:18
Then Scripture adds four haunting words:
“But he lied unto him.”
The Hebrew text says:
כִּחֵשׁ לוֹ
(Kichesh lo)
Meaning:
“He deceived him.”
Not accidentally.
Intentionally.
And suddenly the story becomes terrifyingly modern.
Because now the danger is not persecution.
It is spiritual deception wrapped in spiritual language.
The young prophet believed a voice simply because it sounded spiritual.
He abandoned the direct word God gave him because another religious voice sounded convincing.
And this still destroys people today.
People abandon biblical truth because someone charismatic told them “God understands.”
People compromise conviction because culture repackages rebellion as compassion.
People slowly drift from Scripture because another voice feels easier.
But God never told us to obey what feels easier.
He told us to obey His voice.
Even when it costs us.
Even when it isolates us.
Even when nobody else understands.
The young prophet returned with the old prophet.
He ate.
He drank.
And then something shocking happened.
The same old prophet who lied… suddenly began speaking the true judgment of God.
This is one of the most sobering moments in the Bible.
God can speak through someone and still not approve of their character.
Anointing is not the same as intimacy.
Giftedness is not the same as obedience.
Platforms are not proof of holiness.
And many believers have destroyed themselves following gifted voices instead of grounded truth.
The old prophet declared:
“Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD…” — 1 Kings 13:21
The Hebrew phrase for “mouth of the LORD” is:
פִּי יְהוָה
(Pi Yahweh)
Literally:
“The mouth of Yahweh.”
Meaning the prophet did not merely ignore advice.
He violated direct revelation.
And then came the lion.
Scripture says:
“And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him.” — 1 Kings 13:24
But this was no ordinary attack.
The lion did not eat the body.
The donkey was untouched.
The lion simply stood beside the corpse.
Almost like heaven itself was making a statement.
Judgment had fallen.
And the entire scene feels surreal.
A dead prophet.
A silent lion.
A living donkey.
And travelers staring at a mystery they could not explain.
Because sometimes the greatest tragedies are not caused by ignorance.
But by disobedience after revelation.
This story terrifies mature believers for a reason.
The young prophet was not pagan.
He was not atheistic.
He was not spiritually dead.
He heard God accurately.
He moved in power.
He confronted corruption.
He carried truth.
And still… he fell.
That should humble every one of us.
Especially in an age where people idolize charisma more than character.
The New Testament echoes this warning repeatedly.
In Galatians 1:8, Paul writes:
The Greek word for “gospel” is:
εὐαγγέλιον
(Euangelion)
Meaning:
Good news.
Not altered news.
Not customized truth.
Not convenient spirituality.
The real Gospel.
And Paul says even if an angel appears… if the message contradicts God’s revealed truth… reject it.
That is exactly where the young prophet failed.
He treated a secondary voice as greater than the original command of God.
And modern Christianity struggles with this constantly.
People elevate influencers over Scripture.
Experiences over truth.
Emotions over obedience.
Crowds over conviction.
But God never asked us to follow trends.
He asked us to follow Him.
There is another layer to this story most people miss.
The older prophet lived in Bethel.
Bethel once meant intimacy with God.
The Hebrew name בֵּית־אֵל (Beit-El) means:
“House of God.”
But by Jeroboam’s reign, Bethel had become corrupted.
A place once associated with revelation became contaminated by compromise.
And that is how compromise always works.
Nobody wakes up one day fully destroyed.
Drift happens slowly.
A small compromise.
A quiet rationalization.
A little disobedience defended long enough.
Until eventually people still sound spiritual… while no longer obeying God.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of the story is this:
The young prophet died outside his assignment.
Not because God stopped speaking.
But because he stopped listening carefully.
How many believers are spiritually exhausted today because they kept entertaining voices God never told them to follow?
How many people once heard God clearly… but now live confused because they traded conviction for comfort?
How many callings have been wounded by compromise disguised as wisdom?
This story is not merely about punishment.
It is about the holiness of God.
Modern culture hates that word.
Holiness.
But holiness is not cruelty.
Holiness means God is utterly pure, utterly true, utterly incapable of corruption.
The Hebrew word often connected to holiness is:
קָדוֹשׁ
(Qadosh)
Meaning:
Set apart.
Sacred.
Completely other.
God does not bend truth to accommodate rebellion.
And that should both terrify us… and comfort us.
Because if God compromises truth, then evil wins.
But He doesn’t.
Truth remains truth.
Even when culture changes.
Even when opinions shift.
Even when compromise becomes popular.
And yet hidden underneath this tragic story is mercy.
Because warnings themselves are acts of love.
God preserved this painful story in Scripture because He wanted future generations to survive what destroyed that prophet.
The lion was not merely about judgment.
It became a warning echoing through generations.
Guard your obedience.
Guard your discernment.
Guard your intimacy with God.
Not every spiritual voice should be trusted.
Not every emotional feeling is revelation.
Not every religious teacher speaks truth.
This is why Jesus said in John 10:27:
“My sheep hear my voice.”
The Greek says:
τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούει
(Ta probata tes phones mou akouei)
Meaning:
“My sheep continually recognize and hear My voice.”
Not random voices.
His voice.
And perhaps somewhere while reading this, you realized something painful.
Maybe you once knew exactly what God told you.
But compromise slowly entered.
Maybe it was through relationships.
Culture.
Bitterness.
Influence.
Success.
Lust.
Pride.
Exhaustion.
Or simply wanting an easier path.
And now your spirit feels distant.
Conviction feels quieter.
Prayer feels heavier.
You still look spiritual externally… but internally something is grieving.
The good news of the Gospel is this:
Jesus Christ came precisely for people who drifted.
The lion in 1 Kings brought death.
But Jesus is called:
“The Lion of the tribe of Judah.”
And unlike the lion of judgment… Christ came to rescue sinners crushed beneath sin.
Where the prophet failed in obedience, Jesus remained perfectly obedient.
Philippians 2:8 says:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death…”
The Greek word for obedient is:
ὑπήκοος
(Hypekoos)
Meaning:
Attentively submissive.
Jesus obeyed perfectly where humanity repeatedly failed.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness became available even for compromised people.
Even for wandering believers.
Even for exhausted Christians.
Even for people who ignored God’s voice.
If you are still breathing… repentance is still possible.
The enemy wants compromised believers to believe restoration is impossible.
But Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us…” — 1 John 1:9
The Greek word for confess is:
ὁμολογῶμεν
(Homologomen)
Meaning:
To agree honestly.
To stop hiding.
To speak the same truth God already sees.
And maybe that is what this article is really about.
Not merely a dead prophet.
But living people pretending they are spiritually okay.
God is still calling people back.
Back from compromise.
Back from hidden drift.
Back from performative Christianity.
Back from dead religion.
Back to truth.
Back to holiness.
Back to Christ.
And maybe tonight this story exposed something you have been avoiding.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Some people are not destroyed because God stopped speaking.
They are destroyed because they kept listening to every other voice.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind Rhoda Forgetting to Open the Door for Peter
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind Rhoda Forgetting to Open the Door for Peter
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost too human to belong beside miracles.
Moments so painfully relatable that they expose us before we even realize we have been seen.
Acts 12 is one of those moments.
Most people remember Peter escaping prison.
The angel.
The chains falling off.
The iron gate opening by itself.
But buried inside one of the most intense supernatural rescue stories in the New Testament is a trembling servant girl named Rhoda.
And somehow… her tiny mistake became immortal.
She forgot to open the door.
Not because she was careless.
Not because she lacked faith.
Not because she was foolish.
But because joy overwhelmed her.
And maybe that says more about the human heart than we are prepared to admit.
The story is found in Acts 12:12–16.
The original Greek text says:
“Καὶ ἐπιγνοῦσα τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ Πέτρου ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς οὐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸν πυλῶνα…”
Transliteration:
“Kai epignousa tēn phōnēn tou Petrou apo tēs charas ouk ēnoixen ton pylōna…”
Literal translation:
“And recognizing the voice of Peter, because of joy she did not open the gate…”
Not fear.
Joy.
That detail changes everything.
The Greek phrase “ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς” (apo tēs charas) literally means “from joy” or “because of joy.”
Her emotions overpowered her actions.
Her heart moved faster than her hands.
And suddenly the Bible stops feeling like distant stained-glass religion.
Because how many of us have done the same thing spiritually?
Prayed for something for so long that when God finally answered… we almost did not know how to respond.
We begged heaven to move.
Then heaven moved and we froze.
That is Rhoda.
And that is us.
The chapter begins under darkness.
King Herod Agrippa I had already executed James, the brother of John.
The early church was bleeding.
Fear filled Jerusalem.
Believers were being hunted.
Prison cells were becoming tombs.
Acts 12:5 says:
“So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church.”
The Greek word for “earnest” is “ἐκτενής” (ektenēs).
It means stretched out.
Persistent.
Straining.
This was not casual prayer.
This was desperate prayer.
Prayer from exhausted people.
Prayer from grieving people.
Prayer from believers running out of strength.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You are smiling in public while privately begging God not to let your soul collapse.
You know how to post verses online while secretly wondering if heaven still hears you.
You know how to encourage others while feeling spiritually numb yourself.
That room in Acts 12 was full of people like that.
And then God did something impossible.
Peter was sleeping between two soldiers.
Bound with chains.
Guarded by multiple squads.
Waiting for execution.
But heaven entered the prison.
The angel struck Peter on the side to wake him up.
Chains fell.
Doors opened.
And Acts 12:10 says:
“The iron gate leading into the city opened for them by itself.”
The Greek phrase is astonishing.
“αὐτομάτη” (automatē).
It means automatically.
By itself.
It is where we get the English word “automatic.”
The gate opened without human power.
Without human strength.
Without Peter forcing it.
There are some doors God opens that human effort could never unlock.
You cannot manipulate them open.
You cannot earn them open.
You cannot scheme them open.
When God decides to move, chains break and gates surrender.
Peter eventually arrived at the house where believers were praying.
And then the story suddenly becomes strangely funny.
Peter knocks.
Rhoda comes.
She hears his voice.
She realizes it is him.
And instead of opening the gate… she runs away screaming.
Imagine Peter standing outside after escaping a death sentence.
Still in danger.
Still vulnerable.
Still hunted.
Knocking.
Waiting.
While inside the prayer meeting everybody argues.
The Bible says:
“They said to her, ‘You are out of your mind.’”
The Greek expression here is “μαίνῃ” (mainē).
It literally means:
“You are insane.”
The believers were praying for Peter while simultaneously struggling to believe God had answered.
That hurts because it exposes something uncomfortable.
Sometimes believers pray faithfully while emotionally expecting disappointment.
We know the language of faith.
But trauma has conditioned us to brace for loss.
The early church had already watched James die.
Now Peter was imprisoned.
They had learned heartbreak.
And heartbreak changes people.
Some people stop praying.
Others keep praying but secretly stop expecting miracles.
Yet God moved anyway.
That alone should make somebody cry.
Because if God only answered perfect faith, none of us would survive.
The miracle did not happen because their emotions were flawless.
The miracle happened because God is merciful.
Rhoda becomes one of the most overlooked examples of emotional realism in Scripture.
The Bible could have omitted her mistake.
But Scripture preserves it forever.
Why?
Because God does not erase human weakness from redemption stories.
He includes it.
The Bible is brutally honest about people.
Moses doubted.
Elijah collapsed.
Thomas questioned.
Peter denied Christ.
And Rhoda forgot to open the door.
Yet heaven still moved.
That is grace.
There is another layer hidden inside this story that many miss.
Rhoda was likely a servant girl.
In Greek, Acts 12:13 calls her a “παιδίσκη” (paidiskē).
A young female servant.
In the social hierarchy of the ancient world, she was insignificant.
Invisible.
Disposable.
Yet God allowed her to become the first person to recognize Peter’s miracle.
Not an apostle.
Not a religious leader.
Not a powerful man.
A servant girl.
The kingdom of God repeatedly elevates overlooked people.
She recognized Peter’s voice before the prayer warriors recognized God’s answer.
Read that again.
The servant girl discerned the miracle before the spiritual adults accepted it.
There are people society overlooks who hear God more clearly than those with titles.
There are broken people carrying discernment.
There are exhausted mothers carrying wisdom.
There are anonymous believers whose prayers shake heaven while the world never learns their names.
Rhoda matters because God wanted us to see that heaven notices people earth ignores.
And perhaps the most devastating part of the story is this:
Peter kept knocking.
Acts 12:16 says:
“But Peter continued knocking.”
The Greek word implies persistence.
Repeated knocking.
Continuous knocking.
Can you feel the tension?
Inside the house:
Confusion.
Fear.
Disbelief.
Outside the gate:
The answered prayer.
Still knocking.
How many believers today are doing the same thing?
Jesus answered.
Grace arrived.
Freedom came.
Healing knocked.
But trauma, fear, shame, disappointment, or unbelief kept the door closed.
Some people are still emotionally imprisoned even after God opened the prison.
And this is why Rhoda’s story hits so deeply.
Because it is not merely about forgetting a door.
It is about what happens when joy collides with disbelief.
It is about what happens when heaven answers prayers that suffering taught us not to expect.
Somebody reading this stopped expecting God to surprise you.
You still attend church.
Still quote Scripture.
Still say “God is good.”
But deep inside, disappointment built walls around your expectations.
You are praying through caution now.
Rhoda reminds us that God still moves even through emotionally overwhelmed people.
And perhaps that is why her story survived centuries.
Because she represents every believer who was caught off guard by grace.
There is something else hidden inside this narrative.
Peter recognized the praying church even while fleeing danger.
He knew where to go.
When darkness surrounded him, he moved toward people who prayed.
That is not accidental.
Your spiritual community matters.
The people surrounding your soul matter.
Some people are close enough to hear your pain but too spiritually asleep to pray for your freedom.
Others may have no influence, no status, no platform, but they know how to shake heaven with prayer.
Choose your circle carefully.
And notice this:
Even though they struggled with unbelief, they were still gathered together.
Still praying.
Still seeking God.
Imperfect faith gathered in prayer is still powerful.
That truth alone can resurrect someone’s hope today.
Because many believers are drowning in guilt over not feeling spiritually strong enough.
You think your fears disqualify you.
You think your doubts cancel God’s willingness to move.
But Acts 12 destroys that lie.
The church doubted.
Rhoda panicked.
Peter stumbled through the miracle half awake.
Yet God still intervened.
Because the Gospel was never about human perfection.
It was always about divine mercy.
And maybe the reason this story feels so unforgettable is because every person alive knows what it means to stand emotionally conflicted at the door of hope.
We all know what it feels like to pray for restoration while secretly fearing another disappointment.
We know what it feels like to beg God for healing while preparing emotionally for heartbreak.
We know what it feels like to ask heaven for miracles while wrestling internal exhaustion.
Rhoda is humanity.
And the knocking never stopped.
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 7:7:
“Knock, and it will be opened to you.”
But in Acts 12, the irony flips.
Now heaven is knocking.
The question becomes:
Will we open the door?
Some people reading this have spent years locking Jesus outside wounded areas of your life.
You let Him into your Sunday language but not your hidden addiction.
You let Him into your worship music but not your bitterness.
You let Him into your religious image but not your secret loneliness.
Yet He still knocks.
Patiently.
Relentlessly.
Mercifully.
The book of Revelation echoes this invitation.
Jesus says:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
The Greek word in Revelation 3:20 is “κρούω” (krouō).
It means to knock continuously.
Persistent knocking.
Not one gentle tap.
A continued appeal.
This is the heart of Christ.
He keeps knocking on hearts that keep hesitating.
And maybe today you finally realize something.
The greatest tragedy was never that Rhoda forgot to open the gate.
The greatest tragedy would have been Peter stopping his knocking.
But grace kept knocking.
Mercy kept knocking.
God kept knocking.
And He still does.
So many believers today are exhausted.
Burned out.
Secretly grieving.
Pretending they are spiritually fine while internally unraveling.
This story reminds us that God works through emotionally overwhelmed people.
Not polished robots.
Not perfect Christians.
Real people.
People who cry unexpectedly.
People who panic.
People who doubt.
People who are trying to believe again.
And perhaps somebody needed to hear this today:
God is not intimidated by your emotional mess.
He already knew Rhoda would forget the door.
And He still sent Peter there.
That means your weakness is not shocking heaven.
Your exhaustion is not confusing God.
Your tears are not evidence of divine abandonment.
Sometimes grace arrives while your emotions are still catching up.
And if this reminded you of someone silently struggling with fear, burnout, grief, depression, disappointment, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them.
Some people are one moment away from giving up entirely.
Because sometimes the miracle is already outside the door… and grace is still knocking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Cain Didn’t Kill Abel in One Day
paragraphs: Cain Didn’t Kill Abel in One Day
Most people think Cain became a murderer in a single moment.
One field. One argument. One violent act. One dead brother.
But Scripture paints something far more terrifying.
Cain did not wake up one morning suddenly transformed into evil.
Murder was growing inside him long before Abel’s blood ever touched the ground.
Genesis does not merely tell the story of the first murder.
It reveals the anatomy of hidden sin. The slow corrosion of the human soul. The quiet birth of resentment. The danger of wounded pride left unsubmitted before God.
And if we are honest… many people are far closer to Cain than they want to admit.
Because people rarely destroy relationships, marriages, ministries, purity, faith, or even themselves in one day.
The fall always starts underground.
The resentment. The comparison. The insecurity. The silent offense. The unhealed rejection. The refusal to repent.
Cain’s hands killed Abel later. But Cain’s heart abandoned God first.
Genesis 4 opens with one of the most tragic spiritual contrasts in human history.
“Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, ‘I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD.’ And again, she bore his brother Abel.”
The Hebrew text says:
וַתֹּסֶף לָלֶדֶת אֶת־אָחִיו אֶת־הָבֶל
“Va-tosef laledet et-achiv et-Hevel.”
“And she again bore his brother Abel.”
The name “Abel” in Hebrew is הֶבֶל (Hevel).
It literally means:
vapor, breath, mist, something fleeting.
His very name prophetically whispers the brevity of his life.
Cain’s name, קַיִן (Qayin), is connected to acquisition, possession, or producing. Eve believed she had “acquired” a man from the Lord.
One brother’s identity became wrapped in achievement. The other’s identity reflected fragility.
And hidden inside this contrast is already a warning.
When identity is built on performance instead of surrender to God, jealousy is never far away.
Scripture says:
“In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions.” — Genesis 4:3–4
The Hebrew phrase for “firstborn” is:
מִבְּכֹרוֹת צֹאנוֹ
“mibbekhorot tsono”
Meaning:
the first, the best, the honored portion.
Abel did not merely give something. He gave first.
Then Scripture adds:
וּמֵחֶלְבֵהֶן
“u’mechelvehen”
“The fat portions.”
In ancient Hebrew thought, the fat represented richness, honor, and the choicest part.
Abel’s offering revealed trust. Faith. Honor. Dependence.
Hebrews 11:4 later confirms this:
“By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain.”
The Greek says:
Πίστει πλείονα θυσίαν
“Pistei pleiona thusian”
“By faith, a greater sacrifice.”
The issue was never vegetables versus animals. The issue was the heart.
God was not rejecting agriculture. God was exposing motive.
Cain brought an offering. Abel brought his best.
One gave religious activity. The other gave surrendered worship.
And this is where the internal collapse of Cain truly begins.
Genesis 4:5 says:
“So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.”
The Hebrew language is extremely vivid here.
וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד
“Vayichar leQayin me’od.”
Literally:
“It burned to Cain exceedingly.”
His anger was not mild irritation. It was an internal fire.
Then:
וַיִּפְּלוּ פָּנָיו
“Vayippelu panav.”
“His face fell.”
This describes visible emotional collapse. Bitterness was now shaping his countenance.
The condition of his heart became visible on his face.
And this matters deeply.
Because before Cain ever attacked Abel physically, sin was already consuming him emotionally.
Many believers think hidden bitterness is harmless because nobody can see it yet.
But God saw Cain.
God always sees the war happening underneath the smile.
Then comes one of the most merciful warnings in all Scripture.
“The LORD said to Cain, ‘Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not be accepted?’” — Genesis 4:6–7
The Hebrew word translated “accepted” is:
שְׂאֵת
“se’et”
Meaning:
lifting up, restoration, being raised again.
God was offering Cain restoration before judgment.
Think about that.
God did not immediately destroy Cain. He confronted him. Warned him. Invited him back.
This is the mercy many people ignore.
Before destruction, God often sends conviction. Before collapse, He sends warnings. Before exposure, He whispers repentance.
But Cain refused.
Then comes the terrifying line:
“And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking.
לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ
“Lappetach chatta’t rovetz.”
“Sin is crouching at the door.”
The word רֹבֵץ (rovetz) was often used of a predatory animal lying in wait.
God describes sin like a beast. Not passive. Not harmless. Not sleeping.
Waiting. Watching. Hungry.
Sin was already outside Cain’s heart searching for permission.
And many people still misunderstand this today.
Sin rarely arrives screaming. It crouches.
Quiet compromise. Small offense. Unforgiveness. Private lust. Secret pride. Hidden rage. Spiritual apathy.
Then God says:
וְאַתָּה תִּמְשָׁל־בּוֹ
“Ve’attah timshal-bo.”
“You must rule over it.”
This destroys the modern lie that people are helpless victims of sin.
God told Cain responsibility still existed.
Temptation was real. But surrender was still a choice.
Cain could have repented. Cain could have humbled himself. Cain could have changed.
But wounded pride often prefers destruction over repentance.
Then comes one of the coldest verses in Genesis.
“Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.” — Genesis 4:8
The Hebrew wording is chillingly simple.
וַיָּקָם קַיִן אֶל־הֶבֶל אָחִיו וַיַּהַרְגֵהוּ
“Vayaqam Qayin el-Hevel achiv vayahargehu.”
“And Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him.”
Notice something devastating.
The murder appears sudden in the text. But spiritually, it was years in the making.
The killing in the field was merely the visible manifestation of an invisible spiritual decay.
Cain had already allowed jealousy to grow unchecked. Already resisted conviction. Already rejected correction. Already entertained bitterness. Already nourished wounded ego.
The murder simply revealed what had already conquered him internally.
Jesus later confirms this spiritual principle.
In Matthew 5:21–22 He says:
“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder.’ … But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.”
The Greek word for anger here is:
ὀργιζόμενος
“orgizomenos.”
Persistent anger. Sustained wrath. Nursed hostility.
Jesus exposes something humanity hates admitting.
Murder begins in the heart before it ever reaches the hands.
Hatred is embryonic violence.
This is why unchecked resentment is spiritually deadly.

Some people think they are righteous because they never physically harmed someone. Meanwhile they assassinate people daily through gossip, slander, contempt, envy, bitterness, humiliation, and secret hatred.
Cain’s spirit still exists.

Every time someone secretly resents another person’s blessing. Every time comparison becomes poison. Every time offense becomes identity. Every time pride rejects repentance. Every time someone hardens their heart against conviction.
The spirit of Cain survives.
And notice what happens after the murder.
“Then the LORD said to Cain, ‘Where is Abel your brother?’” — Genesis 4:9
God was not asking for information. God was exposing Cain’s condition.
Cain replies:
“I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?”
The Hebrew word for “keeper” is:
שֹׁמֵר
“shomer.”
Meaning:
guardian, watchman, protector.
Cain had not merely killed Abel. He rejected responsibility for him.
Sin hardens people until compassion disappears.
Then comes one of the most haunting statements in Scripture.
“The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground.” — Genesis 4:10
In Hebrew:
קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי
“Qol demei achikha tso’aqim elai.”
“The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me.”
Notice something profound.
The Hebrew word for blood here is plural.
דְּמֵי
“demei.”
Many Jewish scholars understood this to imply not only Abel’s blood, but the generations that would never exist because Abel’s life was stolen.
Sin always kills more than people expect.
One act of rebellion creates ripple effects across generations.
One affair. One addiction. One hidden compromise. One moment of rage. One secret sin.
The consequences spread farther than people imagine.
Cain thought he buried Abel. But Abel’s blood still had a voice before God.
Nothing hidden stays hidden forever.
Luke 8:17 says:
“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest.”
The Greek word for hidden is:
κρυπτόν
“krypton.”
Concealed. Covered. Secret.
God sees everything beneath the surface.
This article is not really about Cain and Abel.
It is about every human heart.
Because many people are slowly becoming spiritually dangerous while still appearing outwardly functional.
Smiling publicly. Bleeding privately. Applauding outwardly. Resenting inwardly. Serving externally. Decaying internally.
Cain teaches us that unrepented sin evolves.
Jealousy becomes bitterness. Bitterness becomes hatred. Hatred becomes spiritual blindness. Blindness becomes destruction.
Nobody suddenly collapses overnight.
The compromise was growing long before the consequences arrived.
This is why repentance matters immediately.
Not tomorrow. Not after exposure. Not after consequences. Not after the relationship dies. Not after the addiction deepens. Not after the heart hardens.
Now.
The Apostle Paul later writes in Ephesians 4:26–27:
The Greek word for “opportunity” is:
τόπον
“topon.”
Meaning:
place, territory, foothold.
Unresolved anger gives territory to darkness.
Cain gave sin room to live inside him.
And eventually what lived inside him manifested outside him.
But the Gospel reveals a greater truth.
Jesus Christ came to succeed where Cain failed.
Cain murdered his righteous brother in a field. Jesus willingly died for His guilty brothers on a cross.
Hebrews 12:24 says Jesus’ blood:
“speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”
The Greek says:
κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἅβελ
“kreitton lalounti para ton Habel.”
“Speaking better than Abel.”
Abel’s blood cried for justice. Jesus’ blood cries for mercy.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
