The Law of Moses treated contact with dead bodies as ceremonially unclean.
Yet here…
The dead body becomes the location of life.
Why?
Because God was foreshadowing something greater.
The grave itself would eventually become defeated territory.
This is why the resurrection of Christ shattered history.
The Greek word used in Matthew 28:6 says:
ἠγέρθη
(ēgerthē)
Meaning:
“He has been raised.”
Not metaphorically. Not emotionally. Not symbolically.
Physically. Historically. Literally.
Christianity does not stand upon inspirational philosophy.
It stands upon an empty tomb.
And if Christ truly rose…
then despair is not final. Addiction is not final. Failure is not final. Your hidden shame is not final.
Even death itself is not final.
That is why stories like Elisha’s bones matter.
Because they whisper forward toward the greater resurrection coming through Christ.
But there is another terrifying possibility hidden here.
Imagine being close to resurrection power but never touching it.
Close enough to hear testimonies. Close enough to attend church. Close enough to quote verses. Close enough to look religious.
Yet still spiritually dead.
That is one of the greatest tragedies in modern Christianity.
Many know Christian culture. Few truly surrender.
The Pharisees knew Scripture. But they crucified the Messiah standing in front of them.
Judas walked beside Jesus. Yet still betrayed Him.
Being near holy things is not the same as transformation.
And maybe that is why this story feels so emotionally violent.
Because the dead man had no strength left.
No religious performance. No spiritual résumé. No ability to impress God.
He was entirely helpless.
And that is exactly where resurrection met him.
Somebody reading this has spent years pretending to be spiritually alive while quietly dying inside.
You know the language. You know the worship songs. You know how to smile in church.
But your soul feels exhausted.
You are carrying secret sin. Secret bitterness. Secret grief. Secret disappointment with God.
And you wonder if anything inside you can still live again.
Hear this clearly.
Jesus specializes in resurrecting what humans already buried.
The enemy keeps telling people:
“It’s over.”
But resurrection always begins where humans think the story ended.
Lazarus was already decomposing. Peter already failed. Thomas already doubted. Mary Magdalene already broke. Paul already persecuted Christians.
Yet grace still found them.
This is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
And resurrection only matters when something is truly dead.
That changes how we see salvation itself.
Ephesians 2:1 in Greek says:
καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκροὺς
(kai hymas ontas nekrous)
Translation:
“And you being dead…”
Not sick. Not struggling. Not slightly damaged.
Dead.
Spiritually dead.
And yet Christ intervenes.
That is why salvation is miracle territory.
No motivational speaker can resurrect a dead soul.
Only Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why this story refuses to leave people alone once they truly understand it.
Because deep down…
all of us know what dead places feel like.
Dead dreams. Dead marriages. Dead faith. Dead joy. Dead hope.
And we spend enormous amounts of energy trying to hide the smell of spiritual decay.
But God never asked people to resurrect themselves.
He asked them to come near Him.
The cross of Christ was heaven stepping directly into human death.
The sinless One carrying guilty sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 says in Hebrew:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
(uvachavurato nirpa-lanu)
Translation:
“And by His wounds we are healed.”
Not by our perfection. Not by religious performance. Not by pretending.
By His wounds.
The Gospel humiliates human pride because it reveals we could never save ourselves.
But it also heals human despair because Christ accomplished what we never could.
And maybe the reason this article is hitting your spirit harder than expected is because part of you knows you need resurrection too.
Not fake inspiration. Not temporary emotional hype.
Real surrender.
Real repentance.
Real transformation.
Some people reading this are exhausted from carrying hidden darkness alone.
You have smiled publicly while collapsing privately.
You have posted filtered happiness while fighting invisible battles.
But Jesus still calls dead things out of graves.
And the invitation remains open.
Repent. Return. Surrender.
Not because God hates you.
Because He wants you alive.
Completely alive.
There is a reason the enemy fights biblical truth so aggressively.
Because resurrected believers become dangerous.
People healed by Christ love differently.
People forgiven deeply worship differently.
People rescued from darkness carry a fire religion alone cannot imitate.
And once someone truly encounters Jesus…
they can never fully return to spiritual numbness again.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Not by accident.
Not randomly.
But because God still reaches into graves.
And maybe yours is not beyond His voice.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than information.
It touched something buried.
One touch from resurrection changed everything death thought it had already claimed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Elijah Slept Before Hearing God Again
paragraphs: Why Elijah Slept Before Hearing God Again
There are moments when even the strongest believers no longer feel strong.
Moments where the prophet who once called down fire from heaven suddenly wants to disappear.
Moments where a man who outran chariots collapses under a tree and whispers:
“God… I cannot do this anymore.”
And maybe that is why the story of Elijah hits differently.
Because this is not just the story of a prophet.
It is the story of exhausted people.
People who kept serving while bleeding internally.
People who smiled publicly while privately begging heaven to let them rest.
People who feel guilty because they love God… but they are tired.
Deeply tired.
Spiritually tired.
Emotionally tired.
Mentally tired.
And hidden inside 1 Kings 19 is one of the most overlooked truths in Scripture:
Before God spoke to Elijah again…
God let Elijah sleep.
That changes everything.
Because many people think every spiritual problem is solved by another sermon.
Another rebuke.
Another Bible study.
Another lecture.
But heaven itself shows us something shocking.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a broken servant of God can do…
is sleep.
The story begins after one of the greatest victories in biblical history.
Elijah had just stood on Mount Carmel against 450 prophets of Baal.
Fire fell from heaven.
The nation witnessed the power of Yahweh.
Rain finally returned after drought.
It looked like revival.
It looked like triumph.
It looked like the kind of moment Christians post online with celebration captions.
But victories do not automatically remove exhaustion.
Public miracles do not erase private collapse.
And after the crowd disappeared… Elijah crashed.
1 Kings 19:3 says:
“He was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life.”
The Hebrew phrase used for “ran for his life” carries the idea of fleeing to preserve the soul itself.
This was not dramatic exaggeration.
This was a shattered man.
A man emotionally crushed after prolonged spiritual warfare.
Then Scripture says he sat under a broom tree.
The Hebrew word is רֹתֶם (rotem).
A desert shrub.
Dry.
Lonely.
Barely enough shade to survive under.
And there Elijah prayed something many believers are terrified to admit they have felt before.
1 Kings 19:4:
“It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life.”
This was not theatrical despair.
This was burnout.
The kind pastors hide.
The kind worship leaders cry about in parked cars.
The kind mothers feel after carrying everyone else emotionally.
The kind fathers feel when they silently collapse under pressure.
The kind young believers feel after fighting temptation for years.
And here is the shocking part.
God did not answer Elijah with a lecture.
God did not say:
“Pray harder.”
“Have more faith.”
“Stop being emotional.”
“Real prophets do not feel this way.”
Instead…
God let him sleep.
The text says:
“And he lay down and slept under a broom tree.”
The Hebrew word for slept is יָשֵׁן (yashen).
It means deep rest.
To relax.
To cease striving.
To stop activity.
And suddenly the story becomes deeply personal.
Because many believers today are trying to hear God while functioning in complete exhaustion.
They are spiritually awake but emotionally collapsing.
They are posting verses while privately drowning.
They are serving nonstop but never recovering.
And they feel guilty for needing rest.
But Elijah’s story destroys the lie that exhaustion automatically means spiritual failure.
Sometimes exhaustion simply means you have been fighting for too long without recovering.
Even Jesus rested.
Mark 4:38 says Jesus slept in the storm.
The Greek word used is καθεύδων (katheudōn).
Not pretending.
Not meditating.
Actually sleeping.
The Son of God in human flesh experienced physical exhaustion.
This matters because Christianity has sometimes accidentally glorified burnout.
People applaud constant activity.
Constant production.
Constant ministry.
Constant emotional labor.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that God created human beings with limits.
Psalm 127:2 says:
“He gives to His beloved sleep.”
The Hebrew word for beloved is יְדִידוֹ (yedido).
His dearly loved ones.
Sleep itself becomes evidence of God’s care.
Think about that.
Some people punish themselves for resting.
Meanwhile Scripture presents rest as a gift.
And Elijah’s story gets even more beautiful.
Because while Elijah slept… God stayed near.
The Lord did not abandon him during his collapse.
An angel touched him.
Fed him.
Protected him.
Watched over him.
The prophet was too exhausted to sustain himself.
So heaven sustained him.
That detail destroys religious performance culture.
Because some believers secretly think God only loves the strong version of them.
The productive version.
The victorious version.
The emotionally stable version.
But Elijah encountered God in weakness.
Not just strength.
And maybe someone reading this needs to hear that.
God is not only present in your Mount Carmel moments.
He is present under the broom tree too.
He is present when the tears finally come.
He is present when your body shuts down.
He is present when anxiety drains you.
He is present when trauma exhausts your soul.
He is present when you no longer know what to pray.
Romans 8:26 says:
“The Spirit helps us in our weakness.”
The Greek word for weakness is ἀσθενείᾳ (astheneia).
Frailty.
Exhaustion.
Human limitation.
Not fake perfection.
Not spiritual performance.
Weakness.
Then comes one of the most profound moments in Elijah’s life.
After rest.
After food.
After recovery.
God finally speaks.
Not through fire.
Not through earthquake.
Not through wind.
But through what many English translations call:
“A still small voice.”
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַקָּה
Qol demamah daqqah.
Literally:
“A voice of thin silence.”
Or:
“A delicate whispering stillness.”
That changes the atmosphere of the entire story.
Because Elijah expected God in power.
But encountered Him in quietness.
And maybe that is why exhaustion is so dangerous.
Exhaustion makes it difficult to hear gentle things.
When the nervous system is overloaded… whispers get drowned.
Many believers are begging God to shout while heaven is speaking softly.
But Elijah could not hear the whisper until he first rested.
This article is not permission for laziness.
It is permission to be human.
There is a difference.
Elijah eventually got up again.
He obeyed again.
Served again.
Walked with God again.
But first… he slept.
Some of you have been attacking yourselves for needing rest.
You call yourself weak.
Undisciplined.
Spiritually dry.
But maybe your soul is not failing.
Maybe your soul is exhausted.
There is a reason Jesus said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for rest is ἀναπαύσω (anapausō).
To refresh.
To restore.
To give relief.
Christianity was never meant to become endless spiritual panic.
Jesus did not die so His people could live emotionally crushed forever.
And this becomes even more powerful when we understand the broader biblical pattern.
God often restores people physically before restoring them spiritually.
He fed Elijah before speaking.
Jesus fed crowds before teaching.
After the resurrection, Jesus cooked breakfast for His disciples.
Breakfast.
The risen Christ stood on the shore making food for exhausted fishermen.
That detail feels almost too gentle.
Too human.
Too personal.
But that is exactly who Jesus is.
Some people imagine God as constantly disappointed.
Constantly angry.
Constantly frustrated with exhausted believers.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who understands dust.
Psalm 103:14 says:
“For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust.”
The Hebrew word for frame is יִצְרֵנוּ (yitzrenu).
Formation.
Design.
Construction.
God understands human limits because He designed humanity.
He is not shocked that people get tired.
The enemy wants exhausted believers isolated.
Ashamed.
Silent.
Pretending.
Because hidden exhaustion eventually becomes spiritual collapse.
That is why Elijah isolated himself.
And isolation magnified despair.
Some of you are carrying battles silently because you fear judgment.
But hidden exhaustion can become dangerous.
You were never meant to carry everything alone.
Not because comments magically fix pain.
But because honest confession breaks isolation.
And somebody else reading this may realize they are not alone anymore.
Maybe you have smiled in church while fighting depression.
Maybe you quote Scripture while privately battling anxiety.
Maybe you lead others while secretly wondering how much longer you can keep going.
Elijah understands that feeling.
And God did not throw Elijah away.
Please hear that clearly.
God did not discard the exhausted prophet.
He restored him.
Slowly.
Tenderly.
Patiently.
That matters because some believers think burnout means God is finished with them.
But the broom tree was not Elijah’s ending.
It was recovery before assignment.
There are people reading this who feel spiritually numb.
You still love God.
But you are tired.
And maybe this article found you at the exact right moment.
Maybe heaven is reminding you that rest is not rebellion.
Maybe God is not demanding another performance from you tonight.
Maybe He is telling you:
“Eat. Rest. Breathe. I am still here.”
That whisper may save someone.
Especially in a generation trained to measure worth through constant output.
Social media rewards nonstop visibility.
The world celebrates overworking.
People feel guilty for stopping.
But even creation itself was built with rhythms of rest.
Genesis reveals Sabbath.
Jesus withdrew to lonely places.
The disciples slept.
Elijah slept.
Rest is woven into creation itself.
And still many believers feel guilty for being human.
The tragedy is that some people only realize they needed rest after breaking completely.
After panic attacks.
After emotional collapse.
After nervous breakdowns.
After losing joy.
After becoming numb.
But maybe this story can interrupt that path.
Maybe someone reading this needs permission to stop pretending they are okay.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if this reminded you of someone who has been carrying invisible battles, share this with them.
Some people are one honest conversation away from finally admitting they are not okay.
Do not let them fight alone.
Because one day you may need to remember that even Elijah collapsed… and God still stayed.

Followers of Gospel Warrior receive daily biblical encouragement, discipleship, conviction, healing, and Scripture-centered truth designed to strengthen weary believers and call people back to Jesus Christ.
Because some battles are too heavy to fight without consistent spiritual nourishment.
And maybe the most beautiful part of Elijah’s story is this:
God still spoke after the breakdown.
The whisper came after the collapse.
The assignment came after the exhaustion.
The presence of God remained after Elijah thought he was finished.
And maybe that is the message someone desperately needed today.
You are exhausted.
But you are not abandoned.
You are tired.
But God has not walked away.
You may be under the broom tree right now…
but heaven still knows your name.
Some whispers from God only become audible after the soul finally stops running.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind the Prophet Who Ate the Scroll
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind the Prophet Who Ate the Scroll
There are moments in Scripture that sound almost impossible to comprehend.
A bush burning without being consumed.
A sea opening in half.
Dead bones rattling back to life.
But buried in the prophetic books is one of the strangest and most emotionally devastating moments in the entire Bible.
God looked at a prophet… and told him to eat a scroll.
Not metaphorically.
Not symbolically in the casual modern sense.
Literally.
The prophet lifted the scroll to his mouth. He swallowed the words of God. And the taste changed everything.
Most believers know the image. Very few understand the terror behind it.
Because the scroll was not merely information. It was grief. Judgment. Suffering. Loneliness. The burden of carrying Heaven’s voice into a generation that did not want God.
And the deeper you study the Hebrew and Greek text behind this moment… the more frighteningly personal it becomes.
Because this story was never only about prophets.
It was about everyone who says they want to hear from God.
The Scroll Before the Mouth
The most famous account appears in the book of Ezekiel.
God speaks to the prophet:
“Son of man, eat what you find; eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.” — Ezekiel 3:1
In Hebrew, the phrase “eat this scroll” is:
אֱכוֹל אֶת־הַמְּגִלָּה הַזֹּאת
Transliterated:
'Ekhol et-haMegillah haZot'
The word “megillah” (מְּגִלָּה) means scroll, roll, or written record. But in ancient Jewish understanding, a scroll was more than paper.
It represented authority. Covenant. Witness. Legal testimony. Divine decree.
God was not merely telling Ezekiel to absorb information. He was commanding him to internalize Heaven itself.
Then Scripture says something shocking:
“So I opened my mouth, and He fed me this scroll.” — Ezekiel 3:2
Notice the intimacy.
Ezekiel did not seize revelation. God fed it to him.
There is a terrifying difference.
Many people today want inspiration. Few want ingestion.
They want motivational Christianity. Not prophetic transformation.
They want sermons that excite them. Not truth that dismantles them.
But Heaven has never released prophetic voices through spectators. The word had to enter him. Consume him. Break him. Live inside him.
And this is where the story becomes deeply emotional.
Because Ezekiel was not living in comfort.
He was among exiles. A displaced people. A broken nation. A generation under judgment.
Jerusalem was collapsing. Hope was dying. People were spiritually numb.
And God chose a wounded man to carry wounded words.
Some of you understand this pain personally.
You know what it feels like to carry burdens nobody sees. To smile while your spirit quietly bleeds. To speak faith while fighting exhaustion.
That is why this story still grips the soul.
Because God often calls broken people to carry living truth.
The Scroll Was Filled With Grief
Then Ezekiel reveals what was written on the scroll.
“And there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.” — Ezekiel 2:10
The Hebrew reads:
קִנִים וָהֶגֶה וָהִי
Qinim va-hegeh va-hi.
Lamentation. Mourning. Wailing.
The scroll was saturated with sorrow.
This completely destroys the modern fantasy that hearing from God is always emotionally easy.
Sometimes God’s word comforts. Sometimes it confronts. Sometimes it crushes pride. Sometimes it exposes hidden sin. Sometimes it forces a person to stop pretending.
And yet… Ezekiel says something that almost seems contradictory.
“Then I ate it, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth.” — Ezekiel 3:3
Sweet?
How could judgment taste sweet?
How could grief feel holy?
Because the sweetness was not in destruction. The sweetness was in truth.
The Hebrew word for honey is “devash” (דְּבַשׁ). In ancient Hebrew thought, honey symbolized delight, abundance, richness, and pleasure.
Even painful truth becomes sweet when a soul is starving for God.
This is why genuine repentance often comes with tears and relief at the same time.
Because conviction hurts. But deception kills.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You remember the sermon that exposed you. The Scripture that pierced you. The prayer moment where God uncovered something hidden.
It hurt.
But it also saved you.
The Prophet Nobody Talks About
Most people stop at Ezekiel. But the scroll appears again in another terrifying prophetic encounter.
This time in the New Testament.
The apostle John. Exiled. Alone. Banished to Patmos.
A prisoner receiving visions from Heaven.
In Revelation 10:9, John approaches an angel holding a little scroll.
“So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, ‘Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.’”
In Greek, the phrase “take and eat” is:
Λάβε καὶ κατάφαγε αὐτό
Labe kai kataphage auto.
“Kataphage” means to devour fully. Consume entirely.
Not nibble. Not sample. Devour.
And suddenly the mystery deepens.
Because now the scroll is sweet in the mouth… but bitter in the stomach.
Why?
Because receiving truth and carrying truth are two different things.
Hearing revelation feels glorious. Living it costs everything.
Many people love Christian inspiration. Few endure Christian surrender.
The mouth celebrates. The stomach suffers.
That bitterness represents the internal cost of obedience.
The loneliness. The rejection. The spiritual warfare. The heartbreak of loving people who refuse God. The burden of watching truth be mocked.
This is why true prophetic ministry always carries tears.
Jeremiah wept. Ezekiel mourned. John suffered exile. Paul carried affliction. Jesus Himself was “a man of sorrows” according to Isaiah 53:3.
The closer someone walks with God, the more deeply they often feel the grief of a fallen world.
And yet modern culture keeps teaching believers that Christianity should never feel heavy.
But Scripture says otherwise.
Even Jesus in Gethsemane declared:
“My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.” — Matthew 26:38
The Greek phrase “perilypos estin” (περίλυπός ἐστιν) describes overwhelming anguish. Deep crushing sorrow.
Holiness has never meant emotional numbness.
Sometimes the people closest to God cry the hardest.
The Scroll Was Never About Information
This is the part many believers miss.
The scroll was not ultimately about prophecy.
It was about transformation.
God did not tell Ezekiel:
“Read this scroll.”
He said:
“Eat it.”
Internalize it. Absorb it. Let it become part of you.
This changes how we understand Scripture entirely.
The Bible was never meant to be skimmed for inspirational quotes. It was meant to invade the human soul.
The early Jewish understanding of meditation on God’s word involved repetition, muttering, and deep internal reflection.
Psalm 1 describes the righteous person as someone who meditates on God’s law day and night.
The Hebrew word is “hagah” (הָגָה). It can mean meditate, murmur, utter softly, ponder deeply.
Biblical meditation was not emptying the mind. It was filling the soul with God’s truth until it reshaped identity.
That is exactly what the scroll represented.
And this confronts modern Christianity in an uncomfortable way.
Many people consume endless content. Very few let Scripture consume them.
They know clips. Quotes. Highlights.
But not surrender. Not depth. Not transformation.
The scroll cannot merely touch your lips. It must enter your life.
The Cost Nobody Warns You About
There is another heartbreaking detail hidden in Ezekiel.
Immediately after eating the scroll, the prophet is sent to stubborn people.
“And the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you.” — Ezekiel 3:7
Imagine that.
God tells Ezekiel beforehand that many will reject the message.
Yet He still sends him.
This is one of the loneliest realities in genuine ministry.
Obedience does not always produce applause.
Sometimes you love people who refuse truth. Sometimes you warn people who mock you. Sometimes you pray for people who walk away anyway.
And still… God says go.
This is why the scroll had bitterness inside it.
Because loving people deeply will wound you eventually.
Jesus Himself looked over Jerusalem and wept.
The Greek word used in Luke 19:41 is “eklausen” (ἔκλαυσεν). Not quiet tears. Open sobbing.
The Son of God publicly wept over resistant hearts.
That changes everything.

Some of you have been mocked for taking your faith seriously. Some of you carry family members who are far from God. Some of you pray for children, spouses, friends, or parents who seem spiritually asleep.
And sometimes it feels exhausting.
But the prophets understood this burden.
So did Jesus.
The Scroll and the Modern Church
There is a dangerous version of Christianity spreading everywhere right now.
A version obsessed with comfort. Entertainment. Self-promotion. Platforms. Popularity.
But almost completely disconnected from surrender.
People want viral moments. God wants transformed hearts.
The scroll reminds us that true encounters with God change a person permanently.
When Isaiah encountered God, he cried out:
“Woe is me!” — Isaiah 6:5
When Peter encountered Jesus’ holiness, he said:
“Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.” — Luke 5:8
When John saw Christ glorified, he fell “as though dead” in Revelation 1:17.
Biblical encounters shattered human pride.
The modern world wants spirituality without repentance. But the scroll confronts sin directly.
And strangely… that confrontation becomes sweetness.
Because nothing is sweeter than finally becoming honest before God.
No more masks. No more pretending. No more fake perfection.
Just surrender.
Some readers needed this reminder tonight.
God is not asking for performance. He is asking for openness.
The Gospel Hidden Inside the Scroll
The deepest revelation hidden in this story is this:
Jesus Himself became the living Word.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
The Greek phrase:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
The eternal Logos entered humanity.
Jesus did not merely deliver truth. He embodied it.
And on the cross, Christ carried the bitterness humanity deserved so sinners could taste the sweetness of grace.
That is the Gospel.
The prophets carried scrolls. Jesus carried the cross.
And through His death and resurrection, the deepest judgment against sin was satisfied.
Mercy became available. Forgiveness became possible. Redemption opened.
This is why repentance is not humiliation. It is rescue.
The enemy wants people trapped in shame. Jesus calls people into freedom.
There are people reading this who have hidden things for years. Secret addictions. Private compromise. Silent despair. Religious performance.
But the Gospel is not merely behavior modification. It is transformation through Christ.
And maybe that is why the scroll still matters.
Because every believer eventually faces the same decision:
Will you merely admire God’s word?
Or will you let it enter you deeply enough to change you?
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some wounds only heal when truth finally enters the places we kept locked away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why King Lemuel’s Mother Warned Him About Women and Power
paragraphs: Why King Lemuel’s Mother Warned Him About Women and Power
There are some warnings in Scripture that feel less like theology… and more like a mother grabbing her son’s face before he walks into a fire.
This is one of them.
Most people read Proverbs 31 searching for the “virtuous woman.”
But before the famous passage about the noble wife… before the poetic descriptions of strength and dignity… there is a trembling warning almost nobody talks about.
A warning from a mother.
A warning to a king.
A warning about women, seduction, authority, lust, weakness, intoxication, and self-destruction.
And if we are honest… this warning feels more relevant now than ever.
Because history keeps repeating itself.
Powerful men still destroy themselves over uncontrolled desire.
Families still collapse because someone could not govern their appetites.
Ministries still fall.
Marriages still bleed.
Nations still suffer because leaders become slaves to pleasure.
And behind the ruins… you often hear the echo of a warning they ignored.
The passage begins in Proverbs 31:1:
“The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him.”
The Hebrew text says:
"דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל מֶלֶךְ מַשָּׂא אֲשֶׁר יִסְּרַתּוּ אִמּוֹ"
Transliteration:
Divrei Lemuel melek massa asher yisseratu immo.
The word "יִסְּרַתּוּ" (yisseratu) comes from the Hebrew root yasar.
It means:
• to discipline • to correct • to instruct through warning • to chasten lovingly
This was not casual advice.
This was deep correction.
A mother saw danger near her son.
And she spoke urgently.
Some scholars debate whether King Lemuel was Solomon under another name or another king entirely. Scripture does not explicitly confirm his identity. But what matters is this:
God preserved a mother’s warning for generations.
That alone should make us pause.
Because heaven does not preserve meaningless conversations.
Then comes the line that strikes like lightning.
Proverbs 31:3:
“Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.”
The Hebrew says:
"אַל־תִּתֵּן לַנָּשִׁים חֵילֶךָ וּדְרָכֶיךָ לַמְחוֹת מְלָכִין"
Transliteration:
Al-titten lanashim cheilekha, u-derakhekha lamchot melakhin.
This verse is often misunderstood.
His mother was not teaching hatred toward women.
Scripture consistently honors godly women.
Deborah led with wisdom.
Ruth displayed covenant loyalty.
Esther risked her life to save a nation.
Mary carried the Messiah.
Priscilla helped disciple believers.
The Bible never teaches misogyny.
So what was Lemuel’s mother actually warning against?
She was warning against surrendering masculine strength, authority, clarity, calling, discipline, and covenant responsibility to destructive lust and ungodly influence.
The Hebrew word for “strength” here is "חֵיל" (chayil or cheil).
This word is powerful.
It can mean:
• strength • wealth • army • vigor • capability • substance • power • efficiency
In other words:
“Do not hand over your God-given power.”
Not your discernment.
Not your calling.
Not your soul.
Not your kingship.
The warning was never against righteous women.
The warning was against uncontrolled appetite.
Against seduction.
Against becoming weak through pleasure.
Against allowing desire to dethrone wisdom.
And history proves this warning mattered.
Samson lost his strength because he played with compromise.
Solomon, despite extraordinary wisdom, allowed foreign wives to turn his heart toward idolatry.
David’s unchecked desire led to adultery, deception, and bloodshed.
Entire kingdoms suffered because kings could not govern themselves.
People think power destroys men.
Scripture teaches that unrestrained desire destroys men holding power.
That is a very different thing.
And if you think this warning only applies to kings… you have missed the point.
Every man rules something.
A home.
A family.
A future.
A mind.
A calling.
A testimony.
And whatever rules you… eventually rules what you lead.
That is why Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
The Hebrew word for “keep” is "נָצַר" (natsar).
It means:
• to guard • to watch over • to protect like a fortress
Your heart is not something Scripture tells you to casually manage.
It tells you to guard like a kingdom under siege.
Because temptation rarely announces itself as destruction.
It usually arrives looking beautiful.
Desired.
Comforting.
Exciting.
Validating.
That is why seduction is powerful.
It speaks to wounds.
To ego.
To loneliness.
To insecurity.
To pride.
To secret hunger.
And eventually people start sacrificing purpose to feed appetite.
That is exactly what Lemuel’s mother feared.
Not merely immoral behavior.
But destroyed destiny.
Destroyed judgment.
Destroyed leadership.
Destroyed legacy.
And what is terrifying is how modern this sounds.
Today people surrender marriages for temporary validation.
They surrender integrity for hidden conversations.
They surrender families for emotional affairs.
They surrender ministries for secret addictions.
They surrender purity because culture normalized lust.
And then society acts shocked when the collapse comes.
But Scripture warned us.
Long ago.
His mother continues in Proverbs 31:4-5:
“It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: Lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted.”
Again, notice the theme.
Self-control.
Discernment.
Sobriety.
Clear judgment.
Why?
Because leaders who lose clarity eventually harm people.
The Hebrew phrase for “forget the law” includes the idea of losing moral clarity and abandoning righteous judgment.
This was not merely about alcohol.
It was about anything that intoxicates judgment.
Anything that numbs discernment.
Anything that weakens conviction.
Today intoxication comes in many forms.
Pride.
Attention.
Pornography.
Greed.
Validation.
Sexual addiction.
Power.
Fame.
Even social media applause.
People can become drunk on influence.
And intoxicated people rarely lead well.
That is why spiritual warfare often begins in private.
Before public collapse… there was usually private compromise.
Before destruction… there was hidden permission.
Before bondage… there was entertained temptation.
The enemy rarely destroys people suddenly.
He erodes them gradually.
One compromise.
One excuse.
One hidden conversation.
One tolerated addiction.
One secret fantasy.
One private rebellion.
Until eventually the soul no longer recognizes itself.
This is why the New Testament repeatedly calls believers to sobriety and vigilance.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.”
The Greek word for “sober” is "νήψατε" (nēpsate).
It means:
• be self-controlled • be spiritually alert • avoid intoxication of mind and soul
The Greek word for “vigilant” is "γρηγορήσατε" (grēgorēsate).
Meaning:
• stay awake • remain watchful • refuse spiritual sleep
Notice how consistent Scripture is across both Testaments.
God repeatedly warns humanity about spiritual carelessness.
Especially when influence and desire collide.
And maybe this article hurts because deep down… many people know exactly where they became weak.
Some lost years chasing lust.
Some lost peace hiding addiction.
Some lost intimacy with God because compromise became easier than surrender.
Some lost themselves trying to feed emptiness through relationships.
And yet Jesus still stands ready to restore.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Scripture warns deeply because God loves deeply.
Conviction is not hatred.
It is rescue.
The same Bible that warns about destruction also reveals redemption.
The woman caught in adultery was not stoned.
Peter was restored after denial.
The prodigal son was embraced.
David repented and found mercy.
Paul went from persecutor to apostle.
Jesus specializes in rebuilding ruined people.
But restoration begins where excuses end.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
The Greek word for repentance is "μετάνοια" (metanoia).
It means:
• a change of mind • a transformation of heart • turning around completely
Biblical repentance is not emotional performance.
It is surrender.
And some people reading this right now know God has been confronting them privately for months.
Maybe through conviction.
Maybe through sleepless nights.
Maybe through sermons.
Maybe through consequences.
Maybe through silence.
Maybe through the slow grief of realizing sin never delivered what it promised.
The terrifying thing about temptation is that it advertises pleasure… but hides chains.
That is why Proverbs repeatedly personifies seduction as something leading people toward death while promising satisfaction.
Sin always exaggerates what it offers.
And minimizes what it steals.
Lemuel’s mother understood something modern culture often rejects:
Self-control is not oppression.
It is protection.
Boundaries are not bondage.
Sometimes they are mercy.
Not every desire deserves obedience.
Not every attraction deserves pursuit.
Not every emotional craving deserves surrender.
And one of the most dangerous lies people believe today is this:
“If I feel it strongly, it must be right.”
Scripture never teaches that.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
Human emotion without God is not a trustworthy compass.
That is why people need truth.
Not merely affirmation.
And perhaps the reason this warning still survives thousands of years later is because humanity still struggles with the exact same battle.
Appetite versus wisdom.
Pleasure versus holiness.
Desire versus obedience.
Flesh versus Spirit.
Kingdom versus self.
And maybe some people expected this article to attack women.
But that would completely miss Scripture.
The real warning is larger.
It is about idolatry.
Anything can become an idol.
Sex.
Relationships.
Approval.
Beauty.
Influence.
Validation.
Attention.
Pleasure.
And idols always demand sacrifice.
Usually your peace first.
Then your clarity.
Then your identity.
Then your future.
Then your relationship with God.
This is why Jesus said in Matthew 5:8:
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
The Greek word for “pure” is "καθαροὶ" (katharoi).
Meaning:
• clean • unmixed • uncontaminated
Purity is not merely about behavior.
It is about undivided devotion.
A heart not fragmented between God and idols.
And that is where this becomes deeply personal.
Because many people are exhausted not from work… but from inner division.
Half surrendered.
Half compromised.
Half obedient.
Trying to follow God while secretly feeding the very thing destroying them.
But eventually divided hearts collapse under pressure.
God never asked people for partial surrender.
He asked for everything.
And yet even now… grace still reaches.
That is the miracle.
You are not too stained.
Not too compromised.
Not too addicted.
Not too hypocritical.
Not too far gone.
Christ still heals people who come honestly.
Completely.
Without pretending.
Without excuses.
Without hiding.
That is why the cross matters.
Jesus did not die merely to improve behavior.
He died to resurrect dead souls.
And some readers right now do not need motivation.
They need deliverance.
They need freedom.
They need repentance.
They need truth.
They need Christ.
And maybe that is why this warning from a mother still echoes across centuries.
Because deep down humanity still needs wisdom.
Still needs restraint.
Still needs holiness.
Still needs redemption.
Still needs Jesus.
Stay there for a moment.
Let God deal with your heart honestly.
One hidden compromise can quietly become the funeral of a calling.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Cain Couldn’t Rest Even After Building a Life
paragraphs: Why Cain Couldn’t Rest Even After Building a Life
There are people who look successful from a distance but are collapsing in silence when nobody is watching.
They built careers. They built businesses. They built families. They built platforms. They built influence. They built entire identities.
But deep inside… they still cannot rest.
Not because they are lazy. Not because they are weak. Not because God abandoned them.
But because unresolved guilt can build cities while simultaneously destroying the soul living inside them.
Cain understood this better than most people realize.
The terrifying part is this: Cain did not fall apart after judgment.
He kept building.
That is what makes his story dangerous.

Most people imagine rebellion against God always looks like visible destruction. Sometimes it looks like productivity. Sometimes it looks like ambition. Sometimes it looks like a man trying to outrun the sound of God’s voice.
Genesis 4 does not read like ancient mythology. It reads like modern humanity.
The first brothers. The first jealousy. The first hidden rage. The first murder. The first attempt to move on without true repentance.
And maybe that is why Cain still feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because there are people reading this right now who are exhausted from building a life while carrying a soul they never surrendered back to God.
The story begins with worship.
Genesis 4:3–5 says:

“Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD. And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering: but unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.”
The Hebrew language reveals something deeper happening beneath the surface.
The phrase “had respect” comes from the Hebrew:
שָׁעָה sha’ah
Meaning: To gaze upon with favor. To regard attentively. To look toward with pleasure.
God was not randomly rejecting Cain. God was exposing the condition of Cain’s heart.
Abel brought the “firstlings.” The best. The first. The costly.
Cain simply brought “of the fruit.”
One brought worship. The other brought obligation.
And heaven always knows the difference.
This was never merely about vegetables versus animals. That shallow interpretation misses the spiritual weight entirely.
Hebrews 11:4 explains:
“By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain…”
Faith was the issue. The heart was the issue. Trust was the issue.
Cain wanted the appearance of worship without the surrender worship requires.
And honestly… that still exists inside churches today.
People sing while secretly hardening. People serve while privately rebelling. People preach while spiritually empty. People post Bible verses while refusing conviction.
External religion can hide internal distance for a while.
But eventually God confronts what performance cannot cover.
Genesis 4:6–7 says:
“And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.”
That phrase “sin lieth at the door” in Hebrew is haunting.
רֹבֵץ rovetz
It paints the image of a beast crouching. Waiting. Ready to devour.
God warned Cain before Cain destroyed himself.
Because God always warns before judgment falls.
People think conviction is rejection. It is not. Conviction is mercy.
The fact God spoke to Cain at all was an act of compassion.
But Cain refused to humble himself.
And pride always turns pain into poison.
Genesis 4:8 says:
“And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass… that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.”
The first murder in human history happened between brothers.
Not strangers. Not enemies.
Brothers.
Sin does not merely break rules. Sin corrupts love.
The Hebrew word for “slew” carries violent force. This was not accidental rage. This was cultivated resentment finally given permission.
And after the murder, God asked one of the most famous questions in Scripture:
“Where is Abel thy brother?”
God already knew.
This question was invitation. Not information gathering.
The same way God asked Adam: “Where art thou?”
Not because God loses people. But because people lose themselves.
Cain answered:
“I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The rebellion in that sentence still echoes through modern culture.
People no longer want responsibility for one another.
Everyone wants independence. Nobody wants accountability.
But Scripture never teaches isolated Christianity.
The Hebrew word for “keeper” is:
שָׁמַר shamar
Meaning: To guard. To watch. To preserve. To protect.
Cain rejected responsibility for his brother because sin had already hardened him internally.
And then judgment came.
Genesis 4:12:
“A fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.”
The Hebrew words are devastating.
נָע וָנָד na va’nad
Restless wanderer. Shaken drifter. One who cannot settle.
This is deeper than physical movement.
Cain’s punishment was internal instability.
And this is where the story becomes terrifyingly modern.
Because many people today are materially successful while spiritually wandering.
They cannot sleep peacefully. They cannot sit quietly. They cannot be still. They constantly need noise. Entertainment. Attention. Achievement. Distraction.
Not because they are fulfilled. But because silence forces confrontation.
And confrontation threatens the false self they built to survive.
Yet Cain did something shocking after all this.
Genesis 4:17:
“And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city…”
Read that again carefully.
Cain built a city.
A marked man. A guilty man. A restless man.
Built a city.
This is one of the most psychologically revealing verses in the entire Bible.
Cain could build externally while collapsing internally.
And humanity has repeated this pattern ever since.

People build empires while neglecting their soul. People build ministries while hiding secret sin. People build wealth while losing peace. People build online influence while privately drowning in emptiness.
Success cannot heal guilt.
Only repentance can.
The world teaches: “Build enough and you will finally feel okay.”
Scripture teaches: “No amount of building can heal separation from God.”
That is why some of the wealthiest people are miserable. That is why some celebrities self-destruct. That is why some powerful leaders secretly collapse emotionally.
You can build a city and still be spiritually homeless.
Cain’s problem was not merely murder. His deeper problem was refusing true repentance.
Notice something carefully.
Cain regretted consequences. But he never demonstrated brokenness before God.
2 Corinthians 7:10 later explains:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation… but the sorrow of the world worketh death.”
Worldly sorrow says: “I hate what this did to me.”
Godly sorrow says: “I broke the heart of God.”
Those are not the same thing.
And many people confuse emotional regret with repentance.
Biblical repentance in Greek is:
μετάνοια metanoia
Meaning: A change of mind. A turning. An inner transformation.
Not temporary sadness. Not public apology. Not image management.
Transformation.
Cain wanted protection. But not surrender.
And there are still people trying to negotiate with God today.
They want peace without repentance. Heaven without holiness. Comfort without surrender.
But Jesus never preached self-preservation. He preached dying to self.
Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
Modern culture says: “Protect your truth.”
Jesus says: “Crucify your flesh.”
That collision is why many people resist the Gospel.
The Gospel does not flatter human pride. It exposes it.
And yet… hidden inside Cain’s story is still mercy.
Even after Cain sinned, God marked him for protection.
Genesis 4:15:
“And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.”
The Hebrew word for “mark” is:
אוֹת oth
Meaning: A sign. A distinguishing mark. A signal.
God judged Cain. But God also restrained total destruction.
Justice and mercy existed together.
The Bible constantly reveals this tension.
God is holy. But God is also compassionate.
And ultimately this tension is resolved at the cross.
Because Jesus became what Cain never could.
Hebrews 12:24 says:
“And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.”
Abel’s blood cried out for justice.
Jesus’ blood cries out for mercy.
That changes everything.
Because the Gospel is not merely about exposing guilt. It is about redeeming the guilty.
Some of you reading this have spent years trying to build enough success to silence conviction.
But it still follows you.
At night. In quiet moments. During achievements. After applause. Inside relationships.
Because unhealed sin does not disappear through distraction.
It waits.
Just like God warned Cain.
“Sin lieth at the door.”
And maybe the exhaustion you feel is not burnout. Maybe it is spiritual separation.
Maybe the anxiety is deeper than stress. Maybe your soul is starving while your external life keeps expanding.
Cain teaches us something brutal: You can continue living without ever truly coming alive.
But Jesus offers something Cain never embraced.
Rest.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for “rest” is:
ἀναπαύσω anapauso
Meaning: To refresh. To give intermission from labor. To cause someone to cease from movement and anxiety.
The kind of rest Jesus offers is not merely physical. It is soul rest.
The kind Cain never found.
The kind money cannot purchase. The kind achievement cannot manufacture. The kind human approval cannot sustain.
Real peace only comes when the war between you and God ends.
And that peace was purchased through the cross.
Romans 5:1:
“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Not peace through success. Not peace through self-help. Not peace through pretending.
Peace through Jesus Christ.
That is why the Gospel is not behavior modification. It is resurrection.
And maybe this article found you because deep down… you know you have been building while internally bleeding.
You smile publicly. You function externally. You continue moving.
But you still cannot rest.
Jesus is not asking you to perform harder. He is asking you to surrender.
Not partial surrender. Not curated surrender.
Total surrender.
The kind that stops hiding. The kind that confesses. The kind that admits: “I cannot save myself.”
And maybe that is the most dangerous illusion modern humanity believes.
That we can build our own salvation.
Cain built a city.
Jesus builds new creations.
One hides guilt. The other destroys it.
One produces wandering. The other produces peace.
One keeps running. The other says: “It is finished.”
Be honest. This hit harder than some people expected.
Some people spend their entire lives building what can never quiet the voice of a restless soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Prophet Who Died Because He Listened to the Wrong Voice
paragraphs: The Prophet Who Died Because He Listened to the Wrong Voice
There are wounds that do not come from demons.
There are destructions that do not come from persecution.
There are graves dug not by enemies… but by deception wearing the voice of someone spiritual.
And one of the most terrifying stories in all of Scripture is not about a wicked king, a pagan nation, or a possessed man.
It is about a prophet.
A man of God.
A man who heard God clearly.
A man who obeyed almost everything.
Almost.
Because partial obedience still buries people.
Most Christians have never truly sat inside the weight of this story.
They skim it.
They summarize it.
But if you slow down long enough to feel the terror inside 1 Kings 13, you realize this is not merely ancient history.
This is the modern Church.
This is believers destroyed because they listened to charisma over God.
This is people abandoning conviction because someone older, louder, famous, spiritual, emotional, or persuasive spoke against what God originally said.
This is the generation dying spiritually because they trusted the wrong voice.
And what makes the story unforgettable…
is that the prophet was not destroyed while rebelling.
He died while trying to obey.
The chapter opens during the reign of Jeroboam, the king who fractured Israel and led people into idolatry. God sends an unnamed prophet from Judah with a terrifyingly specific assignment.
Scripture says:
"By the word of the LORD a man of God came from Judah to Bethel…" (1 Kings 13:1)
The Hebrew phrase used for “word of the LORD” is:
"בִּדְבַר־יְהוָה" (bidvar-YHWH)
This was not imagination.
Not emotion.
Not intuition.
This was direct divine instruction.
God had spoken clearly.
And clarity from God is a dangerous thing to ignore.
The prophet arrives at Bethel where Jeroboam is standing beside a pagan altar.
This man of God suddenly cries out against the altar itself:
“O altar, altar! Thus says the LORD…”
The Hebrew expression:
"כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה" (koh amar YHWH)
means:
“YHWH Himself has declared.”
This was courtroom language.
Final.
Authoritative.
Absolute.
And the prophecy was shocking.
A future king named Josiah would one day destroy this corrupt altar and expose the evil happening there.
Jeroboam becomes furious.
He stretches out his hand and commands the prophet to be seized.
But suddenly the king’s hand dries up.
The altar splits apart.
Ashes pour out.
Everything God said happens instantly.
The false system trembles when truth arrives.
But then comes the dangerous moment.
Success.
Miracles.
Public power.
Because many believers survive warfare…
but fall after spiritual victory.
Jeroboam suddenly changes his tone and says:
“Come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward.”
The enemy always tries to reward the prophet he cannot silence.
But the man of God answers with stunning conviction.
Even if the king gave him half his house, he would not eat bread or drink water there.
Why?
Because God had already spoken.
Scripture records the instruction:
“You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.”
The Hebrew construction here is extremely forceful.
“לֹא־תֹאכַל לֶחֶם וְלֹא תִשְׁתֶּה מָּיִם”
(lo tokhal lechem velo tishteh mayim)
“Do not eat. Do not drink.”
Direct.
Clear.
No ambiguity.
No symbolic interpretation.
No room for negotiation.
And this is where the story should have ended.
The prophet should have gone home alive.
But the most dangerous attacks often happen after obedience.
An old prophet living in Bethel hears about everything that happened.
And immediately something feels wrong.
Because instead of celebrating the purity of the word from God…
he chases the prophet down.
When he finds him resting beneath a tree, he invites him home to eat.
The prophet refuses.
At first.
And here is the moment that should terrify every believer reading this.
The old prophet replies:
“I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD…”
Then Scripture inserts one of the coldest lines in the entire Bible.
“But he lied to him.”
The Hebrew is devastatingly simple:
"כִּחֵשׁ לוֹ" (kicheish lo)
“He lied to him.”
No complication.
No nuance.
No misunderstanding.
A prophet lied.
And another prophet died because he trusted spiritual appearance over God’s original instruction.
Read that again.
The deception did not come from a witch.
Not from Baal worshippers.
Not from atheists.
Not from pagans.
It came through someone who claimed spiritual authority.
This is why discernment matters more than inspiration.
Not every spiritual voice carries God.
Not every preacher speaking softly speaks truth.
Not every viral sermon is anointed.
Not every emotional confirmation came from Heaven.
And one of Satan’s oldest strategies is this:
contradict what God already said… through someone who sounds spiritual.
It happened in Eden.
“Did God really say…?”
It happened in Bethel.
“An angel told me otherwise…”
And it is happening right now.

People are abandoning biblical truth because influencers, compromised leaders, celebrity pastors, culture-driven teachers, and emotionally persuasive voices are telling them God no longer means what He clearly said.
But God is not the author of confusion.
The Greek word for confusion in 1 Corinthians 14:33 is:
"ἀκαταστασία" (akatastasia)
meaning instability, disorder, chaos, double-minded disruption.
God does not contradict Himself.
If God already spoke clearly in Scripture, no emotional experience has authority over His Word.
The prophet should have remembered that.
But exhaustion weakens discernment.
Loneliness weakens discernment.
Flattery weakens discernment.
The desire for comfort weakens discernment.
And sometimes people obey God publicly… while privately craving someone to tell them they can relax the command.
So the prophet goes home with the old man.
He sits.
He eats.
He drinks.
And then the atmosphere shifts.
Suddenly the real word of God comes.
Ironically… through the lying prophet.
Judgment is pronounced.
Because the man disobeyed the mouth of the LORD.
The Hebrew phrase:
"פִּי יְהוָה" (pi YHWH)
literally means:
“the mouth of YHWH.”
Not suggestion.
Not preference.
The very mouth of God.
And now comes one of the strangest and most haunting scenes in Scripture.
The prophet leaves.
A lion meets him on the road.
Kills him.
But does not eat the body.
The donkey stands beside the corpse.
The lion stands beside the donkey.
Everything freezes.
Creation itself becomes a prophetic sign.
This was not natural.
This was judgment.
The lion was not hungry.
The lion was a witness.
Imagine travelers walking by and seeing this impossible scene:
A dead prophet.
A lion beside him.
A donkey untouched.
Silence on the road.
Because God was screaming through the stillness.
The terrifying truth is this:
the prophet was sincere.
But sincerity without obedience still destroys people.
And this generation desperately needs to hear that.
Because modern Christianity often worships sincerity more than truth.
“If their heart was right…”
“They meant well…”
“They were kind…”
“They were spiritual…”
But the road to destruction is filled with sincere people who ignored what God actually said.
Jesus Himself warned:
“Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord…’”
Notice that.
They called Him Lord.
But intimacy language is not the same as obedience.
The Greek word Jesus used in Matthew 7:21 for “does” the will of the Father is:
"ποιῶν" (poiōn)
meaning actively practicing, carrying out, obeying continuously.
Christianity was never meant to be admiration without surrender.
And maybe that is why this story still punches through the soul centuries later.
Because deep down many believers know exactly what this feels like.
God told them something clearly.
But then another voice entered.
A relationship.
A compromise.
A preacher.
A trend.
A YouTube sermon.
A TikTok prophet.
An influencer.
A friend.
A culture.
And slowly they began negotiating with the very thing God already settled.
Some people reading this were once radically sensitive to conviction.
Now they silence it.
Some used to tremble at Scripture.
Now they reinterpret everything to fit comfort.
Some once obeyed immediately.
Now they delay until obedience dies.
And the frightening part is this:
deception rarely feels dangerous in the beginning.
It often feels relieving.
Comforting.
Affirming.
Reasonable.
That is why Scripture repeatedly warns believers to test spirits.
The Greek word in 1 John 4:1 is:
"δοκιμάζετε" (dokimazete)
meaning to examine, scrutinize, prove after testing.
God never told believers to blindly absorb every spiritual voice.
Discernment is not rebellion.
Discernment is survival.
And maybe someone reading this right now has been feeling tension in their spirit lately.
Something feels off.
A compromise has been whispering.
A voice has been pulling you away from what Scripture clearly says.
You keep trying to convince yourself it is harmless.
But conviction keeps returning at night.
That may be the mercy of God trying to stop your destruction.
Because the scariest judgment is not when God warns you.
It is when He stops warning you.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
The Greek word for harden is:
"σκληρύνητε" (sklērynēte)
meaning to make stubborn, resistant, spiritually insensitive.
Every ignored conviction slowly calcifies the soul.
And eventually people no longer recognize the difference between God’s voice and their own desires.
But there is still mercy.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Because while 1 Kings 13 is a warning…
Jesus Christ is the rescue.
Where Adam failed to obey, Jesus obeyed.
Where Israel rebelled, Jesus remained faithful.
Where prophets fell short, Christ fulfilled perfect obedience.
Philippians 2 says He became obedient unto death.
The Greek word:
"ὑπήκοος" (hypēkoos)
means submissively attentive, listening under authority.
Jesus listened perfectly to the Father.
Even in Gethsemane.
Even at the cross.
Even when obedience hurt.
And because of His obedience… there is mercy for every believer who has listened to the wrong voices.
Peter listened to fear.
Thomas listened to doubt.
The prodigal listened to rebellion.
Yet Jesus restored them.
And maybe that is you.
Maybe you have drifted.
Maybe compromise slowly numbed your spirit.
Maybe you trusted voices that pulled you away from truth.
Maybe you still look spiritual publicly while privately collapsing.
But the Shepherd still calls wandering sheep home.
The Gospel is not merely exposure.
It is redemption.
But redemption begins with honesty.
Not pretending.
Not hiding.
Not spiritual performance.
Honesty.
The kind where you finally admit:
“I have been listening to the wrong voice.”
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment God wanted to wake you up before deeper destruction came.
Do not ignore conviction while it is still speaking.
Some warnings are mercy wearing severe clothing.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
One wrong voice can cost years… but one moment of surrender can still save your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Obadiah
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Obadiah
The Prophet Who Stood Between Two Kingdoms While His Soul Trembled Before God
There are names in Scripture that thunder.
Moses. David. Elijah. Paul.
And then there are names that almost disappear into the dust of forgotten pages.
Names most believers skip. Names buried between wars, judgments, and genealogies. Names preached less than once every few years.
Obadiah is one of those names.
Only twenty-one verses.
One chapter.
A prophet with no recorded miracles. No famous sermons. No dramatic biography. No ark. No lions’ den. No giant slain. No prison chains broken.
Yet hidden inside this shortest book of the Old Testament is one of the fiercest warnings God ever spoke against pride, betrayal, hidden hatred, spiritual arrogance, and silent cruelty.
And maybe that is exactly why so many people avoid Obadiah.
Because Obadiah is not merely a prophecy against a nation.
It is a mirror.
A terrifying mirror.
The Book of Obadiah exposes something most people never admit publicly:
sometimes people do not destroy others with swords.
Sometimes they destroy them by watching them suffer while doing nothing.
And suddenly this ancient prophet stops feeling ancient.
Because entire friendships have died that way. Families have fractured that way. Churches have collapsed that way. Believers have backslidden that way.
People standing nearby. Watching destruction happen. Saying nothing. Doing nothing. Feeling secretly satisfied.
That is the world Obadiah walked into.
And if we are honest...
it is still our world.
The Hebrew name עֹבַדְיָה (‘Ovadyah) means:
“Servant of Yahweh.”
Not celebrity. Not influencer. Not spiritual superstar.
Servant.
That alone already confronts modern Christianity.
Because heaven remembers servants the world forgets.

Very little is known about Obadiah himself. Scholars debate the exact timeline of his ministry, though many place the prophecy shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon around 586 BC. The target of the prophecy was Edom — descendants of Esau.
And that is where the story becomes emotionally devastating.
Because Edom and Israel were not strangers.
They were family.
Jacob and Esau.
Brothers.
The wound began in Genesis.
Two nations struggling inside one womb.
Genesis 25:23 records the Hebrew:
“וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר”
“ve-rav ya’avod tsa’ir”
“The older shall serve the younger.”
From the very beginning there was tension. Competition. Jealousy. Bitterness. Inheritance conflict.
The kind of emotional poison that silently travels through generations.
And centuries later, Edom still carried the bitterness of Esau.
This is why Obadiah is not merely geopolitical.
It is deeply personal.
The prophecy burns because betrayal from enemies hurts.
But betrayal from family cuts differently.
God’s accusation against Edom was horrifying.
When Jerusalem fell...
Edom stood back and watched.
Worse than that.
They celebrated.
Obadiah 1:12 says:
“But do not gloat over your brother in the day of his misfortune.”
The Hebrew word for “gloat” is:
“תֵּרֶא” (tere’eh)
It carries the idea of looking upon with satisfaction. Watching with pleasure. Enjoying someone’s downfall.
That changes everything.
God was not only judging violence.
He was judging hearts that secretly enjoyed seeing others collapse.
That is terrifying.
Because some people never physically attack others.
They simply smile internally when someone fails.
A ministry falls. A marriage breaks. A believer backslides. Someone loses influence. Someone gets exposed. Someone struggles mentally. Someone sins publicly.
And hidden beneath religious language is a secret satisfaction:
“I knew they would fail.”
Obadiah reveals that heaven sees even silent cruelty.
The terrifying thing about Edom is they probably justified themselves.
They did not invade first. They did not light the fires. They only watched.
But God treated passive betrayal as active participation.
That should shake every modern believer.
Because neutrality during evil is not innocence.
The prophet describes Edom standing “at the crossroads” to cut off fugitives fleeing destruction.
Imagine the horror.
People escaping for their lives. Families running through smoke. Children terrified. Jerusalem burning.
And relatives blocked the escape routes.
How cold does a heart become before it can betray blood?
Yet humanity still does this.
People weaponize private pain. Expose vulnerable confessions. Exploit weakness. Use someone’s worst moment as entertainment.
Social media has normalized public executions of broken people.
And many believers participate while calling it discernment.
Obadiah stands like fire against that spirit.
The prophet’s message was not merely political judgment.
It was divine exposure.
God was exposing hidden pride.
Obadiah 1:3 says:
“The pride of your heart has deceived you.”
In Hebrew:
“זְדוֹן לִבְּךָ הִשִּׁיאֶךָ”
“zedon libbekha hishi’ekha”
“The arrogance of your heart has led you astray.”
Notice where the pride lived.
Not merely in behavior.
In the heart.
Pride is most dangerous when invisible.
Edom trusted its mountain fortresses. Its strategic defenses. Its elevated position. Its security. Its wisdom. Its alliances.
They believed they could not be touched.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a terrifying pattern:
whatever people trust more than God eventually becomes the place of their humiliation.
For some it is beauty. For others money. Intelligence. Popularity. Influence. Followers. Control. Relationships. Ministry reputation.
Pride blinds people into believing they are untouchable.
Until God removes the illusion.
And here is where Obadiah becomes deeply uncomfortable.
Because Edom’s greatest sin was not only hatred.
It was distance.
Distance from compassion. Distance from mercy. Distance from grief. Distance from God’s heart.
People can become spiritually sophisticated while emotionally dead.
They know theology. Know verses. Know doctrine. Know apologetics. Know church culture.
Yet feel nothing when people break.
Obadiah destroys performative spirituality.
The prophet reminds us that God notices how people respond to another person’s suffering.
Not only their sermons. Not only their worship playlists. Not only their church attendance.
But their heart posture toward wounded people.
Jesus later echoed this same reality.
In Matthew 25, the Greek language becomes deeply piercing.
“ἐφ’ ὅσον οὐκ ἐποιήσατε”
“eph’ hoson ouk epoiēsate”
“As you did not do it...”
The judgment was connected not merely to evil committed.
But compassion withheld.
That is the terrifying bridge between Obadiah and Christ’s teachings.
Sin is not only what people do.
Sometimes it is what they refused to do.
Refused to say. Refused to help. Refused to heal. Refused to protect.
And somewhere reading this...
someone feels convicted.
Not because you attacked someone.
But because you watched them drown emotionally and justified your silence.
Obadiah reaches directly into modern hearts.
This tiny prophetic book is emotionally enormous.
And yet hidden inside the judgment is one of the greatest revelations of God’s justice.
Evil does not escape heaven’s attention.
People often wonder if God sees betrayal. If He notices manipulation. If He sees hidden cruelty. If He sees what people whispered behind closed doors. If He notices those who exploited weakness.
Obadiah answers clearly.
Yes.
God saw Edom.
Every smirk. Every celebration. Every moment of hidden satisfaction. Every blocked escape route. Every betrayal.
Nothing escaped Him.
That matters deeply for wounded believers.
Because many people carry pain from spiritual betrayal.
Friends who vanished during depression. Churches that abandoned them. Leaders who humiliated them. Family who mocked their faith. People who watched them suffer and offered no mercy.
Obadiah reminds the wounded:
God saw it.
And He still sees it.
But the book also warns the wounded not to become Edom themselves.
Pain can mutate into bitterness.
Victims can become cruel.
The rejected can become rejectors.
The betrayed can become betrayers.
The cycle continues unless grace interrupts it.
And that is where the Gospel enters this ancient prophetic fire.
Because Obadiah ultimately reveals humanity’s desperate need for a Savior.
Every person has traces of Edom hiding somewhere inside.
Jealousy. Hidden pride. Secret satisfaction at someone else’s failure. Emotional distance. Self-righteousness.
The human heart without Christ naturally drifts toward hardness.
This is why the Gospel is not motivational self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is:
“μετάνοια” (metanoia)
It means a transformative change of mind and heart.
Not superficial regret.
Transformation.
Jesus does not merely improve hard hearts.
He replaces them.
Ezekiel 36:26 prophetically declared:
“I will remove the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.”
Obadiah shows us the danger of stone hearts.
Jesus offers new ones.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Even proud people can repent. Even betrayers can be restored. Even spiritually cold hearts can become alive again.
Peter denied Christ. Yet became restored.
Paul persecuted believers. Yet became transformed.
The cross itself proves God specializes in redeeming broken people.
And maybe that is why Obadiah matters now more than ever.
Because modern culture rewards mockery. Rewards exposure. Rewards humiliation. Rewards public destruction.
But the Kingdom of God moves differently.
Mercy. Compassion. Restoration. Truth with tears. Correction with humility.
Not performative outrage.
Obadiah is a warning to every believer becoming emotionally numb.
The book asks uncomfortable questions:
Have you secretly enjoyed someone’s collapse?
Have you become prideful in your spiritual position?
Have you mistaken distance for wisdom?
Have you withheld compassion?
Have you watched people bleed emotionally while protecting your own comfort?
And perhaps hardest of all:
Have you become so wounded that you now resemble the very people who hurt you?
Those questions linger.
Because Scripture was never meant to merely inform minds.
It was meant to expose souls.
And still...
even after judgment...
God leaves room for hope.
The final verse of Obadiah says:
“And the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.”
In Hebrew:
“וְהָיְתָה לַיהוָה הַמְּלוּכָה”
“ve-hayetah l’YHWH ha-melukhah”
“The kingdom belongs to Yahweh.”
That is the ending humanity desperately needs.
Not Edom winning. Not pride winning. Not betrayal winning. Not cruelty winning.
God reigns.
And because He reigns, evil will not write the final chapter.
Jesus Christ already stepped into humanity’s violence, betrayal, mockery, and hatred.
He was betrayed by one of His own. Mocked publicly. Abandoned in suffering. Humiliated before crowds.
The Son of God understands betrayal personally.
Yet from the cross He still prayed:
“Father, forgive them.”
That changes everything.
Because forgiveness is not weakness.
It is proof heaven is stronger than hatred.
Maybe that is why this forgotten prophet still burns after thousands of years.
Obadiah is not merely ancient history.
It is a divine interruption.
A warning. A mirror. A confrontation. A mercy.
And maybe while reading this...
you realized the Holy Spirit exposed something hidden inside you.
Pride. Bitterness. Secret resentment. Spiritual arrogance. Compassion fatigue.
Do not run from conviction.
Conviction is often proof God still wants you.
The most dangerous heart is not the convicted heart.
It is the comfortable one.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this...
Not to shame them.
But because some people are silently becoming emotionally numb and do not even realize it.
One day many people will realize they were losing their soul long before they lost their reputation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Daniel
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Daniel
Most people know Daniel as the man who survived the lions.
But very few people know what the lions were really doing inside that cave.
And even fewer understand what it cost Daniel long before the stone was rolled over the entrance.
Because the greatest battle in Daniel’s life did not happen in the den.
It happened in silence.
It happened when nobody was watching.
It happened when compromise would have been easier.
And if we are honest… that is where many believers are right now.
Smiling publicly.
Breaking privately.
Surrounded by Babylon.
Trying not to lose God.
Daniel’s story is not a children’s bedtime tale.
It is the biography of a kidnapped young man ripped away from his homeland, stripped from his culture, marched into a pagan empire, and pressured daily to slowly forget the God of Israel.
The Book of Daniel opens with devastating words:
“The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand.” — Daniel 1:2
That single sentence destroys the illusion that Israel merely lost politically.
No.
Judgment had come.
Jerusalem had fallen.
The holy vessels of the Temple were stolen.
The people of God were humiliated.
Babylon did not merely want territory.
Babylon wanted identity.
King Nebuchadnezzar specifically selected gifted young Hebrews to be retrained into Babylonian thinking.
This was psychological warfare.
Spiritual assimilation.
The empire wanted their minds before it wanted their loyalty.
Daniel was likely a teenager.
Imagine the fear.
Imagine hearing foreign languages every day.
Imagine watching pagan rituals surround you constantly.
Imagine wondering if God had abandoned His people forever.
Most people would have spiritually collapsed under that pressure.
Daniel did not.
And here is where the untold story begins.
The Hebrew text of Daniel 1:8 says:
“וַיָּשֶׂם דָּנִיֵּאל עַל־לִבּוֹ”
Transliterated:
“Vayyāśem Dānīyyēl ‘al-libbo.”
Literal translation:
“But Daniel set upon his heart…”
Most English translations simplify it to:
“Daniel resolved.”
But the Hebrew meaning is far deeper.
This was not a casual preference.
This was not temporary motivation.
Daniel placed conviction upon his very heart.
He predetermined obedience before temptation arrived.
That changes everything.
Most believers try to decide whether to obey God in the middle of temptation.
Daniel decided long before the pressure came.
That is why Babylon could rename him but could not redefine him.
Babylon changed his Hebrew name “Daniel” — meaning “God is my judge” — into “Belteshazzar,” a name tied to Babylonian deities.
But heaven never called him Belteshazzar.
God still called him Daniel.
And somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that.
This world may try to relabel you by your addiction.
Your trauma.
Your failure.
Your divorce.
Your depression.
Your past.
Your hidden sin.
But hell does not get final authority over your identity.
God does.
Daniel lived in Babylon.
But Babylon never successfully lived inside Daniel.
That is the difference.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply today.
Because many believers attend church while secretly negotiating with Babylon.
We normalize compromise.
We laugh at conviction.
We silence truth to avoid rejection.
We want heaven without holiness.
We want comfort without surrender.
But Daniel understood something terrifying:
Small compromises eventually create spiritual captivity.
The food offered to Daniel was not merely dietary.
It was covenantal.
The king’s food had likely been dedicated to idols.
To eat from it symbolized participation in Babylon’s spiritual system.
Daniel refused.
Not because vegetables were magically holy.
But because worship mattered.
Obedience mattered.
Holiness mattered.
And what happened next is astonishing.
God honored hidden faithfulness before public miracles ever appeared.
Many people want lion’s den deliverance.
Few people want disciplined obedience.
But the miracle was already happening long before the lions arrived.
Daniel survived Babylon without losing intimacy with God.
That may actually be the greater miracle.
Because Babylon is loud.
Babylon is seductive.
Babylon constantly pressures people to compromise slowly.
Not all at once.
Just little by little.
A little less prayer.
A little less Scripture.
A little more sin.
A little more numbness.
A little more worldliness.
Until eventually people wake up spiritually empty while still pretending everything is fine.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Daniel interpreted dreams because Daniel had already learned how to hear God in private.
One of the most misunderstood moments in Scripture is found in Daniel chapter 2.
Nebuchadnezzar demanded that his wise men not only interpret his dream but also reveal the dream itself.
Impossible.
The Chaldeans answered:
“There is not a man on earth who can meet the king’s demand.” — Daniel 2:10
And they were right.
Humanly speaking.
But Daniel did something different.
He went home.
And he prayed.
The Aramaic text says:
“רָזָא גְלִי לְדָנִיֵּאל”
“Rāzā geli le-Dāniyyēl.”
“The mystery was revealed to Daniel.”
Daniel did not manipulate heaven.
He sought God.
And this generation desperately needs to rediscover the difference between performing spirituality and actually knowing God.
Because public gifting without private prayer eventually collapses.
Daniel’s power came from intimacy.
Not performance.
Not charisma.
Not branding.
Not popularity.
Intimacy.
The same God who revealed mysteries to Daniel still sees hidden tears today.
Still hears exhausted prayers.
Still responds to surrendered hearts.
Some of you have been asking God why you feel spiritually exhausted.
But maybe the better question is:
How much Babylon have we allowed into our minds?
Daniel prayed three times daily even after prayer became illegal.
Think about that.
He already knew the decree had been signed.
He already knew he could die.
Yet Daniel 6:10 says:
“He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.”
“As he had done previously.”
That line is devastating.
Daniel did not suddenly become faithful during crisis.
Crisis revealed the faithfulness he had already built.
