Modern culture celebrates emotional hype.
God honors consistency.
Daniel was probably over eighty years old by the time he entered the lions’ den.
This was not reckless youthful passion.
This was decades of tested obedience.
Decades.
Most people quit too early.
Daniel kept praying through regime changes, cultural collapse, threats, loneliness, exile, and spiritual warfare.
And yes — spiritual warfare.
Because one of the most terrifying passages in Daniel is rarely discussed.
In Daniel chapter 10, an angel explains that the answer to Daniel’s prayer had been delayed because of spiritual conflict.
The text says:
“But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days.” — Daniel 10:13
This reveals something staggering.
There are battles happening beyond what human eyes can see.
Some prayers involve warfare we do not fully understand.
Some delays are not denial.
Some silence is not abandonment.
Daniel fasted and mourned while heaven battled on his behalf.
And somebody reading this has been tempted to give up because you assumed God was ignoring you.
He is not absent.
There are realities beyond what you can currently see.
The Hebrew word often associated with perseverance in these contexts carries the idea of enduring strength under pressure.
Faith is not pretending pain does not exist.
Faith is continuing to seek God while carrying pain.
Then came the lions.
But even here, most people miss the deeper horror.
Ancient Near Eastern lion dens were execution chambers.
The lions were intentionally starved.
The den was designed to erase hope.
Daniel spent an entire night inside a place specifically engineered for death.
And yet Scripture says:
“My God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths.” — Daniel 6:22
The Aramaic phrase “סְגַר פֻּם אַרְיָוָתָא”
“Segar pum aryāvātā.”
Literally means:
“He closed the mouths of the lions.”
Not Daniel.
God.
Daniel’s survival was not self-help.
It was divine intervention.
And this matters deeply because modern culture constantly teaches people to save themselves.
Heal yourself.
Fix yourself.
Redeem yourself.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals humanity’s inability to rescue itself fully.
We need God.
We need grace.
We need mercy.
We need Jesus Christ.
Daniel’s story ultimately points beyond Daniel.
It points to a greater Deliverer.
Jesus also faced an unjust government.
Jesus was also falsely accused.
Jesus was also sealed behind a stone.
And unlike Daniel, Jesus actually entered death fully.
But on the third day, the stone was rolled away.
The Gospel is not merely about surviving lions.
It is about resurrection after judgment.
It is about sinners receiving mercy they did not deserve.
It is about prodigals coming home.
It is about broken people becoming new creations through Christ.
Daniel was faithful.
Jesus was flawless.
And that distinction matters.
Because Daniel still needed grace.
We all do.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek word for “sinned” is:
“ἥμαρτον” (hēmarton)
Which carries the idea of missing the mark.
Humanity was designed for God.
But sin distorted us.
Separated us.
Corrupted us.
Yet Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
And maybe that is why Daniel’s story still wrecks people emotionally.
Because deep down, we know what Babylon feels like.
We know compromise.
We know temptation.
We know exhaustion.
We know hidden battles.
We know what it feels like to smile publicly while privately wondering whether we are spiritually surviving.
But Daniel’s life proves something powerful.
God is able to preserve people even inside hostile environments.
You are not beyond redemption.
You are not too compromised for mercy.
You are not too broken for Christ.
The cross remains sufficient.
The tomb remains empty.
And Jesus Christ is still calling people out of Babylon.
Maybe that is why you were led to read this today.
Not by accident.
Not randomly.
But because somewhere deep inside your spirit, you know God has been confronting you.
Maybe you have been spiritually numb.
Maybe secretly addicted.
Maybe exhausted.
Maybe pretending.
Maybe drifting.
Maybe angry at God.
Maybe carrying hidden shame nobody else knows.
But hear this clearly.
Conviction is not hatred.
Conviction is an invitation home.
The enemy condemns people into hopelessness.
God convicts people toward restoration.
And right now, some people reading this can feel the Holy Spirit pulling on places they buried long ago.
Do not ignore that.
Babylon promises freedom while creating chains.
Jesus calls people into surrender that leads to life.
And if you know someone silently battling compromise, addiction, fear, depression, spiritual numbness, or secret pain… share this with them.
Some people are smiling online while collapsing internally.
One day you will realize the lions were never the greatest danger.
Forgetting God in Babylon was.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are moments in Scripture that seem small at first glance.
paragraphs: There are moments in Scripture that seem small at first glance.

A dinner.
A house.
Two sisters.
Jesus sitting in a living room while ordinary life unfolds around Him.
But underneath that quiet scene in Luke 10 is a war most believers never realize they are fighting.
Not the war between good and evil.
Not even the war between faith and unbelief.

But the war between serving Jesus…
and actually being with Him.

The war between Martha’s movement…
and Mary’s surrender.
And if we are honest, many modern Christians have built entire spiritual lives around avoiding the stillness Mary chose.
The story begins in Luke 10:38–42.
The Greek text opens with this line:
“Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ πορεύεσθαι αὐτούς…”
“Now it happened as they went…”
Jesus enters a village.

The village was Bethany.
A place that would later witness tears, resurrection, perfume poured on feet, and the grief of death itself.

But here…
before Lazarus dies…
before resurrection power shakes the tomb…
Jesus walks into a home.
Luke writes:
“A certain woman named Martha…”
The name Martha comes from the Aramaic “מַרְתָּא” (Marta).

It means:
“lady.”
“mistress of the house.”
And that detail matters deeply.
Because Martha immediately steps into responsibility.

Hosting.
Preparing.
Managing.
Serving.
Everything looked honorable.
Everything looked spiritual.
Everything looked necessary.
And that is what makes this battle so dangerous.
Because the enemy rarely tempts devoted believers away from Jesus through obvious evil first.
Sometimes he distracts them with religious activity that slowly replaces intimacy with Christ Himself.
Luke says Martha was:
“περιεσπᾶτο περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν”

Most English translations say:
“Distracted with much serving.”
But the Greek word here is devastating.
“περιεσπᾶτο” (periespato)

It means:
dragged away.
pulled apart.
drawn in different directions.
This was not simple busyness.
Martha’s soul was being internally torn apart.
And how many believers know that feeling?

Always doing.
Always fixing.
Always producing.
Always carrying.
Always exhausted.
But internally fragmented.

Smiling publicly.
Breaking privately.

Still attending church.
Still posting verses.
Still serving ministries.
But slowly losing the ability to simply sit at the feet of Jesus without anxiety crawling inside their chest.
The tragedy is not that Martha served.
Service is holy.
The issue was that her service became louder than her surrender.
Then Scripture shifts toward Mary.
Luke writes:
“And she had a sister called Mary.”
Mary comes from the Hebrew name “מִרְיָם” (Miryam).

Scholars debate its meaning:
beloved,
rebellious,
bitterness,
wished-for child.

Yet in this moment…
Mary becomes the image of surrendered discipleship.
The text says:

“ἣ καὶ παρακαθεσθεῖσα πρὸς τοὺς πόδας τοῦ Κυρίου”
“Who also sat beside the feet of the Lord.”
This was not casual posture.
In Jewish culture, sitting at the feet of a rabbi meant discipleship.

Learning.
Receiving.
Remaining.
Mary took the position of a disciple.
And that alone was culturally shocking.
Women were rarely welcomed into formal rabbinical learning spaces in that society.
But Jesus allowed it.
Because the Kingdom of God was already overturning human pride and religious hierarchy.
Mary was not merely listening to Jesus.
She was surrendering herself to Him.
Then comes one of the most revealing phrases in the entire passage.
Luke says:

“ἤκουεν τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ”
“She was hearing His word.”
Not merely hearing sounds.
The Greek tense implies ongoing attention.
She kept listening.

While Martha’s hands were full…
Mary’s heart was open.
And eventually Martha explodes.
Because distracted souls eventually become resentful souls.
That is one of the clearest signs a believer has drifted from intimacy with God.
Resentment.

Toward others.
Toward ministry.
Toward responsibilities.
Toward people who seem “less busy.”
Martha says:

“Κύριε, οὐ μέλει σοι…”
“Lord, do You not care…?”
That sentence is heartbreaking.
Because this is where distraction eventually leads.

A person can serve Jesus so intensely…
that they begin quietly accusing Him of not caring.
Notice the progression.

Distraction became frustration.
Frustration became comparison.
Comparison became accusation.
And hidden beneath all of it was exhaustion.
Martha continues:

“εἰπὲ οὖν αὐτῇ ἵνα μοι συναντιλάβηται”
“Tell her to help me.”
In other words:

“Jesus…
make Mary become more like me.”
That spirit still exists everywhere today.

People angry at those who prioritize prayer.
People uncomfortable with deep intimacy with God.
People who secretly measure spirituality by visible productivity alone.
But then Jesus responds with astonishing tenderness.
“Μάρθα Μάρθα…”
“Martha, Martha…”
In Hebrew thought, repetition carries emotional weight.

“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Moses, Moses.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
It signals deep affection.
Jesus was not condemning Martha.
He loved her.
And that matters because many exhausted believers secretly think Jesus only loves them when they are producing.
But Christ’s love was never earned by performance.
Then Jesus says:
“μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά”
“You are anxious and troubled about many things.”
The word “μεριμνᾷς” means anxious, divided by cares.
Its root implies being mentally pulled apart.

Again…
fragmentation.
The soul split in pieces by worry.
And “θορυβάζῃ” means disturbed, agitated, inwardly noisy.
That is modern Christianity for many people.
Constant inward noise.

Notifications.
Pressure.
Image management.
Endless content.
Ministry branding.
Performative spirituality.
Emotional exhaustion hidden behind inspirational captions.

Many believers are physically near Jesus…
while internally miles away from resting in Him.
Then comes the line that pierces through centuries.
“ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία”
“But one thing is necessary.”
One thing.
Not twenty.
Not endless striving.
Not proving yourself.
One thing.
Jesus continues:

“Μαριὰμ γὰρ τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο”
“For Mary has chosen the good portion.”
The phrase “good portion” carries covenant language.
In the Old Testament, God Himself was often called someone’s “portion.”
Psalm 73:26 in Hebrew says:
“צוּר־לְבָבִי וְחֶלְקִי אֱלֹהִים לְעוֹלָם”
“God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”
Mary was not merely choosing silence over work.
She was choosing God Himself as her inheritance.
That is the battle.
Not laziness versus discipline.
Not responsibility versus irresponsibility.

The real battle is whether Jesus remains the center…
or whether ministry, survival, productivity, and distraction slowly replace Him while still using His name.
Martha’s danger was not wickedness.
It was nearness without surrender.
And that is terrifying because it can happen inside churches every single day.

People preaching without prayer.
Serving without intimacy.
Leading without abiding.
Singing without worshiping.
Posting about Jesus without sitting with Him.
The Greek word for “abide” in John 15 is:
“μένω” (menō)

It means:
remain.
stay.
dwell.
continue.
Not visit occasionally.
Remain.
And modern believers struggle deeply with remaining.

Silence feels uncomfortable.
Stillness feels unproductive.
Waiting feels weak.
But the Kingdom has always functioned differently than the world.
In Hebrew thought, presence mattered more than performance.
That is why Psalm 46:10 says:
“הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים”
“Be still and know that I am God.”

The phrase “הַרְפּוּ” (harpu) literally means:
let go.
release.
stop striving.
Many people cannot hear God clearly because their inner world never becomes quiet enough to recognize His voice.

And eventually…
activity becomes a hiding place.
Some serve constantly because silence would expose how spiritually dry they actually feel.
Some stay endlessly busy because stillness would force them to confront grief, sin, fear, addiction, loneliness, or the emptiness they keep outrunning.
But Mary sat down.
And surrender always begins there.
At His feet.

Not building your own kingdom.
Not curating your image.
Not proving your worth.
Just Jesus.
This is also why Jesus later says in John 6:27:

“μὴ ἐργάζεσθε τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν ἀπολλυμένην”
“Do not labor for food that perishes…”
Christ was constantly redirecting people from temporary obsession toward eternal reality.
Because eventually every accomplishment fades.

Every platform fades.
Every applause fades.
Every earthly identity fades.
But intimacy with Christ remains eternal.
And there is another layer hidden in this story many overlook.
Martha welcomed Jesus into her house.
But Mary welcomed Jesus into her attention.

One can host Him externally…
while resisting Him internally.
That is why surrender feels threatening.
Because true surrender means Jesus has the right to interrupt your pace, your plans, your identity, your ambitions, your habits, your schedule, and even your version of spirituality.
Mary surrendered control.
Martha maintained control.

One rested.
One managed.

One listened.
One performed.

One chose presence.
One chose pressure.
And Jesus said only one was necessary.
Not because service is evil.
But because intimacy must always come first.
Otherwise service eventually becomes self-powered religion instead of Spirit-filled obedience.
This is why so many believers burn out.
They try to carry what only intimacy with Christ can sustain.
The early church understood this deeply.
In Acts 6, when ministry demands increased, the apostles said:
“We will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”
The Greek word for “devote” is:
“προσκαρτερήσομεν”

It means steadfast continuation.
Persistent adherence.
Refusing to drift away.
Prayer was not secondary support work.
It was survival.
Because no public ministry can remain spiritually healthy while private intimacy with God is dying.
And maybe that is the hidden ache in many hearts right now.
Not lack of information.
Not lack of sermons.
Not lack of Christian content.
But lack of communion with Jesus Himself.

Many know about Him…
while rarely slowing down enough to truly be with Him.
And Christ is still speaking the same invitation.
Come sit.
Come listen.
Come rest.
Come surrender.
Not because responsibilities disappear.
But because peace is only found at His feet.

The world teaches:
produce more.

Jesus says:
abide in Me.
The world rewards noise.
God often speaks in whispers.
The world glorifies exhaustion.
Jesus says:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for rest there is:
“ἀναπαύσω”

Refresh.
Restore.
Give intermission from burden.
Not temporary distraction.
True soul rest.
And that rest only comes through Him.

Not success.
Not ministry.
Not productivity.
Not online validation.
Not religious performance.
Only Christ.
Maybe that is why this little story still unsettles hearts thousands of years later.
Because most people see themselves in Martha before they ever become like Mary.
The good news is that Jesus loved Martha enough to confront her gently.
And He still does the same today.

Not to shame exhausted believers…
but to call them back to the “one thing necessary.”
Himself.

If your soul has become noisy…
fragmented…
restless…
numb…
Maybe this is your invitation to stop running for a moment and return to the feet of Christ again.
Not for performance.
Not for appearance.
But for real communion.
Because no amount of serving Jesus can replace actually knowing Him.
And someday, when every distraction dies and eternity stands unveiled before us, the only thing that will matter is whether we truly remained near to Him.

author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Lesson Hidden in the Bronze Serpent
paragraphs: The Untold Lesson Hidden in the Bronze Serpent
Most people read the story of the bronze serpent and stop at the miracle.
Israel sinned.
Venomous serpents entered the camp.
People were dying.
Moses lifted up a bronze serpent.
Whoever looked lived.
But hidden beneath that moment is one of the deepest prophetic revelations in all of Scripture.
Not just about healing.
Not just about judgment.
But about the terrifying reality of sin, the holiness of God, the humiliation of Christ, and the way heaven destroys death through the very image of the curse itself.
This story is far more uncomfortable than most sermons allow it to become.
Because the bronze serpent forces humanity to stare directly at what has poisoned us.
And many people still refuse to look.
In Numbers 21:4–9, Israel was once again complaining against God after deliverance.
The Hebrew text says:
“וַיְדַבֵּר הָעָם בֵּאלֹהִים וּבְמֹשֶׁה”
Vayedabber ha‘am be’Elohim uveMosheh
“Then the people spoke against God and against Moses.”
The word used for “spoke against” carries the sense of hostile accusation, contempt, and rebellion.
This was not frustration.
This was open resistance against the God who rescued them.
Then Scripture says:
“וַיְשַׁלַּח יְהוָה בָּעָם אֵת הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים”
Vayeshalach YHWH ba‘am et hanechashim hasseraphim
“And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people.”
The phrase “fiery serpents” is deeply important.
The Hebrew word is:
“שָׂרָף” — saraph
Plural: seraphim
Most believers immediately recognize “seraphim” from Isaiah 6.
The burning heavenly beings surrounding God’s throne.
But here the word is attached to serpents.
Why?
Because the term points to burning.
Consuming.
Fiery judgment.
The venom burned through the body.
Sin was no longer theoretical.
The poison was now visible.
And this is where the hidden lesson begins.
God did not remove the serpents immediately.
That matters.
Instead, He provided a way to live in the middle of judgment.
Moses is instructed:
“עֲשֵׂה לְךָ שָׂרָף וְשִׂים אֹתוֹ עַל־נֵס”
Aseh lekha saraph vesim oto al-nes
“Make for yourself a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole.”
The word for pole is:
“נֵס” — nes
This word does not merely mean a stick.
It means banner.
Standard.
Something lifted publicly for all to see.
The same root idea later becomes associated with exaltation and visible salvation.
Isaiah uses similar language prophetically concerning the Messiah.
The serpent was lifted high where everyone could see it.
And then comes the shocking command:
“וְהָיָה כָּל־הַנָּשׁוּךְ וְרָאָה אֹתוֹ וָחָי”
Vehayah kol-hanashukh vera’ah oto vachai
“And it shall be that everyone who is bitten, when he looks at it, shall live.”
Not touches.
Not earns.
Not performs.
Looks.
The Hebrew verb:
“רָאָה” — ra’ah
Means more than casual sight.
It carries the idea of perceiving, regarding, fixing attention upon.
Faith-filled recognition.
God was teaching Israel something terrifying about salvation.
Healing would come through looking directly at the image of the curse.
That sounds strange until Jesus Himself explains the meaning.
In John 3:14–15, Jesus says:
“Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, οὕτως ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.”
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō, houtōs hypsōthēnai dei ton Huion tou anthrōpou
“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
This is not accidental symbolism.
Jesus directly connects Himself to the bronze serpent.
And this is where many believers become uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not compare Himself to Moses in this passage.
He compared Himself to the serpent.
Why?
Because on the cross, Christ became the visible bearer of the curse.
Not sinful.
But treated as sin.
2 Corinthians 5:21 says:
“Τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν.”
Ton mē gnonta hamartian hyper hēmōn hamartian epoiēsen
“He made Him who knew no sin to become sin for us.”
Not merely carry sin.
Become sin.
The holy Son stood in the place of poisoned humanity.
Galatians 3:13 deepens this:
“Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα.”
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou genomenos hyper hēmōn katara
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us.”
The serpent represented the curse killing Israel.
Christ took the curse killing humanity.
And heaven’s answer was not to hide the horror.
It was to lift it up publicly.
Roman crucifixion itself was designed around humiliation.
Exposure.
Public shame.
Jesus was not merely executed.
He was displayed.
Just like the bronze serpent.
This is why John uses the Greek word:
“ὑψόω” — hypsoō
Lifted up.
Exalted visibly.
But there is another layer almost nobody talks about.
The bronze serpent itself had no power.
The healing did not come from bronze.
The healing came from trusting the word of God enough to look.
Imagine the scene.
People collapsing.
Bodies burning.
Panic everywhere.
And then comes a command that sounds foolish.
“Look and live.”
Some probably mocked it.
Some probably delayed.
Some probably wanted another method.
Some likely died arguing.
But the ones who looked lived.
That is the Gospel.
Humanity wants self-salvation.
Religion wants performance.
Pride wants control.
But heaven says:
Look to the One who bore the curse.
Live.
Isaiah foresaw this mystery centuries earlier.
Isaiah 45:22 says:
“פְּנוּ־אֵלַי וְהִוָּשְׁעוּ”
Penu elai vehivvashe‘u
“Turn to Me and be saved.”
The act of looking in Scripture is deeply connected to trust, surrender, dependence, and faith.
This is why the enemy constantly distracts humanity.
Because Satan understands something many believers ignore:
Whatever captures your gaze eventually shapes your soul.
Israel was healed when their eyes turned toward God’s provision.
Peter sank when his eyes left Christ.
Lot’s wife died looking backward.
David fell after staring at Bathsheba.
The eyes are gateways of allegiance.
And modern culture is fighting aggressively for human attention.
Infinite scrolling.
Pornography.
Vanity.
Comparison.
Addiction.
Covetousness.
Distraction.
Fear.
The enemy does not need to destroy everyone instantly.
He only needs to redirect their gaze long enough.
But there is still another hidden lesson.
Years later, the bronze serpent itself became an idol.
In 2 Kings 18:4, King Hezekiah destroys it.
The text says:
“וְכִתַּת נְחֻשְׁתָּן”
Vekhittat Nechushtan
“He broke into pieces the bronze serpent.”
Israel had started worshiping the symbol instead of the God who saved them.
This happens constantly in religion.
People worship:
tradition,
buildings,
preachers,
denominations,
rituals,
platforms,
experiences,
while forgetting Jesus Himself.
The serpent was never the Savior.
It pointed to the Savior.
And this exposes a devastating spiritual danger.
Anything God once used can become an idol when people love the instrument more than His presence.
Even ministry.
Even Christian content.
Even theology.
Even gifted leaders.
Some people know sermons better than Scripture.
Some defend traditions harder than they pursue holiness.
Some can debate doctrine but have no intimacy with Christ.
The bronze serpent warns us that even sacred things can become spiritually deadly when disconnected from worship of the living God.
And yet the beauty of the Gospel still shines through this story.
The people who were bitten were the ones invited to look.
Not the perfect.
Not the strong.
Not the morally impressive.
The dying.
The poisoned.
The desperate.
That means the invitation of Christ is for sinners aware of their condition.
The cross only makes sense to people who realize they are dying without Him.
This is why pride is so dangerous.
Pride convinces poisoned people they are healthy.
But conviction is mercy.
When the Holy Spirit exposes sin, He is not trying to destroy you.
He is trying to save you before the poison finishes its work.
Somebody reading this has been trying to numb spiritual venom instead of bringing it into the light.
Hidden lust.
Secret compromise.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
Double life Christianity.
Performing holiness publicly while privately collapsing.
And the Holy Spirit keeps whispering:
Look to Christ.
Not later.
Now.
Because sin always spreads farther than people expect.
The bronze serpent also reveals something profound about God’s justice.
God did not pretend rebellion was harmless.
The serpents were real.
The bites were real.
The deaths were real.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God making a way for guilty people to survive righteous judgment.
That way cost Jesus everything.
The cross was not symbolic pain.
It was wrath absorbed.
Justice satisfied.
Mercy unleashed.
And the invitation remains exactly the same today.
Look and live.
Not look at yourself.
Not look at culture.
Not look at politics.
Not look at human strength.
Look at Christ crucified.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 1:23:
hēmeis de kēryssomen Christon estaurōmenon
“But we preach Christ crucified.”
The Gospel has always offended human pride.
Because salvation comes through surrender, not self-glory.
The bronze serpent humbles humanity.
The cure comes entirely from God.
And there is one final mystery hidden in this story.
Bronze throughout Scripture is repeatedly associated with judgment.
The altar of sacrifice was overlaid with bronze.
The serpent made of bronze symbolized judgment already executed.
In a prophetic sense, the image represented cursed death already condemned before the eyes of the people.
That means when believers look at Christ crucified, they are not staring at defeat.
They are staring at sin already judged.
Death already confronted.
Hell already challenged.
The cross looked like Satan’s victory.
But it became his ultimate defeat.
Colossians 2:15 says Christ:
“ἀπεκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας ἐδειγμάτισεν ἐν παρρησίᾳ.”
apekdysamenos tas archas kai tas exousias edeigmatisen en parrēsia
“He disarmed rulers and authorities and put them to open shame.”
Open shame.
Public defeat.
The enemy thought he was watching the destruction of Jesus.
Instead, he was witnessing the destruction of his own authority.
That is why believers do not merely admire the cross.
We cling to it.
Because the cross is where poisoned sinners become healed sons and daughters.
It is where condemnation meets mercy.
Where wrath meets grace.
Where justice and love embrace without compromising either.
And maybe the deepest untold lesson hidden in the bronze serpent is this:
God often heals people by forcing them to confront the very reality they have spent their lives avoiding.
Humanity avoids sin.
Avoids repentance.
Avoids mortality.
Avoids surrender.
Avoids holiness.
Avoids truth.
But healing begins when people finally look honestly at both their condition and God’s provision.
The Israelites had to acknowledge the poison.
Then they had to look upward.
So do we.
And maybe that is why so many people remain spiritually dying.
Not because Christ is unwilling to save.
But because pride still refuses to look.
Send this to someone who has been spiritually poisoned by shame, addiction, compromise, fear, or hopelessness.
Some wounds only heal when you finally stop hiding the poison.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Jesus Christ
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Jesus Christ
There are parts of Jesus Christ people sing about…
and there are parts people survive because of.
Most people know the cross. Most people know the manger. Most people know the miracles.
But very few truly know the loneliness. The exhaustion. The human tears. The silence between the verses. The hidden suffering that never made it into paintings.
Because the untold story of Jesus was never just about dying for humanity.
It was about loving people who would still reject Him while He was already bleeding for them.
And if we are honest… that part feels personal.
Because some of us have spent our whole lives trying to be loved by people who only loved us when we were useful.
Yet Christ stayed.
Even knowing Judas would kiss Him with betrayal. Even knowing Peter would deny Him three times. Even knowing the crowd screaming “Hosanna” would later scream “Crucify Him.”
He still walked toward the cross.
The world sees nails. He saw names.
Your name.
The Gospel of John tells us something terrifying and beautiful:
“In the beginning was the Word.”
But the Greek text says:
“Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος” (En archē ēn ho Logos)
The word “Λόγος” (Logos) means far more than “Word.”
It means divine expression. Reason. Meaning. The eternal self-revelation of God.
Jesus was not created. He was not merely a prophet. He was not simply a moral teacher.
He was God revealing Himself to a broken world.
John 1:14 continues:
“Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο” (Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto)
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not symbolism. Not metaphor.
Flesh.
The Greek word “σὰρξ” (sarx) means vulnerable human flesh. Weakness. Mortality. Pain-capable humanity.
The Creator entered creation.
Imagine that.
The God who created oceans had to learn how to walk. The God who formed galaxies felt hunger. The God who spoke stars into existence experienced exhaustion.
Jesus did not come pretending to be human.
He became one of us completely.
That is why Hebrews 4:15 says He is able to sympathize with our weaknesses.
The Greek word for sympathize is:
“συμπαθῆσαι” (sympathēsai)
It literally means: “To suffer together with.”
Jesus does not watch your pain from a distance.
He entered it.
Somebody reading this has been smiling publicly while silently collapsing privately.
You know what it feels like to cry without making a sound. To feel abandoned in rooms full of people. To wonder if God still sees you after everything you have done.
But the untold story of Jesus is this:
He moved toward broken people. Not away from them.
Religion in Jesus’ day avoided the unclean. Jesus touched them.
Lepers. Prostitutes. Tax collectors. The demonized. The rejected. The forgotten.
The people society buried emotionally… Jesus resurrected spiritually.
One of the most misunderstood moments in Scripture happens in Gethsemane.
Most people read it too quickly.
Matthew 26:38 says:
“My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death.”
The Greek phrase is:
“περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου” (perilypos estin hē psychē mou)
“Perilypos” means deeply grieved, surrounded by sorrow, crushed emotionally.
Jesus was not emotionally numb.
He felt agony so intense that Luke records His sweat became like drops of blood.
This medical condition is known as hematidrosis. Extreme anguish. Extreme stress.
The Son of God experienced emotional suffering beyond what many people can comprehend.
Why?
Because He was carrying not only the physical terror of crucifixion…
but the full weight of sin.
Every hidden addiction. Every betrayal. Every abortion. Every lie. Every act of hatred. Every secret nobody knows. Every moment humanity chose darkness instead of God.
He carried it.
Isaiah 53 was written centuries before Jesus was born. Yet it describes Him with terrifying precision:
“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew phrase “אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת” (ish mak'obot) means: “A man intimately familiar with pain.”
Not distant from pain. Familiar with it.
Jesus understands trauma. Jesus understands rejection. Jesus understands abandonment. Jesus understands betrayal.
Some of you were taught that God is angry every time you fail.
But the untold story is that Jesus knew every sin you would commit before Calvary… and still chose the nails.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you fixed yourself. Not after therapy. Not after church attendance. Not after becoming morally clean.
While you were still a sinner.
That changes everything.
Because many people think Christianity is about earning love.
The Gospel says: You could never earn what Jesus already paid for.
And yet people still run.
Adam ran in the garden. Jonah ran from calling. Peter ran after failure.
And maybe you have been running too.
Running into distractions. Running into relationships. Running into addictions. Running into achievement. Running into lust. Running into money. Running into numbness.
But eventually every human soul discovers something terrifying:
Nothing in this world can heal what only Christ can resurrect.
Ecclesiastes calls it “hevel” in Hebrew.
“הֶבֶל” (hevel)
Vapor. Breath. Temporary emptiness.
Everything without God eventually slips through human hands.
Careers. Beauty. Status. Money. Applause. Followers. Even relationships.
That ache inside people is not weakness.
It is eternity calling.
Ecclesiastes 3:11 says God placed eternity in the human heart.
You were made for more than survival.
You were made for Him.
And this is where the untold story becomes deeply uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to inspire people.
He came to confront sin.
The first recorded public words of Jesus in Mark’s Gospel are:
“Repent and believe the Gospel.”
The Greek word for repent is:
“μετανοεῖτε” (metanoeite)
It means: “To change the mind so deeply that life changes direction.”
Biblical repentance is not guilt. It is surrender.
Not perfection. Surrender.
Jesus never preached self-improvement.
He preached death to self.
Luke 9:23 says:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.”
Modern culture says: “Follow your heart.”
Jesus says: “Follow Me.”
And sometimes those directions collide violently.
Because the untold story of Jesus includes something modern Christianity often avoids:
Following Christ costs something.
It may cost relationships. Comfort. Popularity. Sin you secretly love. The version of yourself you built without God.
But what He gives in return cannot be bought.
Peace. Forgiveness. Purpose. Eternal life. Transformation. Identity. Freedom.
Real freedom.
Not the world’s version.
The freedom to finally stop pretending.
There is a reason demons trembled around Jesus.
The Kingdom of darkness recognized authority humans could not fully comprehend.
Even the name “Jesus” carries deep meaning.
In Hebrew:
“יֵשׁוּעַ” (Yeshua)
Meaning: “Yahweh saves.”
His very name was a prophecy.
And the cross was not accidental.
Isaiah 53 again says:
“He was pierced for our transgressions.”
The Hebrew word for pierced is:
“מְחֹלָל” (mecholal)
Meaning wounded through, pierced through violently.
Hundreds of years before Roman crucifixion existed… Scripture described the suffering Messiah.
This is not mythology.
The Bible contains historical manuscripts, prophetic consistency, eyewitness testimony, archaeological support, and textual preservation unmatched by ancient literature.
The resurrection itself changed terrified disciples into bold witnesses willing to die proclaiming they saw the risen Christ.
People may die for a lie they think is true.
But people do not willingly suffer torture for something they know they invented.
Something happened.
The tomb was empty.
And history has never recovered from it.
But maybe the most untold part of Jesus’ story is not His death.
It is His patience.
The fact that after everything humanity has done… He is still calling people home.
Even now.
Even after your rebellion. Even after your addiction. Even after your hypocrisy. Even after your hidden life. Even after your bitterness. Even after the nights nobody knows about.
Grace still knocks.
Revelation 3:20 says:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
Not kick down. Knock.
Love does not force surrender.
But eventually every heart answers one way or another.
Some people reading this feel conviction right now.
Not shame. Conviction.
There is a difference.
Shame says: “You are too filthy to come to God.”
Conviction says: “Come home.”
And maybe this article found you during a season where your soul has been exhausted.
Maybe you have money but no peace. Friends but no trust. Entertainment but no joy. Religion but no intimacy with God.
Jesus did not die to make you religious.
He died to reconcile you back to the Father.
The veil tearing in the temple was not random symbolism.
It represented access.
The barrier between holy God and sinful humanity was opened through Christ.
That is why Jesus cried:
“Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai)
“It is finished.”
Not “I am finished.”
“It is finished.”
The debt. The punishment. The payment. The mission.
Completed.
Paid in full.
Somebody needs to hear this clearly:
You are not too far gone.
The thief on the cross had no time for religious performance. No baptism. No years of discipleship. No opportunity to repair his past.
Yet Jesus told him:
“Today you will be with Me in paradise.”
Grace still reaches dying people.
And maybe that is why this story has survived empires, persecution, mockery, intellectual attacks, and centuries of hatred.
Because deep down humanity knows something is missing.
And the empty tomb still whispers hope into hopeless places.
One day every crown will fall. Every nation will fade. Every celebrity will be forgotten. Every empire will collapse. Every human achievement will turn to dust.
But Jesus Christ remains King.
Philippians 2 says:
“At the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
The Greek says:
“ἵνα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ”
Every knee. Not some.
Kings. Atheists. Celebrities. Politicians. Religious leaders. Demons. All creation.
The untold story of Jesus ends where every human story eventually arrives:
At surrender.
Because one day every person will stand before the Christ history tried to reduce into philosophy.
And in that moment nobody will care about followers, wealth, status, beauty, political identity, or public image.
Only one question will matter:
Did you know Him?
Not know about Him. Know Him.
This world is exhausting people.
People are pretending they are okay while spiritually bleeding internally.
And Jesus is still saying:
“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Not temporary escape. Rest.
The kind your soul has been starving for.
And if somebody came into your heart while reading this… share this with them.
And maybe the reason this article shook you… was because part of your soul still remembers it was created for Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Barnabas
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Barnabas
Nobody talks about the men who disappear so someone else can become greater.
Nobody builds monuments for the ones who willingly step out of the spotlight.
We celebrate the apostles who preached to thousands. We quote the bold voices. We remember the miracles. We remember the sermons. We remember the names that shook nations.
But hidden behind one of the greatest missionary movements in human history was a man whose heart looked more like Jesus than most people realize.

A man who gave away his land. A man who defended the rejected. A man who believed in failures. A man who saw potential where others saw danger. A man who was willing to become smaller so Christ could become greater in someone else.
His name was Barnabas.
And most believers have never truly heard his story.
The world celebrates stars. Heaven celebrates sons who strengthen others.
Barnabas first appears in Scripture in a moment most people read too quickly.
Acts 4:36-37 says:

“Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.”
The name Barnabas comes from the Greek:
Βαρναβᾶς (Barnabas)
Luke himself explains its meaning:
υἱὸς παρακλήσεως (huios paraklēseōs)
Literally: “Son of encouragement,” “Son of consolation,” or even, “Son of exhortation.”
The word παράκλησις (paraklēsis) is powerful. It carries the idea of comfort, strengthening, urging forward, helping someone stand again.
This was not a nickname people gave lightly.
His entire life preached encouragement.
And maybe that is exactly why Satan fights encouragement so hard today.

Because discouraged people stop praying. Discouraged people stop believing. Discouraged people isolate. Discouraged people quit churches. Discouraged people abandon callings. Discouraged people slowly stop hearing God.
There are people reading this right now who are physically alive but spiritually exhausted.
You still post smiles. You still answer messages. You still show up at church. But internally? You are tired.
Tired of pretending. Tired of failing. Tired of fighting thoughts nobody knows about. Tired of carrying wounds you never healed from.
And maybe that is why God wanted you to read about Barnabas today.
Because some people carry anointings that do not look dramatic.
Some people are called to strengthen broken souls.
And heaven takes that seriously.
The first shocking thing about Barnabas is this: He was generous before he was famous.
Before influence. Before ministry recognition. Before missionary journeys. Before church history remembered his name.
He surrendered what he owned.
The early church was exploding with need. Widows needed food. Families were struggling. Believers were being persecuted.
And Barnabas sold land.
Not because he was forced. Not because it looked spiritual. Not because cameras were watching.
He simply loved Jesus more than possessions.
That kind of Christianity barely exists anymore.
Modern culture teaches people to protect everything. Protect your image. Protect your platform. Protect your comfort. Protect your money. Protect your future.
But the Gospel teaches surrender.
The Hebrew concept behind sacrificial surrender flows deeply through Scripture. One powerful word is:
חֶסֶד (chesed)
Often translated as: “lovingkindness,” “steadfast love,” “covenant mercy.”
But Hebrew scholars note it carries covenant loyalty expressed through action. Not merely emotion.
Barnabas did not just feel compassion. He embodied covenant love.
And that is uncomfortable.
Because many believers today love inspiration more than sacrifice.
We want the crown without the cross. The resurrection without the death. The influence without the surrender.
But Barnabas understood something eternal: Everything surrendered to Jesus multiplies forever.
Then comes one of the most emotionally powerful moments in the New Testament.
Saul.
The future Apostle Paul.
Before the churches. Before Romans. Before Corinthians. Before miracles. Before missionary journeys.
He was feared.
Christians were terrified of him.
And honestly? For good reason.
Acts 8:3 says Saul was ravaging the church.
The Greek word used is:
ἐλυμαίνετο (elymaineto)
It paints the picture of brutal destruction. Savage devastation. Violent ruin.
This was not a harmless skeptic.
He hunted believers. Dragged men and women from homes. Approved executions.
Imagine hearing someone like that suddenly says: “I met Jesus.”
Most people would not believe him.
And the disciples did not.
Acts 9:26 says they were all afraid of Saul.
But then comes one of the greatest acts of spiritual courage in Scripture.
Barnabas stepped forward.
Not Peter. Not James. Not John.
Barnabas.
Acts 9:27:
“But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles…”
That single sentence changed Christian history.
Read it again.
“But Barnabas took him…”
When others kept distance, Barnabas moved closer.
When others saw danger, Barnabas saw redemption.
When others remembered Saul’s past, Barnabas believed Jesus could rewrite a future.
Do you understand how powerful this is?
If Barnabas had acted like everybody else, Paul may have remained isolated from the church much longer.
Barnabas became a bridge.
And bridges are rarely celebrated.
They are stepped on. Walked across. Used so others can move forward.
Yet without them, people stay separated.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You were there for people during divorce. During addiction. During depression. During panic attacks. During spiritual collapse. During nights nobody saw.
And later? They moved on. Others celebrated them. Others benefited from their healing.
Meanwhile you stayed hidden.
Barnabas understands hidden faithfulness.
God sees it too.
The untold story of Barnabas is not about fame. It is about becoming the kind of person heaven can trust with wounded people.
There is another detail most believers overlook.
Acts 11 describes a powerful revival happening in Antioch. People were turning to Jesus in massive numbers.
Jerusalem sends Barnabas.
Why?
Because mature believers recognized his spiritual character.
Acts 11:24 says:
“For he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
The Greek phrase:
πλήρης πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ πίστεως (plērēs pneumatos hagiou kai pisteōs)
Means he was saturated. Filled. Governed by the Spirit.
Not just emotionally inspired. Not religious externally.
Spirit-filled.
And what did Barnabas do when revival started growing?
He went looking for Saul.
Think about that.
Barnabas could have kept leadership for himself.
He could have protected influence. Protected authority. Protected recognition.
Instead, he traveled to find someone more gifted.
That level of humility is rare.
Especially today.
Modern culture is addicted to being seen.
But Barnabas was addicted to helping others become who God called them to be.
Some believers secretly compete with people they are called to disciple.
Barnabas did the opposite.
He empowered. Strengthened. Released.
And eventually something astonishing happens.
At first Scripture says: “Barnabas and Saul.”
But later it changes.
“Paul and Barnabas.”
The order shifts.
Paul becomes more prominent.
Barnabas decreases from center stage.
And there is no evidence of jealousy.
No public bitterness. No ego war. No insecurity.
That kind of humility can only exist in someone whose identity is rooted in Christ instead of applause.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly warn against pride because pride corrupts worship.
One Hebrew word for pride is:
גָּאוֹן (ga’on)
It carries the idea of exaltation, arrogance, self-elevation.
Barnabas resisted that spirit.
He was content helping others rise.
Can you imagine how many churches would heal if believers stopped competing?
How many ministries would flourish if leaders genuinely celebrated other people’s growth?
How many broken Christians would recover if someone simply believed restoration was possible?
Barnabas understood something modern Christianity desperately needs again: Encouragement is spiritual warfare.
The enemy wants isolation. Jesus builds family.
The enemy whispers: “You are finished.”
Barnabas-type believers remind people: “Jesus still redeems.”
The enemy weaponizes shame.
Barnabas weaponized hope.
Then comes another painful chapter.
John Mark.
A young man who abandoned the mission during hardship.
Paul no longer trusted him.
Barnabas did.
Acts 15 reveals a sharp disagreement. So sharp that Barnabas and Paul separated.
Many people quickly side with Paul because Paul wrote much of the New Testament.
But slow down.
Barnabas once again believed someone deserved another chance.
And history suggests Barnabas was right.
Later, Paul himself writes positively about Mark.
Even more powerful, 2 Timothy 4:11 says:
“Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry.”
The rejected young man became useful again.
Because Barnabas invested in failure instead of abandoning it.
Somebody reading this feels disqualified.
You failed morally. Failed spiritually. Failed relationally. Failed privately.
You think your story ended.
But Barnabas’ life screams a truth many churches forget: Failure is not always final when Jesus is involved.
The Gospel is filled with restorations.
Peter denied Christ. Thomas doubted. Mark quit. Paul persecuted believers.
Yet Jesus still transformed them.
The Greek word often translated repentance is:
μετάνοια (metanoia)
It means more than feeling guilty.
It carries the idea of a transformed mind. A turning. A reorientation of the soul toward God.
Christianity is not the worship of perfect people.
It is the surrender of broken people to a perfect Savior.
And Barnabas lived like he truly believed redemption was real.
That is why his story still matters.
Because modern believers are drowning in hidden exhaustion.
Many are secretly wondering:
“Can God still use me?”
Barnabas answers: “Yes.”
“Can broken people recover?”
“Yes.”
“Can failures become fruitful again?”
“Yes.”
“Can Jesus transform someone everybody fears?”
Yes.
That is the Gospel.
Not behavior modification. Not religious performance. Not image management.
Transformation.
Real transformation.
The kind only Christ can produce.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because deep down, many believers know what it feels like to need someone like Barnabas.
Someone who believes God is not finished with them.
And maybe the Holy Spirit is asking a harder question right now:
What if you are called to become that person for someone else?
What if your ministry is not a stage?
What if your ministry is strengthening exhausted souls?
What if heaven measures greatness differently than social media does?
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 23:11:
“The greatest among you shall be your servant.”
The Kingdom does not function like the world.
In the world, people climb over others.
In the Kingdom, people kneel.
Barnabas kneeled.
And heaven remembered.
There are people one encouraging message away from quitting. One prayer away from collapse. One moment away from giving up on faith.
Never underestimate what Spirit-filled encouragement can do.
One conversation changed Saul. One investment restored Mark. One surrendered life strengthened entire churches.
And maybe one act of obedience from you could rescue somebody who is silently drowning.
Some people were sent by God not to shine brighter than everyone else… but to keep others from losing their light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Nabal Refused to Help David
paragraphs: Why Nabal Refused to Help David
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully modern.
Moments where pride speaks louder than compassion.
Moments where wealth hardens the heart.
Moments where someone stands face-to-face with a divine opportunity… and completely misses God.
The story of Nabal is not just about a foolish rich man refusing food to David.

It is the terrifying story of what happens when a person becomes so consumed with self-preservation, ego, control, status, and bitterness that they can no longer recognize the hand of God standing right in front of them.
And if we are honest… many people today are closer to Nabal than they realize.
This story is not just ancient history.
It is a mirror.
A warning.
A prophetic exposure.
And hidden inside this uncomfortable story is one of the deepest revelations about pride, spiritual blindness, selfishness, rebellion, and divine mercy found anywhere in the Old Testament.
The Bible introduces Nabal in 1 Samuel 25.
The Hebrew text says:
"וְהָאִישׁ קָשֶׁה וְרַע מַעֲלָלִים"
Transliteration:
"Veha’ish qasheh vera ma'alalim"
Literal translation:
"The man was harsh and evil in his dealings."
(1 Samuel 25:3)
The Hebrew word "קָשֶׁה" (qasheh) means hard, stubborn, severe, cruel, difficult.
This was not merely a man with a bad attitude.
This was a man whose heart had become spiritually rigid.
Cold.
Unteachable.
Unmoved.
And Scripture intentionally contrasts him with his wife Abigail.
The text says she was:
"טוֹבַת שֶׂכֶל וִיפַת תֹּאַר"
"Tovat sekel veyifat to’ar"
Meaning:
"Intelligent and beautiful."
(1 Samuel 25:3)
One house.
Two completely different spirits.
One heart hardened by pride.
Another heart guided by wisdom.
David at this point was not yet king publicly enthroned over Israel.
He was hunted.
Exhausted.
Rejected.
Living in caves.
Pursued by Saul.
Carrying a promise from God while simultaneously surviving betrayal, loneliness, and injustice.
And yet despite being under pressure, David and his men protected Nabal’s shepherds in the wilderness.
They acted like a living wall around his servants.
Nabal prospered partly because David restrained violence and protected what belonged to him.
Then came shearing season.
A season of celebration.
Abundance.
Feasting.
Generosity.
David simply requested provisions.
Not as a thief.
Not as an extortionist.
But respectfully.
Humbly.
The Hebrew wording in 1 Samuel 25:8 carries humility many modern readers miss.
David says:
"Tenah-na"
Meaning:
"Please give."
This was not demand language.
It was gracious.
Honorable.
Respectful.
David even called himself Nabal’s “son.”
An expression of humility and peace.
But Nabal answered with contempt.
Mockery.
Dishonor.
And this is where the story becomes terrifyingly relevant.
Nabal said:
"מִי דָוִד וּמִי בֶן־יִשָׁי"
"Mi David umi ben-Yishai?"
Literal translation:
"Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse?"
(1 Samuel 25:10)
At first glance this sounds like a casual insult.
But in Hebrew culture this was deeply intentional dishonor.
Nabal was not ignorant of David’s identity.
Everyone knew David.
The slayer of Goliath.
The warrior.
The anointed future king.
The worshipper.
The giant killer.
The national hero.
Nabal’s question was not lack of information.
It was rejection.
Contempt.
Dismissal.
He was essentially saying:
“David means nothing to me.”
And this is where the spiritual danger intensifies.
Because pride always minimizes what God is doing.
Pride mocks divine calling.
Pride dishonors anointing.
Pride refuses generosity.
Pride becomes blind to grace.
Nabal had wealth.
But no discernment.
Possessions.
But no wisdom.
Success.
But no spiritual vision.
And many people today are the same.
They can recognize business opportunities faster than divine opportunities.
They can detect market shifts but not movements of God.
They know luxury brands but not spiritual authority.
They protect money more fiercely than relationships.
They fear financial loss more than becoming spiritually empty.
Nabal’s real problem was not greed alone.
It was self-exaltation.
The spirit of self-made pride.
The delusion that what he possessed belonged entirely to him.
Yet Scripture quietly reveals the irony.
Without David’s protection, Nabal’s wealth would have been vulnerable.
The very man he dishonored had helped preserve the prosperity he loved.
How many people insult the very people God used to protect them?
How many destroy relationships that carried grace into their life?
How many mock the voices God sent to help them?
How many reject correction because ego is louder than humility?
And then the story shifts violently.
David is enraged.
Deeply enraged.
The rejection triggered something dangerous.
David tells his men to strap on their swords.
Four hundred men prepare for bloodshed.
This moment reveals something painfully human.
Even godly people can respond wrongly when dishonored.
Even anointed people can be tempted toward revenge.
Even future kings can battle emotional reactions.
Scripture never paints its heroes as flawless.
It tells the truth.
Raw truth.
Messy truth.
Human truth.
And this is why the Bible feels alive.
Because it does not read like propaganda.
It reads like reality.
Then Abigail enters the story.
And suddenly wisdom interrupts destruction.
Abigail acts quickly.
Urgently.
Humbly.
She prepares food.
Bread.
Wine.
Sheep.
Grain.
Raisins.
Figs.
Abundance.
Generosity.
Peace offerings.
But more importantly… she brings discernment.
The Hebrew root connected to Abigail’s wisdom points toward insight, understanding, prudence.
She recognized something her husband could not.
David was tied to God’s future.
Nabal saw inconvenience.
Abigail saw destiny.
Nabal saw cost.
Abigail saw covenant.
Nabal saw a man.
Abigail saw God’s hand.
And this becomes one of the deepest lessons in the entire story:
Spiritual wisdom can recognize what pride cannot.
Abigail falls before David.
And her speech is extraordinary.
One of the most powerful speeches spoken by a woman in the Old Testament.
She appeals to David’s conscience.
His calling.
His future.
His relationship with God.
She essentially tells him:
“Do not let this moment stain the future God has prepared for you.”
And David listens.
That matters.
Pride refuses correction.
Wisdom receives it.
David could have ignored her.
Could have justified revenge.
Could have massacred Nabal’s household.
But instead he recognizes the voice of God through Abigail.
This is one reason David remained a man after God’s own heart despite his failures.
He could still repent.
Still listen.
Still soften.
Still yield.
Meanwhile Nabal is inside partying.
Drunk.
Detached.
Blind to the danger surrounding him.
The text says his heart became like stone.
In Hebrew:
"וַיָּמָת לִבּוֹ בְּקִרְבּוֹ וְהוּא הָיָה לְאָבֶן"
"Vayamot libbo bekirbo vehu hayah le’even"
Literal meaning:
"His heart died within him, and he became like a stone."
(1 Samuel 25:37)
Ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal and he died.
This part makes modern readers uncomfortable.
Because we prefer sanitized spirituality.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that persistent pride, arrogance, cruelty, and rebellion are spiritually dangerous.
God is patient.
Merciful.
Compassionate.
But human pride should never mistake divine patience for divine approval.
Nabal had every opportunity to choose humility.
He chose contempt instead.
And perhaps the most tragic part of the story is this:
Nabal had enough wealth to help David easily.
Helping would not have destroyed him.
Generosity would not have impoverished him.
Humility would not have weakened him.
His downfall came from the condition of his heart.
Not the size of the request.
And this reaches directly into modern life.
Some people sabotage marriages because pride refuses apology.
Some destroy friendships because ego refuses vulnerability.
Some reject truth because correction feels offensive.
Some cling to money so tightly they lose compassion entirely.
Some become spiritually numb while appearing externally successful.
A hardened heart is one of the most dangerous conditions a human being can develop.
And the frightening part is that hardness develops slowly.
A little bitterness.
A little arrogance.
A little selfishness.
A little greed.
A little entitlement.
A little spiritual neglect.
Until eventually compassion disappears.
Discernment disappears.
Humility disappears.
And a person can stand directly in front of God’s movement while mocking it.
That was Nabal.
And this story ultimately points beyond David.
It points toward Christ.
Because humanity has often responded to Jesus the same way Nabal responded to David.
Dismissal.
Contempt.
Mockery.
Rejection.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:
"He was despised and rejected by men."
(Isaiah 53:3)
In Greek, the New Testament says:
"ἐξουθενημένος"
"Exouthenemenos"
Meaning:
Despised.
Treated as nothing.
Rejected as insignificant.
Humanity looked at the Son of God and said in essence:
“Who is this?”
The same spirit of pride.
The same blindness.
The same refusal to recognize heaven standing nearby.
Yet unlike Nabal, Jesus responded to rejection with mercy.
The Gospel reveals a shocking contrast.
Where Nabal’s hardness produced death… Christ’s sacrifice produces life.
Where human pride rejected grace… Jesus still stretched out His hands.
Where humanity deserved judgment… Jesus offered forgiveness.
This is why the Gospel is so staggering.
Because God continues offering mercy to people who repeatedly resist Him.
And maybe that is why this story unsettles people so deeply.
Because somewhere inside, many realize:
“I have acted like Nabal before.”
We have all had moments where pride spoke louder than humility.
Moments where selfishness overpowered compassion.
Moments where ego resisted truth.
Moments where spiritual blindness kept us from recognizing God.
But the beauty of the Gospel is this:
Jesus can still soften a hardened heart.
Even now.
No matter how cold someone has become.
No matter how prideful.
No matter how spiritually numb.
Christ still transforms people.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
"I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh."
In Hebrew:
"וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת־לֵב הָאֶבֶן"
"Vahasiroti et-lev ha’even"
"I will remove the stone heart."
Only God can do that.
Only Christ can break spiritual hardness without destroying the person.
Only grace can heal what pride corrupted.
And maybe someone reading this has been carrying hidden hardness for years.
Anger.
Bitterness.
Control.
Greed.
Spiritual arrogance.
Unforgiveness.
Emotional numbness.
Outward success.
Inner emptiness.
But God still calls people back.
Even now.
Even here.
The terrifying thing about Nabal was not merely that he insulted David.
It was that he lost the ability to recognize what truly mattered.
Do not let pride make you spiritually blind.
Do not become so consumed with protecting your ego that you resist God Himself.
Do not become wealthy in possessions while bankrupt in soul.
Do not become externally successful while internally hardened.
And if this story exposed something hidden inside you… do not run from conviction.
Conviction is often mercy in disguise.
Because the heart that still feels conviction has not become completely stone.
Be honest.
This story hits differently when you realize Nabal is not just a character from history.
He is a warning.
A mirror.
And sometimes… a reflection of who we become without God.
Some hearts become stone slowly… one proud decision at a time.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Bartholomew
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Bartholomew
Nobody talks about Bartholomew.
Peter gets the sermons. John gets the intimacy. Paul gets the theology. Moses gets the miracles. David gets the songs. But Bartholomew?
Most Christians could not tell you a single thing he said.
And maybe that is exactly why his story is one of the most terrifying and convicting stories in the entire Gospel narrative.

Because Bartholomew represents the disciple nobody notices. The believer who is hidden. The servant who is forgotten. The Christian who stays faithful even when heaven seems silent and the world never applauds.
His story is not loud. It bleeds quietly.
And if we are honest… most believers know exactly what that feels like.
To pray and feel unseen. To serve and feel forgotten. To love Jesus while secretly wondering if your life even matters.
This article may expose wounds you buried years ago.
But before this ends, you may realize heaven remembers names earth forgets.
And that changes everything.

The disciple we call “Bartholomew” is likely the same man identified elsewhere as Nathanael. The name “Bartholomew” is not actually a personal name in the normal sense. It comes from the Aramaic expression:
“Bar-Talmai”
In Aramaic:
ܒܪ ܬܠܡܝ
Which literally means:
“Son of Talmai.”
This means Bartholomew was likely a family designation, while Nathanael was his personal name.

The Gospel accounts repeatedly pair Bartholomew alongside Philip, while the Gospel of John pairs Nathanael with Philip. This has led many biblical scholars throughout church history to conclude they are the same person.
And the first time we truly meet him… he is deeply skeptical.
John 1:45–46 records:

“Philip found Nathanael and said to him, ‘We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.’ Nathanael said to him, ‘Can anything good come out of Nazareth?’”
In Greek, Nathanael’s response carries a sharper emotional force than many English readers realize.
The phrase:
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
Comes from:
“Ἐκ Ναζαρὲτ δύναταί τι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι;”
The wording carries skepticism, almost disbelief.
Nazareth was obscure. Insignificant. Unimpressive.
Nobody expected Messiah to come from there.
And if we are honest… many people still reject Jesus for the same reason.
He comes wrapped in forms they did not expect.
Too humble. Too ordinary. Too simple. Too broken-looking.
People want a Messiah crowned in visible glory. But God often hides eternity inside things the world overlooks.
Inside mangers. Inside fishermen. Inside rejected people. Inside crosses.
Inside you.
That is why Bartholomew’s story feels painfully personal.
Because he almost missed Jesus due to assumptions.
And some people reading this are doing the exact same thing.
You have already decided what God cannot use. Your past. Your trauma. Your addiction. Your anxiety. Your failures. Your hidden shame.
You have looked at the ruins of your life and whispered:
“Can anything good come from this?”
But heaven specializes in resurrection.
Philip does not argue with Nathanael. He simply says:
“Come and see.”
That sentence still carries power today.
Christianity was never meant to survive merely through debates. Jesus invites people into encounter.
Come and see.
See the grace. See the scars. See the mercy. See the cross. See the empty tomb.
And when Nathanael approaches Jesus, something shocking happens.
Jesus says:
“Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”
John 1:47
In Greek:
“Ἴδε ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν.”
The word “δόλος” (dolos) means deceit, manipulation, hidden falseness.
Jesus immediately identifies Nathanael as spiritually honest.
Not perfect. Honest.
There is a difference.
Some people appear righteous while hiding corruption. Others openly wrestle but refuse to fake devotion.
Jesus sees through both.
And apparently, He loved Nathanael’s honesty.
This destroys the illusion many believers live under.
God is not asking you to impress Him. He is asking you to stop pretending.

Some people attend church every week while spiritually dying behind polished smiles. They know worship lyrics but have forgotten intimacy. They raise hands publicly while privately drowning in lust, bitterness, fear, envy, pride, addiction, secret compromise, and exhaustion.
But Nathanael came honestly. Skeptical. Questioning. Unfiltered.
And Jesus drew him closer.
Somebody reading this needs to hear that.
God can heal the honest sinner faster than the religious actor.
Then Jesus reveals supernatural knowledge.
“Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
John 1:48
At first glance, this sounds simple. But Jewish context makes this moment explosive.
The fig tree symbolized meditation upon the Scriptures, prayer, and seeking God.
Many scholars believe Nathanael had been praying privately. Possibly wrestling with messianic hopes. Possibly crying out for truth. Possibly carrying secret burdens nobody knew.
Yet Jesus saw him.
Not physically. Supernaturally.
And suddenly Nathanael responds:
“Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
This is astonishingly early recognition of Jesus’ identity.
Why?
Because being seen changes people.
Not casually noticed. Deeply seen.
Most humans spend their entire lives starving for that.
Children crave it. Wives crave it. Husbands crave it. The depressed crave it. The anxious crave it. The lonely crave it.
Social media exploded partly because humanity is desperate to be acknowledged.
“See me.” “Notice me.” “Tell me I matter.”
But algorithms cannot heal loneliness. Only God can.
Jesus saw Nathanael beneath the fig tree. And Jesus still sees people hidden beneath silent suffering today.

He sees the believer crying at 2 AM. He sees the exhausted mother. He sees the father silently collapsing under pressure. He sees the addict trying to quit. He sees the church leader losing strength. He sees the teenager battling suicidal thoughts. He sees the secret grief nobody else notices.
You are not invisible to heaven.
And Bartholomew’s story proves one encounter with the real Christ can completely shatter unbelief.
But after this moment… something strange happens.
Bartholomew almost disappears from Scripture.
No famous sermons. No spotlight moments. No long speeches.
Just faithfulness.
And maybe that is where the deepest lesson begins.
Because modern culture worships visibility.
Followers. Platforms. Recognition. Fame. Influence. Metrics. Applause.
But the Kingdom of God measures differently.
Heaven remembers hidden obedience.
Many believers quietly wonder:
“If my life never becomes publicly significant… did it matter?”
Bartholomew answers that question.
Yes.
The Kingdom was built not merely by famous voices. It was built by surrendered lives.

Church history records that Bartholomew carried the Gospel into dangerous territories including parts of India, Armenia, and possibly Arabia. Though some historical details are debated, early traditions consistently describe him as a fearless missionary who suffered brutally for Christ.
One ancient tradition states he was flayed alive.
Skin removed from his body.
Because he would not deny Jesus.
Imagine that.
The forgotten disciple. The quiet disciple. The overlooked disciple.
Died one of the most horrifying deaths imaginable because he refused to betray the Savior who saw him under a fig tree.
This is what modern Christianity rarely confronts.
The Gospel is not merely motivational inspiration. It is surrender.
The early disciples did not follow Jesus for brand expansion. They followed Him unto death.
And still… Bartholomew stayed faithful.
Even when history barely remembered him.
That confronts our generation hard.

Would we still follow Christ if nobody applauded? Would we still obey if nobody reposted us? Would we still stay pure if compromise looked easier? Would we still stand for truth if culture hated us? Would we still preach repentance if it cost popularity?
Bartholomew’s hidden life exposes performative Christianity.
Some people love being seen serving God more than actually serving God.
But heaven sees motives.
The Greek word often used regarding faithful endurance is:
“ὑπομονή” (hypomonē)
Meaning: steadfast endurance, remaining under pressure, unshaken perseverance.
That is Bartholomew.
And maybe that is the kind of Christianity Jesus is calling back in this generation.
Not celebrity Christianity. Cross-carrying Christianity.
Not performance. Presence.
Not image management. Inner transformation.
Not emotional hype without surrender. True repentance.
The terrifying reality is that many people know church culture but do not know Christ.
They know sermons. Not surrender.
They know theology. Not intimacy.
They know Bible quotes. Not holiness.
But Bartholomew encountered Jesus personally. And that encounter became stronger than torture.
That is real faith.
Not convenience. Conviction.
Somebody reading this is exhausted because your Christianity has become external performance instead of relationship.
Jesus did not die merely to make you religious. He died to reconcile you to God.
The Hebrew understanding behind covenant relationship was never merely transactional. It was relational, intimate, binding.
The Hebrew word:
“יָדַע” (yada)
Often translated “to know,” means far more deeply:
To know intimately. To encounter personally. To experience relationally.
God does not merely want humans informed about Him. He wants them reconciled to Him.
And Bartholomew’s life demonstrates what happens when somebody truly encounters Christ.
Everything changes.
Even suffering becomes survivable.
Even obscurity becomes meaningful.
Even death loses ultimate power.
Because resurrection rewrites endings.
That is why the Gospel is not self-help. It is supernatural rebirth.
The same Jesus who saw Nathanael under the fig tree sees you now.
Your compromise. Your fear. Your hidden addictions. Your loneliness. Your exhaustion. Your secret grief. Your numbness. Your hunger for purpose.
And somehow… He still calls people closer.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved. Power to become transformed.
Real grace does not merely comfort sinners. It changes them.
Bartholomew’s story is proof that ordinary people become dangerous when they truly encounter Jesus Christ.
History may ignore them. Heaven will not.
And maybe the greatest tragedy is not being forgotten by people. Maybe the greatest tragedy is spending an entire life applauded by earth while remaining unknown to God.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:23:
“I never knew you.”
In Greek:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Again the language points toward relational knowing. Not surface association.
That should shake every soul reading this.
Christian branding cannot save you. Church attendance cannot save you. Religious performance cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
The crucified Son of God. The risen King. The Lamb who carried sin. The Savior who conquered death.
And He is still calling people today.
Not into fake perfection. Into repentance. Into transformation. Into truth. Into holiness. Into relationship.
Maybe you feel forgotten. Overlooked. Invisible. Unimportant.
So did Bartholomew.
Yet his hidden faithfulness echoes through eternity.
Because heaven measures differently than earth.
The world celebrates platforms. God celebrates surrender.
And maybe tonight somebody needs to stop chasing visibility and start pursuing Jesus again.
Not for influence. For intimacy.
Not for applause. For eternity.
Some moments are heaven knocking.
Heaven still remembers the names earth forgets.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why David Refused to Drink the Water His Men Risked Their Lives For
paragraphs: Why David Refused to Drink the Water His Men Risked Their Lives For
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost unbearable once you truly understand them.
Not because they are complicated.
Because they expose us.
This is one of those moments.
Three exhausted warriors break through enemy lines while death breathes down their necks… just to bring a thirsty king a drink of water.
And when they finally place it in David’s trembling hands…
he refuses to drink it.
At first glance, it almost feels offensive.
Ungrateful.
Confusing.
Even heartbreaking.
But buried inside this story is one of the deepest revelations about worship, sacrifice, leadership, honor, conviction, and the fear of God in the entire Bible.
Most people have read this story.
Very few have actually seen it.
And once you do…
you will never read it the same way again.
The account is found in 2 Samuel 23:13–17.
David is hiding in the cave of Adullam while the Philistines occupy Bethlehem.
The future king of Israel is exhausted.
Worn down.
Surrounded by war.
The shepherd boy who once stood before Goliath is now hunted, burdened, and carrying the crushing weight of leadership.
Then Scripture says:
“David longed and said, ‘Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!’”
The Hebrew wording is breathtaking.
The phrase “David longed” comes from the Hebrew:
וַיִּתְאַוֶּה דָוִד
“Vayyit’avveh David.”
The root word is:
אָוָה (avah)
which means:
to crave, to desire deeply, to long for emotionally.
This was not casual thirst.
This was emotional longing.
Homesickness.
Memory.
Pain.
Bethlehem was not just a location.
It was childhood.
It was simpler days.
It was before betrayal.
Before war.
Before crowns.
Before responsibility crushed his shoulders.
Sometimes people are not thirsty for water.
They are thirsty for peace.
For innocence.
For the feeling of who they used to be before life shattered them.
And suddenly… this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because there are people reading this right now who smile publicly but secretly whisper inside:
“I miss who I used to be.”
You miss sleeping peacefully.
You miss joy.
You miss hope.
You miss praying without feeling numb.
You miss laughing without pretending.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because David’s thirst was not really about water.
It was about the soul.
Then something shocking happens.
Three mighty men hear David’s longing.
He did not command them.
He did not ask them directly.
He simply spoke a desire out loud.
But loyal men hear what casual listeners ignore.
Scripture says they broke through the Philistine camp.
The Hebrew phrase implies violent penetration through enemy resistance.
These men risked torture.
Capture.
Death.
For water.
Not for military victory.
Not for treasure.
Not for promotion.
For water.
Imagine the scene.
The Philistines occupy Bethlehem.
The city gate is heavily guarded.
Every movement could expose them.
Steel clashes.
Dust rises.
Blood spills.
Three men carve their way through enemy soldiers because their king once whispered a longing.
This is loyalty at terrifying levels.
And maybe that alone convicts us.
Because modern culture celebrates convenience.
But covenant loyalty costs something.
These men were willing to bleed for a desire David barely voiced.
And when they finally return…
they place the water before him.
Can you imagine their faces?
Sweat.
Exhaustion.
Adrenaline.
Maybe smiling.
Maybe expecting David to finally drink.
Maybe believing the mission was accomplished.
Then Scripture says something unforgettable.
“But he would not drink of it.”
Everything pauses.
Why?
Why refuse it?
Why reject what cost them so much?
Because David suddenly realizes something terrifying.
This water carries blood on it.
Not literally.
Spiritually.
The men had risked their lives for his craving.
And David understood something many leaders never learn:
you must never consume selfishly what cost others their suffering.
The text says:
“He poured it out to the LORD.”
The Hebrew says:
וַיַּסֵּךְ אֹתָהּ לַיהוָה
“Vayassekh otah l’YHWH.”
The word:
נָסַךְ (nasakh)
means:
to pour out as a drink offering.
This was worship language.
Temple language.
Sacrificial language.
David turns the water into an offering.
Why?
Because he believes only God is worthy to receive something purchased at such cost.
Then David says:
“Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Is this not the blood of the men who went in jeopardy of their lives?”
The Hebrew phrase:
הֲדַם הָאֲנָשִׁים
“Hadam ha’anashim”
Literally:
“The blood of the men.”
David sees beyond the liquid.
He sees sacrifice.
Risk.
Love.
Devotion.
And suddenly the water becomes holy.
This is where the story becomes devastating.
Because most of humanity consumes sacrifices casually.
People destroy faithful spouses who gave them loyalty.
People waste parents who sacrificed everything for them.
People mock pastors who spent years pouring themselves out.
People use friendships until there is nothing left.
People treat Jesus casually while claiming they love Him.
But David trembled at consuming something that cost too much.
And maybe that is the missing fear of God in modern Christianity.
We have become experts at receiving sacrifice without reverence.
We casually drink what heaven paid dearly for.
The cross becomes decoration instead of devastation.
But when you understand Calvary…
when you understand the lashes, the nails, the mocking, the abandonment, the wrath carried by Christ…
you stop treating grace cheaply.
The Greek of John 19:34 says:
ἀλλ’ εἷς τῶν στρατιωτῶν λόγχῃ αὐτοῦ τὴν πλευρὰν ἔνυξεν, καὶ εὐθέως ἐξῆλθεν αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ.
“Blood and water came out.”
Water again.
But this time it flows from the pierced side of Jesus.
And suddenly David’s story becomes prophetic.
David would not drink water purchased by men risking their lives.
