but to finally obey the last thing He already spoke.
That hidden conviction.
That compromise.
That relationship.
That habit.
That delayed surrender.
Because sometimes the breakthrough people are praying for is waiting on the other side of obedience.
And the terrifying thing about delayed obedience…
is that over time it trains the heart to resist conviction itself.
But the mercy of Jesus is still reaching.
Still calling.
Still restoring.
Peter failed terribly.
Yet Christ restored him.
Jonah ran.
Yet God pursued him.
The prodigal rebelled.
Yet the Father waited.
This is the beauty of the Gospel:
Jesus Christ came to save disobedient sinners and give them new hearts.
Not merely forgiven hearts.
New ones.
Ezekiel prophesied this:
“I will remove the heart of stone…”
The Hebrew imagery is breathtaking.
God replacing spiritual deadness with living responsiveness.
That is what true salvation produces.
Not flawless performance.
But growing surrender.
If you feel conviction reading this…
do not run from it.
Conviction is mercy.
It means God is still calling you back before numbness fully hardens the soul.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years asking God for blessings while quietly resisting Him in private.
He already sees it.
The hidden bitterness.
The pornography.
The pride.
The unforgiveness.
The secret compromise.
The double life.
But He also sees the exhaustion behind it.
The shame.
The emptiness.
The constant cycle.
And Christ still stands with nail-scarred hands offering repentance and mercy.
Not condemnation for those who truly turn to Him.
But transformation.
Deep transformation.
The kind religion cannot manufacture.
Because the greatest tragedy is not unanswered prayer.

It is hearing the voice of God repeatedly…
while refusing to obey Him.
And the greatest blessing is not wealth, success, or comfort.
It is becoming a person who can finally say:
“Speak, Lord… Your servant is listening.”
Not merely hearing.
But shamaʿ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There was a time when the Gospel sounded like thunder.
paragraphs: There was a time when the Gospel sounded like thunder.

Not because preachers were louder.
Not because churches were bigger.
But because people trembled under the weight of holiness.
Now much of modern Christianity sounds more like a motivational seminar wrapped in Bible verses.

We have sermons without repentance.
Worship without surrender.
Grace without holiness.
Salvation without lordship.
Churches filled with people who know Christian language but have never truly died to themselves.
And somewhere along the way, many stopped asking a terrifying question:
Have we softened the Gospel to make it more acceptable to a world that still hates the cross?
Jesus never softened it.
Not once.
In fact, the closer crowds got to Him, the harder His words often became.
When thousands followed Him for bread and miracles, He looked at them and said:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.” — Luke 9:23
The word “deny” there is deeply confrontational in the Greek.
ἀπαρνησάσθω — aparnēsasthō
It means to utterly disown, to reject association with self-interest, to renounce oneself completely.
Jesus was not inviting people to “add Him” to their already comfortable lives.
He was calling them to die.

Modern Christianity often says:
“Jesus will improve your life.”

Biblical Christianity says:
“Your old life must be crucified.”
Paul wrote in Galatians 2:20:
“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”
The Greek word for crucified:
σταυρόω — stauroō

Not wounded.
Not inconvenienced.
Executed.
That changes everything.
The modern softened Gospel often removes the offense of sin because sin makes people uncomfortable.
But Scripture never hides humanity’s condition.
The Hebrew Scriptures are painfully honest about the human heart.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.”
The Hebrew phrase:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב — aqob halev
Literally carries the idea of being twisted, crooked, deceptive beyond understanding.

Yet today many messages tell people:
“You’re basically good.”
“Just believe in yourself.”
“God mainly wants your happiness.”
But the Gospel begins with devastating news:
Humanity is separated from God by sin.

Not misunderstood.
Not merely struggling.
Rebellious.
Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek word for sin:
ἁμαρτάνω — hamartanō

To miss the mark.
To fail God’s holy standard.

And the tragedy is deeper than behavior.
Sin is not merely what we do.
It is what we are apart from Christ.
This is why Jesus spoke so directly about repentance.
The modern church often avoids that word because it sounds harsh.
But Jesus preached it constantly.
Matthew 4:17:
“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
The Greek word:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite
It does not mean merely feeling bad emotionally.
It means a complete change of mind resulting in a transformed life.

A turning.
A surrender.
A radical reorientation toward God.

Biblical repentance is not:
“I’m sorry I got caught.”

It is:
“I see my sin for what it truly is before a holy God.”
And this is where many modern presentations collapse.
We preach comfort before conviction.
But in Scripture, conviction came first.

At Pentecost, Peter did not say:
“God has a wonderful plan for your life.”

He declared:
“You crucified the Messiah.”
Acts 2:37 says:
“They were cut to the heart.”
The Greek:
κατενύγησαν τὴν καρδίαν — katenygēsan tēn kardian

Pierced violently inwardly.
Deeply convicted.
The Gospel wounded before it healed.
And that is what much of modern Christianity fears.

Because conviction empties arenas.
Holiness offends consumers.
Truth costs attendance.
Repentance does not market well.
So we create versions of Christianity where nobody feels confronted.

Jesus becomes a life coach.
The cross becomes jewelry.
Sin becomes “brokenness.”
Hell becomes metaphor.
Holiness becomes optional.
Obedience becomes legalism.
But Scripture never speaks this way.
Jesus Himself spoke more about hell than many modern pulpits.
The word He used often was:
γέεννα — Gehenna

A place of judgment.
Not symbolic discomfort.
Not temporary inconvenience.
And yet the same Jesus who warned about judgment also stretched His hands toward sinners with unimaginable mercy.
That is what makes the true Gospel beautiful.
The Gospel is not softened by removing truth.
It becomes beautiful because grace shines brightest against the darkness of what we truly deserved.
The cross only makes sense when sin is seen honestly.
If humanity is merely “slightly flawed,” then Calvary becomes unnecessary.
But if humanity is spiritually dead…
Then the cross becomes everything.
Ephesians 2:1 says:
“And you were dead in your trespasses and sins.”
Dead.

Not sick.
Not bruised.
Dead.
The Greek:
νεκρούς — nekrous
Spiritually lifeless.
And dead people cannot resurrect themselves.
That is why salvation is entirely dependent upon Christ.

Not church attendance.
Not emotional experiences.
Not moral improvement.
Not Christian culture.
Jesus Christ alone.
The Hebrew prophecy in Isaiah 53 revealed this centuries earlier:
“He was pierced for our transgressions.”
The Hebrew word:
מְחֹלָל — mecholal

Pierced through.
Profaned.
Wounded violently.
The Messiah absorbing wrath for sinners.
This is not soft.

This is bloody.
Costly.
Holy.
Terrifying.
Beautiful beyond words.
The early church understood this.
Following Jesus could cost them families, livelihoods, imprisonment, even death.
Today many presentations of Christianity barely cost inconvenience.
But Jesus never hid the cost.
Luke 14:27:
“Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after Me cannot be My disciple.”
Cannot.

Not “might struggle.”
Cannot.

The Gospel invitation is free.
But discipleship costs everything.
And strangely…
That is exactly what makes it powerful.
A watered-down Gospel creates shallow believers because it asks for nothing.
But the true Gospel creates transformed people because it demands surrender to a King.

Not partial surrender.
Not weekend Christianity.
Not religious performance.
Everything.

Mind.
Body.
Desires.
Identity.
Future.
Sin.
Ambition.
Secrets.
Everything laid before Christ.
And here is the miracle:
When people truly encounter the real Gospel, they do not merely become religious.
They become new creations.

Not perfect overnight.
But changed.
The Greek phrase in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
A new creation of an entirely different kind.
That is what modern culture desperately needs.

Not softer sermons.
Not trendier churches.
Not Christianity blended safely into entertainment culture.
People need truth powerful enough to wake dead souls.
The Gospel was never meant to be safe.
It was meant to save.
And salvation only makes sense when people understand what they are being saved from.

Wrath.
Sin.
Judgment.
Eternal separation from God.
And also what they are saved into:

Reconciliation.
Holiness.
Adoption.
Transformation.
Eternal life in Christ.
Romans 1:16 still stands undefeated:
“For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.”
The Greek word for power:
δύναμις — dynamis

Explosive power.
Miraculous force.
Heaven-breaking authority.
But power disappears when truth is diluted.
A Gospel that never confronts sin cannot produce repentance.
And a Gospel without repentance is not the Gospel Jesus preached.
Some people reading this already feel the tension in their chest.

Because deep down…
you know when Christianity has become performance instead of surrender.
You know when worship became emotional entertainment instead of reverence.
You know when sermons comforted you while your hidden sin remained untouched.
You know when you learned church language but stopped trembling before God.

And maybe tonight…
God is exposing something deeper.
Not to destroy you.
To call you back.
The mercy of God is not proven by His willingness to ignore sin.
It is proven by the fact that Jesus Christ absorbed the punishment sinners deserved.
That is why the cross will always offend pride.

Because it declares that humanity was so lost…
the Son of God had to die.

But it also declares that God loved sinners so deeply…
He was willing to come Himself.
This is the Gospel.

Not softened.
Not reshaped for culture.
Not edited for acceptance.
Truth wrapped in mercy.
Holiness meeting grace.
Justice satisfied in Christ.
And maybe the most dangerous thing happening in modern Christianity is not persecution from outside the church…
But dilution from within.
Because Satan does not always destroy truth by removing it completely.
Sometimes he simply softens it enough that nobody is transformed anymore.
And the terrifying thing is this:
Crowds can gather around a version of Jesus while never truly surrendering to the real Christ revealed in Scripture.
Jesus said in Matthew 7:21:
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”
That should shake us.

Not into panic.
But into honest examination.

Have we followed Christ…
or merely a comfortable version of Christianity that asks little and changes nothing?
The true Gospel still saves.

Still transforms addicts.
Still restores marriages.
Still convicts hearts at 2 a.m.
Still breaks chains of pornography, pride, greed, bitterness, and unbelief.
Still raises spiritually dead people into new life.
Jesus Christ has not lost His power.
But many have stopped preaching the fullness of who He truly is.
Not merely Savior.
Lord.
King.
Holy.
Risen.
Returning.
And worthy of absolute surrender.
The world does not need a softer Gospel.
It needs the real one again.

The kind that wounds pride.
Breaks chains.
Exposes darkness.
Leads sinners to repentance.
And leaves people face down before a holy Savior who still changes everything.
Because the cross was never meant to be admired from a distance.
It was meant to become the place where the old you dies.
And Christ becomes everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Emotional Weight of Carrying Goliath’s Armor After David Won
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Weight of Carrying Goliath’s Armor After David Won
The valley had gone silent.
Moments earlier, it sounded like death.
Metal clashing. Breathing shaking. Thousands of soldiers frozen between fear and hope. Philistine mockery echoing through the dust. Israel trembling under forty days of humiliation.
And then suddenly… one stone.
Not an army. Not a strategy. Not Saul’s armor.
One stone.
The giant collapsed.
But almost nobody talks about what happened after.
Because after David cut off Goliath’s head, Scripture quietly says something that carries more emotional and spiritual weight than most people realize:
“וַיִּקַּח דָּוִד אֶת־רֹאשׁ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּי וַיְבִאֵהוּ יְרוּשָׁלָ‍ִם וְאֶת־כֵּלָיו שָׂם בְּאָהֳלוֹ”
Transliteration: “Vayikach David et-rosh haP’lishti vay’vi’ehu Yerushalayim, v’et-kelav sam b’ohelo.”
Translation: “David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.” — 1 Samuel 17:54
His armor.
David carried Goliath’s armor home.
Sit with that for a moment.
The armor that terrified an entire nation. The armor attached to trauma. The armor soaked in intimidation. The armor nobody believed could be defeated.
Now sitting inside the tent of a shepherd boy.
Can you imagine the emotional weight of touching it?
The smell of battle still trapped in the leather. Blood still drying on the metal. The giant’s presence still haunting the silence.
This was not a trophy for David. This was evidence.
Evidence that fear can fall. Evidence that impossible things can bleed. Evidence that God was stronger than what traumatized Israel.
And maybe that is why some of you cannot move forward.
Because even after God gives victory… you still carry emotional armor from old giants.

The abuse. The betrayal. The addiction. The panic attacks. The shame. The manipulation. The rejection. The secret sin. The church hurt. The father wound. The nights you cried silently while pretending you were spiritually strong.
The battle ended. But the armor stayed.
Most Christians celebrate David killing Goliath. Very few understand what it means to carry the remains of what once terrified you.
There are people reading this right now who survived things nobody knows about.
You smile in public. You worship in church. You quote Scripture online. But deep inside, pieces of old battles still sit inside your emotional tent.
And every now and then… you hear the armor move.
A memory. A trigger. A smell. A song. A location. A random conversation.
Suddenly the giant feels alive again.
This is why the story matters. Because Scripture never hides human emotion.
The Bible is not a collection of plastic heroes. It is a revelation of broken people learning to trust a perfect God.
David was courageous. But David was also human.

The Hebrew word used for “armor” here is “כֵּלִים” (kelim). It can refer to articles, weapons, instruments, vessels, or objects connected to warfare and function. This was not merely decorative equipment. These were instruments of intimidation. Tools of oppression. Visible reminders of domination.
David literally brought home the instruments that once psychologically enslaved Israel.
That changes everything.
Because sometimes healing is not pretending the battle never happened. Sometimes healing is placing the evidence of God’s victory where you can remember what He brought you through.
The enemy wanted Israel to believe Goliath was untouchable. Invincible. Unstoppable.
But David dragged the evidence home.
And some of you need to do the same spiritually.
Not to glorify trauma. Not to worship pain. Not to stay emotionally imprisoned.
But to remember: Jesus already defeated what tried to destroy you.
The cross itself is proof.
Rome intended crucifixion to symbolize humiliation and terror. Instead, Christ transformed the symbol of torture into the eternal declaration of redemption.
What hell meant for shame… God turned into victory.
That is why the Gospel is so emotionally overwhelming.
Jesus does not merely remove sin. He transforms the meaning of what wounded you.
The scars remain. But now they testify.
Even the resurrected Christ still carried scars.
“φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε”
Transliteration: “Phere ton daktylon sou hode.”
Translation: “Put your finger here.” — John 20:27
The risen Savior still bore the marks of crucifixion. Not because death won. But because grace rewrote the story.
There are wounds in your life that God may not erase completely on this side of eternity. But He can transform them into living proof that He carried you through hell and did not abandon you there.
Somebody needed to hear that.
Because there are exhausted believers secretly asking: “If God healed me, why do I still feel emotional weight sometimes?”
Because surviving battle changes people.
Even victorious people.
David won publicly. But internally? He still had to process everything.
Nobody throws a stone at a giant without adrenaline. Nobody walks through warfare without emotional consequence. Nobody faces darkness without carrying memories afterward.
And yet modern Christianity sometimes pressures people to heal unrealistically fast.
We celebrate miracles. But we rarely disciple people through emotional aftermath.
David carried armor after victory. Elijah collapsed emotionally after spiritual triumph. Jeremiah wept openly. Peter carried shame after denial. Thomas wrestled with doubt. Paul spoke of affliction.
The Bible never teaches emotional numbness as holiness.
Real faith is not pretending pain never existed. Real faith is continuing to trust God while carrying the memory of what He brought you through.
And this becomes even more powerful when you understand another layer of the story.
David first tried Saul’s armor.
“וַיַלְבֵּשׁ שָׁאוּל אֶת־דָּוִד מַדָּיו”
Translation: “Saul clothed David with his armor.” — 1 Samuel 17:38
But David removed it.
Why?
Because borrowed armor cannot win spiritual battles.
David refused to fight as somebody else.
And some of you are exhausted because you are trying to wear spiritual armor God never assigned to you.
Trying to imitate influencers. Trying to perform Christianity. Trying to sound spiritually impressive. Trying to hide weakness. Trying to look unshakable.
Meanwhile God is asking for honesty.
David fought authentically. Then later carried the evidence of victory personally.
That combination matters.
You cannot defeat giants by pretending.
And maybe that is why this article found you.
Because beneath the worship music and Bible verses… you are tired.
Tired of carrying hidden grief. Tired of fighting temptation. Tired of acting okay. Tired of trying to appear spiritually perfect while silently breaking apart emotionally.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not die only for the version of you people applaud. He died for the exhausted version too.
The ashamed version. The addicted version. The anxious version. The lonely version. The version crying at 2 AM. The version still carrying emotional armor from battles nobody else understands.
That is why the Gospel is not behavior modification. It is resurrection.
The Greek word often used for repentance is “μετάνοια” (metanoia). It means a transformative change of mind and heart. Not merely feeling guilty. Transformation. Reorientation. A turning.
Jesus does not simply improve people. He makes dead things alive.
And some of you have mistaken survival for healing.
You survived the giant. But you still live emotionally chained to the armor.
You still define yourself by what hurt you. Still hear condemnation. Still replay failure. Still believe you are too damaged for deep intimacy with God.
But hear the truth clearly: The giant fell.
The accusation fell. The shame fell. The chains fell. The curse fell. The penalty of sin fell at Calvary.
“Τετέλεσται”
Transliteration: “Tetelestai.”
Translation: “It is finished.” — John 19:30
Not “partially finished.” Not “finished if you become perfect first.” Not “finished once people approve of you.”
Finished.
Paid. Accomplished. Completed.
Jesus carried what you could not.
And maybe the reason this story stays unforgettable is because deep down, we all know what it feels like to carry emotional armor.

Some people carry armor from divorce. Some from pornography. Some from abandonment. Some from childhood trauma. Some from losing someone they loved. Some from abuse inside churches. Some from secret hypocrisy. Some from years wasted in rebellion.
And the terrifying part? Sometimes people become so familiar with the armor that they forget freedom exists.
But David did not keep Goliath alive.
He carried proof that the giant was dead.
That changes the entire meaning.
Your testimony is not evidence that darkness won. Your testimony is evidence that Jesus rescued you from it.
Never let Satan convince you that your scars disqualify you.
Some of the people God uses most powerfully are those who remember exactly what He saved them from.
David never forgot the valley. Paul never forgot grace. Peter never forgot forgiveness. Mary Magdalene never forgot deliverance.
People who have been rescued deeply often worship differently.
Because forgiveness feels personal.
This article is not for people performing religion. This is for people desperate for Jesus.

For the believer hanging on by a thread. For the exhausted mother silently praying through tears. For the man trapped in hidden addiction. For the prodigal wondering if God still wants them. For the Christian leader secretly battling burnout. For the person who feels spiritually numb. For the soul carrying armor from old giants.
Jesus still saves. Still restores. Still heals. Still calls broken people. Still redeems ruined stories.
And maybe tonight… God is asking you to stop staring at the armor and start remembering who defeated the giant.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
And if somebody you love is silently carrying emotional armor from old battles, share this with them.
Because you will need this reminder again.
The armor may still exist… but the giant that wore it is already gone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Drink Alcohol?
paragraphs:
Can Christians Drink Alcohol?
The Question Sitting Quietly at Dinner Tables, Church Pew Rows, Secret Addictions, and Wounded Homes
There are questions believers ask out loud.

And then there are the questions whispered internally while scrolling late at night… while hiding bottles in cabinets… while remembering drunk fathers… while watching Christians argue online with absolute certainty.
“Is drinking alcohol a sin?”
“Can Christians drink wine?”
“Did Jesus actually drink alcohol?”
“Why do some churches condemn it while others celebrate with it?”
“Am I free… or am I slowly dying spiritually without realizing it?”
This conversation has divided families, churches, denominations, ministries, friendships, and consciences for generations.
Some believers grew up hearing alcohol was demonic.
Others grew up watching pastors laugh over wine at dinner.
Some were abused by drunk parents.
Others came to Christ after alcoholism nearly destroyed them.
Some feel condemned for one glass.
Others hide addiction behind the word “freedom.”
And somewhere inside all this noise… there are exhausted believers genuinely trying to honor Jesus Christ.
Not justify sin.
Not weaponize religion.
Just honor Christ.
So let’s remove culture for a moment.
Let’s remove church politics.
Let’s remove pride.
Let’s remove social media theology.
And let’s walk slowly through Scripture.
Because eternity is too serious for emotional opinions.
And freedom without truth eventually becomes bondage.
But legalism without grace becomes another prison too.
The Bible does not ignore alcohol.
It speaks about it constantly.
Honestly.
Directly.
Without manipulation.
Without confusion.
Without modern agendas.
And the answer may confront both sides harder than expected.
The first shock for many Christians is this:
Jesus did not drink grape juice.
The Greek word repeatedly used in the New Testament for wine is “οἶνος” (oinos).
It means fermented wine.
Real wine.
Not symbolic juice.
Not modern revisionism.
Real fermented drink.
At the wedding in Cana, when Jesus turned water into wine, Scripture says:
“Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.” — John 2:10
The Greek phrase “μεθυσθῶσιν” (methysthōsin) comes from a root associated with becoming intoxicated or having drunk abundantly.
The point of the passage is not drunkenness.
The point is quality.
The master of the feast recognized the wine Jesus created was exceptionally good.
That reality makes some believers uncomfortable.
Because many were taught Jesus would never create actual alcohol.
But Scripture says what it says.
And biblical truth cannot survive if we force the Bible to submit to our preferences.
But before someone uses Cana to justify reckless drinking… keep reading.
Because the same Bible that refuses legalistic distortion also refuses fleshly compromise.
The Bible never condemns alcohol itself as inherently sinful.
But it repeatedly and aggressively condemns drunkenness.
There is a difference.
A massive difference.
Ephesians 5:18 says:
“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.”
The Greek word for “drunk” is “μεθύσκεσθε” (methyskesthe).
It means becoming intoxicated, losing sobriety, surrendering control.
The issue throughout Scripture is not merely the presence of wine.
It is surrendering mastery of yourself to something other than God.
That changes the conversation entirely.
Because many believers ask:
“How much can I drink before it becomes sin?”
But Scripture asks a deeper question:
“What is mastering you?”
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
The Greek word for “dominated” is “ἐξουσιασθήσομαι” (exousiasthēsomai).
It means to be brought under the power or authority of something.
That should terrify more people than it does.
Because addiction rarely announces itself loudly in the beginning.
It whispers.
It negotiates.
It comforts.
It slowly becomes necessary.
One drink to relax.
One drink to sleep.
One drink to survive stress.
One drink to numb grief.
One drink to silence loneliness.
And eventually what once felt like freedom becomes chains.
Some of you reading this are not asking a theological question.
You are asking for permission.
And deep down… the Holy Spirit already warned you.
That’s why conviction keeps interrupting your peace.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
The Bible also shows wine being used positively.
Psalm 104:14–15 says God gave wine “to gladden the heart of man.”
Paul even told Timothy:
“Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” — 1 Timothy 5:23
Again, the Greek word is “oinos.”
Fermented wine.
Not fantasy.
Not rewritten history.
But Scripture refuses to romanticize it.
Proverbs speaks with terrifying realism about alcohol abuse.
“Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine.” — Proverbs 23:29–30
Then comes one of the most haunting warnings in all Scripture:
“Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.” — Proverbs 23:31–32
That verse has buried itself inside countless broken testimonies.
People who thought they controlled it.
People who thought addiction only happened to “other people.”
People who slowly lost marriages, ministries, purity, money, credibility, children, and intimacy with God.
Sin rarely looks dangerous at first.
That’s why temptation works.
And alcohol becomes even more serious when we remember this:
The Christian life is not merely about personal liberty.
It is about love.
Romans 14 changes the entire tone of this debate.
Paul explains that even if something is technically permissible, believers should willingly limit freedoms if those freedoms spiritually harm others.
Imagine sitting across from someone rescued from alcoholism.
A person whose childhood was destroyed by drunken rage.
A believer trying desperately not to relapse.
Now imagine carelessly mocking caution as “religious.”
That is not Christian maturity.
That is selfishness disguised as liberty.
Paul says in Romans 14:21:
“It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.”
The Greek word for “stumble” is “προσκόπτει” (proskoptei).
It means causing someone to spiritually fall or strike against something destructively.
That should sober every believer.
Because Christians are not called merely to defend rights.
We are called to protect souls.
And yet another danger exists too.
Legalism.
Some believers condemn anyone who drinks at all as rebellious or compromised.
But Scripture itself does not make that universal prohibition.
When humans add laws God did not give, spiritual pride quietly enters.
And pride can intoxicate a soul faster than wine.
Jesus Himself was falsely accused of being “a glutton and a drunkard” because He spent time eating and drinking with sinners.
Of course the accusation was false.
Christ never sinned.
But notice something powerful:
Religious people often weaponize external appearances while ignoring internal corruption.
Some people never touch alcohol yet remain drunk on arrogance, lust, greed, gossip, rage, or self-righteousness.
Sin is bigger than bottles.
The heart is the real battlefield.
Still… some of you know alcohol is not spiritually safe for you.
Not because drinking automatically condemns you.
But because your flesh cannot handle it wisely.
And wisdom matters.
Deeply.
The Bible never commands Christians to drink.
Never.
So abstinence can be a beautiful, wise, holy decision.
Especially for protecting your testimony, family, mind, or freedom.
And if alcohol repeatedly pulls you toward compromise, temptation, hidden sin, aggression, escapism, or addiction… walking away completely may not be legalism.
It may be survival.
There are believers reading this who secretly cry after nights of drinking.
Not because they lost salvation.
But because they know something unhealthy is growing.
Conviction is not hatred.
Conviction is mercy before destruction.
The Holy Spirit warns because God loves.
And for others reading this, your struggle is different.
You’ve lived under crushing fear.
Constant condemnation.
A belief that one sip makes God disgusted with you.
Listen carefully:
Your righteousness is not built on beverage performance.
Your salvation is not earned through perfect rule-keeping.
You are saved through Jesus Christ alone.
By grace.
Through faith.
The cross is bigger than your confusion.
But grace is never permission to casually flirt with sin.
True grace transforms desires.
True grace produces wisdom.
True grace asks:
“Will this help me love Jesus more?”
That question changes everything.
Not:
“How close can I get to sin?”
But:
“How close can I stay to Christ?”
There is a reason Scripture repeatedly calls believers to sobriety.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.”
The Greek word “νήψατε” (nēpsate) literally means be sober, self-controlled, clear-minded.
Spiritual warfare requires alertness.
And anything consistently dulling spiritual sensitivity deserves serious examination.
Especially in a culture drowning itself in escape.
People today numb everything.
Pain.
Loneliness.
Trauma.
Anxiety.
Regret.
Silence.
And many Christians are not addicted to alcohol itself.
They are addicted to not feeling.
But healing does not happen through numbing.
Healing happens through surrender.
Jesus never promised escape from every storm.
He promised His presence inside them.
Some of you need prayer more than another drink.
Some need community.
Some need repentance.
Some need counseling.
Some need deliverance.
Some need rest.
Some need honesty.
And some need to finally admit:
“This is controlling me.”
You are not alone in this battle.
God often whispers before consequences scream.
Send this to someone wrestling silently.
One day, many people will realize too late that the thing they used to numb pain was quietly numbing their ability to hear God clearly.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 5 Signs You’re in a Waiting Season
paragraphs: 5 Signs You’re in a Waiting Season
There are seasons where heaven feels loud.
Doors open. Prayers get answered quickly. Everything seems aligned.
And then there are seasons that feel painfully different.
The prayers still rise. But the silence grows heavier.
You keep asking God for clarity. For breakthrough. For movement. For healing. For restoration. For purpose.
But instead of acceleration... there is delay.
Instead of certainty... there is stretching.
Instead of arrival... there is waiting.
And if we are honest, waiting can make even strong believers question themselves.
“Did I miss God?” “Did He forget me?” “Am I being punished?” “Why does everyone else seem to move forward while I stay stuck?”
But Scripture reveals something deeply uncomfortable:
God often does His deepest work in hidden seasons.

Before Joseph wore the robe of leadership, he wore chains. Before Moses led nations, he wandered deserts. Before David sat on a throne, he hid in caves. Before Jesus entered public ministry, He spent years in obscurity.
The waiting season is not always rejection. Sometimes it is preparation.
And the terrifying part is this: Preparation rarely feels glorious while you are inside it.
The Hebrew language carries extraordinary depth in understanding biblical waiting.
One of the primary words used for waiting is:
קָוָה (qavah)
This word does not simply mean “to sit passively.”
It carries the idea of tension like a cord being stretched tightly.
Biblical waiting is not inactivity. It is spiritual stretching.
Isaiah 40:31 says:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength.”
The phrase “wait upon” comes from qavah.
The image is not weakness. The image is tension before strengthening.
God stretches people before He strengthens them.
And many believers misinterpret stretching as abandonment.
But what if your delay is not proof God left? What if it is proof He is still shaping you?
Here are 5 signs you may be in a waiting season God is using for something far bigger than you understand right now.
The first sign is that God is removing your dependence on control.
This is one of the hardest things for human beings to endure.
We want timelines. We want guarantees. We want visible progress. We want explanations.
But waiting exposes how addicted we are to control.
Proverbs 3:5 says:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.”
The Hebrew word for trust here is:
בָּטַח (batach)
It means to place full confidence and security in something.
Not partial trust. Not backup-plan trust. Not temporary trust.
Complete dependence.
And sometimes God allows uncertainty because certainty would keep us self-reliant.
You say you trust Him.
But waiting reveals whether your peace depends on God... or on outcomes.
That hurts.
Because many people do not actually want God Himself.
They want immediate relief.
And waiting exposes the difference.
Some of you are exhausted because you are trying to force doors God never told you to open.
You keep pushing. Networking. Manipulating. Panicking. Obsessing.
Meanwhile heaven remains silent.
Not because God hates you.
But because He refuses to let your future be built on flesh-driven striving.
Psalm 27:14 says:
“Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart.”
The phrase “be of good courage” comes from the Hebrew:
חָזַק (chazaq)
It means to grow strong, firm, courageous.
Notice something powerful.
Strength often comes after waiting. Not before.
Some of you keep praying for strength while resisting the very season producing it.
The second sign is that old idols are losing their grip on your heart.
Waiting exposes what you worship.
When distractions disappear... when doors close... when people leave... when achievements stop satisfying... when entertainment no longer numbs the emptiness...
hidden idols begin surfacing.
Sometimes God allows waiting because He is detoxing your soul.
The Greek New Testament often uses the word:
δοκιμάζω (dokimazō)
This word means to test, refine, examine for authenticity.
Just as gold is refined by fire, hearts are refined through testing.
1 Peter 1:7 says:
“That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire...”
Real faith survives fire.
Counterfeit faith survives convenience.
And some people only realize they built their identity on relationships, money, status, appearance, success, or validation when God temporarily removes those things.
That is why waiting feels so emotionally violent sometimes.
God is not only delaying external things.
He is exposing internal attachments.
You thought you were waiting for a relationship.
But God may be healing your fear of loneliness.
You thought you were waiting for ministry.
But God may be purifying your hunger for recognition.
You thought you were waiting for financial breakthrough.
But God may be confronting your dependence on security instead of Him.
The third sign is that your prayer life is becoming more honest.
Waiting destroys superficial Christianity.
When heaven feels silent long enough, performance-based religion starts collapsing.
You stop pretending.
You stop giving polished church answers.
You stop performing spirituality.
And suddenly your prayers sound like David.
Raw. Broken. Desperate.
Psalm 13 begins with:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?”
That does not sound polished.
It sounds human.
And God included it in Scripture.
Why?
Because biblical faith is not pretending pain does not exist.
Biblical faith is bringing pain honestly before God.
The Greek word for prayer used often in the New Testament is:
δέησις (deēsis)
It carries the idea of desperate supplication arising from deep personal need.
Not robotic repetition.
Not performance.
Desperation.
Some of the deepest intimacy with God is born in seasons where nobody else can fix what you are feeling.
And if we are honest... many of us only learned how to truly pray after life shattered our illusions of control.
Some of you reading this have cried in silence recently.
Smiled publicly. Collapsed privately.
You still worship. Still serve. Still show up.
But deep down you are tired.
And maybe nobody around you fully understands the weight you carry.
But God does.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle.”
Think about that.
Scripture presents a God who notices tears.
Not just victories. Not just sermons. Not just platforms.
Tears.
The fourth sign is that God is teaching you endurance instead of emotional impulsiveness.
Modern culture worships immediacy.
Fast success. Fast pleasure. Fast answers. Fast healing. Fast escape.
But spiritual maturity is slow.
Painfully slow sometimes.
Romans 5:3-4 says:
“Tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope.”
The Greek word for patience here is:
ὑπομονή (hypomonē)
This does not mean passive tolerance.
It means steadfast endurance under pressure.
Remaining faithful while carrying weight.
That changes everything.
Because many believers think spiritual maturity means emotional excitement.
But biblical maturity often looks like staying faithful when emotions disappear.
Still praying. Still obeying. Still believing. Still worshipping.
Even while confused.
Anyone can praise God during visible victory.
But worship during silence reveals depth.
The fifth sign is that your identity is being rebuilt in God alone.
This may be the deepest purpose behind waiting seasons.
God strips away false identities.
Some people only know who they are when they are succeeding.
Others only feel valuable when desired by someone.
Others only feel secure when financially stable.
But what happens when all those things disappear temporarily?
Who are you then?
Galatians 2:20 says:
“I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.”
The Greek phrase:
Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι (Christō synestaurōmai)
means “I have been crucified together with Christ.”
Biblical identity requires death before resurrection.
That is the part modern Christianity rarely wants to talk about.
Everybody wants resurrection.
Few people want crucifixion.
But God often uses waiting seasons to kill false versions of ourselves.
The pride. The self-reliance. The image management. The people-pleasing. The hidden addictions. The counterfeit identities.
And yes... that process hurts.
Deeply.
But God does not destroy identities to leave people empty.
He removes false foundations so people can finally become whole.
Some of you have mistaken this season for failure.
But heaven may call it reconstruction.
You are not buried. You are planted.
There is a difference.
A buried thing is forgotten.
A planted thing is preparing for growth nobody can yet see.
And maybe this is why your spirit has felt so conflicted lately.
Part of you wants to trust God.
Another part is terrified the waiting will never end.
That tension is real.
But Scripture never promises that waiting will be comfortable.
It promises God will remain faithful inside it.
Lamentations 3:25 says:
“The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.”
The Hebrew word for soul there is:
נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh)
It refers to the entire inner being.
God is not merely after surface obedience.
He is shaping souls.
And soul-work takes time.
Some prayers are answered quickly.
Others are answered through transformation.
One changes circumstances.
The other changes you.
And sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God immediately removes the storm...
but that He transforms the person walking through it.
Be honest. This hit harder than some people expected.
And if you know someone silently struggling in a waiting season right now, share this with them.
Some people are losing hope privately while appearing strong publicly.
One day you may realize the season that almost broke you was the same season God used to remake you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND SAMSON BREAKING NEW ROPES LIKE THREAD
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND SAMSON BREAKING NEW ROPES LIKE THREAD
There are moments in Scripture that people read too quickly.
Moments so supernatural… so emotionally violent… so spiritually symbolic… that generations reduce them into children’s stories while missing the terrifying reality unfolding underneath.
Samson snapping brand-new ropes like burned thread is one of those moments.
Most people imagine a muscular man flexing his arms.
That is not what happened.
This was not entertainment.
This was not mythology.
This was not a comic-book scene.
This was the collision between covenant power and spiritual compromise.
And hidden inside those ropes is a warning almost nobody talks about.
Because the ropes were never just ropes.
They represented an entire nation trying to restrain what God had anointed.
And maybe that is why this story still feels disturbingly personal.
Because some people reading this are still tied by invisible ropes nobody else can see.
Addiction.
Lust.
Shame.
Fear.
Depression.
Secret compromise.
Church hurt.
The exhaustion of pretending to be spiritually okay.
The unbearable weight of carrying a calling while privately bleeding.
And suddenly Samson’s story stops feeling ancient.
It feels like us.
Judges 15 does not begin in victory.
It begins with betrayal.
Samson had already begun drifting emotionally long before the ropes touched his body.
Sin almost never destroys people instantly.
It slowly numbs discernment.
The Hebrew narrative repeatedly reveals Samson’s weakness for impulsive desire, emotional rage, and compromised relationships. Yet despite his instability, God still used him.
That alone destroys the pride of religious people.
Because many believers secretly think God only works through flawless people.
But the Bible tells the truth about human beings.
Messy.
Conflicted.
Emotionally impulsive.
Wounded.
Contradictory.
Capable of carrying divine purpose while simultaneously battling private weakness.
That is Samson.
And if we are honest… that is many of us.
The Philistines feared Samson because they recognized something supernatural resting on him.
Not even Israel fully understood him.
The tragedy is heartbreaking.
Sometimes enemies recognize God’s power in your life before your own people do.
Judges 15:13 says:
“So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.”
The Hebrew phrase for “new ropes” is:
"בַּעֲבֹתִים חֲדָשִׁים"
Transliterated:
“ba'avotim chadashim”
The word "חֲדָשִׁים" (chadashim) means fresh, new, unused.
These were not weak ropes.
These were not old restraints ready to tear.
The Philistines intentionally chose fresh restraints because they understood Samson’s previous escape.
This time they wanted certainty.
Control.
Finality.
And that is exactly how sin operates.
The enemy never wants partial restraint.
He wants complete captivity.
He wants people spiritually immobilized while still appearing outwardly functional.
Still attending church.
Still posting Bible verses.
Still smiling publicly.
But privately tied.
Bound.
Numb.
Drained.
The deeper tragedy is that Samson allowed himself to be tied.
That detail matters.
The text says the men of Judah bound him themselves.
His own people surrendered him.
That cuts deep.
Because sometimes the greatest emotional wounds do not come from Philistines.
They come from people close enough to know your name.
The people who should have protected you.
Defended you.
Prayed for you.
Covered you.
Instead, they helped tie the ropes.
Some readers know exactly what that feels like.
You survived betrayal that still echoes in your chest years later.
Family betrayal.
Church betrayal.
Friendship betrayal.
Ministry betrayal.
And maybe the hardest part was pretending it did not break you.
But Scripture keeps pulling us deeper.
Because the real explosion happens in Judges 15:14.
“Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him…”
That phrase changes everything.
The Hebrew says:
"וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה"
Transliterated:
“vatitzlach alav Ruach YHWH”
This is not passive inspiration.
The verb “צָלַח” (tsalach) carries the idea of rushing forcefully, overpowering, advancing mightily.
The Spirit of God did not gently encourage Samson.
The Spirit surged upon him with violent divine empowerment.
And suddenly the ropes became powerless.
The text continues:
“…and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.”
The imagery is astonishing.
The ropes did not merely snap.
They disintegrated.
The Hebrew comparison points to flax fibers instantly collapsing under flame.
Fast.
Violent.
Irreversible.
One moment Samson was restrained.
The next moment the restraints ceased to exist.
That is what happens when the Spirit of God touches bondage.
Chains lose authority.
Sin loses dominance.
Darkness loses ownership.
Hell loses its grip.
People love talking about self-improvement.
The Gospel talks about resurrection.
Because human effort can modify behavior.
But only God can destroy chains from the inside.
And this is where the story becomes terrifyingly personal.
Because many believers know what it means to look tied externally while internally praying:
“God… if You do not help me… I will never break this.”
Some struggles are too deep for motivational speeches.
Too deep for discipline alone.
Too deep for image management.
Too deep for pretending.
This is why Romans 8:11 matters so much.
The same Spirit that raised Jesus from the dead still gives life.
Not symbolic life.
Real transforming power.
The Greek word used for Spirit is:
“Πνεῦμα” (Pneuma)
Meaning breath, wind, spirit.
The same divine breath that moved over creation in Genesis is still moving through broken lives today.
And maybe somebody reading this has been surviving spiritually instead of living.
You pray, but you feel exhausted.
You worship, but you feel numb.
You smile around people while privately collapsing.
You keep saying “I’m fine” because explaining the truth feels too heavy.
Samson’s ropes were visible.
Many modern ropes are hidden.
Hidden pornography addictions.
Hidden bitterness.
Hidden self-hatred.
Hidden compromise.
Hidden spiritual fatigue.
Hidden resentment toward God.
And the frightening thing about hidden bondage is how normal it eventually feels.
People adapt to chains.
Until freedom starts feeling impossible.
But Samson’s story reminds us that impossible is not difficult for God.
And yet there is another layer many people miss.
Samson’s strength was never actually his.
That is the entire point.
The story was never glorifying human power.
It was revealing divine empowerment.
This is why Delilah becomes so tragic later.
Because Samson eventually started treating God’s anointing casually.
Familiarity with divine gifts can create spiritual arrogance.
People begin assuming grace will always cover rebellion.
That power will always remain.
That compromise has no consequence.
But Scripture never teaches careless living.
Grace is not permission to drift from God.
Grace is the reason we run back to Him.
The heartbreaking truth is that Samson was strongest physically when he was weakest spiritually.
And many people today are exactly the same.
Successful publicly.
Dying privately.
Applauded outwardly.
Bleeding inwardly.
Functioning externally.
Crushed internally.
The world celebrates image.
God searches the hidden places.
First Samuel 16:7 reminds us:
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
The Hebrew word for heart is:
“לֵבָב” (levav)
Meaning the inner self, mind, will, emotions, desires.
God sees beneath performance.
Beneath filters.
Beneath ministry platforms.
Beneath curated spirituality.
Beneath exhausted smiles.
He sees the real person.
And somehow… He still calls us toward Himself.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus did not come for people pretending to be whole.
He came for the broken.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The chained.
The hiding.
The people silently wondering if they have gone too far.
Luke 4:18 records Jesus declaring:
“He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives.”
The Greek word for liberty is:
“ἄφεσιν” (aphesin)
Meaning release, pardon, deliverance.
Not temporary relief.
Release.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not behavior modification.
It is deliverance through Christ.
And maybe this is why Samson’s ropes still preach centuries later.
Because people are still searching for freedom.
Still searching for peace.
Still searching for healing.
Still searching for hope strong enough to survive the darkness.
Somebody reading this has been carrying silent spiritual exhaustion for years.
You still believe in God.
But you are tired.
Tired of fighting temptation.
Tired of battling anxiety.
Tired of pretending your heart is not heavy.
Tired of feeling spiritually inconsistent.
Tired of secretly fearing you will never truly change.
But the Gospel is not the story of people saving themselves.
It is the story of Christ entering human brokenness.
Jesus stepped into our bondage willingly.
He carried nails so we could lose chains.
He wore a crown of thorns so shame would not own us forever.
He entered death itself and walked out victorious.
And unlike Samson, Jesus never compromised.
Never sinned.
Never drifted.
Never failed.
The perfect Son of God became the final Deliverer humanity needed.
Isaiah 53 still devastates the human heart:
“He was pierced for our transgressions…”
The Hebrew word for pierced:
“מְחֹלָל” (mecholal)
Carries the idea of being wounded through, profaned, pierced violently.
Christ absorbed judgment so mercy could reach sinners.
That is not weak love.
That is terrifyingly powerful love.
And maybe this article found somebody at the exact moment they were about to give up spiritually.
Do not ignore that.
Because sometimes God reaches people through the very thing they almost scrolled past.
Some readers need to stop pretending.
Some need repentance.
Some need healing.
Some need to finally confess what they have hidden.
Some need to return to Jesus after drifting for years.
Some need to forgive.
Some need to believe God still wants them.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because some chains do not break quietly… they burn off when the Spirit of God steps into the fire.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was one of the greatest kings Judah ever had.
paragraphs: He was one of the greatest kings Judah ever had.

A reformer.
A warrior.
A worshipper.
A man who watched God stop an empire with a single night of divine judgment.
And yet…
many believers never realize that the final chapters of King Hezekiah’s life almost dismantled the very legacy he spent decades building.
Not because he stopped believing.
Not because he abandoned God publicly.
But because pride entered quietly after survival.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment in a believer’s life is not the battle…
it’s what happens after God rescues them from it.
The tragedy of Hezekiah is terrifying because it feels so human.

You can pray faithfully for years…
walk in obedience…
fight sin…
serve God sincerely…
and still slowly drift into self-glory without even noticing it.
That is why this story is not ancient history.
It is a mirror.
And if you read this honestly, you may find yourself somewhere inside it.
The Bible says in 2 Kings 18 that Hezekiah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD.” The Hebrew says:

“וַיַּעַשׂ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה”
(Vayya'as hayashar b'einei Adonai)
“He did what was straight/right in the eyes of Yahweh.”
That word “יָשָׁר” (yashar) means upright, level, morally straight.
Hezekiah was not fake righteous.
He was genuinely devoted.

He destroyed idols.
He broke pagan altars.
He restored worship.
He trusted God when Assyria threatened Judah.
Scripture even says:

“After him was none like him among all the kings of Judah.”
(2 Kings 18:5)
Imagine that.
God Himself honoring your faithfulness.
And then came the impossible crisis.
Hezekiah became deathly sick.
Isaiah the prophet entered the room with devastating words:

“Set your house in order, for you shall die.”
(2 Kings 20:1)

No escape.
No optimism.
No earthly hope.
Just death standing at the foot of the bed.
And Hezekiah broke.
Scripture says he turned his face to the wall and wept bitterly.
The Hebrew expression is deeply emotional:

“וַיֵּבְךְּ בְּכִי גָדוֹל”
(Vayevk bechi gadol)
“He wept a great weeping.”
This was not polished religious prayer.
This was ugly crying before God.
And some of you understand that kind of prayer.

The prayer whispered through panic attacks.
The prayer spoken through grief.
The prayer that comes when nobody else can save you.
And God answered him.
Before Isaiah even left the courtyard, God reversed the verdict.
Fifteen more years.

Healing.
Mercy.
More time.
But hidden inside that miracle was the beginning of Hezekiah’s greatest danger.
Because suffering often keeps people dependent on God…
but success can quietly convince people they no longer need Him as desperately.
That is exactly what happened next.
After Hezekiah’s miraculous healing, envoys arrived from Babylon.
At first this seems harmless.

Diplomatic visitors.
Political conversation.
Royal honor.
But Scripture exposes the deeper issue.
2 Chronicles 32:25 says:
“But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done unto him, for his heart was lifted up…”
The Hebrew phrase is chilling:

“גָּבַהּ לִבּוֹ”
(Gavah libbo)
“His heart became high.”
Pride.

Not loud arrogance.
Not public rebellion.
Internal elevation.
The subtle poison of self-exaltation.
And pride almost always enters quietly after answered prayers.

After promotions.
After blessings.
After healing.
After survival.
After success.
After recognition.
When Babylon came, Hezekiah showed them everything.

The silver.
The gold.
The armory.
The treasures.
The kingdom.
Every hidden thing.
Why?
Because pride craves validation.
The text never says Babylon asked to see everything.
Hezekiah volunteered it.
Because pride desperately wants to impress people.
And this is where the story becomes painfully modern.
Some believers begin with deep dependence on God…
but later start building platforms around themselves.

The ministry becomes about image.
The testimony becomes self-centered.
The blessings become performance.
The gifts become ego fuel.
The danger is not always abandoning God publicly.
Sometimes the danger is slowly taking credit for what only God accomplished.
Isaiah confronted Hezekiah afterward.
And the prophecy was devastating.
Everything he proudly displayed would eventually be carried to Babylon.
His descendants would suffer because of it.
The very thing he flaunted became the thing the enemy targeted.
Read that again slowly.

What pride exposes…
the enemy studies.
And some people reading this are exhausted because you have been advertising treasures God never asked you to display.

Not every blessing needs public validation.
Not every victory needs applause.
Not every spiritual moment needs an audience.
Some things die when pride touches them.
This is why Jesus later warned in Matthew 6 about practicing righteousness “to be seen by men.”
In Greek, the phrase is:

“πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι”
(pros to theathēnai)

“To be gazed at.”
“To become a spectacle.”
That spirit still exists today.

Performative Christianity.
Curated holiness.
Public spirituality with private emptiness.
And the frightening part is that Hezekiah probably did not realize how far his heart had drifted.
Because pride rarely announces itself.

It disguises itself as confidence.
Leadership.
Influence.
Success.
Importance.
But eventually God reveals it.
2 Chronicles 32:31 gives one of the most sobering verses in Scripture:
“God left him, to try him, that He might know all that was in his heart.”
Not abandoned permanently.
Tested.
Exposed.
Revealed.
The Hebrew concept behind “try him” carries the idea of proving what is truly inside.
God allowed the hidden condition of Hezekiah’s heart to surface.
And that should terrify every believer who thinks spiritual longevity automatically guarantees spiritual purity.

You can have history with God…
and still need humility.

You can have miracles in your testimony…
and still become vulnerable to pride.

You can build a godly legacy…
and still wound it near the finish line.
That is why Paul later wrote:

“Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.”
(1 Corinthians 10:12)
Because spiritual pride is often strongest in people who think they are beyond it.
But here is what makes this story even more heartbreaking.
Hezekiah’s response after hearing judgment feels shockingly self-focused.
He essentially found comfort in knowing disaster would not happen during his own lifetime.
In other words:
“As long as there is peace and security while I’m alive…”
That response exposes how pride shrinks a person’s spiritual vision.
A once selfless king became inwardly consumed with personal comfort.
And if we are honest…
modern Christianity struggles with this too.
Many people care more about temporary peace than eternal impact.
More about personal comfort than future generations.
More about protecting image than protecting truth.
But the Gospel calls believers higher than self-preservation.
Jesus did not die to produce comfortable Christians.
He died to produce surrendered disciples.
And this is why the end of Hezekiah’s story feels so emotionally heavy.
Because we see ourselves in him.
We know what it feels like to cry desperately for God’s help…
then slowly become less dependent once life improves.
We know what it feels like to seek God intensely during crisis…
then drift during blessing.
We know what it feels like to secretly crave recognition after God uses us.
This article is not about condemning Hezekiah.
It is about warning us.
Because one of Satan’s oldest strategies is this:

If he cannot destroy you through suffering…
he will try to destroy you through success.
And some of you reading this have survived things that should have broken you.

God carried you through depression.
Through addiction.
Through betrayal.
Through sickness.
Through financial collapse.
Through suicidal thoughts.
Through hidden shame.
But now another danger has appeared.
The temptation to slowly forget the desperation that once kept you close to Jesus.
Do not lose your dependency after deliverance.
Do not lose your humility after healing.
Do not lose your reverence after victory.
Because the finish matters too.
Paul said in 2 Timothy 4:7:
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Not just started well.
Finished well.
And maybe that is why this story lingers so painfully in the soul.
Because many people destroy their witness slowly at the end rather than suddenly at the beginning.

A compromised heart.
A growing ego.
A secret pride.
A craving for applause.
Tiny fractures eventually become spiritual collapse.
But there is still hope.
Because the same God who exposed Hezekiah’s pride is the same God who still offers mercy to humbled hearts today.
James 4:6 says:
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
The Greek word for humble is:

“ταπεινός”
(tapeinos)

Lowly.
Dependent.
Brought down before God.
Not self-hating.
Just fully aware that without Christ, we are nothing.
And maybe that is exactly where some readers need to return tonight.
Not to religious performance.
Not to image management.
Not to public appearance.
But back to broken dependence on Jesus.

Back to secret prayer.
Back to repentance.
Back to humility.
Back to surrender.
Because legacies are not preserved by talent.
They are preserved by humility before God.
And maybe the scariest part of Hezekiah’s story is this:
he almost ruined decades of faithfulness in only a few years of pride.
Do not let temporary success corrupt eternal purpose.
Do not let applause become your addiction.
Do not let blessings make you forget the One who gave them.
And if this exposed something hidden in your spirit…
be honest about it.
Some people reading this need to send this to the friend who used to burn passionately for God but slowly became spiritually numb after life improved.
Not to shame them.
To wake them up.
Because some people lose God long before they lose ministry.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Demas did not leave ministry overnight.
paragraphs: Demas did not leave ministry overnight.
That is the part most people never talk about.
Nobody wakes up one morning and suddenly decides they no longer love Jesus.
It happens slowly.
Quietly.
Almost invisibly.

A compromise here.
A wound there.
A disappointment nobody noticed.
A prayer that felt unanswered.
A hidden exhaustion buried beneath public faithfulness.
And eventually…

someone who once stood beside apostles
starts craving the world more than the presence of God.
That was Demas.

Not a random unbeliever.
Not a pagan enemy of the Gospel.
Not an outsider mocking Christianity.
Demas was close.
Dangerously close.
He walked beside the Apostle Paul himself.

He witnessed miracles.
He heard revelation firsthand.
He saw churches planted.
He watched persecution unfold with his own eyes.
And still…
he walked away.
That should terrify every believer who thinks proximity to ministry automatically means intimacy with God.

Because you can stand near anointing…
and still secretly drift.
The Bible mentions Demas only three times.
But those three verses feel like a slow-motion spiritual funeral.
The first mention sounds hopeful.
In Colossians 4:14, Paul writes:
The Greek text says:

“ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς Λουκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς καὶ Δημᾶς.”
(Aspazontai hymas Loukas ho iatros ho agapētos kai Dēmas.)
Demas is there among faithful workers.

Present.
Trusted.
Included.
No warning signs are recorded.

No scandal.
No betrayal yet.
No public collapse.
Just a man standing beside spiritual giants.
Then later, in Philemon 1:24, Paul calls Demas a “fellow worker.”
The Greek phrase:

“Δημᾶς οἱ συνεργοί μου”
(Dēmas hoi synergoi mou.)
“Synergoi.”

Co-laborer.
Partner in ministry.
Worker together with God’s mission.
Demas was not sitting in the back row spiritually disconnected.
He was involved.
Serving.
Building.
Ministering.
And that may be one of the most sobering realities in all Scripture:
You can serve publicly while dying privately.
You can preach sermons while losing your first love.
You can lead worship while secretly becoming numb.
You can build ministries while your soul quietly starves.
Then comes the final verse.
The heartbreaking one.
The verse that echoes like shattered glass through church history.
2 Timothy 4:10:
“For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world…”
The Greek devastates even deeper:

“Δημᾶς γάρ με ἐγκατέλιπεν, ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα.”
(Dēmas gar me enkatelipen, agapēsas ton nyn aiōna.)
“Enkatelipen.”

He abandoned.
Deserted.
Left behind completely.
This was not a scheduling conflict.
Not ministry burnout alone.
Not merely relocation.
Demas deserted Paul.
But the next phrase exposes the true disease:
“Agapēsas ton nyn aiōna.”
“Having loved this present age.”
The word “ἀγαπήσας” (agapēsas) comes from “agapaō.”
Love.

Deep affection.
Devoted attachment.
Treasured desire.
The tragedy is not merely that Demas left ministry.
The tragedy is that something else captured his heart.
The “present world.”
The Greek word “αἰῶνα” (aiōna) means age, system, spirit of the times.
Demas fell in love with the atmosphere of this fallen world.

Its comforts.
Its pleasures.
Its safety.
Its approval.
Its distractions.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so much today.
Because modern Christianity is filled with people trying to love Jesus and the present age at the same time.

We want the cross…
without dying.

We want resurrection…
without surrender.

We want anointing…
without holiness.

We want influence…
without intimacy.

We want heaven eventually…
but the world right now.
And slowly, secretly, quietly…
many hearts are becoming Demas.
The frightening thing about spiritual drift is that it rarely feels dangerous in the beginning.
Hebrews warns repeatedly about hardening hearts.
The Greek word for hardened is “πωρόω” (pōroō).

To become calloused.
Insensitive.
Covered over.
Nobody notices a callous forming at first.
It develops through repetition.

Pressure.
Friction.
Neglect.
And spiritually, that is exactly what happens when believers repeatedly ignore conviction.
At first, sin grieves you.

Then eventually…
it entertains you.

Then later…
it controls you.

Then finally…
it no longer bothers you at all.

That is how people drift from tears at the altar
to numbness in secret.
Demas likely did not plan to abandon Paul when he first joined ministry.
Something happened over time.
Maybe persecution exhausted him.
Maybe prison scared him.
Maybe suffering disappointed him.

Remember:
Paul wrote 2 Timothy from prison.

Cold.
Abandoned.
Awaiting execution.
Following Jesus stopped looking victorious.
It started looking costly.

And many people love a Gospel that shines…
until it bleeds.
Jesus warned about this in the Parable of the Sower.

Some receive the Word with joy.
But when affliction or persecution comes…
they fall away.
The Greek word there is “σκανδαλίζω” (skandalizō).

To stumble.
To become offended.
To turn away in disillusionment.
Sometimes people do not leave God because they stop believing He exists.
They leave because He did not become who they expected Him to be.
The Messiah they imagined was supposed to make life easier.

Instead…
He asked for everything.
And maybe somebody reading this understands that tension more than you want to admit.
You are tired.

You still post Bible verses…
but your soul feels empty.

You still attend church…
but secretly wonder if your fire is dying.

You still smile publicly…
while battling private compromise.

You still call yourself Christian…
but the world has slowly become easier to love than prayer.
If that is you…
hear this carefully:
The story of Demas is not written merely to condemn you.
It is written to warn you before it is too late.
Because the enemy rarely destroys believers suddenly.
He distracts them gradually.

One compromise.
One unchecked appetite.
One neglected prayer life.
One hidden bitterness.
One secret addiction.
One silent offense.
And eventually the soul no longer burns for eternity.
It burns for comfort.
That is why Jesus said:
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Not your church attendance.
Not your Christian vocabulary.
Not your ministry title.
Your treasure reveals your true devotion.

Demas once walked beside Paul…
but his heart belonged somewhere else.
And the terrifying part?
Paul never says Demas stopped believing intellectually.
Only that he loved the present world more.
That may describe millions sitting in churches today.
Not atheists.
Not pagans.

People who still know Christian language
while emotionally belonging to another kingdom.
But there is another side to this story nobody talks about enough:

If Demas drifted…
then so can we.
That realization should destroy spiritual pride.

Peter walked on water…
and still denied Jesus.

Solomon received divine wisdom…
and still fell into idolatry.

Judas preached with the disciples…
and still betrayed Christ.
The human heart is never beyond deception.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
“The heart is deceitful above all things…”
Hebrew:

“עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל”
(‘Aqov halev mikkol.)

Crooked.
Twisted.
Deceptive.
That is why believers must remain close to Jesus daily.
Not yesterday’s intimacy.
Not old encounters.
Not past revelations.
Daily surrender.
Daily repentance.
Daily dependence.
Because drift happens naturally.
Nobody accidentally becomes holy.
And maybe the most painful question in the Demas story is this:
What did Demas trade eternity for?

Comfort?
Safety?
Pleasure?
Acceptance?
Romance?
Money?
Relief from suffering?
Scripture does not say.

Because maybe God intentionally left it unnamed
so every generation could see its own temptations inside the silence.
For some, the “present world” is lust.
For others, ambition.
For others, political identity.
For others, fame.
For others, entertainment.
For others, bitterness.
For others, secret sin nobody knows exists.

Whatever slowly becomes more desirable than Christ…
becomes your “present age.”
And this is why Jesus spoke so radically:
“What shall it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
The Greek word for soul there is “ψυχή” (psychē).
Not merely existence.

The deepest self.
The eternal inner life.

Demas may have gained temporary relief…
but history remembers him as the man who walked away.
Three verses.
That is all Scripture gives him.

Imagine standing beside Paul…
yet becoming remembered for abandoning him.
What a warning.
What a tragedy.

But maybe…
what mercy.

Because God allowed Demas’ story to survive Scripture
so ours does not have to end the same way.
Right now, some people reading this know you are drifting.
You have been feeding your flesh more than your spirit.
Prayer has become occasional.
Conviction has become weaker.
Secret compromise has become easier.
The things that once broke your heart no longer move you.
But if your heart still feels conviction reading this…
there is still hope.
A dead heart does not tremble.
The fact this hurts means God is still calling you back.
The Gospel is not merely about exposing wanderers.
It is about rescuing them.

Peter failed terribly…
yet Jesus restored him.

The prodigal son rebelled openly…
yet the Father ran toward him.
Grace still pursues people who drift.
But repentance cannot wait forever.
One of the most dangerous lies modern believers tell themselves is:
“I’ll come back later.”
But hearts harden.
Appetites deepen.
Chains tighten.

And eventually what once convicted you…
starts defining you.
That is why Scripture says:
“Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
Today.
Not someday.
Today.
Maybe this article exposed something hidden inside you.

Maybe you realized you have been physically near God
while emotionally running from Him.
Maybe you recognized pieces of Demas inside your own life.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Some people do not need another motivational speech.
They need a warning before they become Demas.
One day Demas realized he had walked farther from God than he ever intended.
Do not wait until your soul feels unfamiliar to you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Stephen
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Stephen
The First Christian Martyr Who Saw Heaven Open
Most people remember Stephen for one thing.
He was stoned.
That is usually where the story begins and ends.

A brave man.
A tragic death.
A few verses in Acts.
But Stephen's story is far bigger than his execution.
His story is the story of what happens when an ordinary believer becomes so consumed by Christ that even death loses its power.
It is the story of a man who was not an apostle.
Not one of the Twelve.
Not a famous miracle worker when his journey began.
Not a bestselling author of Scripture.
Stephen was simply a faithful servant.
And yet heaven opened for him in a way that Scripture records for almost nobody else.
His story is not ultimately about dying for Jesus.
It is about seeing Jesus more clearly than everyone around him.
And once you see Christ that clearly, everything changes.
Everything.
Imagine Jerusalem around AD 34–36.
The city is still buzzing from the crucifixion of Jesus.
Rumors are spreading.
People are whispering.
Some claim He rose from the dead.
Others call it blasphemy.
The religious leaders are terrified because the movement they thought they buried is growing faster than ever.
Thousands are becoming followers of Christ.
The early church is exploding.
But growth brings problems.
Widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.
Tensions are rising.
The apostles cannot personally manage every need.
So seven men are selected to serve.
One of them is Stephen.
Acts describes him this way:
"A man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 6:5).
Notice something remarkable.
Before Stephen performs a miracle.
Before he preaches a sermon.
Before he becomes a martyr.
God first notices his character.
The Kingdom of God often promotes people differently than the world.
The world notices charisma.
God notices faithfulness.
The world notices platforms.
God notices obedience.
The world notices influence.
God notices surrender.
Stephen's public ministry began because of private faithfulness.
That pattern has never changed.
The Greek text of Acts 6:5 uses the phrase:

πλήρης πίστεως καὶ Πνεύματος Ἁγίου
(plērēs pisteōs kai Pneumatos Hagiou)
A careful translation is:
"Full of faith and the Holy Spirit."
The word πλήρης (plērēs) means completely filled, saturated, overflowing.
Stephen was not partially devoted.
He was consumed by God.
His life had become a vessel overflowing with Christ.
And people could see it.
Many believers want the power Stephen had.
Few want the surrender Stephen embraced.
Acts 6:8 says:
"And Stephen, full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people."
Notice the order.
Grace first.
Power second.
God's power is never intended to replace God's character.
The Spirit forms holiness before He entrusts influence.
Stephen became dangerous to darkness because heaven had already transformed his heart.
Soon opposition arose.
It always does.
Truth attracts hunger.
But it also exposes pride.
Members of several synagogues began arguing with Stephen.
Acts says they could not withstand his wisdom.
The Greek text says:

οὐκ ἴσχυον ἀντιστῆναι
(ouk ischuon antistēnai)
Meaning:
"They were not strong enough to resist."
Not because Stephen was intellectually superior.
Not because he had better debating skills.
Because truth empowered by the Spirit carries a weight that human arguments cannot overcome.
When God speaks through surrendered people, something happens that logic alone cannot explain.
Unable to defeat him honestly, they turned to false accusations.
The same strategy used against Jesus.
The same strategy often used against God's people throughout history.
Stephen was dragged before the Sanhedrin.
The highest religious court in Israel.
The room was filled with powerful men.
Men who believed they were defending God.
Men who had already rejected God's Messiah.
Men who knew Scripture but missed its Author.
And then something astonishing happened.
Acts 6:15 says:
"They saw that his face was like the face of an angel."
Stephen is standing on trial.
Yet the people accusing him appear more troubled than the man facing death.
Why?
Because peace is one of the strongest evidences of God's presence.
A person controlled by fear cannot radiate heaven.
Stephen did.
Then comes one of the longest sermons in the entire New Testament.
Acts chapter 7.
Many people skip it.
They should not.
It is one of the most important messages ever preached.
Stephen walks through Israel's entire history.
Abraham.
Joseph.
Moses.
The Tabernacle.
The Prophets.
The Temple.
Again and again he shows a devastating pattern.
Israel repeatedly rejected the very people God sent to save them.
Joseph was rejected.
Moses was rejected.
The prophets were rejected.
And ultimately Jesus was rejected.
Stephen's argument is simple.
The problem was never God's faithfulness.
The problem was humanity's resistance.
At the heart of his message stands a powerful phrase.
Acts 7:51.
Stephen declares:
"You stiff-necked people."
The Greek:

σκληροτράχηλοι
(sklērotrachēloi)
The expression comes from Hebrew imagery.
A stiff-necked ox refuses the farmer's guidance.
Stephen is saying:

"You know the Scriptures.
You know the Law.
You know the Prophets.
But your hearts remain resistant to God."
Knowledge without surrender is spiritual danger.
A person can know Scripture and still miss Christ.
The Sanhedrin proved it.
Then Stephen delivers the sentence that enrages them.
Acts 7:52:
"Which of the prophets did your ancestors not persecute?"
The room erupts.
They are no longer hearing a sermon.
They are hearing an indictment.
And deep down they know he is right.
Conviction often feels like attack when pride refuses repentance.
Then comes the moment that changes everything.
Acts 7:55.
"But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God."
Not sitting.
Standing.
This detail matters.
Throughout the New Testament, Jesus is normally described as seated at the Father's right hand.
But here He stands.
Many scholars have noted the uniqueness of this moment.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us why.
But the image is breathtaking.
The King rises for His faithful servant.
The Savior welcomes His witness home.
The One Stephen preached now appears before Stephen's eyes.
The Greek text reads:

θεωρῶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς διηνοιγμένους
(theōrō tous ouranous diēnoigmenous)
Meaning:
"I see the heavens opened."
Not imagined.
Not symbolic.
Opened.
For one brief moment the curtain separating earthly suffering and heavenly reality is pulled back.
Stephen sees what everyone else in the room cannot.
The throne.
The glory.
The risen Christ.
The crowd cannot tolerate it.
They cover their ears.
They rush him.
Drag him outside the city.
Pick up stones.
And begin the execution.
