But this is where Stephen's story becomes astonishing.
Because as stones crush his body, his heart reveals who truly lives within him.
His final words echo another voice.
The voice of Jesus.
Stephen prays:
"Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Then:
"Lord, do not hold this sin against them."
The Greek phrase:

μὴ στήσῃς αὐτοῖς ταύτην τὴν ἁμαρτίαν
(mē stēsēs autois tautēn tēn hamartian)
Meaning:
"Do not charge this sin against them."
Who speaks like that while being murdered?
Only someone transformed by Christ.
The miracle of Stephen is not merely that he died bravely.
The miracle is that he loved radically.
Even at the end.
Especially at the end.
And standing nearby was a young man named Saul.
Watching.
Approving.
Learning.
Perhaps hearing every word.
Perhaps seeing every prayer.
Perhaps unable to forget the face of the man he helped destroy.
The story of Stephen does not end with Stephen.
His death becomes one of the seeds that eventually leads to Saul's conversion.
Saul becomes Paul.
The greatest missionary in Christian history.
One faithful witness helped change the world.
You may never know what your obedience is accomplishing.
Stephen did not see Paul's future.
But God did.
The untold story of Stephen is not really about martyrdom.
It is about vision.
Everyone in that courtroom saw the same circumstances.
Only Stephen saw Jesus.
And what you see determines how you endure.
When you see only your pain, despair grows.
When you see only your enemies, bitterness grows.
When you see only your limitations, fear grows.
But when you see Christ, courage grows.
Hope grows.
Faith grows.
Love grows.
Stephen lost his life.
Yet he gained something infinitely greater.
The final thing he saw on earth was hatred.
The first thing he saw in eternity was Jesus.
And suddenly every stone became insignificant.
Maybe you feel overlooked.
Stephen started as a servant.
Maybe you feel misunderstood.
Stephen was falsely accused.
Maybe you feel attacked for your faith.
Stephen stood alone before powerful opposition.
Maybe you feel exhausted.
Stephen remained full of the Spirit.
His story reminds us that God often does His greatest work through people history barely remembers.
Heaven remembers them.
Jesus sees them.
And eternity will reveal what faithfulness accomplished.
Because in God's Kingdom, success is not measured by popularity.
It is measured by obedience.
And Stephen was faithful until the very end.
The same Jesus who stood to welcome Stephen still welcomes surrendered believers today.
The same Christ who strengthened Stephen still strengthens His people.
The same Lord who opened heaven for Stephen still reigns on the throne.
And one day, every faithful servant will finally see what Stephen saw.
The King.
Standing.
Waiting.
Welcoming.
The stones stopped falling.
But the story never ended.
It was only beginning.
One day every voice that mocked Christ will fall silent, but every eye that longs for Him will finally see Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 5 Subtle Forms of Pride You Might Not Notice
paragraphs: 5 Subtle Forms of Pride You Might Not Notice
There are people who would never cheat on their spouse. Never steal. Never walk into a club. Never touch drugs. Never publicly deny Jesus.
But pride still owns them.
Not loud pride. Not arrogant pride. Not the kind that flexes money or demands attention.
The terrifying kind.

The kind that knows how to wear worship music. The kind that cries during sermons. The kind that serves in ministry. The kind that says “God bless you” while quietly believing it is spiritually superior.
The kind that can sit in church every Sunday while slowly becoming unreachable by conviction.
That is the most dangerous pride of all.
Because hidden pride does not usually feel evil. It feels reasonable. Mature. Defensive. Wise. Even righteous.
And that is why so many believers never notice it growing.
The enemy rarely walks into a Christian’s life screaming rebellion. Sometimes he simply whispers:
“You’re right.” “You deserve better.” “You already know enough.” “You’re more spiritual than them.” “You don’t need correction.”
And suddenly the heart that once trembled before God becomes untouchable.
Scripture warns us about this kind of blindness.
In Proverbs 16:18, the Hebrew says:
“לִפְנֵי־שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן וְלִפְנֵי כִשָּׁלוֹן גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ”
Transliteration: “Lifnei-shever ga’on; velifnei kishalon govah ruach.”
True translation: “Before destruction comes pride, and before stumbling, a haughty spirit.”
The Hebrew word “גָּאוֹן” (ga’on) does not merely mean confidence. It carries the idea of self-exaltation. An inflated elevation of self. A lifting of the heart above where God intended it to stand.
Pride is not just thinking you are better than people. Pride is whenever self rises above surrender.
And some forms are so subtle they hide inside good behavior.
The first subtle form of pride is refusing correction.
Not outwardly. Not aggressively.
You still listen. You nod. You smile.
But internally? You have already decided nobody can really teach you.
You explain away every rebuke. You defend every weakness. You reinterpret conviction into misunderstanding.
The terrifying thing is that spiritually proud people often believe they are spiritually humble.
The Pharisees were not cartoon villains. They were deeply religious. Disciplined. Scripture-memorizing men.
Yet Jesus spoke some of His harshest words toward them.
Why?
Because pride had made them unreachable.
In Luke 18:11, Jesus describes the Pharisee this way:
“Ὁ Φαρισαῖος σταθεὶς πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ταῦτα προσηύχετο…”
Transliteration: “Ho Pharisaios statheis pros heauton tauta proseucheto…”
Literal rendering: “The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed these things toward himself…”
That phrase matters deeply.
Toward himself.
The prayer sounded directed toward God. But heaven heard self-worship.
That is what pride does.
It can turn prayer into admiration of self. Worship into performance. Serving into spiritual vanity.
Some people no longer seek truth. They seek confirmation.
And the moment correction feels offensive instead of refining, pride has already begun building walls around the heart.
The second subtle form of pride is secretly needing recognition.
This one hides inside serving.
You help. You sacrifice. You give. You show up.
But deep down? You feel wounded when nobody notices.
You become discouraged not because God was absent… but because applause was.
Jesus directly confronted this in Matthew 6.
The Greek word He uses repeatedly is:
“ὑποκριτής” (hypokritēs)
Which originally referred to a stage actor. Someone performing a role before an audience.
That changes everything.
Because religious pride often performs spirituality instead of living surrendered.
Some believers are exhausted not because ministry is heavy… but because performance is.
The soul was never designed to survive on human validation.
There are people who post every act of generosity. Every prayer moment. Every worship tear. Every sacrifice.
Not always because they love God deeply. Sometimes because they fear invisibility.
But heaven does not reward performance. Heaven rewards surrender.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:1:
“Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before men to be seen by them.”
The phrase “to be seen” comes from the Greek “πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι” (pros to theathēnai). It literally carries the sense of performing for observation.
Being watched becomes the reward.
That is terrifying.
Imagine losing eternal reward because human attention became enough.
Some people do not serve God. They serve the image of being seen serving God.
And slowly, the heart forgets intimacy while chasing visibility.
The third subtle form of pride is spiritual comparison.
This one destroys churches quietly.
You hear someone preach. And instead of learning, you compare.
You see someone blessed. And instead of celebrating, you compete internally.
You see someone growing. And suddenly insecurity starts disguising itself as discernment.
Pride cannot celebrate what it secretly envies.
The older brother in Luke 15 looked obedient externally. But his heart revealed pride the moment grace touched someone else.
That is one of the clearest signs of hidden pride: resentment when mercy reaches people you do not think deserve it.
The older brother could not rejoice because comparison had poisoned compassion.
There are believers who love grace for themselves but struggle seeing it overflow onto others.
And the worst part? Comparison can disguise itself as spiritual concern.
People will say: “I’m just discerning.”
But sometimes it is jealousy wearing church clothes.
James 3:16 says:
“For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there is disorder and every evil thing.”
The Greek word for selfish ambition is “ἐριθεία” (eritheia). It describes rivalry. Self-seeking competition. A desire to elevate oneself above others.
That spirit destroys unity.
And social media has amplified this temptation massively.
Now believers compare ministries. Followers. Platforms. Views. Influence. Attention.
People no longer ask: “Am I obeying God?”
They ask: “Am I doing better than them?”
That is not Kingdom thinking.
The Kingdom is not a competition.
When one soul comes home, heaven rejoices. Not competes.
The fourth subtle form of pride is refusing dependence on God.
This is the pride that says: “I’ve got this.”
It looks responsible. Strong. Capable.
But underneath it is self-reliance.
And self-reliance is often socially celebrated pride.
There are people who pray less not because they stopped believing in God… but because they started believing too much in themselves.
That is why trials sometimes expose what success concealed.
Success can quietly convince people they no longer need daily dependence.
In John 15:5, Jesus says:
“χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν”
Transliteration: “Chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden.”
True translation: “Apart from Me you are not able to do anything.”
Not little. Not less.
Nothing.
The Greek construction is absolute. Jesus was not exaggerating.
The illusion of independence is one of pride’s favorite disguises.
And sometimes God allows weakness because weakness destroys the lie that we were ever sustaining ourselves.
Paul understood this deeply.
That is why he wrote:
“When I am weak, then I am strong.”
Because weakness can become the doorway back into dependence.
Some people only pray passionately when life collapses. But intimacy was never supposed to be crisis-driven.
The goal was daily surrender.
Daily dependence.
Daily awareness that every breath is mercy.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The fifth subtle form of pride is thinking repentance is mostly for other people.
This one is deadly.
Because the moment conviction stops reaching you, spiritual decay has already begun.
There are believers who still repent over obvious sins… But no longer repent over pride. Harshness. Coldness. Unforgiveness. Self-righteousness. Prayerlessness.
They have become experts at identifying darkness in others while excusing it within themselves.
Jesus warned about this spirit in Matthew 7.
Why do you notice the speck in your brother’s eye while ignoring the plank in your own?
Pride magnifies other people’s failures while minimizing our own.
Humility does the opposite.
The holiest people in Scripture were usually the most aware of their need for mercy.
Isaiah cried: “I am undone.”
Peter cried: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.”
Paul called himself the chief of sinners.
True intimacy with God does not produce arrogance. It produces awe. Conviction. Dependence. Brokenness.
One of the clearest evidences of spiritual maturity is not perfection.
It is remaining teachable before God.
David fell horribly. But the difference between David and Saul was not sinlessness.
It was response.
Saul defended himself. David broke.
And brokenness is where restoration begins.
Psalm 51:17 says:
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.”
The Hebrew word for contrite is “דַּכָּא” (dakka’). It means crushed. Broken down. Shattered.
God is near to hearts that stop pretending.
And maybe that is the real reason hidden pride is so dangerous.
Because pride protects the image while humility exposes the wound.
Pride says: “I’m fine.”
Humility says: “Lord, heal what I keep hiding.”
One heart keeps performing. The other finally surrenders.
And maybe while reading this, the Holy Spirit quietly revealed something you have been defending for years.
Not to shame you.
To free you.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came to resurrect dead hearts.
Even proud ones.
Even religious ones.
Even exhausted ones.
Even yours.
And if you know someone silently battling hidden pride, compromise, performance, burnout, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them.
Some people do not need more motivation. They need honest conviction.
And sometimes we need reminders before the heart hardens.
One day we will realize that the greatest enemy in the room was not always temptation… sometimes it was the version of ourselves that no longer thought we needed mercy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Solomon
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Solomon
There are people who look blessed in public… while privately dying in silence.
People admire their wisdom. Their success. Their influence. Their gifts. Their accomplishments.
But almost nobody sees the war happening behind their eyes.
That was Solomon.
Most people know him as the richest king who ever lived. The wisest man in history. The builder of the Temple. The author of Proverbs. The man who prayed and fire came down from heaven.
But very few people talk about how Solomon slowly became a warning.
Not because he lacked wisdom.
Because he stopped guarding his heart.
And honestly… that might be the most terrifying truth in Scripture.
Because if Solomon could fall while possessing wisdom God Himself gave him… what makes us think we are untouchable?
The untold story of Solomon is not really about a king.
It is about every believer who once burned for God… but slowly drifted while nobody noticed.
And the scariest part? Drift rarely feels dangerous while it is happening.
It feels small. Harmless. Manageable. Explainable.
Until one day your heart no longer trembles in God’s presence.
And that is exactly where Solomon’s tragedy began.
When Solomon first appears in Scripture, he is not introduced as a powerful ruler. He is introduced as a young man overwhelmed by responsibility.
In 1 Kings 3, Solomon stands before God feeling inadequate. Not arrogant. Not prideful. Broken. Dependent.
The Hebrew text says Solomon asked for:
לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ (lev shomea)
A “hearing heart.”
Not merely intelligence. Not intellectual brilliance.
A heart capable of hearing God.
That changes everything.
Because biblical wisdom was never about being smart. It was about staying surrendered.
Modern culture celebrates information. God celebrates obedience.
And God was pleased with Solomon’s request.
So pleased that Scripture says God gave him wisdom unlike anyone before or after him.
People traveled across nations just to hear him speak. Kings feared him. Queens admired him. Entire economies flourished because of him.
He wrote thousands of proverbs. Songs. Scientific observations. Leadership principles. Judgments that stunned nations.
Imagine possessing that level of divine insight.
Imagine hearing God so clearly that entire kingdoms recognized heaven’s hand on your life.
Now imagine losing it.
Not instantly. Slowly.
That is the part many sermons skip.
Solomon’s destruction did not begin with open rebellion. It began with tolerated compromise.
1 Kings 11 says:
“King Solomon loved many foreign women.”
At first glance, people reduce this to romance. But the deeper issue was covenant corruption.
God had already warned Israel’s kings in Deuteronomy 17 not to multiply wives because their hearts would turn away.
And that exact phrase appears later.
“His wives turned away his heart.”
The Hebrew word used for “turned away” carries the idea of bending, stretching, or inclining something away from its intended direction.
Solomon did not wake up one morning hating God.
His heart was slowly redirected.
And that is how spiritual compromise almost always works.
Very few people suddenly abandon God.
Most drift through gradual desensitization.
A little compromise. A little secrecy. A little pride. A little lust. A little self-worship.
And eventually the soul no longer recognizes how far it has wandered.
What makes Solomon’s story devastating is this:
He still looked successful while spiritually collapsing.
That sentence should shake every church.
Because visible success is not proof of God’s approval.
Solomon still had wealth. Influence. Power. Status. Buildings. Public honor.
But internally? Something sacred was dying.
There are people reading this right now who understand exactly what that feels like.
You still smile publicly. Still post online. Still attend church. Still know the right verses. Still look “blessed.”
But secretly? You know your fire has weakened.
And maybe nobody around you notices.
But God does.
That is why Solomon’s story hurts so deeply.
Because it exposes how possible it is to gain the world while starving your soul.
Ecclesiastes may be the clearest window into Solomon’s internal collapse.
This was not written by a man who lacked success.
This was written by a man who had experienced everything the world promises will satisfy you.
Pleasure. Money. Women. Architecture. Gardens. Music. Entertainment. Education. Luxury. Power.
And after consuming all of it… he arrived at one haunting conclusion.
“Vanity of vanities.”
In Hebrew:
הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים (hevel havalim)
The word “hevel” literally means vapor. Mist. Breath. Smoke. Something impossible to hold.
Solomon was saying:
“I chased everything people said would fulfill me… and it disappeared in my hands.”
That is not depression speaking.
That is exposure.
The world keeps promising people satisfaction through accumulation.
More money. More attention. More followers. More lust. More applause. More possessions. More experiences.
But Solomon had more than almost any human in history.
And he still felt empty.
That should terrify every person chasing worldly fulfillment without God.
Because Solomon already tested the experiment for humanity.
And his conclusion was devastating.
Without God, even success becomes exhausting.
Without God, pleasure becomes numbing.
Without God, wealth becomes meaningless.
Without God, accomplishments become temporary monuments over starving souls.
One of the most heartbreaking realities in Solomon’s life is that the very gifts God gave him became dangerous once intimacy with God weakened.
Wisdom without obedience becomes pride.
Influence without holiness becomes corruption.
Success without surrender becomes idolatry.
And many believers are silently experiencing this right now.
Gifted. Talented. Capable. Influential.
But disconnected from the secret place.
The public sees their fruit. God sees their heart.
Jesus later warned about this exact danger.
In Greek, Jesus says:
τί γὰρ ὠφελεῖται ἄνθρωπος (ti gar opheleitai anthropos)
“For what does it profit a man…”
“…to gain the whole world and lose his soul?”
Mark 8:36 was not merely philosophical.
It was prophetic.
Solomon lived it.
He gained almost everything earth could offer.
Yet nearly lost the very thing that mattered most.
His soul.
And maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because Solomon’s story is not ancient history.
It is modern Christianity.

People building platforms while neglecting prayer. People chasing influence while starving spiritually. People desiring visibility more than holiness. People protecting reputation more than intimacy with God.
And slowly… without realizing it… hearts drift.
The frightening part about drift is that it rarely announces itself.
Nobody wakes up planning to become spiritually cold.
It happens through neglect.
One compromised decision at a time.
One tolerated sin at a time.
One prayerless season at a time.
One hidden addiction at a time.
One moment of pride at a time.
Until eventually people know church language… but no longer know God deeply.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because some of you remember when your relationship with Jesus felt alive.
You remember praying with tears. Reading Scripture with hunger. Worshiping with sincerity. Repenting quickly. Feeling conviction deeply.
But somewhere along the journey… life distracted you. Pain hardened you. Sin seduced you. Success blinded you. Exhaustion weakened you.
And now you feel spiritually numb.
Solomon’s story proves something most people desperately need to hear.
Wisdom alone cannot save you.
Knowledge alone cannot protect you.
Ministry alone cannot preserve you.
Only continual surrender keeps the heart alive.
That is why David — despite his catastrophic failures — was described differently.
David repented.
Solomon accumulated.
David broke before God. Solomon drifted away from Him.
One collapsed into repentance. The other slowly decayed into compromise.
And this is where grace enters the story.
Because even inside Ecclesiastes — buried underneath Solomon’s grief and regret — there remains a cry pointing humanity back toward God.
After testing everything under the sun, Solomon finally writes:
That was the conclusion.
Not wealth. Not women. Not achievement. Not applause. Not luxury.
God.
Only God.
The Hebrew word for “fear” here is:
יָרֵא (yare)
It means reverence. Awe. Holy trembling.
The kind of heart posture modern culture desperately tries to erase.
Because the world teaches self-exaltation.
But Scripture teaches surrender.
And maybe Solomon’s greatest contribution was not his wisdom at all.
Maybe it was his warning.
Maybe God allowed Solomon’s collapse to become permanent Scripture so future generations would stop worshiping earthly success.
Maybe Ecclesiastes exists to expose the emptiness of life without intimacy with God.
And maybe someone reading this right now needed to hear that before it was too late.
Because some people are succeeding publicly while their soul quietly bleeds.
Some people are gaining followers while losing purity.
Some people are building careers while neglecting eternity.
Some people are entertaining crowds while spiritually suffocating.
And God is calling them back before the drift becomes destruction.
You do not need more applause.
You need Jesus.
You do not need another worldly distraction.
You need repentance.
You do not need another temporary pleasure.
You need the presence of God.
The Gospel does not merely expose Solomon.
It rescues us from becoming him.
Because where Solomon failed, Jesus succeeded.
Solomon was a king consumed by compromise. Jesus is the King without sin.
Solomon accumulated wives. Jesus pursues a spotless Bride.
Solomon built a temporary temple. Jesus builds eternal salvation.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured. Jesus’ Kingdom will never end.
And through Christ, even wandering hearts can come home again.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
No matter how far your soul has drifted… repentance is still possible.
Grace is still available.
Mercy still flows.
Jesus still saves.
One day many people will realize they spent their whole life building kingdoms they could not keep… while neglecting the only Kingdom that lasts forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room was silent when she died.
paragraphs: The room was silent when she died.
No prophet showed up.
No miracle interrupted the violence.
No fire fell from heaven.
No angel stopped the door from breaking open.
And maybe that is what makes the story of the Levite’s concubine one of the most terrifying chapters in all of Scripture.
Because it feels horrifyingly familiar.

A woman used.
A nation morally collapsing.
Religious people failing.
Cowards protecting themselves.
Violence normalized.
Human life treated as disposable.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it…
God stayed silent.

The story is found in Book of Judges chapters 19 through 21, and many believers avoid it because it feels too dark to preach, too uncomfortable to explain, too disturbing to read aloud in church. But Scripture does not hide humanity’s ugliness. The Bible is brutally honest about what sin does when people reject God.
The book of Judges repeatedly says:
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
“Ish ha-yashar b’einav ya’aseh.”
אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה

Literally:
“Each man did the straight/right thing in his own eyes.”
Not God’s eyes.
Their own.
That single line is the heartbeat of the entire tragedy.
Because the story of the Levite’s concubine is not merely about one woman.
It is about what happens to a society when truth becomes subjective.
When people stop trembling before God.
When morality becomes self-defined.

When religious identity survives…
but righteousness dies.
The story begins with a Levite.
That matters.
Levites were supposed to serve God, preserve holiness, teach the Law, and represent spiritual leadership among Israel. Yet this Levite already enters the story morally compromised.
The text says he had a “concubine.”

In Hebrew:
“Pilegesh” (פִּילֶגֶשׁ)
A concubine was not exactly a wife, but more than a servant. She occupied a vulnerable social position with limited protection and reduced dignity compared to a covenant wife.
Already, imbalance exists.
Already, exploitation lurks underneath the surface.

The woman leaves him and returns to her father’s house in Bethlehem. Some translations soften the wording, but the Hebrew strongly implies relational betrayal and sexual unfaithfulness or severe relational fracture.
Months later, the Levite travels to retrieve her.
And this is where the story becomes emotionally chilling.
The father welcomes him warmly.
They feast repeatedly.
Days pass with eating, drinking, delaying.
The narrative slows down intentionally.
It almost tricks you into feeling comfortable before the nightmare begins.

Finally, the Levite leaves late in the day with the concubine and a servant. Darkness approaches. They avoid staying among foreigners and instead choose Gibeah, an Israelite city in the tribe of Benjamin.
That decision changes everything.
Because sometimes the greatest danger is not outside the people of God.
Sometimes it is inside.
No one initially welcomes them.
That alone violates sacred hospitality laws in ancient Israel.
Eventually an old man brings them into his home.
Then the pounding starts.
Men surround the house demanding the Levite be brought out for sexual assault.
The language intentionally mirrors the depravity of Book of Genesis 19 and Sodom.
Israel had become what they once condemned.

Religious identity.
Pagan morality.
And then comes one of the most heartbreaking moments in all Scripture.
The Levite pushes his concubine outside to save himself.
Read that again.
The spiritual leader sacrificed her body for his own protection.
She is abused all night.
No rescue comes.
No hero appears.
At dawn she collapses at the doorway.
The Hebrew wording is devastatingly cinematic.
“She fell at the entrance of the house…”
Her hands on the threshold.

Almost inside.
Almost safe.
Almost rescued.
But not quite.
Then the Levite opens the door in the morning and says:
“Get up, let us be going.”

No compassion.
No horror.
No tenderness.
Just coldness.
And the text says:
“But there was no answer.”

In Hebrew:
“Ve’ein oneh.”
וְאֵין עֹנֶה
“And there was no response.”
Silence.
Death.
The woman in the story is never even named.
That should disturb us deeply.
Because sin dehumanizes people until they become objects instead of souls.
The Levite then does something almost impossible to comprehend.
He cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
Modern readers recoil at this, and they should.
The act was horrifying.
But in the ancient Near Eastern context, it was also a national alarm signal — a declaration that something unspeakably evil had occurred inside Israel itself.
And the nation erupts into civil war.
But here is the part most people miss.
Israel becomes outraged over the violence…
while barely acknowledging their own collective spiritual corruption.
They grieve the symptom while protecting the disease.
That still happens today.
People mourn public scandals while privately feeding the sins that created them.
Churches condemn visible collapse while ignoring hidden compromise.
Nations cry over evil after spending decades redefining righteousness.
The Levite’s concubine is not merely a story about brutality.
It is an autopsy of a civilization that abandoned God slowly.
Not instantly.
Slowly.

One compromise at a time.
One excuse at a time.
One normalization at a time.
One spiritual drift at a time.
Until evil no longer shocked them.
And perhaps the most terrifying detail of all…
Everyone in the story seems spiritually numb.
No one cries out to God in repentance.
No one falls broken before holiness.

No one says:
“We have become monsters.”
The conscience of the nation had died long before the woman did.
That is why Judges is so emotionally exhausting to read.
It is watching moral collapse in slow motion.
And if we are honest…
modern culture is not far away from it.

We live in a generation where people redefine truth according to feelings, preferences, politics, desires, and self-expression. What God calls sin, culture celebrates. What God calls holy, culture mocks.
And sadly, even many churches now soften Scripture to remain culturally acceptable.
But truth does not evolve because society becomes uncomfortable.
God does not modernize holiness.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is:
“Metanoia” (μετάνοια)

It means:
a change of mind leading to transformation.

Not guilt alone.
Not emotional regret alone.
A complete turning.
Because the Gospel is not behavior management.
It is resurrection.
And this is where the darkness of Judges makes the light of Christ even more overwhelming.
Because Jesus entered a world just as broken.

Women exploited.
Religious hypocrisy everywhere.
Violence normalized.
Spiritual leaders corrupted.
Crowds driven by lust, power, and hatred.
Yet unlike the Levite…
Jesus did not sacrifice another person to save Himself.
He sacrificed Himself to save others.
That difference changes everything.
Where the Levite abandoned the vulnerable…
Christ became vulnerable.
Where the Levite protected himself…
Jesus stretched out His hands willingly.
Where the concubine was thrown outside the door to suffer…
Jesus was crucified outside the city gates.
The Gospel reverses the horror story.
Isaiah prophesied it centuries earlier:
“He was despised and rejected by men…”

In Hebrew:
“Nivzeh va-chadal ishim.”
נִבְזֶה וַחֲדַל אִישִׁים

Rejected.
Forsaken.
Broken.
Jesus entered humanity’s violence and absorbed it upon Himself.
Not because humanity deserved it.
But because mercy is who He is.
And maybe that is why this story still matters.
Because there are people reading this right now who feel unnamed too.

Used.
Discarded.
Silenced.
Ashamed.
Forgotten.
Spiritually exhausted.
Some of you were betrayed by people who claimed to represent God.
Some of you were wounded inside churches instead of healed.
Some of you survived things nobody knows about.

And the enemy has whispered for years:
“You are disposable.”
But the cross says otherwise.
Jesus knows every hidden wound.

Every violation.
Every betrayal.
Every silent cry.
Every night you survived.
Every moment you thought nobody saw you.
He saw.
The Levite’s concubine had no earthly defender.
But the Gospel reveals a Savior who defends the brokenhearted Himself.
The Hebrew word for compassion often connected to God is:
“Rachamim” (רַחֲמִים)
It comes from the root word for womb.
It carries the idea of deep, visceral mercy from the innermost being.
God’s compassion is not detached sympathy.
It is fierce love.
And this is why repentance matters so deeply.
Because sin does not merely break rules.
Sin destroys people.
Entire civilizations collapse when God is removed from the center.

Families collapse.
Churches collapse.
Souls collapse.
Judges 19 is not ancient history preserved for shock value.
It is a warning flare for every generation.
A mirror held up to human nature without God.
And yet somehow…
even here…
grace whispers through the ruins.
Because the darkest stories in Scripture make the redemption of Christ shine brighter.
The Bible never hides humanity’s evil because it wants us to understand how desperately we need a Savior.

Not self-help.
Not religion alone.
Not moral performance.
Jesus.
Only Jesus.
And maybe tonight, after reading this, you realize your soul has drifted farther than you admitted.
Maybe you became numb slowly.
Maybe compromise stopped bothering you.
Maybe secret sin has been eating your conscience alive.
Maybe you look spiritually alive publicly while privately collapsing.
Come back to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Because civilizations are not the only things that collapse slowly.
So do souls.
And if someone came into your heart while reading this, share this with them immediately. Some people are silently drowning while smiling publicly.

Some stories in Scripture do not exist to comfort you first.
They exist to wake you up before your soul goes silent too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: People fear demons.
paragraphs:
People fear demons.
They fear persecution.
They fear the mark of the beast, deception, antichrists, false prophets, collapsing nations, and coming judgment.
But many still do not fear their own mouth.

Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals something terrifying:
God connects the tongue to destruction more often than most believers notice.
Not merely because words hurt feelings.
But because the tongue exposes the true spiritual condition of the heart.
Jesus said something that should shake every careless soul awake:

“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
— Matthew 12:34
The Greek phrase for “abundance” is περισσεύματος (perisseumatos), meaning overflow, surplus, excess spilling outward.

Your words are not random.
They are overflow.
Heaven hears what keeps leaking out of you.

That sarcastic bitterness.
That hidden rage.
That constant gossip.
That manipulation disguised as “concern.”
That filthy joking nobody sees online.
That passive-aggressive tone.
That lying.
That flattering.
That slander.
That mockery.
That endless complaining.
The tongue becomes a spiritual autopsy.
And the Bible treats this issue with terrifying seriousness.
In Hebrew thought, words were never viewed as empty sounds.
The Hebrew word for “word” is דָּבָר (dābār).

It means word…
speech…
matter…
thing…
action.
In biblical understanding, words are not detached from reality.

Words create movement.
Words carry authority.
Words reveal covenant.
Words establish judgment.
Words release blessing or corruption.

This is why Genesis begins not with human action…
but divine speech.
“And God said…”

Again.
And again.
And again.
Creation itself responds to speech.

Then humanity—made in God’s image—uses speech either to reflect heaven…
or rebellion.
The first recorded human sin after the Fall involving words was blame-shifting.
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me…”
Then Cain lies.
Then humanity corrupts itself through violence and pride.
By Genesis 11, words unite rebellion at Babel.
Speech becomes an instrument of collective defiance against God.
Nothing has changed.
Entire cultures now sin together through words.

Social media proved what God already said thousands of years ago:
the human heart overflows constantly.
And most people are drowning in their own overflow.
James does not soften this reality.
He writes:
— James 3:6
The Greek here is staggering.
κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας (kosmos tēs adikias)

Literally:
“a world-system of unrighteousness.”
Not merely “bad speech.”
James describes the tongue as an entire ecosystem of evil.

A small member…
with massive destructive capability.
Then he says:

“It setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.”
— James 3:6
The Greek word translated “hell” is γέεννα (Gehenna).
This refers to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, historically associated with child sacrifice and later burning refuse and corruption.
James intentionally connects uncontrolled speech with imagery of judgment, death, uncleanness, and destruction.
Imagine that.

A believer can attend church…
post worship lyrics…
quote theology…
and still have a tongue being fueled by hell itself.
That should terrify us.
Especially because modern Christianity often treats sins of speech as “minor.”
Sexual sin shocks people.
Drunkenness alarms people.

But gossip?
Slander?
Division?
Prideful speech?
False witness?
Cruel humor?
Verbal abuse?
People excuse those daily.
Yet Scripture repeatedly lists these among the marks of spiritual corruption.
Paul writes in Romans 1 describing a society under judgment:

“Backbiters, haters of God…”
— Romans 1:30
The Greek word for backbiters is καταλάλους (katalalous).

It means slanderers.
Secret defamers.
Those who speak against others maliciously.

Notice something devastating:
slander appears in the same chapter as sexual depravity, violence, rebellion, and hatred of God.
Heaven does not categorize sin the way culture does.
We rank sins socially.
God judges them holistically.
Proverbs speaks with brutal clarity:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”
— Proverbs 18:21
The Hebrew word for power is יַד (yad), literally “hand.”

The tongue carries the “hand” of death…
or life.
Speech becomes an instrument.

A weapon.
Or healing.
Never neutral.
This is why Satan attacks language constantly.
In Hebrew, the devil is associated with accusation.
In Greek, διάβολος (diabolos) means slanderer, accuser, false accuser.
Think about that carefully.

When believers constantly accuse, tear down, gossip, distort, mock, humiliate, or spread division…
they imitate the linguistic behavior of the enemy.
Not Christ.

Jesus spoke truth sharply when necessary…
but never corruptly.
Even His rebukes were holy.
Many modern Christians confuse carnality with boldness.
Not every “harsh truth” comes from righteousness.
Some people speak from unresolved pride while calling it discernment.
Others weaponize “truth” because they secretly enjoy tearing people apart.
But Scripture says:

“Speaking the truth in love…”
— Ephesians 4:15

Truth without love becomes brutality.
Love without truth becomes compromise.
Jesus embodied both perfectly.
And then there is gossip.
One of the most normalized sins in the church.
The Hebrew word רָכִיל (rākhîl) refers to a talebearer, scandal-monger, one who walks around spreading information destructively.

Notice the imagery:
someone moving from place to place carrying poison.
Digital culture turned millions into professional talebearers.

People now monetize outrage.
Monetize rumors.
Monetize humiliation.
Monetize exposure.
Monetize division.
Entire platforms run on verbal fire.
And Christians participate in it daily.
Then wonder why their hearts feel spiritually dry.
Jesus warned:

“Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.”
— Matthew 12:36
The Greek phrase for “idle word” is ῥῆμα ἀργόν (rhēma argon).

Careless.
Useless.
Unproductive.
Empty.
Not merely overtly evil words.
Careless ones.
That alone should humble every person reading this.
Because most people think judgment only concerns visible acts.
But God hears everything.

The private conversation.
The deleted message.
The voice note.
The hidden insults.
The manipulative compliments.
The secret mockery.
The exaggerated story.
The flirtation.
The verbal abuse nobody else witnessed.
He hears all of it.
And words leave spiritual fingerprints on the soul.
This is why repentance must involve speech.
Not merely behavior modification.
Isaiah understood this when he encountered the holiness of God.
He cried:

“Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips…”
— Isaiah 6:5

Notice:
in the presence of divine holiness, Isaiah became deeply aware of his speech.

Not his résumé.
Not his accomplishments.
Not his status.
His lips.
The Hebrew word for unclean is טָמֵא (ṭāmē’).

Defiled.
Polluted.
Impure.
He recognized that sinful speech revealed inward corruption.
Then God cleansed him.
Because redemption does not merely change destinations after death.

Jesus transforms the heart…
which transforms the mouth.
This is why true conversion eventually changes speech patterns.

Not instantly perfect.
But progressively transformed.

The vulgarity begins dying.
The constant rage weakens.
The lying convicts the conscience.
The gossip grieves the Spirit.
The appetite for verbal destruction decreases.
Why?
Because the Holy Spirit sanctifies language.
Paul commands:

“Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth…”
— Ephesians 4:29
The Greek word for corrupt is σαπρός (sapros).

Rotten.
Decaying.
Putrid.
Used for spoiled fruit.
Imagine rotten fruit coming from someone’s mouth spiritually.
That is how heaven views corrupt speech.
And yet…
Some believers speak with more venom online than unbelievers.

Mocking.
Humiliating.
Devouring each other publicly.
No wonder the church often lacks power.
James says:

“Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.”
— James 3:10
The issue is not perfection.
The issue is surrender.
Who owns your mouth?

Your flesh?
Your anger?
Your insecurity?
Your ego?
Your political tribe?
Your bitterness?
Or Christ?
Because eventually, everyone’s speech reveals their true master.
Peter failed with his mouth repeatedly.

He rebuked Jesus.
Denied Jesus.
Spoke impulsively constantly.
But after being broken and restored…
his speech changed.
Not because he became polished.
But because grace transformed him.
That is the hope of the Gospel.

Jesus died not only for visible sins…
but verbal ones too.

Every lie.
Every curse.
Every cruel sentence.
Every manipulative word.
Every blasphemy.
Every hidden conversation.
The cross reaches even there.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Holy Spirit convicts us because God intends to purify His people.
Including their words.
Maybe that is why mature believers often speak less.
Not because they have nothing to say.
But because they finally understand how dangerous words truly are.

One sentence can destroy a child’s identity.
One conversation can destroy a marriage.
One rumor can destroy a church.
One careless post can harden thousands.
One lie can alter generations.
Or…

One Spirit-filled word can save a life.
Restore hope.
Lead someone to Christ.
Heal wounds.
Bring repentance.
Strengthen faith.
Reveal truth.
The tongue carries enormous spiritual weight.
Far more than most people realize.

And perhaps one of the clearest signs of genuine spiritual maturity is not merely how loudly someone worships…
but how they speak when angry,
how they speak when wounded,
how they speak when nobody applauds them,
how they speak about people who are absent,
and whether Jesus still governs their mouth when emotions rise.
Some people need to repent tonight not because of what they did with their hands…
…but because of what they did with their words.
And the beautiful thing is this:
Christ still cleanses unclean lips.

He still transforms hearts.
Still softens bitterness.
Still convicts gossipers.
Still restores liars.
Still heals verbal abusers.
Still changes the overflow.

If this convicted you deeply, do not ignore it.
Sit with the Lord honestly.
Ask Him to search your speech.
Ask Him to expose what your mouth has been revealing about your heart.
You can join here:
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nobody talks about the years Paul disappeared.
paragraphs: Nobody talks about the years Paul disappeared.

One moment, he is breathing threats against Christians.
The next, he vanishes into obscurity.

No sermons.
No missionary journeys.
No crowds.
No churches planted.
Just silence.
And that silence may be one of the most important seasons in the entire New Testament.

Because God did not merely save Saul of Tarsus.
He dismantled him.

Most people know the road to Damascus.
Few understand what came after.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Apostle Paul — the man who would write much of the New Testament — spent years hidden before God released him publicly.
Years.

Not preaching to nations.
Not writing epistles.
Not standing before kings.
Just being broken.
And if you skip those silent years, you will misunderstand the man completely.
The Man Called Saul
Before he was Paul, he was Saul.

Hebrew:
שָׁאוּל (Sha’ul) — “asked for” or “desired.”
Born in Tarsus, educated under Gamaliel, Saul was not ignorant of Scripture. He was elite. Brilliant. Zealous.
Philippians 3:5–6 says:
“Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews…”
In Greek:

Ἑβραῖος ἐξ Ἑβραίων
(Hebraios ex Hebraiōn)
A Hebrew from Hebrews.

Pure pedigree.
Pure religious confidence.
And completely blind.
Not intellectually blind.
Spiritually blind.
Acts 9 describes Saul hunting believers. The Greek wording is violent.
Acts 9:1:

ἔτι ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου
(eti empneōn apeilēs kai phonou)

Literally:
“Still breathing threats and murder.”

Christianity was not merely something Saul disliked.
He inhaled hatred.
God saw it.
And then Jesus interrupted him.
The Damascus Road Was Not the End — It Was the Collapse
Acts 9:3–5:
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?”
Greek:

Σαούλ, Σαούλ, τί με διώκεις;
(Saoul, Saoul, ti me diōkeis?)

The word διώκεις (diōkeis) means:
to pursue, hunt down, persecute aggressively.
Jesus took Saul’s violence personally.

Not:
“Why are you hurting Christians?”

But:
“Why are you persecuting Me?”
Because Christ is one with His people.
This shattered Saul’s theology instantly.

The crucified Jesus was alive.
The Messiah had come.
And Saul had been fighting God Himself.
Imagine the horror of that realization.
Everything he trusted collapsed in one encounter.

His righteousness.
His status.
His certainty.
Gone.
Three days blind.
Three days unable to see physically while, for the first time, beginning to see spiritually.
And then something strange happened.
Paul disappeared.
Arabia: The Years Nobody Preaches About
Galatians 1:15–18 gives details Acts barely mentions.
Paul writes:
Greek:

ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἀραβίαν
(apēlthon eis Arabian)
“I departed into Arabia.”

Not Jerusalem.
Not seminary.
Not ministry conferences.
Arabia.
Most likely the Nabataean desert region near Sinai.

The same wilderness region associated with Moses.
The same wilderness pattern God repeatedly used.
Because God often isolates before He commissions.

Moses.
David.
Elijah.
John the Baptist.
Even Jesus Himself.
And now Saul.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Most believers want public anointing without private crushing.
But Scripture shows a different pattern.
God hides men before He uses them.
Why?
Because gifted flesh is still flesh.
Saul had knowledge, but his knowledge was poisoned with pride.
He knew Scripture intellectually while missing its fulfillment standing in front of him.
Jesus later became the center of everything.

Not law apart from Christ.
Not morality apart from grace.
Not religion without transformation.
What Happened in Arabia?
Scripture does not give every detail.
And that silence is intentional.
But Galatians reveals enough to understand the magnitude.
Galatians 1:11–12:
“I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ.”
Greek:

δι’ ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
(di’ apokalypseōs Iēsou Christou)
“Through revelation of Jesus Christ.”
Paul was being taught directly by Christ.
Think about that.
The Pharisee who memorized Torah now had to relearn Scripture through the lens of Jesus.

Every prophecy.
Every sacrifice.
Every feast.
Every covenant.
Everything pointed to Christ.
The Hebrew Scriptures suddenly opened.

Isaiah 53 was no longer theoretical.
Psalm 22 was no longer poetic mystery.
Genesis 22 was no longer merely Abraham and Isaac.
It was Jesus.
All of it.
Luke 24:27 says Jesus explained:
“Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.”
The Greek word:

διερμήνευεν
(diermēneuen)

Means:
to interpret thoroughly.
That is what was happening to Paul.
Years of theological reconstruction.
Years of repentance.
Years of ego dying.
You knew.
There are seasons when God removes the noise because He is trying to destroy the version of you that religion built.
The Crushing of Saul
Most people imagine Paul emerging from Damascus instantly bold and fully formed.
But Scripture paints something deeper.
He entered Damascus preaching Christ immediately, yes.
But after opposition rose, he withdrew.
Acts and Galatians together reveal a long hidden process.
This matters because modern Christianity often idolizes instant platform ministry.
But God spent more time preparing Paul than most people realize.
Silence was not punishment.
It was surgery.
Philippians 3 later shows Paul reevaluating everything he once treasured.
“What things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.”
Greek:

ζημίαν
(zēmian)

Loss.
Damage.
Forfeit.
The things he once celebrated became spiritual bankruptcy compared to knowing Jesus.
Then comes one of the strongest lines Paul ever wrote.
Philippians 3:8:
“I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord…”
The phrase:

τὸ ὑπερέχον
(to hyperechon)

Means surpassing greatness.
Supreme value.

Christ became greater than reputation.
Greater than religion.
Greater than intellectual superiority.
That transformation was not produced overnight.
It was forged in hiddenness.
Why God Hides His Servants
Because exposure without death creates dangerous ministers.
Knowledge without brokenness creates Pharisees.
Power without surrender creates corruption.

Saul needed more than information.
He needed crucifixion of self.
Galatians 2:20:
“I am crucified with Christ…”
Greek:

Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι
(Christō synestaurōmai)
“I have been co-crucified with Christ.”

Not improved.
Not slightly adjusted.
Crucified.
This is where many stop following Jesus seriously.

They want inspiration.
Not death to self.
But the Gospel does not merely add Jesus to your existing life.
It kills the old man.
Romans 6:6:
“Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him…”
The Greek:

συνεσταυρώθη
(synestaurōthē)
Crucified together with.
The old identity dies so new life can emerge.
That process is painful.
And often hidden.
God saw it.

The insecurity.
The secret sin.
The pride disguised as spirituality.
The performance.
The double life.

You can fool crowds.
You cannot fool Christ.
Barnabas Finds the Broken Man
Years later, Barnabas searched for Saul in Tarsus.
Acts 11:25:
“Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul.”
The Greek word:

ἀναζητῆσαι
(anazētēsai)

Means:
to search out carefully.
Why?
Because the hidden years were ending.
God had prepared him.

Not perfected him.
Prepared him.
There is a difference.

Paul would still suffer.
Still struggle.
Still battle weakness.
But now his confidence was no longer in himself.
2 Corinthians 12:9:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
Greek:

ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου
(arkei soi hē charis mou)
“My grace is enough for you.”
Enough.
That sentence can only be written by a man who has already been emptied.
The Silent Years Were the Foundation

Without Arabia, there is no Romans.
No Ephesians.
No Galatians.
No missionary journeys.
The hidden years built the visible ministry.
And many of you are fighting the very season God is using to save you from yourself.

You call it delay.
God calls it preparation.

You call it isolation.
God calls it consecration.

You call it silence.
God calls it transformation.
But here’s the danger…
Some people remain hidden because they refuse surrender.

Paul’s silence was not passive.
It was repentance.
Relearning.
Submission.
There is a difference between being hidden by God and running from obedience.

One produces holiness.
The other produces decay.
The Gospel Paul Finally Preached
After the crushing came clarity.
1 Corinthians 2:2:
“For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”
Greek:

Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον
(Iēsoun Christon kai touton estaurōmenon)
“Jesus Christ and Him crucified.”
That became everything.
Because Paul understood something religion cannot produce:

You are not saved by heritage.
Not by ritual.
Not by moral performance.
Not by knowledge.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith…”
Greek:

χάριτί
(chariti)

Grace.
Unearned favor.
The persecutor became the preacher because Jesus saves sinners.

Even violent ones.
Even hypocrites.
Even religious frauds.
Even broken people pretending to be strong.
That is the Gospel.

Christ died for sinners.
Rose again.
And calls men everywhere to repent and believe.
Not admire Him from distance.
Follow Him.
Some of you are in your Arabia right now.

Hidden.
Confused.
Stripped down.
And you think God abandoned you.
No.
He may be dismantling the version of you that cannot carry what He intends to give you.

Read Galatians again.
Read Philippians again.
Read Acts again.
Slowly.
And watch how God transforms a murderer into a missionary through hiddenness, truth, and grace.

If this exposed something in you, say it plainly.
No pretending.

And if someone you know is stuck in silence wondering where God is, send this to them.
They may be closer to transformation than they realize.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 6 Signs You Are in Spiritual Pride
paragraphs: 6 Signs You Are in Spiritual Pride
There is a kind of pride that does not wear arrogance openly.
It prays. It quotes Scripture. It serves in church. It lifts hands during worship. It corrects theology. It posts sermons. It knows doctrine.
And yet heaven still resists it.
One of the most terrifying truths in Scripture is that spiritual pride can make someone feel close to God while drifting farther from Him.

The Pharisees knew the Torah better than most people alive during the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ. They fasted publicly, prayed publicly, gave publicly, and taught publicly. Yet the Son of God looked directly at them and said:
“You are of your father the devil.” (John 8:44)
That should shake every believer.
Because spiritual pride is dangerous precisely because it hides behind religious activity.
The Greek word often associated with pride in the New Testament is:
ὑπερήφανος (hyperēphanos)
Meaning: “showing oneself above others,” “appearing over,” “elevated in self-estimation.”
It describes someone who sees themselves as spiritually superior.
James 4:6 says:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”
The Greek word for “resisteth” is:
ἀντιτάσσεται (antitassetai)
Meaning: “to oppose,” “to set oneself against in battle.”
Imagine that.
God Himself positioning against a believer because pride took root in the heart.
Not because of weakness. Not because of struggle. Not because of imperfection.
But because the soul secretly started worshipping itself.
Spiritual pride is subtle. It slowly replaces brokenness with performance. Dependency with image. Repentance with reputation.
And many people trapped in it have absolutely no idea.
So here are 6 signs you may be walking in spiritual pride.
Not to condemn you. But to expose what can silently destroy intimacy with Christ.
The first sign is when correction offends you more than conviction.
Proverbs 12:1 says:
“Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.”
The Hebrew word for “reproof” is:
תוֹכַחַת (tokhachath)
Meaning: “rebuke,” “correction,” “evidence that exposes error.”
Spiritually humble people can be corrected. Spiritually proud people protect their image.
You can often identify spiritual pride by how violently someone reacts when their behavior, theology, attitude, or motives are questioned.
Instead of praying, “Lord, search me,” they immediately defend themselves.
Saul did this.
When Samuel confronted him in 1 Samuel 15 after his disobedience, Saul cared more about preserving public honor than repenting before God.
“Honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people.”
That is spiritual pride.
Wanting appearance preservation more than heart transformation.
Some people cry harder over embarrassment than over sin.
That is dangerous.
David, despite terrible failures, remained tender before God because he repented quickly.
Psalm 51 is not the language of image management. It is the language of spiritual collapse before a holy God.
The Hebrew word David used for “broken” in Psalm 51:17 is:
נִשְׁבָּרָה (nishbarah)
Meaning: “shattered,” “crushed into pieces.”
God can heal broken people. But proud people rarely admit they are broken.
The second sign is when you constantly compare yourself spiritually to others.
Jesus warned about this directly in Luke 18.
The Pharisee stood praying:
“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are…”
Notice the deception.
He sounded thankful. But underneath the prayer was self-exaltation.
Spiritual pride often disguises itself as discernment.
You begin measuring your holiness against people instead of measuring your life against Christ.
Suddenly your identity becomes:
“I pray more.” “I know more Scripture.” “I’m not lukewarm like them.” “I’m more set apart.”
But holiness is not proven by superiority.
The closer Isaiah came to God in Isaiah 6, the less impressive he felt.
He did not say: “Look how holy I am.”
He cried:
“Woe is me! for I am undone.”
The Hebrew phrase:
אוֹי־לִי כִּי־נִדְמֵיתִי (Oy-li ki nidmeiti)
Carries the idea: “I am ruined.” “I am undone before holiness.”
Real encounters with God destroy self-righteousness.
The deeper you truly go with Jesus Christ, the more aware you become of your desperate need for grace.
The third sign is when serving God becomes more about being seen than surrender.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:
“Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them.”
The Greek phrase:
πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι (pros to theathēnai)
Means: “for the purpose of being noticed,” “to become a spectacle.”
That cuts deeply in the social media generation.
Not every public act is pride. But spiritual pride craves visibility.
It wants applause disguised as ministry. Validation disguised as service. Influence disguised as obedience.
You can preach sermons and still be feeding your ego. You can lead worship and secretly hunger for admiration more than God’s presence. You can post Bible verses while privately neglecting prayer.
The Pharisees loved public recognition. Jesus said they loved “the chief seats.”
The Greek word:
πρωτοκαθεδρίας (prōtokathedrias)
Refers to places of highest honor.
Spiritual pride loves platforms. Humility loves hidden obedience.
Some of the holiest people on earth will never become famous. But heaven knows their names.
The fourth sign is when repentance becomes rare in your life.
Proud hearts explain sin. Humble hearts confess sin.
1 John 1:8 says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
The Greek word for “deceive” is:
πλανῶμεν (planōmen)
Meaning: “to wander,” “to lead astray,” “to drift into error.”
One of the clearest indicators of spiritual pride is the gradual disappearance of repentance.
Not because the person became holy. But because conviction became weaker than ego.
People in spiritual pride usually confess generalized weakness while hiding specific sin.
They say things like: “I’m not perfect.”
But rarely say: “I lied.” “I was jealous.” “I was manipulative.” “I was proud.” “I need forgiveness.”
True repentance is specific.
The Greek word for repentance is:
μετάνοια (metanoia)
Meaning: “a change of mind that transforms direction.”
Repentance is not emotional damage control. It is surrender.
One reason revival tarries in many churches is because people want inspiration without repentance.
But God never pours fresh oil on hearts determined to protect idols.
The fifth sign is when you stop depending on prayer because you trust your own spirituality.
This is one of the most dangerous stages.
At first believers desperately seek God. They pray constantly. They know they are weak.
But over time, knowledge can create false independence.
Ministry experience. Bible knowledge. Reputation. Years in church.
And slowly the soul begins functioning without deep dependence on God.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“For without me ye can do nothing.”
The Greek phrase:
χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν (chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden)
Literally means: “Apart from Me you possess no power to accomplish anything.”
Spiritual pride quietly believes: “I already know enough.”
But spiritually mature believers never outgrow desperation for God.
Paul had revelations, miracles, authority, and deep theological understanding. Yet he still called himself:
“chief of sinners.”
Not because he glorified sin. But because genuine proximity to holiness creates deeper awareness of mercy.
The sixth sign is when love grows cold while theology grows louder.
This one is devastating.
You can defend truth while lacking Christlike character.
1 Corinthians 13 says:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass.”
The Greek word for love here is:
ἀγάπη (agapē)
Meaning: self-sacrificial love rooted in God’s nature.
Spiritual pride often produces harshness.
People become obsessed with winning arguments instead of restoring souls.
Correct theology without love becomes a weapon.
Jesus was full of truth. But He was also full of grace.
Some believers know doctrine well but cannot show mercy. Cannot apologize. Cannot listen. Cannot weep with people. Cannot restore gently.
Galatians 6:1 says:
“Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.”
The Greek word for meekness is:
πραΰτης (prautēs)
Meaning: “strength under control,” “gentle humility.”
If your theology has made you colder, harsher, more arrogant, more self-righteous, and less compassionate, something is spiritually wrong.
Jesus never called us merely to sound biblical. He called us to become like Him.
And perhaps the scariest thing about spiritual pride is this:
It can grow inside people who genuinely believe they are defending God.
That is why humility is not optional.
Micah 6:8 says:
“He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good… to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.”
The Hebrew word for “humbly” is:
הַצְנֵעַ (hatznea)
Meaning: “to walk carefully,” “modestly,” “with lowliness.”
Humility is not self-hatred. It is accurate vision.
It is seeing God as holy. Yourself as dependent. Grace as undeserved. And Christ as everything.
The proud heart says: “Look at me.”
The humble heart says: “Look at Jesus.”
And maybe while reading this, the Holy Spirit exposed something hidden. Not to shame you. But to rescue you before pride hardens your soul.
Because the terrifying thing about pride is that it can sit in church every Sunday while remaining far from repentance.
But there is still mercy.
Peter was proud. Yet Jesus restored him.
The disciples argued over greatness. Yet Jesus washed their feet.
God resists the proud. But He still gives grace to the humble.
If this convicted you, do not run from conviction. Run toward Christ.
Be honest. This hit harder than some expected.
One day every hidden motive will stand exposed before a holy God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Once Saved, Always Saved—Biblical Truth or Dangerous Assumption?
paragraphs: Once Saved, Always Saved—Biblical Truth or Dangerous Assumption?
There are few doctrines that ignite more passion, comfort, controversy, confusion, and division within the Church than the question:
Can a truly saved person ever fall away?
For some believers, the answer comes instantly.
"Once saved, always saved."
For others, the warning passages of Scripture thunder with equal force:
"Take heed lest you fall."
Entire denominations have divided over it. Friendships have fractured over it. Pastors have built ministries defending one side or the other.
But beneath the theological arguments is a far more personal question.
The young man who once preached passionately but now mocks Christianity.
The worship leader who once filled churches with praise but abandoned the faith years later.
The grandmother who worries every night that one mistake might send her to hell.
The exhausted believer wondering if God's grip is stronger than their failures.
This debate is not merely academic.
It touches fear.
Assurance.
Perseverance.
Grace.
Salvation itself.
And if we approach the subject carelessly, we can either rob genuine believers of biblical assurance or hand false assurance to people who may never have truly known Christ.
That is why we must go directly to Scripture.
Not traditions.
Not slogans.
Not denominational loyalties.
Scripture.
Because eternity deserves nothing less.
The Problem with Slogans
The phrase:
"Once Saved, Always Saved"
never appears anywhere in Scripture.
Not once.
That does not automatically make it false.
Many theological terms are not found verbatim in Scripture.
The real question is whether the phrase accurately reflects biblical teaching.
Unfortunately, the slogan itself often creates confusion because different people mean very different things when they say it.
Some mean:
"Anyone who genuinely belongs to Christ will ultimately persevere because God preserves His people."
Others mean:
"Since I prayed a prayer years ago, nothing I do matters anymore."
Those are not remotely the same doctrine.
The first seeks to magnify God's power.
The second often becomes a license for spiritual complacency.
And Scripture never permits such a conclusion.
Jesus' Promise: No One Can Snatch His Sheep
One of the strongest passages used in support of eternal security comes from the words of Jesus Himself.
In John 10:27–28:
"My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand."
The Greek phrase translated "shall never perish" is:

οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται
(ou mē apolōntai)
This is one of the strongest negations possible in Greek.
Literally:
"Absolutely never perish."
Jesus is not offering tentative security.
He is declaring divine certainty.
His sheep belong to Him.
His hand holds them.
His Father holds them.
No external force can overpower God.
No demon.
No government.
No persecution.
No enemy.
No power in existence can rip a true believer from Christ's grasp.
This is not weak assurance.
This is thunderous assurance.
And every believer should rejoice in it.
But Notice Something Most People Miss
Jesus does not merely describe sheep as people who once made a profession of faith.
He describes them as people who:
"hear My voice"
and
"follow Me."
The verbs are ongoing.
Present tense.
The mark of Christ's sheep is not merely a past decision.
It is a present relationship.
The evidence of salvation is not that someone once walked an aisle.
The evidence is that they belong to Jesus today.
The Warning Passages We Cannot Ignore
Then we encounter passages that make many Christians uncomfortable.
Hebrews 3:12 says:
"Beware, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God."
The Greek word translated "departing" is:

ἀποστῆναι
(apostēnai)
The root gives us our English word:
apostasy.
The warning is serious.
Very serious.
The author is speaking to people within the visible covenant community.
And throughout Hebrews he repeatedly warns against drifting, hardening the heart, and abandoning faith.
Hebrews 10:26–27 intensifies the warning.
So does Hebrews 6:4–6.
These texts cannot simply be ignored.
Any theology that skips these passages is incomplete.
Scripture does not whisper these warnings.
It shouts them.
The Difference Between Falling Into Sin and Falling Away
This distinction changes everything.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed adultery and murder.
Jonah ran from God's calling.
Yet all were restored.
Why?
Because stumbling is not the same as apostasy.
The Bible never teaches that genuine believers achieve sinless perfection.
Far from it.
The Apostle John writes:
(1 John 1:8)
Believers stumble.
Believers fail.
Believers sometimes wander.
But apostasy involves a hardened rejection of Christ.
Not temporary failure.
Not weakness.
Not struggle.
Not doubt.
A decisive turning away from the Lord.
The Apostle John Gives a Critical Key
In 1 John 2:19 we find one of the most important verses in this entire discussion.
John writes:
The Greek phrase:

οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν
(ouk ēsan ex hēmōn)
means:
"They were not truly from among us."
John's explanation for those who permanently abandoned the faith is not that salvation failed.
His explanation is that their departure revealed their true spiritual condition.
Their leaving exposed what was hidden.
The visible church had mistaken profession for possession.
Attendance for conversion.
Activity for regeneration.
The Doctrine Jesus Actually Taught
Jesus never taught:
"Pray a prayer and live however you want."
In fact, He taught the opposite.
In Matthew 7:21:
"Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven."
Those words should shake every church.
These people are not atheists.
They are religious.
They know Christian language.
They even point to ministry accomplishments.
Yet Christ says:
"I never knew you."
Not:
"I knew you once."
Not:
"I saved you and lost you."
Not:
"You belonged to Me but then escaped."
He says:
"I never knew you."
The issue is not lost salvation.
The issue is false conversion.
What About the Greek Word for Eternal?
Jesus repeatedly speaks of:

ζωὴ αἰώνιος
(zōē aiōnios)
"Eternal life."
If eternal life can cease, was it truly eternal?
This argument carries significant weight.
The New Testament consistently presents salvation as rooted in God's eternal purpose.
Romans 8:30 declares:
"Whom He justified, these He also glorified."
Notice something remarkable.
Paul speaks of future glorification as though it has already happened.
Why?
Because God's saving purpose is certain.
The chain remains unbroken.
Yet Scripture Also Teaches Perseverance
The Bible's solution is not careless assurance.
Nor is it constant terror.
It is perseverance.
The believer perseveres because God preserves.
The two truths work together.
Philippians 2:12–13 captures the balance perfectly:
"Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling."
Why?
"For it is God who works in you."
Both realities stand together.
Human responsibility.
Divine preservation.
The believer continues because God's grace continues.
The Dangerous Assumption
The greatest danger may not be believing eternal security.
The greatest danger may be believing a distorted version of it.
A person who says:
"I accepted Jesus twenty years ago, but I have no desire for Christ, no repentance, no obedience, no love for God, no evidence of spiritual life—but I'm saved because I repeated a prayer."
That person should not find comfort in "Once Saved, Always Saved."
Scripture never offers assurance apart from genuine faith.
Biblical assurance grows from union with Christ.
Not from a forgotten moment in the past.
The Hebrew Picture Hidden in the Covenant
The Hebrew concept of covenant is:

בְּרִית
(berit)
A covenant is not merely a contract.
It is a binding relationship.
God's covenant faithfulness is one of the dominant themes of Scripture.
Again and again, Israel fails.
God remains faithful.
The New Covenant is grounded not in human perfection but in God's faithfulness.
This is why believers rest in Christ.
Not in their own ability to hold on.
But because Christ holds on to them.
The Question That Changes Everything
Instead of asking:
"Can I lose my salvation?"
Perhaps the better question is:
"Do I belong to Jesus?"
Do you hear His voice?
Do you follow Him?
Do you love Him?
Do you repent when you sin?
Do you hunger for Him?
Do you trust Him?
Not perfectly.
But genuinely.
Because the evidence of saving faith is not flawless performance.
It is a transformed direction.
Where Scripture Ultimately Leads
After examining the whole counsel of God, the strongest biblical conclusion appears to be this:
A genuinely regenerated believer cannot be ultimately lost because salvation is God's work from beginning to end.
However, Scripture simultaneously warns that not everyone who appears saved truly is saved.
Therefore, warning passages function as God's means of preserving His people, exposing false faith, and calling believers to perseverance.
Biblical assurance is not found in a past decision alone.
It is found in a present, living relationship with Jesus Christ.
The New Testament does not teach careless security.
It teaches confident perseverance.
Not:
"I prayed a prayer."
But:
"Christ is my life."
And that changes everything.
Because one day every argument will end.
Every denomination will fall silent.
Every theological debate will cease.
And only one question will matter:
Did we know Him?
Or did we merely know about Him?
The difference is eternal.
Which passage speaks most strongly to you—John 10, Hebrews 6, Hebrews 10, Romans 8, or 1 John 2:19? Thoughtful discussion sharpens the Church.
The most dangerous deception is not losing Christ—it is believing you belong to Him while refusing to follow Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are sins people hide.
paragraphs: There are sins people hide.
Then there are sins people baptize.
That second kind is more dangerous.

Because once lust learns how to quote Scripture, mimic intimacy with God, and speak the language of destiny, conviction starts sounding like persecution. Suddenly what should have led to repentance becomes “confirmation.” What should have been crucified becomes “God understands my heart.”
And people perish there.
Not because God was silent.
Because they trained themselves not to hear Him anymore.
“But here’s what most people don’t realize…”
The flesh does not always tempt you with rebellion that looks evil.
Sometimes it tempts you with spirituality that feels holy.
You can pray and still be in lust.
You can fast and still be in lust.
You can preach, lead worship, speak in tongues, post Bible verses, cry during worship… and still have a heart mastered by desire instead of God.
Jesus never said outward spirituality proved inward purity.
In fact, He warned the opposite.
In Matthew 5:28, Jesus says:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek word for “lust” is:
ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō)

It means:
“to covet,”
“to intensely desire,”
“to set one’s heart upon.”
This is not accidental attraction.
This is cultivated desire.
Internal agreement.
A heart feeding itself forbidden intimacy.
And notice something terrifying:
Jesus places the battlefield in the heart before the body ever moves.
Because heaven sees sin earlier than humans do.
God saw it.
You knew.

The modern world says:
“If you didn’t physically do anything, it’s fine.”

Jesus says:
“If your heart embraced it, heaven already witnessed it.”
That changes everything.
When Lust Starts Wearing Church Clothes
One of the most deceptive forms of lust is not obvious immorality.
It is emotional-spiritual manipulation disguised as divine permission.
People say things like:
“God brought us together.”
“We just understand each other spiritually.”
“Our connection is deeper than labels.”
“God knows my marriage is dead.”
“The Lord told me this person is my kingdom partner.”
Meanwhile there is secrecy.
Fantasy.
Emotional dependency.
Private intimacy that keeps increasing.
Boundaries dissolving under spiritual vocabulary.
And because no one has “officially crossed the line,” people call it harmless.
But Scripture exposes the heart.
James 1:14–15 says:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin…”
The Greek word for “drawn away” is:
ἐξελκόμενος (exelkomenos)
It paints the image of bait dragging prey away from safety.
Lust isolates before it destroys.
That is why hidden conversations matter.
That is why secret emotional attachment matters.
That is why fantasy matters.
Sin grows in concealment.
And the terrifying part is this:
People often ask God to bless what He already called impurity.
The Hebrew Pattern Most Ignore
In Proverbs 7, Solomon describes seduction with terrifying precision.
The Hebrew language reveals something deeper than mere sexual temptation.
The strange woman says in Proverbs 7:14:
“I have peace offerings with me; this day have I paid my vows.”
She mixes seduction with spirituality.
Religious language.
Sacred imagery.
Worship language.
The Hebrew phrase for “peace offerings” is:
זִבְחֵי שְׁלָמִים (zivchei shelamim)
These were legitimate sacrificial offerings connected to fellowship and communion.
Do you see the deception?
She uses sacred symbolism to legitimize sinful desire.
This is ancient.
Not modern.
Lust has always tried to wear spiritual garments.
And people still fall for it.
A worship leader can be in lust.
A pastor can be in lust.
A ministry team can be united by shared rebellion instead of shared holiness.
A relationship can sound spiritually mature while being completely governed by flesh.
Because spiritual language does not sanctify sinful motives.
Read that again.
“God Told Me” Is Not a Shield Against Sin
One of the most dangerous phrases in modern Christianity is:
“God told me.”
Because many believers use God’s name to authorize what their flesh already decided.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
The Hebrew word for “deceitful” is:
עָקֹב (‘aqob)

Meaning:
“crooked,”
“insidious,”
“treacherous.”
Your heart can preach to you while betraying you.
That is why feelings are not final authority.
Scripture is.
The Holy Spirit will never contradict the Word He inspired.
Never.
God will not bless adultery because you “feel peace.”
God will not authorize impurity because you “feel connected.”
God will not sanctify lust because worship music was playing while you felt it.
Feelings can be real and still be deceptive.
That is why discernment matters.
Samson Did Not Fall in One Night
People imagine destruction as sudden.
Biblically, it is usually progressive.
Samson kept approaching what God warned him about.
Touching compromise.
Playing near temptation.
Treating covenant lightly.
Eventually desire blinded him before the Philistines ever did.
Judges 16:1 says:
“Then went Samson to Gaza, and saw there an harlot…”
The Hebrew structure shows intentional movement.
He went.
He saw.
Desire progressed toward action.
Sin rarely appears full-grown.
It is fed.
Protected.
Justified.
Repeated.
Then eventually normalized.
That is why secret lust eventually reshapes theology.
People start changing doctrine to protect desire.
Suddenly repentance sounds “judgmental.”
Holiness becomes “legalism.”
Conviction becomes “toxicity.”
And surrender becomes optional.
But Scripture never changed.
Only the compromised heart did.
The Difference Between Conviction and Condemnation
Some people reading this feel exposed right now.
Not attacked.
Exposed.
There is a difference.

Condemnation says:
“Hide from God.”

Conviction says:
“Run back to Him.”
Romans 8:1 says:
