“Now it came about at the lodging place on the way that the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.” — Exodus 4:24
In Hebrew:
וַיְהִי בַדֶּרֶךְ בַּמָּלוֹן וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁהוּ יְהוָה וַיְבַקֵּשׁ הֲמִיתוֹ
Transliteration:
Vayehi baderekh bammalon vayifgeshehu YHWH vayevakesh hamito.
Literal understanding:
“YHWH encountered him and sought to kill him.”
Not discipline him.
Not scare him.
Kill him.
This is terrifying.
Moses had just encountered God through the burning bush.
He had just been commissioned to confront Pharaoh.
He had just received divine authority.
Miracles.
Signs.
Purpose.
Calling.
Destiny.
And yet before Moses ever reached Egypt…
God nearly ended his life.
Why?
Because Moses carried a public calling while privately neglecting covenant obedience.
His son was apparently uncircumcised.
The covenant given to Abraham in Genesis 17 had not been honored.
God had already spoken:
“Any uncircumcised male… shall be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.” — Genesis 17:14
In Hebrew:
וְעָרֵל זָכָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִמּוֹל אֶת־בְּשַׂר עָרְלָתוֹ וְנִכְרְתָה
Ve'arel zakhar asher lo-yimmol et-besar orlato venikhretah
“An uncircumcised male… shall be cut off.”
Moses knew this.
He was raised in Hebrew identity by his mother before Pharaoh’s palace ever shaped him.
So how did this happen?
Scripture does not fully explain.
But the emotional clues are everywhere.
Zipporah was not Hebrew.
She was Midianite.
The daughter of Jethro.
Circumcision among Midianites may not have held the same covenant meaning it held for Israel.
There may have been disagreement inside the marriage.
Tension.
Resistance.
Delay.
Maybe Moses compromised peace at home to avoid conflict.
Maybe he delayed obedience because he feared hurting his wife.
Maybe Zipporah did not fully understand why covenant blood mattered so deeply.
And honestly…
many modern marriages still carry this exact tension.
One spouse burns for obedience.
The other does not fully understand.
One partner feels conviction.
The other feels frustration.
And compromise slowly enters the home.
Until one day the spiritual consequences become unavoidable.
Then comes the moment almost nobody emotionally enters.
The terror.
The confusion.
The scream.
The panic of Zipporah realizing her husband is suddenly dying under divine judgment.
Imagine the horror.
No warning.
No explanation.
No gentle conversation.
Just the crushing realization that God Himself is against them.
And somehow…
Zipporah immediately understands the reason.
That alone is astonishing.
The text says:
“So Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son’s foreskin and touched Moses’ feet with it…” — Exodus 4:25
Hebrew:
וַתִּקַּח צִפֹּרָה צֹר וַתִּכְרֹת אֶת־עָרְלַת בְּנָהּ
Vatikkach Tzipporah tzor vatikhrot et-orlat benah
“Zipporah took a flint and cut off the foreskin of her son.”
No priest.
No ceremony.
No celebration.
Only urgency.
Blood.
Fear.
A mother cutting her child in desperation to stop death from entering her home.
This was not peaceful Sunday-school obedience.
This was covenant crisis.
And then comes the line that reveals her emotional agony.
“A bridegroom of blood you are to me.”
Hebrew:
חֲתַן דָּמִים אַתָּה לִי
Chatan damim attah li.
The phrase is emotionally loaded.
Scholars debate the exact nuance.
But the pain inside the sentence is undeniable.
Some understand it as bitterness.
Others as shock.
Others as covenant recognition.
But one thing is clear:
Zipporah was emotionally shattered.
Blood had suddenly invaded her marriage.
She had to save her husband herself.
And the covenant Moses neglected became her burden to carry.
Can you imagine how traumatizing that moment was?
The man chosen to deliver Israel almost dies because of hidden disobedience inside his own house.
And his wife becomes the one forced to fix it.
Many women understand this pain more than they admit.
Carrying spiritual weight the husband ignored.
Holding families together while privately bleeding.
Praying while exhausted.
Correcting what someone else neglected.
Trying to save marriages, homes, children, and futures while silently breaking emotionally.
Zipporah’s story is not ancient distance.
It is still happening.
Some people reading this are spiritually exhausted because they keep carrying responsibilities somebody else should have handled.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because covenant neglect always wounds more than one person.
Private disobedience creates public pain.
Hidden compromise eventually spills blood emotionally, spiritually, relationally, or generationally.
What is terrifying is that Moses was still called.
Still chosen.
Still anointed.
Still assigned.
Yet God did not ignore covenant rebellion simply because Moses had ministry.
This destroys modern celebrity Christianity.
Because gifting does not cancel obedience.
Calling does not excuse compromise.
Public influence does not protect private sin.
God was willing to stop Moses before letting him represent divine holiness falsely.
That should shake every believer.
Especially leaders.
Especially people building platforms while neglecting obedience at home.
Especially people posting Scripture publicly while privately resisting surrender.
And yet…
there is mercy hidden in this terrifying scene.
God confronted Moses before Egypt.
Before greater responsibility.
Before national leadership.
Before public miracles.
Because real love confronts what destroys us.
The Hebrew worldview never separated covenant from life.
Obedience was not symbolic.
It was relational.
God was not demanding ritual perfection.
He was demanding covenant faithfulness.
And covenant always costs blood.
That thread runs through all Scripture.
From circumcision.
To Passover.
To sacrifice.
To Calvary.
The deeper prophetic shadow inside this story points toward Jesus Christ.
Because ultimately humanity also stood under judgment unable to save itself.
And blood became necessary.
But this time not the blood of a child’s circumcision.
The blood of the Son of God.
In Greek, Jesus says during the Last Supper:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης” — Matthew 26:28
Transliteration:
Touto gar estin to haima mou tes diathekes.
“This is My blood of the covenant.”
The word διαθήκη (diatheke) means covenant.
Jesus became the covenant blood humanity could never provide for itself.
Where Moses nearly died because covenant blood was absent…
Jesus willingly died to provide covenant blood forever.
That is why this story matters.
It is not random.
It is part of the larger rescue story of Scripture.
A God who takes holiness seriously.
A God who confronts compromise.
A God who provides mercy through blood.
And maybe somebody reading this feels exposed right now.
Because outwardly your life looks spiritual.
But privately something has been neglected.
Delayed obedience.
Hidden compromise.
Unaddressed sin.
Half surrender.
And deep down you know God has been confronting you about it.
Not because He hates you.
Because He refuses to let destruction quietly grow.
Some of you feel like Zipporah.
Emotionally exhausted from carrying spiritual burdens inside your home.
You love deeply.
You pray deeply.
But you are tired.
Tired of bleeding emotionally.
Tired of trying to save what others neglect.
Tired of silent pain nobody notices.
Please hear this clearly:
God sees hidden faithfulness.
God sees private tears.
God sees the burdens nobody applauds.
And God does not waste suffering surrendered to Him.
Zipporah’s pain became part of the preservation of Israel’s deliverer.
What she carried in private affected generations.
Some of your unseen obedience is protecting futures you cannot even imagine yet.
Do not quit.
Do not harden your heart.
Do not mistake hidden faithfulness for invisibility.
Heaven sees what people overlook.
And maybe this article exposed something you have been hiding.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this… send this to them.
Some people are slowly drowning behind spiritual appearances.
They need this reminder before hidden compromise destroys what God wants to heal.
Some wounds never become visible until obedience cuts deeper than comfort.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They memorized Scripture.
paragraphs: They memorized Scripture.
They fasted twice a week.
They tithed down to the smallest herb.
They guarded holiness with terrifying seriousness.
And yet when God stood in front of them in flesh, they wanted Him dead.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Pharisees did not reject Jesus because they loved Scripture too much.
They rejected Him because they misunderstood what Scripture was actually pointing to.
Jesus exposed the terrifying possibility that a person can know the words of God and still not know God Himself.
That is why His presence enraged them.
And if we are honest, it still enrages religious pride today.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The Pharisees were not ignorant pagans. They were experts in Torah. The name “Pharisee” likely comes from the Hebrew word:
פָּרוּשׁ (parush) — “separated one.”

They believed separation from impurity would prepare Israel for the kingdom of God. Their movement rose during centuries of foreign oppression when many Jews feared national compromise and spiritual corruption.
On the outside, their mission sounded righteous.
Protect holiness.
Preserve truth.
Defend the Law.
But something happened over time.
The traditions built around God’s commandments slowly became equal to God’s commandments.
Then eventually greater than them.
Jesus confronted this directly in Mark 7:8:
“You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.”
The Greek text is devastating:

ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων
(aphentes tēn entolēn tou Theou krateite tēn paradosin tōn anthrōpōn)
Literal sense:
“You abandoned God’s command while gripping tightly the traditions of men.”
Read that again.
They were gripping religion while rejecting the God religion was meant to reveal.
One of the deepest reasons the Pharisees could not accept Jesus was because He shattered their entire system of righteousness.
In Hebrew thought, righteousness is often connected to the word:
צְדָקָה (tzedakah)
Not merely moral behavior, but covenant faithfulness before God.
The Pharisees turned righteousness into external performance.
Jesus turned righteousness back into a matter of the heart.
That terrified them.
Because external religion can be controlled.
Heart surrender cannot.
Jesus said in Matthew 23:27:
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs…”
The Greek word for hypocrites:
ὑποκριταί (hypokritai)
Originally referred to stage actors.
Men performing a role.
God saw it.
They cleaned the outside while the inside remained spiritually dead.
And Jesus exposed it publicly.
That is why they hated Him.
Not because He lacked power.
But because His holiness revealed their hidden corruption.
Another reason they rejected Jesus was because He did not fit their expectation of Messiah.
Many expected a political deliverer.
A warrior king like David.
Someone who would crush Rome.
But Jesus came first to crush sin.
Isaiah 53 already foretold this suffering Messiah centuries earlier:
“He was despised and rejected by men…”
The Hebrew says:

נִבְזֶה וַחֲדַל אִישִׁים
(nivzeh vachadal ishim)
“Despised and forsaken by men.”
The Pharisees knew this text.
But they interpreted messianic prophecy selectively.
They embraced glory passages.
They ignored suffering passages.
They wanted a Messiah who would vindicate them publicly.
Instead, Jesus confronted them personally.
You knew.
The greatest collision came over authority.
The Pharisees believed authority came through lineage, scholarship, tradition, and institutional recognition.
Jesus had none of those credentials in their eyes.
Yet He spoke with authority that shook crowds.
Matthew 7:29 says:
“For He taught them as one having authority…”
The Greek word:
ἐξουσία (exousia)
Meaning delegated power, rightful authority, sovereign jurisdiction.
Jesus was not borrowing authority from rabbis.
He was the authority.
That shattered their hierarchy.
Because if Jesus truly carried divine authority, then their entire religious system stood exposed.
This is why in John 5:39–40 Jesus said:
“You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me that you may have life.”
The Greek phrase:

καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με
(kai ou thelete elthein pros me)
“And you are unwilling to come to Me.”
Not unable.
Unwilling.
That changes everything.
The issue was never lack of evidence.
It was resistance of the heart.
Pride blinded them.
And pride is still one of the greatest barriers to Christ today.
The Pharisees could tolerate sinners seeking mercy.
What they could not tolerate was being told they themselves needed mercy.
That is why Jesus said in Luke 18:9–14 that the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
Because the tax collector cried:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
The Greek:

ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
(hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō)
“Make atonement for me, the sinner.”
The Pharisee trusted his performance.
The sinner trusted God’s mercy.
Only one left justified.
There is another layer many miss.
Jesus threatened not only their theology, but their identity.
Their social honor.
Their influence.
Their control over the people.
John 11:48 reveals their fear after Jesus raised Lazarus:
“If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him…”
Everyone.
Their fear was not merely doctrinal.
It was personal loss.
Religious systems built on human glory cannot survive when true glory appears.
And Jesus carried the glory of God openly.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us…”
The Greek says:

Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
(Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto)
“The Logos became flesh.”
Not philosophy.
Not symbolism.
God entered human history.
And many religious leaders could not endure what that meant.
Because if God truly stood before them, then repentance was required immediately.
But the tragedy is deeper still.
Many Pharisees believed they were defending God while fighting against Him.
That should terrify every religious person alive.
Paul himself was once a Pharisee.
In Philippians 3 he lists his credentials:
“As to the law, a Pharisee…”
Yet after encountering Christ, Paul called his former righteousness:
σκύβαλα (skybala)
Refuse.
Garbage.
Compared to knowing Jesus.
Because salvation was never earned through law-keeping.
The Law revealed sin.
Christ fulfilled the Law.
The Hebrew word for law:
תּוֹרָה (Torah)
Means instruction.
It was always meant to lead people toward dependence on God.
Galatians 3:24 says the Law was a tutor leading us to Christ.
But the Pharisees turned the tutor into the savior.
And many still do.
Church attendance cannot save you.
Bible knowledge cannot save you.
Religious reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
This is why Jesus spoke such severe words in John 8:44:
“You are of your father the devil…”
People read that and recoil.
But Jesus was exposing a terrifying spiritual reality:
You can outwardly defend religion while inwardly resisting God.
That is what Satan has always done.
External appearance.
Internal rebellion.
And Jesus saw through all of it instantly.
God saw it.
Yet even in this darkness, grace appeared.
Not all Pharisees stayed hardened.
Nicodemus came to Jesus at night.
Joseph of Arimathea honored Him at burial.
Paul became an apostle.
Grace can break religious pride.
Jesus can rescue even the self-righteous.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sinners cleaned themselves enough for God.
But that Christ died for sinners who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Pharisees stumbled over grace because grace destroys boasting.
At the cross, nobody earns a place.
The immoral need mercy.
The religious need mercy.
The broken need mercy.
The proud need mercy.
Everyone stands equal before the crucified Christ.
And maybe that is why this story still cuts so deeply today.
Because many people are not rejecting a false version of Jesus.
They are rejecting the real Jesus.
The Jesus who confronts pride.
The Jesus who demands repentance.
The Jesus who refuses to be reduced into a religious accessory.
The Jesus who sees the hidden heart.
You knew.
Sit with it.
Read the Gospels again slowly.
Ask yourself whether you love Jesus Himself… or merely the comfort of religion around Him.
There is a difference.
A terrifying difference.
And eternity hangs on it.
There are truths many churches avoid because they confront the heart too directly. But freedom begins where honesty begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You didn’t run because you were weak.
paragraphs: You didn’t run because you were weak.
You ran because God was merciful.
That is the part most people miss about Jonah.
Most sermons reduce the story to a stubborn prophet swallowed by a great fish. A children’s story. A lesson about obedience.
But the Book of Book of Jonah is far darker than that.
Jonah was not merely afraid.
He was angry at the mercy of God.
And once you understand the historical brutality of Nineveh, the Hebrew language behind the text, and the terrifying spiritual tension beneath the narrative, the entire story changes.
Because Jonah did not flee from danger.
He fled from grace.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The story opens with a direct command from God:

“Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.”
— Jonah 1:1–2
The Hebrew phrase for “cry against it” is:

קְרָא עָלֶיהָ
qĕrā’ ‘ālêhā
It carries the sense of proclaiming judgment publicly and forcefully.
God was sending Jonah to confront one of the most violent empires in human history.
Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.
The Assyrians were infamous for torture, impalement, skinning enemies alive, beheadings, mass deportations, and psychological terror. Their own inscriptions bragged about brutality.
This was not a random pagan city.
These were enemies of Israel.
People Jonah likely hated with reason.
People who would later devastate the northern kingdom.
And God says:
Go warn them.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jonah’s problem was not fear of dying.
The text itself reveals the deeper issue later.
Jonah eventually admits why he ran:

“Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.”
— Jonah 4:2
Read that again.
Jonah fled because he knew God might forgive them.
The Hebrew wording here is devastatingly important.

חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם
ḥannûn wĕraḥûm
“Gracious and compassionate.”

אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם
’erekh ’appayim
“Slow to anger.”

וְרַב־חֶסֶד
wĕrav-ḥesed
“Abounding in steadfast covenant love.”
Jonah knew the character of God.
That was the problem.
He wanted justice without mercy.
Judgment without redemption.
Wrath without repentance.
And if you are honest, so do many people today.
You want mercy for yourself.
But vengeance for your enemies.
God saw it.
Jonah boards a ship to Tarshish.
The exact location is debated, but most scholars believe it represented the far western edge of the known world—possibly southern Spain.
Nineveh was east.
Tarshish was west.
Jonah was not confused.
He was intentionally moving in the opposite direction from the presence of God.
The Hebrew says:

מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה
millip̄nê YHWH
“From before the face of the LORD.”
That phrase matters.
Jonah was not merely leaving geography.
He was attempting to escape divine confrontation.
You knew.
And this is where the story stops being about Jonah alone.
Because many people still run from God for the same reason.
Not because they doubt Him.
But because they know what obedience will cost.
Some run because forgiveness feels unjust.
Some run because surrender threatens their pride.
Some run because they secretly want control over who deserves grace.
Jonah wanted God to destroy Nineveh.
Instead, God wanted to transform it.
Then the storm comes.
Not random weather.
Divine interruption.
The pagan sailors panic while the prophet sleeps below deck.
That detail is spiritually humiliating.
The unbelievers are praying.
The prophet is unconscious.
The captain confronts Jonah:

“What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God.”
— Jonah 1:6
There is irony everywhere in this book.
The pagan sailors fear God before Jonah does.
The sailors eventually throw Jonah into the sea.
And immediately the waters calm.
Then comes the most famous moment:

“Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.”
— Jonah 1:17
The Hebrew says:

דָּג גָּדוֹל
dāg gādôl
“A great fish.”
Not necessarily a whale specifically.
And notice something critical:
The fish was not judgment alone.
It was rescue.
Jonah should have drowned.
The fish became mercy in terrifying form.
Sometimes God’s rescue does not feel comfortable.
Sometimes grace feels like confinement before freedom.
Inside the fish, Jonah finally prays.
And the language echoes death imagery repeatedly.

“Out of the belly of hell cried I.”
— Jonah 2:2
The Hebrew word translated “hell” is:

שְׁאוֹל
Sheol
The realm of the dead.
Jonah describes descending to “the bottoms of the mountains.”
This is resurrection imagery before resurrection theology is fully revealed.
Which is why Jesus later connects Jonah directly to Himself.
In Gospel of Matthew 12:40, Jesus says:
“For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”
Jonah becomes a prophetic shadow.
A rebellious prophet enters symbolic death and emerges alive.
Christ enters actual death and rises victorious.
But unlike Jonah…
Jesus did not run.
Jonah hated his enemies.
Jesus died for His enemies.
That contrast changes everything.
When Jonah finally enters Nineveh, his message is shockingly short.
In Hebrew, only five words:

עוֹד אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְנִינְוֵה נֶהְפָּכֶת
‘ôd ’arbā‘îm yôm wĕnînĕwê nehpāket
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
Jonah 3:4
No softness.
No compassion.
No hope explicitly stated.
And yet the city repents.
From king to commoner.
They fast.
They mourn.
They cry out for mercy.
Even the animals are covered in sackcloth.
And God relents from destroying them.
Then comes the darkest revelation in the book.
Jonah becomes furious.
Not relieved.
Furious.

“But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry.”
— Jonah 4:1
The Hebrew intensifies this:

וַיֵּרַע אֶל־יוֹנָה רָעָה גְדוֹלָה
wayyēra‘ ’el-yônāh rā‘āh gĕdôlāh
“It was exceedingly evil to Jonah.”
Think about that.
The repentance of an entire city offended him.
Mercy looked evil to Jonah because hatred had hardened his heart.
And before criticizing him too quickly, remember how often people do the same thing.
You celebrate grace until it reaches someone you despise.
You rejoice in forgiveness until God forgives the person who wounded you.
That is why Jonah is uncomfortable Scripture.
It exposes the human heart.
God then grows a plant over Jonah to shade him.
Jonah loves the plant.
Then God destroys it.
Jonah mourns the plant more than he mourned thousands of souls.
And God asks the crushing final question:

“And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?”
— Jonah 4:11
The book ends there.
Abruptly.
No resolution.
Because the unresolved issue is not Jonah alone.
It is the reader.
Will you accept a God whose mercy reaches beyond your comfort?
Will you rejoice when grace rescues the undeserving?
Because that is the entire Gospel.
None of us deserved mercy.
Not Jonah.
Not Nineveh.
Not you.
Not me.

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8
The Greek phrase:

ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν
eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn
“While we were still sinners.”
Not cleaned up.
Not worthy.
Still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
And that is the real reason Jonah ran from God.
He could not bear the thought of mercy reaching people he believed deserved destruction.
But Jesus came precisely for people who deserved destruction.
That includes Nineveh.
That includes Jonah.
That includes you.
And maybe the reason this story still convicts people thousands of years later is because many are still running.
Not from religion.
From surrender.
From forgiveness.
From the terrifying possibility that God’s mercy is bigger than your bitterness.
God saw it.
You knew.
Say it plainly. Confess where bitterness has replaced mercy. Someone else reading your words may realize they are running too.
And if you are serious about growing deeper in biblical truth, spiritual discernment, and uncompromising Gospel teaching, join here:
One day you may need to read Jonah again when God shows mercy to someone you think does not deserve it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can a Christian Lose Their Salvation?
paragraphs:
Can a Christian Lose Their Salvation?
The Question That Has Kept Believers Awake at 2 A.M.
There are few questions that have haunted the hearts of Christians more deeply than this one:
"What if I fail God one too many times?"
Not because people are trying to win theological debates.
Not because they enjoy arguing doctrine.
But because somewhere beneath the question is something far more personal.
A hidden fear.
A trembling uncertainty.
A memory of a sin they swore they would never commit again.
A season of wandering.
A prayer that felt unanswered.
A night when they looked at themselves and wondered:
"Am I really saved?"
For many believers, this is not an academic discussion.
It is a soul-level crisis.
It is the difference between resting in Christ and living every day wondering if heaven's door might suddenly slam shut.
And to answer this question honestly, we must go deeper than modern opinions.
We must go back to the Scriptures themselves.
Back to the original languages.
Back to the words God inspired.
Back to Jesus.
Because salvation is not ultimately about our grip on Him.
It is about His grip on us.
Imagine a father walking through a crowded marketplace with his small child.
The child occasionally stumbles.
Sometimes gets distracted.
Sometimes lets go.
But the father's hand never releases the child.
The child's safety does not ultimately depend upon the strength of the child's grip.
It depends upon the strength of the father's.
That image captures one of the greatest tensions in Scripture.
God commands believers to persevere.
Yet God also promises to preserve them.
Both truths appear repeatedly throughout the Bible.
The mistake comes when people embrace one and ignore the other.
Jesus spoke some of the most comforting words ever recorded regarding salvation.
In John 10:27–29 He says:
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish."
The Greek phrase translated "never perish" is:

οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται
(ou mē apolōntai)
This is one of the strongest negative constructions in the entire Greek language.
It could be understood as:
"They will absolutely never perish."
Not "probably."
Not "unless they have a bad year."
Not "unless they struggle."
Not "unless they stumble."
Jesus continues:
"Neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
The Greek word for "pluck" is:

ἁρπάσει
(harpasei)
Meaning to seize, snatch, or violently take away.
Christ's promise is breathtaking.
No external force can remove His sheep from His hand.
No demon.
No government.
No persecution.
No devil.
No human being.
No power in existence.
The Apostle Paul expands this confidence in Romans 8.
After listing tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword, he arrives at one of the most triumphant declarations ever written:
"For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers... shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Romans 8:38–39
The Greek phrase:

οὐ δυνήσεται χωρίσαι
(ou dynēsetai chōrisai)
Means:
"Will not be able to separate."
Paul is not expressing wishful thinking.
He is proclaiming certainty.
Nothing in creation possesses the power to sever God's saving love from those who belong to Christ.
Yet many readers immediately think of warning passages.
And they should.
Because Scripture contains them.
Hebrews 6.
Hebrews 10.
The warnings in the Gospels.
The warnings in Revelation.
These texts cannot simply be ignored.
The Bible does not treat apostasy lightly.
The writer of Hebrews repeatedly warns against falling away.
The Greek word often associated with apostasy is:

ἀποστασία
(apostasia)
Meaning rebellion, departure, abandonment.
This raises a crucial question:
If salvation cannot be lost, why do these warnings exist?
The answer may surprise many believers.
Warnings are one of God's tools for preserving His people.
A road sign that says:
"DANGER. CLIFF AHEAD."
Is not evidence that the government wants drivers to crash.
It exists to prevent them from crashing.
Likewise, biblical warnings are instruments God uses to keep genuine believers persevering in faith.
The warnings are real.
The danger is real.
But so is God's preserving grace.
One of the most misunderstood passages is Hebrews 6:4–6.
Many conclude it teaches that a saved person can lose salvation.
However, the text never explicitly says the individuals were regenerated.
It describes people who experienced extraordinary exposure to spiritual realities.
They were enlightened.
They tasted.
They shared in blessings.
Yet the passage carefully stops short of saying they were truly born again.
This interpretation aligns with Jesus' own teaching.
In Matthew 7:21–23 many people claim spiritual experiences, ministry accomplishments, and religious activity.
Yet Jesus says:
"I never knew you."
Not:
"I knew you once."
Not:
"I knew you until you lost salvation."
But:
"I never knew you."
The issue was not lost salvation.
The issue was false conversion.
This distinction becomes even clearer in 1 John 2:19.
John writes:
The Greek says:

οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν
(ouk ēsan ex hēmōn)
Meaning:
"They were not truly from among us."
John's explanation for their departure is not that they lost salvation.
It is that their departure revealed they never genuinely belonged in the first place.
Their leaving exposed what had always been true.
Yet none of this should create spiritual arrogance.
Because another danger exists.
Some people hear "eternal security" and conclude:
"Then I can live however I want."
Scripture utterly rejects that idea.
The Apostle Paul asks:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?"
Romans 6:1
His answer:
"God forbid."
True salvation transforms.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
But genuinely.
The evidence of salvation is not sinless perfection.
It is a new direction.
A new affection.
A new hunger.
A new battle.
The person who belongs to Christ does not become sinless.
But they can no longer comfortably make peace with sin.
This is where many struggling believers need relief.
You may be reading this while carrying guilt.
Maybe you failed recently.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe publicly.
Maybe secretly.
Maybe you're exhausted from fighting the same temptation.
And because of it, you've started asking:
"Have I finally crossed the line?"
Consider the Apostle Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not privately.
Publicly.
Repeatedly.
Profanely.
Yet Christ restored him.
Why?
Because Peter's salvation rested on Christ's faithfulness more than Peter's performance.
Jesus had already told Peter:
"I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not."
Luke 22:32
Peter fell.
But he was not abandoned.
The Hebrew concept behind God's covenant faithfulness is often expressed by the word:

חֶסֶד
(chesed)
A word difficult to translate fully.
It carries the idea of covenant loyalty.
Steadfast love.
Faithful mercy.
Unfailing commitment.
God's love toward His people is not fragile.
It is covenantal.
It is anchored in His character.
Not ours.
So can a Christian lose their salvation?
The answer depends on what we mean.
Can a genuine believer stumble?
Yes.
Can a genuine believer experience seasons of doubt?
Yes.
Can a genuine believer fall into serious sin?
Yes.
Can a genuine believer experience God's discipline?
Absolutely.
But Scripture overwhelmingly teaches that those whom God truly regenerates, justifies, and adopts will ultimately be preserved by His grace and brought safely home.
As Jesus declared:
"It is finished."
The Greek:

τετέλεσται
(tetelestai)
Means:
"Paid in full."
Not partially paid.
Not conditionally paid.
Paid in full.
The cross was not a down payment awaiting human completion.
It was a finished redemption accomplished by a perfect Savior.
Maybe the deeper question is not:
"Can a Christian lose salvation?"
Maybe the deeper question is:
"Have I truly surrendered my life to Jesus Christ?"
Because assurance is not found by staring endlessly at ourselves.
Assurance grows when we look to Christ.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who saves.
The One who keeps.
The One who still welcomes repentant sinners.
And the One who promised:
"Whoever comes to me I will never cast out."
Have you ever struggled with assurance of salvation?
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
The hands that were pierced for you are stronger than the hands that keep failing Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They called him “Father.”
paragraphs: They called him “Father.”
Not because he pointed people to Jesus Christ… but because he slowly replaced Jesus in their hearts.
At first, it looked holy.

The church was loud with worship.
People cried at the altar.
Scriptures were quoted.
The preacher sounded powerful.
He spoke about “kingdom,” “authority,” “covering,” and “submission.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Satan rarely walks into a church wearing red.
He comes carrying a Bible.

And one of the oldest marks of a false prophet throughout history has been this:
a man who craves spiritual power eventually begins craving sexual power too.
That is why so many cult leaders drift toward polygamy, secret relationships, “spiritual wives,” manipulation of women, or distorted teachings about marriage.
God saw it.
And Scripture already warned us.

The danger is not merely a sinful preacher.
The danger is when sin becomes doctrine.
When rebellion is preached as revelation.
When manipulation is renamed “submission to God.”
And thousands sit in pews believing they are serving Christ while slowly being enslaved to a man.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The New Testament repeatedly warns believers that false teachers would arise from inside the visible church.
Not outside.
Inside.
Jesus Himself said:
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.” — Matthew 7:15

The Greek phrase for “ravening wolves” is:
λύκοι ἅρπαγες (lykoi harpages)
It means predators who seize, plunder, and exploit.
Not shepherds.
Predators.
Read that again.

A cult does not begin with obvious evil.
It begins with subtle replacement.
Christ is slowly dethroned while the leader becomes untouchable.
One of the clearest biblical signs appears when leaders begin distorting God’s design for marriage and sexuality.
From the beginning, God established marriage as covenant union between one man and one woman.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 2:24 says:

עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
Al-ken ya'azov ish et-aviv ve'et-immo vedavaq be'ishto
Translation:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife...” — Genesis 2:24
Not wives.
Wife.
Singular.
Jesus later reaffirmed this in Matthew 19:4–6.
And the Greek becomes devastatingly clear.

οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi duo eis sarka mian
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Two.

Not three.
Not five.
Not a hidden spiritual harem disguised as “biblical revelation.”
Yet cult leaders throughout history repeatedly revive polygamy because lust always seeks theological camouflage.
That is exactly what happened in many destructive sects.
The pattern never changes:

First comes “special revelation.”
Then isolation.
Then unquestioned authority.
Then sexual corruption.
Because false doctrine eventually produces false living.
The Apostle Paul warned Timothy about leaders whose lives disqualify their ministry.
In 1 Timothy 3:2:

δεῖ οὖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
dei oun ton episkopon anepilempton einai, mias gynaikos andra
Literal meaning:
“An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife.”

The phrase:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (mias gynaikos andra)

Literally means:
“a one-woman man.”

Not spiritually divided.
Not sexually scattered.
Not secretly collecting women while preaching holiness.
A preacher practicing polygamy while claiming divine authority is not restoring biblical Christianity.
He is resurrecting rebellion.
And many people miss the warning signs because cults often imitate revival language.

They speak constantly about “anointing.”
“Honor.”
“Kingdom.”
“Prophetic covering.”
“Touch not God’s anointed.”
But biblical leadership never demands worship-like loyalty.
Peter refused it.
In Acts 10:25–26, when Cornelius bowed before Peter, Scripture says:

Ἀνάστηθι· καὶ ἐγὼ αὐτὸς ἄνθρωπός εἰμι
Anastēthi; kai egō autos anthrōpos eimi
Translation:
“Stand up; I myself am also a man.”
True servants of Christ redirect glory back to Jesus.
Cult leaders absorb it.
One of the strongest signs you may be trapped in a cult disguised as a church is this:
You fear the pastor more than you fear God.

You cannot question leadership.
You cannot examine doctrine openly.
Members who leave are demonized.
Families become divided.
Independent thinking becomes “rebellion.”
The leader’s words carry more emotional weight than Scripture itself.
God saw it.
You knew something felt wrong.
But fear kept you silent.
Another sign is when the church gradually separates itself from the Body of Christ and begins claiming exclusive truth.

They become “the only real church.”
“The remnant.”
“The chosen movement.”
“the final revelation.”
Yet Scripture says in Galatians 1:8:
“But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you... let him be accursed.”

The Greek word is:
ἀνάθεμα (anathema)

Meaning:
devoted to destruction under divine judgment.
Paul did not tell believers to blindly trust charisma.
He commanded them to test doctrine.
Even the Bereans were praised because they examined Paul’s teachings against Scripture daily.
Acts 17:11 says:
“They received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
A true church invites examination under God’s Word.
A cult fears it.
And when a preacher begins justifying polygamy, secret marriages, spiritual wives, or sexual “revelation,” you are no longer dealing with mere error.
You are witnessing a direct attack against God’s created order.
The Old Testament records polygamy among fallen men, yes.
But description is not endorsement.

David practiced polygamy.
Solomon multiplied wives.
And the consequences were catastrophic.

Division.
Idolatry.
Judgment.
Broken families.
Corrupted worship.
Jesus did not point back to Solomon’s excess.
He pointed back to Eden.
Back to God’s original design.
Back to covenant purity.
False prophets often appeal to Old Testament figures while ignoring Christ’s fulfillment and clarification.
That is deception.
And the deeper danger of cult systems is not merely doctrinal confusion.
It is spiritual captivity.
People begin outsourcing conscience itself to the leader.
That is why abusive leaders become enraged when members study Scripture independently.
Because truth threatens control.
2 Corinthians 11:13–14 warns:
“For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.”

The Greek phrase:
μετασχηματιζόμενοι (metaschēmatizomenoi)

Means:
disguising outward appearance.
Counterfeiting.
Performing spirituality externally while corruption grows internally.
This is why emotional experiences alone cannot validate a ministry.

People can cry in deception.
People can sing in deception.
People can even witness miracles around deception.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that many would prophesy and cast out demons in His name and still hear:
“I never knew you.”

Not:
“I knew you once.”
Never.
The true test is not charisma.
It is submission to Christ and fidelity to Scripture.

If your church protects the reputation of leaders more than the holiness of God…
if women are manipulated through “submission” language…
if questioning doctrine is treated like betrayal…
if the preacher claims special revelation beyond Scripture…
if sexual sin is normalized through twisted theology…
if loyalty to the leader overshadows loyalty to Christ…
You are not witnessing biblical Christianity.
You are witnessing spiritual abuse wearing church clothes.
And some of you reading this already know.

You have ignored the discomfort.
Ignored the contradictions.
Ignored the manipulation because leaving felt terrifying.
God saw it.
But hear this clearly:
Jesus Christ does not enslave people to human control.
He sets captives free.

The Gospel is not:
“Submit blindly to a leader.”
The Gospel is this:

You are a sinner separated from God.
Christ died for your sins.
Jesus rose again.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Him alone.

Not through a cult.
Not through a prophet.
Not through “covering.”
Not through spiritual intimidation.
Only through Jesus Christ.
John 8:36 says:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”

The Greek word for “free” is:
ἐλεύθεροι (eleutheroi)

Liberated.
Released from bondage.
That includes spiritual manipulation disguised as Christianity.
And some people reading this need courage right now.

Courage to test everything by Scripture.
Courage to leave systems that exalt men over Christ.
Courage to stop calling control “discipleship.”
Because eternity is too serious to gamble on deception.
If this exposed something you’ve been wrestling with in silence, say it plainly.
“No man replaces Jesus.”
Somebody else needs to read this before they surrender their mind, family, and soul to spiritual counterfeit.
Send it to someone trapped in manipulative religion.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You can spend decades looking righteous while slowly drifting from God.
paragraphs: You can spend decades looking righteous while slowly drifting from God.
That is the terrifying story of Asa.

He didn’t begin as a hypocrite.
He began as a reformer.

He tore down idols.
He confronted corruption.
He called an entire nation back to God.
And for a while, heaven blessed everything he touched.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
A strong beginning can hide a weak foundation.
And if pride is never crucified, even a godly season can become the setup for a tragic ending.

“Nevertheless the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days.”
— 2 Chronicles 15:17
Read that again.

His heart was sincere toward God for much of his life.
Yet his story still ended in spiritual decline.
That should shake anyone who thinks yesterday’s obedience guarantees tomorrow’s faithfulness.
Because it doesn’t.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The Rise of a Godly King
When Asa became king of Judah, the nation was spiritually polluted.

Idolatry had infected the land.
False worship had become normal.
Compromise had become culture.
But Asa did something rare.
He acted.

“He took away the altars of the strange gods, and the high places, and brake down the images, and cut down the groves.”
— 2 Chronicles 14:3

He didn’t negotiate with sin.
He destroyed it.

He commanded Judah to seek the Lord.
He rebuilt fortified cities.
He restored spiritual order.
And God responded.

“The LORD gave him rest.”
— 2 Chronicles 14:6
That word “rest” matters.

Because peace is not always the absence of enemies.
Sometimes peace is the presence of God.
And Asa experienced both.
Then came the invasion.
Zerah the Ethiopian marched against Judah with an army of a million men.
A million.
Humanly speaking, Asa had no chance.
But this is where his faith shined brightest.

“LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power.”
— 2 Chronicles 14:11

That prayer reveals the secret of Asa’s early strength:
he knew he was helpless without God.
And heaven answered.
God crushed Judah’s enemies so decisively that Asa’s kingdom entered one of its strongest periods.
This is where most people stop reading.

Victory.
Revival.
Blessing.
Strength.
The perfect spiritual success story.
But the danger of success is subtle.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to your soul arrives after the battle is over.
The Warning Asa Ignored
After the victory, God sent the prophet Azariah with a warning.

“The LORD is with you, while ye be with him.”
— 2 Chronicles 15:2

Simple.
Direct.
Conditional.
God’s blessing was never meant to replace dependence on Him.
That message still destroys modern Christianity.

Many people want God’s protection without God’s authority.
God’s blessings without surrender.
God’s promises without obedience.
But covenant relationship has always required continual trust.
And at first, Asa responded correctly.

He renewed the altar of the Lord.
The people entered covenant.
Revival spread across Judah.

“And all Judah rejoiced at the oath.”
— 2 Chronicles 15:15
Imagine it.

A nation publicly seeking God.
Idols destroyed.
Worship restored.
Peace everywhere.
It looked unshakable.
But hidden compromise survives quietly.
Years passed.

Comfort increased.
Pressure returned.
And Asa slowly became the kind of man he once opposed.
That’s how spiritual drift works.
Nobody wakes up planning to abandon dependence on God.

It happens gradually.
Silently.
Reasonably.
One compromise at a time.
The Turning Point
In Asa’s later years, Baasha king of Israel moved against Judah.
This time, Asa didn’t pray.
That detail matters.
The man who once cried out to God against a million soldiers suddenly trusted political strategy instead.

“And Asa brought out silver and gold out of the treasures of the house of the LORD… and sent to Benhadad king of Syria.”
— 2 Chronicles 16:2
Did you catch it?
He emptied God’s treasury to purchase worldly help.

And technically…
it worked.

That is one of the most dangerous moments in a believer’s life:
when disobedience appears successful.
Because immediate success can disguise spiritual decay.
God then sent Hanani the seer to confront Asa.

“Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God…”
— 2 Chronicles 16:7
The issue wasn’t merely strategy.
The issue was trust.
Asa no longer depended on God the way he once did.
And then came one of the saddest verses in Scripture.

“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.”
— 2 Chronicles 16:9
God was still looking for surrendered hearts.

Still searching for dependence.
Still ready to show Himself strong.
But Asa responded with anger instead of repentance.

“Then Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house.”
— 2 Chronicles 16:10
The reformer became the oppressor.
The man who once received correction now punished it.
That is what pride does.

At first you resist sin.
Then you defend it.
Then you attack anyone who exposes it.
God saw it.
You knew.
The Tragic Ending
Near the end of his life, Asa became diseased in his feet.
But the disease itself wasn’t the tragedy.
The real tragedy was this:

“Yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.”
— 2 Chronicles 16:12
Scripture is not condemning doctors.
The issue again was dependence.
Even in suffering, Asa refused to return fully to God.
The king who once trusted God against impossible odds now trusted human solutions without seeking the Lord.
And then he died.

No dramatic repentance recorded.
No final restoration described.
Just silence.
That ending feels heavy because it should.
Asa proves something many people refuse to accept:
You can start well and still finish poorly.

Church attendance cannot preserve your heart.
Past victories cannot sustain present faith.
Anointing cannot replace ongoing surrender.
Some people are still living off spiritual momentum from years ago.
But intimacy with God cannot survive on old obedience.
Yesterday’s prayer life will not protect today’s compromise.
And this generation desperately needs to hear that.
Because modern Christianity often celebrates beginnings while ignoring endurance.

We celebrate conversions.
Platforms.
Influence.
Moments.
But heaven watches faithfulness over time.

Jesus did not say,
“He who starts well shall be saved.”
He said:

“He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.”
— Matthew 24:13
That endurance is not human willpower.
It is continual dependence on Christ.
The Gospel Beyond Asa
Here is the hope hidden inside Asa’s warning.
Your confidence was never supposed to rest in your own consistency.
Because if salvation depended on human perfection, nobody would survive.

Not Asa.
Not David.
Not Peter.
Not you.
This is why the Gospel matters so deeply.
Jesus succeeded where every human king failed.

Every earthly leader eventually revealed weakness.
Every human heart eventually drifted.
Every sinner eventually fell short.
But Christ remained perfectly faithful.

Perfect obedience.
Perfect righteousness.
Perfect sacrifice.
And on the cross, Jesus took the judgment our spiritual failures deserved.

Including the sins of pride.
Self-reliance.
Drift.
Hypocrisy.
Coldness.
Compromise.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works.”
— Ephesians 2:8-9

That grace does not excuse rebellion.
It transforms hearts.

Real salvation produces repentance.
Real faith continues following Christ.
Real discipleship keeps returning to God even after failure.
That is the difference between religion and redemption.

Religion performs outwardly while drifting inwardly.
Redemption creates ongoing dependence on Jesus.
And maybe this is why Asa’s story unsettles people so deeply.
Because parts of his decline feel familiar.

You used to pray more.
Used to hunger for Scripture more.
Used to repent faster.
Used to depend on God more fully.
But somewhere along the way, self-reliance replaced surrender.

Outwardly you still look functional.
Internally the fire weakened.
God saw it.
You knew.
But the mercy of Christ still calls sinners back.
Right now.
Before the drift becomes permanent.
Before pride hardens completely.
Before your ending becomes a warning instead of a testimony.
Write “Lord, keep my heart” if you know you need Him again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There is a reason the Bible keeps returning to the image of the watchman.
paragraphs: There is a reason the Bible keeps returning to the image of the watchman.

Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because God was obsessed with military towers.
But because humanity has always drifted toward spiritual sleep.

The watchman stood between danger and the people.
Between truth and destruction.
Between warning and judgment.
He was not chosen because he was powerful.
He was chosen because he stayed awake while others slept.
And that image becomes one of the most haunting spiritual pictures in all of Scripture.

The modern world celebrates distraction.
God still searches for watchmen.
In Hebrew, the primary word for “watchman” is שֹׁמֵר — shomer.

It comes from the Hebrew root שָׁמַר (shamar), meaning:
to guard,
to keep,
to preserve,
to watch carefully,
to protect attentively.
This word appears constantly throughout the Old Testament because watching was never merely physical.
It was spiritual responsibility.
The first time the concept appears powerfully is in Genesis when God asks Cain:
“Where is Abel thy brother?”
And Cain responds:

“Am I my brother’s keeper?”
— Genesis 4:9
The Hebrew word there for “keeper” is:
שֹׁמֵר (shomer).
Cain was essentially asking:
“Am I supposed to watch over him?”
And the terrifying answer throughout all Scripture is:
Yes.
Humanity was created with responsibility toward one another.
The watchman motif begins there.
Not on a wall.
But in the heart.
By the time Israel became a nation, watchmen became literal figures stationed upon city walls.
Ancient cities depended entirely on elevated watch towers because enemies often attacked at night. A sleeping watchman could doom an entire city.
This is why Isaiah writes:
— Isaiah 62:6
The Hebrew text says:
עַל־חוֹמֹתַיִךְ יְרוּשָׁלִַם הִפְקַדְתִּי שֹׁמְרִים
‘Al chomotayikh Yerushalayim hifqadti shomrim.
“Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have assigned guardians/watchers.”
But these were not merely soldiers.
Notice the next phrase:
“They will never keep silent.”
Because biblical watchmen were also prophetic voices.

They warned.
They confronted.
They cried out when danger approached.
The watchman was spiritually responsible to speak even when nobody wanted to listen.
That becomes devastatingly clear in Ezekiel.
God tells Ezekiel:

“Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel.”
— Ezekiel 3:17
The Hebrew reads:

צֹפֶה נְתַתִּיךָ
(Tzofeh netattikha)
“I have made you a watcher.”

The word here changes from shomer to צָפָה (tsaphah), which means:
to peer into the distance,
to lean forward watching,
to observe attentively,
to keep lookout.
This is deeper than guarding.
This is discernment.
A biblical watchman saw what others ignored.
God then gives Ezekiel one of the heaviest responsibilities imaginable:

“When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning… his blood will I require at thine hand.”
— Ezekiel 3:18
This is why watchmen appear repeatedly in Scripture.
Because God holds silence accountable.
That should shake modern Christianity.

We live in a generation terrified of confrontation.
Terrified of offending people.
Terrified of speaking truth plainly.
But biblical watchmen were never called to popularity.
They were called to faithfulness.

Jeremiah stood as a watchman.
Isaiah stood as a watchman.
Ezekiel stood as a watchman.
Even Habakkuk says:

“I will stand upon my watch.”
— Habakkuk 2:1
The Hebrew phrase is stunning:

עַל־מִשְׁמַרְתִּי אֶעֱמֹד
(‘al mishmarti e’emod)
“I will station myself at my post.”
That is spiritual discipline.
That is attentiveness to God.

Not casual Christianity.
Not emotional religion.
Not occasional conviction.
Watchfulness.
Jesus carries this exact imagery into the New Testament.
In Greek, one major word connected to spiritual watchfulness is γρηγορέω (grēgoreō).

It means:
to stay awake,
to remain alert,
to remain vigilant.
Jesus repeatedly says:

“Watch therefore.”
— Matthew 24:42
Greek:

γρηγορεῖτε οὖν
(grēgoreite oun)
“Stay awake therefore.”
This was not merely about prophecy charts or end-times curiosity.
Christ was warning against spiritual numbness.
Because sleep is one of the central metaphors of sin in Scripture.
People stop watching slowly.
Not instantly.

One compromise.
One distraction.
One hidden sin.
One season of prayerlessness.
One gradual desensitization.
And eventually people who once burned with conviction cannot even discern darkness anymore.
That is why Jesus warned His disciples in Gethsemane:

“Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.”
— Matthew 26:41
The disciples physically slept while spiritual warfare intensified around them.
And that still happens now.

People sleep spiritually while marriages collapse.
While addictions deepen.
While truth is corrupted.
While churches entertain goats instead of feeding sheep.
While souls walk toward destruction smiling.
The watchman sees what comfort tries to ignore.
Paul continues this imagery in the New Testament:

“Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober.”
— 1 Thessalonians 5:6
The Greek word for “sober” is νήφω (nēphō).

It means:
clear-minded,
self-controlled,
free from intoxication.
Not merely alcohol.
Spiritual intoxication.
The world is drunk on distraction.

Constant noise.
Constant scrolling.
Constant stimulation.
Constant entertainment.
And many believers have lost the ability to hear God because silence feels unbearable to them now.
Biblical watchmen lived differently.

They listened.
They discerned.
They examined themselves.
They warned others.
They prayed through the night.
They carried burdens for people who often mocked them.
The prophet Isaiah even describes blind watchmen:

“His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant.”
— Isaiah 56:10
The Hebrew there is terrifying.

צֹפָיו עִוְרִים
(tzofav ivrim)
“His watchers are blind.”
A blind watchman is catastrophic.
And spiritually, Scripture warns repeatedly about leaders who cannot discern truth anymore yet continue speaking confidently.
That is not merely ancient history.
That is modern reality.
This is why the Bible repeatedly returns to watchmen.
Because God is emphasizing a permanent spiritual principle:
someone must stay awake.

Someone must pray when others do not.
Someone must warn when culture celebrates sin.
Someone must stand when compromise becomes normal.
Someone must guard truth when false doctrine spreads.
Someone must love people enough to tell them the truth.

And ultimately…
the greatest Watchman is God Himself.
Psalm 121 says:
“Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.”
The Hebrew word again:

שׁוֹמֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל
(Shomer Yisrael)
“The Keeper of Israel.”

Human watchmen fail.
God never does.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because humanity failed its watch.

Adam failed in the garden.
Israel failed repeatedly.
The disciples slept in Gethsemane.
But Jesus remained faithful.

While others slept, He prayed.
While others fled, He endured.
While others denied Him, He drank the cup of wrath fully.
At the cross, Christ bore judgment for sleeping sinners.
And through His resurrection, He awakens dead souls.
This is why Paul writes:
— Ephesians 5:14
The Christian life is not passive existence.
It is awakened living.

Not paranoia.
Not fear.
Not obsessive speculation.
But spiritual alertness.

Holiness.
Discernment.
Prayer.
Truth.
Repentance.
Readiness.
The repeated mention of watchmen throughout Scripture is God’s mercy.
Warnings are mercy.
Conviction is mercy.
Truth is mercy.
Because God warns before judgment comes.
And maybe the most frightening reality today is not open wickedness.
It is spiritual sleep inside people who still think they are awake.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.

The conviction used to be stronger.
Prayer used to feel alive.
Sin used to bother you more deeply.
Scripture used to pierce your heart more often.
But little by little…
the soul drifted.
And maybe this is your warning.
Not condemnation.
A warning.
Because watchmen in Scripture were never sent to destroy people.
They were sent because God desired repentance before destruction.
Jesus Christ still saves spiritually sleeping people.
Completely.
Fully.
Freely.
But repentance cannot happen while pretending everything is fine.
The Gospel begins with honesty.

You are not saved by vigilance.
You are saved by Christ.
But those truly awakened by Christ begin watching again.

They begin guarding their soul.
Guarding truth.
Guarding prayer.
Guarding holiness.
Guarding their heart against compromise.
Not perfectly.
But genuinely.
There are believers right now crying out for deeper biblical understanding because shallow Christianity no longer satisfies them. That hunger matters.
Do not sleep through the season God is trying to wake you in.
Some warnings are actually mercy wearing a severe face.

And sometimes the most loving thing God does…
is send a watchman.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Battle of Barak Fighting Under Deborah’s Command
paragraphs: The Untold Battle of Barak Fighting Under Deborah’s Command
When Heaven Chooses a Different Kind of Warrior
There are battles that begin on battlefields.
And there are battles that begin inside the human heart.
The story of Barak is both.
Most Christians know the names.
Deborah. Barak. Sisera.
But few truly understand what happened beneath the surface of one of Israel's most dramatic military victories.
This was not merely a story about war.
It was a story about fear.
About hesitation.
About leadership.
About surrender.
About what happens when God chooses unexpected people to accomplish impossible things.
And perhaps most importantly...
It is a story that feels painfully familiar to every believer who has ever known exactly what God was asking them to do—and hesitated anyway.
The Book of Judges records one of the darkest periods in Israel's history.
The nation had entered a devastating cycle.
They would serve God.
Then drift.
Then rebel.
Then suffer oppression.
Then cry out.
Then God would rescue them.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Judges 4 opens with chilling words:
"And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the LORD..." (Judges 4:1)
The Hebrew phrase is:

וַיֹּסִפוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת הָרַע
(Vayosifu B'nei Yisrael La'asot Hara)
Literally:
"The children of Israel continued doing evil."
Not a single mistake.
Not a temporary failure.
A lifestyle of rebellion.
And rebellion always has consequences.
God allowed Israel to fall under the oppression of King Jabin of Canaan.
For twenty years they suffered.
Twenty years.
An entire generation growing up beneath fear.
An entire generation wondering if freedom would ever come.
The commander of Jabin's army was a man named Sisera.
A terrifying military leader who possessed nine hundred iron chariots.
In the ancient world, iron chariots were the equivalent of modern tanks.
Against them, Israel looked hopelessly outmatched.
Humanly speaking, victory was impossible.
And that is exactly when God loves to move.
Enter Deborah.
One of the most remarkable leaders in Scripture.
Judges 4:4 introduces her:

דְּבוֹרָה אִשָּׁה נְבִיאָה
(Devorah Ishah Nevi'ah)
"A woman, a prophetess."
Not merely someone who predicted the future.
The Hebrew word נְבִיאָה (Nevi'ah) means one who speaks the words of God.
Deborah was God's voice to a nation that had stopped listening.
She judged Israel beneath a palm tree.
People traveled from all over the land seeking wisdom.
Imagine that.
While military leaders trembled.
While tribes argued.
While oppression increased.
A woman sat beneath a tree faithfully hearing from God.
History often remembers warriors.
Heaven often remembers listeners.
Then God gave Deborah a message.
She summoned Barak.
His name in Hebrew is:

בָּרָק
(Barak)
Meaning:
"Lightning."
A powerful name.
A warrior's name.
A name that sounds fearless.
Yet names do not always reveal what is happening inside a person.
God's command was crystal clear.
Gather ten thousand men.
March to Mount Tabor.
Fight Sisera.
Victory is already promised.
No ambiguity.
No confusion.
No uncertainty.
God had spoken.
The mission was clear.
The outcome was guaranteed.
Yet Barak's response reveals one of the most human moments in Scripture.
Barak answered:
"If you will go with me, I will go. But if you will not go with me, I will not go."
Many modern readers immediately criticize him.
Coward.
Weak.
Faithless.
But perhaps we should be careful.
Because many of us have done exactly the same thing.
God says go.
We say:
"Only if someone comes with me."
God says trust Me.
We say:
"Can I have a backup plan?"
God says step forward.
We ask for guarantees.
Additional confirmations.
Extra signs.
More reassurance.
Barak was not merely facing soldiers.
He was facing fear.
The same fear that has stopped countless believers from obeying God's call.
Deborah agreed to go.
But she also delivered a startling prophecy.
The honor of the victory would not belong to Barak.
Instead, God would hand Sisera over to a woman.
At first glance this sounds like a rebuke.
And perhaps it partly was.
Yet there is something deeper happening.
God was teaching Israel a lesson.
Victory never belongs to human strength.
Victory belongs to God.
He can use a military commander.
A prophetess.
A housewife.
A shepherd.
A fisherman.
A tax collector.
A former persecutor.
Or a carpenter from Nazareth.
The power is never in the vessel.
The power is in the God who fills it.
The battle itself is described in greater detail in Judges 5.
What appears at first to be a normal military victory reveals something supernatural.
Deborah's victory song hints that Heaven itself entered the fight.
Judges 5:20 declares:
"The stars fought from heaven."
The Hebrew reads:

מִן־שָׁמַיִם נִלְחָמוּ הַכּוֹכָבִים
(Min-shamayim nilchamu hakokhavim)
"From the heavens the stars fought."
This poetic language suggests divine intervention.
Then Judges 5:21 mentions the Kishon River sweeping away the enemy.
Many scholars believe God sent a massive storm.
Sisera's iron chariots suddenly became useless in mud-filled terrain.
The very weapon that made him powerful became his weakness.
What looked unstoppable collapsed in a single day.
The God who controls weather does not fear iron.
The God who created rivers does not fear armies.
The God who spoke galaxies into existence does not fear impossible odds.
Sisera fled on foot.
Desperate.
Defeated.
Broken.
And then came one of the most shocking moments in Scripture.
He arrived at the tent of Jael.
A woman who appeared harmless.
Safe.
Insignificant.
Forgettable.
The kind of person military leaders overlook.
Exactly the kind of person God often uses.
While Sisera slept, believing he had escaped judgment, Jael carried out the prophecy Deborah had spoken.
The mighty commander who terrorized Israel for twenty years fell not on a battlefield but in a tent.
Not before an army.
Not before kings.
Not before generals.
Before God.
Because ultimately every earthly power answers to Him.
What does Barak's story mean for us today?
Everything.
Because many believers are living inside Barak's struggle.
You know God is calling you.
You know the next step.
You know the conversation that needs to happen.
You know the ministry He wants you to begin.
You know the sin He wants you to leave.
You know the forgiveness He wants you to offer.
You know the obedience He has already asked for.
But fear keeps negotiating.
Fear keeps delaying.
Fear keeps requesting more evidence.
More certainty.
More guarantees.
Yet faith was never designed to operate after certainty arrives.
Faith moves because God has spoken.
The Greek word for faith in the New Testament is:

πίστις
(Pistis)
Meaning trust.
Confidence.
Reliance.
Not confidence in ourselves.
Confidence in God.
Barak's story reminds us that God can still use imperfect faith.
That may be the most encouraging truth in the entire account.
Barak hesitated.
Yet Hebrews 11 still includes him among the heroes of faith.
Think about that.
The Bible remembers his hesitation.
But Heaven remembers his obedience.
God does not require flawless people.
He requires surrendered people.
Maybe you feel like Barak.
Maybe God has called you somewhere frightening.
Maybe the battle looks too large.
Maybe the opposition feels overwhelming.
Maybe your confidence has disappeared.
Maybe you're waiting for Deborah to walk beside you.
The lesson is not that fear disqualifies you.
The lesson is that fear must not govern you.
Courage is not the absence of fear.
Courage is obedience despite it.
And perhaps that is the untold battle.
Not the battle against Sisera.
Not the battle against chariots.
Not even the battle for Israel's freedom.
The greatest battle was the one inside Barak himself.
The war between fear and faith.
The war between hesitation and obedience.
The war every believer eventually faces.
And the same God who met Barak still meets His people today.
Still calling.
Still leading.
Still empowering.
Still delivering victories that human strength could never accomplish.
Because the battle has never belonged to us.
As Deborah declared in essence through her leadership, the Lord Himself goes before His people.
And when God goes before you, impossible odds become opportunities for His glory.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The battle that almost stopped your obedience may become the testimony that inspires someone else's faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nebuchadnezzar had everything men kill for.
paragraphs: Nebuchadnezzar had everything men kill for.
Power. Armies. Wealth. Influence. Palaces wrapped in gold. Nations trembling at the sound of his name.
He was not merely a king.
He was the king of Babylon.
The ruler of the greatest empire on earth.
And yet…
Scripture records one of the most terrifying psychological collapses in human history.

A king who once commanded empires ended up crawling through fields like an animal, drenched in dew, fingernails growing like claws, hair matted like eagle feathers, mind shattered beneath the judgment of God.
This is not mythology.
This is not metaphorical poetry.
This is a warning.
Because the most dangerous mental condition in the Bible was never madness.
It was pride.
And many people carrying it still look completely normal.

The story unfolds in the Book of Daniel, written partly in Aramaic, the imperial language of Babylon itself. That detail matters deeply because Daniel was not writing distant folklore. He was documenting events inside the very empire that ruled the known world.
In Daniel 4:30, Nebuchadnezzar stands over Babylon and says:
“Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…”
But the original Aramaic hits with far more force:

“הֲלָא־דָא הִיא בָבֶל רַבְּתָא דִּי אֲנָה בְנֵיתַהּ”
“Hălā dā hî Bāḇel rabbəṯā dî ʾănā bənêṯah”
Literally:
“Is this not Babylon the Great which I myself built…”
That phrase “אֲנָה” (“ʾănā”) means “I myself.”
Not God.
Not providence.
Not mercy.
Not blessing.
Not stewardship.
The disease had already consumed him long before the collapse came.
And that is how pride works.
It convinces people they are self-created.
Self-sustained.
Self-glorified.
Modern culture celebrates this sickness.

“Self-made.”
“Your truth.”
“You are your own god.”
“You manifested it.”
But Scripture keeps exposing the lie humanity keeps reposting.
The breath in your lungs is borrowed.
The mind in your skull is sustained by mercy.
The heartbeat in your chest is not self-generated.
One microscopic interruption in the brain and the strongest billionaire, athlete, celebrity, pastor, politician, influencer, or entrepreneur becomes fragile overnight.
Nebuchadnezzar forgot that.
And heaven interrupted him publicly.
Daniel 4:31 says:
“While the word was in the king’s mouth…”
Before he even finished speaking.
Judgment arrived mid-sentence.
There are moments where God allows people to continue in pride for years.
And then there are moments where heaven suddenly says:
Enough.
The decree came:
“the kingdom has departed from you.”
Not “might.”
Not “possibly.”
Departed.
Done.
Finished.
Then comes one of the most haunting descriptions in Scripture.
Daniel 4:33:
“He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox…”
The Aramaic phrase is devastating:

“וּמִן־אֲנָשָׁא טְרִיד”
“ū-min-ʾănāšā ṭərîḏ”
“Driven away from humanity.”
Not merely isolated.
Separated from human normalcy itself.
Some scholars associate this with a rare psychological condition called boanthropy — a disorder where a person believes they are cattle or an animal.
But Scripture does not reduce this merely to psychology.
This was spiritual humiliation.
God was showing the most powerful king alive what man truly is without Him.
Dust wearing temporary glory.
And suddenly the man who ruled empires could not rule his own mind.
Read that again slowly.
The man who controlled nations lost control of himself.
Because success without humility is lethal to the soul.
Many people ask:
“Why would God do something so severe?”
Because Nebuchadnezzar’s pride was not merely personal arrogance.
It was self-deification.
The ancient kings of Babylon viewed themselves as almost divine. Nebuchadnezzar had crossed into the oldest satanic temptation in history:
“You shall be as gods.”
The same lie whispered in Eden still destroys people now.
You can see it everywhere today.

People worship followers.
Worship beauty.
Worship intellect.
Worship influence.
Worship politics.
Worship platforms.
Worship money.
Worship themselves.
And society applauds narcissism as confidence.
But heaven sees deeper than branding.
God was not destroying Nebuchadnezzar.
He was breaking him to save him.
That changes everything.
Because Daniel had warned him beforehand.
Daniel 4:27:
“Break off your sins by practicing righteousness…”
The Aramaic word for “break off” is “פְּרֻק” (“pərūq”).
It carries the idea of tearing away decisively.
Repentance is not cosmetic adjustment.
It is violent separation from sin.
Nebuchadnezzar was given mercy before judgment came.
Just like many people reading this right now.
Warnings ignored eventually become consequences experienced.
Still…
The story does not end in madness.
And that may be the most beautiful part.
After the humiliation…
After the isolation…
After the collapse…
After losing everything…
Nebuchadnezzar finally looked upward.
Daniel 4:34 says:
“I lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me.”
Do not miss that.
His sanity returned when his gaze changed direction.
The Aramaic phrase:

“וּמַנְדְּעִי עֲלַי יְתוּב”
“ū-mandəʿî ʿălay yəṯūḇ”
“My understanding returned to me.”
The restoration of the mind came after surrender.
That is devastatingly relevant right now.
Because many people are mentally exhausted not only from stress…
…but from carrying the crushing weight of self-rule.
Trying to be their own savior.
Their own god.
Their own source of worth.
Their own healer.
Their own redeemer.
Human beings were never designed to carry that throne.
Only God can sit there without destroying the soul beneath it.
Nebuchadnezzar finally understood this.
And listen carefully to what he says next.
Daniel 4:37:
“Those who walk in pride He is able to humble.”
Not “might.”
Able.
The Hebrew mindset behind biblical pride is not mere confidence.
The Greek New Testament later uses the word “ὑπερήφανος” (“hyperēphanos”) for the proud — literally meaning someone who appears above others, elevated beyond proper measure.
Pride is elevation beyond truth.
Humility is agreement with reality.
And reality is this:
Without God, every human being is fragile.

One diagnosis.
One accident.
One stroke.
One economic collapse.
One tragedy.
One phone call.
One breath.
That is all it takes.
The terrifying thing about pride is that it blinds people while convincing them they see clearly.
Nebuchadnezzar lost his kingdom long before he lost his mind.
His insanity simply exposed what pride had already done internally.
And honestly…
Some people reading this are exhausted because they have spent years pretending to be strong while spiritually collapsing inside.
Smiling publicly.
Bleeding privately.
Building Babylon externally.
Breaking internally.
You can fool followers.
You can fool family.
You can fool church people.
You can fool social media.
But eventually the soul reveals who sits on the throne.
This story is unforgettable because it exposes every human heart.
We all want control.
We all want glory.
We all want to believe we built ourselves.
And yet the Gospel confronts us with something humbling:
You cannot save yourself.
That is why Jesus Christ came.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is surrender.
It is the Son of God stepping into human weakness to rescue people consumed by sin, pride, rebellion, fear, shame, lust, addiction, bitterness, and spiritual blindness.
Philippians 2 describes Jesus with stunning contrast to Nebuchadnezzar.
Nebuchadnezzar exalted himself and was humbled.
Jesus humbled Himself and was exalted.
The Greek says Christ:

“ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν”
“Heauton ekenōsen”
“He emptied Himself.”
The King of Heaven became low to save the proud.
That is the scandalous beauty of grace.
And maybe that is why this story hits so deeply.
Because somewhere inside, many people know pride has been eating them alive too.
Not just arrogance.
But silent self-dependence.
Secret control.
Refusal to surrender.
Performing strength while drowning internally.
Nebuchadnezzar’s story proves something terrifying and hopeful at the same time:
God can break a man completely…
…and still restore him mercifully.
That means your collapse is not automatically your end.
Your failure is not beyond redemption.
Your mental exhaustion is not beyond Christ.
Your pride is not stronger than grace.
Your past is not too filthy for the cross.
But pride must die.
And that is the part many people resist.
Because pride would rather lose everything than kneel.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone you love is slowly destroying themselves through pride, anger, control, ego, or self-worship, share this with them before life humbles them publicly.
And never forget this:
The same God who humbled a king in the wilderness still knows how to rescue people lost inside themselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Herodias is one of the most haunting women in all of Scripture.
paragraphs: Herodias is one of the most haunting women in all of Scripture.
Not because Scripture spends many chapters on her.
It does not.
But because in only a few verses, God exposes something terrifying about the human heart when lust, pride, bitterness, political ambition, and hatred toward truth are left unrepented.
Her story is not ultimately about seduction.
It is about rebellion against God’s order.
It is about a woman who hated the voice that confronted her sin.
And in the end… that hatred demanded a prophet’s head.
The tragedy of Herodias is not merely historical.
It is spiritual.

Because there are still people today who do not mind hearing preaching…
until the preaching touches the thing they refuse to surrender.
And that is where Herodias becomes terrifyingly relevant.
The primary accounts concerning Herodias are found in Gospel of Matthew 14:1–12 and Gospel of Mark 6:14–29.
To understand her properly, we must first understand the corrupted family she belonged to.
Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great.
The same Herod who attempted to murder the infant Christ in Bethlehem.
Already, the spiritual atmosphere surrounding this dynasty was dark, paranoid, violent, and consumed with power.
Herodias first married Herod Philip, who was her half-uncle.
Later, she abandoned him and entered into a relationship with another uncle — Herod Antipas.
This was not simply scandalous culturally.
It was unlawful before God.
John the Baptist publicly confronted this union.
And that confrontation ignited the rage that would eventually lead to his death.
The Greek text in Mark 6:18 says:
“Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.”
Transliterated:
“Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gunaika tou adelphou sou.”
Literal translation:
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
The phrase “οὐκ ἔξεστίν” (ouk exestin) means “it is not permitted” or “it is unlawful.”
John was not giving personal opinion.
He was declaring divine law.
This statement reaches back into the Torah itself.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, Leviticus 18:16 says:
“עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה”
Transliteration:
“Ervat eshet achikha lo tegalleh.”
Literal meaning:
