And perhaps one of the greatest tragedies is that millions have formed strong opinions about Paul's words without ever examining what Paul actually wrote, what his audience actually heard, and what the original language actually meant.
Because when we slow down and enter the world of the first century, the picture becomes far more profound—and far more beautiful—than many realize.
The story begins long before Paul ever picked up a pen.
It begins in Eden.
The Hebrew word for man is:
אָדָם (Adam)
The Hebrew word for woman is:
אִשָּׁה (Ishah)
Genesis does not portray woman as an afterthought.
When God says:
"It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18)
The helper God creates is described as:
עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (ezer kenegdo)
Many English readers mistakenly hear "helper" and imagine an assistant.
Yet the Hebrew word ezer is frequently used of God Himself helping Israel.
It describes strength.
Rescue.
Support.
Not inferiority.
From the beginning, Scripture presents men and women as equally bearing God's image.
Genesis 1:27 says:
"So God created mankind in His own image... male and female He created them."
The image of God was never reserved for one gender.
Yet when we arrive at Paul's letters, something seems to change.
Particularly in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35:
"The women should keep silent in the churches."
In Greek:

αἱ γυναῖκες ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν
(hai gynaikes en tais ekklēsiais sigatōsan)
The critical word is:
σιγάτωσαν (sigatōsan)
Many assume it means permanent silence.
But here's where context changes everything.
Earlier in the same chapter, Paul uses the same root word when instructing tongue-speakers to remain silent if no interpreter is present.
He also tells prophets to remain silent when another receives revelation.
The command isn't absolute.
It's situational.
Temporary.
Orderly.
Paul is regulating disruptions.
Not erasing voices.
This matters enormously.
Because only three chapters earlier, Paul explicitly acknowledges women praying and prophesying publicly in worship.
1 Corinthians 11:5 says:
"Every woman who prays or prophesies..."
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say women cannot speak.
He assumes they already are.
And prophecy in the New Testament was hardly silent.
How could Paul prohibit all female speech in chapter 14 if he already recognized female prayer and prophecy in chapter 11?
Something else is happening.
Something contextual.
Something many modern readers miss.
Corinth was chaotic.
Wildly chaotic.
The church gatherings often resembled disorder more than worship.
People interrupted one another.
Prophets competed for attention.
Tongues erupted without interpretation.
The wealthy shamed the poor.
Communion became divided.
Everything Paul addresses in 1 Corinthians revolves around restoring order.
The silence command appears inside a larger section about preventing interruptions during worship.
Many biblical scholars believe certain women were publicly disrupting teachings by asking questions across the assembly.
Why?
In the first-century Greco-Roman world, many women had little formal education compared to men.
New converts often entered church gatherings eager but inexperienced.
Paul's instruction may specifically address disruptive questioning rather than faithful participation.
Notice verse 35:
"If they desire to learn something, let them ask their husbands at home."
The issue appears connected to learning and interruptions—not preaching, praying, or prophesying.
The context matters.
The audience matters.
The language matters.
And suddenly the passage becomes less about suppression and more about order.
But the discussion does not end there.
Many point to another difficult text.
1 Timothy 2:12.
"I do not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man."
The Greek reads:

οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω δὲ γυναικὶ διδάσκειν
(ouk epitrepō de gynaiki didaskein)
The controversy often centers around:
αὐθεντεῖν (authentein)
Translated in many versions as "exercise authority."
But this word is extraordinarily rare.
It appears nowhere else in the New Testament.
Its historical usage often carried ideas of domineering, controlling, or usurping authority rather than simply possessing legitimate leadership.
The city where Timothy ministered was Ephesus.
Ephesus was saturated with false teaching.
Paul repeatedly warns Timothy about deception spreading through the congregation.
Some scholars believe Paul was addressing a specific local crisis involving false doctrine and abusive authority rather than issuing a universal ban for all churches throughout all history.
Regardless of where one lands in that debate, one fact remains undeniable.
Paul consistently partnered with women in ministry.
Consider the evidence.
Paul commends Phoebe.
Romans 16:1 calls her:
διάκονον (diakonon)
A servant or deacon of the church.
He praises Priscilla, who alongside Aquila helped instruct Apollos more accurately in doctrine.
He greets Junia, whom many scholars identify as being notable among the apostles.
He repeatedly acknowledges women as fellow workers in the Gospel.
If Paul fundamentally opposed women participating in ministry, his own ministry partnerships become difficult to explain.
The deeper we look, the more we discover a man concerned not with silencing women but with protecting truth, order, and faithful discipleship.
And perhaps that brings us to the real issue.
Because many believers are not actually wrestling with Paul.
They're wrestling with pain.
Some women have been dismissed, overlooked, or wounded using isolated verses as weapons.
Some men have inherited interpretations they never personally examined.
Some churches have elevated traditions above context.
Some have reacted by abandoning biblical authority altogether.
The answer is not to ignore difficult passages.
Nor is it to weaponize them.
The answer is to wrestle honestly with Scripture.
To study carefully.
To seek truth humbly.
To love deeply.
Because Jesus never feared women.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman when others would not.
He welcomed Mary as a disciple at His feet.
He healed women publicly.
He defended women repeatedly.
And in one of history's most astonishing moments, the first witnesses of His resurrection were women.
The risen Christ entrusted world-changing news to voices society often ignored.
That should make all of us pause.
The debate over Paul's words will likely continue.
Faithful Christians reach different conclusions regarding church leadership roles.
Yet whatever position one holds, Scripture is crystal clear on this truth:
Women are not second-class citizens in the Kingdom of God.
They are image bearers.
Disciples.
Co-heirs of grace.
Valuable members of Christ's body.
Loved by the same Savior who shed His blood for men and women alike.
Maybe that's why this conversation matters so much.
Because behind every theological argument stands a real person.
A daughter.
A mother.
A sister.
A believer trying to understand God's heart.
And perhaps the greatest question is not:
"What can women do?"
But:
"How can the Church faithfully honor everything God actually said?"
That question requires humility from all of us.
Sit with it.
Open your Bible.
Read the passages yourself.
Search the context.
Ask God for wisdom.
And if you've ever felt wounded by how these verses were used against you, remember that Christ invites honest seekers closer—not farther away.
The verses that trouble us most are often the ones that force us to dig deep enough to discover the heart of God hiding beneath the surface.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who look spiritually alive… but inwardly, they are exhausted.
paragraphs: There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who look spiritually alive… but inwardly, they are exhausted.
Not because they stopped loving Jesus.
But because somewhere along the way, they confused serving Christ with sitting at His feet.
And the terrifying part is this…
Martha never stopped believing in Jesus.
She simply became too distracted to enjoy Him.
That is why the story of Martha and Mary is one of the most misunderstood and emotionally dangerous passages in the entire Bible.
Because this story is not merely about two sisters.
It is about two kinds of Christians.
And if we are honest…
both women are living inside many of us at the exact same time.
In Luke 10:38–42, Scripture says:
“Now it happened as they went that He entered a certain village; and a certain woman named Martha welcomed Him into her house.”
At first glance, Martha appears admirable.
Responsible.
Faithful.
Productive.
Dependable.
The type every church depends on.
The Greek word used in Luke 10:40 says Martha was:
“περιεσπᾶτο” (periespato)

Meaning:
“dragged away,”
“pulled apart,”
“distracted in many directions.”
This is far deeper than being “busy.”
The word paints the image of a soul being internally torn apart.
Martha was not simply cooking dinner.
Her spirit was being violently fragmented.
And this is where modern Christianity quietly breaks people.
Because many believers are applauded for spiritual productivity while their intimacy with Christ is slowly dying in silence.
Martha welcomed Jesus into the house…
but Mary welcomed Jesus into her heart.
That distinction changes everything.
Luke writes:
The phrase “sat at His feet” in Jewish culture carried massive spiritual meaning.
This was the posture of a disciple.
In Acts 22:3, Paul says he was educated “at the feet of Gamaliel.”

To sit at someone’s feet meant:
“I surrender to your authority.”
“I want your wisdom.”
“I belong to your teaching.”
Mary was not being lazy.
Mary chose devotion over performance.
And religion hates that.
Because religious systems often reward visible labor more than hidden intimacy.
But heaven does not measure faithfulness the way crowds do.
Then comes one of the most emotionally revealing moments in Scripture.
Martha finally explodes.
“Lord, do You not care…?”
That sentence exposes the human heart.
People overwhelmed by serving eventually begin questioning the love of God.
That still happens today.

People pray:
“Lord, do You not care that I’m carrying this family?”
“Do You not care that I’m burned out?”
“Do You not care that I’m doing everything alone?”
Martha’s frustration was not ultimately with Mary.
It was with God.
Busyness had distorted her perception of Jesus.
And then Christ responds with heartbreaking tenderness.
“Martha, Martha…”
Whenever names are repeated in Scripture, it signals deep emotion.

“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
“Saul, Saul.”
Jesus was not rebuking her with cruelty.
He was grieving for her.
Then He says:
“You are anxious and troubled about many things.”
The Greek words here are devastatingly revealing.

“μεριμνᾷς” (merimnas)
means:
to be mentally pulled apart by anxiety.

“θορυβάζῃ” (thorybazē)
means:
inner turmoil,
noise,
restlessness,
emotional disturbance.
Martha’s problem was never cooking.
Her problem was internal noise.
And that describes countless Christians today.
Always active.
Always posting.
Always serving.
Always doing ministry.
Yet spiritually starving.
Some people know church culture better than they know the voice of God.
That sentence hurts because many of us recognize ourselves inside it.
Then Jesus says something revolutionary:
“But one thing is necessary.”
The Greek says:

“ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία”
(Henos de estin chreia)
“Only one thing is truly needed.”
Not ten things.
Not endless striving.
Not spiritual image management.
One thing.
Presence with Him.
And then comes the line that destroys the performance-based mindset of modern Christianity:
“Mary has chosen the good portion.”
The phrase “good portion” echoes Psalm 16:5:
“The LORD is the portion of my inheritance.”
Mary chose Christ Himself as her inheritance.
Not activity.
Not appearance.
Not reputation.
Jesus was enough.
This is the untold truth most people miss:
Martha represents Christians who know how to work for Jesus.
Mary represents Christians who know how to love Jesus.
And many churches unconsciously produce Marthas faster than Marys.
We train people to lead before teaching them to linger.
To perform before they learn surrender.
To preach before they learn silence.
To serve before they learn worship.
And eventually souls collapse under the weight of religious performance.
Because activity without intimacy always becomes exhausting.
But intimacy with Christ transforms obedience into delight.
The shocking part is this:
Martha was close to Jesus physically…
while remaining emotionally distant internally.
That still happens every Sunday.
People can sing worship songs while their hearts are miles away.
They can quote Scripture while privately feeling numb.
They can lead ministries while secretly feeling spiritually dead.
Outward closeness does not guarantee inward communion.
Mary understood something Martha did not yet understand:
Jesus did not come merely to be used.
He came to be loved.
And here is the part almost nobody talks about…
Martha eventually changed.
In John 11, after Lazarus dies, Martha runs to Jesus again.
But this time something is different.
She says:
“Yes, Lord; I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God…”
Pain transformed her theology into surrender.
Sometimes heartbreak becomes the doorway into deeper intimacy with Christ.
Some of you reading this have spent years being Martha.

Serving.
Carrying.
Fixing.
Managing.
Performing.
Pretending you’re spiritually okay.

But inwardly…
you are tired in places nobody sees.
And Jesus is not asking you to abandon responsibility.
He is asking you to stop trying to earn closeness with Him through constant striving.
Because salvation was never built on your performance.
The Hebrew concept of rest throughout Scripture is deeply connected to trust.
The word “שָׁלוֹם” (shalom) does not merely mean peace.

It means:
wholeness,
completeness,
nothing missing,
nothing broken.
Mary found shalom at the feet of Christ.
Martha found fragmentation inside distraction.
And many believers today are collapsing emotionally because they are trying to carry burdens Jesus never asked them to carry.
You do not have to become spiritually famous to be deeply loved by God.
You do not have to constantly prove your worth to heaven.

Jesus never said:
“Come to Me all who are productive.”
He said:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for “rest” there is:
“ἀναπαύσω” (anapausō)

Meaning:
to refresh,
to revive,
to give calm strength again.
Not temporary escape.
Deep restoration.
And maybe that is why this story survives across centuries.
Because every generation creates more Marthas.
Anxious believers.
Exhausted disciples.
Overstimulated Christians trying to earn what Jesus already purchased at the cross.
But heaven still honors Marys.

People who know how to stop.
Listen.
Weep.
Worship.
Remain.
People who choose presence over applause.
The frightening reality is this:
A Christian can spend years working in God’s house while neglecting God Himself.
And eventually the soul notices the difference.
Be honest…
When was the last time you sat with Jesus without rushing?
Without multitasking?
Without checking notifications every few minutes?
Without turning prayer into a performance?
Without secretly measuring your spiritual worth by productivity?
This story was never meant to shame hardworking believers.
It was meant to rescue them.
Because Jesus loved Martha too much to leave her trapped inside anxious striving.
And He loves you too much to leave you there either.
And if you know someone silently drowning beneath pressure, burnout, anxiety, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them today.
Some people are not losing faith…
they are losing intimacy.
And never forget this:
Some people are busy serving God while starving for God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people never notice this.
paragraphs: Most people never notice this.
The first man in Scripture to take more than one wife was not introduced as wise, blessed, righteous, or favored by God.
He was introduced as violent.
That is not an accident.

The first polygamist in the Bible was Lamech, a descendant of Cain — the same bloodline that flowed from the first murderer in human history. And the moment Scripture introduces polygamy into the human story, it places it inside a family line already corrupted by rebellion, pride, vengeance, and bloodshed.
God saw it.
And He recorded it exactly as it happened.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Bible often describes things without approving them.

Many people assume that because certain men in the Old Testament practiced polygamy, God must have endorsed it. But Scripture repeatedly shows the destruction, jealousy, division, and spiritual decay that followed it.
The very first appearance of polygamy sets the tone.

Violence.
Pride.
Self-exaltation.
Defiance against God’s design.
You knew there was something deeper there.
God’s Original Design Was One Man and One Woman
Before sin entered the world, God established marriage in Eden.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
In Hebrew:

וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-davaq be-ishto ve-hayu le-vasar echad
Key phrases matter here.
“His wife” — Singular
The Hebrew word:

אִשְׁתּוֹ (ishto)
“his wife”
Singular.
Not wives.
From the beginning, God’s covenant pattern was covenantal unity between one man and one woman becoming “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself later reaffirmed this in the Greek text of Matthew 19:4–6.
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female…”
Greek:

ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς
arsen kai thēly epoiēsen autous
“male and female He made them”
Then Christ quotes Genesis directly and concludes:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Jesus did not point to polygamy as the model.
He pointed back to Eden.
Back before sin multiplied corruption.
Back before human rebellion distorted covenant.
Cain’s Line: Civilization Without God
Genesis 4 presents two family lines developing in parallel.

Cain’s descendants advanced culturally:
cities,
music,
metalworking,
technology.
But spiritually, the line became increasingly corrupted.
Then suddenly Genesis 4:19 says:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives…”
Hebrew:

וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
vayyiqqach-lo Lemech shtei nashim
Literally:
“Lamech took for himself two women/wives.”
The wording matters.
“Taken for himself.”
Self-directed desire.
Not divine instruction.
Not covenant blessing.
Not God speaking.
Lamech becomes the first human in biblical history to violate the one-man-one-woman pattern established in Eden.
And immediately after introducing his polygamy, Scripture records a chilling song of violence.
That sequence is intentional.
Lamech’s Song of Violence
Genesis 4:23–24 is one of the darkest speeches in early human history.
Lamech says to his wives:

“Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech:
for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.”
Hebrew:

כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי
ki ish haragti le-fitz‘i
“For I killed a man for wounding me”
And then:
“If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.”
Hebrew:

שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה
shiv‘im ve-shiv‘ah
“seventy-sevenfold”
This is not repentance.
This is boastful escalation.
Cain murdered and feared judgment.
Lamech murders and celebrates himself.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this moment reveals something terrifying about unchecked sin: it never stays still.

Violence grows.
Pride grows.
Sexual rebellion grows.
Human self-worship grows.
Sin always evolves toward greater corruption unless God intervenes.
The Connection Between Violence and Sexual Corruption
The placement of this passage matters deeply.
The Bible could have introduced polygamy anywhere.
But God chose to introduce it in the context of a violent, arrogant man descended from Cain.
That literary structure is theological.
Scripture is showing the unraveling of creation order.
One rebellion leads to another.
When humans reject God’s authority in one area, corruption spreads into others.
Paul later explains this spiritual principle in Romans 1.

People suppress truth,
exchange God’s design,
then become consumed by disordered desires and violence.
Sin never remains isolated.
You see this pattern throughout the Old Testament.

Nearly every major polygamous household becomes marked by:
jealousy,
division,
competition,
sexual sin,
family destruction,
or bloodshed.

Abraham and Hagar.
Jacob with Leah and Rachel.
David’s fractured household.
Solomon’s downfall.
The pattern repeats again and again.
Not because God approved of it.
But because Scripture tells the truth about fallen humanity.
God saw it.
What About the Patriarchs?
Many skeptics ask:
“If polygamy was wrong, why did God allow it?”
Because God often permits what He does not endorse.

The same Scriptures that record polygamy also record:
divorce,
slavery,
idolatry,
human sacrifice,
murder,
and rebellion.
Description is not approval.
Jesus explained this principle regarding divorce in Matthew 19:8:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
From the beginning.
Christ keeps bringing humanity back to God’s original design.

Not cultural normalization.
Not fallen tradition.
Not human appetite.
Truth.
The Hebrew Structure Reveals a Warning
There is another detail many readers miss.

Genesis 4 contrasts two voices:
Cain’s corrupted lineage
and Seth’s godly lineage in Genesis 5.
Lamech from Cain’s line boasts in violence.
But later another Lamech — from Seth’s line — speaks hope over Noah.
Genesis 5:29:
“This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands…”
Hebrew:

זֶה יְנַחֲמֵנוּ
zeh yenachamenu
“This one will comfort us”
One Lamech glorifies vengeance.
The other longs for redemption.
The contrast is intentional.

Two spiritual paths.
Two legacies.
Two kingdoms.

One built on pride and self-rule.
The other waiting for God’s mercy.
Christ Reverses the Curse of Violent Men
The Gospel does not merely condemn sinners.
It rescues them.
Lamech bragged about seventy-sevenfold vengeance.
But Jesus later transformed that number entirely.
In Matthew 18:22, when Peter asked how many times forgiveness should be offered, Jesus answered:
“Until seventy times seven.”
Greek:

ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta
Lamech used “seventy-seven” for revenge.
Jesus used it for mercy.
That is not coincidence.
That is redemption overturning the spirit of Cain.

The kingdom of darkness multiplies vengeance.
The kingdom of Christ multiplies forgiveness.
Only Jesus can reverse what sin has corrupted.
Only Christ can transform violent hearts into redeemed hearts.
Only the cross can reconcile what rebellion destroyed.
Because at the center of human corruption is not merely bad behavior.
It is sin.
And sin separates humanity from God.
That is why Jesus came.

Not simply to improve morality.
Not merely to repair culture.
But to save sinners through His blood.
The Greek of John 3:16 declares:

Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho Theos ton kosmon
“For God so loved the world…”
Christ entered the violence of humanity and absorbed judgment at the cross.
The innocent One died for the guilty.
The sinless One carried sinners.
The risen Christ now calls every person to repentance and faith.

Not self-justification.
Not religious performance.
Repentance.
Faith.
Surrender.
Because the same sinful nature that existed in Cain and Lamech still exists in humanity now.

Pride.
Lust.
Violence.
Self-rule.
You knew.
God saw it.
And yet Christ still offers mercy.
If this exposed something inside you, don’t ignore it. Write “Jesus is Lord” if you know only Christ can change the human heart.
And if you want deeper teachings that uncover Scripture in its original context, grow your understanding of biblical truth, and strengthen your walk with Christ, join here:
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He looked strong enough to tear apart lions… but weak enough to be destroyed by the thing he never crucified inside himself.
paragraphs: He looked strong enough to tear apart lions… but weak enough to be destroyed by the thing he never crucified inside himself.
That is the terrifying part about Samson.
It wasn’t Delilah.
It wasn’t the Philistines.
It wasn’t even betrayal.
Samson was destroyed by appetites he kept entertaining while still expecting God to keep empowering him.
Most people preach Samson like he was simply a victim of a seductive woman.
Scripture tells a far more uncomfortable story.
Because long before Delilah ever touched his life… Samson had already been drifting away from consecration.
Judges 13 says Samson was called before birth. An angel of the LORD appeared to his mother and declared that the child would be a Nazirite “from the womb.”

The Hebrew word used is:
נָזִיר (nāzîr)

It means:
“consecrated,”
“separated,”
“devoted unto God.”
Samson was not ordinary.
His hair was not magic.
His calling was covenant.
That matters.
Because people keep misunderstanding the source of his strength.
The power was never in the hair itself.
The hair represented separation.
Holiness.
A visible covenant.
The tragedy of Samson is not that he lost his hair.
The tragedy is that he slowly stopped valuing the God the covenant belonged to.
Judges 14 begins exposing the deeper issue.
“And Samson went down to Timnath, and saw a woman…”
That phrase “went down” is spiritually important throughout Scripture.
He kept going down.

Down morally.
Down spiritually.
Down internally.
The pattern repeats.

He sees.
He desires.
He takes.
No restraint.
No surrender.
No self-government.
The Hebrew mindset connected wisdom with mastery over desires.
Proverbs 25:28 says:
“He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.”

The Hebrew word for spirit there is:
רוּחַ (ruach)

It can mean:
spirit,
mind,
breath,
inner impulses.

Samson could overpower armies…
but not his own impulses.
That is the real warning.

Some people can preach publicly…
and still be collapsing privately.

Some can cast out demons…
while secretly feeding lust.

Some can lead worship…
while entertaining compromise they refuse to kill.
Giftedness can hide dysfunction for a season.
But what you refuse to control will eventually control you.
That is exactly what happened to Samson.
By the time Delilah appears in Judges 16, Samson is already spiritually compromised.
He had touched dead things despite Nazirite laws.
He had reckless anger.
Unrestrained lust.
Pride.
Spiritual carelessness.
Delilah was not the beginning of his destruction.
She was the exposure of what was already rotting inside him.
Judges 16:16 says:
“And it came to pass, when she pressed him daily with her words…”
That phrase matters deeply.
Because temptation is rarely instant destruction.

It is pressure.
Repetition.
Erosion.
Fatigue.
The enemy studies persistence.

Little compromises.
Little lusts.
Little entertainments.
Little hidden conversations.
Little secret addictions.
Until conviction gets quieter.
Then eventually…
you stop noticing how far you drifted.
The Hebrew idea behind temptation was often connected to being enticed or lured away internally.
James explains this perfectly in Greek.
James 1:14 says:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.”
The Greek says:

ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται
ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας
ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος
“Each person is tempted by his own desire, being dragged away and baited.”

ἐπιθυμία (epithymia)
means:
craving,
desire,
longing,
lustful appetite.
Notice this carefully.
James does not say Satan forced him.
It says his own desires dragged him away.
That is Samson.
People want to rebuke devils while protecting appetites.
But spiritual warfare means nothing if the flesh remains enthroned.
Galatians 5:16 says:
“Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.”

The Greek word for flesh is:
σάρξ (sarx)
Not merely the physical body.
It refers to the fallen human nature that rebels against God.

Samson had moments of supernatural strength…
while still feeding the flesh.
And eventually the flesh collected its payment.
That is why Judges 16:20 is one of the saddest verses in Scripture:
“But he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.”
“He did not know…”
That should terrify every believer.
Imagine falling so slowly that you no longer recognize the absence of God’s presence.
Imagine becoming so numb that compromise feels normal.
That is why secret sin is deadly.
Not because God stops loving you.
But because repeated compromise hardens sensitivity.
The strongest man in Israel became weak long before his hair was cut.
The haircut was merely the visible manifestation of an invisible surrender.
Then comes the devastating image.
The Philistines gouged out his eyes.

The man ruled by what he saw…
ended blind.
Sin often judges symbolically.
The thing you refuse to surrender eventually becomes the thing that humiliates you publicly.
But even here…
God’s mercy appears.
Judges 16:22 says:
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again…”
That line is soaked in grace.
Because God was not finished with him.
Broken people still matter to God.
Failed people still matter to God.
Repentant people still matter to God.
Samson’s final prayer in Hebrew is powerful:

אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא
(Adonai YHWH zokhreni na)
“O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee.”

Not:
“Make me famous again.”

Not:
“Restore my image.”

Not:
“Protect my reputation.”

Simply:
“Remember me.”
And God answered.
Hebrews 11 later includes Samson among the faithful.
Think about that.

A flawed man.
A compromised man.
A fallen man.
Still remembered by grace.
Because the Gospel has always been about redemption, not human perfection.
But do not miss the warning buried inside his story.

You can be called…
and still careless.

Anointed…
and still undisciplined.

Used by God…
and still secretly feeding the thing trying to destroy you.
The real enemy in Samson’s life was never merely Delilah.
It was the unchecked appetite he kept defending.
And many believers are doing the same thing now.
Entertaining what should be crucified.
Normalizing what should be repented of.
Negotiating with sin while asking God for power.
You cannot consistently feed the flesh and expect spiritual authority to remain untouched.
Eventually something breaks.

Your peace.
Your purity.
Your discernment.
Your marriage.
Your calling.
Your intimacy with God.
Whatever you refuse to surrender will eventually demand more than you planned to give.
Romans 8:13 says:
“For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.”

The Greek word for “mortify” is:
θανατοῦτε (thanatoute)

It literally means:
“put to death.”

Not manage it.
Not rename it.
Not excuse it.
Kill it.
Because tolerated sin never stays small.
And maybe this is why Samson’s story still shakes people centuries later.
We see ourselves in him.

Strong outside.
Undisciplined inside.

Public victories.
Private compromise.

A calling from God…
while secretly wrestling appetites we keep postponing surrendering.
But Jesus came precisely for people like Samson.

People who failed.
People who drifted.
People who compromised.
People who are tired of pretending they are still spiritually healthy while slowly dying inside.
The cross is proof that God still pursues people who made a mess of their consecration.
But grace is not permission to continue drifting.
Grace is the power to finally surrender.
Completely.
Not partially.
Not emotionally.
Actually.
Maybe that hidden thing has already started cutting away at your spiritual strength and you know it.

The conversations.
The lust.
The addiction.
The pride.
The anger.
The secret double life.
The compromise nobody sees.
And maybe this hit harder because deep down… you know Delilah is not your real problem either.
The most dangerous chains are the ones you defend while calling yourself free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS SAY TO LOVE YOUR ENEMIES?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SAY TO LOVE YOUR ENEMIES?
The Command That Feels Impossible… Until You Understand the Cross
There are verses that comfort us.
There are verses that encourage us.
And then there are verses that stop us in our tracks.

Verses that confront our pride.
Our wounds.
Our desire for revenge.
Our secret wish to see certain people suffer for what they did.
Few teachings of Jesus cut deeper than these words:

"But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
(Matthew 5:44)
For many people, this may be the most difficult command in the entire Bible.
Love your enemies?
The person who betrayed you?
The family member who abandoned you?
The spouse who shattered your trust?
The friend who spread lies about you?
The person who took advantage of your kindness?
Surely Jesus could not mean that literally.
But He did.
And the reason He did may reveal one of the greatest mysteries of the Gospel.
Because Jesus was not merely teaching us how to treat our enemies.
He was revealing how God treated us.
The Day the Crowd Wanted Blood
Imagine standing in first-century Judea.
Dust fills the air.
The Roman Empire rules with an iron fist.
Religious leaders compete for power.
Hatred divides groups into camps.

People despise tax collectors.
Zealots despise Romans.
Pharisees despise sinners.
Samaritans and Jews avoid one another.
The world Jesus entered was not very different from ours.

Political division.
Religious hostility.
Cultural hatred.
Personal grudges.
And into that atmosphere Jesus spoke words no one expected.
The Greek text records His command as:

"ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν"
(agapate tous echthrous humōn)
Literally:
"Love your enemies."
The word used is not emotional affection.
It is not romance.
It is not friendship.
It is the Greek word "ἀγαπάω" (agapaō).
A deliberate, sacrificial, covenantal love.
A love that chooses the good of another regardless of personal cost.
Jesus was not commanding feelings.
He was commanding actions flowing from transformed hearts.
That changes everything.
Because many believers spend years feeling guilty for not having warm emotions toward those who hurt them.
Jesus never said you must feel affection.
He said you must choose love.
The Difference Changes Lives.
The Ancient Roots Hidden in Hebrew Scripture
To understand Jesus' command, we must go back hundreds of years.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a God whose mercy extends beyond human expectations.
One of the most powerful Hebrew words is:

חֶסֶד
(chesed)
Often translated as:

"Lovingkindness"
"Mercy"
"Steadfast love"
"Covenant faithfulness"
No English word fully captures it.
Chesed is God's faithful love toward people who often fail Him.
It is love that remains when justice alone would walk away.
This divine pattern appears throughout the Old Testament.
God continually pursues rebellious people.
He calls wandering nations back.
He forgives repeated failures.
He extends mercy where punishment seems deserved.
Jesus was not introducing a new God.
He was revealing the heart of the same God.
The God of chesed.
The God who keeps loving people who keep running.
The Problem We Never Notice
Most people read Matthew 5 assuming they are the righteous victims.
We picture ourselves loving difficult people.
We imagine ourselves extending grace.
But Scripture forces a painful realization.
Before we had earthly enemies...
We were enemies of God.
The Apostle Paul writes:
(Romans 5:8)
A few verses later:

"For if when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son..."
(Romans 5:10)
Read that again.
Enemies.
Not strangers.
Not neutral observers.
Enemies.
The Gospel begins with a shocking truth:
The greatest enemy God ever loved was humanity itself.
Including you.
Including me.
Before we loved Him.
Before we obeyed Him.
Before we sought Him.
Christ moved toward us.
Not away from us.
The Cross Changes Everything
The command to love enemies cannot be separated from Calvary.
At the crucifixion, Jesus experienced betrayal, mockery, false accusations, torture, abandonment, humiliation, and execution.
If anyone ever had the right to seek vengeance, it was Him.
The crowds mocked Him.
The soldiers beat Him.
The religious leaders celebrated His suffering.
Yet from the cross He prayed:

"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
(Luke 23:34)
This was not weakness.
This was divine strength.
The Aramaic language spoken by Jesus contains a rich concept behind forgiveness.
The idea is not pretending evil never happened.
It is releasing the right to personally repay evil.
That is exactly what Jesus modeled.
He entrusted justice to God while extending mercy to sinners.
This is why Christian forgiveness is not denial.
It is surrender.
It is saying:

"God, I trust You to judge rightly.
I refuse to become what wounded me."
That is supernatural.
And that is why the world struggles to understand it.
Loving Enemies Does Not Mean What Many Think
Biblical love is often misunderstood.
Loving enemies does not mean approving sin.
It does not mean enabling abuse.
It does not mean remaining in dangerous situations.
It does not mean abandoning wisdom.
It does not mean removing healthy boundaries.
Jesus loved people perfectly.
Yet He still confronted evil.
He rebuked hypocrisy.
He exposed corruption.
He challenged falsehood.
Love and truth were never enemies in His ministry.
Real biblical love speaks truth without hatred.
Offers mercy without surrendering righteousness.
Extends grace without compromising holiness.
The Freedom Hidden Inside Forgiveness
Many people believe forgiveness benefits the offender.
Sometimes it does.
But often the first person liberated is the one doing the forgiving.
Bitterness feels powerful at first.
It feels like justice.
It feels like protection.
Yet over time it becomes a prison.
The person who hurt you may move on.
But bitterness stays behind.
Living rent-free in your heart.
Stealing peace.
Stealing joy.
Stealing worship.
Jesus commands enemy-love because He knows what unforgiveness becomes.
A chain.
A cage.
A slow spiritual death.
Love breaks the chain.
Not because evil was acceptable.
But because Christ is greater than the evil done against us.
The Most Convicting Question
Imagine standing beneath the cross.
Looking at Jesus.

Bruised.
Bleeding.
Rejected.
And then hearing Him pray for His killers.
Now ask yourself:
Who is your enemy?
Who still occupies space in your heart?
Whose name immediately triggers anger?
Whose face still awakens old wounds?
Now ask something harder.
If Jesus loved His enemies enough to die for them...
Can we continue refusing to pray for ours?
The question is uncomfortable because it exposes something deep.
The Gospel is never merely about receiving grace.
It is about becoming people who extend it.
Why Jesus Really Said It
Jesus told us to love our enemies because that is exactly what God did.
The command is not random.
It is not unrealistic.
It is not detached from reality.
It is the very center of the Gospel.
We love because He first loved us.
We forgive because we were forgiven.
We extend mercy because mercy was extended to us.
The cross is not merely the place where sinners were saved.
It is the place where enemies became family.
And perhaps the greatest evidence that Jesus truly lives in us is not how we treat those who love us.
It is how we respond to those who do not.
Maybe that person who hurt you does not deserve your forgiveness.
Neither did we.
Yet Christ opened His arms anyway.
And that changes everything.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
One day you may discover that the person God used to heal your heart was the very person you once struggled to forgive.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The valley was not empty because there were no people left.
paragraphs: The valley was not empty because there were no people left.
The valley was empty because hope had already died before the bodies did.
That is the terrifying part of Ezekiel 37.
Not death.
Not bones.
Not judgment.
But people who still technically existed… while believing restoration was impossible.
And if we are honest, some of us know exactly what that feels like.

You can sit in church while your spirit feels abandoned.
You can worship publicly while grieving privately.
You can smile for family photos while something inside you has already collapsed.
You can survive years after the trauma… but still feel emotionally buried beneath it.
The Valley of Dry Bones is not merely a prophecy about ancient Israel.
It is one of the most psychologically devastating and spiritually revealing chapters in all of Scripture.
Because God was not only speaking to exiles in Babylon.

He was exposing every generation that secretly believes:
“My situation is too dead for God to restore.”
And then heaven answered that lie.
The prophet Ezekiel writes:
The Hebrew phrase for “full of bones” is:

מְלֵאָה עֲצָמוֹת
mele’ah atzamot

Not scattered remains.
Not a few casualties.
An overwhelming field of devastation.
And Scripture says the bones were not merely dead.
They were “very dry.”
In Hebrew:

וְהִנֵּה יְבֵשׁוֹת מְאֹד
vehinneh yeveshot me’od

Extremely dried out.
Long dead.
Beyond human recovery.
Beyond medical intervention.
Beyond emotional repair.
This was not CPR territory.
This was impossible territory.
And that detail changes everything.
Because God intentionally brings Ezekiel into a situation where human strength has absolutely no answer.
Some of you have been asking God why He allowed things to become this broken.
But sometimes God waits until every human solution dies… so nobody can confuse the resurrection with self-improvement.
Then came the question that still shakes the soul today.
“Son of man, can these bones live?” — Ezekiel 37:3
In Hebrew:

הֲתִחְיֶינָה הָעֲצָמוֹת הָאֵלֶּה
ha-tichyeynah ha-atzamot ha-elleh
“Can these bones live again?”

Not “Can they be repaired?”
Not “Can they improve?”
Can death itself reverse?
And Ezekiel answers carefully:
“O Lord GOD, thou knowest.”
Because when you stand in front of impossible situations long enough, certainty disappears.
Some readers know this feeling intimately.

The marriage looked alive publicly but died years ago privately.
The addiction returned after every promise.
The anxiety became exhausting.
The betrayal changed you permanently.
The ministry collapsed.
The prayer seemed unanswered.
The child walked away from God.
The depression became so normalized that numbness started feeling safer than hope.
Dry bones.
Very dry bones.
But then God commands something bizarre.
He tells Ezekiel to preach to dead things.
“Prophesy upon these bones.” — Ezekiel 37:4
The Hebrew word for “prophesy” is:

הִנָּבֵא
hinabe

To speak forth under divine inspiration.
To declare heaven’s reality into earthly impossibility.
This is critical.
Because heaven often speaks life before life becomes visible.

The world says:
“I’ll believe it when I see it.”

God says:
“Speak My truth before you see anything change.”
And suddenly the valley begins to move.

Bones start rattling.
Fragments reconnect.
Structures reform.
Tendons appear.
Flesh grows.
Skin covers them.
Imagine the horror and wonder of that moment.
An entire graveyard reassembling itself under the authority of God’s voice.
But then Scripture delivers one of the most haunting lines in the chapter:
“But there was no breath in them.” — Ezekiel 37:8
Everything looked restored externally…
…but something was still missing internally.
And this is where the hidden meaning becomes deeply personal.
Because many people today have structure without breath.

Church attendance without intimacy.
Knowledge without transformation.
Appearance without surrender.
Routine without fire.
Activity without life.
Bodies standing.
Souls exhausted.
The Hebrew word for breath here is one of the most profound words in all Scripture:

רוּחַ
Ruach

It means:
breath,
wind,
spirit.
The same word used in Genesis when God breathed life into Adam.
The same divine force now enters the valley.
Then God says:
“Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.” — Ezekiel 37:9
This is resurrection language.
Not symbolic motivation.
Not positive thinking.
Resurrection.
And when the Ruach enters them…
they stand.
Not as survivors.
As an army.
That detail is often overlooked.
God did not merely revive individuals.
He rebuilt identity, purpose, and calling.
The valley was transforming into warfare preparation.
Which reveals one of the deepest truths hidden inside this prophecy:
The enemy wanted Israel scattered, hopeless, ashamed, and spiritually dead because broken people rarely believe they still have purpose.
But God specializes in rebuilding what shame declared unusable.
Some of you still define yourselves by your worst season.
God does not.
Some still believe failure disqualified them permanently.
God does not.
Some think emotional collapse means spiritual abandonment.
God does not.
The Valley of Dry Bones is proof that God enters places people consider too ruined to redeem.
And then comes the direct interpretation from God Himself:
“These bones are the whole house of Israel.” — Ezekiel 37:11
This prophecy originally addressed Israel’s exile in Babylon.
The people believed their covenant future was over.
They said:
“Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost.”
In Hebrew:

אָבְדָה תִקְוָתֵנוּ
avdah tikvatenu
“Our hope has perished.”
This was national despair.
Spiritual trauma.
Collective grief.
Yet God responds with covenant restoration.
Not because Israel earned it.
But because God remains faithful even when people collapse emotionally.
And this points directly toward Jesus Christ.
Because Ezekiel’s valley foreshadows a greater resurrection still to come.
In the New Testament, the Greek word for resurrection is:

ἀνάστασις
anastasis
“To stand again.”
That is exactly what happened in the valley.
And ultimately, it is exactly what Christ accomplishes through the Gospel.
Jesus entered humanity’s valley of death Himself.

Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
And on the third day…
the stone moved.
Death lost authority.
The grave lost permanence.
Hope stopped being theoretical.
Because Christianity is not built upon self-help principles.
It is built upon resurrection power.
The Apostle Paul writes:
Dead spiritually.
Just like the valley.
Until the breath of God entered again.
This is why the Valley of Dry Bones still destroys hearts emotionally today.
Because deep down, people recognize themselves inside it.

The exhausted father pretending he is okay.
The woman silently battling shame from years ago.
The believer secretly questioning whether God still wants them.
The addict tired of lying.
The pastor emotionally burned out.
The anxious teenager terrified nobody understands.
The prodigal convinced they went too far.
Dry bones.
And then Jesus walks into valleys nobody else wants to enter.
That is who He is.

He touched lepers.
He restored failures.
He forgave adulterers.
He called doubters.
He ate with sinners.
He rebuilt Peter after denial.
He saved Saul after persecution.
He still resurrects impossible things.
Not every restoration looks identical.

Sometimes God restores marriages.
Sometimes He restores identity.
Sometimes He restores peace.
Sometimes He restores purpose.
Sometimes He restores faith after years of numbness.
But Scripture never teaches that dryness has authority greater than God.
And maybe that is why this chapter refuses to leave people alone emotionally.
Because most people are not afraid of failure.
They are afraid nothing inside them can ever truly live again.
But Ezekiel 37 screams across generations:
God still breathes into impossible places.
Even now.
Especially now.
Do not hide in silence.
Someone reading your honesty may realize they are not alone tonight.
And share this with the person who feels spiritually numb, emotionally exhausted, or too far gone for restoration.
And never forget this:
The valley looked like the end… until God spoke to what everyone else had already buried.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD BATTLE OF RELIGIONS
paragraphs:
THE UNTOLD BATTLE OF RELIGIONS
The War Most People Think Is About Churches, But Is Actually About Thrones
There is a battle raging across the earth that most people have completely misunderstood.
Many think it is a battle between Christianity and Islam.
Others think it is a battle between Christianity and atheism.
Some believe it is a battle between denominations.
Catholics against Protestants.
Orthodox against Evangelicals.
Conservatives against Progressives.
Religion against science.
Faith against reason.
But Scripture reveals something far deeper, older, and more terrifying.
The true battle has never been about religions.
It has always been about worship.
And worship is ultimately about one question:
Who sits on the throne?
Not merely the throne of nations.
Not merely the throne of churches.
The throne of the human heart.
Because every religion, every philosophy, every ideology, every worldview, and every rebellion is ultimately answering the same question:
"Who deserves ultimate authority?"
The untold battle of religions is not primarily a battle between people seeking God.
It is a battle between humanity's endless attempts to reach heaven on its own terms and God's invitation to be saved by grace through Jesus Christ.
That battle began long before the first church building.
Long before denominations.
Long before modern religions.
It began in Eden.
The serpent's temptation was not merely disobedience.
It was replacement.
In Hebrew, the serpent tells Eve:

"וִהְיִיתֶם כֵּאלֹהִים"
(vihyitem ke'elohim)
"You shall be like God."
(Genesis 3:5)
Not merely knowing.
Not merely learning.
Becoming.
Ruling.
Defining truth.
Determining right and wrong.
The first false religion was born the moment humanity decided God was no longer enough.
And every false system since then has carried the same ancient heartbeat.
"You can become your own savior."
Different language.
Different rituals.
Different symbols.
Same serpent.
Same lie.
Same throne.
Human history became a graveyard of towers.
The most famous was Babel.
The Hebrew text calls it:

"בָּבֶל"
(Bavel)
A monument to human self-exaltation.
People united not to worship God but to elevate themselves.
Genesis 11 records their ambition:
"Let us make a name for ourselves."
Notice the focus.
Not God's name.
Their name.
Religion often becomes exactly that.
People attempting to climb upward.
People building ladders to heaven.
People constructing systems designed to reach God through human achievement.
More rituals.
More works.
More effort.
More performance.
More climbing.
But Christianity begins with the exact opposite movement.
Not man climbing upward.
God coming downward.
This is what makes the Gospel unlike every human-made religious system.
The Apostle Paul writes:
(Ephesians 2:8)
The Greek word for grace is:

"χάρις"
(charis)
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift.
Not earned.
Not purchased.
Not achieved.
Given.
Every religion says:
"Do."
Jesus says:
"It is finished."
The Greek word He cried from the cross was:

"Τετέλεσται"
(Tetelestai)
"It is finished."
An accounting term meaning:
"Paid in full."
Not partially paid.
Not mostly paid.
Not waiting for human completion.
Paid.
In full.
That single word shattered every system built upon human merit.
Because if Jesus finished the work, then salvation cannot be earned.
And if salvation cannot be earned, then pride loses its throne.
This is where the battle becomes deeply personal.
Because most people are not merely trapped in false religions.
Many are trapped in religious versions of Christianity.
Church attendance without surrender.
Bible knowledge without repentance.
Worship songs without worship.
Christian labels without Christ.
Jesus warned about this repeatedly.
He reserved His strongest rebukes not for pagans.
Not for tax collectors.
Not for prostitutes.
But for religious leaders.
People who appeared righteous while their hearts remained far from God.
In Matthew 15:8 Jesus quotes Isaiah:
"This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me."
Religion can disguise rebellion.
A person can know theology and still not know God.
A person can quote Scripture and still reject Christ.
A person can sit in church for decades while never surrendering the throne.
Because the battle was never primarily external.
It was always internal.
What makes Jesus so offensive to every religious system is that He destroys human boasting.
The religious mind says:
"I am good enough."
The Gospel says:
"No one is righteous."
The religious mind says:
"I can earn God's acceptance."
The Gospel says:
"You need a Savior."
The religious mind says:
"Look what I have done."
The Gospel says:
"Look what Christ has done."
This is why the Apostle Paul, once among the most religious men alive, eventually declared:
"I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord."
(Philippians 3:8)
Paul had status.
Education.
Authority.
Religious credentials.
Yet compared to Christ, he considered them worthless.
Because religion gave him rules.
Jesus gave him life.
The untold battle of religions becomes even more intense when we realize that modern culture has not abandoned religion.
It has simply created new ones.
Self-worship.
Political worship.
Celebrity worship.
Success worship.
Technology worship.
Identity worship.
Pleasure worship.
Money worship.
The ancient idols changed forms.
The human heart did not.
John Calvin famously observed that the human heart is a factory of idols.
And Scripture confirms it.
Anything that takes God's place becomes a functional god.
Anything we trust more than Christ becomes an idol.
Anything we fear more than God becomes a master.
The battle continues.
Not only in temples.
Not only in churches.
Not only in mosques.
Not only in shrines.
But in offices.
Homes.
Phones.
Bank accounts.
Relationships.
And secret places where nobody else is watching.
Perhaps the most shocking truth is this:
The greatest enemy of the Gospel is not always atheism.
Sometimes it is religious pride.
The belief that we are spiritually superior.
The belief that we have earned what God freely gives.
The belief that our performance deserves God's favor.
Yet the cross crushes all pride.
At Calvary, every human being stands equally guilty.
And every believer stands equally dependent upon mercy.
The cross is the place where kings and beggars kneel on the same ground.
Because none of us are saved by our achievements.
We are saved by Jesus Christ alone.
The Hebrew prophet Isaiah declared:

"כֻּלָּנוּ כַּצֹּאן תָּעִינוּ"
(kullanu katzon ta'inu)
"All we like sheep have gone astray."
(Isaiah 53:6)
Not some.
All.
And that same chapter reveals the solution:
The suffering servant who would bear our sins.
Centuries before Christ walked the roads of Galilee.
Centuries before the nails.
Centuries before the empty tomb.
God already declared His rescue plan.
Not religion.
Redemption.
Not human effort.
Divine mercy.
Maybe that is why this battle feels so exhausting.
Because many people have spent years trying to earn what Jesus already purchased.
Trying harder.
Performing better.
Hiding failures.
Pretending holiness.
Carrying burdens Christ never asked them to carry.
The Gospel invitation remains unchanged.
Come.
Not because you are worthy.
Come because He is merciful.
Come not because you have climbed high enough.
Come because Christ came down far enough.
Come not because your record is clean.
Come because His blood cleanses sinners.
Come not because religion succeeded.
Come because Jesus saves.
And perhaps right now, someone reading this has been fighting the wrong battle.
You thought the war was against another denomination.
Another religion.
Another group.
Another ideology.
But the real battlefield has always been much closer.
The throne inside your own heart.
Who sits there today?
Your pride?
Your fears?
Your achievements?
Your wounds?
Your desires?
Or Jesus Christ?
Because every religion eventually leads to that question.
And eternity depends upon the answer.
Be honest. This may have hit closer than expected.
The throne you refuse to surrender today may become the prison you cannot escape tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are stories in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
paragraphs: There are stories in Scripture that most people read too quickly.

Cain kills Abel.
God curses Cain.
Cain leaves.
Then suddenly… one sentence appears that should disturb every serious believer.
“So Cain went away from the presence of the LORD… and he built a city.” — Genesis 4:16–17
A city?

Not an altar.
Not repentance.
Not brokenness.
Not worship.
A city.
And if you don’t slow down there, you’ll miss one of the most terrifying spiritual patterns in all of Scripture.
Because Cain became the first man in history to build a civilization without God.
And millions are still following his blueprint today.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 4:16 says:

וַיֵּצֵא קַיִן מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה
Vayetze Qayin milifnei YHWH
Literally:
“Cain went out from before the face of Yahweh.”

Not merely geographically.
Spiritually.

He didn’t just leave a location.
He abandoned Presence.
And that changes everything.
Most people think Cain’s greatest sin was murder.
It wasn’t.
Murder was the fruit.
The deeper sin happened earlier when Cain brought God an offering without surrender.
Genesis 4:3–5 says Cain brought “some of the fruits of the soil,” while Abel brought “the firstborn” and “fat portions.”
The Hebrew wording matters.

Abel brought:
מִבְּכֹרוֹת צֹאנוֹ
mibbekhorot tsono
“The firstborn of his flock.”

The best.
The first.
The costly.

Cain simply brought:
מִפְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה
mipri ha’adamah
“From the fruit of the ground.”

Not firstfruits.
Not sacrifice language.
Not costly devotion.
Just… something.
Religion without surrender.
And God sees the difference every single time.
That’s why Hebrews 11:4 in Greek says:

Πίστει πλείονα θυσίαν Ἅβελ παρὰ Κάϊν προσήνεγκεν τῷ Θεῷ
Pistei pleiona thysian Habel para Kain prosēnenken tō Theō
“By faith Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain.”
The issue was never vegetables versus animals.
It was heart posture.

Abel built worship.
Cain preserved self.

One surrendered.
One performed.
And when God confronted Cain, the Lord actually gave him a path back.
This is what makes the story devastating.
Genesis 4:6–7 is one of the earliest recorded moments of divine mercy after human rebellion.
God tells Cain:
“Sin is crouching at the door.”
In Hebrew:

לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ
Lappetach chatta’t rovetz
The imagery is terrifying.
“Sin crouches” like a predator waiting outside a doorway.
God warns Cain before he falls.
Which means Cain was not abandoned by God.
He was pursued by God.
But wounded pride can become more dangerous than open rebellion.
Cain could not handle being exposed.
And people still react the same way today.

Some leave churches not because God failed them…
but because conviction touched something they refused to surrender.

Some build careers to avoid emptiness.
Some build platforms to avoid repentance.
Some build relationships to silence guilt.
Some build entire identities so they never have to hear the voice of God asking:
“Why are you angry?”
Cain murdered Abel because Abel’s obedience exposed Cain’s imitation.
Real holiness irritates counterfeit worship.
That has never changed.
After the murder, God says something chilling:
“The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.”
The Hebrew word for blood here is not singular.

דְּמֵי
demei
“Bloods.”

Ancient rabbis noted this implies not only Abel’s blood cried out…
but every future generation that would come through him.
One act of sin carried generational consequence.
And Cain knew it.
That’s why Genesis says he became “a restless wanderer.”
In Hebrew:

נָע וָנָד
na va’nad

Shaking.
Wandering.
Unsettled.
This is the condition of a soul disconnected from God.
People think peace comes from success.
Scripture says peace comes from Presence.
And here is where the story becomes painfully modern.
Cain feared vulnerability more than separation from God.

So instead of building an altar…
he built infrastructure.
Genesis 4:17:
“And Cain built a city.”
The Hebrew word is:

עִיר
‘ir
A fortified human settlement.
This was not merely architecture.
It was theology.
Cain creates a system of human security apart from dependence on God.
Think about it.

His parents knew altars.
Abel knew sacrifice.
Cain knew cities.

One generation removed from Eden…
humanity was already replacing Presence with production.
Instead of returning to God, Cain distracts himself with construction.
And isn’t that exactly what many people do now?

We build businesses because we cannot face silence.
We chase applause because we fear stillness.
We consume endlessly because conviction is uncomfortable.
We curate perfect online identities while our souls quietly decay.

Cain discovered something dangerous:
you can succeed publicly while collapsing spiritually.
A city can hide a cursed soul.
And what’s even more haunting is this:
Cain named the city after his son, Enoch.
Not after God.
Humanity’s first city was built for human legacy.
Not divine glory.
And this becomes the seed of Babylon later in Scripture.
From Genesis to Revelation, Babylon represents human civilization attempting greatness without God.

Achievement without surrender.
Power without holiness.
Culture without repentance.
Cain planted the first brick.
This is why the story matters so deeply now.
Because modern culture celebrates what Cain invented.

Build.
Scale.
Expand.
Accumulate.
Brand yourself.
Protect your image.
Silence conviction.
Never slow down long enough to hear God.
But the soul was never designed to survive apart from Presence.

Augustine later wrote:
“Our hearts are restless until they rest in You.”
Cain is the biblical picture of restless humanity.

Busy.
Productive.
Innovative.
Advanced.
Yet spiritually homeless.
And the terrifying part?
You can sit in church while still living in the spirit of Cain.

You can sing worship songs while secretly building your own kingdom.
You can know Scripture while avoiding surrender.
You can serve publicly while privately resisting repentance.
Cain’s story is not merely about murder.
It is about what happens when wounded pride refuses brokenness.
And there are people reading this right now who know exactly what that feels like.

You’ve built routines to avoid pain.
Built humor to hide trauma.
Built ambition to numb emptiness.
Built success so nobody notices your soul is exhausted.
But cities cannot heal what only God can restore.
Cain built walls because he lost intimacy.
And many people are still doing the same thing.

Yet even here…
the Gospel whispers something extraordinary.
Because another blood eventually cried out from the ground.
Hebrews 12:24 says the blood of Jesus speaks “a better word than the blood of Abel.”
In Greek:

κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἅβελ
kreitton lalounti para ton Habel
“A better speaking word than Abel.”

Abel’s blood cried for justice.
Jesus’ blood cries for mercy.
That changes everything.

Cain ran east of Eden.
Christ came into our exile.

Cain built a city to hide shame.
Jesus carried shame publicly on a cross.

Cain shed his brother’s blood.
Jesus shed His own blood for His brothers.

And Revelation ends not with humanity’s city…
but with God’s city descending from heaven.
The New Jerusalem.

Not built by restless men.
Given by a redeeming God.

The Bible begins with exile from Presence…
and ends with restored Presence.
That is the Gospel.
Not human achievement reaching heaven.
But God descending to rescue broken humanity.

So maybe the real question is not:
“Why did Cain build a city?”
Maybe the real question is:
What are you building instead of surrendering?

A platform?
An image?
A distraction?
A relationship?
A career?
A version of yourself that keeps people impressed but keeps God distant?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone you love is exhausting themselves trying to build a life without true peace, share this with them gently. They may need this more than you realize.
Some people are not running from failure anymore.
They are running from the silence where God is waiting.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Hell has been reduced in many modern conversations to flames, torture, screaming, and fear imagery. Paintings imagined it. Movies exaggerated it. Preachers weaponized it. But when Scripture is carefully read in its original languages and full context, something even more terrifying emerges.
paragraphs: Hell has been reduced in many modern conversations to flames, torture, screaming, and fear imagery. Paintings imagined it. Movies exaggerated it. Preachers weaponized it. But when Scripture is carefully read in its original languages and full context, something even more terrifying emerges.
The deepest horror of hell is not fire.
It is separation.

Not merely separation from comfort.
Not merely separation from loved ones.
Not merely separation from earthly pleasure.
But eternal separation from the presence, goodness, light, mercy, peace, and relational nearness of God Himself.
And the terrifying truth is this:
Every beautiful thing humanity has ever experienced was still touched by the mercy of God.

The breath in your lungs.
The warmth of sunlight.
The feeling of love.
Music.
Laughter.
Rain.
Rest.
Hope.
The ability to sleep peacefully after pain.
The conviction that still calls sinners home.
All of it exists because God still allows His goodness to spill into creation.
Hell is what remains when His relational presence is eternally rejected.

Jesus described hell with images of fire because human language struggles to describe spiritual devastation. Fire communicates destruction, agony, exposure, and judgment. But the fire points toward something deeper.
When Jesus cried from the cross in Matthew 27:46:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
the Greek says:

“Θεέ μου Θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;”
(Thee mou Thee mou, hina ti me enkatelipes?)

The word “ἐγκατέλιπες” (enkatelipes) means:
to abandon,
to forsake,
to leave behind,
to withdraw presence from.
Even on the cross, the agony was not merely physical torture.
It was bearing the weight of separation.
Jesus experienced what sin produces.

Not because He sinned —
but because He carried ours.
And that reveals something horrifying:
The cross shows us that separation from the Father is unbearable even for the Son who had eternally existed in perfect communion.
Hell is terrifying because it is the full and final reality of existence apart from God.
Second Thessalonians 1:9 says:
“They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of His might.”
The Greek phrase is devastating:

“ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Κυρίου”
(apo prosōpou tou Kyriou)

Literally:
“from the face of the Lord.”

Not merely away from a location.
Away from His face.
Away from relational nearness.
Away from intimacy.
Away from divine fellowship.
In Hebrew thought, the “face” of God represented favor, peace, blessing, relationship, covenant closeness.
That is why the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26 says:
“The LORD make His face shine upon you.”
In Hebrew:

“יָאֵר יְהוָה פָּנָיו אֵלֶיךָ”
(Ya’er YHWH panav eleikha)

His face shining meant:
presence,
acceptance,
communion,
peace.
Hell is the exact opposite.

No light from His face.
No comfort from His voice.
No invitation home.
Only the eternal consequence of choosing existence apart from Him.
And this changes how we understand darkness in Scripture.
Jesus repeatedly called hell “outer darkness.”
Matthew 8:12:
“In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
The Greek phrase:

“τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον”
(to skotos to exōteron)

Literally:
“the outer darkness.”

Darkness in Scripture is not merely visual absence.
It symbolizes separation from truth, life, God’s presence, order, and peace.
Because God Himself is light.
1 John 1:5 says:

“ὁ Θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν”
(ho Theos phōs estin)
“God is light.”

Not metaphorically only.
Morally.
Spiritually.
Existentially.
To be separated from Him is to exist where light no longer reaches.

That is why hell is described with paradoxes:
fire and darkness together.
Because the imagery is attempting to communicate realities beyond human categories.

The fire represents torment.
The darkness represents abandonment.
Together they reveal complete ruin.
One of the most chilling verses about hell is actually found in the words of Jesus concerning judgment:
“Depart from Me.”
Matthew 7:23:

“ἀποχωρεῖτε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ”
(apochōreite ap’ emou)
“Go away from Me.”
That is the tragedy.

Not merely pain.
Not merely punishment.
But exile from the One humans were created for.
Because humanity was designed for communion with God from the beginning.

Genesis describes Eden not primarily as paradise because of scenery —
but because God walked with humanity there.
The Hebrew imagery in Genesis 3:8 suggests intimate nearness:
“They heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden.”
Sin fractured relationship before it ever produced physical death.
Adam and Eve hid.
That is what sin always does.
It separates.
Isaiah 59:2 says:
“But your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God.”
The Hebrew word for separation here is:

“הִבְדִּילוּ”
(hivdilu)

Meaning:
divided,
cut off,
made distinct from.
Hell is simply the eternal completion of what sin naturally produces when grace is finally refused.
C.S. Lewis once wrote that hell is the greatest monument to human freedom.
And Scripture agrees more than many realize.

God does not force love.
He invites.
Calls.
Convicts.
Warns.
Pursues.
But eventually, the final judgment honors humanity’s ultimate choice.

Life with God —
or existence without Him.
And many people misunderstand hell because they imagine sinners begging for God while He cruelly withholds Himself.
But Scripture paints a darker reality.
Romans 1 describes humanity continually suppressing truth, exchanging God for idols, rejecting His authority, and wanting autonomy over communion.
Hell is the final trajectory of eternal self-rule.
The terrifying reality is not merely that people are sent away.
It is that apart from grace, humanity naturally runs from God already.
This is why Jesus spoke so urgently.

Not because He enjoyed fear-based preaching.
But because He loved people enough to warn them.
And the most beautiful part of the Gospel is this:
Jesus entered abandonment so humanity would not have to remain there.
On the cross, Christ absorbed wrath, judgment, curse, and separation so reconciliation could become possible.
Second Corinthians 5:18 says:
“God… reconciled us to Himself through Christ.”
The Greek word for reconciled:

“καταλλάσσω”
(katallassō)

To restore relationship.
To bring back into harmony.
To end hostility.
To reunite.
The Gospel is not merely about escaping punishment.
It is about restoration to God Himself.
Eternal life is not simply living forever.
Jesus defined eternal life in John 17:3:
“That they know You.”

Not merely know about Him.
Know Him.

Relationship.
Communion.
Presence.
That is heaven’s greatest treasure.
God Himself.
Revelation does not climax with golden streets.
It climaxes with this:
“Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.”
The final victory of salvation is restored presence.
And the final horror of hell is eternal absence.
That is why the Gospel matters so deeply.

Because every human soul is moving toward one of two eternities:
eternal communion with God,
or eternal separation from Him.
And every heartbeat is mercy.
Every conviction is mercy.
Every chance to repent is mercy.
You reading this right now is mercy.

There are people pretending they are spiritually fine while slowly becoming numb to God’s voice. Some have mastered church language while privately feeling distant from Christ. Some are entertaining sin they once feared. Some are exhausted, ashamed, hiding things nobody knows.
But the terrifying thing about separation is that it rarely begins suddenly.
It begins quietly.

A hardened conscience.
A prayer life disappearing.
Conviction fading.
Sin becoming normal.
Worship becoming emotionless.
The heart slowly drifting from the presence it was created for.
And maybe this is why this message unsettled you.

Not because you fear flames.
But because deep down you know your soul was made for Him.
it is about returning home to the Father.
And the scariest part of eternity is not burning forever…
It is realizing too late that the soul was created to live in the presence of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room smelled like death before anyone said a word.
paragraphs: The room smelled like death before anyone said a word.
Not metaphorically.
Literally.

A concubine violated through the night.
A nation collapsing morally in real time.
An old man trembling in silence.
A Levite standing in a doorway.
And a body cut into pieces and shipped across Israel like a warning flare from hell itself.
Most churches never preach this story.
Not because it is unimportant.
Because it is horrifying.
Because it exposes what humanity becomes when people still claim to know God… while living completely surrendered to darkness.
This is not just one of the darkest stories in the Bible.
It may be the darkest.
And what makes it even more terrifying…
is that the Book of Judges says this exact sentence repeatedly like a funeral bell ringing over an entire civilization:

“In those days there was no king in Israel. Every man did what was right in his own eyes.”
— Judges 21:25
In Hebrew:

אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
“Ish hayashar b’einav ya’aseh.”

Literally:
“Each man did what was straight/right in his own eyes.”
Not God’s eyes.
Their own.
That sentence is not freedom.
It is judgment.
And maybe that is why this story feels so painfully modern.
Because we are watching an entire generation redefine morality based on feelings, preferences, trends, politics, lust, trauma, pride, and self-worship.
And the Book of Judges shows exactly where that road ends.
Not in enlightenment.
In destruction.
The story begins in Judges 19.
A Levite and his concubine are traveling near Gibeah, a city belonging to the tribe of Benjamin.
An old man offers them hospitality for the night because even he understands the streets are unsafe.
Then the nightmare begins.
Scripture says wicked men surrounded the house demanding to violate the Levite.
The Hebrew text uses language echoing Genesis 19 in Sodom.
They are not merely sinful.
They are consumed.
Possessed by violence.
Drunk on humiliation and domination.
The old man says something horrifying:
“Do not do this vile thing.”
Hebrew:

אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
“Al-tare’u.”

Meaning:
“Do not act wickedly.”
But wickedness had already taken over.
Then comes one of the most disturbing moments in all Scripture.
The concubine is thrown outside.
And all night long they abused her until morning.
The Bible does not sanitize evil.
Modern culture romanticizes darkness constantly.
Scripture exposes it naked.
At dawn she collapses at the doorway.
Her hands stretched toward the entrance.
Possibly reaching for help that never came.
Possibly dying alone while the man inside stayed silent.
Then comes the verse that feels like a knife to the chest.
Judges 19:28:
“Get up, let us be going.”

No compassion.
No mourning.
No recorded tears.
Just silence.
Coldness.
Moral decay so severe that human suffering no longer shocks anyone.
And this is exactly what sin does.
Sin never stays contained.
The Greek word for sin in the New Testament is:
ἁμαρτία — hamartia

Meaning:
“To miss the mark.”
But biblical sin is not merely making mistakes.
It is separation from God that progressively hardens the heart until evil becomes normal.
That is what happened in Judges.
And if we are honest…
many hearts today are slowly becoming numb too.

Laugh at wickedness.
Celebrate rebellion.
Mock purity.
Normalize pornography.
Treat covenant like inconvenience.
Treat repentance like weakness.
And still wonder why anxiety, emptiness, addiction, loneliness, rage, and spiritual confusion are consuming people everywhere.
Judges is not ancient history.
It is a mirror.
The Levite takes her body home.
Then he does something so shocking it almost feels impossible to read.
He cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
The nation erupts in horror.
Civil war follows.
Thousands die.
Entire cities burn.
The tribe of Benjamin is nearly annihilated.
And all of it traces back to one terrifying reality:
When people abandon God, darkness never remains private.
It spreads.
Always.
The Bible never tells this story to entertain us.
It tells this story to warn us.
Romans 15:4 says:
“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning…”
The Greek word for “learning” is:
διδασκαλία — didaskalia

Meaning:
Instruction.
Doctrine.
Teaching meant to transform behavior.
Judges 19 is not there accidentally.
God preserved this horrifying account because humanity keeps repeating it.
Civilizations collapse morally long before they collapse politically.
A nation dies spiritually first.
And the terrifying part is this:
Israel still had religion during Judges.

They still had rituals.
Still had traditions.
Still had identity.
But they no longer feared God.
And external religion without repentance always becomes corruption eventually.
Jesus confronted this same issue centuries later.
In Matthew 15:8, He quotes Isaiah:
“These people honor Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.”
In Greek:

ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ
“he de kardia auton porro apechei ap emou”
“Their heart remains far away from Me.”

Not their songs.
Not their gatherings.
Their hearts.
And maybe that is the part nobody wants to confront.
Because it is possible to look spiritually alive publicly while rotting privately.

Possible to quote Scripture while secretly addicted.
Possible to worship while hating people.
Possible to preach while living in hidden sin.
Possible to wear Christianity culturally while being completely disconnected from Christ relationally.
Judges proves something terrifying:
Human beings do not slowly drift toward holiness naturally.
Without God, we drift toward darkness.
Always.
That is why the Gospel matters so much.
Because Christianity is not behavior modification.
It is resurrection.
The solution to Judges was never “try harder.”
Humanity had already proven it could not save itself.
That is why Jesus came.
And when you understand how dark humanity truly is…
the cross becomes infinitely more beautiful.
Because Christ entered THIS world.
Not a clean one.
This one.
The Greek word used when John says:
“The light shines in the darkness…”
is:
φαίνει — phainei

Meaning:
To shine continuously.
To keep shining.
John 1:5 says:
“And the darkness did not overcome it.”
Greek:

καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν
“kai he skotia auto ou katelaben”

Meaning:
Darkness could not overpower,
comprehend,
or extinguish the Light.
That means no matter how corrupted humanity becomes…
Jesus remains undefeated.

Still saving addicts.
Still healing trauma.
Still rescuing suicidal souls.
Still restoring marriages.
Still forgiving secret sin.
Still calling prodigals home.
Still breaking chains.
Still raising spiritually dead people back to life.
