It was the resurrection of this woman’s ability to trust God again.
That was the true healing.
Because some people can survive suffering…
but cannot survive disappointment with God.
That is why this story matters so deeply today.
There are believers sitting in churches every Sunday secretly terrified to hope again.
People who still sing worship songs while emotionally numb.
People who serve faithfully while inwardly asking:
“God… will You disappoint me again?”
And this story whispers something eternal into exhausted souls:
God is not intimidated by wounded faith.
He is not offended by trembling hope.
He is not shocked by your emotional exhaustion.
The Bible is filled with people whose faith limped before it walked.
Even Sarah laughed.
In Genesis 18:12, the Hebrew says:
"וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה"
Vatitzchak Sarah.
“Sarah laughed.”

The root word צָחַק (tsachaq) means:
to laugh,
to mock,
to play,
to express incredulous joy or disbelief.
Yet God still named the covenant child Isaac — יִצְחָק (Yitzchak).

Literally:
“He laughs.”
God turned wounded laughter into covenant fulfillment.
Only God can do that.
Only Jesus can walk into human disappointment and still resurrect hope.
And this is why the Gospel changes everything.
Because the cross itself looked like the death of every promise.
The disciples thought hope had died.
Heaven looked silent.
Darkness covered the earth.
But three days later, resurrection rewrote the ending.
Some of you thought your story ended in grief.
But Jesus specializes in impossible endings.
The Greek word for resurrection in the New Testament is:
ἀνάστασις (anastasis)

It means:
a standing up again,
a rising,
a restoration to life.
That is what Christ still does.
He raises what people buried.
He restores what shame destroyed.
He breathes into hearts that have forgotten how to hope.
And maybe this article found you at the exact moment you were about to emotionally quit on God.
Not publicly.
Just internally.
Quietly.
Secretly.
But heaven sees silent heartbreak too.
The woman who laughed at Elisha was not evil.
She was wounded.
And God still met her there.
Be honest.
Some of you have been surviving spiritually, but not truly living.
And if you know somebody silently carrying disappointment with God, share this with them tonight.

Some people desperately need this reminder:
God has not abandoned their story.
Sometimes the loudest cry for help is hidden behind the quietest laugh.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 6 Lies You Thought Could Save You… But They Never Could
paragraphs:
6 Lies You Thought Could Save You… But They Never Could
The Quiet Deceptions We Cling To Before We Finally Meet Jesus
There is a terrifying moment many people experience but rarely talk about.
It usually happens in silence.
Not in church.
Not during worship.
Not while posting Bible verses online.
It happens when life strips away the distractions and leaves a person alone with their own soul.
The promotion finally comes.
The relationship finally happens.
The money finally arrives.
The addiction finally gets hidden well enough.
The image finally looks perfect.
And yet...
Something still feels empty.
Because deep down, every human being is searching for salvation.
Not merely survival.
Salvation.
The problem is that most people spend years trying to save themselves with things that were never designed to save them.
The Bible calls these false refuges.
The prophet Isaiah described them as lies people make agreements with while avoiding the truth of God.
And if we're honest, many of us have believed them too.
Not because we're stupid.
Because we're desperate.
Desperate people grab whatever promises relief.
But relief is not redemption.
Comfort is not salvation.
And temporary escape is not eternal rescue.
Here are six lies millions believe can save them.
None of them can.
Only Jesus can.
The first lie says:
"If I become successful enough, I'll finally be okay."
The world preaches this gospel every day.
More money.
More influence.
More recognition.
More followers.
More achievements.
Then you'll finally have peace.
But the wealthiest king who ever lived shattered that illusion.
King Solomon possessed riches, power, influence, knowledge, luxury, and pleasure beyond imagination.
Yet he wrote:
"Meaningless! Meaningless! Everything is meaningless." (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
The Hebrew word used here is:
הֶבֶל (hevel)
Literally meaning:
"Vapor."
"Mist."
"Breath."
Something visible for a moment and then gone.
Solomon discovered something many people spend their entire lives learning too late.
Success can fill your calendar.
It cannot fill your soul.
Many people have achieved everything they wanted and still go to sleep feeling empty.
Because purpose isn't found in what you accomplish.
It's found in Who created you.
Jesus never said:
"Come to Me if you're successful."
He said:
"Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28)
The rest you've been chasing was never found at the top.
It was always found at the cross.
The second lie says:
"If people love me, I'll finally feel complete."
This one is dangerous because love itself is good.
But human love makes a terrible savior.
People change.
People fail.
People leave.
People die.
Even the best marriages cannot carry the weight of a soul looking for God.
Many enter relationships hoping another person will heal wounds only Jesus can heal.
Then disappointment arrives.
Not because the person was evil.
Because they were never designed to be your Messiah.
In Greek, Jesus says in John 10:10:

ἐγὼ ἦλθον ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσιν
(egō ēlthon hina zōēn echōsin)
"I came that they may have life."
The word ζωή (zōē) means more than existence.
It means true life.
Full life.
God-given life.
The kind of life no boyfriend, girlfriend, spouse, parent, or child can create.
The deepest longing in your heart is not for another human being.
It's for reconciliation with the God who made you.
The third lie says:
"If I'm a good person, God will accept me."
This sounds humble.
It sounds reasonable.
It sounds fair.
But Scripture demolishes it.
Paul writes:
The Greek word for righteous is:
δίκαιος (dikaios)
Meaning:
Perfectly just.
Completely upright.
Morally flawless before God.
Not better than average.
Not nicer than most.
Perfect.
And suddenly the problem becomes obvious.
Nobody qualifies.
Not pastors.
Not missionaries.
Not saints.
Not you.
Not me.
Salvation isn't about being better than someone else.
It's about standing before a holy God.
And every human being falls short.
That's why Christianity is different from every man-made religion.
Most religions teach:
"Work your way to God."
The Gospel says:
"God came down to you."
Jesus did not come to make bad people slightly better.
He came to make dead people alive.
The fourth lie says:
"My past is too broken for God to use me."
This lie keeps countless people trapped.
Shame whispers:
"You've ruined everything."
"You've gone too far."
"God may forgive others, but not you."
Yet Scripture tells a different story.
Moses was a murderer.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
And God still used them.
Why?
Because grace is not earned.
It is given.
The Aramaic roots behind mercy reveal a beautiful picture.
The concept behind mercy points toward deep compassion flowing from the innermost being.
Not reluctant tolerance.
Not divine annoyance.
Compassion.
The cross proves God knew your worst day before you ever lived it.
And Jesus went there anyway.
Your sin is serious.
But His blood is greater.
The fifth lie says:
"I still have plenty of time."
Few lies are more dangerous.
Because it feels true.
Until it isn't.
Nobody plans their final day.
Nobody schedules their last breath.
James writes:
The same reality Solomon described with hevel.
Vapor.
Breath.
Mist.
Temporary.
Modern culture teaches people to postpone eternity.
Later.
Tomorrow.
Next year.
After I enjoy life.
After I fix myself.
After I get serious.
But salvation is never promised tomorrow.
Only today.
Every heartbeat is a gift.
Every breath is borrowed.
Every moment is grace.
And every moment is one moment closer to standing before God.
The sixth lie says:
"Something other than Jesus can save me."
At the root of every false hope is this final deception.
Money.
Politics.
Self-improvement.
Religion.
Good works.
Spirituality.
Success.
Relationships.
Personal enlightenment.
None of them can carry the weight of eternity.
In Acts 4:12, Peter boldly declares:
"There is salvation in no one else."
The Greek word for salvation is:
σωτηρία (sōtēria)
Deliverance.
Rescue.
Preservation.
Complete redemption.
And Peter says that rescue is found nowhere else.
Not because Christianity is arrogant.
But because Jesus is unique.
No other religious leader claimed to be God in flesh.
No other religious leader died for the sins of the world.
No other religious leader conquered death.
No other religious leader walked out of a sealed tomb.
Jesus did not merely show a way.
Jesus declared:
"I am the way, and the truth, and the life." (John 14:6)
Not a way.
The way.
Maybe while reading this, one of these lies exposed something you've been trusting.
Maybe success has become your savior.
Maybe approval has become your savior.
Maybe religion has become your savior.
Maybe your own goodness has become your savior.
Maybe you've spent years trying to rescue yourself.
And you're exhausted.
Because carrying the weight of your own salvation was never a burden you were created to bear.
The Gospel begins where self-salvation ends.
Jesus lived the life you could not live.
Died the death you deserved.
Rose from the grave defeating sin and death.
And now offers forgiveness, reconciliation, adoption, eternal life, and true peace to everyone who believes.
Not because you've earned it.
Because He paid for it.
The greatest tragedy is not that people are sinners.
The greatest tragedy is that many keep reaching for lifeboats that cannot float while rejecting the Savior who already crossed the storm for them.
One day every false savior will fail you, but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus never will.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You said you wanted God’s will.
paragraphs: You said you wanted God’s will.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Most people do not want the will of God.
They want the blessings of God while protecting the idols He told them to surrender.

They want peace without repentance.
Purpose without obedience.
Heaven without holiness.
And deep down…
You knew.

God saw the hidden compromise.
The delayed obedience.
The private rebellion covered in Christian language.
The terrifying thing about deception is that you can sing worship songs while slowly drifting from God.

That is why Scripture does not merely call believers to “believe.”
It calls them to align.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind…” — Romans 12:2

The Greek word for “conformed” is:
συσχηματίζεσθε (syschēmatízesthe)

It means:
“To be pressed into a pattern.”
“To take the outward shape of something else.”
Paul was warning believers not to let the world shape their identity, desires, values, and decisions.
Because something is always discipling you.

Social media.
Fear.
Lust.
Money.
Pain.
Pride.
Or God.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And if your life is going to align with God’s will, Scripture shows us the path clearly.

Not perfectly.
But truthfully.
The first alignment begins where most people refuse to go.
Repentance.
Jesus began His ministry with these words:
“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” — Matthew 4:17

The Greek word for repent is:
μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite)
It does not merely mean “feel bad.”

It means:
“To change the mind.”
“To turn inwardly.”
“To reverse direction.”

Biblical repentance is not emotional guilt alone.
It is surrender that produces transformation.

Many people cry during conviction but return unchanged.
That is not repentance.
That is temporary emotion.
David understood this after his sin shattered him.
He prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…” — Psalm 51:10

The Hebrew phrase:
לֵב טָהוֹר (lev tahor)
means “a purified heart.”

Not improved behavior.
A purified inner being.
Because God is not merely after your habits.
He wants your heart.
The second alignment is obedience over feelings.

Modern culture teaches:
“Follow your heart.”
Scripture says something radically different.
“The heart is deceitful above all things…” — Jeremiah 17:9

The Hebrew word for deceitful is:
עָקֹב (aqov)

Meaning:
“Crooked.”
“Insidious.”
“Twisted.”

Your emotions are real.
But they are not always righteous.

That relationship felt right.
That compromise felt harmless.
That secret sin felt manageable.
Until it consumed you.
Jesus said:
“If you love Me, keep My commandments.” — John 14:15
Notice what He did not say.

He did not say:
“If you feel spiritual.”
“If it is convenient.”
“If culture approves.”
Love for Christ is revealed through obedience.

Not perfection.
Obedience.
And obedience often costs you something.

Sometimes your comfort.
Sometimes your reputation.
Sometimes people you thought would stay forever.
But alignment with God will always require dying to self.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily…” — Luke 9:23

The Greek word for deny is:
ἀπαρνησάσθω (aparnēsasthō)

Meaning:
“To completely disown.”
That is violent language against pride.
Because the Christian life is not self-improvement.
It is crucifixion before resurrection.
The third alignment is renewing your mind with Scripture.
Many believers are spiritually starving while holding a Bible they rarely open.
And then they wonder why confusion dominates their life.
God’s will is never disconnected from God’s Word.
The psalmist declared:
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” — Psalm 119:105

The Hebrew word for word is:
דָּבָר (dabar)

Not merely written text.
It carries the sense of divine utterance, revealed truth, authoritative speech.
When God speaks, reality changes.

But here is the danger:
You cannot align your life with a voice you refuse to listen to.
Some people spend five hours scrolling through content that feeds anxiety, lust, envy, and pride…
Then give God five distracted minutes.
And they wonder why they feel spiritually numb.
God saw it.
You knew.
The fourth alignment is surrendering hidden sin.

Not managing it.
Not renaming it.
Killing it.
Paul wrote:
“Put to death therefore what is earthly in you…” — Colossians 3:5

The Greek phrase:
νεκρώσατε οὖν (nekrōsate oun)
means:
“Make dead.”
“Execute completely.”
Scripture does not negotiate with sin.
It crucifies it.

The pornography.
The bitterness.
The greed.
The manipulation.
The secret addiction nobody knows about.
You may have hidden it from people.
But not from God.
Hebrews says:
“All things are naked and exposed to the eyes of Him…” — Hebrews 4:13

The Greek word:
τετραχηλισμένα (tetrachēlismena)
Carries the imagery of being fully exposed, laid bare, unable to hide.
That should terrify the rebellious heart.
But it should comfort the repentant one.
Because Jesus already knows the worst thing about you…
And still went to the cross.
This is the Gospel.

Not that humanity was good enough.
Not that religion could save itself.
But that Christ stepped into our guilt.
Isaiah prophesied:
“He was pierced for our transgressions…” — Isaiah 53:5

The Hebrew word for pierced:
מְחֹלָל (mecholal)

Meaning:
“Wounded through.”
“Profaned.”
“Pierced violently.”
Jesus did not die symbolically.
He bled literally.
For sinners literally condemned under the holiness of God.
That includes you.
That includes me.
And salvation is not earned through works.
Paul wrote:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…” — Ephesians 2:8

The Greek word for grace:
χάριτι (chariti)

Meaning:
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.

You cannot earn mercy.
You can only receive it through Christ.
The fifth alignment is walking in the Spirit daily.

Not occasionally.
Not emotionally.
Daily.
Paul says:
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.” — Galatians 5:16

The Greek word for walk:
περιπατεῖτε (peripateite)

Meaning:
“To conduct your entire way of life.”
Christianity was never meant to be a Sunday performance.
It is a surrendered lifestyle.

The Spirit of God changes desires.
Convicts sin.
Produces holiness.
Creates endurance.
Transforms identity.
And when the Holy Spirit convicts you…
Do not silence Him.
Respond quickly.
The sixth alignment is seeking God’s kingdom above your own ambition.
Jesus said:
“Seek first the kingdom of God…” — Matthew 6:33

The Greek word for seek:
ζητεῖτε (zēteite)

Meaning:
“To pursue relentlessly.”
“To crave.”
“To prioritize above all else.”

Many people ask:
“What is God’s will for my life?”
While ignoring the revealed will already written in Scripture.

God’s will is not first about your platform.
Your status.
Your career.
Your image.

It is about becoming holy.
Knowing Christ.
Reflecting Him in a dying world.

Because one day, your money will disappear.
Your body will fail.
Your achievements will fade.
But eternity will remain.
And one day every hidden thing will stand before God.
That is why alignment with God is urgent.

Not later.
Not when life calms down.
Not after one more compromise.
Now.
If this exposed something in you, do not ignore it.
Conviction is mercy before judgment.
Read that again.
Maybe you have been spiritually drifting for years while pretending everything was fine.
Maybe this was the warning you were not expecting.
Jesus Christ is still calling sinners home.

Still forgiving.
Still restoring.
Still transforming.
But surrender cannot stay theoretical.
If you are tired of lukewarm Christianity…
And if this reached your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
And if you are done pretending, write:
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You keep praying for breakthrough while protecting the very mindset that keeps you bound.
paragraphs: You keep praying for breakthrough while protecting the very mindset that keeps you bound.
That is the tragedy most people never confront.
They want God to change their circumstances without allowing Him to change their thinking.
But Scripture is painfully clear: before God transforms a season, He often confronts a mindset.
Israel left Egypt physically in one night, but Egypt stayed in their minds for years.
And some people reading this are still carrying mental chains into places God already opened.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Breakthrough in Scripture was rarely just external.

It was spiritual.
Internal.
Foundational.
God changed the mind before He changed the outcome.
“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind...” — Romans 12:2
The Greek word for “renewing” is anakainōsis (ἀνακαίνωσις).

It means:
“A complete renovation.”
“A renewal that makes something qualitatively new.”
Not behavior modification.
Transformation.

God is not trying to decorate the old you.
He is trying to crucify the old mind entirely.
And there are five mindsets throughout Scripture that repeatedly positioned people for divine breakthrough.

Not self-help.
Not motivational psychology.
Biblical transformation.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The first mindset is surrender over control.
Most people want breakthrough while still demanding control over timing, outcomes, methods, and comfort.
But breakthrough often begins where control dies.
Abraham understood this.
Genesis 12:1 says:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house...”
The Hebrew phrase for “Get thee out” is:
Lekh-lekha (לֶךְ־לְךָ)

Literally:
“Go yourself.”
“Go toward yourself.”
God was not merely relocating Abraham geographically.
He was stripping him psychologically.
Leaving comfort was part of becoming who God called him to be.
Many people never enter promise because they worship predictability.
They need guarantees before obedience.
But faith never demanded full visibility.
Hebrews 11:8 says:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called... obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Read that again.
“Not knowing.”
That destroys modern Christianity’s obsession with certainty.
Sometimes breakthrough begins when you obey without complete explanations.
You knew God was calling you higher.
But fear negotiated with obedience.
God saw it.
The second mindset is repentance instead of self-justification.
This is where many people collapse spiritually.
Because pride would rather defend sin than destroy it.
David understood this after his fall.

Psalm 51 is not performance religion.
It is spiritual brokenness.
The Hebrew word David uses for “broken” in Psalm 51:17 is:
Shabar (שָׁבַר)

Meaning:
“To be shattered.”
“To be crushed into pieces.”
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart...”
God responds to repentance because repentance stops pretending.
Most people are exhausted because they are managing appearances instead of surrendering honestly.
And Scripture never teaches breakthrough through image management.
Jesus confronted this directly.
In Luke 18, the Pharisee justified himself while the tax collector cried for mercy.

One impressed people.
The other moved heaven.
The Greek phrase:
Hilastheti moi (ἱλάσθητί μοι)

Means:
“Be merciful to me.”
“Provide atonement for me.”
The tax collector understood something modern culture hates:
You cannot heal what you refuse to confess.
And some people keep calling spiritual warfare what is actually unrepented compromise.
The third mindset is kingdom vision instead of temporary vision.
Esau lost a birthright over one meal.
One craving destroyed a generational inheritance.
Hebrews 12:16 calls him “profane.”
The Greek word is:
Bebēlos (βέβηλος)

Meaning:
“Common.”
“Worldly.”
“Spiritually careless.”
That is terrifying.
Because Scripture teaches that people can trade eternal value for temporary appetite.
And culture trains people to think short-term constantly.

Immediate pleasure.
Immediate validation.
Immediate gratification.
But God often works through delayed fulfillment.
Joseph endured betrayal, slavery, false accusation, and prison before elevation.
Why?
Because God prepares the vessel before releasing the assignment.
Genesis 50:20 says:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good...”
The Hebrew word for “meant” is:
Chashab (חָשַׁב)

Meaning:
“To weave.”
“To devise.”
“To skillfully plan.”
Even suffering was being woven strategically.
You thought your delay meant abandonment.
But heaven may have been building endurance inside you.
The fourth mindset is spiritual hunger instead of spiritual comfort.
Jesus said:
“Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness...” — Matthew 5:6
The Greek word for hunger is:
Peinaō (πεινάω)
It describes desperate starvation.
Not casual interest.
This is where lukewarm Christianity gets exposed.
Because many people want inspiration without surrender.

Church without holiness.
Worship without obedience.
Encouragement without repentance.
But breakthrough consistently followed spiritual desperation in Scripture.
Blind Bartimaeus cried louder when others tried to silence him.
The woman with the issue of blood pressed through the crowd.
Jacob wrestled until blessing came.
Comfort never produced those moments.
Hunger did.
Jeremiah 29:13 says:
“And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.”
The Hebrew phrase:
Bekhol levavkhem (בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם)

Means:
“With your entire inner being.”
Not partial pursuit.
Total pursuit.
And this generation is drowning in distraction while starving spiritually.

Infinite scrolling.
Endless entertainment.
Constant noise.
Meanwhile the soul quietly dies from distance from God.
The fifth mindset is eternal identity instead of shame identity.
This may be where the enemy has held many people hostage.
Because shame rewrites identity.
Peter denied Jesus publicly.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
But after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter instead of discarding him.
That matters deeply.
Because religion often defines people by their worst moment.
Jesus defines redeemed people by His grace.
In John 21, Jesus asks Peter:
“Lovest thou me?”
The Greek word Jesus first uses is:
Agapaō (ἀγαπάω)
Sacrificial love.
Peter responds with:
Phileō (φιλέω)
Brotherly affection.
Peter could not even confidently claim higher devotion anymore after failure.
And yet Jesus still called him forward.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue sinning.
But redemption after repentance.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus...”
The Greek word for condemnation:
Katakrima (κατάκριμα)

Means:
“A guilty verdict carrying punishment.”
Jesus absorbed that verdict at the cross.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities...”
The Hebrew word for wounded:
Mecholal (מְחֹלָל)

Meaning:
“Pierced through.”
“Profaned violently.”
Christ was crushed so sinners could be restored.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Substitution.
Jesus took the judgment sin deserved so repentant sinners could receive mercy they never deserved.
And breakthrough without Christ is temporary at best.

Because the greatest breakthrough is not financial.
Not emotional.
Not circumstantial.
It is being rescued from sin and reconciled to God.
Some people keep asking God for open doors while refusing the Savior standing in front of them.
But salvation is the true breakthrough.

You can gain money and still be empty.
Gain influence and still be lost.
Gain applause and still stand condemned before God.
Jesus said:
“What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36
The Greek word for soul is:
Psychē (ψυχή)

Your eternal self.
Your life beyond the body.
And one day every mask will fall.
Every excuse will die.
Every secret will stand exposed before God.
But grace is still available right now.
Repentance is still open right now.
Mercy is still calling right now.
You felt something because truth was confronting you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There was a reason Pharaoh feared Hebrew babies.
paragraphs: There was a reason Pharaoh feared Hebrew babies.
But there was a deeper reason hell feared one specific child.

Before Moses ever parted the sea…
before Sinai trembled…
before plagues shattered Egypt…
before Israel even knew his name…
a hidden war was already happening around his life.
Most people read the story of baby Moses like a simple survival account.

A grieving mother.
A cruel king.
A basket on a river.
A miraculous rescue.
But underneath Exodus chapter 2 is one of the most prophetic mysteries in all of Scripture.
Because Moses was not only hidden from Pharaoh…
he was hidden by God Himself.
And once you understand the original Hebrew language, the ancient context, and the spiritual symbolism inside this story…
you realize this was never just about protecting a baby.
It was about preserving a deliverer before the world knew it needed one.
In Exodus 1, Egypt had become spiritually intoxicated with fear. Israel was multiplying rapidly, and Pharaoh believed the Hebrews were becoming too powerful.
So he issued a demonic decree:
Every Hebrew son must die.
Exodus 1:22 says:
“Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river…”
The Hebrew phrase is:

“כָּל־הַבֵּן הַיְלֹד הַיְאֹרָה תַּשְׁלִיכֻהוּ”
(Kol-ha’ben hayyilod haye’orah tashlikhuhu)

Literally:
“Every born son you must throw into the Nile.”
This was not random violence.
The Nile represented Egypt’s power, economy, religion, and false gods.
Pharaoh was essentially demanding Hebrew sons be sacrificed into the bloodstream of Egypt itself.
This mirrors later satanic patterns throughout Scripture.

When deliverers are about to rise…
mass attacks against children suddenly appear.
Pharaoh against Moses.
Herod against Jesus.
The dragon against the male child in Revelation 12.
Hell attacks infancy whenever heaven sends liberation.

And somehow…
Amram and Jochebed — Moses’ parents — discerned something unusual about their son.
Hebrews 11:23 says:
“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child…”
The Greek phrase for “proper child” is:

“ἀστεῖον τὸ παιδίον”
(asteion to paidion)

Meaning:
“beautiful,”
“extraordinary,”
“marked out,”
or “divinely favored.”
Acts 7:20 gives even deeper language when Stephen says Moses was:

“ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ”
(asteios tō Theō)

Literally:
“beautiful to God.”
Not merely cute.
Not merely healthy.
There was something visibly marked by divine purpose upon him.
His parents sensed heaven resting on this child.
And this is where the mystery deepens.
Exodus 2:2 says:
“The woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.”
The Hebrew for “hid” is:

“צָפַן”
(tsaphan)
This word does not simply mean concealed.

It means:
to treasure,
to reserve,
to protect secretly,
to store up with intention.
This exact Hebrew word is used elsewhere for hidden treasure, concealed wisdom, and things reserved by God.
Psalm 119:11:
“Thy word have I hid in mine heart…”
Same root idea.
Moses was not hidden out of panic alone.
He was hidden prophetically.
Protected as concealed treasure.
Reserved for an appointed time.
And then comes one of the most overlooked prophetic symbols in Scripture.
The basket.
Exodus 2:3 says Jochebed placed Moses into an “ark” of bulrushes.
The Hebrew word is:

“תֵּבָה”
(tevah)
And this is astonishing…
because the word “tevah” is only used in TWO stories in the entire Old Testament.
Noah’s ark.
And Moses’ basket.
Not a coincidence.
The Holy Spirit intentionally connected Moses to Noah.

Both were hidden inside an ark.
Both passed through waters of judgment.
Both emerged to preserve humanity.
Both became agents of covenant transition.
Moses was essentially floating in a miniature ark.
A vessel of preservation carrying future deliverance.
And the basket itself was covered with slime and pitch.
The Hebrew:

“חֵמָר וָזָפֶת”
(chemar va’zapheth)
This mirrors Noah’s ark being sealed for protection.
The imagery screams one truth:
God preserves what hell tries to drown.
But the Nile itself reveals an even deeper mystery.
In ancient Egypt, the Nile was associated with life, fertility, and divine sovereignty.
Pharaoh believed the river belonged to Egypt’s gods.
Yet God sends Moses — the future destroyer of Egypt’s idols — floating directly through the center of their false worship system.
The enemy was unknowingly carrying the instrument of his own defeat.
Read that again.
The very waters assigned to kill Hebrew sons became the pathway preserving Israel’s deliverer.
That is how God works.
The cross looked like Satan’s victory…
until it became his destruction.
And then something unbelievable happens.
Pharaoh’s daughter finds Moses.
The house that ordered death becomes the house that finances deliverance.
Only God can write stories like this.
Exodus 2:10 says:
“And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.”

The Hebrew:
“מֹשֶׁה”
(Mosheh)

Connected to:
“מָשָׁה”
(mashah)

Meaning:
“to draw out.”
Moses would first be drawn out himself…
before later drawing Israel out of bondage.
His identity was prophetic from infancy.
Everything about Moses’ hiddenness pointed toward future redemption.
But here is the part many believers miss.
Hidden seasons are not wasted seasons.

Moses spent:
3 months hidden by his mother,
40 years hidden in Pharaoh’s palace identity confusion,
40 years hidden in Midian,
before publicly stepping into destiny.
God often conceals people before He reveals them.
Jesus spent 30 hidden years before 3 public years.
David was hidden in fields before the throne.
Joseph was hidden in prison before the palace.
Paul disappeared into Arabia before ministry exploded.
Our culture worships visibility.
God often develops power in obscurity.
Some of you are frustrated because your life feels hidden.

Unnoticed.
Delayed.
Buried.
Forgotten.
But hidden does not mean abandoned.
Sometimes God hides what He refuses to let the enemy destroy prematurely.
Sometimes concealment is protection.
Sometimes isolation is preparation.
Sometimes heaven covers what hell is searching for.
Moses was hidden because deliverance was inside him before he understood it himself.
And maybe that is why this story hits so deeply.

Because many people reading this have spent years wondering why life feels delayed…
why doors closed…
why seasons became lonely…
why you feel unseen.
But what if God has been preserving you?
What if the hidden season was never punishment?
What if you were being protected from destruction before your assignment fully matured?
The enemy attacks what carries future freedom.
That is why some of you have faced warfare since childhood.
The battle around your life may reveal the weight of your calling.
And the beautiful truth of the Gospel is this:
Moses points beyond himself.

Like Moses:
Jesus survived a child massacre under Herod.
Jesus came as a deliverer.
Jesus passed through waters at baptism.
Jesus leads His people out of slavery — not Egypt, but sin itself.
Moses was hidden in an ark.
But Christ Himself became the ark for us.

The place of salvation.
The covering from judgment.
The vessel of mercy carrying sinners into covenant grace.

And maybe today…
God is still drawing people out of deep waters.

Out of addiction.
Out of shame.
Out of secret sin.
Out of depression.
Out of bondage.
Out of spiritual numbness.

And if you know someone in a hidden season…
someone battling discouragement…
someone questioning God’s timing…
They may not realize it yet…
but heaven sometimes hides what hell cannot stop.
The God who hid Moses in the river still knows how to hide His people inside mercy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room probably went silent when the Spirit of God first began moving on Samson.
paragraphs: The room probably went silent when the Spirit of God first began moving on Samson.
Not because people feared him yet.
But because deep down… they knew he had been marked.

Before Samson ever touched a lion…
before he shattered ropes…
before gates were ripped from cities…
before Delilah ever whispered his name…
there was a mother trembling under prophecy.
Judges says the Angel of the LORD appeared and declared:
“For behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb…” — Judges 13:5

The Hebrew word used is:
נָזִיר (nāzîr)

It means:
“consecrated,”
“set apart,”
“devoted unto God.”
Not normal.
Not common.
Not allowed to belong to himself anymore.
That sounds beautiful when preached from a stage.
But almost nobody talks about the emotional weight of being chosen before you even understand what choice means.
Samson did not wake up one day and volunteer for greatness.
He inherited separation.
And there are people reading this right now who understand exactly what that feels like.
You grew up feeling different.
You could never fully enjoy what everyone else enjoyed.
You tried fitting in, but something in your spirit always felt disturbed afterward.

You laughed with them…
but went home empty.

You joined them…
but felt God grieving inside you.

You wanted peace with the world…
while carrying a war inside your soul.
That is the hidden loneliness of calling.

People celebrate the strength.
They rarely survive the isolation behind it.
Samson’s life was not simply about muscles.
The Hebrew Scriptures never even emphasize his physical appearance the way modern imagination does.
His real burden was consecration.
Because consecration creates tension.
You begin loving God while still wrestling flesh.
You know truth while still battling appetite.
You are called higher while still trapped inside human weakness.
And Samson’s life becomes terrifyingly relatable when you stop reading him like a cartoon hero and start reading him like a bleeding human being.
The Spirit of God came upon him powerfully.

The Hebrew phrase repeatedly used is:
וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה
(vattitslaḥ alav Ruach YHWH)
“The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him.”
Not lightly touched him.
Rushed upon him.
Overwhelmed him.
Possessed the moment with divine force.
Imagine carrying that kind of spiritual intensity while still fighting human desire.
Some believers know exactly what this feels like.

You can pray with tears…
yet still fight temptation after midnight.

You can hear God clearly…
yet still sabotage relationships.

You can carry anointing publicly…
while privately feeling exhausted by your own weakness.
This is why Samson’s story hurts.
Because it exposes the terrifying possibility of being spiritually gifted while emotionally undisciplined.
And the Church often misunderstands people like Samson.

We either idolize them…
or destroy them.
Rarely do we understand them.
Samson was not merely rebellious.
He was internally divided.
Paul later describes this exact war in Romans 7.
The Greek reads:

“ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω”
(ho gar katergazomai ou ginōskō)
“For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

Paul describes a fractured internal condition:
wanting holiness while battling another law inside himself.
That was Samson long before Paul wrote Romans.
A man carrying heaven’s assignment inside a nervous system still vulnerable to earthly cravings.

And eventually…
that tension began crushing him.
People talk about Delilah like she was merely seductive.
But the deeper tragedy is that Samson kept searching for rest in places that could never protect his calling.
That is the real danger of emotional exhaustion.

When you grow tired of carrying spiritual weight…
you eventually become vulnerable to counterfeit comfort.
Sometimes people do not fall because they hate God.
Sometimes they fall because they are tired.
Tired of resisting.
Tired of carrying expectations.
Tired of being “strong.”
Tired of fighting secret wars nobody sees.
And some of the strongest believers are actually the loneliest believers.

Because everybody admires their gifting…
while almost nobody notices their bleeding soul.
Judges 16 says Delilah pressed him daily.

The Hebrew says:
וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ
(vatte'altzehu)

“She pressured him.”
“She squeezed him emotionally.”
This was not one moment of weakness.
This was prolonged soul exhaustion.
The enemy rarely destroys people instantly.
Usually he drains them slowly.

One compromise.
One hidden conversation.
One private fantasy.
One exhausted surrender at a time.
And eventually Samson tells her everything.
Not because sin suddenly appeared.
But because prolonged compromise finally wore down his spiritual resistance.
Then comes one of the coldest verses in all Scripture.
“But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him.” — Judges 16:20

The Hebrew:
וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו
(vehu lo yada ki YHWH sar me'alav)
“He did not know…”
That phrase should terrify every believer.
Because spiritual drift is often silent before it becomes visible.
Nobody wakes up planning to lose intimacy with God.
It happens gradually.
Prayer becomes optional.
Conviction becomes negotiable.
Compromise becomes explainable.
Presence becomes unfamiliar.

And eventually you keep performing externally…
without realizing something internally has already died.
But this is where the mercy of God becomes overwhelming.
Because Samson’s story should have ended in humiliation.

Blind.
Broken.
Grinding grain like an animal.
The mighty judge reduced to chains.
Sin always humiliates what pride once celebrated.
But then…
one tiny sentence appears like a whisper of resurrection.
“But the hair of his head began to grow again…” — Judges 16:22

The Hebrew:
וַיָּחֶל שְׂעַר רֹאשׁוֹ לְצַמֵּחַ
(vayyachel se'ar rosho letzammeach)
“It began to grow.”
Not fully restored yet.
Not instantly powerful again.

Just…
beginning.
And somebody reading this needs that hope desperately.
Because you think failure disqualified you forever.
You think your compromise canceled God’s purpose.
You think your weakness shocked Heaven.
But Scripture keeps showing us the same truth repeatedly:
God still pursues broken people.
Peter denied Christ.
David collapsed morally.
Jonah ran.
Elijah burned out.
Thomas doubted.
Samson compromised.
Yet God still moved toward repentant hearts.
The enemy wants you ashamed enough to hide.
Jesus wants you surrendered enough to return.
That is the Gospel.
Not human perfection.
Redemption.
The final prayer of Samson is one of the most emotionally devastating prayers in the Bible.
“Lord GOD, remember me, I pray!” — Judges 16:28

The Hebrew:
אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא
(Adonai YHWH zokhreni na)
“Remember me…”

Not:
“Make me famous again.”

Not:
“Restore my image.”

Not:
“Prove them wrong.”

Just:
“Remember me.”
There comes a stage in brokenness where reputation no longer matters.
Only God’s presence matters.

And honestly…
some of the deepest intimacy with God is born after collapse.
Because pride finally dies there.
Masks finally die there.
Performance finally dies there.
Samson destroyed more Philistines in his death than his life.
But the greater tragedy is realizing how much destruction could have happened through surrender instead of self-destruction.
His life becomes a warning to gifted believers.
Anointing is not intimacy.
Calling is not character.
Power is not purity.
And public impact can never substitute private surrender.
But Samson is also hope for exhausted believers.

Because even after blindness…
failure…
bondage…
humiliation…
God still heard him.
That means God can still hear you too.
Even now.
Especially now.
Somebody else needs to know they are not fighting alone.
And maybe the most dangerous moment in your life was never your weakness…
maybe it was pretending you were strong while slowly dying inside.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nobody talks about the silence of Mephibosheth.
paragraphs: Nobody talks about the silence of Mephibosheth.
Not really.

People preach David’s kindness.
People celebrate covenant.
People quote “a seat at the king’s table.”
But very few stop long enough to feel the humiliation that sat inside the bones of the crippled prince.

Because some wounds don’t bleed publicly.
Some pains survive by hiding behind survival.
And Mephibosheth knew exactly what that felt like.
His story begins in catastrophe.
2 Samuel 4:4 says:

“And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame…”
The Hebrew language carries enormous emotional weight here.

The word used for “lame” is:
פִּסֵּחַ
(pisseach)
It means crippled, impaired, disabled in movement.
But this was not merely physical limitation.
This child was dropped while everybody was running from death.
Imagine the trauma.

One moment he belongs to royalty.
The next moment panic fills the palace.
People scream.
War is lost.
His grandfather Saul is dead.
His father Jonathan is dead.
The kingdom is collapsing.
And while being carried by someone trying to save him…
he falls.

Some people were not destroyed by rebellion.
They were damaged during somebody else’s panic.
That is the secret pain of many believers.

You were dropped by exhausted people.
Dropped by distracted people.
Dropped by fearful people.
Dropped by wounded people trying to survive themselves.
And now you walk through life carrying injuries you never asked for.

Somebody reading this still wonders:
“Why did God allow me to be dropped?”
That question lives quietly inside many hearts.
Especially the people who smile the most online.
Especially the ones who say “I’m good” automatically.
Especially the ones who keep serving while privately feeling emotionally crippled.
Because Mephibosheth teaches us something terrifying about pain:
unhealed wounds create hidden identities.
Years later, when David finally calls for him, Mephibosheth says something heartbreaking in 2 Samuel 9:8:
“What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?”
Dead dog.

In Hebrew:
כֶּלֶב מֵת
(kelev met)
This was not casual language.

In ancient Israel, dogs were not viewed the way modern culture views pets.
Calling yourself a dead dog meant:
worthless,
unclean,
discarded,
humiliated,
beneath dignity.
This crippled prince no longer saw royalty when he looked at himself.
He saw shame.
And that is what trauma does when it sits too long inside the soul.
It changes the mirror.

Some people love Jesus…
but still secretly hate themselves.
They worship publicly while internally agreeing with every accusation the enemy whispers at night.

“You’re broken.”
“You’re damaged.”
“You’ll never belong.”
“You’re too ruined.”
“You’re too weak.”
“You’re too compromised.”
And after years of pain, people stop fighting those lies.
They start introducing themselves through them.
That was Mephibosheth.
Not just crippled feet.
Crippled identity.
The text says David found him living in a place called Lo-debar.

לֹא דְבָר
(Lo Debar)

Scholars note the meaning carries the idea of:
“no pasture,”
“no word,”
“barren place,”
“place of nothingness.”
What a picture.

A prince living in emptiness.
A covenant heir hiding in isolation.
A royal son surviving in obscurity.
Because pain loves isolation.
The enemy wants wounded believers hidden.

Hidden in shame.
Hidden in pornography.
Hidden in bitterness.
Hidden in fake peace.
Hidden in emotional numbness.
Hidden behind church smiles.
Hidden behind ministry activity.
Hidden behind constant scrolling and endless distraction.

Some people don’t hate God.
They just stopped believing they belong near Him anymore.
Because the enemy is not only attacking morality anymore.
He is attacking identity.
But then comes one of the most beautiful verses in Scripture.
2 Samuel 9:1:
“And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
Notice this carefully.
David was not searching because Mephibosheth earned restoration.
He searched because of covenant.

That phrase “kindness” is the Hebrew word:
חֶסֶד
(chesed)
This word is almost impossible to fully translate into English.

It means covenant love,
faithful mercy,
steadfast lovingkindness,
unearned loyalty flowing from covenant relationship.
David pursued Mephibosheth because of a covenant established with Jonathan long before.
This is the Gospel.
Jesus Christ pursues broken people because of covenant mercy.

Not because we walk perfectly.
Not because we healed ourselves.
Not because we appear strong.

Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek here is powerful.

“Commendeth” comes from:
συνίστησιν
(synistēsin)

Meaning:
to demonstrate,
to prove,
to establish visibly.
God did not merely say He loved us.
He demonstrated it through Christ.
And this matters deeply because wounded people often believe love must be earned.
But covenant mercy searches for people hiding in Lo-debar.
Even when they feel disqualified.
Even when shame became their identity.
Even when they cannot explain why they still feel broken after all these years.
And then comes the moment that probably shattered Mephibosheth emotionally.
David tells him:
“Fear not.”

In Hebrew:
אַל־תִּירָא
(al-tira)
Do not fear.
Because traumatized people expect rejection automatically.
Mephibosheth likely thought this summons meant execution.
After all, ancient kings often killed rival heirs.
But David restores him instead.
Not partially.
Completely.

His land.
His inheritance.
His dignity.
His position.
And then David says:
“Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall eat bread at my table continually.”
Continually.

Not temporarily.
Not conditionally.
Not occasionally.
Continually.
This is grace.
And here is the part that destroys me emotionally every time:

At the king’s table…
nobody could see Mephibosheth’s crippled feet anymore.
The table covered what shame tried to expose.
This does not mean God ignores sin.
It means grace redefines identity.
The cross of Jesus Christ does not merely forgive sinners.
It restores sons and daughters.
Ephesians 2:8 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith…”

The Greek word for grace:
χάριτί
(chariti)

Meaning:
favor,
gift,
unearned kindness,
divine generosity.
Mephibosheth lived because covenant kindness was greater than inherited shame.
And many believers desperately need to hear this:
Your injury is not your identity.
Your trauma is not your name.
Your failure is not your final sentence.
Jesus Christ still calls wounded people to His table.

Not because they are strong.
But because He is merciful.
Somebody reading this has spent years hiding emotional paralysis behind humor, ministry, productivity, relationships, or social media performance.
But exhausted souls cannot heal pretending forever.
Because there are still modern-day Mephibosheths sitting in dark rooms wondering if God remembers them.
He does.
The Gospel is not Jesus searching for impressive people.
The Gospel is the King searching for crippled heirs hiding in Lo-debar.

And maybe that secret ache you carry…
the one nobody knows how to explain…
is exactly where Christ plans to reveal covenant mercy most powerfully.
Because grace has always walked toward the broken.
The terrifying thing is not that Mephibosheth had wounded feet.
The terrifying thing is that he almost believed wounded feet meant he no longer belonged at the King’s table.
And many believers are still believing that lie tonight.
And never forget this:
The King did not ask Mephibosheth to fix his feet before coming to the table.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room was full of men.
paragraphs: The room was full of men.

Prophets.
Priests.
Warriors.
Voices history never stopped repeating.
But hidden in the silence of Scripture was a woman most believers have either skipped over… or never truly seen.
Not because she lacked faith.
Not because she lacked courage.
But because heaven often hides its greatest heroes behind ordinary names.
Her name was Rizpah.
And what she did was so powerful… it may be one of the most heartbreaking displays of love, loyalty, grief, justice, and spiritual warfare in the entire Bible.
Most people never preach about her.
Few songs mention her.
She has no book named after her.

No crown.
No throne.
No famous miracles.

Just a shattered heart…
and a terrifying kind of faithfulness.
The kind that stays when everyone else leaves.
The kind that remains after death.
The kind that watches over broken things when nobody else thinks they matter anymore.
Her story appears in 2 Samuel 21.
Israel was under judgment.
A famine had lasted three years.
King David sought the face of God concerning why heaven had shut itself over the nation.
And the answer was devastating.
Saul, the former king, had committed bloodguilt against the Gibeonites by violating an ancient covenant Israel had sworn before God.
The land was bleeding from unresolved sin.

Justice had been delayed.
Truth buried.
Covenants broken.
So restitution was demanded.
Seven descendants of Saul were handed over for execution.
Among them were the sons of Rizpah.
Imagine that.

Not because they personally committed the crime.
Not because they led rebellion.
Not because they were murderers.
But because sin always leaves wreckage beyond the original sinner.
That alone should stop us.

The modern world teaches:
“Your sin only affects you.”
Scripture says otherwise.
The Hebrew concept of covenant carried communal consequences.

The word often tied to covenant is:
בְּרִית (Berith)
A sacred binding agreement.

Not casual.
Not disposable.
Not temporary.
And when covenant was violated, the consequences could spread across generations, communities, and nations.
That is why sin is never “private.”

Your hidden compromise can become your family’s storm.
Your secret rebellion can become your children’s confusion.
Your spiritual laziness can become generational darkness.
People want the freedom to sin without the responsibility of consequence.
But the Bible never teaches isolated rebellion.
It teaches ripple effects.
And Rizpah stood in the middle of those ripples.
Then came the horror.
The bodies of her sons were exposed publicly after execution.
Unburied.
Humiliated.
Left vulnerable to scavenging birds during the day and wild beasts at night.
In ancient Israel, denial of burial was not merely emotional pain.
It represented disgrace.
The Hebrew understanding of honor after death mattered deeply because humanity bears the image of God.
Even in death, dignity mattered.
And this is where Rizpah becomes unforgettable.
Scripture says:
“She took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell from the heavens…” — 2 Samuel 21:10
Read that again.

From harvest season…
until rain came.
This was not one night of mourning.
This was months.
Months.
She stayed beside the bodies.

Day after day.
Night after night.

Driving away birds.
Fighting beasts.
Guarding what everyone else abandoned.

No applause.
No recognition.
No guarantee anyone cared.

Just a mother…
refusing to leave.
The Hebrew phrase describing her action carries violent persistence.
She “drove away” the birds and beasts.
Not symbolically.
Literally.
Can you picture her?

Exhausted.
Weeping.
Sleepless.
Starving.
Sunburned by day.
Frozen by night.
Yet still standing guard over the broken remains of what she loved.
This is not weak faith.
This is terrifying endurance.
This is covenant love refusing to disappear.
And suddenly Rizpah becomes more than a grieving mother.
She becomes a prophetic picture.
Because this is exactly what faithful love does.
It stays.

Even when things smell like death.
Even when prayers seem unanswered.
Even when heaven feels silent.
Even when everybody else moved on.
Modern culture glorifies quitting.
God honors staying.

Some of you are one painful season away from abandoning your marriage.
Your calling.
Your prayer life.
Your purity.
Your faith.
But Rizpah teaches something the modern church rarely preaches:
Holy endurance changes history.

The Greek New Testament later uses the word:
ὑπομονή (Hypomonē)

Meaning:
steadfast endurance,
patient perseverance,
remaining under pressure without surrendering.
Not shallow positivity.
Not fake smiles.
Endurance.

The kind Jesus described in Matthew 24:13:
“He who endures to the end shall be saved.”

Not the loudest believer.
Not the trendiest preacher.
Not the most visible Christian.
The one who remains faithful.
And Rizpah remained.
Then something astonishing happened.
David heard about what she was doing.

One grieving mother sitting on a rock…
moved a king.
Her faithfulness awakened national conscience.
David finally gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan along with the executed descendants and gave them honorable burial.
Then Scripture says:
“After that, God responded to the plea for the land.”
Do not miss this.

Rain came after remembrance.
Healing came after honor.
Restoration came after somebody refused to abandon the forgotten.
Rizpah’s faithfulness became part of national restoration.
One hidden woman changed the atmosphere of an entire nation.
And maybe that is exactly why hell fights faithful people so hard.
Because quiet obedience terrifies darkness.
You may feel unseen right now.

Forgotten.
Overlooked.
Emotionally exhausted.

You kept praying for your child.
Still serving.
Still forgiving.
Still showing up.
Still resisting temptation.
Still believing while secretly breaking inside.
Rizpah understands you.
And more importantly…
Jesus does too.
Because the Gospel itself is the story of Someone who stayed beside the condemned.

When humanity was spiritually exposed in shame…
Christ did not walk away.

Isaiah 53 describes Him as:
“despised and rejected.”

The Hebrew word for rejected there is:
חֲדַל (Chadal)

Meaning forsaken,
abandoned,
left behind.
Jesus entered abandonment so sinners could be brought near to God.
At the cross, while many fled…
He stayed.
And after His death, something extraordinary happened.
Joseph of Arimathea requested His body.
Why?
Because dignity still mattered.
Love still stayed.
Burial still mattered.

Rizpah guarded the dead.
Christ conquered death.
And through resurrection, Jesus transformed every grieving rock into a future testimony.
Some of you reading this have been sitting beside emotional graves for years.

The grave of betrayal.
The grave of addiction.
The grave of divorce.
The grave of regret.
The grave of the person you used to be.
But the Gospel says graves are not final places when Christ steps in.
The resurrection was heaven’s declaration that abandoned things are not beyond redemption.
That forgotten people are still seen.
That hidden faithfulness matters.
That tears are counted.
Psalm 56:8 says God keeps our tears in His bottle.

Not one forgotten.
Not one wasted.
Maybe that is why Rizpah’s story still cuts so deeply.
Because everyone knows what it feels like to guard pain nobody else understands.

To sit beside something broken.
To feel unseen.
To wonder if faithfulness still matters.
And yet heaven recorded her name forever.
Not because she was famous.
Because she stayed faithful when nobody was watching.
That is real spiritual warfare.

Not platform Christianity.
Not performance.
Not image management.
Faithfulness in hidden places.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if somebody you love feels forgotten, abandoned, or emotionally exhausted, share this with them today.
Some people look forgotten on earth while heaven is writing their name in eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS DELAYED OBEDIENCE STILL DISOBEDIENCE?
paragraphs: IS DELAYED OBEDIENCE STILL DISOBEDIENCE?
The question sounds simple until it becomes personal.
Not theoretical.
Personal.
Because almost everyone reading this can remember a moment when they knew exactly what God was asking them to do.
Apologize.
Forgive.
Leave.
Stay.
Speak.
Repent.
Serve.
Surrender.
Give.
Trust.
And instead of saying no...
they said, “Later.”
That is what makes this question so uncomfortable.
Most believers would never openly tell God no.
But many have quietly told Him not yet.
And sometimes, those two answers are far closer than we would like to admit.
The silence in the room after God speaks is often where some of the greatest spiritual battles are fought.
Not rebellion in public.
Delay in private.
Not fists raised against heaven.
Just a heart negotiating with the King.
The tragedy is that delayed obedience often feels spiritual.
We tell ourselves we are praying about it.
Thinking about it.
Seeking confirmation.
Waiting for better timing.
Preparing.
Learning.
Growing.
Yet beneath all the spiritual language, there can sometimes be a hidden reality.
God already spoke.
The decision was already made in heaven.
We are simply delaying what we know we should do.
The Bible repeatedly confronts this uncomfortable truth.
One of the clearest examples comes from the life of King Saul.
When God commanded Saul to completely destroy the Amalekites, Saul obeyed partially while preserving what God explicitly said to remove.
When confronted, Saul defended himself.
He explained.
Justified.
Rationalized.
Yet the prophet Samuel delivered one of the most devastating statements in Scripture:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
(1 Samuel 15:22)
The Hebrew word translated “obey” is שָׁמַע (shamaʿ).
It means far more than merely hearing words.
It carries the idea of hearing with the intention of responding.
Listening that produces action.
In biblical thought, hearing and obeying were inseparable concepts.
A person had not truly heard God if they refused to act on what He said.
This changes everything.
Because in Scripture, delayed obedience is not merely a timing issue.
It becomes a hearing issue.
If God has spoken clearly and we refuse to respond, have we actually listened?
The ancient Hebrew mindset would often answer no.
Many believers imagine obedience as a destination.
The Bible presents obedience as a response.
The moment God speaks, faith moves.
This is why Abraham remains one of Scripture’s greatest examples of faith.
Genesis records that God called him to leave everything familiar.
His homeland.
His security.
His future plans.
His comfort.
The remarkable part of the story is not simply that Abraham obeyed.
It is how quickly he obeyed.
God spoke.
Abraham moved.
There is no record of years spent negotiating.
No committee meetings.
No strategic planning sessions.
No endless requests for additional signs.
God called.
Abraham responded.
The New Testament later celebrates this as faith itself.
Because biblical faith was never intended to be mere intellectual agreement.
Faith moves.
Faith trusts.
Faith acts.
The Greek word often translated faith is πίστις (pistis).
While modern readers often reduce faith to belief, pistis carries the sense of trust, loyalty, confidence, and faithful commitment.
Biblical faith is not passive.
It demonstrates itself through action.
This explains why James writes:
(James 2:17)
James is not teaching salvation by works.
He is teaching that genuine faith inevitably produces obedience.
A living faith moves.
A dead faith delays indefinitely.
Yet before anyone reading feels condemned, there is another side of this conversation that must be understood.
Not all waiting is disobedience.
Scripture also contains examples of holy waiting.
David waited for God's timing.
The disciples waited for the promised Holy Spirit.
The early church often sought God's direction before acting.
The issue is not waiting.
The issue is whether God commanded action or commanded waiting.
There is a profound difference.
Waiting because God said wait is obedience.
Waiting because we fear obedience is delay.
The challenge is that only the heart truly knows which one it is.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes delayed obedience is not really confusion.
It is fear.
Fear of loss.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of change.
Fear of sacrifice.
Fear of what happens next.
Jonah knew exactly what God wanted.
His problem was not lack of clarity.
His problem was lack of willingness.
The storm that followed was not caused by ignorance.
It was caused by delayed obedience.
How many storms in our own lives are not caused by the absence of God's guidance but by resistance to guidance already given?
That question is uncomfortable because it forces us to examine ourselves honestly.
Many believers spend years asking God for new directions while ignoring old instructions.
Praying for another word.
Seeking another revelation.
Waiting for another sign.
Meanwhile, heaven remains silent.
Not because God has abandoned them.
Because God is still waiting for them to obey the last thing He said.
Jesus Himself addressed this issue directly.
In Luke 6:46 He asks:
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?”
The question cuts through every excuse.
The title “Lord” comes from the Greek word κύριος (kyrios).
It means master.
Owner.
Sovereign ruler.
One possessing authority.
Jesus essentially asks:
If I truly am your Lord, why is My authority ignored?
Christianity has never been about admiration without submission.
The Gospel calls us to both.
To love Christ and follow Christ.
To worship Christ and obey Christ.
To trust Christ and surrender to Christ.
This is why delayed obedience is so spiritually dangerous.
The longer obedience is postponed, the easier compromise becomes.
Conviction weakens.
Urgency fades.
The voice once clear becomes easier to ignore.
What felt impossible yesterday begins to feel normal tomorrow.
The heart slowly adjusts to disobedience.
Not all at once.
Little by little.
That is how spiritual drift often begins.
Not with rebellion.
With delay.
And yet there is extraordinary hope.
Because the Gospel is not a story about perfect people who obeyed immediately every time.
It is the story of a perfect Savior who rescues imperfect people who failed.
Peter delayed.
Jonah ran.
Moses resisted.
David stumbled.
Yet God's grace met them all.
The answer to delayed obedience is not despair.
It is repentance.
The New Testament word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a change of mind resulting in a change of direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad.
It is turning back.
Turning toward God.
Turning toward obedience.
The beautiful truth is that if you are reading this and feeling conviction, it is not too late.
The same God who spoke before is still calling today.
The same grace that saved you still invites you.
The same Christ who died for your sins still extends mercy.
Perhaps the question is no longer whether delayed obedience is disobedience.
Perhaps the greater question is:
What has God already asked you to do?
The conversation you keep postponing.
The sin you keep excusing.
The forgiveness you keep withholding.
The surrender you keep resisting.
The calling you keep delaying.
The answer may already be sitting quietly in your heart.
Waiting.
Not for another sign.
Not for another confirmation.
Not for another sermon.
Just obedience.
If this article exposed something God has been speaking to you about, be honest.
One day we will discover that many of life's greatest regrets were not the times God was silent—but the moments He spoke clearly and we waited too long.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There is a reason the enemy did not begin with Adam.
paragraphs: There is a reason the enemy did not begin with Adam.
That detail has haunted theologians, historians, rabbis, and believers for centuries.

Out of all the creatures in Eden…
Out of all the moments in human history…
Out of all the strategies hell could have used…
the serpent went to Eve first.
Not because she was weaker.
But because the enemy understood something most people still do not.
The first attack in human history was not against strength.

It was against identity.
Against trust.
Against sacred intimacy with God.
And if you are not careful, you will read Genesis too quickly and completely miss the psychological warfare unfolding beneath the surface.
Because the story in Eden was never simply about fruit.
It was about worship.
It was about authority.
It was about whose voice humanity would trust.
And some of you are still fighting that same serpent every single day.
The book of Genesis introduces the serpent with chilling precision:
“Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made.” — Genesis 3:1
The Hebrew word for “subtil” is עָרוּם (ʿārûm).

It means:
crafty,
shrewd,
strategic,
psychologically calculating.
This was not a wild beast attacking randomly.
This was an intelligent spiritual assassination.

The serpent studies.
The serpent watches.
The serpent waits.
Hell does not waste temptation.

It studies wounds.
Patterns.
Loneliness.
Silence.
Insecurities.
Fatigue.
Curiosity.
Isolation.
And then it whispers.
The Hebrew text becomes even more revealing when the serpent approaches Eve:
“Yea, hath God said…” — Genesis 3:1

In Hebrew:
אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים
(ʾaph kî-ʾāmar ʾĕlōhîm)
The structure carries the tone of manipulation and distortion.
It was not a direct denial at first.
It was suggestion.
Subtle reframing.
The enemy rarely begins with rebellion.
He begins with confusion.
He introduces uncertainty into what God already made clear.
That is still how darkness operates today.
Not usually through obvious evil.
But through altered truth.

“Did God really say purity matters?”
“Did God really say forgiveness is necessary?”
“Did God really say marriage is sacred?”
“Did God really say obedience matters?”
“Did God really say you are loved?”
The first satanic strategy in history was theological distortion.
And Eve was standing in the middle of it.
But here is where the story becomes deeply emotional.
Most people assume Eve was targeted because she was gullible.
Scripture never says that.
Not once.
In fact, the text suggests something far more devastating.
Eve was targeted because she carried influence.
When Satan attacked humanity, he did not go first to the one formed from dust.
He went to the one created from intimacy.
Genesis 2:22 says:
“And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman…”
The Hebrew word for “rib” is צֵלָע (ṣēlāʿ).
It does not simply mean rib bone.
It can also mean side, chamber, support structure, sacred architecture.

Eve was not created beneath Adam.
Not from his feet to be trampled.
Not from his head to dominate him.
From his side.
Near his heart.

Close enough to protect.
Close enough to love.
Close enough to reflect divine companionship.
The first woman carried relational power.
She represented connection.
And Satan understood something terrifying:

If he could fracture trust inside the relationship…
he could fracture humanity itself.
So the serpent did not begin with brute force.
He began with conversation.
Notice something else most people overlook.
The serpent speaks to Eve while she is separated from Adam.
Isolation has always been one of hell’s favorite environments.
Because voices become louder when accountability disappears.
That is why so many spiritual collapses happen in secret.

Private compromises.
Hidden addictions.
Silent bitterness.
Unspoken wounds.
The enemy loves isolated minds.
1 Peter 5:8 says:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.”
The Greek word for “devour” is καταπιεῖν (katapiein).

It means:
to swallow whole,
to consume completely.
Satan never wanted Eve slightly distracted.
He wanted humanity consumed.
And then comes the most dangerous sentence in Eden.
“You shall not surely die.” — Genesis 3:4

In Hebrew:
לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן
(lō-mōṯ təmuṯūn)
This was the first direct contradiction of God in human history.

The serpent moves from questioning God…
to replacing God.
And humanity has been wrestling with that temptation ever since.

To redefine morality.
To edit truth.
To crown personal desire above divine authority.
This is why the fall was catastrophic.
Because sin was not merely eating forbidden fruit.
Sin was humanity choosing autonomy over intimacy with God.
And suddenly shame enters the world.
Genesis 3:7 says:
“And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked…”
The Hebrew word for naked here is עֵירֹם (ʿêrōm).
Not merely physically exposed.

Vulnerable.
Ashamed.
Stripped.
Emotionally uncovered.
Sin always promises elevation.
But delivers exposure.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.

The hidden habit.
The fake smile.
The secret compromise.
The late-night regret.
The exhausting performance.
The fear that if people truly knew you, they would walk away.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because while Adam and Eve hid…
God came looking.
Genesis 3:9:
“And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?”

In Hebrew:
אַיֶּכָּה
(ʾayyekkāh)
Not because God lacked information.
But because God was inviting confession.
That question still echoes through every generation.

Where are you spiritually?
Where are you emotionally?
Where are you in your obedience?
Where are you in your secret life?
Where are you in your relationship with Christ?
Some of you reading this have mastered pretending.
But heaven still sees the hiding places.
And yet…
God still comes searching.
That is the part that breaks me every time.
Humanity sinned.
Humanity hid.
Humanity blamed.
Humanity fractured.
But God pursued.
Even in judgment, mercy appeared.
Genesis 3:15 contains what theologians call the Protoevangelium — the first Gospel prophecy.
Speaking to the serpent, God says:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.”
The Hebrew word for “bruise/crush” is שׁוּף (šūp̄).

Crush.
Strike fatally.
This was the first prophetic announcement of Jesus Christ.

Before humanity ever escaped Eden…
God already revealed redemption.
The serpent would wound the Messiah temporarily…
but Christ would crush the serpent ultimately.
That is why the cross terrified hell.
Because Satan thought Eden was victory.
But Calvary became reversal.
Jesus became the second Adam.

Where Adam failed in a garden…
Christ surrendered in a garden.

Where humanity hid in shame…
Jesus was publicly stripped on a cross.

Where the serpent brought death through a tree…
Christ brought life through a tree.
And maybe that is why this story still wrecks people emotionally.
Because deep down, we recognize ourselves in Eve.
We know what it feels like to hear conflicting voices.

We know temptation.
Curiosity.
Confusion.
Shame.
Fear.
Hiding.
But we also recognize the voice of God still calling into our darkness:
“Where are you?”
Not to destroy us.
To bring us home.
Be honest.
This hit harder than some of you expected.
And somebody you know desperately needs this reminder that the enemy’s oldest weapon is still deception… but Christ is still greater.

The serpent spoke first in Eden…
but God gets the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF GOLIATH
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY OF GOLIATH
The Giant Was Bigger Than You Think
Most people think they know the story.

A giant.
A shepherd boy.
A stone.
A victory.
But the real story is far more disturbing.
Because Goliath was never the biggest giant on that battlefield.
Fear was.
And fear still walks among us today.
The tragedy is that millions of believers know David's victory, but they have never understood Goliath's purpose.
Because Goliath was not merely a warrior.
He was a weapon of psychological warfare.
He was designed to make God's people forget who God was.
And if we're honest...
That strategy still works.
Every day.
Everywhere.
In homes.
In marriages.
In churches.
In private battles nobody talks about.
The story begins long before David ever picked up a stone.
The story begins with a nation that forgot how to trust.
The Valley of Fear
Scripture tells us:
"And the Philistines stood on a mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on a mountain on the other side: and there was a valley between them."
(1 Samuel 17:3)
This was not merely geography.
It was theology.
Two kingdoms.
Two worldviews.
Two futures.
Separated by a valley.
The Hebrew word for valley here is:

עֵמֶק
(emeq)
A deep place.
A low place.
A place between destinations.
A place where battles happen.
And isn't that where most of us live?
Between promise and fulfillment.
Between faith and fear.
Between what God said and what we currently see.
The valley is where giants appear.
Goliath Was a Monster of a Man
The Bible says:
"And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath..."
(1 Samuel 17:4)
The Hebrew word translated "champion" is fascinating.

אִישׁ הַבֵּנַיִם
(ish ha-benayim)
Literally:
"The man between."
The middle man.
The representative warrior.
The one who stood between two armies and declared:
"If I win, you lose."
"If I conquer, you serve."
Goliath represented more than himself.
Just as David represented more than himself.
This battle was never merely personal.
It was covenantal.
Kingdom against kingdom.
Truth against deception.
Faith against intimidation.
How Tall Was Goliath Really?
The traditional Hebrew text describes Goliath as:
Six cubits and a span.
Approximately:
9 feet 9 inches.
Nearly 3 meters tall.
Whether slightly shorter or exactly that height, the point remains unchanged.
He was terrifying.
His armor alone weighed approximately 125 pounds.
His spearhead weighed around 15 pounds.
He looked unbeatable.
And that was the point.
Satan has always specialized in appearances.
The enemy wants problems to look larger than God's promises.
He wants sickness to look permanent.
Failure to look final.
Sin to look stronger.
Addiction to look unbeatable.
The giant's first weapon was not his spear.
It was perception.
The Forty-Day Attack Nobody Talks About
Many people miss this detail.
Scripture says:
"And the Philistine drew near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days."
(1 Samuel 17:16)
Forty days.
Twice a day.
Eighty public humiliations.
Eighty threats.
Eighty reminders of fear.
This wasn't combat.
This was psychological conditioning.
Every morning.
Every evening.
The same voice.
The same intimidation.
The same threat.
Until Israel began believing the giant's version of reality.
Sound familiar?
You wake up.
The anxiety speaks.
You go to sleep.
The anxiety speaks.
Morning.
Evening.
Morning.
Evening.
The voice repeats itself until it sounds true.
Many believers are not losing battles because the giant is stronger.
They are losing because they have listened too long.
Why Saul Could Not Fight
The Bible says:
"When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid."
(1 Samuel 17:11)
The Hebrew phrase implies being shattered internally.
Broken emotionally.
Crushed mentally.
Overwhelmed psychologically.
Saul was the obvious choice.
He was the king.
He was trained.
He was armed.
He was physically impressive.
Yet he could not move.
Why?
Because fear had already defeated him before the battle ever started.
Many people believe courage means not feeling fear.
Biblically, courage means obeying God while fear is screaming.
David did not have less fear.
David had greater trust.
David Saw Something Nobody Else Saw
When David arrived, everybody saw a giant.
David saw an uncircumcised Philistine.
Listen carefully.
He did not identify Goliath by his size.
He identified him by his spiritual condition.
David said:
"Who is this uncircumcised Philistine?"
(1 Samuel 17:26)
The Hebrew word:

עָרֵל
(arel)
Uncircumcised.
Outside covenant.
Outside God's promises.
Outside God's protection.
Outside God's relationship.
Everyone else saw size.
David saw status.
Everyone else saw power.
David saw a man disconnected from the living God.
Perspective changes everything.
The Secret Nobody Knew About David
David's confidence did not begin in public.
It began in private.
Long before Goliath.
Long before applause.
Long before recognition.
David fought lions.
David fought bears.
David worshiped in obscurity.
David learned dependence where nobody was watching.
The greatest victories in your life will rarely begin on public stages.
They begin in hidden places.
Prayer nobody sees.
Repentance nobody applauds.
Faithfulness nobody rewards.
Private obedience creates public courage.
The Stone That Changed History
Then came the moment.
The moment every child remembers.
The shepherd ran toward the giant.
Not away.
Toward him.
The Hebrew text paints a picture of urgency.
David did not hesitate.
He did not negotiate.
He did not wait for ideal conditions.
He trusted God.
The stone struck.
The giant fell.
The earth shook beneath a warrior everyone thought could never be defeated.
And suddenly everybody discovered something.
The giant was never invincible.
He was simply unchallenged.
Read that again.
The giant was never invincible.
He was simply unchallenged.
The Deeper Prophetic Picture
The story points beyond David.
Far beyond David.
David is ultimately a shadow.
A foreshadowing.
A glimpse.
A prophetic picture of Jesus Christ.
Like David:
Jesus appeared unlikely.
Like David:
Jesus was underestimated.
Like David:
Jesus represented His people.
Like David:
Jesus fought a battle others could not fight.
And just as David defeated the giant on behalf of Israel...
Christ defeated sin, death, and hell on behalf of humanity.
The Greek word used in the New Testament for Savior is:

Σωτήρ
(Sōtēr)
Deliverer.
Rescuer.
