Redeemer.
The victory of Jesus was not merely an example.
It was a substitution.
He fought where we could not.
He conquered what we could not conquer.
He carried what we could not carry.
And because He rose again, the greatest giant humanity ever faced has already fallen.
The Giant Standing In Front Of You
Maybe your giant is not nine feet tall.
Maybe it's depression.
Maybe it's shame.
Maybe it's addiction.
Maybe it's regret.
Maybe it's grief.
Maybe it's a secret sin nobody knows.
Maybe it's the voice in your head telling you you'll never change.
The same God who stood with David still reigns.
The same Christ who defeated death still saves.
The same Holy Spirit still empowers believers.
Your giant may be large.
But it is not larger than God.
Never has been.
Never will be.
Somebody reading this has spent months listening to the giant.
Months believing the threats.
Months believing defeat is inevitable.
But today is your reminder:
The giant's voice is loud.
God's voice is true.
And truth always outlives intimidation.
Someone else may need your story today.
The giant that terrified an entire nation became the testimony of a shepherd who trusted God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Isaac thought he was choosing a son.
paragraphs: Isaac thought he was choosing a son.
But he was actually shaping generations.
And one quiet sentence buried in Scripture reveals a tragedy most people skip past too quickly:
“Now Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob.” — Genesis 25:28
Read that again.
Isaac loved Esau because of what Esau gave him.

Not because Esau walked with God.
Not because Esau valued spiritual things.
Not because Esau carried the heart of the covenant.
Isaac loved him because Esau satisfied his appetite.
And that one misplaced affection changed everything.

Most people don’t realize how dangerous favoritism becomes when it blinds spiritual discernment. Isaac was not just a father. He was the patriarch chosen in the covenant line of Abraham. The promises of God were flowing through his household. Nations were in the womb of Rebekah. Heaven itself had already spoken concerning the boys before they were born:
“The elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23
God already declared Jacob would carry the covenant promise.
But Isaac kept leaning toward Esau anyway.
Why?
Because Esau appealed to his flesh.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can love someone emotionally and still be blind spiritually.

Isaac saw Esau’s strength.
His masculinity.
His hunting skills.
His outdoorsman spirit.
The wild game he brought home.
But God saw deeper.
God saw a man who would eventually despise his birthright for a bowl of stew.
A man willing to trade eternal inheritance for temporary hunger.
“And Esau despised his birthright.” — Genesis 25:34
That line should terrify people.
Because many still do the same thing today.

Trading purity for pleasure.
Truth for popularity.
Calling for comfort.
Conviction for temporary satisfaction.
God saw it.
You knew.

Esau was impulsive.
Driven by appetite.
Controlled by the immediate.

And Isaac either ignored it…
or refused to confront it.

That is one of the most painful realities in Scripture:
parents can sometimes strengthen what God is trying to expose.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The house of Isaac slowly became divided by favoritism.

Rebekah clung to Jacob.
Isaac clung to Esau.
And eventually deception entered the home because spiritual leadership had already weakened long before Jacob stole the blessing.
People often focus only on Jacob’s deception. And yes, Jacob sinned. Deeply.
But the fracture started earlier.
It started when affection became partial instead of righteous.

Isaac knew the prophecy.
Isaac knew God’s word concerning the boys.
Yet in Genesis 27, when Isaac became old and his eyes were dim, he still attempted to give the covenant blessing to Esau privately.
That matters.

His physical blindness mirrored something deeper:
spiritual blindness.
“And Isaac said unto Esau… make me savory meat, such as I love… that my soul may bless thee before I die.” — Genesis 27:4

Again…
his appetite appears.
The blessing moment was surrounded by craving.
That should shake people.
Because unchecked flesh can distort judgment even in spiritual leaders.

You can preach.
Lead.
Teach.
Raise children.
Carry history with God…
…and still allow personal desires to cloud obedience.
This story is not just about ancient brothers.
It is about what happens when families stop seeing through God’s eyes.

One child becomes “the successful one.”
Another becomes “the difficult one.”
One receives affection more freely.
Another grows up starving for approval.
And slowly division grows in silence.
Some people reading this still carry wounds from partial love.

You remember trying harder.
Performing better.
Hoping someone would finally choose you.
God saw it.
But this story is also a warning to parents.

Love cannot be governed by preference.
It must be governed by truth.

Isaac preferred Esau’s personality.
God chose according to purpose.
That difference changed history.
Romans 9 later explains that God’s choice was never based merely on human effort or natural status:
“For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil… it was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger.” — Romans 9:11-12
This was about God’s sovereign plan.
Not human favoritism.

Not charisma.
Not talent.
Not natural strength.
Because the Kingdom of God has always overturned human expectations.

David was overlooked.
Joseph was hated.
Moses stuttered.
Peter failed.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God chose them.
Meanwhile Esau looked powerful externally…
…but spiritually he was careless.
Hebrews gives one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament about him:
“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” — Hebrews 12:16
Profane.
Meaning he treated holy things casually.
That spirit still exists everywhere now.

People casually ignore conviction.
Casually compromise.
Casually mock repentance.
Casually trade eternity for temporary pleasure.

One relationship.
One addiction.
One hidden sin.
One appetite.
And suddenly eternal things no longer matter.
That is Esau’s spirit.
And Isaac could not fully see it because his affections were clouded.
This is why spiritual discernment matters more than emotional attachment.

A person can be charming and still spiritually dangerous.
Talented and still rebellious.
Successful and still lost.

The flesh notices appearance first.
God examines the heart.
“For the Lord seeth not as man seeth… man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7
But here is where the Gospel enters the story.
Because if we are honest…
there is Esau in all of us.
Every person has traded eternal things for temporary desires.
Every person has chosen appetite over obedience at some point.

Sin is not merely “mistakes.”
It is rebellion against God.

And the terrifying reality is this:
without Christ, we naturally drift toward Esau’s path.

Living for the now.
Living for self.
Living for appetite.
But Jesus came to rescue people enslaved to the flesh.
Where Esau failed, Christ obeyed.

Esau surrendered inheritance for food.
Jesus refused Satan’s temptation in the wilderness despite extreme hunger.
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4
Do you see the contrast?

Esau said yes to appetite.
Jesus said yes to the Father.
That obedience led Christ to the cross.
There, Jesus bore the punishment for sinners who traded holiness for sin again and again.
The cross is where mercy met rebels.

Not because we deserved it.
Not because we performed well enough.
But because God loved sinners enough to send His Son.
And through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, even people who wasted years chasing temporary things can be redeemed.
That is the hope Esau never truly sought.
Some of you feel the Holy Spirit exposing things right now.

The appetite.
The compromise.
The hidden idol.
The resentment.
The favoritism.
The spiritual blindness.
Do not harden your heart.
Because eventually repeated compromise numbs conviction.
That is why Scripture says:
“Today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.” — Hebrews 3:15
Today.
Not later.
Some people keep waiting for a “better season” to surrender to God while feeding the very desires destroying them.
You already know the emptiness isn’t leaving.
You knew.
But Jesus Christ still saves.

Still restores.
Still forgives.
Still changes hearts.
If you are ready to go deeper in Scripture, discipleship, spiritual warfare, and Gospel-centered transformation, join here:
Because one path feeds the flesh until eternity is lost.
The other leads to Christ, repentance, and life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jonah sat outside the city angry that mercy had won.
paragraphs: Jonah sat outside the city angry that mercy had won.
That sentence sounds almost impossible until you realize how many believers secretly live there too.
Not in Nineveh.
Not on a hillside east of the city.
But inside a silent war between obedience and bitterness.

Jonah preached one of the greatest repentance revivals in recorded history. Entire streets collapsed into mourning. Violent men fasted. Kings stepped down from their thrones. An empire trembled before God.
And Jonah hated every second of it.
That is what makes the Book of Book of Jonah so terrifying.
Because the prophet was not rebelling openly anymore.
He was obeying externally while rotting internally.
Most people think Jonah’s story is about a fish.
It is not.
It is about resentment hidden beneath religious duty.
It is about a man who could preach repentance to others while refusing healing for himself.
And if we are honest…
many Christians today are doing exactly the same thing.
The book opens with God’s command:
“Arise, go to Nineveh…” (Jonah 1:2)
The Hebrew word for arise is קוּם (qum).

It means:
rise,
stand up,
take action,
move immediately.
God was not merely giving Jonah a travel assignment.
He was confronting the posture of his heart.
Because Nineveh was not just another city.
It was Assyria.
A brutal empire.

Violent.
Cruel.
Merciless.
Ancient Assyrian records describe horrifying torture practices. Entire populations lived in fear of them. They were known for mutilation, public executions, psychological warfare, and terror.
And now God was asking Jonah to preach mercy to them.
This changes everything.
Jonah was not merely afraid.
He was offended by grace.
That is why Jonah 4 becomes one of the most emotionally exposing chapters in Scripture.
After Nineveh repents, Jonah says something shocking:
“I knew that You are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger…” (Jonah 4:2)

The Hebrew phrase:
אֵל־חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם
(El-ḥannun ve-raḥum)

means:
“a God full of compassion and tender mercy.”
Jonah was quoting God’s own self-description from Exodus 34:6.
He knew the theology perfectly.
That was not the problem.

The problem was that Jonah wanted mercy for himself…
but justice for his enemies.
And suddenly the story becomes deeply personal.
Because many believers celebrate grace until God gives it to someone they secretly believe does not deserve it.
The addict who destroyed the family.
The ex who lied.
The hypocrite who embarrassed the church.
The person who wounded you and now seems blessed.
The prodigal who comes home after years of rebellion.
The people we smile at publicly while privately hoping God “deals with them.”
Jonah exposes the hidden ugliness inside selective compassion.
And what makes bitterness so dangerous is that it often disguises itself as righteousness.
Jonah probably thought his anger was justified.
That is how bitterness survives.
It baptizes itself in moral language.
“I’m just discerning.”
“I’m just protecting myself.”
“I just care about justice.”
But bitterness rarely announces itself honestly.

In Greek, the New Testament word often associated with bitterness is:
πικρία (pikria)

It literally refers to sharpness,
poison,
corrosive hostility.
Hebrews 12:15 warns:
“lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you…”

The phrase “root of bitterness” in Greek is:
ῥίζα πικρίας
(rhiza pikrias)
Roots grow underground before they become visible.
That is why bitterness is terrifying spiritually.
It hides.
It smiles in worship services.
It posts Bible verses online.
It serves in ministry.
It sings with hands lifted high while secretly keeping score of wounds.
And eventually the poison spreads.
Jonah’s bitterness became so irrational that he was more emotionally devastated over a dead plant than thousands of human souls.
That is the frightening progression of unresolved resentment.
It disorders love.
It warps priorities.
It shrinks compassion.
Jonah 4:10–11 reveals God’s devastating response.
God asks Jonah why he cares more about a plant than people created in His image.

The Hebrew word for compassion there is:
חוּס (chus)

It means:
to pity,
to spare,
to have mercy upon.
God was exposing Jonah’s emotional inconsistency.
And perhaps He is exposing ours too.
Some believers have spent years asking God for healing while secretly nurturing hatred.

Some people are exhausted spiritually not because God abandoned them…
but because bitterness became a hidden altar in their heart.
You can obey God externally while internally resisting His character.
That is Jonah’s tragedy.
He became angry at the very mercy that once saved him.
And here is what many people miss:
Jonah himself was rescued by undeserved grace first.
Inside the fish, Jonah cried out for mercy.
Inside Nineveh, he became angry when others received it.
That contradiction still exists inside many churches today.
We love testimonies until they involve people we dislike.
We celebrate redemption until it costs our pride.
We preach forgiveness while replaying offenses in our minds every night.
And slowly bitterness becomes identity.
Some people no longer know who they are without resentment.
That is why Jesus attacked unforgiveness so directly.

In Matthew 6:15, the Greek word for forgive is:
ἀφίημι (aphiēmi)

It means:
to release,
to let go,
to send away.
Biblical forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened.
It means refusing to chain your soul permanently to the offense.
Because bitterness keeps wounds alive long after the moment has passed.
Some readers carrying this pain right now have spent years smiling while internally bleeding.
You still replay conversations from years ago.
Still rehearse betrayal.
Still feel rage rise when certain names appear.
Still secretly want God to punish people who hurt you.
And the terrifying part?
You may still be deeply religious while emotionally imprisoned.
That was Jonah.

Near God…
but unlike Him.

Active prophet…
but bitter soul.
And the ending of Jonah is intentionally unresolved.
The book ends with a question from God.

No emotional closure.
No triumphant ending.
No final repentance scene.
Why?
Because the Holy Spirit hands the final answer to us.
Will we cling to resentment…
or surrender to the mercy we ourselves desperately needed?
Some people reading this are realizing their exhaustion is not merely stress.
It is spiritual corrosion.
Bitterness is heavy.

It drains joy from worship.
Softness from prayer.
Tenderness from relationships.
Peace from the heart.
And eventually it can make a believer emotionally numb to grace itself.
But the Gospel still reaches people like Jonah.
Because Jesus did what Jonah refused to do.
Jonah ran from his enemies.
Christ wept over His.
Jonah wanted judgment.
Jesus absorbed judgment Himself.
While hanging on the cross, Jesus said:
“Father, forgive them…”

The Greek:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς
(Pater, aphes autois)

Even in agony…
mercy still flowed from Him.
That is the difference between wounded humanity and divine love.
And maybe tonight some people need to stop asking God merely to remove pain…
and start asking Him to uproot bitterness.
Because hidden resentment can quietly separate the heart from intimacy with God while religious activity continues outwardly.
Be honest.
Who are you still angry survived without your permission?
Who are you struggling to accept God might redeem?
Who hurt you so deeply that you built an identity around the wound?

And if someone came to your mind while reading this…
do not ignore that conviction.
Send this to them.
Some people do not need another motivational quote.
They need freedom.

Some wounds do not destroy the soul immediately…
they slowly teach the heart how to stop loving.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD MIRACLE BEHIND JESUS MULTIPLYING BREAD THROUGH THE DISCIPLES’ HANDS
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD MIRACLE BEHIND JESUS MULTIPLYING BREAD THROUGH THE DISCIPLES’ HANDS
What if the greatest part of the miracle was not the bread in Jesus’ hands—but what happened after it left them?
The crowd had no idea.
Thousands stood scattered across the green hillsides near the northeastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Men. Women. Children. The sick. The desperate. The curious. The skeptical.
Some came because they believed.
Others came because they were hungry.
Most came because they heard stories about a rabbi who could make blind eyes see and crippled legs walk.
But on that day, they were about to witness something deeper than a miracle of provision.
They were about to witness a miracle of participation.
And almost nobody talks about it.
The story is recorded in all four Gospels, a distinction shared by very few miracles. That alone should make us stop.
Something about this event was so important that the Holy Spirit inspired Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John to preserve it for every generation of believers.
Yet most people focus on one detail.
Jesus multiplied bread.
True.
But there is another detail hidden in plain sight.
The multiplication did not happen in front of the crowd.
Nobody saw the exact moment it occurred.
The Gospel writers never describe bread exploding into piles.
They never describe baskets magically refilling before everyone’s eyes.
Instead, they tell us something astonishing.
Jesus placed the bread into the hands of His disciples.
Then the disciples distributed it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
And somehow...
it never ran out.
That changes everything.
John tells us there were five barley loaves and two fish.
The Greek text reads:
"πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους καὶ δύο ὀψάρια"
Pente artous krithinous kai duo opsaria.
"Five barley loaves and two fish."
(John 6:9)
Not five bakery carts.
Not five wagonloads.
Five loaves.
Two fish.
Human logic looked at the resources and declared the mission impossible.
Jesus looked at the same resources and asked His disciples to organize the crowd.
Imagine being one of them.
You know exactly how little food exists.
You watched the boy hand it over.
You counted it.
You touched it.
You know the numbers.
And now Jesus tells you to feed thousands.
The Gospel of Matthew records:
"καὶ ἔδωκεν τοῖς μαθηταῖς τοὺς ἄρτους, οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ τοῖς ὄχλοις"
Kai edōken tois mathētais tous artous, hoi de mathētai tois ochlois.
"He gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds."
(Matthew 14:19)
Look carefully.
Jesus gave.
The disciples distributed.
The miracle flowed through human hands.
This is where many believers miss the deeper lesson.
God often chooses not to work around His people.
He works through them.
The disciples became living conduits of divine provision.
The bread passed from Christ's hands into theirs.
Then from theirs into the crowd.
The miracle moved through obedience.
Not understanding.
Obedience.
There is no indication the disciples understood what Jesus was doing.
No indication they had a strategy.
No indication they could explain the mathematics.
All they had was a command.
And sometimes that is exactly where God meets us.
We want explanations before obedience.
Jesus often asks for obedience before explanations.
The pattern appears throughout Scripture.
Noah built before rain.
Abraham walked before seeing.
Moses stretched out the staff before the sea opened.
Joshua marched before the walls fell.
The disciples distributed bread before they understood multiplication.
Faith has never been the absence of questions.
Faith is moving when God has not answered every question yet.
The Hebrew concept of faith is richer than many modern definitions.
The Hebrew word אֱמוּנָה (emunah) does not merely mean intellectual belief.
It carries the idea of faithfulness, steadfastness, trust expressed through action.
Biblical faith is not simply believing God can.
It is moving because God said so.
That day, every disciple became a living picture of emunah.
Imagine carrying the basket.
You reach inside.
There is bread.
You hand it out.
Reach inside again.
More bread.
Again.
More bread.
Again.
Still more bread.
At what moment did panic become wonder?
At what moment did confusion become worship?
At what moment did they stop counting and simply trust?
We are not told.
Perhaps because the Holy Spirit wants us to see ourselves in the story.
Most believers know what it feels like to stand before something impossible.
A marriage hanging by a thread.
A diagnosis nobody expected.
A ministry with no resources.
A calling larger than our ability.
A burden too heavy for our strength.
A future we cannot afford.
And God says the same thing He effectively said to the disciples.
"Start distributing."
Not because your resources are sufficient.
Because His are.
The miracle was never about bread.
The bread was evidence.
The miracle was about revealing who Jesus is.
In John 6, the feeding miracle is immediately connected to one of the most profound declarations Jesus ever made:
"ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς"
Egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs.
"I am the Bread of Life."
(John 6:35)
The bread in the baskets was temporary.
The Bread standing before them was eternal.
Physical hunger would return.
Spiritual hunger could be satisfied forever.
The miracle pointed beyond provision.
It pointed to Christ Himself.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Many people spend their entire lives chasing things they believe will satisfy them.
Success.
Money.
Recognition.
Relationships.
Pleasure.
Status.
Achievement.
Yet the human soul remains restless.
Because the deepest hunger was never physical.
It was spiritual.
It was the hunger for reconciliation with God.
The hunger for forgiveness.
The hunger for purpose.
The hunger for peace.
The hunger for home.
Only Jesus satisfies that hunger.
Only Jesus can feed what the world cannot fill.
And perhaps that is why this miracle continues to speak across centuries.
Because every person reading this is carrying some form of emptiness.
Something unfinished.
Something aching.
Something longing.
Something waiting.
The disciples learned that what seemed insufficient became abundant when surrendered to Christ.
The same remains true today.
Your strength may feel insufficient.
Your resources may feel insufficient.
Your wisdom may feel insufficient.
Your past may feel irredeemable.
Your future may feel impossible.
But surrendered things behave differently in the hands of Jesus.
Five loaves became enough.
Two fish became enough.
A cross became salvation.
A tomb became victory.
A sinner became redeemed.
A broken life became a testimony.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps the most overlooked miracle of all is this:
The disciples themselves were being multiplied.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
Every trip through the crowd expanded their faith.
Every handful of bread deepened their trust.
Every impossible moment revealed more of Christ.
The bread was multiplying.
But so were they.
Maybe that is what God is doing in your life right now.
Maybe the miracle is not only what He is providing.
Maybe the miracle is what He is producing inside you while you carry the basket.
Maybe the season you want Him to end is the season He is using to transform you.
Maybe your greatest breakthrough is not ahead of you.
Maybe it is already happening within you.
And years from now, you may discover the greatest miracle was never what passed through your hands.
It was what happened to your heart while it did.
The basket never became empty because the Source never became limited.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The grave was already four days old when Jesus arrived.
paragraphs: The grave was already four days old when Jesus arrived.

Not one day.
Not two.
Four.

In Jewish understanding during the first century, many believed the spirit lingered near the body for three days, hoping to return. By the fourth day, decomposition confirmed finality. Death was no longer debated. Lazarus was not unconscious. He was not revivable by medicine. He was gone.
That is why Martha said:
“Lord, by this time there is a stench…” — John 11:39
The Greek text is brutally honest.

ἤδη ὄζει
“Already he smells.”

Not poetic.
Not softened.
Not sanitized.
The Bible refuses to romanticize death.
And maybe that is why this story still reaches into modern hearts like a hand through the grave.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like when hope already smells dead.

Marriages.
Purity.
Prayer lives.
Mental health.
Families.
Faith.
Things people publicly buried while secretly wishing Jesus would still come.
But the untold story of Lazarus was never just about resurrection.
It was about what happens after God brings someone back.
Because surviving the grave is one thing.
Living after it is another.
The village of Bethany sat less than two miles from Jerusalem. Small enough for everybody to know everybody. Which means Lazarus did not quietly disappear and quietly return.
Everyone saw the funeral.
Everyone heard the mourning.
Everyone watched the burial stone seal his death.
And then everyone watched him walk back out.
Can you imagine the silence when that dead man emerged?
John records Jesus shouting:

Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω
“Lazarus, come out!” — John 11:43

Not whispered.
Not symbolic.
A command into death itself.
And the dead obeyed.
The Hebrew mindset behind resurrection was never merely spiritual inspiration. Resurrection meant bodily return. Tangible restoration. Flesh and breath. This is why John carefully writes:
He walked out still wearing burial garments.
Still wrapped like a dead man.
Still carrying evidence of where he had been.
And if we are honest, many believers today know exactly what that feels like.

Alive…
but still wrapped in old grave clothes.

Smiling in church while secretly bound by shame.
Worshipping while dragging old addictions.
Preaching sermons while privately exhausted.
Posting Bible verses while mentally drowning.
Jesus did not only call Lazarus out.
He then told the community:
“Unbind him, and let him go.”
λύσατε αὐτὸν καὶ ἄφετε ὑπάγειν
Notice this carefully.

Jesus raised Lazarus.
But people helped remove the grave clothes.
Some healing only happens in godly community.

Some chains break in confession.
Some freedom comes through discipleship.
Some restoration happens when believers stop pretending.
Because the untold story gets even heavier after the miracle.
Most people stop reading at the resurrection.
But resurrection made Lazarus a marked man.
John 12 reveals something chilling:
“So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well…” — John 12:10
Read that again slowly.
They wanted to kill the man Jesus already resurrected.
Why?
Because Lazarus himself became evidence.
His existence threatened unbelief.
Scripture says:
“Because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.” — John 12:11
Lazarus did not become famous because he preached.
He became dangerous because he was living proof.
And that still terrifies darkness today.

There are people who hate the Gospel not because of arguments…
but because transformed lives expose what they cannot explain.

A healed addict.
A restored marriage.
A former atheist now in tears during worship.
A suicidal person still alive years later because Jesus intervened.
Evidence unsettles people.
Especially when grace rewrites someone completely.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
The Bible never records a single word Lazarus said after resurrection.

Not one sermon.
Not one quote.
Not one testimony paragraph.
The man who literally came back from the dead is silent in Scripture.
Why?
Because maybe his life became the sermon.
Maybe some encounters with Jesus are too deep for vocabulary.
Maybe resurrection changes a person so profoundly that explanation becomes impossible.
You can almost imagine Lazarus sitting quietly at dinner in John 12 while others stared at him in disbelief.
The same hands that once folded funeral linens now breaking bread.
The same lungs once filled with death now breathing evening air beside the Messiah.
And somewhere in the room sat Mary.
The same Mary who poured expensive perfume on Jesus’ feet.
John says the fragrance filled the house.

ἐπληρώθη ἡ οἰκία ἐκ τῆς ὀσμῆς τοῦ μύρου
“The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.” — John 12:3
Earlier, Lazarus smelled like death.
Now the house smells like worship.
That contrast is not accidental.
Jesus transforms atmospheres.
Some people remember when your life smelled like destruction.
But Jesus can make your future carry worship instead of decay.
That is the Gospel.
Not behavior modification.
Resurrection.
The Hebrew concept behind salvation carries this depth beautifully.
The word for salvation is often יְשׁוּעָה (yeshuah).

Deliverance.
Rescue.
Victory.
Life restored by God.
And the name Yeshua — Jesus — comes from this same root.
Jesus does not merely improve dead things.
He resurrects them.
And maybe the most haunting part of Lazarus’ story is this:
He eventually died again.
Think about that.
Lazarus was not resurrected into eternal glorified immortality like Christ after the Resurrection. Lazarus returned temporarily to mortal life. One day, Bethany buried him again.

Another funeral.
Another tomb.
Another goodbye.
So why raise him at all?
Because Lazarus was never the final point.
He was a sign.
A preview.
A prophecy in flesh.
Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection and the life.” — John 11:25
In Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή

Not:
“I can perform resurrection.”
“I AM resurrection.”
Death itself stood in front of the Author of Life.
And death lost.
Lazarus became living evidence that the grave is not ultimate.
Which is why believers throughout history clung to this story while standing beside coffins.
Because Christianity does not deny grief.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’ tomb.

δάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
“Jesus wept.” — John 11:35

The shortest verse in English.
But immeasurable in depth.

The Son of God knew resurrection was minutes away…
and still cried.
Why?
Because love grieves.
This destroys the lie that strong faith means emotional numbness.

Jesus was not weak for weeping.
He was holy in love.
Somebody reading this has been trying to stay emotionally “strong” while silently breaking inside.
But even Christ wept beside a grave.
And perhaps the deepest untold truth behind Lazarus is this:
Jesus intentionally delayed.
John 11:6 says:
“So, when He heard that Lazarus was ill, He stayed two days longer…”
At first this feels cruel.
Until you realize Jesus was not late.
He was revealing something bigger than healing.
Anyone can celebrate God when He prevents the grave.
But Lazarus teaches us who Jesus is when the grave already happened.

When the prayer seemed unanswered.
When the relationship died.
When hope collapsed.
When heaven felt silent.
Bethany teaches us that silence is not abandonment.
Sometimes God waits because resurrection reveals His glory deeper than prevention ever could.
And some people reading this are in the “fourth day” season right now.

Everything feels over.
Prayers exhausted.
Faith weak.
Heart numb.
But the stone has not intimidated Christ yet.
And never forget this:
The man everybody buried became the evidence nobody could silence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You would have never chosen that job.
paragraphs: You would have never chosen that job.
Not if you understood what it meant in the first century.
The night before the cross, the One who commanded storms to stop… picked up a towel.

Not a sword.
Not a crown.
Not a throne.
A towel.
And most people completely miss the terror and beauty hidden in that moment.
Because Jesus washing feet was not merely “an example of humility.”
It was a prophetic confrontation.
It was God exposing the filth humanity keeps pretending isn’t there.
And the original language reveals something deeper than most translations ever show.
The scene begins in The Gospel of John 13:4–5:
“He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself. After that he poureth water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet…”
The Greek phrase for “laid aside” is:

“τίθησιν τὰ ἱμάτια”
(tithēsin ta himatia)
It literally carries the idea of voluntarily setting something down.
The same root idea appears later when Jesus says:

“I lay down My life…”
— John 10:17
That was not accidental.
John is connecting the towel to the cross.
Jesus removing His outer garment was symbolic of Him laying down His glory.
Read that again.
The King dressed Himself like a servant before He dressed Himself in wounds.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Foot washing in ancient Judea was considered the lowest task in the household.
Not even Jewish servants were always required to do it.

It was degrading.
Dirty.
Humiliating.
The roads of first-century Israel were covered in dust, mud, animal waste, sewage runoff, and human filth. People wore sandals. Feet arrived filthy everywhere.
And Jesus knelt before men who would soon betray Him.
That changes the entire moment.
He washed Peter’s feet knowing Peter would deny Him.
He washed Thomas’ feet knowing Thomas would doubt Him.
He washed Judas’ feet knowing Judas already sold Him for silver.
God saw it.
And He still knelt.
The Greek word used for “wash” here is profound:
“νίπτειν” (niptein)
This does not mean a full bath.
It refers specifically to washing a part of the body.
That matters because later Jesus tells Peter:

“He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet…”
— John 13:10
Two different Greek words appear there.

“λελουμένος” (leloumenos) = fully bathed
“νίψασθαι” (nipsasthai) = to wash partially
Jesus was teaching something spiritual.
Salvation is the full cleansing.
Daily repentance is the foot washing.
A believer may belong to Christ and still pick up dirt while walking through a fallen world.
You knew that already.

You felt it after the compromise.
After the hidden sin.
After the bitterness.
After the pornography.
After the lies you justified because nobody found out.
Saved people still need cleansing fellowship with God.
Not re-salvation.
Restoration.
That is why Peter’s reaction is so powerful.
In Greek, Peter says:

“Οὐ μὴ νίψῃς μου τοὺς πόδας εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα”
(Ou mē nipsēs mou tous podas eis ton aiōna)
Literally:
“You shall NEVER wash my feet forever.”
Peter was horrified.
Because in Jewish understanding, the greater person never lowered himself beneath the lesser.
Yet here was the Messiah kneeling.
Peter’s theology could not process a suffering Servant.
And many people still cannot.

They want a Jesus who inspires them.
Motivates them.
Empowers their dreams.
But not a Jesus who kneels in front of their filth.
Not a Jesus who confronts sin directly.
Not a Jesus who says:

“If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me.”
— John 13:8
That sentence changes everything.
The Greek phrase:

“οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετ’ ἐμοῦ”
(ouk echeis meros met’ emou)

Means:
“You have no share with Me.”
“No participation with Me.”
“No inheritance with Me.”
Jesus was declaring a terrifying truth:
If you refuse His cleansing, you cannot belong to Him.
Not because works save you.
But because pride refuses grace.
And pride is the religion of hell.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Now watch what happens next.
Jesus says:

“For I have given you an example…”
— John 13:15
The Greek word for “example” is:
“ὑπόδειγμα” (hypodeigma)
Not merely a suggestion.

A pattern.
A model to imitate.
But modern Christianity often turns this into shallow politeness.

“Serve others.”
“Be nice.”
“Stay humble.”
That is not the full weight of this moment.
Jesus was teaching crucified leadership.
Kingdom authority bends low.
Real spiritual power serves.
The Son of God was showing that holiness is not self-exaltation.
It is self-sacrifice.
And here is the untold lesson most sermons never touch:
Nobody wanted their feet exposed.
Because exposure is uncomfortable.

You can sing worship songs while hiding sin.
You can preach while secretly rotting.
You can post Bible verses while your private life collapses.
But eventually Jesus kneels in front of the very thing you hoped nobody would touch.
And you have two choices:
Pull your feet away like Peter…
Or surrender.
That is why revival always begins with brokenness.
Not performance.
Not religious branding.
Not emotional hype.
Brokenness.
In Hebrew thought, feet often symbolized one’s walk or way of life.

The Hebrew word:
“דֶּרֶךְ” (derekh)
Means “way,” “path,” or “journey.”
Psalm 119:105 says:
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.”
Feet represented how a person lived before God.
So when Jesus washed feet, He was symbolically addressing the disciple’s walk.

Their daily life.
Their hidden failures.
Their direction.
And some of you are exhausted because you keep trying to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
That will never work.
You cannot wash your own soul with dirty hands.
Only Jesus cleanses sin.

The cross was the final basin.
Calvary was the final towel.
His blood became the final cleansing.
This is why the Apostle John later writes:
— 1 John 1:7
The Greek word for “cleanses” is:
“καθαρίζει” (katharizei)
Present tense.
Continual action.
He keeps cleansing those who keep coming.
That does not excuse sin.
It destroys hopelessness.

Because the enemy whispers:
“You failed again.”

But Jesus says:
“Come here. Let Me wash your feet.”
God saw it.
And He still made room at the table.
The terrifying part is Judas also sat there.
He experienced proximity without surrender.
Presence without transformation.
Religion without repentance.
And many people in church today are repeating Judas’ mistake.

Close enough to hear Jesus.
Close enough to quote Scripture.
Close enough to look saved.
But never truly surrendered.
You knew.
That is why this moment before the crucifixion matters so much.

Before nails pierced His hands…
Before thorns pierced His head…
Before blood ran down the cross…
Jesus gave humanity one final picture of the Gospel:
The Holy One kneeling before the unholy.
Not because humanity deserved it.
But because love chose to descend.
Philippians 2:7 says Christ:
“Made Himself of no reputation…”
In Greek:

“ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν”
(heauton ekenōsen)
“He emptied Himself.”
That is the heart behind the towel.
The incarnation itself was divine humility.
The Creator stepped into dust to rescue dust.
And one day every knee will bow before the same Jesus who once knelt with a basin in His hands.
But here’s the question most people avoid:
Have you actually let Him cleanse you…
Or have you spent your whole life pretending your feet are clean?
Send this to someone who keeps hiding behind church while silently drowning.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There is something terrifying about pride when it no longer sounds arrogant.
paragraphs: There is something terrifying about pride when it no longer sounds arrogant.
Because the most dangerous pride is not loud.

It is wounded pride.
Religious pride.
Moral pride.
The kind that says:
“I know who I am.”
“I deserve better than this.”
“God should work the way I expect Him to.”
That is where the story of 2 Kings becomes painfully personal.
Most people remember Naaman as the leper who got healed.
But the deeper story is about a man whose pride almost kept him from the mercy of God.
And if we are honest…
many believers are standing in the exact same place today.

Successful.
Respected.
Powerful.
Spiritually curious.
Yet still deeply offended by the simplicity of God’s instructions.
The story begins in 2 Kings 5:1:
“Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable… he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.”
The Hebrew is devastating in its structure.

“וְהָאִישׁ הָיָה גִּבּוֹר חַיִל מְצֹרָע”
Veha’ish hayah gibbor chayil metzora.
Literally:
“The man was a mighty warrior… a leper.”

One sentence.
One collision.
Strength and decay living in the same body.
Honor and hidden corruption existing together.
And isn’t that humanity?
People applaud what they can see while hell quietly grows underneath what nobody notices.

Naaman had authority.
Status.
Military success.
But none of those things could heal what was rotting beneath his skin.
The Hebrew word for leper here is “מְצֹרָע” (metzora).

In biblical thought, leprosy was more than physical suffering.
It represented uncleanness.
Separation.
Decay.
A visible picture of inward corruption.
Sin works exactly like that.
At first it hides beneath armor.

Beneath titles.
Church attendance.
Ministry platforms.
Marriage photos.
Business success.
Bible knowledge.
But eventually what lives inside always touches the skin.
And here is where God begins exposing the deeper lesson hidden inside Naaman’s story:
God often sends humility through people we think are beneath us.
A captive servant girl — unnamed, forgotten, powerless — becomes the voice God uses to point Naaman toward healing.

Not a king.
Not a prophet yet.
Not an army.
A servant.
The kingdom of God constantly humiliates human pride.
Jesus would later reveal the same pattern in Matthew 23:12:
“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
The Greek word for “humbled” is “ταπεινωθήσεται” (tapeinōthēsetai).

It means:
to be brought low,
reduced,
leveled.
God does not negotiate with pride.
He crushes it to save us from it.
Naaman arrives expecting spectacle.

He brings wealth.
Silver.
Gold.
Royal letters.
He expects prophetic ceremony.

Something dramatic.
Something worthy of his status.
Instead…
Elisha does not even come outside.
Imagine the offense.

Naaman is a commander of armies.
A national hero.
And the prophet sends a messenger.
Not even personal attention.
Then comes the instruction:
“Go and wash in Jordan seven times.”

Simple.
Unimpressive.
Almost insulting.
The Jordan was muddy compared to the rivers of Syria.
Naaman explodes in anger.
Why?
Because pride always wants God to heal us in ways that preserve our ego.
That is the hidden lesson.
Naaman did not hate the idea of healing.
He hated the method.
He wanted healing without humiliation.
Transformation without surrender.
Power without obedience.
And many people still do.

People want peace without repentance.
Deliverance without holiness.
Blessing without dying to self.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
But God repeatedly chooses foolish-looking obedience to expose human pride.
This is why the Gospel offends people.
Because salvation does not come through human achievement.
It comes through surrender.
The Apostle Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 1:18:
The Greek word for foolishness is “μωρία” (moria).

Absurdity.
Nonsense.
Intellectual embarrassment.
The cross humiliates human self-sufficiency.
You cannot earn grace.
You kneel for it.
Naaman’s servants finally speak wisdom to him:
“My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it?”
That question still exposes the human heart today.

People will climb mountains,
study philosophies,
build platforms,
perform religion,
buy self-help systems,
chase spiritual experiences—
but struggle to simply repent and obey Christ.
Because simple obedience kills pride.
And pride fights for survival.
Then comes the turning point.
Naaman goes down into the Jordan.
The Hebrew repeatedly emphasizes descent.
He went down.
That matters.

Before resurrection there is surrender.
Before cleansing there is humility.
Before grace transforms you, pride must drown.
And when Naaman emerges after the seventh washing:
“his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child.”

The Hebrew phrase carries the imagery of becoming tender again.
Softened.
Restored.
God was not merely healing skin.
He was breaking a warrior into childlike humility.
That is always where true healing begins.
Jesus said in Matthew 18:3:
“Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
Not childish.
Childlike.

Dependent.
Trusting.
Humble.
Naaman entered the river as a proud commander.
He came out as a humbled man touched by mercy.
And maybe that is why some people remain spiritually stuck for years.
Not because God refuses to heal.
But because pride refuses to kneel.
Some people are waiting for God to do something dramatic while ignoring the simple thing He already said.

Forgive them.
Confess it.
Leave the sin.
Destroy the idols.
Repent.
Obey.
Surrender fully to Christ.
But pride keeps negotiating.

Pride says:
“There must be another way.”
There isn’t.
The Gospel itself is a Jordan River moment.

You either humble yourself before Jesus Christ…
or pride will carry you untouched into eternity.
And this is what makes the mercy of God so overwhelming.
Naaman was a foreigner.
An enemy commander.
Yet God pursued him anyway.
Because the heart of God has always been bigger than national borders and human expectations.
This points directly to Jesus Christ.
Our spiritual leprosy — sin — separated us from God completely.

No amount of morality,
religion,
status,
or achievement could cleanse us.
So Christ stepped into our uncleanness Himself.

On the cross, Jesus bore what we deserved so we could receive what we never deserved:
grace.
The Greek word for grace is “χάρις” (charis).

Unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
Divine generosity toward the guilty.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Resurrection.
Not image management.
New creation.
And pride still remains one of the greatest barriers between people and Jesus.
Because pride hates dependency.
But salvation begins precisely there.
At the feet of Christ.

Broken.
Honest.
Empty-handed.
The frightening reality is that some people would rather protect their pride than receive healing.
Naaman almost did.
And many still are.

Late at night…
when the distractions stop…
when the noise fades…
when nobody is clapping anymore…
people know something is wrong inside.

They feel the decay.
The exhaustion.
The numbness.
The hidden chains.
The distance from God.

Yet pride whispers:
“You’re fine.”
“You can handle it yourself.”
“You don’t need to surrender fully.”
That voice has destroyed countless souls.
But Jesus Christ still calls people to come low so He can raise them new.

Not polished.
Not pretending.
Not performing.
Repentant.
And there is mercy waiting there.
Real mercy.
The kind that rewrites entire lives.
You can join here:
Because some messages comfort you.
But others expose the very thing keeping you from freedom.

And sometimes…
that thing is pride.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room smelled like survival.
paragraphs: The room smelled like survival.
Not victory.
Not fulfillment.
Survival.

Joseph stood in a foreign land wearing Egyptian linen while carrying Hebrew wounds nobody around him could see. The palace knew him as a ruler. Egypt knew him as a strategist. Pharaoh knew him as useful.
But heaven still remembered the boy in the pit.
And sometimes the most revealing thing about a man is not what he builds…
…but what he names his children.
Most people read one small verse in Genesis and move on too quickly. But buried inside those names is one of the deepest emotional moments in Scripture. Not because Joseph was celebrating success…
but because he was trying to survive memory.
Genesis 41:51 says:
“And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: ‘For God,’ said he, ‘hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.’”
Then verse 52 says:
“And the name of the second called he Ephraim: ‘For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.’”
At first glance, it sounds beautiful.
Until you realize what he was actually saying.
Joseph did not name his sons after power.
He named them after pain.
The Hebrew behind these names changes everything.

“Manasseh” comes from the Hebrew root נָשָׁה (nashah), meaning:
“to forget,”
“to let go,”
“to cease remembering,”
or even,
“to neglect.”

Joseph was not casually saying,
“God helped me move on.”
No.
This was the cry of a traumatized man begging heaven for relief from memories that still haunted him.
Every time Joseph called his son’s name…
he was confessing what God was healing.
“Manasseh…”
God is helping me forget.
Forget the pit.
Forget the brothers who smiled while selling me.
Forget the robe soaked in blood.
Forget the slavery.
Forget the false accusation.
Forget the prison nights wondering if God abandoned me.
Forget the silence.
Can you imagine that?
A man so wounded that he names his child after his attempt to stop bleeding internally.
Some of you understand that kind of pain.
You smile publicly while privately asking God to erase memories that still wake you up at 2AM.
Certain names still sting.
Certain betrayals still echo.
Certain seasons changed you forever.
And the terrifying part is this:
Joseph’s brothers had no idea what they had done to his soul.
People often underestimate how deeply betrayal marks a human being.
Especially betrayal from family.
Especially betrayal from people who once ate at your table.
Joseph did not just lose freedom.
He lost trust.
There is a reason Genesis specifically says:
“all my toil, and all my father’s house.”
Not just suffering.
His father’s house.
Because trauma changes how you remember home.
Some people survived childhood physically…
but emotionally never escaped it.
Some people are still carrying conversations from fifteen years ago.
Still bleeding from words nobody apologized for.
Still replaying abandonment like a movie they cannot turn off.
And yet Joseph did not become bitter enough to stop believing in God.
That is the miracle.
Not the palace.
Not the promotion.
Not the authority.
The miracle was that suffering did not make him godless.
Be honest.
Some of you almost walked away from God because of what people did to you.
Especially church people.
Especially religious people.
Especially people who quoted Scripture while destroying your heart.
Because there are people reading this right now who look faithful externally while internally battling disappointment with God they are too afraid to admit.
But Joseph’s story gets even deeper.
His second son was named “Ephraim.”

Hebrew:
אֶפְרָיִם (Ephrayim)

It comes from the root פָּרָה (parah), meaning:
“fruitful,”
“to flourish,”
“to multiply.”
Joseph says:
“For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Not after affliction.
In affliction.
That changes everything.
Most people keep waiting to heal before becoming useful.
Joseph became fruitful while still carrying scars.
Read that again.
God did not erase the land of affliction.
He caused fruit to grow there.
Egypt was still not Joseph’s home.
His brothers still had not repented.
His lost years were still lost years.
Yet God brought life out of wounded ground.
Some of you think your life is disqualified because too much damage happened.
But Scripture keeps showing us a God who grows gardens in deserts.
A God who brings water from rocks.
A God who resurrects dead things.
A God who still produces fruit from broken people.
That is the Gospel.
And there is another hidden layer most people never notice.
Joseph gave his sons Hebrew names.
Not Egyptian ones.
That matters.
Because Joseph lived surrounded by Egyptian culture, Egyptian language, Egyptian gods, Egyptian politics, and Egyptian identity.
Yet when it came time to name his sons…
his covenant identity resurfaced.
Deep down, Joseph still belonged to the God of Abraham.
Sometimes the world changes your clothing…
but cannot fully erase your spiritual inheritance.
That hit me hard.
Because some people reading this feel trapped in environments hostile to faith.
You work around darkness.
You live around compromise.
You feel spiritually exhausted trying to stay loyal to Christ in modern Egypt.
But Joseph reminds us something powerful:
You can live in Egypt without Egypt living in you.
And maybe that is exactly why this story destroys me emotionally.
Joseph’s sons became living testimonies.
Every introduction was a sermon.
Every roll call repeated God’s mercy.
Every time Joseph hugged his children, he remembered:
“I survived.”
Not because people were good.
Not because life was fair.
But because God stayed present inside suffering.
The Hebrew word for “affliction” in Genesis 41:52 is עָנְיִי (‘onyi).

It means:
misery,
sorrow,
humiliation,
poverty,
oppression.
Joseph was acknowledging that Egypt was still painful.
Healing is not pretending something never hurt.
Biblical healing is when pain no longer owns your identity.
There are people who still define themselves entirely by what happened to them.
Divorce defines them.
Addiction defines them.
Abuse defines them.
Failure defines them.
Church hurt defines them.
But Joseph teaches us that God can write a future bigger than your trauma.
Not by denying the wound…
but by redeeming it.
And years later, when Joseph finally faced his brothers again, something breathtaking happened.
The boy who once cried in the pit became the man who cried in forgiveness.
Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”

The Hebrew phrase:
חָשַׁב עָלַי אֱלֹהִים לְטֹבָה
(chashav alai Elohim l’tovah)
Literally carries the idea that while humans were “weaving” evil plans…
God was weaving another story simultaneously.
That means betrayal was never the final author.
God was.
Somebody needed that today.
Because you thought your story ended in the pit.
You thought the rejection killed your purpose.
You thought the divorce ruined your future.
You thought your failure disqualified you permanently.
Meanwhile heaven was still writing.
Still weaving.
Still redeeming.
Still transforming.
And maybe the most emotional truth in Joseph’s entire story is this:
The pit was never proof God left him.
It was proof the story was not finished yet.
Let people know they are not alone in their struggle.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only person secretly carrying pain.
And never forget this:
Some of the holiest names you will ever speak are the ones born from seasons you barely survived.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jesus Seated at the Right Hand of the Father
paragraphs:
Jesus Seated at the Right Hand of the Father
If Jesus and the Father Are One, Why Is Jesus Sitting Beside Him?
There are moments in Scripture that seem simple until you stare at them long enough.
Jesus ascends into heaven.
The disciples watch.
The clouds receive Him.
And then Scripture repeatedly tells us something astonishing:
"He sat down at the right hand of God."
For many believers, that single statement creates an uncomfortable question.
If Jesus is God...
If Jesus said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30)...
Why is Jesus sitting next to the Father?
Is there one throne or two?
One God or two?
One divine person or two separate beings?
For centuries skeptics have pointed to this verse as evidence that Christianity contradicts itself.
But the deeper you go into Scripture, the more breathtaking the answer becomes.
This is not a contradiction.
It is one of the most beautiful revelations of the Gospel.
And once you understand it, you will never read the Ascension the same way again.
Imagine a son returning home after winning a war.
His clothes are stained.
His hands bear scars.
The battle is finished.
The enemy has been defeated.
The kingdom is secure.
The father stands waiting.
Then the son walks into the throne room and takes the seat of honor beside his father.
Not because he is less than his father.
Not because he is a different king.
But because the victory has been completed.
This is the picture the New Testament paints of Jesus.
The phrase "right hand" is not primarily about geography.
It is about authority.
Power.
Honor.
Kingship.
Dominion.
In Hebrew thought, the right hand symbolized supreme authority.
The Hebrew word is:
יָמִין (yamin)
It literally means "right hand," but throughout the Old Testament it became a symbol of power, strength, favor, and royal authority.
David writes:
The Psalmist declares:
"The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool." (Psalm 110:1)
The Hebrew text reads:

נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי
(Ne'um YHWH l'Adoni, shev limini)
"The LORD said to my Lord, sit at My right hand."
This became the most quoted Old Testament passage in the entire New Testament.
Not because early Christians were obsessed with seating arrangements in heaven.
Because they understood what it meant.
Jesus had been publicly enthroned.
Then comes the Greek New Testament.
After His resurrection, Mark records:
"The Lord Jesus, after He had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God." (Mark 16:19)
The Greek reads:

ἐκάθισεν ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ
(ekathisen ek dexiōn tou Theou)
"Sat down at the right hand of God."
The phrase ἐκ δεξιῶν (ek dexiōn) means the position of highest honor and authority.
Not a second throne competing with God's throne.
The place of shared rule.
Shared dominion.
Shared glory.
Now comes the question that changes everything.
If Jesus is seated at the Father's right hand...
Are there two Gods?
Scripture answers with a thunderous no.
Israel's foundational confession remains true:

שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל
(Shema Yisrael)
"Hear, O Israel."

יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
(YHWH Eloheinu YHWH Echad)
"The LORD our God, the LORD is One." (Deuteronomy 6:4)
The key word is:
אֶחָד (echad)
One.
But not necessarily solitary.
The same word is used when:
"The two shall become one flesh."
A husband and wife remain distinct persons.
Yet they are one.
United.
Perfectly joined.
The Father and the Son are distinct Persons.
Yet one divine essence.
One God.
Not two gods sharing power.
One God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Jesus Himself explained this mystery.
In John 17:5 He prayed:
"Father, glorify Me in Your own presence with the glory that I had with You before the world existed."
Notice what He did not say.
He did not ask for a new glory.
He asked for the glory He already possessed before creation.
Before Bethlehem.
Before the manger.
Before humanity existed.
The Son eternally shared the Father's glory.
This is why John opens his Gospel:
"In the beginning was the Word."
The Greek:

Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
(En archē ēn ho Logos)
"And the Word was with God."

καὶ ὁ Λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν
(kai ho Logos ēn pros ton Theon)
The phrase πρὸς τὸν Θεόν (pros ton Theon) implies intimate face-to-face fellowship.
Distinct Person.
Yet then John immediately adds:

καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος
(kai Theos ēn ho Logos)
"And the Word was God."
Not merely godlike.
Not a lesser deity.
God Himself.
Distinct from the Father.
Yet fully divine.
Then something extraordinary happens after the resurrection.
For the first time in history, a glorified human body enters heaven.
Jesus remains fully God.
But He is also forever fully human.
The scars remain.
The resurrected body remains.
The humanity remains.
The Son who became flesh returns to heaven as the God-Man.
This is why Hebrews says:
"After making purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." (Hebrews 1:3)
Priests in the Old Testament never sat down.
Their work was never finished.
Sacrifices continued endlessly.
But Jesus offered one perfect sacrifice.
Then He sat down.
Not because He was tired.
Because redemption was complete.
The cross worked.
The debt was paid.
The victory was won.
Stephen saw this reality moments before his martyrdom.
As stones crushed his body, heaven opened.
He cried:
"I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." (Acts 7:56)
Notice something remarkable.
Most passages show Jesus seated.
Stephen sees Him standing.
Almost as if heaven itself rose to welcome its faithful witness home.
The King stood for His servant.
Even in death, Stephen was not abandoned.
So what does Jesus sitting at the Father's right hand mean?
It means He reigns.
It means His sacrifice succeeded.
It means His authority is absolute.
It means the crucified Savior is now the enthroned King.
It means the One who wore a crown of thorns now wears many crowns.
It means the One who was mocked now rules the universe.
It means the One who stretched out His hands on a cross now holds history in those same scarred hands.
And perhaps most beautifully...
It means humanity already has a representative in heaven.
A glorified man sits on the throne.
Jesus did not merely open the door to heaven.
He carried our humanity into the very presence of God.
Maybe that is what makes this truth so personal.
Because many believers imagine Jesus as a distant figure somewhere beyond the stars.
But Scripture presents something far more intimate.
The One seated at the Father's right hand still bears the wounds that purchased your salvation.
The King remembers the nails.
The scars remain visible.
The throne has not erased His love.
The crown has not erased His compassion.
The glory has not erased the cross.
The One ruling heaven is still the Lamb who was slain.
And that means the heart that bled for you is the same heart reigning over eternity.
What part of Christ's exaltation moves you most?
Your testimony may strengthen someone silently scrolling through their darkest season.
And never forget this:
The hands that were pierced for you now hold the scepter of the universe.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The room was silent… but hell was screaming.
paragraphs: The room was silent… but hell was screaming.
Nobody saw it at first.

Not the servants.
Not the king.
Not even Tamar.
Because sexual sin rarely begins in the bed.
It begins in the imagination.

It begins in hidden glances.
Unsubmitted desires.
Private fantasies nobody rebukes.
Thoughts entertained in darkness until they become cravings powerful enough to overthrow reason itself.
And that is exactly how Amnon destroyed himself.

Not with a sword.
Not in battle.
Not through enemies.
But through lust he refused to crucify.
The tragedy of Amnon in 2 Samuel 13 is not just an ancient story.
It is the anatomy of unrestrained desire.

And if we are honest…
some people reading this are closer to Amnon’s mindset than they want to admit.
The terrifying part is this:
Amnon thought what he felt was love.
But heaven called it something else entirely.
The Hebrew text exposes this with chilling clarity.
In 2 Samuel 13:1, the scripture says Amnon “loved” Tamar.
The Hebrew word used is:
אַהֵב — “ahav”
A word often describing affection, covenantal love, desire, or emotional attachment.
But what happened next proved it was never godly love.

Because biblical love protects.
Lust consumes.

Biblical love honors.
Lust takes.

Biblical love sacrifices.
Lust demands.
And one of the most horrifying lines in all of scripture comes after Amnon finally forces himself upon Tamar.
2 Samuel 13:15 says:
“Then Amnon hated her exceedingly…”
The Hebrew intensifies the disgust.

וַיִּשְׂנָאֶהָ — “vayyisna’eha”
“He hated her.”

Not mildly.
Violently.
The scripture says the hatred afterward was greater than the so-called “love” he claimed before.
That is lust.

Lust promises intimacy…
then leaves people empty, ashamed, disgusted, numb, and spiritually hollow.
Because lust never truly sees people.
It only sees consumption.
And millions today are silently being discipled by Amnon’s spirit.

Pornography.
Secret affairs.
Private addictions.
Hidden DMs.
Emotional cheating.
Fantasy addiction.
Lust disguised as “natural urges.”
Modern culture baptizes what scripture warns destroys souls.
But the Bible never romanticizes uncontrolled sexual desire.
It exposes it.
James 1:14-15 reveals the progression with terrifying precision:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
The Greek word for lust there is:
ἐπιθυμία — “epithymia”

A craving.
An overdesire.
A passion that begins ruling the heart instead of God.
Notice the progression.

Desire.
Conception.
Sin.
Death.
Sin never stays where it started.
Amnon did not wake up one morning suddenly capable of destroying Tamar.
He slowly fed desires he refused to surrender.
That is why scripture commands believers not merely to resist sin externally…
but to wage war internally.
Jesus Himself shattered every attempt humanity makes to reduce sexual sin to physical acts alone.
Matthew 5:28 says:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”

The Greek phrase:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
means:
“with the intention of desiring her.”
Jesus goes beneath behavior and exposes motive.
Because heaven sees the hidden chambers nobody else can access.
And some people reading this know exactly what that conviction feels like.
You can worship publicly while rotting privately.
You can quote scripture while hiding addiction.
You can serve in ministry while secretly feeding fantasies that are poisoning your soul.
That is why this story is so devastating.
Amnon was David’s son.

Close to royalty.
Close to spiritual legacy.
Close to power.
Yet proximity to godly things does not equal surrender to God Himself.
And this story becomes even darker when you realize Amnon was not alone in his corruption.
There was Jonadab.
The friend who helped him sin.
2 Samuel 13:3 says:
“But Amnon had a friend…”
Some friendships are assignments from heaven.
Others are accelerants from hell.

Jonadab did not counsel repentance.
He strategized wickedness.
And some people’s destruction began because they kept listening to voices that normalized sin instead of confronting it.

“Everybody struggles.”
“It’s not a big deal.”
“God understands.”
“You’re only human.”
No.
Scripture says:
“Flee sexual immorality.”

Not flirt with it.
Not manage it.
Not negotiate with it.
Flee.

The Greek in 1 Corinthians 6:18 uses:
φεύγετε — “pheugete”

Run.
Escape immediately.
Get out.
Because sexual sin uniquely scars both body and soul.
Paul writes:

Modern culture says:
“Follow your heart.”

Scripture says:
“Your heart can deceive you.”
Jeremiah 17:9:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked…”

The Hebrew:
עָקֹב — “aqob”

Crooked.
Insidious.
Treacherous.
Your feelings are not always trustworthy.
Amnon felt passion.
But his passion was demonic selfishness masquerading as affection.
And perhaps the saddest voice in the entire story is Tamar.
After Amnon violated her, she cried out in anguish.
Not merely because of physical violation…
but because sin steals dignity.

It steals innocence.
Peace.
Trust.
Safety.
Identity.
Sexual sin never affects only one person.
Its consequences ripple through families, futures, generations, ministries, marriages, children, and souls.
Amnon’s sin eventually led to hatred, murder, revenge, division, and bloodshed within David’s house.

Sin always promises secrecy.
But eventually it harvests exposure.
Numbers 32:23 warns:
“Be sure your sin will find you out.”
And yet…
even in this horrifying story…
the Gospel still breathes.
Because the Bible does not merely expose sinners.
It reveals a Savior.
Jesus Christ entered a world drowning in sexual brokenness.

Adulterers.
Prostitutes.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The violated.
The impure.
The hypocrites.
And instead of announcing condemnation first…
He offered redemption.
To the woman caught in adultery He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Notice both grace and truth.

Not condemnation without hope.
Not acceptance without repentance.
Transformation.
The cross proves something many people still struggle to believe:

Sexual sin is serious…
but the blood of Jesus is stronger.

There are people reading this who feel filthy because of what they have watched…
what they have done…
who they became in secret…
who touched them…
who they touched…
what addictions chained them for years.
Listen carefully.

Shame says:
“Hide from God.”

The Gospel says:
“Run to Him.”
1 John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

The Greek word for “cleanse”:
καθαρίσῃ — “katharisē”

To purify.
Wash thoroughly.
Remove contamination.
Jesus does not merely forgive repentant sinners.
He restores them.

That does not erase consequences.
It does not erase trauma overnight.
It does not erase accountability.
But it does mean sin does not get the final word.
Christ does.
And somebody needed to hear this today:
Your struggle is not proof God abandoned you.
Your conviction is evidence He is still calling you back.
Stop feeding what is killing you.
Kill it before it kills everything around you.

Delete the secret conversations.
Confess the hidden addiction.
Leave the compromising relationship.
Stop entertaining fantasies that are slowly reshaping your soul.

Because what you repeatedly desire…
eventually disciples you.
And unlike Amnon…
you still have time to repent.
Somebody else reading your honesty may realize they are not alone in this war.
Follow for daily biblical truth, healing, conviction, spiritual warfare, discipleship, and Gospel-centered encouragement that refuses to water down scripture.
Some sins whisper pleasure before they scream devastation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Adam was not hiding because he heard thunder.
paragraphs: Adam was not hiding because he heard thunder.
He was hiding because, for the first time in human history… he heard himself.

Before sin entered the world, Adam stood naked before God without shame. No insecurity. No pretending. No fear of exposure. No internal war between who he was and who he appeared to be. The garden was not merely beautiful because of rivers and trees. It was beautiful because nothing was fractured yet.
Then one bite changed the human nervous system forever.
The silence after the fruit must have felt unbearable.
One moment Adam was walking in divine intimacy… the next moment he became aware of himself in a way humanity was never designed to experience.

Not self-awareness.
Self-consciousness.
That is the hidden terror of the fall.
Most people think Adam’s greatest fear was punishment.
It was not.
His greatest fear was exposure.
Genesis 3:7 says:
“Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked…”
The Hebrew here is devastatingly important.
The word for “knew” is יָדַע (yadaʿ).

This is not casual awareness.
It means experiential knowing.
Deep realization.
Intimate recognition.
Adam did not simply notice nakedness physically.
He experienced vulnerability spiritually.
For the first time, he saw himself disconnected from holiness.
For the first time, humanity felt deficiency.
And the immediate response was not prayer.
It was covering.
“They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings.” — Genesis 3:7
That word “coverings” in Hebrew is חֲגֹרֹת (ḥăgōrōṯ).

Temporary coverings.
Incomplete coverings.
Human-made solutions to spiritual exposure.
And humanity has been sewing fig leaves ever since.

Careers.
Status.
Filters.
Money.
Pride.
Humor.
Achievement.
Lust.
Performance.
Religion without surrender.
Fake strength.
Fake peace.
Fake holiness.
Modern humanity is still terrified someone will see what’s underneath.
Because sin did not only separate man from God.
It separated man from himself.
The terrifying moment comes next.
Genesis 3:8 says:
“And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day…”

The phrase “voice of the LORD God” is Hebrew:
קוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים (qōl YHWH ʾĕlōhîm)
Qōl does not merely mean sound.
It can imply thunder, resonance, authority, terrifying presence.
The same voice that once brought comfort now produced fear.
Nothing changed about God.
Sin changed Adam.
That is one of the most heartbreaking truths in all Scripture.
God did not become dangerous after the fall.
Adam became afraid of love.

Read this carefully:
the guilty conscience transformed intimacy into terror.
“And Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.”

The Hebrew phrase “from the presence” is:
מִפְּנֵי יְהוָה (mippənê YHWH)

Literally:
“from the face of the LORD.”
Adam was no longer hiding from punishment.
He was hiding from being fully seen.
And this is still the secret fear inside millions of people today.
People fear exposure more than death.
That is why some people sabotage relationships before intimacy deepens.
That is why some believers avoid prayer after sinning.
That is why some people stay busy every waking moment.
Silence becomes dangerous when shame is alive.
Because eventually you hear your soul.
And underneath the noise is a terrifying question:

“If God sees everything…
why has He not abandoned me yet?”
That question haunted Adam.
You can almost hear the panic in Genesis 3:10:
“I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; and I hid myself.”
The Hebrew word for “afraid” is יָרֵא (yārēʾ).
This is not mild nervousness.

It means terror.
Dread.
Overwhelming fear.
But notice something tragic.

Adam feared God more after sinning…
than he feared sin before committing it.
That is exactly what shame does.
Shame distorts reality.

Conviction says:
“You sinned.”

Shame says:
“You are the sin.”
Conviction pulls you toward God.
Shame drives you into hiding.
And Satan understands this deeply.
The enemy’s greatest weapon was never merely temptation.
It was isolation after failure.
Because isolated shame grows in darkness.
This is why many believers secretly suffer while smiling publicly.
Some worship while hiding panic attacks.
Some preach while feeling spiritually numb.
Some serve while secretly believing God is disappointed in them.
Some post Bible verses while battling hidden addictions.
Some look holy publicly while internally repeating Adam’s ancient sentence:
“I was afraid… so I hid.”
Be honest.
This hit deeper than expected.
Because every human being knows what it feels like to hide.

Hide pain.
Hide trauma.
Hide failure.
Hide addiction.
Hide insecurity.
Hide loneliness.
Hide disappointment with ourselves.
But then comes one of the most breathtaking moments in the entire Bible.
Genesis 3:9:
“But the LORD God called to Adam and said to him, ‘Where are you?’”
God was not asking for Adam’s location.
The omniscient Creator was asking for Adam’s condition.

The Hebrew word אַיֶּכָּה (ʾayyekkāh)
means:
“Where are you?”
but carries emotional weight closer to:
“What has happened to you?”
This was not the voice of an executioner.
It was the voice of a grieving Father.
And this changes everything.

Because even after rebellion…
God pursued.

Even after hiding…
God called.

Even after shame…
God came closer.
Adam expected wrath.
Instead, he encountered pursuit.
And buried inside Eden is the first whisper of the Gospel.

Humanity runs.
God follows.

Humanity hides.
God searches.

Humanity covers itself poorly.
God prepares a sacrifice.
Genesis 3:21 says:
“And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.”
This verse is massive.
Animals died so shame could be covered.
Blood entered history because sin entered history.
The Hebrew word for “clothed” is לָבַשׁ (lāḇaš).
It means to fully cover, envelop, or array someone.

God rejected Adam’s fig leaves…
and provided His own covering.
Because human effort can never fully cover spiritual shame.
Only God can.
This points directly toward Jesus Christ.
The second Adam.
Romans 5 calls Christ the greater Adam because where the first Adam failed, Christ overcame.
The first Adam hid among trees.
Jesus carried a cross made from a tree.
The first Adam blamed others.
Jesus took blame He never deserved.
The first Adam brought death through sin.
Jesus brought life through sacrifice.
And perhaps most astonishing…
Adam hid his nakedness.
Jesus was stripped publicly.
Why?
Because Christ entered humanity’s deepest shame to destroy shame’s authority forever.
Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross “despising the shame.”
The Greek word for shame there is αἰσχύνη (aischynē).

Public disgrace.
Humiliation.
Exposure.
Jesus absorbed humanity’s shame so humanity could stop hiding from God.
Read that again slowly.
The Gospel is not merely forgiveness from punishment.
It is freedom from hiding.
That is why the enemy constantly tries to keep believers trapped in shame cycles.
Because ashamed Christians stay distant from intimacy.
But Jesus did not die merely to forgive sinners.
He died to bring them home.
Somebody reading this has been hiding emotionally for years.

Pretending.
Performing.
Distracting.
Avoiding stillness because stillness exposes wounds.
But God is still asking the ancient question:
“Where are you?”
Not because He lost you.
Because He wants you to stop running.

And if someone came to your mind while reading this…
share this with them.
Some people are smiling publicly while spiritually hiding behind trees.
The most dangerous prison is the one built from shame nobody else can see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There is something strangely heartbreaking hidden inside the story of Book of Judges Samson that most people never notice.
paragraphs: There is something strangely heartbreaking hidden inside the story of Book of Judges Samson that most people never notice.

He carried impossible strength in his body…
but almost no authority over his own soul.

People remember the lions.
The jawbone.
The gates of Gaza ripped from the earth.
The Philistines trembling when the Spirit of God rushed upon him.
But buried underneath the violence and miracles is a quiet detail that reveals something tragic.
Samson never cut his own hair.
Not once.
And Scripture is painfully intentional about that detail.
The secret is not merely about hair.
It is about covenant.
Identity.
Consecration.
And a man who was separated unto God before he was even born… yet never fully surrendered his heart to the God who called him.
In Book of Judges 13, before Samson takes his first breath, the Angel of the LORD appears to Manoah’s barren wife and says:

“For behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb…”
— Judges 13:5
The Hebrew phrase is staggering.

“נְזִיר אֱלֹהִים”
Nezir Elohim
A Nazirite of God.

The root word is:
“נָזַר” (nazar)

Which means:
to separate,
to consecrate,
to dedicate,
to set apart.
Samson’s hair was never magical.
The hair represented separation unto God.
That is why the cutting of his hair mattered.
It was visible covenant symbolism.
In the Torah, the Nazirite vow is explained in Book of Numbers 6.
The Hebrew says:

“תַּעַר לֹא־יַעֲבֹר עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ”
(ta'ar lo ya'avor al rosho)
“no razor shall pass over his head.”
The word “ta'ar” means razor.
But here is the detail almost nobody talks about:
The vow forbids the razor from passing over the head…
yet Samson himself is never shown intentionally protecting the covenant.
Others guard it for him.
His mother guards it in the womb.
His parents raise him under it.
Even Delilah becomes the instrument that exposes it.
