Instead, He reinforced monogamous covenant marriage.

The First Polygamist in the Bible Was a Violent Rebel
The first man in Scripture recorded as taking multiple wives was Lamech.

Not a righteous prophet.
Not a godly leader.
A corrupt and violent descendant of Cain.
Genesis 4:19 says:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives…”
Just a few verses later, Lamech boasts about murder and revenge.
The Bible introduces polygamy in the context of human rebellion and moral decline.
That is not accidental.
God saw it.

The Pattern of Polygamy in Scripture Always Produced Pain
Every major polygamous relationship in the Bible carries conflict, jealousy, division, or judgment.

Abraham’s household fractured after taking Hagar beside Sarah.
Jacob’s family became consumed with rivalry between Leah and Rachel.
David’s multiple wives contributed to family chaos, betrayal, and violence.
Solomon’s many wives eventually pulled his heart into idolatry.
1 Kings 11:3–4 says:
“His wives turned away his heart after other gods.”
You knew.
The Bible never presents polygamy as producing peace, covenant purity, or spiritual strength.
It repeatedly reveals its destructive consequences.
That alone should sober people who claim God celebrates it.

God Warned Kings Not to Multiply Wives
This is one of the clearest passages in all of Scripture.
Long before Israel even had kings, God gave instructions about future rulers.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away…”
That is not merely practical advice.
It is divine warning.
God explicitly cautioned leaders against accumulating multiple wives because it would corrupt their hearts.
And exactly that happened to Solomon.

The command exposes God’s position clearly:
multiplying wives was spiritually dangerous and contrary to covenant faithfulness.

The Bible Often Describes Sin Without Immediately Calling It Sin
Some people argue:
“But God never directly said, ‘Thou shalt not practice polygamy.’”
But Scripture often reveals sin through narrative consequence and progressive revelation.

For example:
The Bible records Lot’s drunkenness without an immediate command beside the event.
It records Jephthah’s tragic vow.
It records slavery, corruption, and violence in fallen societies.
Descriptive does not mean prescriptive.
The presence of something in biblical history does not equal divine approval.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

The New Testament Establishes Monogamy Clearly
When you move into the New Testament, the standard becomes unmistakably clear.
Church leaders were instructed to be:

“the husband of one wife”
—1 Timothy 3:2
Also repeated in Titus 1:6.
That phrase matters because the early Church was being called back to covenant purity and order under Christ.
Ephesians 5 presents marriage as a picture of Christ and the Church:

One husband.
One bride.
Jesus does not have multiple brides.
The covenant picture itself points toward singular devotion and faithful union.

Polygamy Distorts the Gospel Symbolism of Marriage
Marriage was never merely about romance or reproduction.
It was designed to reflect covenant faithfulness.
That is why idolatry is often described spiritually as adultery throughout Scripture.
God is not presented as sharing His covenant bride with rivals.
The exclusivity of marriage reflects the exclusivity of covenant love.
This is why the Gospel matters here.

Humanity continually distorted God’s design—including marriage itself.
But Jesus came not merely to forgive sin…
He came to restore what sin corrupted.
Including covenant faithfulness.

Sin always multiplies desires.
Grace restores order.

What About the Patriarchs?
This is where many people struggle.
“How could God use men who practiced polygamy?”
Because God has always worked through flawed people.

Noah got drunk.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
God using someone does not mean He approved every decision they made.
The mercy of God toward sinners should not be confused with endorsement of their actions.
And when you study the lives of the patriarchs honestly, their polygamy consistently produced sorrow.
The Bible is warning you while telling the story.
But most people never slow down enough to notice.

Jesus Restores God’s Original Design
The clearest answer is not found in isolated Old Testament narratives.
It is found in Christ.

Jesus restored the original creation pattern:
one man and one woman united in covenant before God.

Not because God wants to restrict joy…
but because covenant faithfulness reflects His character.
The deeper issue underneath polygamy is often the human desire for self-rule, lust, power, control, or dissatisfaction.

Sin always tells you:
“One is not enough.”

But covenant love says:
“I give myself fully.”
That is why biblical marriage points beyond itself to Christ.
And this confronts all of us—not just people debating polygamy.
Because the real issue is whether we submit to God’s design or reshape truth around our desires.
God saw it.
You knew.
And maybe this is the moment you stop defending what Scripture warns about and start letting God correct what culture—and even religion—has normalized.
There are people sitting in churches quoting verses while resisting the God who wrote them.
Do not become one of them.
“Polygamy can’t be wrong because it’s in the Bible.”
The Bible records many things.
But Jesus reveals God’s standard clearly.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Samson did not truly sound powerful when he was strongest.
paragraphs: Samson did not truly sound powerful when he was strongest.
He sounded powerful when he was finally broken.
That is what makes his final prayer so terrifyingly beautiful.

Most people remember Book of Judges for the violence, the riddles, the lion, the jawbone, the gates of Gaza, and Delilah cutting his hair while he slept. But buried underneath the chaos is one of the most emotionally devastating spiritual transformations in all of Scripture.
Because Samson’s final prayer was not the prayer of a confident warrior.
It was the prayer of a man who finally saw himself clearly.
And for the first time in his life…
he stopped talking like he was invincible.
The Hebrew text in Book of Judges repeatedly shows Samson living as a man empowered by God but not surrendered to God.
That distinction changes everything.

From birth, Samson was called to be a Nazirite. In Hebrew:
“נָזִיר אֱלֹהִים”
Nazir Elohim
“Consecrated unto God.”
His life was supposed to represent holiness, separation, obedience, covenant identity, and divine purpose.
But Samson spent most of his life treating God’s calling like a weapon instead of a relationship.
He had divine strength without divine intimacy.
And honestly?
That is where many believers secretly live today.

Strong in gifting.
Weak in surrender.

Publicly powerful.
Privately compromised.
Samson killed lions, destroyed armies, and terrified nations, yet could not conquer his own appetites.
The tragedy of Samson is not merely that Delilah cut his hair.
The tragedy is that long before the haircut, compromise had already been cutting pieces off his soul.
The frightening part is how gradual it happened.

One compromise.
One lust.
One secret.
One rationalization.
One flirtation with darkness at a time.
Judges says something haunting after Delilah betrayed him:

“He did not know that the LORD had left him.”
— Judges 16:20
In Hebrew:

“וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו”
Vehu lo yada ki YHWH sar me’alav.
“He himself did not know that Yahweh had departed from upon him.”
That line should shake every believer to the core.
He still thought he was Samson.

Still thought the anointing was there.
Still thought strength guaranteed God’s presence.
Still thought yesterday’s victories protected today’s disobedience.
But heaven had gone silent.
And he didn’t even notice.

That is one of the most terrifying spiritual conditions imaginable:
being spiritually empty while still appearing spiritually functional.
Then came humiliation.
His eyes were gouged out.
The man who spent his life following his eyes lost them.
The Philistines chained him like an animal.
The mighty judge of Israel became entertainment for pagans.
And suddenly the man who once walked in supernatural strength was grinding grain in darkness.

Blind.
Broken.
Humiliated.
Alone.
But something happened in the prison.
Something deeper than physical suffering.
For the first time, Samson stopped relying on Samson.
And that is where his final prayer becomes radically different from his earlier life.
Earlier Samson often spoke impulsively, emotionally, and self-centeredly. His life was driven by desire, revenge, appetite, anger, ego, and impulse.
But in his final recorded prayer, the tone changes completely.
Judges 16:28 says:
“Then Samson called to the LORD and said, ‘O Lord GOD, remember me, please strengthen me only this once, O God.’”
In Hebrew:

“אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא וְחַזְּקֵנִי נָא”
Adonai YHWH zokhreni na vehazzekeni na.
“Lord Yahweh, remember me please, and strengthen me please.”
Do you hear the difference?

No arrogance.
No boasting.
No swagger.
No entitlement.
Just desperation.
The strong man finally became weak enough to pray honestly.
And strangely…
that was the strongest moment of his entire life.
Because brokenness introduced Samson to dependence.
Earlier in his life, Samson wanted God’s power.
At the end of his life, he wanted God Himself.
That changes a person.
The phrase “remember me” is deeply important in Hebrew thought.
It does not merely mean “think about me.”

The Hebrew word:
“זָכַר” (zakar)
means to remember with covenant action.
Samson was not asking God for sentimental attention.
He was crying out for mercy.

For restoration.
For covenant compassion.
For undeserved grace.
And God answered him.
That alone is shocking.
Because Samson failed repeatedly.

He violated boundaries repeatedly.
He played with sin repeatedly.
He ignored warnings repeatedly.
Yet in his final humbled prayer…
God still listened.
Somebody reading this has secretly believed you ruined your relationship with God beyond repair.

You think your compromises were too deep.
Your hypocrisy too ugly.
Your addictions too hidden.
Your failures too repetitive.
But Samson’s story destroys the lie that God only uses perfect people.
No.
God restores surrendered people.
Even shattered people.
Especially shattered people.
And then comes the moment that feels cinematic beyond comprehension.
Blind Samson stands between the pillars of the Philistine temple.
Thousands are watching him.
Mocking him.
Laughing at the fallen warrior.
But heaven was about to turn humiliation into judgment.
Samson pushes against the pillars.
And in his death, he destroys more enemies than he did in his life.
That line is often misunderstood.
This was not merely revenge.
It was redemption through surrender.
The man who wasted so much of his life finally fulfilled his calling completely when he stopped depending on himself.
That is the paradox of the Kingdom of God.
Sometimes your greatest spiritual breakthrough happens after your greatest collapse.
Sometimes God does His deepest work after pride dies.
Sometimes the strongest prayer comes from the weakest moment.
The Apostle Paul the Apostle would later write in Greek:
Hotan gar asthenō, tote dynatos eimi.

“For when I am weak, then I am strong.”
— Second Epistle to the Corinthians 12:10
Samson became living proof of that truth before it was ever written.
And maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Because many people see themselves in Samson.

Gifted but inconsistent.
Called but compromised.
Used by God yet secretly battling destructive appetites.
Looking spiritually alive while internally exhausted.
And maybe you have been wondering whether God still hears you after everything.
Samson’s final prayer answers that question.
Yes.
God still hears broken people who truly turn back to Him.
Not because they deserve it.
Because He is merciful.
The frightening reality is that some people only meet their true self after losing everything they built their identity around.

Samson lost his eyes.
His strength.
His freedom.
His reputation.

But finally…
he found humility.
And humility brought him closer to God than strength ever did.
That is why Samson’s final prayer was so different from his earlier life.
Earlier Samson used God’s strength.
At the end, Samson sought God’s mercy.
Earlier he moved with confidence in himself.
At the end, he trembled with dependence upon God.
Earlier he was externally unstoppable but internally unstable.
At the end, blind and broken, he finally saw clearly.
And maybe that is the part nobody forgets.
The strongest man in Israel only discovered true strength after his pride collapsed.

Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Some people lose everything before they finally stop running from God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Judas didn’t wake up one morning and randomly decide to betray Jesus.
paragraphs: Judas didn’t wake up one morning and randomly decide to betray Jesus.
That’s the part people skip.

We reduce him to thirty pieces of silver… a kiss in the garden… a villain in the story. But the deeper lesson hiding inside Judas Iscariot is far more terrifying because it exposes something many believers secretly carry while still sitting in church, still lifting their hands, still walking near Jesus externally.
Hidden disappointment.
Not open rebellion.
Not atheism.
Not immediate hatred toward Christ.
Disappointment that stayed unspoken long enough to become darkness.
The tragedy of Judas was not merely betrayal.
It was proximity without surrender.
It was following Jesus while silently resenting the way Jesus refused to become the Messiah Judas wanted.
Most people never notice that Judas followed Christ for years while internally expecting a different kingdom.
A different outcome.
A different kind of power.
And disappointment hidden long enough can mutate into bitterness while the mouth still says “Rabbi.”
In John 12:4-6, Scripture reveals something chilling:

“But Judas Iscariot, one of His disciples (the one who was about to betray Him), said, ‘Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’ He didn’t say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief.”
The Greek word used for thief is:
κλέπτης (kleptēs)
Not merely someone tempted occasionally.
A stealer.
One who secretly takes.
Judas had already been hiding corruption before the betrayal ever manifested publicly.
That is how spiritual collapse often works.
The betrayal people see publicly usually began privately long before anyone noticed.
What makes Judas terrifying is that nobody at the table initially suspected him.
When Jesus said in Matthew 26:21:
“Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me,”
the disciples began asking:
“Surely not I, Lord?”
None of them immediately pointed at Judas.
Why?
Because hidden disappointment often disguises itself extremely well inside religious behavior.
Judas looked close to Jesus externally.
But inwardly, something was dying.
The Hebrew understanding behind the idea of the “heart” matters deeply here.
In Scripture, the Hebrew word is:
לֵב (lev)
Not merely emotions.
The inner will.
The control center.
Mind, desires, intentions, affections.
Judas physically walked with Jesus while his lev slowly drifted somewhere else.
And many believers are doing the same thing right now.
Still attending church.
Still posting Bible verses.
Still saying “God is good.”
But secretly disappointed because Jesus did not answer the prayer the way they wanted.
Because the healing did not come.
Because the relationship died.
Because the ministry failed.
Because the suffering remained.
Because God did not perform according to their expectations.
And disappointment left unprocessed becomes spiritually dangerous.
Judas likely expected a conquering political Messiah.
Many Jews during that era anticipated a ruler who would overthrow Rome visibly and establish national dominance.
But Jesus kept talking about servanthood.
Dying.
Loving enemies.
Taking up crosses.
Losing your life to find it.
That was not the kingdom Judas envisioned.
And instead of bringing his confusion honestly before Christ… Judas concealed it.
That concealment became rot.
John 13:27 says:
“After Judas ate the piece of bread, Satan entered into him.”
The Greek phrase is deeply sobering:

εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς
(eisēlthen eis ekeinon ho Satanas)
“Entered into him.”
Notice something important.
Satan did not create the disappointment.
He exploited what Judas refused to surrender.
That changes everything.
Because many people think spiritual destruction begins with demons.
Often it begins with hidden wounds we refuse to bring honestly before Jesus.
Judas never openly wrestled.
Never openly confessed.

Never openly cried out:
“I don’t understand You anymore.”
Peter failed loudly.
Thomas doubted openly.
David wept publicly.
Jeremiah questioned God emotionally.
But Judas concealed everything behind the appearance of discipleship.
That is why hidden disappointment is so dangerous.
It can survive inside outward Christianity for years unnoticed.
One of the most heartbreaking moments comes in Matthew 26:50 when Jesus says to Judas:
“Friend, do what you came for.”
The Greek word used for “friend” here is:
ἑταῖρε (hetairos)
A companion.
An associate.
Jesus still addressed Judas with restrained mercy even in the moment of betrayal.
And this is where the article becomes painfully personal.
Some believers are not abandoning Jesus because they hate Him.
They are slowly drifting because He disappointed the version of Christianity they imagined.
They thought obedience would guarantee comfort.
They thought prayer would prevent suffering.
They thought faithfulness would remove warfare.
They thought serving God would make life easier.
Then reality collided with expectation.
And instead of grieving honestly before God… they buried the disappointment beneath religious routine.
But concealed disappointment eventually seeks escape.
For Judas, it became betrayal.
For others, it becomes cynicism.
Compromise.
Secret addictions.
Bitterness.
Deconstruction rooted not in intellectual questions but emotional wounds.
Coldness toward prayer.
Resentment toward God.
Performative Christianity without intimacy.
And the terrifying part is that people can remain around Jesus while internally walking away from Him.
That is the lesson Judas taught me.
Not merely betrayal.
Hidden disappointment left unhealed.
Psalm 62:8 says:
“Pour out your hearts before Him.”
The Hebrew phrase for “pour out” carries the imagery of spilling completely.
God never asked us to pretend before Him.
He already sees what is hidden.
The difference between Peter and Judas was not perfection.
Both failed Jesus.
Both broke under pressure.
But Peter returned weeping.
Judas returned despairing.
Peter ran toward grace.
Judas ran away from it.
And some people reading this are exhausted from pretending they are spiritually okay.
You still attend.
Still smile.
Still serve.
But secretly, there is disappointment toward God buried underneath your worship.
And if you never bring it into the light, the enemy will gladly build lies inside the silence.
Jesus is not afraid of your questions.
He is not intimidated by your confusion.
He is not shocked by your grief.
But hidden disappointment becomes deadly when honesty disappears.
The Gospel was never an invitation to perform emotional perfection.
It was an invitation to surrender truthfully.
Even now, Christ still calls wounded people closer.
Not farther.
The cross itself proves that God understood suffering better than we do.
Isaiah 53 says He was:
“A man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew phrase:

מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
(mak'ovot veyadua choli)
Means deep pains… familiar with sickness, suffering, grief.
Jesus understands disappointment from the inside.
That is why you do not have to hide it from Him.
And maybe that is the real warning inside Judas’ story.

Not simply:
“Don’t betray Jesus.”
But:
“Don’t silently drift from Him while pretending everything is fine.”
Bring the disappointment into the light before it becomes something darker.
Because concealed wounds eventually speak.
And when they do, they often speak destructively.
And if you know someone silently drifting while pretending they’re okay, share this with them tonight.
Some people do not need another motivational message.
They need permission to finally be honest before God.
Some betrayals begin long before the kiss ever happens.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You were never meant to worship yourself.
paragraphs: You were never meant to worship yourself.
That is the hidden war behind Lucifer.
Most people think Lucifer wanted power. Authority. A throne. Control.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Lucifer already had unimaginable access to glory.
He stood in the presence of God.
He moved among the stones of fire.
He was covered in beauty, splendor, brilliance, music, and heavenly authority.
Yet it still was not enough.
Why?
Because Lucifer did not merely want influence.
He wanted worship.
And worship belongs only to God.
That is the part many miss.
The rebellion in Heaven was not ultimately political.
It was theological.
It was an assault on the uniqueness of God Himself.

And once you understand what worship truly is in Scripture, you begin to understand why Satan has spent human history fighting for your attention, your affection, your obedience, your fear, your identity, and your devotion.
Because worship was always the target.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The first major passage tied to Lucifer’s fall appears in the book of Ezekiel. While the immediate context addresses the king of Tyre, the language reaches beyond any human ruler.
Listen carefully.
Ezekiel 28:12–17 says:

“You were the seal of perfection,
full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.
You were in Eden, the garden of God…”
Then it says:
“You were the anointed cherub who covers…”
The Hebrew phrase is:

“כְּרוּב מִמְשַׁח הַסּוֹכֵךְ”
(Keruv Mimshach HaSokekh)
Meaning:
“The anointed guardian cherub.”
This was not a low-ranking being.
This was a throne guardian.
A being associated with proximity to divine glory.
Then Scripture says:
“Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty.”
The Hebrew says:

“גָּבַהּ לִבְּךָ בְּיָפְיֶךָ”
(Gavah libbekha beyofyekha)
Literally:
“Your heart became high because of your beauty.”
Pride was born from self-contemplation.
Lucifer became intoxicated with his own splendor.
God gave him beauty…
But instead of reflecting glory back to God, Lucifer absorbed it into himself.
That is the origin of corrupted worship.
Romans 1 describes this exact spiritual pattern later in humanity:
“They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”
Read that again.
Lucifer was the first creature to desire worship that belonged to the Creator.
Isaiah 14 reveals even more.
Again, the immediate audience is the king of Babylon, but the language pierces deeper into cosmic rebellion.
Isaiah 14:13–14 says:

“For you said in your heart:
‘I will ascend into heaven,
I will exalt my throne above the stars of God…
I will be like the Most High.’”
The Hebrew phrase for “Most High” is:

“עֶלְיוֹן”
(Elyon)
A title reserved for God’s supreme sovereignty.
Lucifer did not merely want a higher position.
He wanted divine distinction.
He wanted what made God uniquely God.
Worship.
The terrifying part is hidden in the Hebrew structure.
Five times Lucifer says:
“I will.”

“I will ascend.”
“I will exalt.”
“I will sit.”
“I will ascend above.”
“I will be like.”
Sin began with self-exaltation.

The center shifted from God…
to self.
That is why Satan’s core temptation to humanity has never changed.

“You shall be as gods.”
(Genesis 3:5)
The same poison that destroyed Lucifer was offered to mankind.
Self-exaltation.
Self-rule.
Self-worship.
God saw it.
And deep down…
You knew.
Because humanity still fights this same rebellion daily.
Not always through satanic rituals.
Not always through obvious evil.

Sometimes through obsession with self-image.
Sometimes through pride disguised as ambition.
Sometimes through building identities where God becomes secondary.
Sometimes through wanting Christianity without surrender.
Lucifer’s fall explains why worship is so central in spiritual warfare.
In the Greek New Testament, the primary word for worship is:

“προσκυνέω”
(Proskuneō)
It literally means:

“To bow down.”
“To kiss toward.”
“To prostrate oneself in reverence.”
Worship is not merely singing.
It is surrender.
Allegiance.
Adoration.
Submission.
This is why Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness with worship.
Matthew 4:8–9 says:
“Again, the devil took Him to an exceedingly high mountain and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.

And he said to Him,
‘All these things I will give You if You will fall down and worship me.’”
The Greek says:

“ἐὰν πεσὼν προσκυνήσῃς μοι”
(ean pesōn proskynēsēs moi)
“If falling down you worship me.”
Do you see it?

Satan offered Jesus kingdoms…
for worship.
Because worship was always the real prize.
Not money.
Not politics.
Not influence.
Worship.
And Jesus answered with Scripture immediately.
“You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.”
The Greek word for “serve” there is:

“λατρεύω”
(latreuō)
Meaning sacred service reserved for deity.
Jesus reaffirmed the absolute exclusivity of worship.
Only God deserves it.
Only God can sustain it without corruption.
Only God is holy enough to receive it.
Lucifer wanted worship because worship carries glory, authority, devotion, identity, and spiritual alignment.
What you worship shapes you.
Psalm 115 says idols have eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear…
Then it says:
“Those who make them become like them.”
That principle still operates today.
People become what they worship.

If you worship power, you become hardened by power.
If you worship lust, you become consumed by appetite.
If you worship self, you become enslaved to insecurity.
If you worship Christ, you are transformed into His image.
That is why Satan fights worship so aggressively.
Not because songs matter alone…
But because worship determines ownership.
This is also why Heaven revolves around worship in Revelation.
The angels cry:
“Holy, holy, holy…”
The Greek word is:

“Ἅγιος”
(Hagios)
Meaning utterly separate, sacred, transcendent.
Lucifer rebelled because he could not tolerate God’s uniqueness.
Pride cannot coexist with divine holiness.
One must bow.
The other must break.
And eventually Lucifer chose rebellion over surrender.
That is the untold reason worship matters so deeply.
Worship declares who sits on the throne.
Not merely in Heaven.
In you.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your behavior.
He came to restore rightful worship.

Sin fractured worship.
The cross restored it.
Colossians says all things were created through Christ and for Christ.
For Him.
Not for self-glory.
Not for self-rule.
Not for personal kingdoms.
For Him.
But here is the hope Satan never understood.
God takes broken worshipers and redeems them through grace.
Lucifer fell while standing in glory.
Humanity can rise from the dust through mercy.
That is the scandal of the Gospel.
The enemy who once stood in Heaven can never be redeemed.
But sinners covered in shame can be washed clean through the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why Satan hates the Gospel so violently.
Because grace creates redeemed worshipers he can never become again.
And maybe that is why this unsettled you while reading.
Because the Holy Spirit is exposing what sits on the throne of your heart.

Success?
Approval?
Pleasure?
Control?
Self?
Religion without surrender?
Or Christ?
You were created to worship God, not yourself.
And every day you choose one throne.
One kingdom.
One master.
If this convicted you, do not ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF HABAKKUK
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY OF HABAKKUK
When God Does Not Explain Himself
By Gospel Warrior
Some stories in Scripture are remembered because of miracles.
Others because of kings.
Others because of battles.
But one of the most emotionally devastating books in the entire Bible begins with something most believers secretly experience and rarely admit.
Confusion.
Not rebellion.
Not unbelief.
Not hatred toward God.
Confusion.
The story of Habakkuk is not primarily about prophecy.
It is not primarily about judgment.
It is not even primarily about Babylon.
The untold story of Habakkuk is the story of every believer who has stared into heaven and wondered why God appears silent while evil seems to be winning.
It is the story of faith when answers never arrive.
It is the story of trust when explanations are withheld.
It is the story of a man who dared to bring his questions directly to God instead of hiding them behind religious language.
And because of that, his story may be one of the most relatable books ever written.
The book opens with a cry that feels astonishingly modern.
Habakkuk 1:2 records:
"How long, O LORD, must I call for help and You do not listen?"
The Hebrew is painfully raw.

עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה
('Ad-anah YHWH)
"How long, LORD?"
This phrase appears repeatedly throughout the Old Testament whenever God's people feel abandoned, oppressed, or forgotten.
It is not the language of atheism.
It is the language of wounded faith.
Habakkuk still believes God exists.
That is exactly why he is struggling.
If he did not believe in God, there would be nobody to question.
His pain is born from faith, not the absence of it.
He sees violence.
Corruption.
Injustice.
Lawlessness.
The wicked prosper.
The righteous suffer.
And heaven appears silent.
Sound familiar?
Many believers know exactly what that feels like.
The diagnosis comes back positive.
The marriage falls apart.
The child walks away from God.
The prayer remains unanswered.
The betrayal arrives from someone trusted.
The darkness lingers longer than expected.
And somewhere in the middle of it all comes the ancient cry:
"How long, Lord?"
Habakkuk expected God to intervene.
God did answer.
But the answer was not what Habakkuk wanted.
God reveals He is raising up Babylon as an instrument of judgment.
This shocked the prophet.
Babylon was infamous for cruelty.
Violence.
Paganism.
Brutality.
Habakkuk could understand God judging sin.
What he could not understand was why God would use people even more wicked to accomplish it.
Again he questions.
Again he wrestles.
Again he struggles.
This is where Habakkuk becomes unlike many modern portrayals of faith.
He does not pretend.
He does not suppress his questions.
He does not perform spirituality.
He brings every confusion directly before God.
The prophet teaches us something many believers desperately need to remember:
God is not threatened by honest questions.
The Lord rebukes pride.
He rebukes unbelief.
He rebukes arrogance.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that He welcomes sincere wrestling.
The God who gave Jacob a night of wrestling is not intimidated by your questions.
The turning point comes in Habakkuk 2.
The prophet declares:
"I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the lookout tower."
Habakkuk 2:1
He waits.
Not for a quick answer.
Not for immediate relief.
Not for circumstances to improve.
He waits for God.
Many people want God's hand.
Habakkuk wanted God's voice.
There is a difference.
Then comes one of the most important declarations in all of Scripture.
Habakkuk 2:4:

וְצַדִּיק בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ יִחְיֶה
(Ve-tzaddiq be'emunato yichyeh)
"The righteous shall live by his faith."
The Hebrew word אֱמוּנָה (emunah) means more than intellectual belief.
It carries the idea of faithfulness, steadfast trust, firmness, reliability, and enduring confidence.
This verse becomes foundational throughout the New Testament.
The Apostle Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.
The writer of Hebrews echoes it in Hebrews 10:38.
The message is profound.
The righteous do not live by explanations.
The righteous live by faith.
Habakkuk wanted answers.
God gave him Himself.
And that changed everything.
Then comes one of the most beautiful transformations in Scripture.
By chapter three, Habakkuk is no longer demanding explanations.
He is worshiping.
Not because every question was answered.
But because he has encountered the character of God.
The prophet begins remembering.
He remembers God's power.
God's faithfulness.
God's deliverance.
God's holiness.
Sometimes faith grows strongest not when we learn something new about God but when we remember what He has already done.
Then we reach one of the greatest declarations of trust ever recorded.
Habakkuk 3:17-18 says:

"Though the fig tree should not blossom,
and there be no fruit on the vines,
though the yield of the olive should fail,
and the fields produce no food,
though the flock should be cut off from the fold
and there be no cattle in the stalls,

Yet I will exult in the LORD,
I will rejoice in the God of my salvation."
This was not poetic exaggeration.
For an ancient society, this represented complete economic collapse.
Food gone.
Income gone.
Security gone.
Future gone.
Everything failing.
Yet Habakkuk says:
"Still."
Still I will trust.
Still I will worship.
Still I will rejoice.
This is not denial.
This is not pretending.
This is not positive thinking.
This is biblical faith.
Faith is not confidence that everything will work out the way we want.
Faith is confidence that God remains worthy of trust regardless of how circumstances unfold.
That is the untold story of Habakkuk.
It is the journey from questions to trust.
From confusion to confidence.
From demanding explanations to resting in God's character.
Many people believe faith begins when all doubts disappear.
Habakkuk reveals something deeper.
Faith often begins when answers disappear.
The prophet never receives a complete explanation for everything he asks.
Yet he ends with something greater.
He ends with God.
And ultimately that is the Gospel itself.
At the cross, humanity witnessed what appeared to be God's greatest silence.
The innocent Son of God suffered.
The wicked seemed victorious.
Darkness covered the land.
Hope appeared dead.
Yet three days later the resurrection revealed what nobody could see in the moment.
God had been working all along.
The same truth remains today.
You may not understand what God is doing.
You may not understand why He has delayed.
You may not understand the suffering, the waiting, the loss, or the silence.
But Habakkuk stands across thousands of years and whispers:
God's silence is not God's absence.
God's delay is not God's neglect.
God's mysteries are not God's abandonment.
The God who was faithful then remains faithful now.
And perhaps that is why Habakkuk continues to speak so powerfully today.
Because every generation eventually asks the same question:
"How long, Lord?"
And every generation must learn the same answer:
"The righteous shall live by faith."
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Sometimes God's greatest answer is not an explanation... but His presence in the waiting.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He did not lose the kingdom in one moment.
paragraphs: He did not lose the kingdom in one moment.
That is what most people miss when they read the story of Saul.

They remember the dramatic ending.
The torment.
The collapse.
The jealousy toward David.
The witch at Endor.
The battlefield death.
But Saul lost the kingdom long before he lost the throne.
He lost it one decision at a time.
And that is exactly how many people lose what God entrusted to them now.

Not instantly.
Gradually.

A compromise here.
A delayed obedience there.
A moment of pride nobody notices.
A secret rebellion hidden behind religious language.

Until one day the crown is still on your head…
but God has already departed from your heart.

“You have done foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God.”
— 1 Samuel 13:13
Read that again.
Saul did not begin as a wicked man.
He began humble.
Scripture says he once hid among the baggage when people tried to present him as king. He looked small in his own eyes. There was trembling in him. Dependency. Fear of God.
But power reveals what humility hides.
And little by little, Saul stopped trusting God and started protecting himself.
That is where kingdoms die.

Not first in public failure.
First in private independence.
The first major crack came when Saul refused to wait for Samuel.

The Philistines were gathering.
The pressure was rising.
The people were scattering.
Fear was choking the camp.
And Saul panicked.
Instead of waiting for the prophet as God commanded, Saul performed the sacrifice himself.
To many people, that sounds small.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The issue was never the ceremony.
It was the heart.
Saul believed partial obedience was acceptable if it produced faster results.
That spirit still destroys people today.

You say:
“I know what God said… but this situation is different.”
“I know it’s compromise… but I have no choice.”
“I know I should wait… but I’m afraid of losing control.”
God saw it.
You knew.

Saul’s problem was not weakness.
It was impatience mixed with self-preservation.
And impatience is often disguised rebellion.
Because when you refuse God’s timing, you are declaring your wisdom superior to His.
Then came the next decision.
The deeper one.
The deadly one.
In 1 Samuel 15, God gave Saul a direct command concerning the Amalekites.
Destroy everything.

Not because God is cruel.
Because Amalek represented a persistent evil that opposed God’s covenant people for generations.

But Saul spared King Agag.
He kept the best animals.
He preserved what God said destroy.
Then he wrapped his rebellion in spirituality.
“I obeyed the Lord,” Saul insisted.
But Samuel answered with words that still shake the soul:

“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
— 1 Samuel 15:22
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
That verse exposes an entire generation.

People who want worship without surrender.
Church without repentance.
Christian identity without crucifixion of the flesh.

Saul still talked about God.
Still used spiritual language.
Still appeared religious.
But obedience was gone.
And once obedience disappears, religion becomes performance.
That is terrifying.
Because you can look anointed in public while being rejected in private.
You can still hold position while heaven has already written Ichabod over your life.

“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today.”
— 1 Samuel 15:28
Notice this carefully.
Saul did not lose the kingdom because he stumbled once.
He lost it because every confrontation from God was met with excuses instead of repentance.
That is the real difference between Saul and David.
Both sinned.

But Saul defended himself.
David broke before God.
When Saul was confronted, he blamed the people.

“I feared the people and obeyed their voice.”
— 1 Samuel 15:24
There it is.
The fear of man.
The invisible idol.
Saul cared more about public approval than divine approval.
And many people are doing the same now.

You know what God is calling you to abandon.
You know the relationship is ungodly.
You know the secret sin is killing you.
You know the compromise is grieving the Holy Spirit.
But you fear people more than God.
So you preserve what should be destroyed.
Just like Saul.
And every act of disobedience hardens the heart a little more.
That is why Saul eventually became consumed with jealousy toward David.
Because disobedience creates insecurity.
When people abandon intimacy with God, they start competing with people instead.

Saul heard women sing:
“Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
And something broke inside him.
From that moment forward, he watched David with suspicion.

Jealousy turned into obsession.
Obsession turned into rage.
Rage turned into spiritual darkness.
The man who once prophesied now threw spears.
Sin always mutates.
It never stays small.
That hidden compromise you protect today will become tomorrow’s torment.
And the most frightening line in Saul’s story may be this:

“Now the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul.”
— 1 Samuel 16:14
Imagine that.

The crown remained.
The title remained.
The palace remained.
But God’s presence left.
This is why outward success can deceive you.

A person can still have followers, influence, money, ministry, applause…
and yet be spiritually abandoned inside.
Saul spent the rest of his life trying to hold together what obedience once sustained naturally.
That is exhausting.
When grace lifts from a life, people start forcing what God once blessed freely.
Then came the final descent.
Instead of returning to God in broken repentance, Saul sought a medium at Endor.
The same king who once expelled witchcraft from Israel now pursued darkness because he refused surrender.
Sin makes people become what they once condemned.
Read that again.
The tragedy of Saul is not merely that he died.
The tragedy is that he kept resisting every opportunity to truly repent.
And this story is not in Scripture merely to inform you.
It is warning you.
Because kingdoms are still lost one decision at a time.

Marriages.
Ministries.
Purity.
Calling.
Conviction.
Peace.
Rarely destroyed overnight.
Usually eroded slowly through tolerated compromise.
But there is another King in Scripture.
One greater than Saul.
Jesus Christ obeyed where Saul rebelled.

Saul grasped for control.
Jesus surrendered completely.

Saul feared people.
Jesus feared the Father.

Saul preserved his throne.
Jesus carried a cross.
And because of Christ, failure does not have to become final.
That is the Gospel.

The answer is not pretending you are strong.
The answer is repentance.
Real repentance.

Not emotional regret.
Not image management.
Not spiritual performance.
Surrender.

The kind that destroys Agag instead of hiding him.
The kind that waits when flesh wants control.
The kind that says:
“Lord, expose whatever in me still resists You.”
Because the terrifying part is not that Saul fell.
The terrifying part is that he kept hearing truth and refused to fully bow.
Do not do the same.
If this convicted you, say “Lord, remove Saul from my heart” and mean it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SOMEONE LIVE IN SIN AND STILL BE SAVED?
paragraphs:
CAN SOMEONE LIVE IN SIN AND STILL BE SAVED?
The Question Nobody Wants to Ask—But Everyone Needs Answered
Some questions are whispered.
Not because they're unimportant.
Because they terrify us.
Questions like:
What if I've gone too far?
What if I keep committing the same sin?
What if I say I believe in Jesus... but my life still looks like a battlefield?
What if someone claims to be a Christian while openly living in sexual immorality, greed, drunkenness, deception, unforgiveness, pornography, rebellion, or habitual disobedience?
Can they still be saved?
Or perhaps the question is even more personal.
Can I?
That question has kept people awake at 2:17 in the morning.
It has haunted church pews.
Filled prayer rooms with tears.
Driven some people into despair.
And given others a false peace that could cost them eternity.
Because there are two deadly lies circulating through modern Christianity.
The first lie says:
"If you profess faith once, nothing you do afterward matters."
The second lie says:
"If you struggle with sin, you're probably not saved."
Both are dangerous.
Both distort the Gospel.
Both miss the heart of what Scripture actually teaches.
To answer this question correctly, we must walk through some uncomfortable territory.
We must allow Jesus, Paul, John, Peter, James, and the writers of Scripture to speak for themselves.
Not through modern slogans.
Not through denominational traditions.
Not through social media theology.
But through the inspired Word of God itself.
And what we discover may be both more frightening and more hopeful than many people realize.
Because the real issue is not whether Christians ever sin.
The real issue is whether they can comfortably live there.
The Difference Between Falling Into Sin and Living In It
One of the greatest misunderstandings in Christianity is confusing a struggle with sin and a lifestyle of sin.
The Bible never teaches that genuine believers become sinless.
In fact, the Apostle John wrote:

"If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."
(1 John 1:8)
The Greek word used here is:
ἁμαρτία (hamartia)
Meaning:

"missing the mark,"
"failing God's standard,"
"falling short of His holiness."
John is speaking to believers.
Even redeemed people still battle the flesh.
Even mature Christians stumble.
Even the strongest saints have moments of weakness.
The Apostle Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery and murder.
Noah became drunk.
Jonah rebelled.
Thomas doubted.
The Bible never hides the failures of God's people.
But it does reveal something critically important.
Their failures did not become their identity.
Their sin did not become their permanent residence.
They stumbled.
They repented.
They returned.
They fought.
They grieved over their sin.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because Scripture repeatedly warns against something far more dangerous than occasional failure.
It warns against ongoing, unrepentant, deliberate rebellion.
The Word That Changes Everything
One of the most important passages in this discussion is found in 1 John 3:6.
Many English readers miss its full force because translations often smooth out the grammar.
The Greek reads:
πᾶς ὁ ἐν αὐτῷ μένων οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει
Transliterated:
Pas ho en autō menōn ouch hamartanei.
Literally:
"Everyone abiding in Him does not keep on sinning."
The key phrase is the present active verb.
John is not describing a single act.
He is describing a continuous pattern.
A lifestyle.
An ongoing practice.
Many scholars therefore translate the idea as:
"No one who lives in Him keeps on practicing sin."
John is not saying Christians never commit a sin.
If he were, he would contradict what he wrote earlier.
Instead, he is saying that someone genuinely transformed by Christ cannot make peace with rebellion against God.
The Holy Spirit will not allow it.
There will be conviction.
Conflict.
Correction.
Discipline.
A war inside the soul.
Because salvation changes more than destination.
It changes nature.
When Jesus Spoke of Trees
Jesus often used simple images to reveal profound truths.
One day He said:

"Every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit."
(Matthew 7:17)
Notice what He did not say.
He did not say every good tree produces perfect fruit.
He said good fruit.
Fruit that reflects the nature of the tree.
The Greek word for fruit is:
καρπός (karpos)
Meaning:

fruit,
result,
evidence,
outcome.
Jesus was teaching that the reality inside eventually reveals itself outside.
Not instantly.
Not flawlessly.
But genuinely.
A genuine believer may struggle.
May fail.
May need restoration.
But over time there will be evidence of divine life.
Not perfection.
Direction.
That distinction matters.
Because many people are looking at isolated moments while God examines patterns.
A person can fall into sin.
But can someone remain there year after year without repentance, conviction, change, or concern and still claim Christ?
Scripture repeatedly raises serious warnings about that possibility.
Warnings too important to ignore.
The Passage That Makes People Uncomfortable
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10:
Notice those four words.
Do not be deceived.
Paul knew deception would become a major issue in the church.
The Greek phrase is:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε
(Mē planasthe)
Meaning:

"Stop being misled."
"Do not wander into error."
Then Paul lists persistent sinful lifestyles and says those who practice such things will not inherit the Kingdom of God.
This is not describing someone who fell and repented.
It is describing people whose lives are characterized by rebellion.
Then comes one of the most beautiful statements in Scripture.
"And such were some of you."
Not are.
Were.
Past tense.
Because the Gospel transforms people.
The drunkard can become sober.
The immoral can become pure.
The liar can become truthful.
The addict can become free.
The self-righteous can become humble.
Not because human effort saves.
But because Christ changes what He saves.
This is where the modern conversation often breaks down.
Some preach grace without transformation.
Others preach transformation without grace.
The Bible refuses both extremes.
Grace saves.
Grace transforms.
Grace preserves.
Grace sanctifies.
And grace never signs a peace treaty with sin.
The most terrifying possibility is not that you are struggling against sin.
The most terrifying possibility is that you are no longer fighting at all.
Because dead things do not struggle.
Only living things do.
And sometimes the very fact that your heart aches over your sin may be evidence that God is still working inside you.
But there is another side to this discussion that many churches avoid entirely.
What did Jesus mean when He said, "Why do you call Me Lord, Lord, and not do what I say?"
And what about the frightening words, "I never knew you"?
Because answering whether someone can live in sin and still be saved requires us to confront one of the most sobering warnings Christ ever gave.
To be continued in Part 2.
If this exposed something you've been wrestling with, be honest.
The soul at war with sin is in a very different place than the soul at peace with it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Mystery Behind Why Jesus Healed on the Sabbath
paragraphs: The Mystery Behind Why Jesus Healed on the Sabbath
There was a reason the religious leaders became furious every time Jesus healed on the Sabbath.
It was never just about miracles.
It was about authority.
It was about identity.
It was about exposing a system that had learned how to protect rules while neglecting people.
And hidden underneath every Sabbath healing was a declaration so powerful that it threatened the entire religious structure of the day:
Jesus was revealing Himself as Lord of the Sabbath.
Most modern readers miss the weight of this because we read the Sabbath as merely “a day off.”
But to first-century Jews, the Sabbath was sacred covenant identity.
The Sabbath was woven into creation itself.
In Hebrew, the word Sabbath is:
שַׁבָּת (Shabbat)

Derived from the Hebrew root:
שָׁבַת (shavat)
meaning:
“to cease,”
“to rest,”
“to stop striving.”
The Sabbath was first introduced in Genesis:

“On the seventh day God ended His work… and He rested.”
(Genesis 2:2)
The Hebrew does not imply exhaustion.
God was not tired.

The word implies completion.
Fulfillment.
Perfect satisfaction.

The Sabbath was meant to remind humanity:
You are not slaves.
You were not created merely to produce.
You were created to dwell with God.
But by the time Jesus walked the earth, the Sabbath had become surrounded by layers of human traditions.
The Pharisees built countless additional regulations around it.
What began as holy rest slowly became spiritual pressure.

Instead of freedom…
people feared violating technical rules.

Instead of restoration…
people carried anxiety.
And this is exactly where Jesus steps in.
One of the most explosive moments happens in Mark 3.
A man with a withered hand stands inside the synagogue.
Everyone watches Jesus carefully.
Not because they care about the suffering man.
But because they want to accuse Jesus.
The Greek text says:

“παρετήρουν αὐτὸν”
(paretēroun auton)

Meaning:
“They were watching Him closely,”
“spying on Him,”
“observing maliciously.”
The atmosphere was hostile.
And Jesus asks a devastating question:

“Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?”
(Mark 3:4)

The Greek phrase:
ἀγαθοποιῆσαι ἢ κακοποιῆσαι
(agathopoiēsai ē kakopoiēsai)

Literally means:
“To do beneficial good or harmful evil.”
Jesus exposes the deeper issue immediately.
The Sabbath was never intended to prevent mercy.
Refusing to help when you have the power to help is itself evil.
That shattered their religious logic.
Then Scripture says something many people overlook.

“He looked around at them with anger, grieved at the hardness of their hearts.”
(Mark 3:5)
The Greek word for hardness is:
πώρωσις (pōrōsis)

It means:
callousness,
spiritual blindness,
a petrified heart.
Jesus was not angry because they loved holiness too much.
He was angry because they used religion to avoid compassion.
That changes everything.
Because every Sabbath healing was actually a living prophecy.
Jesus was restoring what Sabbath was always supposed to mean.
Freedom.
Wholeness.
Release.
Healing.
Restoration.
In Luke 13, Jesus heals a crippled woman who had been bent over for eighteen years.
The ruler of the synagogue becomes indignant because the healing happened on the Sabbath.
Jesus answers:

“Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham… be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath?”
(Luke 13:16)
The Greek word for “loosed” is:
λυθῆναι (lythēnai)

Meaning:
to untie,
to release,
to liberate from bondage.
Do you see the picture?
The Sabbath was always about liberation.
In fact, Deuteronomy connects Sabbath directly to freedom from slavery in Egypt.

The Sabbath was God’s declaration:
“You are no longer enslaved.”
So when Jesus heals on the Sabbath, He is proclaiming something massive:

The Kingdom of God has arrived.
Captivity is breaking.
True rest is here.
This is why Jesus says in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto Me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for rest:
ἀναπαύσω (anapausō)

Meaning:
to refresh,
to give relief,
to cause someone to finally breathe again.
Jesus was not abolishing Sabbath.
He was fulfilling it.
The Pharisees reduced Sabbath to external regulation.
Jesus restored it to covenant restoration.
And then comes one of the most controversial declarations ever spoken:

“The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
(Mark 2:28)
In Greek:

κύριος τοῦ σαββάτου
(kyrios tou sabbatou)
“Lord of the Sabbath.”
This was not merely a statement about authority over a day.
This was a divine claim.
Because in Jewish understanding, the Sabbath belonged to God alone.
Jesus was revealing His divine identity openly.
The healing miracles were signs pointing toward something greater:
The Creator Himself had stepped into human suffering.
That is why these moments triggered such violent reactions.
The religious leaders understood exactly what Jesus was implying.
And many people still miss the deeper meaning today.
Some people still live exactly like the Pharisees.

Perfect at defending appearances.
Terrible at displaying mercy.

Quick to quote rules.
Slow to heal wounds.

Careful about religious image.
Careless about broken people.
But Jesus consistently revealed this truth:
Mercy is not a violation of holiness.
Mercy is the fulfillment of God’s heart.
The Sabbath healings reveal something deeply personal about Christ.
Jesus is not intimidated by human bondage.

Not physical bondage.
Not spiritual bondage.
Not emotional bondage.
Not generational bondage.
And He does not delay restoration simply to protect religious performance.
Some of you reading this have spent years bent over spiritually like the woman in Luke 13.

Smiling publicly.
Breaking privately.

Looking religious externally.
Exhausted internally.
But Jesus still heals on the Sabbath.

Meaning:
He still steps into impossible situations to announce freedom.
Not because you earned it.
But because restoration is part of who He is.

Religion says:
“Fix yourself first.”

Jesus says:
“Come to Me first.”

Religion says:
“Perform harder.”

Jesus says:
“Receive rest.”
Religion burdens.
Jesus restores.
And maybe that is why this story still unsettles people.
Because grace offends every system built on human pride.
The deeper mystery behind the Sabbath healings is this:
Jesus was never merely healing bodies.
He was announcing the arrival of the true eternal Sabbath.

A rest not found in rituals…
but in reconciliation with God.
Hebrews 4 echoes this powerfully:
“There remains therefore a rest for the people of God.”
The Greek word used there is:
σαββατισμός (sabbatismos)

Meaning:
“Sabbath rest.”
Not merely a weekly observance.
But a spiritual resting place found in Christ Himself.
The final invitation of Jesus has never changed.
Stop striving to save yourself.
Stop exhausting yourself trying to appear righteous.
Stop carrying burdens you were never meant to carry alone.
The Lord of the Sabbath is still calling weary people home.
And some of you know this message exposed something deep inside you.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Jesus did not come merely to make you religious.
He came to make you free.
The same hands they criticized for healing are the same hands that were pierced to save humanity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The most terrifying sentence Jesus ever said was not about flames.
paragraphs: The most terrifying sentence Jesus ever said was not about flames.
Not about outer darkness.
Not about weeping and gnashing of teeth.
It was seven words that almost nobody talks about deeply enough.
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.”
“Amen, I tell you… I do not know you.”
— Matthew 25:12
Not “you never went to church.”
Not “you never posted Bible verses.”
Not “you weren’t religious enough.”
“I do not know you.”
And if that sentence does not shake something inside your soul… you may not understand what Jesus was actually saying.
Because in Scripture, to be “known” by God was never casual recognition.
The Greek word Jesus used here is “οἶδα” (oida).

It means:
to truly know,
to recognize intimately,
to perceive deeply,
to be personally connected with.

This was not Jesus saying,
“I forgot your name.”

This was Jesus saying,
“You stood near Me… but never belonged to Me.”
That is horrifying.
Because it means proximity to Christianity is not the same as intimacy with Christ.
You can sing worship songs and still be spiritually unknown.
You can quote Scripture and still be spiritually unknown.
You can build an online ministry and still be spiritually unknown.

You can preach sermons and still hear:
“I never knew you.”
The terrifying part is that many people Jesus warned were completely convinced they were safe.
“Κύριε, κύριε…”
“Lord, Lord…”
Matthew 7:22
Notice that.
They called Him Lord.

Not atheist.
Not pagan.
Not unbeliever.
Religious people.
Church people.
People who thought they were fine.
And Jesus says something so emotionally devastating that it almost feels unbearable to read honestly.
“Καὶ τότε ὁμολογήσω αὐτοῖς ὅτι· Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
“And then I will declare to them: I never knew you.”
— Matthew 7:23
The word “ἔγνων” (egnōn) comes from “γινώσκω” (ginōskō).
This is even deeper than intellectual awareness.

It speaks of relational knowing.
Experiential knowing.
Covenantal intimacy.
The same word used for deep personal union.
Jesus was not exposing weak church attendance.
He was exposing counterfeit intimacy.
And suddenly the conversation becomes personal.
Because many people today know Christian culture better than they know Christ Himself.

They know worship trends.
Podcast theology.
Denominational arguments.
TikTok sermons.
Motivational Christianity.
But they do not know Jesus in secret.

No surrender.
No repentance.
No hidden prayer life.
No real obedience when nobody is watching.
Only performance.
Only appearance.
Only carefully edited spirituality.
And the scariest part?
It can fool everyone around you.
But not Him.
In Revelation 3:1, Jesus speaks to the church in Sardis with another terrifying statement:
“ὄνομα ἔχεις ὅτι ζῇς, καὶ νεκρὸς εἶ.”
“You have a reputation for being alive, but you are dead.”
Dead people can still look religious.
That should terrify every one of us.
Because Christianity was never meant to be cosmetic.
The Hebrew understanding of knowing God was always relational.

In Hebrew, the word “יָדַע” (yada) means:
to know intimately,
to experience personally,
to walk closely with.
Genesis says Adam “knew” Eve.
Not information.
Intimacy.
Connection.
Union.
So when Scripture speaks of knowing God, it is not talking about memorizing verses while your heart remains distant.
It is talking about surrender.
Transformation.
Communion.
Walking with Him when nobody applauds you.
There are people who know theology but do not know Jesus.
And there are broken people with trembling prayers that heaven recognizes instantly.
That is why the tax collector in Luke 18 went home justified while the proud religious man did not.
One performed.
One surrendered.
One impressed people.
One cried for mercy.
And heaven responded to the honest sinner.
This is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because some people reading this have mastered appearing Christian while secretly being exhausted from pretending.
You post strength while privately collapsing.
You post faith while privately numb.
You know how to sound spiritual while your prayer life has gone silent.

And deep down, there is this quiet fear:
“What if I have been near Jesus… without truly knowing Him?”
Listen carefully.
Conviction is not condemnation.
If your heart is being pierced right now, that is not proof God abandoned you.
It may be proof He is calling you back before your heart hardens completely.
Because the same Jesus who warned with terrifying honesty also invited with terrifying mercy.
In John 10:14, Jesus says:
“ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, καὶ γινώσκω τὰ ἐμά.”
“I am the Good Shepherd. I know My own.”
He knows His sheep.
Not perfectly polished sheep.
Not flawless sheep.
His sheep.

The struggling.
The weary.
The repentant.
The honest.
The broken who still run toward Him instead of away from Him.
That is the difference.
Not perfection.
Relationship.
Real repentance is not pretending you never failed.
It is refusing to hide from God after you fail.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Jesus once.
One ran back in repentance.
One ran away in despair.
The difference was not the size of the sin.
The difference was surrender.
And maybe that is why this subject cuts so deeply.
Because many people fear hell while still avoiding intimacy with Christ.
But eternal life itself was never merely about escaping punishment.
Jesus defined eternal life personally.
“αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωή, ἵνα γινώσκωσίν σε…”
“And this is eternal life: that they may know You…”
— John 17:3
Eternal life begins with knowing Him now.
Not someday.
Now.
Not religious performance.
Relationship.
Not image management.
Surrender.
Not public Christianity with private rebellion.
Real communion with Christ.
And maybe somebody reading this needed to hear this today:
God is not asking you to become impressive.
He is asking you to become honest.
The enemy loves fake perfection because fake perfection never seeks healing.

But broken honesty?
That is where transformation begins.
Some of you have spent years trying to look spiritually alive while quietly dying inside.
Jesus never asked for your performance.
He asked for your heart.

And the terrifying sentence:
“I never knew you”
was never meant to drive repentant people away from Him.
It was meant to wake up those hiding behind religious masks before it is too late.
So stop pretending.
Stop performing.
Stop curating holiness while secretly starving spiritually.
Run back to Christ honestly.
Cry honestly.
Pray honestly.
Repent honestly.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be failing publicly.
The greatest tragedy would be standing before Jesus after spending your whole life pretending to know Him… only to discover you never truly surrendered to Him at all.
And maybe that is why this sentence is more terrifying than descriptions of hell itself.
Because separation from Christ was always the real horror.
Not flames.
Not darkness.

Him saying:
“You wanted religion without relationship.
You wanted salvation without surrender.
You wanted My benefits without Me.”
And suddenly every fake mask becomes meaningless forever.
Somebody else reading your confession may realize they are not alone tonight.
One day, every performance will die… but your relationship with Jesus Christ will remain forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story Behind Samson Killing a Lion Bare-Handed
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind Samson Killing a Lion Bare-Handed
There are moments in Scripture that feel larger than life.
A man tears apart a lion with his bare hands.
No sword.
No spear.
No shield.
Just a young man walking alone through a vineyard... and suddenly standing face-to-face with death.
Most people read the story and focus on the miracle.
But the real story isn't the lion.
The lion was merely the warning.
The lion was the prophecy.
The lion was the shadow of a far greater battle Samson didn't realize was already beginning.
And if we're honest...
Many of us are fighting our own lions right now.
Not in the wilderness.
Inside our hearts.
The story begins in Judges 14.
Samson is traveling toward Timnah when something terrifying happens.
The Hebrew text says:
"וְהִנֵּה כְּפִיר אֲרָיוֹת שֹׁאֵג לִקְרָאתוֹ"
Ve-hinneh kefir arayot sho'eg liqrato.
"Behold, a young lion came roaring toward him."
(Judges 14:5)
The word כְּפִיר (kefir) specifically refers to a young lion in its prime.
Not weak.
Not wounded.
Not old.
This was a predator at the height of its strength.
The kind hunters feared.
The kind that rarely lost.
The text paints a sudden scene.
No warning.
No preparation.
No escape route.
One moment Samson is walking.
The next moment death is charging directly at him.
And isn't that how many of life's greatest battles begin?
You weren't looking for the diagnosis.
You weren't expecting the betrayal.
You weren't prepared for the temptation.
You didn't wake up planning for your marriage to struggle.
You didn't see depression coming.
You didn't expect your faith to be tested.
One moment everything is normal.
The next moment a lion is roaring in your face.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary statements in the entire Old Testament.
The Hebrew says:
"וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה"
Vatitzlach alav Ruach YHWH.
"And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him."
(Judges 14:6)
The word צָלַח (tsalach) means to rush, break forth, overpower, or come mightily upon someone.
This wasn't Samson discovering hidden strength.
This wasn't adrenaline.
This wasn't human courage.
The power came from God.
The lion was stronger than Samson.
But God was stronger than the lion.
Scripture then says:
"וַיְשַׁסְּעֵהוּ כְּשַׁסַּע הַגְּדִי"
Vayeshasse'ehu keshassa ha-gedi.
"He tore the lion apart as one tears apart a young goat."
The image is shocking.
The victory is immediate.
Decisive.
Absolute.
The lion never stood a chance once God's Spirit moved.
But something strange happens next.
Most readers miss it.
The text says Samson told no one.
Not his father.
Not his mother.
Nobody.
Why?
Because this story was never about impressing people.
It was about preparation.
God was showing Samson something.
A lesson.
A warning.
A revelation.
The lion wasn't merely an enemy.
It was a preview.
A glimpse of what Samson would spend the rest of his life fighting.
Because lions don't always come with fur and teeth.
Sometimes they arrive disguised as pride.
Sometimes as lust.
Sometimes as compromise.
Sometimes as self-confidence.
The lion outside was easier to kill than the lion inside.
Months later Samson returns.
The carcass remains.
Inside it he discovers something astonishing.
A swarm of bees.
And honey.
Death had become a source of sweetness.
Judges 14:8 says:
"וְהִנֵּה עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים בִּגְוִיַּת הָאַרְיֵה וּדְבָשׁ"
Ve-hinneh adat devorim bigviyat ha-aryeh udevash.
"Behold, a swarm of bees and honey were in the carcass of the lion."
From a dead lion came sweetness.
From what once threatened his life came nourishment.
From what was meant to destroy him came provision.
The symbolism is breathtaking.
God often brings sweetness from places that once brought pain.
The marriage that nearly collapsed becomes stronger than before.
The addiction that broke you becomes part of your testimony.
The grief that crushed your heart becomes the place where compassion grows.
The wound becomes wisdom.
The scar becomes ministry.
The lion becomes honey.
Yet Samson never fully learned the lesson.
That is the tragedy.
God gave him victory over the lion.
But Samson never gained victory over himself.
The strongest man in Scripture was eventually defeated by weaknesses no muscle could overcome.
His greatest enemy wasn't the lion of Timnah.
It was the pride within his own heart.
Again and again he played with temptation.
Again and again he ignored warning signs.
Again and again he assumed God's power would always cover his disobedience.
Until one day it didn't.
The man who once tore apart a lion was eventually bound by ropes.
The man who once inspired fear became a prisoner.
The man who once saw victory became blind.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because many believers pray for Samson's strength.
Few pray for Samson's humility.
We want lion-killing faith.
We want mountain-moving power.
We want supernatural victories.
But God often wants to teach us something greater:
Dependence.
Obedience.
Faithfulness.
Character.
The lion wasn't Samson's greatest test.
Success was.
Victory was.
Power was.
And sometimes the blessings God gives us reveal more about our hearts than the battles we survive.
There is another lion in Scripture.
Centuries later, the Apostle Peter wrote:
"Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour."
The Greek text says:
"ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος"
ho antidikos hymōn diabolos hōs leōn ōryomenos
"Your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion..."
(1 Peter 5:8)
Notice the connection.
Samson faced a roaring lion.
Believers face a roaring lion.
The battle never ended.
The battlefield simply changed.
But unlike Samson, we have Someone greater.
Someone who did not merely kill a lion.
Someone who conquered sin, death, hell, and the grave itself.
Jesus Christ.
The Lion of Judah.
In Hebrew:
"אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה"
Aryeh Yehudah.
The Lion of Judah.
The true Deliverer.
The true Judge.
The true Champion.
Where Samson failed, Jesus succeeded.
Where Samson was overcome by temptation, Jesus remained sinless.
Where Samson lost his strength, Jesus willingly laid down His life.
Where Samson's story ended in tragedy, Christ's story ended in resurrection.
And because He lives, our lions do not have the final word.
Maybe you're staring at a lion today.
Fear.
Anxiety.
Shame.
Temptation.
Addiction.
Loss.
Depression.
A broken relationship.
A secret struggle nobody knows about.
The same God who empowered Samson still reigns.
The same Spirit who rushed upon Samson still transforms lives.
The same Christ who conquered the grave still saves.
And sometimes God doesn't just destroy the lion.
Sometimes He turns the lion into honey.
Sometimes the very thing that nearly destroyed you becomes the testimony that helps save someone else.
That's how redemption works.
That's how grace works.
That's how Jesus works.
Maybe that is why you're reading this right now.
Not because of the lion.
But because of the honey God plans to bring from it.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The lion that terrified you yesterday may become the testimony that feeds someone tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The rain had stopped… but heaven still felt silent.
paragraphs: The rain had stopped… but heaven still felt silent.

Imagine Noah standing at the opening of the ark after months trapped between judgment and uncertainty. The screams of humanity were gone. The violence was gone. The mocking voices were gone. But something terrifying remained:
Silence.
The earth had survived judgment, but Noah still did not know if the world was ready for life again.
Most people read quickly past the moment Noah released the birds. But hidden inside this scene is one of the deepest prophetic mysteries in all of Scripture.
Why did Noah send out birds twice?
Why a raven first… then a dove repeatedly afterward?
This was not random survival behavior.
This was revelation.
This was prophecy.
This was a mirror of the human heart.
In the Hebrew text of Genesis 8:6–12, the wording becomes incredibly important.
The Scripture says:
“And it came to pass at the end of forty days, that Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made: and he sent forth a raven…”
The Hebrew word for raven is:
“עֹרֵב” (ʿōrēḇ)
Strong’s H6158
The root carries associations connected to darkness, dusk, obscurity, and wandering.
Then later Noah sends a dove:
“יוֹנָה” (yônāh)
Strong’s H3123
The dove throughout Scripture symbolizes peace, innocence, gentleness, covenant, and eventually the Holy Spirit.
This contrast is not accidental.
The raven and the dove represent two completely different spiritual natures.
The raven feeds on death.
The dove searches for life.
The raven was comfortable in a judged world.
The dove was not.
That changes everything.
Genesis 8:7 says:
“And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.”
The phrase “to and fro” in Hebrew is:

“יָצֹוא וָשׁוֹב”
(yāṣôʾ wāšôḇ)

Literally:
“going and returning.”
The raven never truly came back into covenant rest.
Why?
Because ravens are scavengers.
The flood had left floating carcasses across the earth.
The raven found satisfaction in death.
It could survive among corruption.
But then Noah sent the dove.
The dove could not.
Genesis 8:9 says:
“But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot…”
The Hebrew word for “rest” is:
“מָנוֹחַ” (mānôaḥ)

Meaning:
resting place,
comfort,
settling,
peace.
This is deeply connected to Noah’s own name:
“נֹחַ” (Nōaḥ)

Which means:
rest,
comfort,
peace.
The dove could not find “Noah” outside the ark.
Think about that carefully.
The unclean bird adapted to death.
The clean bird longed for covenant rest.
That is humanity today.
Some people become comfortable in spiritually dead places.
Others cannot breathe unless God is near.
The raven represents the flesh.
The dove represents the Spirit.
This pattern becomes even more powerful when viewed through the New Testament Greek.
When Jesus is baptized in Matthew 3:16, Scripture says:
“And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove…”
Greek:

“περιστερὰν”
(peristeran)
A dove.
The same symbol from Noah returns.
Why?
Because Noah’s ark was a prophetic shadow of salvation through Christ.
Peter confirms this directly.
1 Peter 3:20–21 says the ark symbolized salvation.
The flood was judgment.
The ark was mercy.
The dove was the Spirit searching for a resting place after judgment.
And where did the dove finally rest?
Not on dead flesh.
Not on floating corruption.
Not on destroyed civilization.
But on an olive branch.
Genesis 8:11:
“And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off…”
The olive tree throughout Scripture represents covenant, anointing, endurance, and reconciliation with God.
The Hebrew word for olive leaf is connected to:
“זַיִת” (zayith)
Olive tree.
Oil came from olives.
Anointing came from oil.
The dove returned carrying evidence that life had begun again.
Mercy survived judgment.
But here is the mystery most people miss completely:
Noah sent the dove three separate times.
Not once.
Three times.

The first time:
No rest.

The second time:
Evidence of life.

The third time:
The dove never returned.
Why?
Because the earth was finally ready for habitation.
This mirrors the entire story of redemption.
The Spirit searches humanity.
At first there is no resting place.
Then signs of transformation appear.
Finally the Spirit abides permanently where life has truly been restored.
This is why Jesus says in John 14:17:
“He dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.”
The dove no longer merely visits.
The dove remains.
Even deeper still…
Jewish rabbis noticed something ancient readers often understood instinctively:
The raven and the dove may also symbolize two kingdoms.
One kingdom feeds on corruption, violence, pride, and death.
The other seeks purity, peace, holiness, and communion with God.
One adapts to a cursed world.
One waits for a restored world.
And every human soul eventually chooses which bird it becomes.
This is why the sequence matters.
Noah tested the world first with a creature comfortable in death.
Then with a creature that could only survive where peace existed.
Some people can sit inside sin for years without conviction.
Others feel miserable the moment God’s presence lifts.
That difference reveals what spirit is leading them.
Romans 8:5 says:
“For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit.”
The raven found enough in death.
The dove did not.
And maybe that is what terrifies some people reading this right now.
Because deep down you know this world has been feeding parts of you that should have died long ago.
Maybe you have adapted to spiritual numbness.
Maybe compromise stopped bothering you.
Maybe you learned how to survive around dead things instead of pursuing God’s presence.
But if there is still a dove inside you…
You will never truly be comfortable far from Him.
That restlessness is mercy.
That conviction is mercy.
That discomfort is mercy.
The Spirit still searches for a resting place.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you…”
God does not merely improve people.
He transforms their nature.
Ravens survive on death.
Doves search for peace.
And the Gospel changes what kind of creature lives inside a person.
This is why repentance matters.
This is why surrender matters.
This is why Jesus came.
Not merely to make bad people nicer…
But to make dead people alive.
The untold mystery behind Noah sending out birds twice was never really about birds.
It was about humanity after judgment.
It was about the Spirit searching the earth.
It was about the condition of the heart.
It was about whether we love darkness… or long for God’s rest.
And even now…
The dove is still searching.

Be honest…
This hit harder than some expected.
Some souls are starving because they learned to feed where God never meant them to live.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are moments in Scripture where silence becomes louder than explanation.
paragraphs: There are moments in Scripture where silence becomes louder than explanation.
One of the most debated questions in the entire Bible is this:
“Where did Cain’s wife come from?”

Skeptics mock it.
Believers wrestle with it.
Many pastors avoid it.
And countless Christians quietly wonder if Genesis somehow forgot to explain one of the most important details in human history.
But the answer was never hidden.
It was simply overlooked.

To understand Cain’s wife correctly, we cannot read Genesis through modern assumptions, modern biology, modern culture, or modern morality alone. We must return to the ancient Hebrew text itself, the context of creation, the timeline of early humanity, and the original intent of the narrative.
Because Genesis was never written like a modern Western history textbook.
It was written as sacred covenant history.
And once you understand that, the confusion begins to disappear.
The story begins in Genesis 1:27:
“So God created man in His own image…”
The Hebrew reads:

אָדָם — ’Āḏām
“Adam” or “mankind”
This is important because Adam is both a personal name and a collective term for humanity itself.
Then Genesis 2 narrows the focus onto the first man and first woman.
In Genesis 2:22:

וַיִּבֶן יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הַצֵּלָע
Vayyiven YHWH Elohim et-hatzela
“And the LORD God built the rib…”
