הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Hapa‘am odeh et-YHWH
“This time I will praise Yahweh.”
Notice what disappeared.
Jacob.
For the first time, Leah names a son without mentioning her husband’s approval.

The son’s name was Judah.
יְהוּדָה (Yehudah)

Which comes from:
יָדָה (yadah)
meaning:
to praise,
to worship,
to surrender gratitude.
This is the turning point.
Leah stops measuring her worth through human affection.
And heaven responds.
Because from Leah came Judah.
From Judah came King David.
And from David eventually came Jesus Christ.
The rejected woman carried the Messianic bloodline.
Rachel had beauty.
Leah carried destiny.
And this is where people misunderstand God.
God often plants eternal significance inside the people the world overlooks.
The cross itself proves this pattern.
Isaiah 53 says of Christ:
“He had no beauty or majesty to attract us to Him.”
Even Jesus understands rejection.
Even Jesus knows what it feels like to be unwanted by people He came to save.
That is why Leah’s tears matter so deeply.
Because they prophetically echo toward Christ Himself.
And there is another detail many never notice.
When Jacob finally died, where was he buried?
Not beside Rachel.
Beside Leah.
Genesis 49:31 reveals it quietly.
In the cave of Machpelah.
Leah ended up in the covenant resting place beside Jacob.
The woman who spent years feeling unseen was never forgotten by God.
Not once.
Some of you have been crying like Leah.

Quietly.
Privately.
Exhaustedly.

Trying to earn love.
Trying to compete.
Trying to be enough for people who only see Rachel.
But heaven is not measuring your worth through human preference.
God saw Leah before Jacob ever did.
And sometimes the people who feel least beautiful to the world become the ones God uses most eternally.
Maybe Leah kept crying because rejection cuts deeply.
But maybe she also cried because God was slowly washing her dependence on human validation away.
Pain became the place where worship was born.
And worship changed her legacy forever.

Somebody reading this has spent years asking:
“Why am I not chosen?”

But maybe the deeper question is:
“What if God is building something eternal through the very pain I wanted removed?”
The terrifying truth is this:
Sometimes God allows the wound of rejection because intimacy with Him grows deepest in the places where human applause dies.
And Leah’s tears still preach thousands of years later.
Not because she was loved correctly by people…
But because she was seen completely by God.
And if you know someone silently carrying rejection, share this with them tonight. Some people are smiling publicly while crying like Leah privately.
The woman nobody wanted became part of the lineage that carried the Savior of the world.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The people who hated Jeremiah still went to church.
paragraphs: The people who hated Jeremiah still went to church.
That’s what makes his story terrifying.

They lifted their hands in worship…
while their hearts quietly belonged to idols.
And the frightening part is this:
most people destroying their souls do not realize it immediately.
Because spiritual death rarely begins with rebellion.
It begins with slow compromise.

One ignored conviction.
One secret habit.
One delayed obedience.
One hidden pride nobody confronts because it still “looks Christian” on the outside.
Jeremiah watched an entire nation slowly drift from God while convincing themselves they were still safe.
That’s why his words cut so deeply even now.

In Jeremiah 2:13, God says:
“My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.”
Read that carefully.

They rejected the Source…
then tried to replace Him with empty substitutes.
That is still happening today.
People are exhausted because they are trying to get eternal peace from temporary things.

Validation.
Attention.
Relationships.
Money.
Secret sin.
Platforms.
Lust.
Control.
Pride disguised as “self-confidence.”
Broken cisterns.
And some of you already know the feeling.

You laugh publicly…
but privately your mind feels exhausted all the time.
You worship in rooms where nobody knows you stopped praying consistently months ago.

You still believe in God…
but your appetite for Him is fading.
That silent drift terrifies you.
God saw it.
You knew.
Jeremiah was called “the weeping prophet” because he carried the grief of watching people reject the very God trying to save them.
Not because God hated them.
Because God loved them enough to warn them.
That changes the entire story.
Conviction is not cruelty.
It is mercy before destruction.
AHA REVELATION LINE:
Sometimes the most loving thing God will do is disrupt the lie you were becoming comfortable inside.
Read that again.
Some people keep asking God for peace while refusing repentance.

But Isaiah 57:21 says,
“There is no peace… for the wicked.”
That doesn’t mean God refuses mercy.
It means sin was never designed to produce peace.
Only surrender does that.

And Jeremiah preached this message while false prophets told everyone exactly what they wanted to hear:
“Peace, peace,” when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).
Sound familiar?
We are living in a generation flooded with inspirational Christianity that rarely confronts sin anymore.

People want sermons that soothe them…
not sermons that expose them.
But Jesus never died merely to make people feel inspired.
He died to rescue sinners from destruction.

That includes you.
That includes me.
And maybe the hardest truth is this:

some people love the idea of Jesus…
while resisting the Lordship of Jesus.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR STATEMENT:
You can say “God knows my heart” while ignoring the fact that Scripture says your heart is deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9).
That verse destroys modern self-worship.
Because the human heart without surrender does not naturally drift toward holiness.
It drifts toward self.

Toward pride.
Toward hidden compromise.
Toward making excuses for sin we once hated.
This might be the warning your soul needed.

Some of you are spiritually tired not because God abandoned you…
but because you’ve been feeding your flesh more than your spirit.
And nobody around you knows.
That’s the hidden battle people rarely admit.
Spiritual fatigue from pretending.

You still post verses.
Still smile.
Still appear “fine.”
But inside, conviction has been fighting with compromise for months.
And every time you silence conviction, your heart hardens a little more.

Hebrews 3:15 says:
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
Today.

Not after another secret conversation.
Not after another hidden addiction.
Not after another week of distance.
Today.
Because here is the hope buried inside Jeremiah’s story:
God kept calling people back even after repeated rebellion.
That’s grace.

Not tolerance of sin.
An invitation out of it.

Jeremiah prophesied about a coming New Covenant in Jeremiah 31:33:
“I will put My law within them, and I will write it on their hearts.”
This pointed directly to Jesus Christ.

The One who would not merely warn sinners…
but save them.
Jesus fulfilled what Jeremiah foresaw.
The cross was not symbolic poetry.
It was substitution.
Christ took the judgment sinners deserved so repentant people could receive mercy they never deserved.
That is the Gospel.

Not self-improvement.
Not behavior management.
Not religious performance.
Salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone.

Ephesians 2:8-9 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works.”
You cannot earn cleansing.
But you must surrender to the One offering it.
And maybe that is why this message found you right now.
Not randomly.
Maybe God is interrupting the version of you that learned how to look spiritually alive while quietly starving inside.
IDENTITY STATEMENT:
You were not created merely to appear holy in public.
You were created to belong completely to Jesus in private too.
And here’s the beautiful part:
Jesus still restores people who failed Him.

Peter denied Him three times.
Thomas doubted.
David collapsed morally.
Paul hunted Christians.
Yet grace rewrote their stories.
Because repentance opens doors pride keeps locked.
Some scholars interpret Jeremiah’s tears as reflecting the very heart of God grieving over people He deeply loved.
And Jesus showed that same heart when He wept over Jerusalem in Luke 19:41.
God is not emotionally distant from human rebellion.
He grieves over what sin destroys.
That means conviction is not proof God abandoned you.
It may be proof He is still pursuing you.

If your heart feels exposed reading this…
good.
Dead hearts feel nothing.
The fact you still feel conviction may be evidence that mercy is still calling your name.

So stop pretending.
Stop negotiating with hidden sin.
Stop waiting for “someday.”
Come back to Jesus fully.

Not halfway.
Not performatively.
Not emotionally for one night.
Fully.
Some wounds need Scripture handled deeply, patiently, and truthfully. If you want to go deeper in your walk with Christ, you can begin here:
And the next message may uncover the very thing your soul has been trying not to face.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There is a verse many people avoid because it feels too harsh to explain.
paragraphs: There is a verse many people avoid because it feels too harsh to explain.
A prophet walks out of a city.
Some young people mock him.

Then suddenly…
judgment falls.
And generations have asked the same question:
“Why would God do something like that?”
But most people were never taught what was really happening in that moment.
Because this was never just about children making jokes.

This was about rebellion.
Desecration.
Hatred of God.
A nation spiritually collapsing from the inside.
And the terrifying part is this:
The same spirit still exists today.
The story is found in 2 Kings 2:23–24.
Most English translations say:
“Little children mocked him.”
But the original Hebrew tells a much deeper story.
The phrase used is:

“נְעָרִים קְטַנִּים”
(ne'arim qetannim)
People often assume this means toddlers or innocent little boys.
It does not.
The Hebrew word ne'arim was used for young men, servants, military-age youths, and even grown men in some contexts.

Isaac was called a na'ar.
Joseph at seventeen was called a na'ar.
Solomon used the term about himself as king.
This was not a playground of harmless six-year-olds.
This was likely a hostile gang of rebellious youths and young men.
And where did this happen?
Bethel.
That matters more than most people realize.
Bethel was one of the main centers of idol worship in northern Israel after the kingdom split.
King Jeroboam had established golden calf worship there in direct rebellion against the worship of Yahweh in Jerusalem.
This city had become spiritually corrupted for generations.
The atmosphere itself was anti-God.
And then Elisha arrives.
Not as a motivational speaker.
Not as a celebrity preacher.
But as the newly appointed prophet carrying the authority of heaven after Elijah had just been taken up.
The timing matters.
Right before this event, Elijah had been taken into heaven in a whirlwind.
The prophetic mantle had fallen onto Elisha.

This moment publicly confirmed whether Israel would honor God’s authority…
or reject it.
Then the mocking begins.
“Go up, thou bald head!”
In Hebrew:

“עֲלֵה קֵרֵחַ”
(aleh qereach)
The word “aleh” means “go up.”
They were not merely insulting his appearance.
Many scholars believe this was mocking Elijah’s ascension.
In other words:

“Why don’t you disappear too?”
“Go die.”
“Get out of here.”
“We don’t want God’s prophet.”
This was open hostility toward the representative of God.
And notice something devastating:
Elisha did not curse them in personal anger.
Scripture says:
“He cursed them in the name of the LORD.”
That phrase changes everything.
This was judicial.
Prophetic.
Covenantal.

Under Mosaic covenant law, persistent rebellion against God and contempt for divine authority carried severe consequences because Israel was not merely a nation…
it was a covenant people directly accountable to Yahweh.
Modern readers often approach this passage through a Western individualistic mindset instead of ancient covenant theology.
But in ancient Israel, rebellion against God spread like infection through generations, families, and entire communities.
The issue was never bald jokes.
The issue was hardened contempt toward God.
And the bears?
Two female bears came from the woods and mauled forty-two of them.

The Hebrew word does not necessarily mean all forty-two died instantly.
It indicates violent tearing or mauling.
Still horrifying.
Still severe.
Still meant to shake the nation awake.
Because sometimes judgment in Scripture was not only punishment…
It was warning.
Mercy had already been ignored repeatedly in Israel.

Prophets had pleaded.
God had warned.
Idolatry had spread.
Truth had been mocked.
Eventually judgment arrived.
That pattern exists all throughout Scripture.
People love verses about grace until they realize grace rejected repeatedly becomes judgment eventually.
And honestly…
many people secretly mock God today exactly the same way.
Not always with words.
But with indifference.
Selective obedience.
Performative Christianity.
Internet Christianity with no repentance.

People wear crosses while hating holiness.
Quote Scripture while sleeping comfortably in sin.
Build entire online identities around God while privately resisting surrender.
This story is uncomfortable because it destroys the modern fantasy that God exists only to tolerate us.
No.
God is merciful beyond imagination.
But He is also holy beyond comprehension.
The same Bible that says “God is love” also says:
“Our God is a consuming fire.”
In Greek:

“πῦρ καταναλίσκον”
(pyr katanaliskon)
A consuming fire.

Not safe.
Not tame.
Not controllable.
Holy.
And maybe the deeper tragedy in this story is not the bears.
Maybe it is that an entire generation had learned to laugh at what should have brought them to repentance.
That spirit still lives now.

People mock conviction.
Mock purity.
Mock repentance.
Mock preachers.
Mock holiness.
Mock the fear of God.
Then wonder why their souls feel empty.
Be honest.

How many times has God tried to get your attention…
but you laughed it off?

How many convictions did you silence?
How many compromises did you rename as “freedom”?
This article is not about bears.
It is about the terrifying danger of a heart that no longer trembles before God.

Because once a culture normalizes mocking truth…
collapse is usually already beginning.
And yet…

even here…
grace still whispers.
Because the fact you are reading this right now may itself be mercy.

You still have breath.
Still have time.
Still have an invitation.
Jesus Christ carried the judgment we deserved so repentance could become restoration instead of destruction.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Substitution.
The innocent Son of God absorbing wrath so rebellious people could become sons and daughters again.
In Aramaic, one of the words Jesus cried from the cross was:
“Eloi.”
“My God.”
The rejection we deserved fell onto Him.
That is why repentance is not humiliation.
It is rescue.

And maybe this story unsettled you because deep down…
you know God has been calling you back for a long time.
Not to religion.
To surrender.
To truth.
To holiness.
To life.

And if someone you love has slowly become spiritually numb, send this to them gently.
Not to condemn them.
To wake them up.

One day people will realize the scariest judgment was never the bears…
it was a heart that stopped fearing God entirely.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: It didn’t feel like a blessing.
paragraphs: It didn’t feel like a blessing.
It felt like silence.
Doors kept closing. Messages left unanswered. Plans you prayed over—stalled. You told yourself to stay patient, but deep down, something started whispering, “Maybe God forgot you.”
You didn’t say it out loud.
But you felt it.
You watched other people move forward—new opportunities, open doors, visible favor. Meanwhile, you were stuck in what felt like divine delay. Same place. Same prayers. Same waiting.
And the hardest part?
You were trying to be faithful.
You were praying. You were believing. You were holding on.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Some of God’s greatest blessings arrive disguised as delays.
Not because He is slow.
But because He is precise.
“Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!” — Psalm 27:14
Read that again.
Waiting isn’t God ignoring you.
Waiting is God forming you.
You thought the delay meant denial.
But what if it meant protection?
What if the thing you were asking for—if it came when you wanted it—would have crushed you instead of blessed you?
God saw it.
He saw what you couldn’t handle yet.
He saw the people you weren’t ready to discern.
He saw the pride still hiding behind your prayers.
You knew.
There were moments you wanted the blessing more than you wanted Him.
And God will not compete with what He intends to give you.
So He delays.
Not to punish you.
But to purify your desire.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
There’s a pattern in Scripture most people miss.
Joseph was delayed in a prison before he stepped into a palace.
David was delayed in the wilderness before he wore a crown.
Even Lazarus… Jesus delayed on purpose.
“When He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days.” — John 11:6
That doesn’t sound loving at first.
Until you realize the delay set the stage for resurrection.
If Jesus had come early, Lazarus would have been healed.
But because He came late, Lazarus was raised from the dead.
Some blessings require a delay… because they’re meant to reveal something greater.
And now it’s getting personal.
Because your delay is exposing something in you.
Impatience.
Fear.
Control.
Maybe even quiet unbelief.
You say you trust God…
But your anxiety tells a different story.
You say He’s enough…
But your restlessness keeps reaching for something else.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because the delay isn’t just about what you’re waiting for.
It’s about who you’re becoming while you wait.
“Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for Him…” — Psalm 37:7
Stillness is not inactivity.
It’s surrender.
It’s choosing to trust when nothing is moving.
It’s believing that God is working even when you see nothing changing.
And here’s the truth most people avoid—
If God gave you everything right now, without transformation, you would misuse it.
Or worse… you would replace Him with it.
So He slows it down.
Not because He’s withholding good.
But because He is good.
“For the Lord God is a sun and shield; the Lord bestows favor and honor. No good thing does He withhold from those who walk uprightly.” — Psalm 84:11
No good thing.
Which means if it’s being withheld…
It’s not ready.
Or you’re not.
That’s not rejection.
That’s mercy.
And here comes the moment you can’t avoid anymore.
Because eventually, the delay forces a decision.
Will you trust God… even if the timeline never matches yours?
Will you love Him… even if the answer takes longer than you expected?
Or were you only faithful as long as He was fast?
This is where many walk away.
Not because God failed them.
But because He didn’t move on their schedule.
But there’s another path.
The one where you stop chasing outcomes…
And start surrendering fully.
Where your faith isn’t anchored in what God gives—
But in who He is.
And that’s where the Gospel breaks through everything.
Because the greatest “delay” in human history…
Was actually salvation being prepared.
For generations, people waited.
Prayed.
Hoped.
And then, at the perfect time—
Jesus came.
“But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son…” — Galatians 4:4
Not early.
Not late.
Perfect.
And what looked like another delay…
Led to the cross.
Where sin was exposed.
Judgment was satisfied.
And grace was released.
Because the real issue was never your timeline.
It was your sin.
Your separation.
Your need for redemption.
And Jesus didn’t delay that.
He finished it.
“It is finished.” — John 19:30
So now the question isn’t just about your waiting…
It’s about your surrender.
Because you can spend your life frustrated over delays…
And still miss the Savior standing right in front of you.
Or…
You can recognize that even this moment—
This waiting, this tension, this uncertainty—
Is God calling you closer.
Not just to trust His plan.
But to receive His Son.
Because the greatest blessing isn’t what you’re waiting for.
It’s Jesus.
Everything else is secondary.
Temporary.
Passing.
But Him?
Eternal.
And if you have Him…
You are not delayed.
You are being prepared.
This is where it changes for you.
Not when the door opens.
But when your heart does.
So say it plainly, if you feel it pressing on you—
“I surrender my timing. I trust Your will.”
Say it.
Mean it.
And if this hit something deep in you, don’t keep it to yourself. Let this reach them.
If conviction is sitting heavy on you, don’t ignore it—respond to it. Write it out. Even one word. “Trust.” “Surrender.” “Wait.” Let it be real.

Follow this journey if you’re done with surface-level faith and ready for truth that actually transforms. Save this—because the next time the delay hits, you’ll need to remember what God is really doing.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—beyond moments like this, into real growth, correction, and daily strengthening in Christ—step into what’s waiting for you here:
Not just to endure the delay—
But to understand it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some people preach holiness in the pulpit while secretly negotiating compromise in private.
paragraphs: Some people preach holiness in the pulpit while secretly negotiating compromise in private.
And one of the clearest compromises Scripture repeatedly confronts is the misuse of marriage, leadership, and spiritual authority.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

This is not merely about culture.
It is about qualification.
The Bible never presents spiritual leadership as a platform for personal indulgence. A preacher is not called to collect women while claiming to represent Christ. He is called to mirror Christ.
And Christ does not have many brides.
He has one Church.
God saw it.
You knew.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

The modern defense of polygamy among spiritual leaders often sounds intellectual, historical, or even “biblical,” but when Scripture is read honestly and completely, the pattern becomes undeniable: God’s design for covenant leadership is faithfulness, purity, self-control, and singular devotion.
Especially for those who stand before people claiming to speak for Him.
Here are six reasons why preachers cannot practice polygamy according to biblical truth.
The first reason is because a preacher must be the husband of one wife.
Scripture does not leave this vague.
In 1 Timothy 3:2, Paul writes:

Other translations say:
“the husband of one wife.”
Read that again.

Not many wives.
Not rotating wives.
Not hidden wives.
Not spiritual wives.
One.
The qualification for leadership was never built around multiplying women. It was built around proven covenant faithfulness.
A preacher who cannot remain faithful to one woman cannot claim authority over the house of God.

Because ministry is not proven by charisma.
It is proven by character.
The second reason is because church leadership reflects Christ and the Church.
Marriage was always prophetic.
Ephesians 5 reveals that earthly marriage reflects the relationship between Christ and His Church.
“And the two shall become one flesh…”
Then Paul says:
“This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church.”
Christ does not divide His covenant among competing brides.
There is one redeemed Church under one Savior.
A preacher practicing polygamy destroys the very picture he was called to represent.
And this is where many become uncomfortable.
Because some people want Old Testament permission without New Testament responsibility.

But Jesus did not come to lower the standard.
He fulfilled and elevated it.
The third reason is because polygamy consistently produced destruction in Scripture.
People love pointing out that certain biblical men had multiple wives.
But they ignore what happened because of it.
Look carefully.
Abraham experienced division and conflict through Hagar and Sarah.
Jacob lived inside rivalry, jealousy, and household chaos between Leah and Rachel.
David watched family disorder, sexual sin, betrayal, and violence explode inside his own house.
Solomon had many wives who turned his heart away from God.
Scripture records these things honestly, not approvingly.
There is a difference between description and endorsement.
God allowed many things humanity chose in its rebellion, but allowance is not approval.
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 19 that some things existed because of the hardness of human hearts.
But from the beginning, it was not so.
That matters.
The fourth reason is because preachers are called to self-control, not fleshly excess.
A true shepherd must crucify the flesh.
Not feed it.
Titus 1 says an elder must be disciplined and self-controlled.
A preacher cannot stand before people preaching purity while building a lifestyle around unchecked appetite.
And let’s be honest.

Many times polygamy is not about biblical conviction.
It is about male desire baptized in religious language.
God saw it.
You knew.
The Gospel calls men to die to themselves, not expand themselves.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross.”
That includes sexual desires, ego, power fantasies, and domination.
Especially for leaders.
The fifth reason is because polygamy damages witness and credibility.
Paul repeatedly emphasized that church leaders must be “above reproach.”
Meaning there should not be legitimate accusations that discredit the Gospel.
A preacher represents Christ publicly.
His household preaches before his mouth ever does.
And in nearly every culture shaped by New Testament Christianity, polygamy creates confusion, scandal, division, favoritism, financial instability, emotional wounds, and spiritual compromise.
People begin defending the preacher instead of following Jesus.
That is dangerous.
Because when leadership becomes self-centered, discipleship dies.
The sixth reason is because Genesis established God’s original design.

Before kingdoms.
Before cultural distortions.
Before human corruption expanded.

There was Adam.
And there was Eve.

One man.
One woman.
One covenant.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”

Not three.
Not four.
Not many.
Two.
Jesus later repeated this exact foundation because heaven never changed its design.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
This conversation is deeper than polygamy.
It is about whether leaders will submit themselves fully to Scripture or reshape Scripture around desire.
That is the real issue.
Because once a preacher starts negotiating clear biblical standards for personal appetite, the compromise rarely stops there.
One compromise opens the door for another.
And another.

Until eventually people no longer hear the voice of Christ.
They hear the voice of a man protecting his flesh.
The Gospel calls preachers higher.

Not because they are superior.
But because they are accountable.
James says teachers will be judged more strictly.
That should terrify anyone handling the Word carelessly.
And maybe this exposed something deeper in you.
Maybe not polygamy physically.
But divided devotion spiritually.

Because many people claim Christ while still keeping other lovers in the heart:
money,
lust,
pride,
secret sin,
self-worship.
You come to church while another god sits on the throne inside you.
God saw it.
You knew.
But this is why Jesus came.

Not merely to condemn sinners.
But to rescue them.
The cross is where divided, sinful, broken people become new.
Through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, hearts can be cleansed, desires transformed, and lives restored.

That includes leaders.
That includes pastors.
That includes you.
And the time to repent is now.
Not later.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You said you forgave them.
paragraphs: You said you forgave them.
But every time their name appears on your screen, your chest tightens.

Every memory still burns.
Every silence still accuses.
And deep down, you keep asking the question nobody wants to answer honestly:
“Why should I forgive someone who never even apologized?”
That question has destroyed marriages, divided families, hardened hearts, and quietly poisoned souls sitting in church every Sunday.
Because forgiveness sounds beautiful… until betrayal becomes personal.

Until it was your trust.
Your innocence.
Your years.
Your tears.
And suddenly forgiveness feels less like righteousness and more like surrendering justice.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Biblical forgiveness was never permission for evil.
It was never pretending the wound didn’t happen.
And it was never saying accountability no longer matters.
Forgiveness is not denial.
It is releasing your right to become consumed by vengeance while trusting God to judge rightly.
That changes everything.

Jesus never said evil was acceptable.
He never minimized sin.
In fact, He exposed sin more severely than anyone else ever did.
But while hanging on a cross—betrayed, mocked, beaten, abandoned—He said words that still shake history:
“Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34
Notice something terrifying.
Most of the people crucifying Him never apologized.

Some never repented.
Some walked away laughing.
Some likely died unchanged.
Yet Jesus revealed the heart of God in the middle of injustice.

Not because sin was small…
but because mercy is divine.
And that’s where people struggle.

Because human instinct says:
“If they don’t apologize, they don’t deserve forgiveness.”
True.
They don’t.
Neither did you.
Neither did me.
That is the scandal of grace.
Scripture says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
While we were still sinners.

Not improved.
Not apologizing perfectly.
Not deserving mercy.
God moved first.
Read that again.
God moved first.

That does not erase repentance.
Repentance still matters deeply.
Salvation itself requires repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
But forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
This is where many believers become confused.

Forgiveness can be given unilaterally.
Reconciliation requires repentance, trust rebuilding, and transformed behavior.
You can forgive someone and still maintain boundaries.

You can forgive and still testify in court.
Forgive and still walk away from abuse.
Forgive and still say, “I cannot trust you right now.”
Even God Himself does not reconcile with unrepentant rebellion apart from repentance through Christ.

So forgiveness is not naïveté.
It is spiritual freedom.
Because unforgiveness does something horrifying to the human soul.
At first, it feels like protection.
Then slowly it becomes identity.

You replay conversations.
You imagine revenge.
You nurture silent bitterness.
You rehearse speeches they may never hear.
God saw it.
You knew.
And eventually the wound they caused begins shaping your entire personality.
Hebrews warns:
“See to it… that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled.” — Hebrews 12:15
Bitterness never stays contained.

It leaks into marriages.
Friendships.
Children.
Churches.
Thoughts.
Sleep.
You think you’re imprisoning the person who hurt you.
But the prison was built around your own heart.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Now here is the harder truth nobody likes discussing:
Sometimes people weaponize “forgiveness” to avoid justice, confrontation, or healing.
That is not biblical forgiveness either.

Jesus forgave sinners…
and still called them to repent.

The Gospel is not:
“Pretend sin doesn’t matter.”

The Gospel is:
“Sin is so catastrophic that the Son of God had to die for it.”

That means your pain matters.
Your wounds matter.
Justice matters.
But vengeance belongs to God.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God…”
Why?
Because you were never designed to carry permanent hatred without spiritual destruction.
Some of you are exhausted because you’ve been feeding anger for years.
You smile publicly while privately arguing with ghosts.
And the person who hurt you may not even be thinking about you anymore.
Meanwhile your soul is drying out.
This is why forgiveness is necessary—even without apology.
Not because evil deserves comfort.
But because Christ deserves your trust.

Forgiveness says:
“God, I release this into Your hands. I refuse to let this poison own me anymore.”
That does not happen once emotionally.
Sometimes forgiveness becomes daily warfare.

Some wounds reopen repeatedly.
Some scars ache for decades.
Some betrayals permanently alter your life.
But every time bitterness tries to reclaim territory, the cross stands there again.
Not excusing evil.
Conquering it.
And if you think forgiveness is impossible, you are finally close to understanding the Gospel.
Because it is impossible without Christ.

Human strength can suppress rage temporarily.
Only Jesus transforms the heart.
That is why the cross is central.
At Calvary, justice and mercy collided.

Your sin was not ignored.
It was judged in Jesus Christ.
And now the same Savior who forgives sinners commands sinners to forgive others.

Not selectively.
Not only when apologies arrive.
Not only when closure feels satisfying.
Forgive as those who have been forgiven.
Ephesians 4:32 says:
“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”
As God forgave you.
That changes the conversation completely.
Because now forgiveness is no longer based on whether they deserve it.
It is rooted in whether Christ is enough.
Somebody reading this has been carrying resentment so long that it feels normal now.

But it’s killing your intimacy with God.
Killing your peace.
Killing your joy.
And maybe tonight the Holy Spirit is exposing something you buried years ago.
Not to shame you.
But to free you.
The question is not whether what they did was wrong.
It was.
The question is whether you will let their sin become your prison forever.
Jesus Christ can heal what bitterness never will.

If this convicted you, say it plainly:
“I need God to help me forgive.”

Not because the pain was fake.
Not because justice disappeared.
But because your soul belongs to Christ now.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t come during the day.
paragraphs: He didn’t come during the day.
That’s where most people rush past the moment and miss the weight of it.

Nicodemus wasn’t just “curious.” He wasn’t just a man asking spiritual questions. He was a Pharisee. A ruler. A teacher of Israel. A man who stood in public light with authority, respect, and religious certainty.
And yet… he waited until night.
You’ve done that too.

Not necessarily physically—but internally. You’ve delayed the real conversation with God until it was quiet enough that no one else could hear it. When the noise died down. When your image was safe. When you didn’t have to perform.
Night is where masks loosen.
“Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus… This man came to Jesus by night…” (John 3:1–2)
By night.
Not because it was convenient.
Because it was costly.
He had everything to lose—status, reputation, control. Coming in the daytime would’ve exposed him. So he came when no one could see the conflict inside him.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Nicodemus didn’t come to surrender.
He came to affirm.
“Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God…” (John 3:2)
Read that again.
He approached Jesus with respect… but not repentance. Acknowledgment… but not submission. He was trying to fit Jesus into his existing framework instead of letting Jesus dismantle it completely.
You’ve done that too.
You’ve said, “God, I know You’re real… I know You’re good…” while quietly holding onto control of your life. Keeping your sin untouched. Keeping your identity intact.
God saw it.
Jesus didn’t entertain his compliments.
He cut straight through him.
“Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” (John 3:3)
No small talk. No validation.
A complete spiritual reset.
Nicodemus came with theology.
Jesus confronted his condition.
Because knowledge doesn’t equal life.
You can know Scripture and still be spiritually dead.
You can teach others and still not be transformed.
Nicodemus was a master of the Law, yet Jesus told him he couldn’t even see the kingdom.
That should disturb you.
Because it means proximity to truth is not the same as possession of truth.
And Nicodemus felt it. You can see it unravel him.
“How can a man be born when he is old?” (John 3:4)
He’s thinking physically.
Jesus is speaking spiritually.
There’s a gap—and it’s exposing him.
You’ve felt that gap before.
Moments where truth hits deeper than your understanding. Where something in you knows you’re not right with God… but you don’t know how to cross that distance.
Here’s the tension most avoid:
Nicodemus had built his identity on being “right.”
Jesus told him he had to start over.
Not improve.
Not adjust.
Start over.
“Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
That’s not behavior modification.
That’s transformation at the core of your being.
And this is where many turn away quietly—just like Nicodemus eventually did that night. The conversation fades. No recorded confession. No immediate surrender.
Just silence.
You’ve had those moments.
Where truth confronted you… and instead of yielding, you paused. You thought about it. You let it linger.
But didn’t act.
You knew.
Then Jesus says something that splits everything open:
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:14–15)
He’s pointing to the cross before it even happens.
In the wilderness, people were dying from snake bites—judgment for their sin. God told Moses to lift up a bronze serpent, and whoever looked at it would live (Numbers 21:8–9).
Not worked.
Not earned.
Looked.
Believed.
Lived.
That’s the Gospel.
Then comes the verse everyone quotes—but few actually feel:
“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.” (John 3:16)
Not admire.
Not agree.
Believe.
Trust completely.
Surrender fully.
That’s where Nicodemus hesitated.
And that’s where you’re standing right now.
Because believing means dying to who you’ve been.
It means your pride doesn’t survive.
Your hidden sin doesn’t stay hidden.
Your control doesn’t remain intact.
This is why he came at night.
And this is why many stay there.
But the story doesn’t end in John 3.
Nicodemus shows up again.
Quietly at first—defending Jesus when others wanted Him condemned (John 7:50–51). Still cautious. Still not fully exposed.
Then later… something shifts.
After the crucifixion.
After the world had rejected Jesus.
After everything looked lost.
Nicodemus steps into the light.
“He… brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.” (John 19:39)
That wasn’t a small gesture.
That was public.
Costly.
Final.
He identifies himself with the crucified Christ.
No more night.
No more hiding.
That’s the part most people miss.
The man who came in secrecy eventually stood in the open.
Something changed.
The question is… has anything changed in you?
You’ve heard the truth.
You’ve felt the tension.
You’ve recognized yourself in this story.
So what are you going to do with it?
Stay in the night?
Or step into the light?
“This is the condemnation, that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.” (John 3:19)
That’s not poetic.
That’s personal.
You already know where you stand.
You knew before you even finished reading this.
Say it.
Acknowledge it.
“I don’t want to stay in the dark anymore.”
Write it. Own it. Don’t soften it.

And if someone came to your mind while reading this—the one who’s hiding, delaying, wrestling—send this to them. Not to argue. Not to prove a point. But because you know what it’s like to be in that place.
Follow this path if you’re done playing with truth and ready to actually be transformed. There’s deeper correction, clarity, and real discipleship waiting—not surface religion.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You thought maturity would feel like strength.
paragraphs: You thought maturity would feel like strength.
Like finally having control… saying the right things… being unshaken.

But that moment you snapped back at them?
That quiet jealousy you tried to justify?
That habit you keep feeding, even though you promised God you’d stop?

God saw it.
You knew.

And somewhere deep down, you felt it…
This isn’t maturity.
It just looks like it on the outside.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior

Most people don’t realize this, but maturity in God’s eyes has almost nothing to do with age, success, or how “put together” you appear. You can lead meetings, raise a family, quote Scripture—and still be spiritually immature where it matters most.
Because true maturity is revealed under pressure… when no one is clapping… when your flesh wants control.
And that’s where the difference shows.
Not in what you say—but in what comes out when you're squeezed.
Scripture cuts through the illusion:
“By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” — John 13:35
Read that again.

Not knowledge.
Not status.
Not image.
Love.

But not the soft, convenient kind.
The kind that costs you something.
The kind that exposes you.

The first sign of real maturity is this: you start taking responsibility instead of shifting blame. You stop crafting excuses for your reactions. You stop rewriting the story to make yourself the victim every time.
Adam blamed Eve. Eve blamed the serpent.
Immaturity always points outward.
But maturity stands still under conviction and says, “It was me.”
David said it plainly:
“I have sinned against the Lord.” — 2 Samuel 12:13
No defense. No spin. No delay.
That’s where growth begins.
And then something uncomfortable happens.
You start choosing silence when your pride wants to speak.
Not because you’re weak… but because you’re learning restraint.
“Whoever restrains his words has knowledge.” — Proverbs 17:27
You feel the urge to prove your point. To win the argument. To correct them publicly.
But something deeper pulls you back.
And it bothers you at first… because your flesh hates losing control.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

That restraint?
That quiet obedience?
That’s strength.
Real maturity doesn’t need to announce itself.
It shows up in how you handle offense.
Because offense reveals everything.
Immaturity reacts immediately. It holds grudges. It replays conversations. It builds quiet resentment while smiling in public.
But maturity absorbs the hit… brings it before God… and chooses forgiveness even when it’s undeserved.
“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.” — Ephesians 4:32
That last part changes everything.
As God forgave you.

Not when you deserved it.
Not when you apologized perfectly.
Not when you “fixed” yourself.
He forgave you while you were still in it.
So now the standard shifts.
And it gets uncomfortable.
Because now you can’t justify holding onto bitterness the same way anymore.
Then comes the part most people avoid entirely.
Correction.
Immaturity resists it. Deflects it. Gets defensive.
But maturity leans in—even when it stings.
“Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.” — Proverbs 12:1
That verse doesn’t soften it.
Because correction is where pride goes to die.
And without that death… there is no growth.
Then something deeper starts forming.
Consistency.

Not emotional bursts of devotion.
Not temporary discipline when you feel inspired.
But steady obedience when nobody sees.
Jesus said:
“He who is faithful in little is faithful also in much.” — Luke 16:10
This is where maturity separates itself completely.
Because anyone can perform when it’s visible.
But can you obey when it’s hidden?
Can you walk away when temptation is quiet and private?
Can you pray when you feel nothing?

God isn’t measuring your moments.
He’s watching your pattern.
And finally… the clearest sign.
You start becoming less of the center.

Your opinions don’t need to dominate every conversation.
Your feelings don’t dictate every decision.
Your identity isn’t built on being right, seen, or validated.
You start decreasing.
And Christ starts becoming more visible in how you think… how you speak… how you respond.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30
That’s maturity.
Not perfection.
Surrender.
But here’s the tension you feel right now…
Because if you’re honest… you saw yourself in more than one of these.

That reaction.
That pride.
That resistance.
God saw it.
You knew.
They feel the conviction… and bury it.
But something in you didn’t.
That’s not accidental.
That’s God pressing on something deeper.
Because maturity isn’t something you achieve—it’s something you surrender into.
And the doorway is always the same:
Repentance.

Not surface regret.
Not “I’ll do better.”
A real turning.
Because Scripture is clear:

“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
That’s the Gospel.
You weren’t waiting to become mature enough for Jesus.
He stepped in while you were still immature… still inconsistent… still struggling.
And through His death and resurrection, He made a way for real transformation—not behavior management, not image correction—but heart change.
So now the question isn’t whether you see the gaps.
You do.
The question is what you’ll do with them.
Because one path keeps you performing.
The other leads you into surrender.
And only one of those produces real maturity.
If something in you is shifting right now—don’t ignore it.
Let it turn into action.
Say it plainly: “Lord, I’ve been immature in ways I didn’t want to admit… change me.”
If that hit something real in you, don’t stay silent. Put it into words. Someone else needs to see it and wake up too.
Follow this journey if you’re done playing surface-level faith and ready for something deeper, something that actually transforms.
And if you’re ready to go deeper, to be sharpened, corrected, and built into real spiritual maturity, step into it here:
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people read that moment too quickly.
paragraphs: Most people read that moment too quickly.

A desperate woman touches the edge of Jesus’ garment…
and suddenly He stops in the middle of the crowd and asks:
“Who touched Me?”
At first glance, the question almost sounds strange.

Because Jesus was surrounded by people.
Pressed on every side.
Crowds touching Him everywhere.

Even Peter basically says,
“Lord… everyone is touching You.”
So why did Jesus ask the question?
Was He unaware?
Did the Son of God suddenly lose divine knowledge?
Or is there a hidden mystery inside this moment most people never notice?
The account appears in multiple Gospels, but Luke captures the tension powerfully:

“And Jesus said, ‘Who was it that touched Me?’ When all denied it, Peter said, ‘Master, the crowds surround You and are pressing in on You!’ But Jesus said, ‘Someone touched Me, for I perceive that power has gone out from Me.’”
— Luke 8:45–46
The Greek text becomes deeply revealing here.
Jesus says:

“τίς ὁ ἁψάμενός μου;”
(Tis ho hapsamenos mou?)
“Who is the one having touched Me?”

The word used for “touched” is:
ἅπτομαι (haptomai)
This is not casual contact.

It means:
to fasten oneself to,
to cling to,
to lay hold of intentionally.
This was not an accidental brush in a crowd.
This was faith reaching.
Everyone else touched Jesus physically.
But one woman touched Him spiritually.
That is the mystery.

The crowd was around Him…
but only one person reached Him.
And suddenly the entire scene changes when you understand the condition of this woman.
Mark 5 tells us she had suffered for twelve years with an issue of blood.
Twelve years.
According to Levitical law, this condition made her ceremonially unclean.
In Hebrew understanding, blood carried deep covenant significance.
Leviticus 17:11 says:
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood.”

The Hebrew word for life is:
נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh)

Meaning:
soul,
living being,
breath-life,
the very essence of existence.
For twelve years, this woman lived isolated, rejected, untouchable.
Anyone she touched became ceremonially unclean.
Imagine the psychological torment.

No embrace.
No public acceptance.
No normal worship life.
No restoration.

She was alive physically…
but socially buried.
And then she hears Jesus is near.
Now here is where the deeper Hebrew context changes everything.
The woman says within herself:

“If I only touch His garment, I will be healed.”
— Matthew 9:21

The Greek says:
κἂν μόνον ἅψωμαι τοῦ ἱματίου αὐτοῦ
(Kan monon hapsōmai tou himatiou autou)

Again:
not casual contact.
Intentional grasping faith.
But what garment was she reaching for?
The text hints toward something profoundly Jewish.
Many scholars believe she reached for the tzitzit — the tassels/fringes on a Jewish man’s garment commanded in Torah.
Numbers 15:38 says:
“Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments…”

The Hebrew word is:
צִיצִת (tzitzit)
These tassels represented covenant remembrance, obedience, and identity under God.
Now listen carefully to Malachi 4:2:
“But unto you that fear My name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in His wings.”

The Hebrew word for “wings” is:
כָּנָף (kanaph)

But kanaph can also mean:
edge,
corner,
hem of a garment.
Ancient Jewish readers understood this messianically.
Healing would be found in the Messiah’s “hem.”
And suddenly this woman is no longer merely touching fabric.
She is reaching toward covenant prophecy.
Toward messianic promise.
Toward the fulfillment of centuries of hope.
She believed healing was in Him before she ever touched Him.
That is faith.
Not intellectual agreement.
Not religious performance.
Complete surrender.
And this explains why Jesus stopped.
Because virtue went out from Him.
The Greek phrase says:

δύναμιν ἐξεληλυθυῖαν
(dynamin exelēlythuian)
Power had gone forth.

This is the word:
δύναμις (dynamis)
Divine miracle-working power.
The same root word connected to supernatural acts throughout the New Testament.
But here is the hidden mystery almost nobody talks about:
Jesus was not exposing the woman to shame.
He was restoring her publicly.
Had she slipped away quietly, she would have remained socially unclean in the eyes of the people.
Jesus stops everything to bring her into the open.

Not to humiliate her…
but to fully restore her identity.
Then He says:

“Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
— Luke 8:48
“Daughter.”
This is the only recorded time in the Gospels where Jesus directly calls a woman “daughter.”
Think about that.

For twelve years she was called:
unclean,
defiled,
untouchable.
Jesus calls her family.
Restoration is not merely physical healing.
It is relational healing.
Spiritual healing.
Identity healing.
And there is still another layer hidden inside this moment.

The crowd was pushing Jesus constantly…
yet no power flowed.
Why?
Because proximity is not intimacy.

Many people surround Jesus culturally.
Few truly reach for Him in faith.

Church attendance is not the same as surrender.
Christian language is not the same as trust.
Religious activity is not the same as desperate dependence on Christ.
One intentional touch of authentic faith moved heaven.
And maybe that is why this story still convicts people today.

Because some people have spent years around Jesus…
without ever truly reaching for Him.

This woman came broken.
Unclean.
Ashamed.
Exhausted.
Hidden.
And still Jesus stopped for her.
Still He healed her.
Still He called her daughter.
Still He restored what religion and society had buried.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus is not repelled by the bleeding parts of your life.
He heals what people hide.
He restores what shame destroys.
He stops for the desperate.
And maybe somebody reading this has been silently bleeding spiritually for years.

Smiling publicly.
Dying privately.

Pretending to be strong.
Pretending to be okay.
Pretending your faith is alive while your soul is exhausted.
But one honest reach toward Christ can change everything.

Not polished religion.
Not performance.
Not fake perfection.
Faith.
Real faith.
Desperate faith.

The kind that says:
“If I can just reach Him…”

Some people touched Jesus with their hands.
One woman touched Him with her faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’ve said “God is good” before.
paragraphs: You’ve said “God is good” before.
But if you’re honest, there are moments you didn’t believe it.

Not when the prayer went unanswered.
Not when the door stayed closed.
Not when the pain didn’t stop.
You said the words… but something in you hesitated.
Because goodness, to you, started to feel conditional.

If God is good—why did He allow that?
If God is good—why didn’t He intervene?
If God is good—why does this still hurt?
And that tension… you never really resolved it.
You just learned how to hide it.
The room was quiet. Too quiet.
You remember that moment—when everything slowed down and reality settled in heavier than you expected. No distractions. No noise. Just you… and the weight of what you were facing.
You tried to pray, but the words felt hollow.
Because deep down, a question had formed that you were almost afraid to say out loud:
“Is God actually good… to me?”

Not in general. Not in theory.
To you.
Because it didn’t feel like it.
And that’s where most people stop. They build their theology on their pain instead of on truth.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God’s goodness was never meant to be measured by your circumstances.
It’s revealed in His character.
“Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in Him.” — Psalm 34:8
Taste and see.
That means you don’t just analyze God’s goodness… you experience it.
But experience requires trust.
And trust is exactly where you started pulling back.
Let’s be honest.

You trusted God when things made sense.
You trusted Him when the outcome matched your expectations.
You trusted Him when the blessing was obvious.

But when confusion came…
When delay came…
When silence came…
You questioned everything.
God saw it.

That moment when you thought, “Maybe He’s holding out on me.”
That whisper: “Maybe He doesn’t actually care.”
You didn’t say it out loud.
But you felt it.
You knew.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
Here’s the truth that disrupts everything you thought you understood:
God’s goodness is not proven by giving you what you want.
It’s proven by giving you what you need… even when you resist it.
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord.” — Isaiah 55:8
You were measuring God’s goodness by comfort.
But God defines His goodness through purpose.
And His purpose is not your temporary happiness—it’s your eternal salvation.
Look at the cross.
That’s where this conversation changes.
Because if you want to understand the goodness of God, you don’t start with your situation…
You start with Jesus Christ.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8

While you were still in sin.
While you were still running.
While you were still choosing everything but Him…
He didn’t wait for you to get it together.
He stepped in.
That’s goodness.
Not reactive. Not conditional. Not dependent on your performance.
Relentless.
But here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because if God is truly good… then your biggest problem was never your situation.
It was your sin.

You didn’t just need help.
You needed rescue.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That includes you.

Every hidden thought.
Every compromise.
Every moment you knew better… and still chose differently.
God saw it.
And instead of condemning you immediately—He made a way.
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
Read that again.
Death is what you earned.
Life is what He offers.
That’s goodness you didn’t deserve.
So why does it still feel like God is distant sometimes?
Because you’ve been trying to experience His goodness without surrendering to His authority.

You want comfort without repentance.
Peace without transformation.
Blessing without obedience.
But God’s goodness leads somewhere.
“Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” — Romans 2:4
That tension you feel?
That conviction you’ve been ignoring?
That’s not rejection.
That’s God being good to you.
Calling you back.
You have two paths in front of you right now, whether you admit it or not.
One where you keep defining God by your feelings… and slowly drift further from truth.
And one where you surrender—fully—and finally see His goodness clearly.
Not because life becomes easy…
But because your heart becomes aligned.
“The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.” — Nahum 1:7
He knows who trusts Him.

Not who talks about Him.
Not who posts about Him.
Who actually trusts Him.
So let’s stop pretending this is just information.
You felt something reading this.
That pull. That conviction.

That quiet moment where you realized…
“This is about me.”

If you know you’ve been doubting God’s goodness… say it.
If you know you’ve been holding back from surrender… admit it.
If you know you need to come back to Him… don’t delay it.
Type it out. Make it real.
Because silence is where resistance hides.
And if something in you is starting to wake up… don’t let it fade.
There’s a deeper walk available—one where you don’t just hear about God’s goodness, you live in it, understand it, and grow in it daily through truth that corrects, challenges, and transforms you.
That’s what you step into when you go further.
Stay. Grow. Be sharpened.
Because surface-level faith won’t survive real life.

And someone you know is still stuck where you were—send this to them.
Let this confront them the way it just confronted you.
You’ll need it again when doubt tries to come back.
This isn’t the end of the conversation.
It’s where it actually begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’ve seen the number before.
paragraphs: You’ve seen the number before.
Not once. Not twice. It keeps showing up—quietly, deliberately—woven into the fabric of Scripture like a signature most people never stop to question.
Seventy.

Seventy elders.
Seventy nations.
Seventy years.
Seventy times seven.
And you were never meant to ignore it.
Because this number isn’t random—it’s revealing something about how God governs, judges, and ultimately redeems.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Seventy is not just a number.
It’s a mirror of humanity under God’s authority.
It begins early—before kingdoms, before Israel, before the Law was written on stone.
In Genesis 10, the table of nations unfolds after the flood. The descendants of Noah spread across the earth, and when you count them carefully, you find something striking.
Seventy nations.
Seventy distinct people groups, flowing from one family, filling the earth God just judged and cleansed.
This wasn’t accidental.
It was a divine structuring of humanity—complete, ordered, accountable.

God didn’t just scatter people.
He defined the world.
And then, not long after, everything fractures at Babel.
Pride rises. Unity turns into rebellion. Humanity tries to reach heaven on its own terms.
God responds—not with annihilation this time—but with division.
Languages split. Nations scatter.
But the number still stands.
Seventy.
Complete… yet divided.
Then God does something unexpected.
Instead of fixing all nations at once, He chooses one man.
Abraham.
From seventy nations, God narrows His focus to one lineage—not because the others didn’t matter, but because He was building a plan to reach them all.
And that plan begins to take visible shape in Exodus.
Moses is overwhelmed. The burden of leading Israel is crushing him. The people are restless, rebellious, constantly complaining.
And God responds with structure again.
“Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel…” (Numbers 11:16)
Seventy elders.
Not fifty. Not one hundred.
Seventy.
God takes the Spirit that is on Moses and distributes it among them. Authority is shared. Leadership is expanded.
Why seventy?
Because Israel is being shaped as a reflection of the nations.
A microcosm of humanity under God.
What God intends to do with Israel… He intends to do with the world.
But Israel struggles. Just like the nations.
You know the pattern.

Obedience… then drift.
Faith… then compromise.
Devotion… then idolatry.
God saw it.
And judgment comes—not immediately, but precisely.
Seventy years.
Jeremiah declares it before it happens:
“This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.” (Jeremiah 25:11)
Not sixty-nine. Not seventy-one.
Seventy.
A full measure of discipline.
A complete cycle of correction.

You knew they deserved it.
But if you’re honest… you’ve followed the same pattern.

You don’t need Babylon to exile you.
Sin already has.
Then something shifts.
In Daniel, after decades of exile, a man begins to pray.
Not casually. Not religiously.
Desperately.
He reads Jeremiah’s prophecy. He realizes the seventy years are almost complete.
And he doesn’t celebrate.
He repents.
“We have sinned and done wrong…” (Daniel 9:5)

He doesn’t blame others.
He doesn’t justify the past.
He confesses.
And that’s when heaven responds.
But not the way you’d expect.
God doesn’t just speak about seventy years anymore.
He expands it.
“Seventy weeks are decreed about your people…” (Daniel 9:24)
Now the number stretches beyond exile—into redemption, into Messiah, into the final dealing with sin itself.
Seventy becomes prophetic.
Not just about punishment…
But about restoration.
About the end of transgression.
About bringing in everlasting righteousness.
Read that again.
God was never just counting years.
He was counting toward Jesus.
And then Jesus steps into the story.

Not as a symbol.
Not as a continuation.
As the fulfillment.
When He sends out His disciples in Luke 10, how many does He appoint?
Seventy.
And He sends them where?
Into the world.
Into towns. Into places that mirror the scattered nations.
The mission expands.
What started with seventy nations…
What was mirrored in seventy elders…
What was purified through seventy years…
What was prophesied in seventy weeks…
Now becomes a movement.
Seventy messengers.
Carrying the Kingdom.
And then Peter asks a question that exposes something deeper in you too.
“How many times should I forgive? Up to seven times?”
Jesus answers:
“Not seven times, but seventy times seven.” (Matthew 18:22)
You wanted a limit.
God gives you a number that breaks your system.
Because forgiveness, like grace, cannot be contained in your calculations.
Seventy times seven isn’t math.
It’s mercy without measure.
So what does seventy represent?
Completion under God’s authority.
The full scope of humanity.
The weight of responsibility.
The certainty of judgment.
And the promise of restoration.
It’s the number that tells you…

God sees all nations.
God appoints leadership.
God disciplines sin.
God fulfills His promises.
God sends salvation.
And still—you hesitate.
Still—you delay.
Still—you think you have more time.
But you’ve already seen the pattern.
God is patient… but not passive.
Merciful… but not indifferent.

The same God who counted seventy nations…
Counted seventy years…
Declared seventy weeks…
Also counted every hidden thing in your life.
God saw it.
You knew.
And yet, here is the part that changes everything.
Jesus stepped into that timeline—not to extend your exile, but to end it.
“To finish transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity…” (Daniel 9:24)
That wasn’t symbolic.
That was the cross.
Where judgment met mercy.
Where your seventy cycles of failure met one act of perfect redemption.
You don’t need another system.
You need surrender.
Not later.
Now.
Let it confront you.
Say it plainly—“Lord, I’ve been running.”
Or, “I need that mercy.”
Or even just, “I’m ready.”
Write it. Don’t hide it.
Someone else needs to see that honesty more than you think.
Follow if you’re done with surface-level faith and want truth that actually changes you.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—to be corrected, sharpened, and built up in what Scripture actually says—step into it fully:
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Solomon could answer questions no man on earth could answer.
paragraphs: Solomon could answer questions no man on earth could answer.

Kings traveled across nations just to hear him speak. The Queen of Sheba stood speechless in his presence. Gold flooded his kingdom. Peace covered the land. Scripture says God gave him wisdom greater than all the people of the East.
And yet…
The wisest man alive still destroyed himself with undisciplined desire.
That should terrify you.

Because intelligence is not holiness.
Knowledge is not obedience.
And discernment means nothing if desire is left uncrucified.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can know what is right and still slowly walk into destruction while convincing yourself you are in control.
That was Solomon.

He did not fall in one night.
He drifted.

One compromise.
One attachment.
One desire he refused to confront.
Then another.
And another.
Until the man who once built the Temple for God was bowing near altars built for idols.
God saw it.
And deep down…
You knew.
You knew wisdom alone was never enough.
Scripture says in 1 Kings that Solomon loved many foreign women, even though God had clearly warned Israel not to intertwine themselves with nations that would turn their hearts away.

The warning was not random.
It was protective.
Because whatever captures your desire eventually shapes your worship.
Read that again.
Whatever captures your desire eventually shapes your worship.
At first Solomon probably thought he could manage it. After all, he was Solomon. The king. The builder. The teacher of Proverbs. The man who asked God for wisdom instead of riches.
But desire is dangerous when it goes undisciplined.
Especially secret desire.
Especially tolerated desire.
Especially desire you excuse because you still look “spiritual” in public.
That is where many people are trapped right now.

You still quote Scripture.
Still attend church.
Still know theology.
Still post Christian content.
Still say “God is good.”
But your private appetites are dragging your soul somewhere your public image refuses to admit.
God saw it.
You knew.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

Solomon’s downfall was not ignorance.
It was affection.
Ecclesiastes reveals a man who tasted everything the world could offer and still found emptiness at the end of it. Pleasure. Women. Achievement. Wealth. Entertainment. Projects. Success.
None of it could heal the soul.
Because desire was never meant to sit on the throne.
Only God belongs there.
The frightening part is that Solomon did not lose wisdom overnight. He kept speaking intelligently while spiritually decaying internally.
That is possible.
You can sound mature while your soul rots quietly.
You can preach truth while secretly entertaining compromise.
You can know doctrine while becoming enslaved to appetite.
That is why knowledge without surrender becomes dangerous.
Paul later wrote in 1 Corinthians:
“Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.”
Knowledge can inflate ego while starving intimacy with God.
And this generation worships knowledge.

People binge sermons but never repent.
Study Greek words but won’t crucify lust.
Debate theology online while secretly addicted to sin.
Wisdom became information instead of transformation.
Solomon is the warning.
Because eventually the desires you refuse to discipline will demand worship from you.

For some people it is lust.
For others money.
Validation.
Control.
Attention.
Power.
Pleasure.
Comfort.

Different idols.
Same throne.
And the terrifying thing about idols is they rarely announce themselves immediately.
They seduce slowly.
That is how hearts drift.

Nobody wakes up one morning planning to destroy their intimacy with God.
Drift happens through tolerated compromise.

A little bitterness.
A hidden addiction.
A private fantasy.
A relationship God warned you about.
A lifestyle you keep defending.
And over time conviction becomes quieter.
Not because God stopped speaking.
Because you stopped listening.
That is where Solomon ended up.
The man who once prayed for wisdom became a king whose heart was divided.
Scripture says:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods.” — 1 Kings
His heart turned.

Not his intelligence.
Not his gifting.
His heart.
That is the real battle.

Not appearance.
Not talent.
Not charisma.
Your heart.
Jesus said in Matthew:
“Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
Your desires reveal your direction.
And some people reading this already feel the conviction rising because the Holy Spirit has been warning you for months.
Maybe years.

About the relationship.
About the addiction.
About the pride.
About the hidden life nobody sees.
God saw it.
You knew.
But here is the mercy Solomon’s story still points toward…
Even after humanity failed over and over again, God sent Someone greater than Solomon.
Jesus Christ.

Solomon had wisdom.
Jesus IS wisdom.

Solomon’s kingdom divided.
Christ’s Kingdom cannot be shaken.

Solomon was consumed by desire.
Jesus conquered temptation in the wilderness without sin.
Where Solomon compromised, Christ obeyed perfectly.
And then Jesus went to the cross carrying the punishment for every idol, every hidden sin, every divided heart, every lust, every rebellion, every compromise.
That is the Gospel.

Not self-improvement.
Not behavior management.
Not “trying harder.”
Transformation through surrender to Jesus Christ.
Because discipline alone cannot save you if your heart still loves sin more than God.
You need a new heart.
And that is exactly what Christ offers.

Grace does not excuse sin.
Grace breaks chains.

Repentance is not punishment.
It is rescue.
The cross is where divided hearts can finally become whole.
But you cannot heal what you continue to hide.
Bring it into the light.

The addiction.
The compromise.
The secret desire.
The thing slowly replacing God in your affection.
Bring it to Jesus before the drift becomes destruction.
Because Solomon’s story is not preserved in Scripture to entertain you.
It is there to warn you.
Wisdom without obedience still ends in ruin.
And some of the most spiritually dangerous people are not the ignorant ones…
They are the ones who know truth while refusing to surrender desire.
Let it confront you.

The drift can stop today.
Jesus still restores divided hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You keep calling it confusion.
paragraphs: You keep calling it confusion.
That’s what you tell people when the conversation gets too close. When someone brings up God, conviction rises in your chest, and suddenly your answer is, “I’m just trying to figure things out.”
But that’s not what’s happening.
You’re not confused.
You just don’t like the truth.
It’s quieter than you admit. It doesn’t shout. It presses. It lingers after the music stops, after the scrolling ends, after the laughter fades and you’re alone with your thoughts.
That moment when you know what’s right—and still don’t do it.
God saw it.
You knew.

You knew when you crossed that line and called it “just once.”
You knew when you silenced your conscience because obedience felt inconvenient.
You knew when you heard the truth and felt something inside you resist it, not because it didn’t make sense… but because it cost too much.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
“But here’s what most people don’t realize…”
Confusion feels safer than confrontation.

If you say you’re confused, you don’t have to change.
If you say you’re still searching, you don’t have to surrender.
If you keep things “unclear,” you can delay obedience without feeling like you’re outright rejecting God.
But Scripture doesn’t play along with that illusion.
“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who suppress the truth in unrighteousness.” — Romans 1:18
Read that again.
Suppress.

Not misunderstand.
Not miss.
Suppress.
You didn’t lose the truth. You pushed it down.
That’s why it keeps resurfacing.

That’s why certain messages hit harder than others.
That’s why conviction doesn’t leave you alone.
That’s why even now, something in you feels exposed.
Because truth doesn’t disappear when you ignore it. It waits.
And the longer you resist it, the heavier it becomes.

You tell yourself, “I just need more clarity.”
But clarity has already come.
Jesus didn’t speak in riddles about your condition.
“The light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.” — John 3:19
That’s the real tension.
It’s not intellectual.
It’s moral.
You don’t struggle to understand—you struggle to surrender.
And that’s where everything breaks open.

Because the truth you’re avoiding isn’t just about rules.
It’s about your condition before a holy God.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
Not some.
You.
Not them.
You.
Every compromise, every hidden thought, every moment you chose yourself over God—it all testifies. And deep down, you don’t need anyone to convince you of that.
You’ve already felt it.
That weight.
That quiet guilt you can’t fully shake.

You tried to outgrow it.
Outwork it.
Outrun it.
But it followed you.
Because sin isn’t just what you do—it’s what you are apart from Christ.
And here’s the part you’ve been avoiding…
If the truth is real, then you’re accountable.
And if you’re accountable, then you need saving.
That’s the breaking point.
That’s where confusion dies and honesty begins.
Because once you admit you’re not confused… you have to decide what you’re going to do with the truth.
And the truth isn’t just about your sin.
It’s about a Savior you’ve been keeping at a distance.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Jesus didn’t wait for you to figure it all out.
He stepped into your mess.
He took the punishment your sin deserved.
The cross wasn’t symbolic. It was substitution.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That’s not confusion.
That’s clarity.

Your sin is real.
Your guilt is real.
But so is His grace.
And grace doesn’t meet you halfway—it calls you all the way out.

Out of hiding.
Out of excuses.
Out of delay.
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.” — Acts 3:19
Not later.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Because every moment you label conviction as “confusion”… you train your heart to resist God.
And hearts that keep resisting… grow hard.
That’s the part no one wants to say out loud.
You don’t stay neutral.
You either soften… or you harden.
There is no middle ground.
So what are you going to do with what you already know?
Because you do know.
You’ve heard enough.
Felt enough.
Seen enough.
This isn’t about needing another explanation.
It’s about whether you’re willing to finally say yes.

Yes to truth.
Yes to repentance.
Yes to Jesus.
Or if you’ll keep calling it confusion… until your conscience stops speaking altogether.
Two paths are in front of you right now.
One where you keep delaying, keep justifying, keep pretending you’re “still figuring things out”… and slowly drift further from God while convincing yourself you’re searching.
And one where you drop the act, face the truth, and fall into the mercy of Christ—fully, honestly, without conditions.
Only one leads to life.
Let it land.
Let it expose.
Let it lead you where you’ve been avoiding.
Write it if you have to—“I’m done running from the truth.”
Say it where you can’t take it back.
There’s someone in your life who’s doing the same thing you’ve been doing—send this to them. Not to argue… but because you know what it feels like to be confronted like this.
Stay close to this kind of truth. You won’t grow if you keep surrounding yourself with what makes you comfortable instead of what makes you honest.
Follow this path if you’re ready to stop playing with conviction and actually walk in transformation. There’s more depth waiting—real correction, real clarity, real growth in Christ.
And if you’re ready to go deeper, to be sharpened, corrected, and discipled without compromise, step into it fully:
Don’t just feel this.
Respond to it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Esau thought he was trading a birthright for a bowl of stew.
paragraphs: Esau thought he was trading a birthright for a bowl of stew.
But Scripture reveals something far more terrifying.

He traded intimacy for appetite.
Legacy for urgency.
Covenant for craving.
Eternity for something temporary that his body demanded in one emotional moment.
And millions are still doing the same thing today.
The story appears in Genesis 25, but if you slow down and truly examine the Hebrew language, the weight of what Esau surrendered becomes devastating.
Genesis 25:29–34 says Jacob was cooking stew when Esau came in exhausted from the field. Esau begged for food, and Jacob asked for his birthright in exchange.
The Hebrew word used for birthright is:
בְּכֹרָה — bekhorah
This was not merely inheritance money.

The bekhorah carried:
spiritual authority,
family leadership,
covenant responsibility,
priestly function,
and generational blessing.
The firstborn in ancient Hebrew culture carried the sacred continuation of the family line and covenant identity.
Esau did not merely lose property.
He treated holy things as disposable.
Genesis 25:32 records Esau saying:
“Behold, I am about to die; so of what use then is the birthright to me?”
The Hebrew phrase reveals shocking exaggeration.

הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ לָמוּת
hinneh anokhi holekh lamut
“I am going to die.”
But Esau was not literally dying.
He was hungry.
His flesh convinced him that temporary discomfort justified permanent compromise.
That is exactly how sin still speaks.

“Just this once.”
“You need this.”
“You deserve relief.”
“God will understand.”
“You can repent later.”
The enemy rarely begins with rebellion.
He begins with appetite.
And appetite becomes dangerous when it grows louder than conviction.
